0.title: The Cross at the Centre: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians
0.overview:
Of all the churches Paul founded, none gave him more grief — or more glory — than the church at Corinth. Corinth was one of the great cities of the ancient world: a rebuilt Roman colony on the narrow isthmus of Greece, sitting athwart the trade routes of the Mediterranean, a cosmopolitan, polyglot, ferociously commercial city where every culture, every religion, and every vice was for sale. The Greek verb korinthiazesthai — to live like a Corinthian — had become a byword for sexual immorality. Into this city Paul came on his second missionary journey around AD 50, stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:11), and planted a church that would make him simultaneously the most celebrated and most embattled apostle in his own lifetime.

He wrote this letter from Ephesus around AD 54–55, provoked by reports from Chloe’s household and a letter from the Corinthians themselves. What he had heard was alarming: the church had fractured into personality factions (“I follow Paul”; “I follow Apollos”; “I follow Cephas”; “I follow Christ”); a man was openly sleeping with his stepmother and the church was arrogant about it; members were suing each other in pagan courts; spiritual gifts had become instruments of status and one-upmanship; the Lord’s Supper had been turned into a class exercise in social humiliation; and some were denying the bodily resurrection entirely. This is a church in crisis — not the crisis of persecution from outside, but the far more dangerous crisis of pride, worldliness, and theological confusion from within.

Paul’s answer to every single one of these crises is the same: the cross. The word of the cross (1:18) is the only wisdom that addresses human arrogance. The crucified Christ (1:23) is the only foundation (3:11) on which a community can be built. The resurrection of Christ (15:20) is the only ground on which the resurrection of the dead makes sense. Every pastoral problem in the letter — from church discipline to spiritual gifts to the collection for the Jerusalem poor — is resolved by returning to the gospel of the crucified and risen Lord. This is why Martin Luther set the theology of the cross (theologia crucis) against the theology of glory (theologia gloriae), and why this letter is the most searching diagnostic of the church’s recurrent temptation to dress the gospel in the clothing of worldly wisdom and power.

The governing conviction is that this letter was written to the twenty-first century as much as the first — because the Corinthian church is every church, and the Corinthian heart is every heart, that has tried to hold the gospel and the values of the world simultaneously.

1.title: Divisions, the Cross, and the Wisdom of God
1.overview:
Corinth in the 50s AD was a boom town. Destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, it was refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC as a Roman colony, settled largely with freed slaves, and grew rich on trade between its two harbours on either side of the isthmus. It hosted the Isthmian Games and was full of people climbing the social ladder: one inscription found there records that a man called Erastus paved a street at his own expense in return for public office, perhaps the same Erastus, “the city treasurer”, who sent greetings in Romans 16:23. Status, eloquence, wisdom and success were prized. Paul spent eighteen months planting the church there (Acts 18), and a few years later, from Ephesus, he wrote this letter after hearing of serious problems.

The first problem is division. Church members were lining up behind favourite teachers (Paul, Apollos, Peter, even “Christ”) as though they were rival schools of philosophy. Paul’s answer goes to the root: the gospel itself overturns human ideas of wisdom and status. Its message is a crucified Messiah, which sounded like nonsense to Greeks and like an outrage to Jews, yet it is God’s power and wisdom. God deliberately chose ordinary, unimpressive people, so that no one could boast except in the Lord, who has given us Christ as our wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, writing with a colleague called Sosthenes, introduces himself as an apostle by God’s calling. He addresses the church in Corinth as God’s own people, made holy in Christ and called to be saints, together with believers everywhere who call on the name of Jesus, the Lord of all, and wishes them grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Called by the Will of God

Paul’s self-designation as an apostle “by the will of God” is not modesty but theology. The divine will is the only ground of any apostolic or ministerial commission. This will become crucial in the letter: when the Corinthians reject Paul’s apostleship, they are not rejecting a self-appointed teacher but the will of the God who sent him. The same logic applies to their own calling: they are saints not because they volunteered but because they were called (v. 2). The sovereignty of grace is the foundation of every sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s apostolic authority was contested at Corinth by those who preferred Apollos’s rhetorical polish or Cephas’s Petrine prestige. His opening — “called by the will of God” — quietly answers the challenge before it is raised. Now: In a church culture that prizes celebrity and charisma, the ground of ministry is still the same: divine calling, not human talent. The pastor who grounds his authority in his own gifts is standing on sand; the one who grounds it in the call of God can stand when the culture turns against him.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus, and our brother Sosthenes,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians is Paul’s letter to a gifted but troubled church. Chapter 1 does two things. First, Paul greets them and thanks God for them: they are a church of God, sanctified in Christ, enriched with every gift, and God will keep them to the end (vv. 1–9). Then he takes up the first problem: the church is splitting into fan clubs around favourite leaders, Paul, Apollos, Peter, even Christ (vv. 10–17). His answer goes to the root. The Corinthians were impressed by worldly wisdom and polished speech, but the gospel is the message of the cross, which the world thinks foolish and weak, and which is in fact the power and wisdom of God (vv. 18–25). God proved this by whom he chose: not many wise, powerful or noble, but the foolish and weak and despised, so that no one can boast before him (vv. 26–29). Everything the believer has, wisdom, righteousness, holiness and redemption, is found in Christ, so let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord (vv. 30–31). Divisions are cured not by better leaders but by a fresh look at the cross, and the chapter that begins with a quarrel over men ends with every eye on one Man.

The setting. Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church on his second missionary journey (Acts 18:1–18; 1 Corinthians 16:8). He had stayed eighteen months. Since then he had written an earlier letter (5:9), heard reports from Chloe’s people (1:11), and received a letter from the church with questions (7:1). 1 Corinthians answers both the reports and the questions: divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, worship, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection.

Paul, called by the will of God to be an apostle of Christ Jesus. Three phrases carry the weight, and each of them takes something away from Paul. Klētos: called. Thelēmatos theou: by the will of God. Apostolos: one sent with authority, a man under orders carrying somebody else’s message, a witness of the risen Lord (9:1; 15:8). He does not write “Paul, who became an apostle”, or “Paul, who trained for this”, or “Paul, whom the church appointed”. Every one of those would have located the commission somewhere in Paul. He puts it outside himself entirely (Galatians 1:15).

Not an application he submitted. And he had reason to. Whatever else the Damascus road was, it was not a job interview. Paul was travelling in the opposite direction with warrants in his luggage, on his way to arrest Christians, when he was knocked to the ground and blinded by the very person he was persecuting (Acts 9:3–9). Nobody has ever entered the ministry with less enthusiasm for the job. That is exactly why he can open a letter to a church that is questioning his authority (4:3; 9:3) by saying, in effect: you may take this up with me if you like, but the appointment was not mine to make and is not mine to resign.

Why it matters for this letter. This letter is about to spend sixteen chapters correcting people who badly do not want to be corrected. If Paul’s standing rests on his personality, his eloquence or his track record, then the Corinthians can simply decide they prefer somebody else’s, and that is precisely what they have done (v. 12). If it rests on the will of God, their preferences are beside the point. Paul begins with the basis of his authority: the will of God, not his own ambition.

And our brother Sosthenes. The second name is easy to read past, and it may be one of the quietest miracles in the New Testament. Luke records that when the Corinthian Jews dragged Paul before the proconsul Gallio and the case was thrown out, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal (Acts 18:17). He held the office Crispus had held before he became a Christian (Acts 18:8), which means he had inherited the leadership of the opposition. We cannot be certain it is the same man; Sosthenes was not a rare name. But the coincidence is considerable: the same name, the same city, and a man now described simply as our brother, sitting beside Paul as the letter is composed and sending it to the church his synagogue had tried to destroy. If it is him, the head of the opposition became the co-sender of the correspondence, and the Christians at Corinth opened this letter and saw a name they remembered from the wrong side of a courtroom.

The gospel recruits its opponents. Hold on to that when you pray for someone who seems entirely closed: the relative who mocks it, the colleague who has heard it all and wants none of it, the person whose hostility feels settled and permanent. Paul was the most dangerous enemy the early church had, and Sosthenes may well have been the second. Both names are at the top of this letter. The gospel does not merely survive its opponents; it has a long history of enlisting them.

Your own calling. There is a test in the first word for anyone who has quietly assumed that his Christian life was fundamentally his own idea. Ask how you came to be reading this at all. Trace it back: who spoke to you, who prayed for you, why you were in that room, what made you willing to listen when a hundred other people heard the same words and did not. Follow it far enough and you will not find a decision you made first. You will find a series of things that happened to you, which is the whole meaning of called, and it is the reason no Christian can boast (John 15:16; Galatians 1:15–16).

What it does not mean. It does not mean apostles still exist today in Paul’s sense. The apostles of Christ, eyewitnesses of the risen Lord sent by him personally, laid the foundation of the church once (Ephesians 2:20). Their authority continues in their writings, the New Testament. When we want to hear an apostle, we open this letter.

Is my job a calling in the same sense? Not quite, though it is not nothing. When Paul says called here, and of all Christians in verses 2, 9 and 24, he means God’s effectual summons into Christ: the call that saves. That call is the same for the apostle and for you. Paul’s particular office was a further, unrepeatable commission. Your work, family and church responsibilities are callings in a secondary sense: the place where God has put you to serve him (7:17–24). So you need not hunt for a dramatic sense of vocation before your life counts. The first call, the one that made you his, is already the greatest thing that will ever happen to you; everything else is lived out of it.

In a sentence. Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes,

On a Tuesday. Whatever place you hold in your church or work, see it as God’s calling, not your achievement. That keeps you humble when it goes well and steady when it goes badly, because the appointment was never yours to secure. And today, pray by name for the person you think least likely to believe. The man who wrote this letter was once that person, and the man beside him may have been too.

For worship. The risen Christ stopped his chief enemy on a road and made him his herald, and very probably took the ruler of the synagogue who opposed him and made him a brother. That is what our Lord is like. He does not wait to be chosen; he chooses. He does not need willing material; he makes it willing. Every name at the top of this letter is a trophy of grace, and so is every name written in the Lamb’s book of life, including the ones that were once at the head of the opposition.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Ephesus, around AD 53–55, a few years after founding the church. Sosthenes may be the synagogue ruler beaten at Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the church of God that is in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus, called to be saints together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

The setting. Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, with ports on two seas. It had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and refounded by Julius Caesar in 44 BC. It was proud, competitive, status-conscious and famous for its immorality; the Greeks had coined a verb from the city’s name, korinthiazomai, to Corinthianise, meaning to live immorally. It hosted the Isthmian Games and many temples, including the temple of Aphrodite, and it was full of new money, competitive display and imported religion.

To the church of God that is in Corinth. The preposition is doing more work than any other word in the sentence. The church (ekklēsia, the assembly, those called out) belongs to God; it merely has an address. It is the church of God, not of Paul or Apollos or any faction. And the address is almost the point of the joke, because every reader in the ancient world knew what Corinth was. To write “the church of God in Corinth” was very nearly a contradiction in terms, and Paul writes it without a flicker of embarrassment. If God can have a church in Corinth, he can have one anywhere.

To those sanctified in Christ Jesus. This is the most important thing in the greeting, and a great deal of Christian anxiety turns on it. “Sanctified” (hagiazō, set apart as holy) is a perfect passive: something that was done to them, at a point in the past, with results that continue (6:11). It is not a report on their conduct. It is a statement about their location. To be sanctified here is to be set apart for God, and they are set apart because they are in Christ, who is holy. The holiness is his, and they are in him. Theologians call this definitive sanctification: God has set them apart as his own, once for all.

Remember who is being described. This is the church that will shortly be rebuked for factions, for a man living with his father’s wife, for suing each other in pagan courts, for getting drunk at the Lord’s Supper while poorer members went hungry, and for a chaotic scramble over spiritual gifts. Paul knows all of it; he has already had the report (v. 11). And he still opens by calling them sanctified saints. He does not withdraw the title in order to motivate them to earn it. He states who they are, and then spends sixteen chapters telling them to become it.

Identity first, instruction second. That order is the gospel, and reversing it is the commonest way to make Christianity unbearable. The world says: behave, and you will belong. Every religion of human effort says: achieve, and you may be accepted. Paul says: you have been set apart, therefore live like it. Nobody in this letter is being asked to work towards a standing. They are being asked to live up to one they already have.

Called to be saints. Saints (hagioi, holy ones) is what all believers are, not a special class. Called means effectively summoned by God, and their calling is to live up to what they already are. Most of us hear the word saint and think of stained glass, or of somebody markedly better than we are, and conclude that it cannot honestly apply. But in the New Testament saint is never a rank awarded to the exceptional. It is the ordinary word for a Christian, and Paul is happily applying it to the worst-behaved congregation in his correspondence. If the Corinthians qualified, the bar is not where you think it is. The question is not whether your record has earned the description. It is whether you are in Christ, because the description follows the location.

Together with all those who in every place call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, both their Lord and ours. The address opens outward. Corinth is not a self-contained religious club with its own arrangements; it is one congregation inside something worldwide, and not independent of the rest. And the phrase call upon the name of the Lord is lifted straight out of the Old Testament, where it means to invoke and worship the LORD, Yahweh himself (Genesis 4:26; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13). Paul applies it to Jesus without argument or apology, as though it needed no defending. To call on Jesus is to worship him as God. It is one of the strongest statements of Christ’s deity in the New Testament, and it arrives disguised as an address label.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. The greeting fuses two worlds: charis, grace, a Christian reshaping of the ordinary Greek greeting, and shalom, peace, the standard Hebrew one, both filled with gospel meaning. And they come from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, one preposition governing both, the Father and the Son named together as the single source of the gift. Paul is not arguing for the deity of Christ here. He is assuming it, in a passing line, which is a far stronger indication of what the earliest church believed than any formal argument would be (Romans 1:7; 2 Corinthians 1:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians were already perfect in conduct. They were saints in Christ who were behaving badly. Paul addresses them first by what God has made them, then corrects them.

If I am already sanctified, why must I still grow in holiness? Because the Bible uses the word in two ways, and both are true of you. Definitively, you were set apart for God the moment you were joined to Christ; that is finished and does not fluctuate (6:11; Hebrews 10:10). Progressively, the Spirit is now making your actual life match that status, a lifelong work that is real but never complete in this life (2 Corinthians 3:18; Westminster 13.1–2). The first is the ground of the second, never its reward. You do not pursue holiness to become God’s; you pursue it because you are his. So when you fail, you have not lost the first; you have found another place where the second still has work to do.

In a sentence. To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be his holy people, together with all those everywhere who call on the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, their Lord and ours: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test that will show you what you actually believe. When you have sinned badly, not a slip but the real thing, what is your first instinct about your standing before God? Do you assume you have dropped out of the category and must work your way back in before you can pray properly? Or do you go to him as someone who is still, at that moment, sanctified in Christ Jesus? The first instinct is nearly universal, and it is not the gospel. The letter that says you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified (6:11) says it to people who were still getting it badly wrong. Go to him today as what he has made you, and ask him to make your life match your name.

For worship. God has a church in Corinth. He looked at the city whose name was a byword for vice and planted his own holy people in the middle of it, and then put his name on them before they had learned to behave. That is the grace of the Father and the Son: holiness given before it is lived, a title conferred on the undeserving and never withdrawn, and a Lord Jesus who receives the worship that belongs to God alone because he is God, their Lord and ours.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth was a wealthy Roman colony and trading city on the narrow isthmus of Greece, with two ports and a mixed, mobile population. “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God constantly for the grace given to the Corinthians in Christ. They have been enriched in every way, especially in their speech and knowledge, because the message about Christ took firm root among them, and so they lack no spiritual gift as they wait for Christ to be revealed. Christ will keep them firm to the end, so that they will be blameless on his day. God is faithful, and it was he who called them into fellowship with his Son.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Faithfulness of God as the Ground of Perseverance

Verse 9 — “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son” — is one of the great perseverance texts in Paul. The guarantee of the Corinthians’ ultimate confirmation (v. 8) is not their grip on Christ but God’s grip on them. The calling is God’s act; the fellowship is God’s gift; the sustaining is God’s work. Reformed theology has always grounded the doctrine of perseverance here: the saints persevere not because they are strong but because the God who called them is faithful.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians had turned their spiritual gifts into status symbols, measuring their standing before God and their superiority over others by the quality of their tongues and the depth of their knowledge. Paul’s thanksgiving subtly reorients them: the gifts are something you “were enriched in” — given, not earned. Now: The same pride attaches to spiritual accomplishment in every generation — the sense that one’s theological sophistication or spiritual experience gives one a higher standing. Paul’s corrective is the same: it is all grace. What do you have that you did not receive? (4:7).

verseByVerse.quote: I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—
verseByVerse.commentary:
I give thanks to my God always for you because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus, that in every way you were enriched in him in all speech and all knowledge—

I give thanks to my God always for you. Before anything else, notice what Paul does first, and remember what he already knows. Chloe’s people have reported the quarrelling (v. 11). He has heard about the immorality, the lawsuits, the disorder. He is holding a list of things that would justify opening with anger, and the first thing he does is thank God for them. He sees God’s work in them before he deals with their sin.

Not a technique. This is not flattery, and it is not a sweetener before the medicine. It is possible because the thanksgiving is not aimed at the Corinthians at all. Read it again: I give thanks to my God because of the grace of God that was given you. He is not congratulating them on being impressive; he is thanking God for something God did. That is precisely why he can do it with complete sincerity about a church he is about to take apart. There is nothing here that their behaviour could invalidate, because none of it was their achievement in the first place.

Because of the grace of God that was given you in Christ Jesus. The grammar carries the theology. The grace was given, a completed action done to them, and they were enriched, another passive. They are wealthy, and every penny of it arrived as a gift. The cause of thanksgiving is not their goodness but God’s grace.

That in every way you were enriched in him. The word for enriched (eploutisthēte) belongs to the same family Paul uses in the most famous sentence he ever wrote about Christian wealth: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). That is where the Corinthian riches came from. Their wealth is the measure of his poverty; what they have in their hands is what it cost him to put it there.

In all speech and all knowledge. The specifics are chosen with care: logos, speech, and gnōsis, knowledge. Anyone reading the whole letter will recognise both immediately, because they are the two things that have gone most badly wrong at Corinth. Speech is the arena of the tongues problem that will occupy chapters 12 to 14. Knowledge is the source of the arrogance Paul confronts at 8:1, where he says flatly that knowledge puffs up. So Paul thanks God for the very gifts that are currently doing the damage, because they were real gifts. The problem was not the gifts but pride in them.

Tracing the gift to the Giver. Pause on this, because our instinct when a gift is being misused is to disparage the gift. Paul does not treat their gifts as the problem, and he does not ask the Corinthians to have less of them. His instinct is to trace each gift back to the Giver and give thanks, and then to spend the letter putting it back in its place. The trouble at Corinth was never that they had too much of God’s grace. It was that they had forgotten it was grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is flattering them. He means it; and later he will show that gifts without love are nothing (13:1–3). Nor does thanksgiving cancel correction. Paul does not overlook a single one of their problems. He simply refuses to let the problems be the first or the truest thing he says.

How can I thank God for someone without pretending his sin is fine? By thanking God for what God has done in him, not for what he is doing wrong. The two are different columns, and Paul keeps them separate: thanks for grace in verses 4–9, correction from verse 10 on. Thanksgiving is not a verdict that the problem is small; it is a confession that God is at work even there. It also changes the correction. You will speak more gently, more hopefully and more accurately to someone whose gifts you have honestly thanked God for that morning, and he is far more likely to hear you, because he can tell you are not his enemy.

In a sentence. Paul always thanks his God for you because of his grace given you in Christ Jesus. For in him you have been enriched in every way, with all kinds of speech and with all knowledge,

On a Tuesday. Before you criticise your church, thank God for what he has given it; it changes how you speak. Then try something harder. Think of the person in your church you find most difficult, the one whose name lowers your mood, whose contributions in a meeting you brace for. Write down, honestly, three things God has genuinely given that person. Not three things you can tolerate about them; three evidences of grace. Most of us discover we have never once tried, and that we have been carrying a mental file on them consisting entirely of the other column. Paul had a far longer file on the Corinthians than you have on anybody, and he opened with thanksgiving (Philippians 1:3–6; Romans 1:8).

For worship. Every gift in that troubled church came from the hand of a Saviour who emptied his own. The eloquence they were proud of, the knowledge they were puffed up with, the riches they had forgotten were riches: all of it was bought by the poverty of the Son of God, who became poor that they might become rich. And he did not take it back when they misused it. He sent an apostle to put it in its place. Such is the grace of God given in Christ Jesus: generous beyond our deserving, and patient beyond our misuse.
verseByVerse.note: The Corinthians prized eloquent speech and knowledge — the very gifts later misused.

verseByVerse.quote: even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you— so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you—so that you are not lacking in any gift, as you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ,

Even as the testimony about Christ was confirmed among you. The testimony (martyrion) about Christ is the gospel Paul preached. “Confirmed” (bebaiōthē) is a word from the world of contracts and guarantees: something ratified and made secure. The gospel took root and was shown true in their lives, including through spiritual gifts. The gifts at Corinth were not decorations. They were the divine signature under the apostolic message, God countersigning what Paul preached, so that nobody could say it was merely one man’s opinion.

So that you are not lacking in any gift. “Gift” (charisma) means the spiritual gifts that chapters 12–14 discuss at length. They had everything they needed. And this is said of this church: a congregation deficient in love, humility, unity, self-control and basic decency is told it lacks no spiritual gift whatever. Both things are true at once, and holding them together is most of the wisdom of this letter.

Gifting is not maturity. They do not arrive together, and one is no evidence of the other. It is entirely possible to be lavishly equipped and badly behaved. That is a warning to the gifted, who may be tempted to read their usefulness as God’s approval of their character, and a considerable relief to everybody else, who may have assumed that the gifted must be the godly.

For the Christian who thinks he has no gift. You watch people who teach, or sing, or organise, or seem to know instinctively what to say in a hospital room, and you can identify nothing comparable in yourself. Paul’s statement is made to a whole congregation, and he says the same thing to them individually later in the letter: to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good (12:7). Not to some. To each. The question is never whether you were given something; it is whether anyone has ever helped you find out what it was. And gifts are ordinarily discovered by serving, not by introspection. Take the job nobody wants, and see what God does with it.

As you wait for the revealing of our Lord Jesus Christ. This phrase reframes all of it. “Revealing” (apokalypsis) is an unveiling, the drawing back of a curtain on someone who is already there: Christ’s return, when he will be seen in glory. The gifts are issued for the waiting. They are equipment for the interval between his going and his coming, provisions for a journey rather than trophies for a cabinet. Some Corinthians acted as if they had already arrived (4:8); Paul reminds them they are still waiting (13:8–12).

Possession or equipment? That single clause would have solved most of the Corinthian problem if they had believed it. A gift understood as a possession becomes a measure of standing; standing invites comparison; and comparison produces the factions of the next paragraph. A gift understood as equipment for a job raises a different question: not what does this say about me, but what is this for? The same gift, held in two ways, builds a church or splits one.

Where Christians differ: do all the gifts continue today? Some hold that the revelatory and sign gifts, prophecy, tongues and gifts of healing, belonged to the apostolic age and ceased once the foundation was laid and the New Testament complete, pointing to the apostles and prophets as a foundation laid once (Ephesians 2:20) and to the signs as God’s attestation of the apostolic message (Hebrews 2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Others hold that they continue until Christ returns, reading the perfect of 13:10 as his appearing rather than the closing of the canon, and noting that this very verse ties the gifts to the period of waiting for the revealing of the Lord, which is plainly not over. Verdict: the first is the better view, and the argument is set out at 13:8–12 and Acts 5:12. The sign gifts authenticated the apostles and their message, and with a closed canon God speaks to his church through Scripture, sufficient for all of life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). This is held charitably: both positions are taken by people who love Scripture and submit to it, and what Paul says here, which neither side disputes, is the main thing. Whatever gifts God has given you were given for the waiting, will not be needed when he appears, and were never intended to tell you or anyone else how you are doing (Romans 8:23–25; 1 Peter 4:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every individual had every gift (12:29–30). The church as a whole lacked nothing.

If the sign gifts have ceased, does God still heal? Yes. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped acting; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing or new revelation as signs authenticating a message. God still hears prayer for the sick and often answers it, sometimes through doctors, sometimes beyond them, and James tells the sick to call the elders to pray (James 5:14–15). So pray boldly for healing, and give thanks when it comes. What you should be wary of is anyone who claims to heal at will or to bring a new word from God that binds your conscience. Test everything by the Scripture God has already given.

In a sentence. God thus confirming our testimony about Christ among you. Therefore you do not lack any spiritual gift as you eagerly wait for our Lord Jesus Christ to be revealed.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are actually waiting for. Not what you would say in a Bible study: what genuinely functions in you as the thing that will make everything all right. For most of us it is a resolution: the diagnosis reversed, the job secured, the child settled, the debt cleared. All legitimate to want. None of them is what Paul says the Christian is waiting for, and every one of them can arrive and leave you exactly where you were. The Corinthians had every gift and were still restless, because gifts were never designed to satisfy the ache that only a Person appearing can end. Then ask what your gift is for this week, and use it on someone.

For worship. The church is not left empty-handed in the interval. The ascended Christ has supplied his people with everything they need to wait well, and the curtain will be drawn back. The one we wait for is not absent but hidden, already there behind the veil, and on the day of his unveiling every gift will be laid down like a lamp at sunrise, because the Light himself will have come.

verseByVerse.quote: who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who will sustain you to the end. The subject of that verb points back to the end of the previous verse. It is Christ who will do the sustaining, or God through him; it is certainly not the Corinthians. The word is bebaiōsei, the same root as “confirmed” in verse 6: the language of legal guarantee, of a contract made secure so that it will hold. As God confirmed the gospel among them, he will confirm them to the end, to the last day. Something has been underwritten here, and the underwriter is not you.

Guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. This is the word the whole verse is built to deliver. Anenklētous is a courtroom term. It does not mean innocent in the sense of never having done anything. It means unaccused: no charge standing, nothing on the sheet, no case to answer. It describes a person against whom the prosecution has nothing to bring. The day of the Lord is the day of judgement and Christ’s return, and on that day believers will stand without accusation, because Christ’s righteousness is theirs (Romans 8:33–34; Colossians 1:22).

Before he names a single sin. Feel the force of that as the Corinthians would have. Paul is about to spend fifteen chapters listing what is wrong with them, and much of it is not trivial: incest in the congregation, drunkenness at the Lord’s table, believers dragging each other before pagan judges. And before he names a single item he tells them how the day of judgement will go for them. They will stand there with no charge against them.

How can that be true? Only one way, and the letter will say it plainly at 15:3: Christ died for our sins. The charges are not being ignored, waived, or quietly dropped for lack of evidence. They were transferred. Every accusation that could be brought against a Corinthian believer on that day was brought against Christ on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem, and answered there. The sheet is clean because someone else’s was filled in.

For the Christian who is afraid of the last day. There are more of them than admit it. You believe in the forgiveness of sins in general, and you are not at all sure it will hold for you in particular, because you know things about yourself that nobody else knows: the thing you did that you have never told anyone, the pattern you have confessed a hundred times and returned to, the person you damaged who never got an apology. Somewhere underneath, you expect that day to be the moment it all finally comes out. Something will indeed come out. But look at what Paul says will be true of you when it does: guiltless. Not forgiven with a permanent asterisk. Not acquitted after a difficult hearing. No charge standing. If a single accusation could still be brought against a believer on that day, then Christ’s death dealt with most sins and not all, and the letter that says he was raised on the third day would be describing a job half done.

The comfort is in the tense. Paul does not write that God may sustain you, or that he will if you hold on tightly enough. He writes who will sustain you to the end: a plain future about something already guaranteed. The delivery is outstanding; the verdict is not.

Where Christians differ: perseverance. Some teach that true believers may fall away and be finally lost. Verdict: Paul says God will sustain them to the end. If it were up to the Corinthians, with all their failings, they would not stand. But God keeps his people. True believers may fall into serious sin, as the Corinthians did, and must be corrected; but God will not let them go (Philippians 1:6; John 10:28–29; Westminster 17.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean sin does not matter. The rest of the letter calls them to repent. God keeps them partly by such warnings, and a person who hears the warnings and runs back to Christ is being kept in exactly the way God keeps.

What about people who seemed to be Christians and then walked away? Scripture gives two answers that must be held together. Some who leave were never truly joined to Christ, however real it looked: they went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2:19). Others are true believers in a long and grievous backsliding, as Peter was for a night and the Corinthians were for a season, and God will bring them home. From the outside we often cannot tell which, so we do not pronounce; we pray, we keep the door open, and we keep calling. What you can know is your own case: if you are still coming to Christ with your sins today, that coming is the evidence that he is keeping you.

In a sentence. He will also keep you firm to the end, so that you will be blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Your assurance rests not on your strength but on God’s keeping. When you fail, run back to him; he is holding you. And here is a test, diagnostic rather than accusing. Imagine the day arriving this evening, and notice what your mind reaches for first as the ground of your confidence. If it reaches for your record, the years of church, the things you gave up, the sins you have avoided, then whatever you believe about grace, you are planning to be assessed on your own paperwork, and it will not survive the audit. The only answer that holds on that day makes no reference to you at all: Christ died, and Christ is risen.

For worship. He is able to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). Not with relief that the business is finally concluded, and not with the weariness of a judge who has found a technicality. With joy, because the one doing the presenting is the one who paid for the presentation, and he has wanted this from before the foundation of the world. The Lord who will sit on that day’s throne is the Lord who bore that day’s charges, and there is no accusation left in the universe that he has not already answered with his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

God is faithful. Pistos ho theos. Three short words in the Greek, and they are the floor under everything Paul has just promised, the reason for the confidence of verse 8. “Faithful” (pistos) means reliable, true to his word. It is a key phrase in this letter (10:13).

But what if I let go? A reader who has taken verse 8 seriously will already have asked it. It is very well to say that God will sustain me to the end, but I have let go before. I know how thin my grip is on a bad week, and I have watched people who seemed far stronger than me walk away. What happens then? Paul’s answer is not to reassure you about your grip. He changes the subject away from your grip altogether, and puts the entire weight on the character of God. The guarantee is not that you are faithful; it is that he is. That is the only guarantee worth anything, because a promise is exactly as reliable as the person making it, and you already know what yours are worth.

By whom you were called. Look at how the sentence is built. God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son. The calling is his act, a passive verb again, something done to them; God called them, effectively, into union with Christ. The fellowship is his gift. And the faithfulness that will keep them in it is his character. There is no point in that sentence at which the Corinthians contribute anything, which is a remarkable thing to say about a church whose behaviour is about to be dismantled for fifteen chapters. What God begins, he finishes.

What perseverance does and does not claim. This is the ground the Reformed doctrine of perseverance stands on, and we need to be exact. It does not claim that a Christian cannot sin badly, or drift for years, or go through a season in which faith is barely detectable. The Corinthians are the standing proof that it claims nothing so comfortable. What it claims is that the God who began the work will not abandon it: that the calling was not experimental and the fellowship is not on probation. The doctrine is often called the perseverance of the saints, and the name can mislead, because it sounds like a statement about the stamina of the saints. It is first a statement about the preservation of the saints by God. Christians persevere, and the reason they persevere is that they are being kept.

Into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord. “Fellowship” (koinōnia) means sharing, partnership, common life: having something in common, holding a share in the same thing. They were not called into a religion, or a set of obligations, or a moral improvement scheme. They were called into a shared life with the Son of God: union with him, sharing in all he is and has. And since every believer shares in Christ, they share in one another. The Corinthians, who have divided themselves into parties over which teacher they prefer, are told in the last line of the thanksgiving that they were all called into partnership with the same Person. That quietly makes every faction in the next paragraph absurd before Paul has even named them. This is the answer to their divisions (v. 10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean fellowship is just friendly activity, coffee after the service. It is first participation in Christ, from which friendship with one another flows.

What does fellowship with Christ look like on an ordinary day? It means that what is his is yours, and what is yours he has taken. His righteousness covers you, his Spirit lives in you, his Father is your Father, and his future is your future. In return he has taken your sin, your burdens and your griefs as his concern. You enjoy it by using it: speaking to him in prayer as one who is welcome, listening to him in Scripture, receiving him at his table, and sharing your life with others who share his. It is not a feeling you must manufacture. It is a relationship you are already in, and feelings tend to follow when you act on it.

In a sentence. God is faithful, who has called you into fellowship with his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

On a Tuesday. For the reader who lies awake over this, ask which of two questions you are actually asking. “Am I holding on tightly enough?” is a question with no answer, because there is no measurement that would settle it, and asking it repeatedly has never once produced assurance in anybody. “Is he faithful?” is a question with an answer, and the answer has a location: a cross, an empty tomb, and the record of a God who has never yet abandoned anyone who called on his name. Rest your weight on that today.

A God who will not leave you. The most dangerous thing in the world is not a God who might abandon you. It is a God of infinite faithfulness who has committed himself to you. Dangerous, because such a God will not leave you as you are; and safe, for exactly the same reason.

For worship. He has never broken a promise. Not to Abraham, waiting twenty-five years for a son; not to Israel, kept through four centuries in Egypt; not to David, whose throne stood empty for six hundred years before a child was born in Bethlehem to fill it. Every one of those promises looked, for a long time, like a promise that had failed. Not one of them did. He is faithful (1 Thessalonians 5:24; 2 Timothy 2:13), and the God who kept his word to them has called you into the fellowship of his own Son, and will not let go of what he has called.

parallels.desc: the faithful God

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul appeals to them, in Christ’s name, to agree with one another and end their divisions. Members of Chloe’s household have told him about quarrels: each person has a favourite, Paul, Apollos, Peter or Christ. Is Christ split into pieces? Was Paul crucified for them, or were they baptised into Paul’s name? He is glad he personally baptised only a handful of them, so no one can claim to be his disciple. Christ sent him not mainly to baptise but to preach the gospel, and not with clever rhetoric, which would empty the cross of its power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cross Against Personality Cults

The Corinthian factions are a cautionary tale about what happens when human personality becomes the centre of Christian community. This text is a permanent warning: the church that rallies around a preacher’s gifts, style, or personality rather than around the crucified Christ has already drifted from the gospel. The preacher is, at most, a herald — the one who announces a message that does not belong to him. Paul’s refusal to preach with “eloquent wisdom” is not anti-intellectualism; it is a deliberate choice to let the gospel speak in its own register, with its own power, rather than dressing it in borrowed clothes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ancient world ran on patronage and sophistry: you attached yourself to the most impressive teacher, displayed his influence on your life, and measured your social standing by his. The Corinthian factions are simply the church doing what Corinthian culture always did. Now: Celebrity pastor culture is the contemporary version. The church that streams a famous preacher rather than investing in local pastors, or that divides over which theological tradition’s champion to follow, is still choosing Apollos over Christ — a more impressive package over the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you, my brothers.

I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. “Appeal” (parakalō) is the verb of urging and pleading, from the same root as the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Paraklētos, the one called alongside. Paul does not command here, though as an apostle he could. He pleads. And he pleads by the name of Christ: by his authority, and by the one name in Corinth that belongs equally to every person he is writing to, which is exactly the point he is about to make. Christ has been named ten times in the first ten verses. Before Paul mentions a single faction, he has filled the room with the one Person they all share.

That all of you agree. Literally, that you all say the same thing: speak with one voice, rather than shouting rival slogans (v. 12).

And that there be no divisions among you. “Divisions” (schismata, from which we get schism) means tears, rents, splits. The word was used of a tear in a garment (Mark 2:21). It is not the word for a difference of opinion. It is the sound of fabric giving way. The church had not yet split into separate congregations, but there were cliques and rivalries. And what makes it worse is what the fabric is: this letter will shortly call the church a body (12:12–27), and a tear in a body is not an untidiness. It is a wound.

But that you be united in the same mind and the same judgment. “United” (katartizō) means mended, restored, put in order; it is the word used of the fishermen mending their nets (Mark 1:19). Paul wants the torn garment mended. Same mind (nous) is a shared way of thinking; same judgement (gnōmē) is a shared opinion and purpose. This is not a demand that every Christian hold identical views on every question. Paul himself makes room for genuine disagreement on real matters, food, days, disputable things (Romans 14), and this same letter will spend chapter 8 handling a question on which believers landed differently. What he is after is a shared orientation: a church so fixed on the same Lord that no rival loyalty can organise a party.

For it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people that there is quarreling among you. “Quarrelling” (erides) is strife, rivalry. Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business, perhaps slaves or employees travelling between Corinth and Ephesus. We do not know who Chloe was. Her people were socially the least significant witnesses available in Corinth, precisely the sort of people whose testimony a status-conscious congregation would be inclined to discount.

Paul names his source. He does two things with that report, and both are instructive. He takes it seriously, though it comes from the bottom of the social order rather than the top. And he says openly where it came from, refusing to deal in anonymous information. He will not build a rebuke on gossip he cannot attribute, and he will not pretend to a knowledge he acquired by some more dignified route. If you are going to confront a church, you say what you have heard and who told you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must agree on every opinion (Romans 14). It means unity in the gospel, in mind and purpose, without factions.

What does this ask of me on Sunday? Most readers are living somewhere inside this passage. Your church has a fault line: a leadership dispute, a music argument, two families who no longer speak, a slow separation into those who liked the last minister and those who wanted the change. Four things are asked of you, and none of them is dramatic. Refuse the party: the factions at Corinth were sustained by people saying I follow, and every division needs recruits; declining to take a side is a positive act, not cowardice. Stop repeating it: much of what tears a congregation is not the original disagreement but its retelling, and the sentence that begins I probably shouldn’t say this has done more damage in more churches than any heresy. Speak to the person, not about them, which is what Paul is doing here, at some cost. And keep eating together: this letter treats a shared table as a theological act, and people who eat together find it much harder to caricature each other.

Unity is not the same thing as quiet. One guard, because this passage can be used as a weapon by the wrong people. A call for unity is not a call to suppress genuine concern, and “you are being divisive” is the standard reply of anyone who wishes an uncomfortable question would go away. Paul himself is prepared to break fellowship over the gospel: he opposed Peter to his face when the gospel was at stake (Galatians 2:11), and told the Galatians that a different gospel is no gospel at all. Nor does unity ever mean covering up sin or abuse; this very letter demands that serious sin be dealt with openly (5:1–13). The unity commanded here is unity around the crucified Christ. The test is whether the thing dividing your church is Christ or preference. If a congregation is splitting over the gospel, that is a grief and may be a necessity. If it is splitting over anything else, and it usually is, then what Paul says next applies without qualification.

When is it right to leave a church? Rarely, and never casually. There are real reasons: the gospel itself is denied or obscured; serious sin or abuse is protected rather than dealt with; you are required to act against Scripture; or you have moved away. Preference about style, music or personality is not one of them, and even real concerns should first be raised humbly, privately and with the elders (Matthew 18:15). If you must go, go openly and peaceably, without recruiting others or leaving a trail of grievance, and join another faithful church promptly. Leaving Christ’s people altogether is never an option Scripture offers.

In a sentence. Paul appeals to you, brothers and sisters, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree with one another in what you say and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly united in mind and thought. Some from Chloe’s household have informed him that there are quarrels among you.

On a Tuesday. If you have a complaint about someone in your church, speak openly and to the right person, not in whispers. And work for mending, not tearing. Before Sunday, find one person on the other side of whatever fault line runs through your church, and do something ordinary and kind with them: a meal, a message, a question about their week. Mending nets is slow work, done knot by knot.

For worship. The Lord whose name Paul pleads by has one body and will not be divided. He prayed on the night he was betrayed that his people would be one, as he and the Father are one (John 17:21), and he bought that oneness with a body that was torn so that ours need not be. Every tear in his church is mended, in the end, by the one whose own flesh was torn for it, and on the last day there will be one flock and one Shepherd.
verseByVerse.note: Chloe’s people were probably members of her household or business who had travelled to Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What I mean is that each one of you says, “I follow Paul,” or “I follow Apollos,” or “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?

What I mean is that each one of you says. Paul reports four slogans without comment before demolishing them: I follow Paul, or I follow Apollos, or I follow Cephas, or I follow Christ. Literally, I am of Paul: I belong to Paul. The names are not random, and each represents a real attraction.

“I follow Paul”. Paul founded the church; his party is the loyalist old guard, the people who were there at the beginning and proud to follow the church’s founder.

Or “I follow Apollos”. Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. He was an eloquent Jew from Alexandria, competent in the Scriptures (Acts 18:24–28): the polished speaker, and in a city that paid to hear professional orators, a considerable draw. Some preferred his style.

Or “I follow Cephas”. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name. Some, perhaps Jewish believers, claimed the leading apostle of the Twelve: the Jerusalem connection, the man who walked with Jesus, apostolic prestige of a kind Paul could not match.

Or “I follow Christ”. Perhaps the most dangerous party, and it deserves its own word, because it looks like the right answer and is rebuked alongside the others. What could be wrong with that? Everything, if it is said in that tone. It is the claim to have risen above the mess: I have no time for your teachers and your traditions and your squabbling church; I have Christ, directly, and I need nothing else. It sounds like maturity and is a subtler form of the same pride, because it has still turned Christ into a party badge, and it has done it by using his name to look down on his people.

Good material, bad division. Notice that nothing here is a heresy. Nobody is teaching error. Every one of these men is a genuine servant of God, and Paul will insist two chapters later that Apollos and he are simply servants through whom the Corinthians believed (3:5). The material of the division is entirely good. That is what makes it so hard to see from the inside. A congregation dividing over false teaching at least knows what it is doing; a congregation dividing over preferences believes it is defending something important.

Is Christ divided? Then come three questions, and each one is a hammer. Has Christ been split up and shared out among factions? If the church is his body, then a factional church is a dismembered Christ. The image is grotesque, and it is meant to be. There are not four Christs to distribute among four parties. Every believer at Corinth has the whole of him, which means no group holds a portion the others lack. To divide the church is to tear him.

Was Paul crucified for you? Here is the only credential that could justify a Christian naming himself after someone. Loyalty of this depth belongs to a person who died for you, and exactly one person qualifies. Paul is not being modest. He is pointing out that the Corinthians have offered him something he has no right to receive, and he refuses to be the head of a party.

Or were you baptized in the name of Paul? Baptism names your owner. To be baptised into the name of someone is to be publicly transferred into his possession, and every Corinthian was baptised into the name of Christ, whoever happened to be standing in the water with him. These are absurd questions with obvious answers: only Christ died for them, and they belong to him alone.

For the one who has withdrawn into a private faith. This passage comes uncomfortably close to a particular reader. You have been hurt by a church, or simply exhausted by one. You have watched Christians behave in ways that embarrassed you, and you have quietly withdrawn: you love Christ, you read your Bible, and you have concluded you can do without the rest. Nothing in this passage doubts the hurt, and a church that damaged you owes you an apology it may never offer. But notice where the fourth slogan sits. Paul does not put it above the others as the one healthy option. He puts it in the same sentence and lets the same three questions fall on it, because Christ has attached himself to a body, and no one can take the Head and decline the rest of him. The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you (12:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should have no preferences among teachers, or that denominations are always sinful. Paul does not rebuke anyone for learning more from Apollos than from Cephas, and churches that hold distinct convictions about baptism or church order are not what he is attacking. It means no human leader may take Christ’s place, and no preference may divide the church. The sin is boasting in a human leader and treating your own side as the measure of who really belongs (3:21). Paul and Apollos are servants through whom you believed (3:5), and both belong to every believer (3:22). A loyalty has become a party spirit when you can no longer gladly receive Christ’s gifts through someone outside it.

Can I just listen to my favourite preacher online instead of my own church? Listen to him gladly, but not instead. Christ gives his gifts through the gathered church you actually belong to: the pastor who knows your name, the elders who will visit you in hospital, the table you share, the people who can see your life and speak into it (Hebrews 10:24–25; 13:17). A celebrity preacher cannot shepherd you, and he will never know if you drift. And comparing your pastor unfavourably with a man edited for an online audience is exactly the Corinthian habit Paul is rebuking. Thank God for both, and give your loyalty to the local body where Christ has placed you.

In a sentence. What he means is this: one of you says, “I follow Paul”; another, “I follow Apollos”; another, “I follow Cephas”; still another, “I follow Christ.” Is Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Were you baptised in the name of Paul?

On a Tuesday. Think of the Christian tribe you belong to: the tradition, the church, the teacher whose books you buy, the theological camp whose language you speak. Now ask what you would find harder to give up: that identity, or the company of a believer who has all of Christ and none of your tribe’s distinctives. Most of us discover our loyalties are considerably more Corinthian than we thought, and the tell is not what we say about Christ. It is who we are content to be in the same room with (Ephesians 4:4–6; John 17:20–21).

For worship. Thank God for the preachers and authors who have helped you, and then remember: none of them died for you. Only Christ did. He alone was crucified for us, he alone owns us by baptism into his name, and he alone is undivided, whole and entire for every one of his people. No servant of his can bear the weight of our hearts, and he never asked them to. He bore it himself.
verseByVerse.note: Apollos had taught at Corinth after Paul. Cephas is Peter’s Aramaic name.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius, so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. (I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)

I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius. Paul is glad he baptised almost nobody, which, said by an apostle, needs explaining before anything else. He is not disparaging baptism. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19), Paul assumes every Corinthian has received it (v. 13), and he treats it in this very letter as bound up with the moment believers were joined into one body (12:13). What he is glad about is narrower and shrewder. Paul probably left most baptisms to others, and the fewer people who could claim a personal bond with him through baptism, the fewer could build a party on it.

Who these people were. Each of the three he does remember was a person of standing. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue who believed with his whole household (Acts 18:8), the most prominent convert in the city. Gaius later hosted not merely Paul but the whole church (Romans 16:23), which suggests a man of means with an open house. Stephanas and his household were the firstfruits of Achaia and devoted themselves to serving the saints (16:15–17). These are exactly the people a personality cult would be built around, and Paul knows it.

So that no one may say that you were baptized in my name. Given what is happening in verses 12–13, his relief is entirely justified. No one can claim a special bond with him through baptism, and so no one can use the water as a badge of loyalty to a man.

I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Paul corrects himself honestly as he dictates. The little parenthesis, oh, and Stephanas’s household as well, is the sound of a real man dictating a real letter and remembering something halfway through.

Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else. Here is a sentence that stops careful readers, and it deserves a proper answer rather than a smile. A man writing Scripture has just admitted, in Scripture, that he cannot remember. How can that be, if the Bible is the word of God? The question rests on an assumption: that inspiration must mean dictation, that God overrode Paul’s mind and used him as a pen, so that anything less than total recall is a flaw in the machinery. But that is not what Scripture claims for itself, and it is not how the Bible reads. Luke opens his Gospel by describing research, following all things closely and consulting eyewitnesses (Luke 1:1–4). The Psalms are full of men saying exactly what they feel. The human authors are not bypassed; they are used.

What inspiration does mean. The doctrine holds that the Spirit so superintended what these men wrote that the result is precisely what God intended to say, without suppressing the men themselves: their vocabulary, their temperament, their circumstances, their memories (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21). On that understanding this verse is not a problem at all. Ask what the sentence asserts. It asserts that Paul, at the time of writing, was not certain whether there had been others. And that assertion is entirely true. Inspiration does not mean Paul had a perfect memory of every detail; it means what he wrote is true, including his statement that he does not remember. Nothing false has been affirmed.

A forger tidies. There is more here than a defence. Consider what this verse does to the character of the document. A man inventing an apostolic letter to bolster his own authority does not portray himself groping after a detail and correcting himself mid-sentence, and he certainly does not leave the correction in. It is the kind of detail that no one puts in on purpose.

God uses ordinary minds. It also tells you something about how God works. He did not require Paul to be superhuman before he would use him. The letter that contains the greatest chapter ever written on love, and the fullest account of the resurrection in the New Testament, also contains its author failing to remember whom he baptised, and God saw no need to remove it. That is a considerable encouragement to anyone who has assumed that God can only work through people whose faculties are impressive.

Where Christians differ: household baptisms. Some argue from household baptisms (here, and Acts 16:15, 33) that infants of believers should be baptised. Verdict: the New Testament never mentions an infant in any household baptism. The text here does not say who was in the household or how old they were, but at the end of the letter this same household is described as devoting themselves to serving the saints (16:15), which describes believers old enough to serve. Elsewhere the households that were baptised are households that heard the word and believed (Acts 16:32–34; 18:8). Baptism in the New Testament follows repentance and faith (Acts 2:38, 41; 8:12). So the app holds believer’s baptism (1689 London Baptist Confession 29), while warmly recognising paedobaptist brothers and sisters as faithful Christians who read the covenant differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism is unimportant. Christ commanded it (Matthew 28:19). Paul simply refuses to let it become a badge of loyalty to him.

I was baptised as an infant and have since come to faith. Should I be baptised? On the view this app holds, yes: the baptism the New Testament describes is the public confession of a believer, and since you did not make that confession as an infant, the step of obedience is still before you. That is not a slight on your parents, who very likely acted in faith and love, and it is not a judgement on paedobaptist churches, which are true churches of Christ. Talk it through with your pastor or elders, read the passages for yourself, and act with a clear conscience. If your church holds the other view, raise it humbly; this is a matter on which godly Christians differ, and love must govern the conversation.

In a sentence. Paul is thankful that he did not baptise any of you except Crispus and Gaius, so no one can say that you were baptised in his name. (Yes, he also baptised the household of Stephanas; beyond that, he does not remember if he baptised anyone else.)

On a Tuesday. Do not tie your faith to a particular minister. Your baptism joined you to Christ, not to a person. And ask whose name is attached to your own service: the group you lead, the class you teach, the work you have built. If it ended tomorrow and someone else’s name went on it, and it flourished, how would you feel? Paul’s answer to that question is in the first words of this passage: I thank God.

For worship. Christ is the one into whose name every believer is baptised, and he shares that name with no one. He used an apostle who could not remember whom he had baptised, a household that gave itself to serving, a synagogue ruler and a generous host, and he wove them all into one church that belongs to him alone. His word comes to us through real men with real memories, and it is still wholly his word, true in every line, so that the very gaps in Paul’s recollection are kept by God for our comfort.
