Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?<sup>14</sup>I thank God that I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius,<sup>15</sup>so that no one may say that you were baptized in my name.<sup>16</sup>(I did baptize also the household of Stephanas. Beyond that, I do not know whether I baptized anyone else.)<sup>17</sup>For Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel, and not with words of eloquent wisdom, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.<sup>18</sup>For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.<sup>19</sup>For it is written, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the discernment of the discerning I will thwart.”<sup>20</sup>Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? Where is the debater of this age? Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?<sup>21</sup>For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.<sup>22</sup>For Jews demand signs and Greeks seek wisdom,<sup>23</sup>but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles,<sup>24</sup>but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.<sup>25</sup>For the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men.<sup>26</sup>For consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth.<sup>27</sup>But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise; God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong;<sup>28</sup>God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are,<sup>29</sup>so that no human being might boast in the presence of God.<sup>30</sup>And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption,<sup>31</sup>so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

2.title: The Spirit, the Cross, and True Wisdom
2.overview:
Paul continues his answer to a church that prized clever speech and secret wisdom. He reminds them how he first came to Corinth: not as a dazzling orator, but weak, nervous and resolved to speak of nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified, so that their faith would rest on God’s power rather than on human brilliance. Yet the gospel is not anti-intellectual. There is a wisdom Paul speaks among the mature, but it is God’s wisdom, hidden in the past and now revealed, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

This wisdom cannot be discovered; it must be revealed, and God has revealed it by his Spirit, who knows God’s depths as a person’s own spirit knows his thoughts. The apostles have received that Spirit, and they speak in words he teaches. A person without the Spirit cannot accept these things; they seem foolish to him, because they can be understood only by the Spirit. But the person with the Spirit can discern them, and believers have the mind of Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul recalls his arrival in Corinth. He did not come with impressive rhetoric or a display of cleverness to announce God’s message. He had made up his mind to know nothing among them except Jesus Christ, crucified. He came in weakness, fear and great trembling, and his preaching did not rely on persuasive technique but on a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that their faith would rest not on human wisdom but on God’s power.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Theology of Proclamation

Paul’s deliberate simplicity in proclamation is not a pastoral strategy; it is a doctrinal commitment. The power of the gospel is the power of the Spirit working through the word of the cross — not the power of the preacher, the brilliance of the argument, or the emotional manipulation of the audience. Reformed theology has always insisted on this: it is the Spirit who regenerates, convicts, and converts; the preacher is the instrument, not the cause. If people are not converted by the preaching of Christ crucified, they will not be converted by anything the preacher can add.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: In first-century Corinth, the travelling sophist was a celebrity figure — a rhetorical virtuoso who could hold an audience spellbound, charge a fee, and move on. The Corinthians expected their teacher to perform at that level. Paul’s refusal to do so was not incompetence but protest: he would not compete on the sophists’ terms. Now: The contemporary equivalent is the pressure to make church services “compelling” through production values, platform charisma, and emotional manipulation. Paul’s counter-word is not to be deliberately boring, but to trust the cross to do what polished performance cannot: actually save people.

verseByVerse.quote: And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 2 carries on the argument against the Corinthians’ love of worldly wisdom. First, Paul reminds them how he preached when he came: not with impressive rhetoric, but with Christ crucified, in weakness, so that their faith would rest on God’s power, not human cleverness (vv. 1–5). Second, there is a true wisdom, but it is God’s wisdom, hidden and now revealed: his plan of salvation in Christ, which the rulers of this age did not grasp, or they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (vv. 6–9). Third, this wisdom is known only by the Spirit. The Spirit searches the depths of God and reveals them to his apostles, who speak them in Spirit-taught words (vv. 10–13). The natural person, without the Spirit, cannot receive these things; the spiritual person, taught by the Spirit, can, and has the mind of Christ (vv. 14–16). The chapter is one of the Bible’s key passages on revelation, inspiration and illumination, and it moves from a frightened preacher in a hostile city to the astonishing claim that ordinary believers have been let into the mind of God.

And I, when I came to you, brothers. Paul goes back to his first visit to Corinth, about AD 50 (Acts 18:1). The church has since heard Apollos and concluded it would have preferred something with more polish, and Paul is defending what he did then.

Did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. “Lofty” (hyperochē) means superiority, excellence: the elevated style of the professional orator. He did not come as a showman. Some manuscripts read mystery of God instead of testimony of God; the ESV notes this. Either way, the content is God’s message about Christ.

For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. “Decided” (ekrina, from krinō) means I judged, I reached a verdict: a deliberate choice. Paul did not drift into a plain style because he had nothing better available. He weighed it and came to a decision.

Not a repentance after Athens. A popular reading says Paul is repenting here: that he had tried philosophy at Athens, quoting their poets on the Areopagus (Acts 17), found it a failure, and arrived at Corinth chastened and determined never to try it again. It is a memorable story and it is almost certainly wrong. Luke does not present Athens as a failure: some joined him and believed, including a member of the council (Acts 17:34). Paul goes on quoting pagan writers for the rest of his ministry. He is not describing a change of tactics but a settled resolve about content.

The centre that governs everything. Nothing except Jesus Christ and him crucified cannot be taken with wooden literalism. This very letter deals with lawsuits, marriage, food offered to idols, head coverings, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual gifts and the resurrection body. What Paul means is that everything he taught was centred on and measured by Christ crucified. The cross was not one topic among many; it was the lens for all of them. Watch how he does this later in the letter: when the Corinthians squabble over food, he ends with the brother for whom Christ died (8:11). When they abuse the Supper, he takes them back to the night he was betrayed (11:23). Every practical problem in this church is finally settled by reference to a cross.

And him crucified. Note the sharpness of the phrase. Not Jesus Christ alone, which could have been made respectable: a great teacher, a moral example, a figure of light. Him crucified. Paul deliberately keeps the offensive part in the centre of the frame, because the moment you remove it you have a religion the world can admire and nobody needs saving by.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only on the crucifixion and nothing else. He taught the whole counsel of God (Acts 20:27), including ethics, marriage, the church and the resurrection, as this letter shows. But all of it flowed from the cross. Nor is it a defence of anti-intellectualism: the man writing it had the best education available to a Jew of his generation and is in the middle of a sustained argument. And a congregation fed only on the mechanics of justification, never told how to be a husband or handle money or forgive, is not being fed the way this letter feeds.

What is the message of Christ crucified, in plain words? That Jesus, the eternal Son of God made man, lived the perfect life we have not lived, and then died on the cross in the place of sinners, bearing the punishment our sins deserved, so that God is just in forgiving us (Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:24). That he was buried and raised on the third day, proving the payment accepted (15:3–4). And that everyone who turns from sin and trusts him is forgiven, counted righteous and made a child of God, freely, without any contribution of his own. If you can say that clearly to a friend, you can do what Paul did at Corinth.

In a sentence. And so it was with Paul, brothers and sisters. When he came to you, he did not come with eloquence or human wisdom as he proclaimed to you the testimony about God. For he resolved to know nothing while he was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified.

On a Tuesday. Let Christ crucified be the centre of your faith; measure your opinions, priorities and plans by the cross. And if you teach anything, a sermon, a class, a Bible study, a conversation with a child, take the last thing you taught and ask how many steps it took to get from your subject to the cross. The test is not whether you mentioned Jesus. It is whether what you said would collapse if the crucifixion were removed from underneath it (Galatians 6:14; 1 Corinthians 15:3).

For worship. Paul could have talked about anything, and he chose to talk about a dying Saviour, because there is nothing greater to talk about. All the wisdom of God is gathered into that one event: the Son of God lifted up on a Roman cross, bearing the sin of the world. A preacher may spend his whole life on it and never reach the bottom. We will spend eternity on it and never tire, singing to the Lamb who was slain.

verseByVerse.quote: And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling, and my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.

And I was with you in weakness and in fear and much trembling. This is the apostle Paul describing his own arrival at Corinth, and it is worth refusing to make it more dignified than it was. Consider what had just happened to him. He had been stripped, beaten with rods and jailed at Philippi. He had been run out of Thessalonica by a mob, and then out of Berea. At Athens he had met a cool reception and polite mockery (Acts 16:22–17:34). He arrived at Corinth alone, without Silas and Timothy, in a city famous for its hardness. And Luke records that during that stay the Lord appeared to him in a vision at night and said: do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent (Acts 18:9–10). You do not say that to a man who is not afraid. Paul was not a confident superstar. He was weak, afraid and trembling.

Arguing from his fear. So the fear was real; it was not a rhetorical device. And Paul puts it in writing to a church that had begun to prefer more impressive speakers. He is not embarrassed by it. He is arguing from it.

And my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom. “Plausible” (peithos, persuasive) means the techniques of rhetoric designed to win over an audience. The sophists produced persuasion, and Paul refused to compete with them on their terms.

But in demonstration of the Spirit and of power. “Demonstration” (apodeixis) was a technical term in rhetoric: a compelling proof, a demonstration that settles a matter. Paul has chosen it deliberately. He claims something better than persuasion, and locates it entirely outside himself. The proof of his message was not his technique but the Spirit’s power: convicting hearts, bringing new birth, and in the apostolic ministry accompanied by signs (2 Corinthians 12:12; 1 Thessalonians 1:5). What proved the message was not the performance of the speaker but the Spirit doing in the hearers what no speaker can do.

So that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God. This is the point of the paragraph. Paul is thinking about foundations: about what happens years later, under pressure, when the church is tested. If their faith had been produced by clever speech, a cleverer speaker could undo it. A faith founded on a persuasive man lasts exactly as long as that man remains persuasive. If the Corinthians had been won by Paul’s brilliance, the arrival of a better speaker would move them, which is precisely what has happened, and it is the trouble this letter is addressing. Worse, when a preacher falls, or is exposed, or simply turns out to be ordinary, everyone whose faith was built on him discovers there was nothing underneath. Faith that rests on God’s power stands.

Fear is not disqualifying. Most readers need this verse more than the argument it serves. There is a very common Christian assumption that the people God uses are the confident ones: that if you were more assured, better spoken, less prone to going dry-mouthed when the conversation turns to Christ, you would be useful, and that your nervousness proves this is not your gift. This verse says the founding missionary of the Gentile world arrived at one of the most important churches of his career weak, frightened and shaking. Not once, in an off week; it is how he describes the whole visit. Fear is not the opposite of usefulness, and confidence is not the qualification. A man who is never nervous may be relying on something Paul had deliberately laid down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should be nervous to be faithful, or that preparation is unspiritual. It means the effectiveness of preaching depends on the Spirit, not the preacher.

What does the Spirit’s demonstration look like today? Chiefly what it looked like at Corinth: people convicted of sin, turning to Christ, and being changed. The church at Corinth was itself the proof: idolaters, thieves and drunkards washed, sanctified and justified (6:9–11). In the apostolic period the Spirit also confirmed the message with signs, and this app holds that those sign gifts belonged to that foundational time (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). But the greatest miracle has never ceased: a dead heart made alive through a plain message. Look for that, pray for it, and do not despise it because it is quiet. Every conversion is the power of God on display.

In a sentence. Paul came to you in weakness with great fear and trembling. His message and his preaching were not with wise and persuasive words, but with a demonstration of the Spirit’s power, so that your faith might not rest on human wisdom, but on God’s power.

On a Tuesday. After you have spoken to someone about Christ, notice what you want to know. If the question in your mind is how did I come across, then the demonstration you were relying on was your own. If it is Lord, do something in him that I cannot do, you have understood this passage. If you feel weak and afraid when you speak of Christ, you are in good company. Pray for the Spirit’s power, and speak.

For worship. Paul trembled his way through eighteen months at Corinth and left behind a church that is still read about two thousand years later, and not one line of it is credited to his nerve. That is how God works: treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us (2 Corinthians 4:7). The Lord who stood by a frightened apostle in the night and said do not be afraid, I am with you, is the same Lord who stands by every trembling witness, and the faith he builds rests on him, and so it cannot fall.
verseByVerse.note: Paul came to Corinth after the cool reception at Athens.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Yet Paul does teach wisdom among those who are mature, though not the wisdom of this age or of its rulers, who are passing away. It is God’s secret wisdom, hidden until now, which God planned before time for our glory. None of the rulers of this age understood it; if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. As Scripture says, no one has seen, heard or imagined what God has prepared for those who love him, but God has revealed it to us by his Spirit, who searches even the depths of God. Just as only a person’s own spirit knows his inner thoughts, only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. Believers have received not the world’s spirit but God’s Spirit, so that they may understand what God has freely given. The apostles speak of these things in words taught not by human wisdom but by the Spirit. The unspiritual person rejects them as foolishness and cannot understand them, because they are discerned only through the Spirit. The spiritual person can evaluate everything but is not subject to merely human judgement. Who has known the Lord’s mind to instruct him? But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Knowledge of God

Verses 10–16 are the locus classicus of the Reformed doctrine of the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit (testimonium Spiritus Sancti internum). Calvin’s Institutes ground the believer’s certainty about Scripture not in external proofs but in the Spirit’s own witness to the heart. Paul’s argument here is the foundation: the things of God are spiritually discerned; the Spirit of God alone can reveal them; the Spirit has been given to those who are in Christ. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos) is not merely unwilling but unable to receive spiritual things — a direct support for the Reformed doctrine of total depravity in its noetic dimension.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians’ preference for Apollos’s sophisticated rhetoric over Paul’s plain proclamation was, at root, a preference for a wisdom they could evaluate by their own natural capacities. Paul’s response: the real wisdom — the wisdom that saves — cannot be evaluated that way. It requires the Spirit to receive it. Now: The recurring temptation to evaluate the gospel by academic or cultural criteria — to ask whether Christianity can hold its own in the university seminar — misses Paul’s point. The knowledge of God is not the endpoint of human inquiry; it is the gift of the Spirit to the humble heart. This is why apologetics serves evangelism but cannot replace it: ultimately, only the Spirit can open eyes to see the Lord of glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom, although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory.

Yet among the mature we do impart wisdom. After two chapters of demolishing wisdom, Paul turns and says the Christian message is wisdom after all, just not of a kind the world can recognise or reach. Paul is not against wisdom. There is a true wisdom.

Not two tiers of Christian. The sentence needs a guard at once, because it sounds like something Paul would hate. Read carelessly, it sets up two tiers: ordinary believers who get the basic gospel, and an inner circle of the mature trusted with deeper material. That is how the mystery religions of Corinth were organised, and how the Gnostic teachers of the following century would organise themselves. Two things rule that reading out. The first is the word itself: teleioi, the mature, the complete, the grown-up. Here it means all who have the Spirit and accept the gospel, as opposed to the natural person (v. 14). It is not a rank; it is an age. Paul’s contrast in the next paragraph is not initiates against outsiders but adults against infants: infants in Christ (3:1). One category, at different stages.

The sting. The second is the sting the Corinthians would have felt. They regarded themselves as the mature elite; that self-assessment is the engine of the whole problem. Paul says among the mature we impart wisdom, and in the next breath tells them he could not do it with them, because they were still on milk and squabbling like children. This is not an invitation into an inner circle. It is a rebuke delivered by holding the door open and observing that they cannot yet walk through it. Paul redefines maturity.

Although it is not a wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are doomed to pass away. The rulers of this age are the political and religious leaders who crucified Jesus (v. 8): Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas. Some also see behind them the spiritual powers (Ephesians 6:12). They are being brought to nothing (katargeō), passing away with this age.

But we impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God. Literally, God’s wisdom in a mystery. Secret and hidden not because God is withholding it now, but because it was concealed until he chose to disclose it. Paul’s word is mystērion, and in his hands a mystery is never a puzzle to be solved but a secret God has decided to tell (Romans 16:25–26; Ephesians 3:4–6). Not a secret for an elite few, but God’s plan once hidden and now revealed.

Which God decreed before the ages. “Decreed” (proorizō) means predestined, determined beforehand. The plan was settled before there was a universe to enact it in. Before time began, God planned salvation through Christ crucified. The cross was not God’s recovery from an unexpected disaster. It was the arrangement, made in eternity, before Adam, before the fall, before there was anybody to be saved by it (Ephesians 1:4; Revelation 13:8).

For our glory. And then the phrase that ought to stop the reader. Not merely for our rescue, or our forgiveness, or our safety. The eternal decree had our glory in view: the glorification of believers, sharing Christ’s glory (Romans 8:30). This letter will spell out later what that means: a body raised imperishable, in glory, in power (15:42–43). Whatever God was intending before the ages, it was not simply to get us out of trouble. It was to bring us somewhere.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is a secret higher teaching for advanced Christians beyond the gospel, as the later Gnostics claimed. The wisdom is the gospel itself, understood more deeply.

Does “for our glory” put us at the centre instead of God? No. Our glory is the glory of sharing his: being made like Christ, seeing his face, reflecting his likeness (Romans 8:29; 2 Corinthians 3:18). It is the glory of a mirror catching the sun, not of a lamp lit by itself. And Scripture says the whole plan is to the praise of his glorious grace (Ephesians 1:6, 12, 14). God’s glory and our good are not rivals. He is most glorified in giving his people the greatest gift, which is himself, and we are most glad when we receive it. So you may long for the glory to come without any embarrassment. It is God’s idea, and it will be all of his doing.

In a sentence. We do, however, speak a message of wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. No, we declare God’s wisdom, a mystery that has been hidden and that God destined for our glory before time began.

On a Tuesday. God planned your glory before the ages; on a hard day, remember where your story is going. If God settled this before the ages, then the thing you are currently most anxious about, the situation you cannot see through, the outcome you are trying to secure, is happening inside a plan that was complete before the world was made. That does not tell you how it will go. It tells you that it is not being improvised, and that the same decree which reaches back before time reaches forward to a glory you have not yet seen (Ephesians 1:4; Romans 8:29–30).

For worship. Before there were stars, the Father, the Son and the Spirit had settled the cross and set their love on a people to bring to glory. Nothing has taken God by surprise, not the fall, not Calvary, not your life. The wisdom the rulers could not see was older than their thrones, and it will outlast them, and its end is a company of sinners shining with the glory of the Son who died for them.

verseByVerse.quote: None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
None of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

None of the rulers of this age understood this. Who are the rulers? Commentators divide. Some take them as the human authorities: Pilate, Herod, Caiaphas, the Sanhedrin, the men who actually signed the order and carried it out. Others take them as the spiritual powers, the rulers and authorities of Ephesians 6:12, working behind the human actors. The best reading is probably both, and Paul may not have felt the need to distinguish them. The New Testament shows Satan operating through named human beings at exactly this point (Luke 22:3; John 13:27). The rulers did not grasp God’s plan. They thought they were getting rid of a troublemaker. In fact they were carrying out God’s plan of salvation.

Was the cross a blunder? If they had known, they would not have done it. Does that mean Satan miscalculated, and that if the powers had been better informed the atonement would never have happened? The New Testament will not let us rest there, and the answer is one of the most important things a Christian can grasp about how God governs the world. Peter puts both halves in a single sentence at Pentecost: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Not one clause qualifying the other. The plan was fixed, and the men who executed it were lawless and guilty. The believers in Jerusalem say the same when they pray, naming Herod, Pontius Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered to do whatever God’s hand and plan had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27–28). They freely did what they wanted. What they wanted had been decreed.

Blind because they were evil. So the ignorance here is real, and it is culpable. The powers were not victims of insufficient briefing; they were blind because they were evil, and their blindness was the very thing God used. This is the pattern of Joseph and his brothers written across cosmic history: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). The devil got exactly what he wanted, and it destroyed him: through death the Son destroyed the one who has the power of death (Hebrews 2:14).

When someone has wronged you. This yields a considerable comfort for anyone on the receiving end of someone else’s malice. You are not obliged to believe that what was done to you was good, or that the person who did it meant anything but harm. The cross settles that God does not require evil to be innocent in order to make it serve him. The worst act in the history of the world is the one he used to save it.

For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. Then the title, the most audacious thing in the verse. “Lord of glory” is a title of God in the Old Testament (Psalm 24:7–10; Acts 7:2). It echoes Psalm 24, where the gates are commanded to lift up their heads so that the King of glory may come in, and the psalm asks twice, who is this King of glory? and answers: the LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD of hosts. Paul takes that title and attaches it, without a word of explanation, to a man his readers knew had been flogged and nailed up outside a city wall between two criminals. The one they crucified was the Lord of glory himself. A stunning phrase: God the Son, the glorious Lord, crucified.

One person, two natures. Because Christ is one person with two natures, what is true of either nature can be said of the person: the Lord of glory died, in his human nature. The theologians call this the communication of properties, and Scripture uses it freely: God purchased the church with his own blood (Acts 20:28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the rulers were innocent because they were ignorant. Jesus prayed for their forgiveness (Luke 23:34), but they were guilty (Acts 3:17; 4:10).

Did God die on the cross? The person who died was God the Son, so in that sense yes, and the Bible says so (Acts 20:28). But he died in his human nature, not his divine nature. His body died and his human soul was separated from it; his divine nature, which cannot die, did not cease, and the Trinity was never broken apart. That is not a technicality. It means the one who bore your sin was not a lesser being but God himself, so the sacrifice has infinite worth; and it means he truly died as a man, so he could stand in a man’s place. Only one who is both God and man could do both.

In a sentence. None of the rulers of this age understood it, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.

On a Tuesday. If someone’s cruelty has shaped your life, bring it to the cross today. Do not call the evil good, and do not tell yourself God was absent. Tell him what was done, and then say with Joseph: you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good. It may take years before you see how. The rulers never saw it at all, and God still saved the world.

For worship. The King of glory came to his own gates and they did not lift up their heads; they crucified him. He made the wood. He made the iron in the nails, and the men who drove them, and held their hearts beating through every hour of it. And he did not come down, because coming down would have saved him and lost us, and he had decreed before the ages which of those he would choose (Psalm 24:7–10; John 1:10–11). The Lord of glory was crucified for you. Let that astonish you again.

verseByVerse.quote: But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”— these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”—these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.

But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined”. This is one of the most misquoted sentences in the Bible, and the misquotation turns it inside out. It is a loose quotation of Isaiah 64:4, with echoes of Isaiah 65:17. You will have heard it at funerals and on cards, often in the old wording, offered as a statement that heaven is beyond imagining, that we cannot know what awaits us and must simply trust. It is used to close a subject.

Read on into verse 10. But look where the sentence actually ends. The main clause is in verse 10: these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. The verse is often quoted as if it were only about heaven, beyond our knowledge. But Paul says God has revealed these things. The quotation is the setup; the revelation is the point. Quoting verse 9 without verse 10 makes Paul say the opposite of what he wrote.

Three faculties ruled out. Notice the three faculties the citation rules out, because they cover every route a person might take. No eye has seen: it cannot be observed, and empirical investigation will not find it. Nor ear heard: it cannot be picked up by report, and no human tradition preserved it. Nor the heart of man imagined: it cannot be reached by intuition or mysticism or the religious imagination working at full stretch. Human senses and imagination could never discover God’s plan of salvation. Sight, hearsay and inspiration all fail, which leaves exactly one possibility, the one Paul names: God had to say it himself.

What God has prepared for those who love him. Those who love him are believers. What God has prepared includes salvation in Christ now, as well as glory to come.

These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. “Revealed” (apokalyptō) means unveiled. “Us” here refers first to the apostles, through whom God gave the revelation that became the New Testament, and then to all believers who receive it.

For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. “Searches” (eraunaō) does not mean that the Spirit is ignorant and must look, as though he were exploring a God he does not yet fully know. It is the language of complete access: he knows everything thoroughly. The depths (bathē) of God are his inmost thoughts and purposes. Only someone who is himself God can know the depths of God. The Spirit is at home there because he is God. This is a strong text for the Spirit’s deity.

The same Spirit in ordinary believers. Hold on to this. The Spirit who has full access to the interior life of God is the same Spirit given to ordinary believers. That is how a person with no education and no religious pedigree can read a page of Scripture and genuinely meet God there, while a hostile expert reads the identical page and finds nothing but literature.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know everything about heaven. Much remains unseen (1 John 3:2). But the heart of God’s plan is revealed.

Is the Holy Spirit a person or a power? A person, and God. Only a person searches, knows, teaches and can be grieved (v. 13; Ephesians 4:30), and only God knows the depths of God. He is not an influence God sends out, like warmth from a fire; he is the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son, who comes to live in believers himself. So we speak of him as he, not it. And we may pray to him, worship him and rely on him as we do the Father and the Son, while knowing that his delight is to point us to Christ (John 16:14).

In a sentence. However, as it is written: “What no eye has seen, what no ear has heard, and what no human mind has conceived, the things God has prepared for those who love him,” these are the things God has revealed to us by his Spirit. The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit who knows the depths of God has revealed God’s heart in Scripture; open it today, and ask him to show you. And ask what you actually expect after death. Notice whether your answer comes from Scripture or from the culture: clouds, a vague reunion, a light, becoming a memory in other people’s heads. Most of us discover that our functional hope is far vaguer than the one we have been given, not because God was reticent but because we took no eye has seen as permission not to look up what he said (Isaiah 64:4; Ephesians 1:17–18).

For worship. Standing at a graveside, we are not reduced to saying that we cannot imagine what has happened to the one we loved. We can say a great deal, because God has told us: that to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8); that the dead in Christ will rise (1 Thessalonians 4:16); that this perishable body will put on the imperishable (15:53); that he will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4). The Christian at a funeral is not the person who knows nothing. He is the one person in the room who has been told. Blessed be the God who did not leave us guessing, but sent his own Spirit out of his own depths to tell us what he has prepared.

parallels.desc: from of old no one has heard or perceived

verseByVerse.quote: For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given us by God.

For who knows a person’s thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? Paul now supplies an analogy so ordinary that it is easy to miss how much it settles. No one can know what you are thinking unless you tell them; only your own spirit knows. Think about someone you have lived alongside for thirty years. You know their face better than your own, you can predict what they will order and how they will react, and they still surprise you. You still cannot get inside. There is a room in every human being that no one else has ever entered, and the only occupant is the person himself.

So also no one comprehends the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. Now scale that up. If one finite creature is finally closed to another, what route is there into the interior life of God? None from the outside. However clever the investigator and however long he works, he is standing outside a door with no handle on his side. Only God’s Spirit knows God’s thoughts. The Spirit is to God as a person’s spirit is to the person: one with God, sharing his inner life. Yet the Spirit is also a distinct person who reveals (v. 10) and teaches (v. 13).

Now we have received not the spirit of the world. The spirit of the world is the mindset and wisdom of fallen humanity, and behind it, perhaps, the evil spirit at work in the disobedient (Ephesians 2:2). It is the whole outlook a person absorbs simply by living here: the instincts about what matters, what success looks like, what is worth fearing, what is faintly ridiculous. It is the air. And it is competent within its own range; it can assess a career, a house, a reputation. It simply has no equipment for the things of God, and never will.

But the Spirit who is from God. Here is the extraordinary sentence. Believers have received the Holy Spirit, the Spirit from God (Romans 8:9). The door was opened from within. God has not merely sent information about himself; he has given the one person who has always been inside, and he has given him to ordinary believers in a quarrelsome congregation in a port city.

That we might understand the things freely given us by God. “Freely given” (charizomai, from the same root as grace) means given by grace: the things graced to us. The Spirit enables us to understand what God has given us in Christ: forgiveness, adoption, glory. And notice the double gift, the heart of the matter. God gives, and then God gives the capacity to know what he has given. Without the second gift the first would sit unrecognised, like a man holding a deed in a language he cannot read.

Why the scholar may see nothing. This explains something every Christian has watched happen. A new believer with no theological education reads a chapter of Paul and comes away genuinely fed, having met God in it. A scholar who has spent a career on the same chapter, and knows far more about it, comes away having met nothing. The difference is not intelligence and it is not diligence. One has the Spirit and the other does not.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have private revelations beyond Scripture. The Spirit helps us understand what God has given and revealed in his word.

If I have the Spirit, why does my Bible reading so often feel dry? Because illumination is not the same as excitement. The Spirit’s work is to make you understand and believe what is there, and he often does it slowly, like rain soaking into soil rather than a flash flood. Dryness can come from tiredness, distraction, unconfessed sin, or simply a season God uses to teach you to keep going by faith. Keep reading, ask him before you open the page, read slowly enough to notice what it actually says, and talk to him about it as you go (Psalm 119:18). Many believers find that a passage which seemed dull on Tuesday is the one that holds them up on Friday.

In a sentence. For who knows a person’s thoughts except their own spirit within them? In the same way no one knows the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God. What we have received is not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may understand what God has freely given us.

On a Tuesday. If you feel disqualified from Scripture, because you were never taught, you find the Bible hard, and you assume real understanding belongs to people with training, hear this. Training helps and is worth having, and God gives teachers to his church for a reason. But the decisive qualification is not education. The Spirit who lives in the depths of God lives in you, and he is entirely capable of showing an ordinary person what he has freely given. Ask him before you read. That is not a pious formality; it is the exact application of this verse (Psalm 119:18; John 16:13–15).

For worship. The God whom no one could reach from outside has come to live inside his people. He did not send us a report; he sent himself. The Spirit who has known the Father’s heart from all eternity now dwells in clay jars in ordinary streets, opening the gifts of grace and teaching us to say Abba, Father. Thank God for the gift of his Spirit, who lets you know God’s heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.

And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit. The claim has moved a step further than most readers notice. Paul is no longer saying merely that the Spirit gave him the message; he is saying the Spirit was involved in the wording. Not only the thoughts but the words of the apostolic message are taught by the Spirit. This is a key text for verbal inspiration: the Spirit guided the apostles’ very words (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21).

Why the words matter. That is a considerable claim, and it is the foundation of what the church has meant by inspiration. Not that God gave the apostles a general impression which they then dressed in whatever language came to hand, but that the Spirit superintended the expression as well as the substance. It is why Scripture can be studied at the level of a single word, and why translators labour over particles and tenses that would not matter in an ordinary document. If the ideas alone were inspired, the words would be packaging. Paul says the words were taught.

Real men, God’s words. This must not be pressed into a claim that the human authors were suppressed. They plainly were not. Paul’s Greek does not read like Luke’s; John writes with a vocabulary a child could follow; and this same letter contains its author failing to remember whom he baptised (1:16). The Spirit used real men, with their own styles and limitations, and the result is exactly what he intended to say. Both halves must be held, and dropping either produces a doctrine the Bible itself contradicts.

Interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual. The last clause is genuinely difficult, and honesty requires saying so. The Greek is compressed (pneumatikois pneumatika synkrinontes): literally, combining spiritual things with spiritual. It may mean explaining spiritual truths to spiritual people (the ESV text), comparing spiritual things with spiritual things, or expressing spiritual truths in spiritual words. The ESV notes these alternatives, and good commentators land differently. What is not in doubt is the direction of Paul’s argument: the Spirit’s truths are conveyed in the Spirit’s words and received by the Spirit’s people. There is no point in the chain at which unaided human capacity is sufficient.

Scripture interprets Scripture. The second rendering describes something Christians do constantly, whether or not it is what Paul meant here. An obscure verse is read in the light of a clear one; a difficult passage is checked against the whole (Westminster 1.9). That is why the Bible is its own best commentary, and why the person who has read all of it will understand any part of it better than the person who knows three favourite chapters very well.

Where Christians differ: inspiration. Some say the Bible contains God’s word but that its words are merely human, and may contain errors. Verdict: Paul says the words, not only the ideas, were taught by the Spirit. Scripture is God-breathed in all its parts, without error in all it affirms, while using the personalities and styles of its human authors (Westminster 1.4–5, 8). The Spirit did not dictate mechanically, but guided the writers so that what they wrote was exactly what God intended.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the human authors were passive, or that every Christian’s words are inspired as the apostles’ were. This was a unique gift for giving Scripture.

If the very words are inspired, which translation is the real Bible? Inspiration belongs strictly to the words as the prophets and apostles first wrote them in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. But God has preserved those words with remarkable care, and a faithful translation into your language is truly the word of God to you, because it carries what God said (Westminster 1.8). The differences between good modern translations are mostly about style and readability, not doctrine. So read a reliable translation with full confidence, compare another when a verse puzzles you, and leave the arguments about manuscripts to those trained for them, knowing that no doctrine of the faith hangs on a disputed reading.

In a sentence. This is what we speak, not in words taught us by human wisdom but in words taught by the Spirit, explaining spiritual realities with Spirit-taught words.

On a Tuesday. Treat the words of Scripture with care; every one was taught by the Spirit. If the words were taught, the actual wording rewards attention in a way no other book’s does. Slow down. Notice the tense, the conjunction, the little word but. Much of what people call deep Bible study is simply the willingness to read what is on the page rather than the summary of it we carry in our heads (2 Timothy 3:16; 2 Peter 1:21).

For worship. God has not left his church to guess at his meaning. The Spirit who searches the depths of God bent down to teach fishermen and a former Pharisee the very words to write, so that a farmer in any century could hold God’s speech in his hands. Every word of it is breathed out by him, every line of it true, and all of it bears witness to the Son. What a gift, and what a God, who speaks.

verseByVerse.quote: The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.

The natural person. Here is the verse that explains the whole chapter, and it is one of the hardest sayings in Paul. The natural person (psychikos anthrōpos, soulish, living only by natural human life) is the human being as he comes into the world, equipped with everything natural birth supplies and nothing more: someone without the Spirit. Not a wicked person particularly, and not a crude or unintelligent one; he can be a brilliant philosopher. The issue is not intellect but spiritual life.

Does not accept the things of the Spirit of God. Paul says two different things about him. First, he does not accept (dechomai): he does not welcome these things, he will not have them. He may understand the words, but he does not welcome the truth.

For they are folly to him. The same word as 1:18. To him the gospel seems foolish.

And he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned. Second, he is not able (ou dynatai): a lack of ability, not just of willingness. Unwilling and unable, and the second is the more uncomfortable claim. “Discerned” (anakrinō) means examined, judged: spiritual truths can only be evaluated rightly with the Spirit’s help. The natural person needs new birth (John 3:3).

Stating it carefully. It is easily caricatured. Paul is not saying that unbelievers cannot follow the words, or that they are less intelligent, or that an atheist cannot give an accurate account of Christian doctrine; many can do it better than most churchgoers. He is saying that such a person cannot receive these things as true and desirable, cannot see them for what they are, because they are spiritually discerned and he has no organ for that discernment. It is like describing a colour to a man born blind; the failure is not in his reasoning, and a better explanation will not help. The damage of sin is not only to the will, so that we will not come; it reaches the understanding, so that we do not see anything worth coming for. And the root is moral rather than intellectual: the cross looks foolish to a man not because he has thought hard and found a flaw, but because he is estranged from the God it reveals.

Where Christians differ: total inability. Some teach that unbelievers have the natural ability to receive the gospel if they choose to, and God’s grace only assists them. Verdict: Paul says the natural person is not able to understand the things of the Spirit. Sin has darkened the mind and enslaved the will (Ephesians 4:18; Romans 8:7). This is total inability: not that unbelievers are as bad as they can be, but that they cannot turn to God by their own power. Only the Spirit, by regeneration, opens the heart (Acts 16:14; Westminster 9.3; 10.2).

Then why say anything to anybody? This verse always raises the question, and it deserves a straight answer. If my brother-in-law cannot receive it, what am I doing at Christmas dinner? The answer is that God has appointed the message as the very instrument by which he gives the capacity. He does not wait for people to become able and then send a preacher; he sends the preacher and makes them able. Luke records it in one line about a businesswoman at Philippi: Paul spoke, and the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said (Acts 16:14). Two things happened, and only one of them was Paul’s. Ezekiel is the picture. Told to preach to a valley of dry bones, the least promising congregation in Scripture, he is not asked whether they are capable of responding. He is told to prophesy, and while he is prophesying the bones come together (Ezekiel 37). The preacher’s job was never to produce life. It was to speak, while God produced it.

The weight comes off your shoulders. So this verse, far from discouraging evangelism, is the reason it is bearable. It takes the outcome off your shoulders. It explains why your best arguments have not worked and why your relative is not persuaded by evidence he cannot fault: not because you argued badly, but because argument was never the missing ingredient. And it tells you what to do instead: keep speaking, and pray for the one thing you cannot supply.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should not reason with unbelievers or present evidence. Paul did. But we must pray, because only the Spirit can open their eyes.

If unbelievers cannot understand, how can God hold them responsible? Because their inability is not like a missing limb; it is the inability of a heart that does not want God. A man who hates his brother so much that he cannot bring himself to forgive him is not excused by his cannot; the cannot is the guilt. So with the natural person: he cannot receive the things of God because he loves darkness rather than light (John 3:19–20; Romans 1:18–21). No one will stand before God and say he wanted Christ but was not allowed. Everyone who wants him may come, and is welcome (John 6:37). The wonder is not that some are lost but that any are saved.

In a sentence. The person without the Spirit does not accept the things that come from the Spirit of God but considers them foolishness, and cannot understand them because they are discerned only through the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Take the person you have been trying to convince for years. Stop preparing the better argument, and start asking God to open their eyes, by name, specifically and often. Keep speaking when the door opens, kindly and clearly. But you have been attempting the one part of the job that was never yours, and neglecting the part that was (2 Corinthians 4:4–6; John 3:3).

For worship. If you see the glory of Christ today, it is because God shone in your heart, as he once said let there be light over the dark waters (2 Corinthians 4:6). You were the natural person once: unwilling, unable, and sure the cross was foolish. He did not wait for you to become able. He spoke, and you lived. The same Spirit is able to open any heart, and the hardest case you know is not too hard for him.
verseByVerse.note: The “natural person” is someone without the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The spiritual person judges all things, but is himself to be judged by no one.

The spiritual person. The spiritual person (pneumatikos) is anyone who has the Spirit: every true believer. Not a superior class of Christian, as some Corinthians thought.

Judges all things. “Judges” (anakrinō) means discerns, examines, evaluates: the same word as verse 14. With the Spirit, a believer can evaluate everything rightly in the light of God’s truth, including the world’s wisdom. This is not a claim to omniscience or to being right about everything. A Christian is not guaranteed to be correct about politics or medicine or his own motives. He is given the capacity to see what the world is, what a life is for, and what the cross means, and no amount of natural brilliance supplies that.

But is himself to be judged by no one. The natural person cannot properly evaluate the spiritual person, because he lacks the Spirit. The world cannot rightly judge the Christian’s faith, any more than a blind person can judge colours. It is a statement about who has standing, and the point is not the Christian’s superiority but the world’s incompetence in this particular court.

A sentence often abused. This is among the most misused sentences in the New Testament, and the misuse always runs in the same direction. It has been used by leaders to place themselves beyond accountability, by teachers to dismiss every objection as carnal, and by ordinary Christians who do not wish to be corrected: you are not in a position to assess me; I am spiritual. Used that way it is a trump card that ends every conversation, and it has protected a great deal of harm. The proof that it cannot mean this is in this very letter. Three chapters later Paul pronounces judgement on a Corinthian believer’s conduct (5:3), tells the congregation flatly that it is their business to judge those inside the church (5:12), and asks whether there is no one among them wise enough to settle a dispute between brothers (6:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are infallible, or above correction or church discipline. Paul himself corrects the Corinthians throughout, and tells them to judge one another’s prophecies (14:29) and to discipline sin (5:12). It means unbelievers are not qualified to judge spiritual truth.

When your family thinks you have thrown your life away. Here the verse genuinely helps. There are Christians whose families think they have wasted themselves: the son who turned down the career for the mission field, the woman whose relatives regard her faith as a phase she should have outgrown, the man whose colleagues have quietly filed him under harmless and rather sad. The verdict is delivered constantly, sometimes kindly, and it lands. Paul’s word is that the verdict is being handed down by people who, on this subject, are not competent to reach one. That is not arrogance. They are assessing a spiritual matter with equipment that does not extend to it, and their conclusion tells you about their instruments rather than about you.

Does “judges all things” mean Christians should have a strong opinion on everything? No. The spiritual person discerns the things of God: what is true about God, sin, Christ and the life that pleases him. On the many questions Scripture does not settle, the best car, the right investment, much of politics and science, a Christian may be no wiser than his neighbour, and should say so humbly. Spiritual discernment shows itself less in having opinions than in seeing ordinary things in God’s light: recognising an idol in a good thing, noticing pride in your own heart, hearing the gospel distorted. It grows by soaking in Scripture (Hebrews 5:14), not by speaking first.

In a sentence. The person with the Spirit makes judgements about all things, but such a person is not subject to merely human judgements.

On a Tuesday. Do not be shaken when the world mocks your faith; it cannot see what you see. But hold that alongside the guard, because the two must travel together. The world’s opinion of your faith is not the final word. Your brother’s opinion of your behaviour very often is, and a Christian who uses this verse to deflect correction from other believers has turned a sentence about the world’s incompetence against the very people God gave him for the purpose. When you last reached for the idea that people do not understand you, was your critic outside the faith, or a Christian who loves you and had noticed something true?

For worship. The Spirit has given ordinary believers eyes the wisest of this world do not have. A child who trusts Christ sees more of what is real than a philosopher who does not. And the one who sees most clearly of all, who judges all things perfectly and is judged by no one, is the Lord Jesus himself, who was judged by the world’s courts and condemned, so that we might stand uncondemned in his.

verseByVerse.quote: “For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

For who has understood the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him? Paul closes the argument with a question from Isaiah and an answer that ought to be impossible. The quotation is Isaiah 40:13 (also Romans 11:34), and its setting matters. Isaiah is at his most soaring, describing a God who measures the waters in the hollow of his hand and weighs the mountains in scales, before whom the nations are a drop from a bucket and dust on the balance. Into that he drops the question: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? The expected answer is nobody, ever. No human can know God’s mind by his own wisdom, much less teach him.

But we have the mind of Christ. Paul quotes it, lets it do its work, and then writes this. It is a breathtaking claim, one of the boldest sentences he ever wrote, and it should not be softened. In Isaiah, the mind of the Lord is the mind of Yahweh; Paul equates it with the mind of Christ. We cannot reach God’s mind ourselves, but we have Christ’s mind given to us by the Spirit: his way of thinking, revealed in the apostolic gospel. “We” is first the apostles, then all believers who receive their teaching. The whole chapter has argued that God’s thoughts are unreachable from below. What Paul claims is that the unreachable has been given.

What it looks like. This is a real participation, not a figure of speech, and it has a shape you can recognise. To have the mind of Christ is to begin valuing what he values and to find yourself unimpressed by what impressed you before. It is to look at a difficult person and see someone he died for. It is to hear about a decision at work and instinctively ask what would be honest rather than what would be advantageous. It is to feel the pull of the poor, the awkward and the unimportant in a way that has no natural explanation. None of that is achieved by effort alone; it grows, because someone else’s mind has been given to you.

The mind of Christ is a servant’s mind. The phrase gets used to end arguments, so it is worth saying what it is not. Having the mind of Christ does not mean your convictions are automatically his, and it is not a claim to be exercised against other Christians. Paul elsewhere describes the mind of Christ at length, and what he describes is not a set of superior opinions but a disposition: he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:5–8). A man who says he has the mind of Christ and is chiefly using it to win is describing something other than what Paul means.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know everything Christ knows, or that we can never be wrong. It means we share his outlook through his word and Spirit, and grow into it (Philippians 2:5; Romans 12:2).

How do I grow in the mind of Christ? By keeping company with him where he speaks. Read the Gospels and watch how he thinks: whom he notices, what angers him, what he refuses, how he prays. Let Scripture correct your instincts, especially where it surprises you, and ask the Spirit to renew your mind (Romans 12:2). Then practise it in small things: choose the lower place, forgive quickly, speak the truth kindly, serve someone who cannot repay you. Spend time with mature Christians in whom you can see it. Growth is slow, and you will often notice it only looking back, but it is sure, because the one who gave you his mind is at work to form it in you.

In a sentence. For, “Who has known the mind of the Lord so as to instruct him?” But we have the mind of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Take one decision in front of you this week, at work, at home, with money or with a difficult person. Before you settle it, ask what Christ, who emptied himself for others, would value here. Then do that, even if it costs you something.

For worship. So the chapter ends where it began, and the distance travelled is enormous. It opened with a frightened man arriving in a hostile city, shaking, refusing to be impressive, determined to talk about nothing but an execution. It ends by claiming that such people, not the philosophers, not the rulers of this age, not the mature of Corinth’s own estimation, have been given access to the mind of God. Nobody has instructed him. Nobody has advised him, or improved his plan, or contributed a single thought he did not already hold. He measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and he decreed before the ages a wisdom hidden from every ruler and power. And then he came, and was not recognised, and was crucified by the men he was dying for. And he has given his own mind to a church at Corinth that could not stop arguing about which preacher it preferred. That is what he is like (Romans 11:33–36).

parallels.desc: who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?
