3.title: God’s Field, God’s Building, God’s Temple
3.overview:
The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual and wise. Paul tells them bluntly that their quarrelling over leaders shows they are still spiritual infants, behaving like ordinary unconverted people. Their leaders are only servants. Using a farming picture, Paul says he planted and Apollos watered, but God made things grow, so the workers are nothing and God is everything. Then a building picture: Paul laid the only possible foundation, Jesus Christ, and others build on it. On the day of judgement, fire will test the quality of each builder’s work; good work will be rewarded, and poor work will burn up, though the builder himself will be saved, as if escaping through flames.

Then a warning: the church is God’s temple, where his Spirit lives, and anyone who destroys it will be destroyed by God. Paul ends where chapter 1 began, with the folly of the world’s wisdom. No one should boast about human leaders, because everything already belongs to believers, Paul, Apollos, Peter, the world, life, death, the present and the future, and they belong to Christ, and Christ to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul could not speak to them as spiritually mature people, but only as people still ruled by the flesh, infants in Christ. He gave them milk rather than solid food, because they were not ready, and they still are not. Their jealousy and quarrels prove it: they are behaving like ordinary people, saying “I follow Paul” or “I follow Apollos”. But Paul and Apollos are only servants through whom they believed, each doing the job the Lord assigned. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth, so the planter and the waterer are nothing; only God, who makes things grow, matters. The workers have one purpose, and each will be rewarded for his own work. They are God’s fellow workers; the church is God’s field and God’s building.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of God in Ministry

The repeated insistence that God gives the growth is not a platitude; it is the Reformed doctrine of sovereign grace applied to the fruit of ministry. Paul preached; Apollos taught; but neither of them converted a single soul. Conversion is the work of God, not the achievement of the preacher. This means that the minister cannot take credit for results, cannot despair over apparent fruitlessness as if it were his own failure, and cannot be compared with another minister as if their different “results” reflected their different competencies. God gives where and when he wills.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian factions were measuring Paul and Apollos by their outputs — converts, rhetorical impact, visible results. Paul refuses this measuring rod: the results belong to God, not to the apostle. Now: The contemporary church is still tempted to evaluate ministry by attendance, conversion numbers, and cultural impact — and to attribute these to the skill and gifting of the human leader. Paul’s corrective: plant faithfully, water patiently, and trust the God of growth.

verseByVerse.quote: But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 3 applies chapters 1–2 to the Corinthians’ divisions. First, their quarrelling proves they are still spiritually immature, acting like mere humans, not people of the Spirit (vv. 1–4). Second, Paul and Apollos are only servants. One planted, one watered, but God gave the growth. The church is God’s field and God’s building (vv. 5–9). Third, Paul laid the only foundation, Jesus Christ; everyone who builds on it must take care, for the Day will test each one’s work by fire. Good work will be rewarded; worthless work will burn, though the builder himself is saved (vv. 10–15). Fourth, the church is God’s holy temple, where his Spirit dwells; whoever destroys it, God will destroy (vv. 16–17). Finally, do not boast in human leaders. All things are yours, Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present and future, because you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (vv. 18–23). The chapter opens by calling them infants and ends by telling them they own the universe, and the hinge between the two is not their growth but whose they are.

But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people. Paul had spent eighteen months at Corinth. He is writing perhaps three or four years later, and the verdict is devastating in its plainness. The Corinthians thought of themselves as spiritual (pneumatikoi), wise and mature; that was the whole basis of their confidence. They had the gifts, the knowledge, the eloquence, the tongues. Paul takes the label off them in his first sentence: you were not acting like it.

But as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ. “Of the flesh” (sarkinos) means made of flesh. Here it describes believers who are still governed too much by the old ways of thinking. “Infants” (nēpioi, babies) in Christ: they are in Christ, truly believers, but immature.

I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. Milk is the basic truths of the gospel; solid food is deeper teaching and application (Hebrews 5:12–14). When Paul first came, they were new believers and could only take milk. That was normal. But notice what milk is not. It is not a different or lesser gospel, a simplified version for beginners while the mature graduate to something else. It is the same food in a form an infant can take. The Christian who moves on from the cross has not advanced; he has wandered off.

And even now you are not yet ready. What makes the diagnosis sting is the tense. Not merely that they were immature when he arrived, since everybody is, but that years have passed and nothing has changed. That is what is not normal. An infant is delightful. A man who has been an infant for four years is a tragedy.

How would you know? This applies to a great many long-standing churchgoers. You cannot see your own growth directly, and the people most confident of their maturity are, in this chapter, precisely the ones who do not have it. Paul is about to give the measurement in the next verse, and it is not the one anybody expects. But notice already that it is not knowledge. The Corinthians knew a great deal; Paul has conceded they are enriched in all speech and all knowledge (1:5), and it has not made them adults. It is entirely possible to accumulate information about God for thirty years and remain a spiritual toddler, because facts are the easiest thing in the Christian life to acquire and the least reliable indicator of anything.

Where Christians differ: the carnal Christian. Some teach that there are two kinds of Christians: spiritual Christians, who have surrendered to Christ as Lord, and carnal Christians, who have accepted Christ as Saviour but live permanently as if unconverted. Verdict: Paul is rebuking immaturity in true believers, not describing a permanent, acceptable category of Christian. The Corinthians were in Christ, and some still behaved in fleshly ways, which Paul calls them to leave behind. The real contrast in these chapters is between the natural person, who does not have the Spirit at all (2:14), and the believer who has the Spirit and is not yet living like it. All true believers have the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and are being changed (2 Corinthians 3:18), though at different speeds. A profession of faith that never produces any change is not saving faith (James 2:17; 1 John 3:9–10; Galatians 5:19–21). Christ is received as both Saviour and Lord.

What it does not mean. It does not mean milk is bad, or that the gospel is only for beginners. The gospel is the food at every stage. Solid food is the same gospel, more deeply understood and applied.

How do I move from milk to solid food? Not chiefly by learning harder doctrines, though that has its place, but by putting into practice what you already know. Hebrews says the mature are those whose powers of discernment have been trained by constant practice (Hebrews 5:14). So read Scripture steadily, not just favourite passages; sit under faithful preaching and ask how it applies to you; obey the thing you were last convicted about; and spend time with older believers whose lives show the fruit. Above all, let the gospel go deeper rather than leaving it behind. Mature Christians do not need the cross less; they see more of it, and it shapes more of them.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul could not address you as people who live by the Spirit but as people who are still worldly, mere infants in Christ. He gave you milk, not solid food, for you were not yet ready for it. Indeed, you are still not ready.

On a Tuesday. Ask honestly: am I growing? Are my reactions and attitudes more like Christ than a year ago? Here is a test that cuts through the self-assessment. Ask what you were like ten years ago in the one area where you are hardest to live with: your temper, your tongue, your resentment of a particular person, your handling of being crossed. Not what you know about it now; what you are actually like. Growth in Christ shows up there or it has not happened, and the person best placed to answer is not you but whoever shares your house. If you are not growing, ask God for growth, and feed on his word (1 Peter 2:2).

For worship. Paul still calls them brothers. He calls them infants, but infants in Christ, and a baby in a father’s arms is no less his child for being unable to walk. God does not disown his children for being slow to grow. He feeds them, patiently, with the same gospel that gave them life, and he has promised that the one who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). His patience with us is the patience of a Father who intends to see his children grown.

verseByVerse.quote: for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?
verseByVerse.commentary:
for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?

For you are still of the flesh. “Of the flesh” here is sarkikos, fleshly: governed by sinful human nature. And here is the measurement, startlingly ordinary.

For while there is jealousy and strife among you. This is the evidence. Two words. Jealousy (zēlos) is the heat of wanting what someone else has, of not being able to be glad about another person’s advantage: envy, rivalry. Strife (eris) is the quarrelling that follows. Paul is not describing exotic wickedness. He is describing the ordinary weather of a church committee. And he treats them with complete seriousness, because in his list of the works of the flesh these two sit alongside idolatry, sorcery and drunkenness (Galatians 5:20). We instinctively grade sins, and jealousy comes low on our list because it is invisible and universal. Paul puts it with sorcery.

The measure they never thought to use. Feel the force of the argument. The Corinthians assessed spiritual maturity by spiritual phenomena: who could speak in tongues, who had the deeper knowledge, whose teacher was most impressive. Paul assesses it by whether they can get on with each other. Everything they were counting is set aside, and the one thing they had never thought to measure is made the whole test. That is not Paul’s invention. It is what Jesus said would identify his disciples to a watching world: not their doctrine or their gifts, but their love for one another (John 13:35). And it is what the most famous chapter of this letter will say: gifts without love are noise (13:1–3).

Are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way? Literally, walking according to man. It is the deadliest phrase in the verse. They are behaving just like unbelievers, like the competitive culture of Corinth around them. The church was running on ordinary human operating principles: rank, rivalry, the instinct to be associated with the winning side. Nothing was happening in that congregation that could not be equally observed in a trade guild or a political faction. Fan clubs and rivalries are normal in the world; they should not be normal in the church. The Spirit had been given to them, and you could not tell from the outside.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sexual sins are fleshly. Paul’s first example of fleshliness is quarrelling and jealousy in church. Respectable sins are still sins of the flesh.

Is every disagreement in church fleshly? No. Christians can disagree honestly about real questions, and Paul himself argues hard in this letter. What makes a disagreement fleshly is the spirit of it: envy, the need to win, taking sides around personalities, contempt for the other person, refusing to listen, spreading the quarrel to others. You can test yourself by asking whether you could pray warmly for the person you disagree with, and whether you would be glad if God blessed him. A disagreement held in love, aimed at the truth and the good of the church, is not strife. A disagreement that has become about me is.

In a sentence. You are still worldly. For since there is jealousy and quarrelling among you, are you not worldly? Are you not acting like mere humans?

On a Tuesday. Think of the person in your church whose success you find hardest to be glad about: whose gift is the one you wish you had, whose praise you find yourself qualifying, whose name you are slightly relieved to hear criticised. You have just located the exact point at which, on Paul’s measurement, you are still an infant. That is not said to condemn. It is said because the Corinthians did not know, and would have gone on not knowing, and a diagnosis is the first mercy. Confess the jealousy to God by name, and then pray for that person’s good today (James 3:14–16).

For worship. The gifts told the Corinthians nothing; the jealousy told them everything. And the God who exposes our envy is the God who has none: the Father who gave his only Son, the Son who did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, the Spirit who delights to glorify another. There is no rivalry in heaven, only self-giving love, and that same Spirit has been given to us to replace our envy with his love.

verseByVerse.quote: For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human? What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.

For when one says, “I follow Paul”, and another, “I follow Apollos”, are you not being merely human? Paul names only himself and Apollos now, perhaps because they were the two who had worked in Corinth, or to avoid naming Peter. He repeats the charge from the previous verse and attaches it to the slogans. The tragedy of a personality faction is that it is so completely unremarkable. Every institution on earth divides this way. A church doing it is not displaying a distinctive failing; it is failing to display anything distinctive at all.

What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Notice what, not who. Paul asks what their function is, not their personal importance. Asking what a person is rather than who he is reduces him, deliberately, to a function. Paul is refusing to be a personality.

Servants through whom you believed. His answer is one word: diakonoi. Servants. It is the ordinary word for household servants, for someone who waits at table: the person who brings the food and is not the reason anyone came. Nobody leaves a dinner party discussing the waiter, and the Corinthians have organised their church around a debate about waiters. And “through whom” is instrumental. They were instruments, not sources. You believed in Christ, through them. You do not thank the pipe for the water.

As the Lord assigned to each. Each servant was given his task by the Lord. Even the differences between them, the very differences the Corinthians are quarrelling over, were handed out by the Lord. Apollos’s eloquence is not Apollos’s achievement; it was assigned. That quietly removes the ground from both factions at once. If Apollos is more polished than Paul, that is not a reason to prefer Apollos; it is a fact about what God gave Apollos. If Paul founded the church, that is not a reason to prefer Paul; it is a fact about what God assigned Paul to do. You cannot build a hierarchy out of gifts that were distributed rather than earned. Paul’s gifts and Apollos’s gifts were both from Christ. No reason for rivalry.

Comparison is an argument with God. This reaches into ordinary Christian life, because most readers do not run a faction but nearly all of us make the comparison. You listen to a gifted preacher and come away either diminished or quietly competitive. You watch someone else’s ministry flourish while yours does not. You measure your church against the one down the road. Paul’s cure is not to try harder at humility. It is to remember the word assigned. What another Christian has was given to him, which means envying it is a complaint about the distribution rather than about the person, and the distributor is the Lord. Comparison, followed all the way down, always turns out to be an argument with God about what he decided to hand out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers deserve no honour. Elders who labour in preaching and teaching are worthy of double honour (1 Timothy 5:17). But they are servants, not masters.

What if I really do benefit more from one preacher than another? That is natural and not sinful. God gives different gifts, and some will help you more than others; Paul himself speaks warmly of particular co-workers. Receive the help gratefully. The danger comes when preference turns into partisanship: when you belittle the other preacher, stay away when your favourite is not speaking, or treat your liking as a measure of spirituality. Thank God for the servant who feeds you best, and be equally willing to be fed by the one who does not suit your taste, because both are bringing food from the same Master’s kitchen.

In a sentence. For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not mere human beings? What, after all, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Only servants, through whom you came to believe, as the Lord has assigned to each his task.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your pastor, and pray for him; but do not put him on a pedestal. He is a servant, as you are. And when you last felt the sting of someone else’s gift, did it occur to you that God gave it to him on purpose, for the good of a church you belong to? A servant does not resent another servant’s tray. Both trays are going to the same table (Romans 12:6; 1 Peter 4:10).

For worship. There is only one Lord in the house, and every servant in it was hired and equipped by him. The greatest of them all was the Lord himself, who came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He took the towel and washed his disciples’ feet. When we stop arguing about the waiters, we see at the head of the table the Master who first waited on us.

verseByVerse.quote: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.

I planted. Paul founded the church in Corinth: he first brought the gospel there (Acts 18:1–11).

Apollos watered. Apollos came later and built up the young church with his teaching (Acts 18:27–19:1).

But God gave the growth. Three verbs, and the first two are ordinary work while the third is a miracle nobody can perform. The tense is different too. Planted and watered are past, completed actions; gave the growth is imperfect: God was continually causing growth. Paul and Apollos did their parts at certain times; God was doing the real work all along.

What no farmer can do. The image is exact and worth staying with. A farmer can do a great deal. He can prepare the ground, choose the seed, get the depth right, water at the correct intervals, keep the weeds down, watch the weather. Every one of those requires skill, and a lazy farmer produces a poor crop. But no farmer in the history of the world has ever made a seed germinate. He creates conditions. Life is not among the things he supplies. That is the exact shape of Christian ministry. Preaching, teaching, hospitality, patient friendship, years of prayer: all real, all demanding, all worth doing well. Not one of them can produce spiritual life in another human being. The most gifted preacher alive stands in exactly the same relation to a hard heart as a farmer to a seed.

So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth. The conclusion is more severe than we usually let it be. Literally, neither of them is anything at all. Not less important than God, not secondary. Nothing. Compared to God, the workers are nothing. No gardener makes a seed grow; only God gives life. Paul has just described his own life’s work and given it the value zero in the column that matters. He does not mean the work was pointless; the next verse says each will receive wages. He means it contributed nothing to the one thing that had to happen. And he says it in a church choosing sides between two men, because if both men are nothing, the argument is over.

For those who have prayed for years. This is the verse for the parent whose adult child has walked away, the wife whose husband has heard it all and remains politely unmoved, the person who has explained, invited, modelled, wept, and watched nothing happen, and who has begun to suspect that the failure is theirs. Read the verse again. You were never able to give the growth. It is not that you have fallen short of a standard other people meet; it is that the thing you long for has never once been within the power of any human being, including the apostle Paul. That does not make your planting and watering worthless. God ordinarily uses exactly such means, and your years of faithfulness are the seed and the water. It removes a burden you were never given and could not carry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean human work is unnecessary. God uses planting and watering. Without them there is no harvest. But the result belongs to God.

If God gives the growth, should a church bother to plan, train and evaluate? Yes. Farmers who trust God for the harvest still plough straight furrows. Paul planned his journeys, trained co-workers and thought hard about how to reach people (9:19–23). Careful planning, good teaching and honest review of what you are doing are part of faithful planting and watering. What the verse rules out is thinking that the right method guarantees results, measuring faithfulness by numbers, or taking credit when things grow. Plan carefully, work hard, and pray as people who know that without the Lord nothing will come up at all.

In a sentence. Paul planted the seed, Apollos watered it, but God has been making it grow. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow.

On a Tuesday. Most of us pray for opportunities and then work very hard at the opportunity when it comes. This week, pray instead for the thing only God does. Name the person you long to see grow, or come to faith, and ask God to give the growth. Then go on planting and watering. He has been giving life to unpromising ground since the beginning, and the man writing this verse was, before Damascus, the least likely convert in the ancient world (Ezekiel 36:26; John 15:5).

For worship. If you have seen anyone grow in faith through your efforts, give God the glory. He gave the growth. Every believer you know is a field where the Lord of the harvest has worked a miracle no farmer could perform: a dead heart made alive, a seed of the word sprouting into faith. He is the God who gives life to the dead, and he has never once needed a gardener to be clever before he made the garden grow.

verseByVerse.quote: He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.

He who plants and he who waters are one. Hen eisin: they are one thing. One in purpose and work, on the same team, serving the same Lord, aiming at the same harvest. Not merely allies, not colleagues who have agreed not to compete. The Corinthians made them rivals; they were partners. The factions set Paul against Apollos, and Paul says there is no gap between them for a faction to occupy.

And each will receive his wages according to his labor. Wages (misthos, reward): each worker will be rewarded individually by God. Not according to success, which belongs to God, but according to labour (kopos, toil): faithfulness in hard work, the kind of work that wears you out. The logic of the preceding verses requires this. If God gives the growth, then results cannot be the measure of the servant, because the results were never his to produce. What is his is the labour. That is what will be assessed, and that is what will be paid.

A different column heading. Think how completely this inverts the way ministry is usually judged, then and now. The Corinthians were comparing outputs: who drew the crowd, whose converts, whose impact. Every generation since has done the same with attendance figures, conversion numbers and reach. Paul says the ledger God keeps has a different column heading altogether.

For the faithful who saw little. This is one of the most quietly liberating sentences in the New Testament, and it is addressed to many people. The missionary who gave forty years to a hard field and saw a handful of converts. The Sunday school teacher who taught for three decades and watched most of them drift. The pastor who has led a small congregation faithfully in a village where nothing has ever grown, while a church in the next town filled up. The mother who prayed and taught and did everything she knew, and whose children do not believe. Every one of them has, at some point, done the arithmetic and concluded the life was wasted. This verse says the arithmetic is wrong, not because results do not matter, but because they were never the thing being weighed. The Lord who gives the growth does not charge his servants for the growth he chose not to give.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by labour. Salvation is a gift (Romans 6:23). Paul has already said that Christ became our righteousness (1:30), and he will shortly say that the man whose work burns is saved anyway (v. 15). The New Testament is unembarrassed about reward for faithful service and treats it as a proper motive. What is being paid for is not your entrance; it is your labour. And rewards for faithful service are themselves gracious, God crowning his own gifts.

Will some believers have more in heaven than others, and will that not cause envy? Scripture does speak of differing rewards (Luke 19:17–19; 2 Corinthians 5:10), but it never pictures heaven as a place of rivalry. Every believer will have all of Christ and will be perfectly satisfied, as a small cup and a large cup may both be full. And envy will be impossible, because sin will be gone and love will be perfect: we will rejoice in every other believer’s reward as gladly as in our own, since every reward will be a display of God’s grace. In the vision of Revelation the elders cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Whatever we receive, we will give back to him.

In a sentence. The one who plants and the one who waters have one purpose, and they will each be rewarded according to their own labour.

On a Tuesday. God rewards faithfulness, not visible success. Keep labouring in your quiet corner; he sees. Change the question you ask yourself. Not what have I achieved, which produces pride or despair depending on the decade, but have I laboured? Have I kept planting and watering in the place I was put, for the years I was given? That question has an answer tonight, and it is the one you will be asked (Matthew 25:21; Galatians 6:9; 1 Corinthians 15:58).

For worship. What a Master we serve. He gives the growth, and then rewards the servants for planting the seeds he made and watering with the rain he sent. He notices the toil nobody else saw and the faithfulness that produced no headlines. And on the last day he will say to servants who did very little, well done, good and faithful servant, enter into the joy of your master, as though the joy were their wages, when it was his gift all along.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are God’s fellow workers. You are God’s field, God’s building.

For we are God’s fellow workers. Three genitives in one short verse: God’s fellow workers, God’s field, God’s building. “God’s” is emphatic in the Greek, three times, hammering a single point by repetition, and the point is ownership. Fellow workers (synergoi) is commonly rendered fellow workers with God, a thrilling idea that has launched a great deal of preaching about partnership with the Almighty. The Greek permits it. But it equally permits, and the context rather demands, fellow workers belonging to God: God’s workmen, labouring alongside each other in a field that is his. The other two phrases are plainly possessive, and the argument since verse 5 has been that the workers are nothing. Paul and Apollos are fellow workers in God’s service, not junior partners. That is not a demotion worth grieving over. The dignity of Christian work has never come from our importance to it. It comes from whose work it is.

You are God’s field. The agricultural picture of verses 6–8. The church belongs to God, not to Paul or Apollos. And this too is aimed at the factions. A field is not divided into plots belonging to different farmers. The Corinthians have been marking out territory in ground that belongs to somebody else.

God’s building. Paul switches pictures to prepare for verses 10–17, and it is not carelessness. A field is organic and forgiving; if a crop fails you plough it in and sow again next season. A building is different. It goes up in a fixed order, every course rests on the one beneath, and what you put in early determines what the whole thing can bear. The church is a building under construction. The stakes have just risen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church belongs to its members or its ministers to run as they please. It is God’s. A church is not a voluntary society belonging to its members, a platform belonging to its minister, or a heritage belonging to the families who have been there longest. The deeds are not in the building.

Then who makes the decisions in a church? Christ does, through his word, and every church structure is a stewardship under him. Christians differ on how that works out: some churches are led by elders with the congregation’s consent, some by a congregational vote, some by a wider presbytery or by bishops, and faithful believers hold each of these views from Scripture. Whatever your church’s order, the principle of this verse applies to all of them: leaders are servants answerable to the owner, members are workmen and not shareholders, and every decision should begin with the question, what does the Lord of this field want? A meeting that forgets that question has forgotten whose meeting it is.

In a sentence. For we are co-workers in God’s service; you are God’s field, God’s building.

On a Tuesday. Most long-standing members have been possessive about a congregation, usually without noticing. Listen to how you talk about it: my church, our chairs, the way we have always done this. Then ask what changes if the field and the building are God’s, and you are one of the workmen. A workman does not get a vote on the design. He gets the considerable honour of being trusted with somebody else’s property. Pray for your church’s growth, and do your part in it (Ephesians 2:20–22; 1 Peter 2:5).

For worship. Your church is God’s field and God’s building. He bought the ground with his Son’s blood, he sows it with his word, he waters it by his Spirit, and he is building it, stone by living stone, into a dwelling place for himself. Every ordinary congregation, however small, is a piece of his property, and he has never yet abandoned a field he planted.

parallels.desc: the planting of the LORD

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: By God’s grace, Paul laid the foundation like a skilled master builder, and others are building on it. Everyone must be careful how they build, because no other foundation can be laid than the one already there, Jesus Christ. On that foundation people build with gold, silver and precious stones, or with wood, hay and straw. The day of judgement will expose each person’s work, because it will be revealed with fire, which will test its quality. If the work survives, the builder will be rewarded; if it burns up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as one escaping through fire. Paul then warns that the church is God’s temple, in which God’s Spirit lives. If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person, because God’s temple is holy, and they are that temple.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church as the New Temple

Paul’s identification of the church as God’s temple carries enormous theological weight in a letter written to a city famous for its pagan temples. The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the temple of Aphrodite; the city was saturated with temple culture, sexual licence, and temple feasts. Paul’s claim is that the living God has abandoned temples made of stone and taken up residence in a community of people — flawed, fractious, sin-prone people — through his Spirit. The church is not a building where God may be found; the church is the people in whom God actually dwells. This is the new covenant fulfilment of every OT temple theology: God with his people, no longer mediated through architecture and ritual, but through the Spirit given to all who belong to Christ.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The divisions at Corinth were not merely social dysfunction; they were a theological emergency. A fragmented community cannot be a temple — the architectural metaphor itself requires unity, all the stones fitting together. The faction wars were, quite literally, demolition work on the place where God had chosen to live. Now: Every church split, every faction, every deliberate destruction of community is an assault on the dwelling of the Holy Spirit. This gives a theological gravity to church unity that mere social concern cannot supply: we are not trying to be nice; we are protecting the home of God.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
According to the grace of God given to me, like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation, and someone else is building upon it. Let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ.

According to the grace of God given to me. Paul’s apostleship and skill were gifts of grace (15:10). Look at how he introduces his competence. He does not say he was skilled and therefore chosen, nor pretend to a modesty he does not feel. He states the skill and assigns its origin in the same breath, which is the only way a Christian can ever speak accurately about his own gifts.

Like a skilled master builder I laid a foundation. “Master builder” (architektōn, from which architect) is the chief builder who oversees the project, responsible for the whole design, who lays out the foundation and hands the site on to others. It is the only time the word appears in the New Testament. “Skilled” (sophos, wise) is the true wisdom, unlike the Corinthians’ worldly wisdom.

And someone else is building upon it. Apollos, and other teachers since. Every generation of teachers builds on the foundation.

Let each one take care how he builds upon it. This warning governs everything to the end of the chapter. It is addressed first to teachers and leaders: be careful what you build with; the quality of your teaching and ministry matters. And notice it is not whether but how. Everyone in a church is building something, whether or not he has noticed. The question is how, and Paul is about to say the answer will be exposed by fire.

For no one can lay a foundation other than that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. The foundation is not open for discussion. Christ crucified, as preached by the apostles, is the only foundation (Isaiah 28:16; Ephesians 2:20). No one may lay a different one. A church built on any other foundation is not a church of God. Note the passive: which is laid. Even Paul did not choose it. He laid it in the sense that a builder lays what the architect has specified; the specification came from elsewhere.

How foundations shift. It is worth being exact about what this rules out, because churches rarely announce a change of foundation. They shift by degrees, and the shift is always onto something good. A congregation can come to rest on its history: the families, the building, the way things have always been done. On a personality, which is the Corinthian version. On a cause, however worthy. On an experience, so that the question becomes whether people felt something. On a doctrinal system, held so tightly that Christ himself becomes a topic within it rather than the one it rests on. Every one of those can coexist with an impeccable statement of faith, and every one of them is a different building.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Paul himself is the foundation. Christ is. Paul laid it by preaching Christ.

What should I look for in a church? First, the foundation: is Jesus Christ, crucified and risen, clearly at the centre of what is preached, sung and prayed, and is the Bible taught faithfully as God’s word? Then the building: is the gospel shaping how people live and love one another, are baptism and the Lord’s Supper observed, is there loving care and discipline, are the leaders godly and accountable? Style, size, music and programmes come far lower. No church is perfect, and if you wait for one you will never join one. Look for one built on Christ and trying, imperfectly, to build well, and then commit yourself to it.

In a sentence. By the grace God has given him, Paul laid a foundation as a wise builder, and someone else is building on it. But each one should build with care. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Whatever you build, a family, a ministry, a life, build it on Christ; nothing else will stand. And ask what would have to be removed before your church noticed something essential had gone. If the minister left, the music changed, the building were sold, would the church still be there? And if the person and work of Jesus Christ were quietly no longer at the centre, how long would it take anyone to notice (Matthew 7:24–27)?

For worship. A congregation can survive the loss of almost anything except one thing. That one thing was laid before any of us arrived, by an Architect who did not consult us, and it is the only surface in the universe able to take the weight of what is being built on it. Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16). Christ is that stone: rejected by the builders, chosen by God, and precious to everyone who believes.

parallels.desc: a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw— each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw—each one’s work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done.

Now if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, straw. Six materials, in two groups of three. Gold, silver and precious stones were what David gathered for the house of God (1 Chronicles 29:2): durable and precious. Wood, hay and straw were the stuff of ordinary huts: cheap and flammable. The first group is what you use when you are building a house for God; the second is what you use when you are throwing something up quickly. The materials stand for the quality of a teacher’s work: sound teaching and faithful ministry, or shallow, worldly ministry. And the difference that matters is not cost or beauty. It is behaviour under fire. Gold, silver and stone come through a blaze; wood, hay and straw do not merely char, they vanish.

Each one’s work will become manifest. Now it may be hard to tell the difference. On the Day, it will be obvious: made visible, brought into the open.

For the Day will disclose it. The definite article, and no further explanation needed. The Day is the day of the Lord, Christ’s return and judgement (1:8; 4:5).

Because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up. Fire here is a picture of God’s searching judgement (Malachi 3:2–3; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–8). It tests the work, not the person’s salvation. And note the phrase what sort, because it settles what is being examined. Not how much work: the fire is not weighing output. Quality, not quantity; kind, not scale.

What makes a work gold? Paul does not give a list, and we should be careful about inventing one. But the letter itself supplies the direction. Work genuinely built on the foundation: Christ crucified, not merely mentioned but load-bearing. Work done in dependence on the Spirit rather than on technique. Work aimed at people’s good rather than at the builder’s standing, which is the very thing that has gone wrong at Corinth. And work done in love, since gifts exercised without it are nothing (13:1–3).

Gold and straw look alike now. The distinction is very largely invisible in this life, and that is the point of the fire. Straw and gold look much alike at ground level, and a straw building can be considerably more impressive than a gold one if it is bigger. Two ministries can produce identical statistics, buildings and reputations, and be made of entirely different substances. Nothing available to us reliably tells them apart. The fire will. So the sobering thought is not that a Christian might be found to have done too little. It is that he might be found to have done a great deal of the wrong kind: a life of visible activity, admired at the time, that turns out to have been made of hay.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only full-time ministers will be judged. Paul speaks first of teachers in the church, but the principle applies to every believer’s service.

Will my sins be exposed in front of everyone on that Day? What this passage says will be revealed is your work, so that it can be rewarded or lost. Your sins, if you are in Christ, have already been judged at the cross; there is no condemnation left for you (Romans 8:1), and God has cast them behind his back (Isaiah 38:17; Micah 7:19). Scripture does say that all will give account and that hidden things will be brought to light (4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:10), so believers should live seriously. But whatever is shown of a believer on that Day will be shown as a sinner fully forgiven, and the point of it will be the glory of the grace that saved him, not his shame.

In a sentence. If anyone builds on this foundation using gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay or straw, their work will be shown for what it is, because the Day will bring it to light. It will be revealed with fire, and the fire will test the quality of each person’s work.

On a Tuesday. Take anything you are doing for God this week and ask what would happen to it if nobody ever knew you had done it. Take away the credit, the recognition, being seen as the sort of person who does such things. Would you still do it, and would you do it as carefully? Fire settles questions of motive that introspection never quite manages, and the honest answer is a fair preview (Matthew 6:1–4; 1 Corinthians 4:5). Ask God to help you build with gold: faithful truth, sincere love, work done for his glory.

For worship. The eyes of the Lord are like a flame of fire (Revelation 1:14), and nothing escapes them. Yet the same Lord who will test every work has already borne the fire of judgement for every builder who stands on him. He is a refiner’s fire for our works and a shelter for our souls. And everything done in his name with love, however small, the cup of cold water, the prayer no one heard, will come through that fire like gold, because he made it, and he keeps what is his.
verseByVerse.note: Fire tests metals; wood and straw burn up.

parallels.desc: like a refiner’s fire

verseByVerse.quote: If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, though he himself will be saved, but only as through fire.

If the work that anyone has built on the foundation survives, he will receive a reward. Two outcomes, and Paul states them without softening either. Faithful work will stand the test and be rewarded (Matthew 25:21).

If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss. Loss of reward: the work is gone, as if a lifetime’s labour went up in smoke.

Though he himself will be saved. The builder is a true believer, built on Christ. His salvation does not depend on the quality of his work but on the foundation. Notice where the sentence lands, because Paul refuses to leave the man in the fire. The clause is unqualified. His life’s work is gone and he is not. Whatever else this verse does, it does not put a single believer’s salvation in question, and it was never meant to be read by an anxious Christian as a threat.

But only as through fire. Like a man escaping a burning house with nothing but his life. He is out, he is alive, he is not going back in, and everything he spent forty years accumulating is behind him in the flames. Saved, but with empty hands.

Where Christians differ: purgatory. The Roman Catholic Church has used this passage to support purgatory, a place of temporal purifying punishment after death for believers before entering heaven. From the medieval period onwards it became a principal text for that doctrine, and the reading is not foolish: there is a fire, there is a Christian, and he passes through it and comes out saved. Verdict: the passage does not teach purgatory. The fire tests works, not people; verse 13 says so twice. What burns is the work; the man is not being purified, he is being rescued from a blaze consuming what he built. It happens on the Day of judgement, not over a period after death; nothing suggests duration, degrees or satisfaction for sin. And it is about the work of teachers, not punishment for sins. Behind that lies the deeper reason: Christ became our righteousness (1:30). If the cross dealt with sin, there is nothing left for a fire to deal with; if a fire is still required, the cross did not finish. Christ’s sacrifice fully paid for his people’s sins, so there is no punishment left for them (Hebrews 10:14; Romans 8:1). At death, believers go immediately to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Westminster 32.1).

Sobering enough without additions. What is left is sobering without importing anything. A Christian can arrive at the end of his life, undoubtedly saved, and have nothing whatever to show for the time. Not because he was a scandal; he may have been busy, respected, even prominent; but because what he built was made of the wrong stuff. That is a real possibility, and Paul puts it in writing to frighten people out of it.

What is the reward? Paul does not describe it in detail, but the New Testament gives its shape: the Lord’s own commendation (4:5; Matthew 25:21), wider trust and service in the age to come (Luke 19:17), and the crown Paul calls imperishable (9:25; 2 Timothy 4:8). Salvation is the same for every believer; reward is not, and Scripture is not embarrassed to say so. Yet the reward is itself grace, a reward for work that God himself enabled, and the elders in heaven lay their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean faithfulness does not matter, since we are saved anyway. Loss of reward is real loss, and there is shame in it (1 John 2:28).

I have wasted years. Is it too late to build with gold? No. As long as you are alive, you can start building on the foundation with materials that last. The thief on the cross had hours, and Christ welcomed him. Paul himself spent his early years destroying the church, and then laboured more than all the apostles by the grace of God (15:9–10). God does not ask how late you started but whether you are faithful now. Confess the wasted time, refuse to waste more on regret, and give yourself to what lasts: loving people, teaching truth, serving in Christ’s name. Work begun late in faith is still gold.

In a sentence. If what has been built survives, the builder will receive a reward. If it is burned up, the builder will suffer loss but yet will be saved, even though only as one escaping through the flames.

On a Tuesday. Will what you are doing today survive the fire? Invest in what lasts: people, truth, love. Take the thing you are pouring most of yourself into, the ministry, the project, the position, the thing you would most want mentioned at your funeral, and ask what it is made of. Not how large it is; what it is made of. There is still time to change materials, and that is the entire reason Paul told them about the fire in advance (2 Corinthians 5:10; Revelation 14:13).

For worship. The man in the burning house is saved because he stands on a foundation no fire can touch. Christ passed through the fire of God’s judgement first, so that no believer will ever be consumed by it. Our works may burn; he will not, and we are in him. And the Lord who saves the empty-handed also delights to reward the faithful, crowning in us the very gifts he gave, so that on the last day every crown will be laid down at his feet and every voice will say: worthy are you, our Lord and God.

parallels.desc: a brand plucked out of the burning

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple.

Do you not know that you are God’s temple. A phrase Paul uses ten times in this letter, always with an edge: this is not new information; you have been told, and your behaviour suggests you have forgotten. And the first thing to get right is the pronoun, because almost everyone reads this verse wrong. “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple. In 6:19 he will say each believer’s body is a temple; here it is you together, the congregation, collectively. One temple, not two hundred little ones. And temple here is naos, the inner sanctuary where God dwelt, not the whole temple complex. Paul says the local church is God’s holy of holies.

In a city full of temples. That is a considerable claim in Corinth. The city was full of temples, to Apollo, to Asclepius, to Aphrodite on the mountain above the town: buildings of stone and marble, with priests and sacrifices and processions. Paul tells a group of mostly ordinary people meeting in somebody’s dining room that they are the place where the living God has taken up residence. The temples on the skyline are empty. The house with the shabby congregation in it is not.

And that God’s Spirit dwells in you? As the glory-cloud filled the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11), so God’s Spirit lives among his gathered people. The church is where God is.

If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. One of the most severe sentences in the letter. The same verb comes twice (phtheirō, ruin, corrupt, destroy): you ruin it, he will ruin you. It is deliberately symmetrical and deliberately alarming. Whoever wrecks the church, by divisive factions, false teaching or corrupting influence, God will ruin. This is not a builder who builds badly (vv. 12–15), but a wrecker. God guards his temple fiercely. And notice what it does to the subject of church division. Everything so far might be heard as a plea for better relationships. This is not that. A church split is not a management problem, a personality clash or a regrettable difference of vision. It is demolition work on the house where God lives, and he defends his property.

For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple. Holy: set apart for God. Damaging the church is an attack on what belongs to God. Not holy because the members are impressive; these are the people Paul has just called infants. Holy because of who lives there. You may think very little of your congregation, and you may have good reason. God has chosen to live in it, and that is what makes tearing at it so serious.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a true believer who causes trouble will lose salvation. It describes those who destroy the church, showing they were never truly of it (1 John 2:19), and warns all of us how seriously God takes the unity and purity of his church. The warnings are real, not stage effects; they are among the means God uses to keep his people, as a fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over. And the person in view is not someone who has been difficult, or held an unpopular position, or raised a hard question, but one set on wrecking the church.

Is this verse about looking after my body? Not directly. People often quote it against smoking or overeating, but here the temple is the church, the gathered people of God, and the sin is damaging that community. Paul does teach that the individual believer’s body is a temple of the Spirit, three chapters later, where the issue is sexual immorality (6:18–20), and caring for your body honours God for that reason. But the first application of this verse is to how you treat your church: your words, your loyalties, your influence. Wrecking a congregation is a far graver thing than most of us realise.

In a sentence. Don’t you know that you yourselves are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in your midst? If anyone destroys God’s temple, God will destroy that person; for God’s temple is sacred, and you together are that temple.

On a Tuesday. Think of the last conversation you had about someone in your church who was not present. Ask honestly whether it was building or quietly taking something down. Most demolition in most churches is not done by anyone who would describe themselves as destroying anything. It is done a sentence at a time, by people who would be horrified to be told what they are standing in (Ephesians 2:21–22; 2 Corinthians 6:16).

For worship. When your church gathers, God is present by his Spirit. The God who would not be contained by the heavens, who filled Solomon’s temple with a cloud so thick the priests could not stand, has chosen to live among a gathering of forgiven sinners in an ordinary room. The true temple is the body of Christ, destroyed and raised in three days (John 2:19–21), and we are built into him. Come to church with reverence and joy, and guard its unity, for the Holy One is there.
verseByVerse.note: “You” is plural: the church together is God’s temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–23 — The Folly of Boasting in Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to fool themselves. Anyone who thinks he is wise by this world’s standards should become a fool, in the world’s eyes, so as to become truly wise. The world’s wisdom is foolishness to God, as Scripture says: God traps the wise in their cunning, and knows how empty their reasoning is. So no one should boast about human leaders. Everything already belongs to them: Paul, Apollos and Peter, the world, life and death, the present and the future. All of it is theirs, and they belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Everything in Christ, Nothing Apart from him

Verses 21–23 are one of the great catalogue texts of what it means to be in Christ. Paul’s list — Paul, Apollos, Cephas, the world, life, death, present, future — is comprehensive: every apostle, every circumstance, every temporal horizon, even death itself, belongs to the believer in Christ. The Corinthians have been acting poor — squabbling over which apostle to claim — while they are infinitely rich. This is union with Christ expanded to cosmic scope: the one who is in Christ owns, in principle, everything that Christ owns. They need not cling to Paul or Apollos; they have all of them, and infinitely more besides.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were each claiming one-third of the apostolic inheritance — “I follow Paul,” etc. — when they could have had the whole. Their factionalism was a self-imposed poverty in the middle of infinite wealth. Now: The Christian who defines himself by his tradition (Calvinist, Arminian, Baptist, Anglican) rather than by Christ is doing the same thing — claiming a slice when the whole belongs to him. The traditions are real and valuable; they are yours in Christ. But Christ is not yours in the tradition.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one deceive himself. If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness,” and again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile.”

Let no one deceive himself. Self-deception is the danger of the clever. They think they are wise, and so cannot see their folly. Paul does not warn them about being deceived by someone else. The danger is self-administered, and it is the hardest kind to detect, because the person doing the deceiving is entirely trusted by the person being deceived.

If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise. To become wise, you must accept being thought a fool by the world, by embracing the foolish message of the cross (1:18–25). The instruction is deliberately shocking, and it describes a real and painful step. It is not a recommendation to stop thinking. It is the requirement to accept a verdict on your thinking: to agree that the equipment you have relied on cannot reach God, and to receive from him what you could not work out.

The door marked fool. Everybody who becomes a Christian does this, and for some it costs more than for others. The person who has never had much confidence in his own cleverness has less to lay down. The person whose whole standing rests on being the one who understands things, the academic, the professional, the man used to being the most informed person in the room, is being asked to walk into the kingdom by a door marked fool, and to keep walking through it afterwards.

For the wisdom of this world is folly with God. In God’s eyes, the world’s wisdom, apart from him, is foolishness.

For it is written, “He catches the wise in their craftiness”. From Job 5:13, the only quotation of Job in the New Testament outside Romans 11. God traps the clever in their own schemes; their cleverness becomes their snare. And there is a fine irony here: Paul is quoting Eliphaz, one of Job’s comforters, whose confident wisdom God himself exposes before the book ends (Job 42:7). The man who said it was caught by it.

And again, “The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are futile”. From Psalm 94:11, where the psalmist writes the thoughts of man; Paul sharpens it to the wise, since that is the group in question at Corinth. Futile (mataios) means empty, vain, leading nowhere. God sees through all human reasoning that leaves him out. He is not described as outwitting the clever in an argument. He knows their reasoning, and knows it goes nowhere, which is a far more devastating verdict than being contradicted.

A permanent posture. What Paul asks for is not a one-off act but a lasting posture: the willingness to let Scripture correct your categories rather than trimming Scripture to fit them. Every Christian who reads seriously meets passages that offend his instincts, about judgement, sexuality, money, God’s sovereignty, hell. At that point one of two things happens, and which one happens is the whole subject of these verses.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. It means that wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 9:10), and all learning must bow to God’s revelation.

Should Christians study at university or work in science and scholarship? Yes, gladly. All truth is God’s truth, the world is his to explore, and Christians have done some of the finest thinking in history in every field. Daniel learned the literature of Babylon without bowing to its gods (Daniel 1:17). What this verse forbids is not learning but letting learning sit in judgement over God. So study hard, think carefully, and take your faith into the lecture room rather than leaving it at the door. Find Christian friends who will help you think, and when a teacher’s claims clash with Scripture, test them humbly and patiently, remembering that the fear of the Lord is where wisdom starts.

In a sentence. Do not deceive yourselves. If any of you think you are wise by the standards of this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise. For the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight. As it is written: “He catches the wise in their craftiness”; and again, “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.”

On a Tuesday. Be willing to look foolish in the world’s eyes for believing God’s word; that is the beginning of real wisdom. And name a conviction you have changed in the last five years because Scripture required it, against your preference and against the opinion of people whose respect you wanted. If nothing comes to mind, ask whether you have been reading the Bible or consulting it, because a person who is never corrected by a book is not being taught by it (Proverbs 3:5–7; Isaiah 5:21; Matthew 11:25).

For worship. The only wise God (Romans 16:27) has no need of our counsel, and he has made his wisdom known in a crucified Christ. He catches the clever in their own nets and gives understanding to the simple. Blessed be the God who hides these things from the wise and understanding and reveals them to little children, because such was his gracious will (Matthew 11:25–26).

parallels.desc: he catches the wise in their own craftiness
the LORD knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath

verseByVerse.quote: So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,
verseByVerse.commentary:
So let no one boast in men. For all things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future—all are yours,

So let no one boast in men. The conclusion of chapters 1–3. Do not boast in human leaders; the party slogans must stop. And the logic is not what we expect. Paul does not say: stop boasting in men, because you have nothing to boast about. He says: stop boasting in men, because you are far too rich for that. The Corinthians are behaving like people fighting over scraps, and Paul’s answer is to open the accounts.

For all things are yours. A glorious reversal. You said, I belong to Paul. Paul says: no, Paul belongs to you. Why pick one teacher when God has given you all of them?

Whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas. The very men the factions were dividing over. All the teachers are God’s gifts to you, to serve you (Ephesians 4:11–12). Each group had claimed one and rejected the others, and Paul tells them they own all three. The faction was not merely wrong; it was a self-imposed poverty. They were each clinging to a third of an inheritance that was entirely theirs.

Or the world. Then the list jumps. The whole created world is yours, as heirs with Christ (Romans 4:13; 8:17), because the meek shall inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5).

Or life or death. Life is yours: not a lease on a few decades, but life as a possession rather than a predicament. And then a word nobody would have put in a list of assets: death. Death is yours. Not survivable, or temporary; it belongs to you, it is on the inventory. Paul means it: the last enemy has been so thoroughly defeated that it now serves the believer, for it brings you to Christ (Philippians 1:21). Death is no longer your master; it is your servant, the servant that carries a Christian home. The thing every human being organises his life around avoiding has been reduced to an item on a list of possessions.

Or the present or the future, all are yours. Present circumstances and future events: all work together for your good (Romans 8:28, 38). Both, notice. Not the future only, as if this were a promise to be endured towards. The present, this month, with its unresolved situation, belongs to you as much as the glory does.

Not a prosperity gospel. A guard is needed, because all things are yours has been used to underwrite a gospel of prosperity: claim your health, claim your finances, everything belongs to you. But look at what is on the list. Nobody preaching that message has ever made much of or death. Paul is writing to a church that is mostly poor and socially insignificant (1:26), and is about to say that the apostles themselves are hungry, poorly dressed and homeless (4:11). The riches he describes are not paid out in the currency such teaching demands.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians own everything now or can grasp at things. It means that in Christ, everything is working for them, and they will inherit it all.

If death is mine, why am I still afraid of dying? Because death is still an enemy, the last one (15:26), and the process of dying can be hard. Jesus himself wept at a grave and was in anguish in Gethsemane. Fear of dying is not unbelief; it is being human in a fallen world. What Christ has removed is the sting: death can no longer separate you from God, condemn you or keep you (15:55–57; Romans 8:38–39). So bring the fear to him honestly. Read what he has promised about the other side. Ask to be with believers who have died well. And remember that he has gone through death ahead of you, and will be with you in it.

In a sentence. So then, no more boasting about human leaders! All things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future, all are yours,

On a Tuesday. If you feel spiritually poor, as most of us do most of the time, write down what you think you are short of: standing, security, a future, a place to belong, someone in your corner. Then read the list again. The Corinthians were quarrelling over which apostle to claim while owning the world, life, death, the present and the future. It is possible to be an heir of everything and live like a man counting coins, and the only thing that has to change is that somebody tells you what is in the account (Romans 8:32; Psalm 24:1).

For worship. Life is yours. Death is yours. The future is yours. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things (Romans 8:32)? The Father has held nothing back. The Son who inherits all things has made us co-heirs, and even the grave has been made to serve those for whom he rose. Praise God for such riches in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.

And you are Christ’s. Eight words in all, and they hold the whole chapter together. All things belong to you, because you belong to Christ. Not to Paul, not to Apollos, but to Christ. This is the true slogan: I am Christ’s. And the reason all things are yours is that they are his, and you are in him.

Owner and owned. The chain runs downwards and the ownership runs upwards. All things belong to you, but you are not the top of the chain, and that is exactly what keeps verse 22 from becoming the fantasy of self-importance the Corinthians would have made of it. You own everything, and you are owned. The inheritance is real because the belonging is real; remove the belonging and the inheritance evaporates. That is why the factions were absurd. A man who says I am Paul’s has swapped an infinite estate for a small allegiance, and has got the direction of ownership wrong in the bargain. You do not belong to a teacher. Teachers belong to you, and you belong to Christ.

And Christ is God’s. Christ, as the Son and Mediator, belongs to God the Father and serves his glory (11:3; 15:28). Everything flows down from God, through Christ, to his people, and everything flows back up to God’s glory. Read carelessly, the clause sounds like a demotion, as though the Son were a lesser being belonging to a greater one, which is precisely what the Arians of the fourth century argued from sentences like this.

Equal in nature, ordered in relation. The church’s answer, set out at Nicaea, is that Scripture speaks of the Son in two registers. As to his being, he is fully and equally God: this same Paul calls him the Lord of glory (2:8) and applies to him the covenant name from Jeremiah (1:31). As to his mission, he willingly took a place of submission: sent by the Father, doing the Father’s will, and at the end handing the kingdom over to the Father (15:24–28). The submission is not evidence of a lesser deity; it is the shape divine love took when it came to fetch us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is less than God in his divine nature. As the eternal Son, he is equal with the Father. As Mediator, the Son incarnate, he willingly serves the Father’s purpose (John 14:28; Philippians 2:6–11).

A chain you did not make. The practical force is considerable. Everything you have depends on a link you did not make and cannot break. Your standing rests on your being Christ’s; his standing rests on nothing outside himself, because he is God’s eternally and by nature. There is no point in that chain at which your grip is what holds it. It is the same comfort as 1:9, arriving by a different road.

What does it mean in practice to belong to Christ? It means your life is not your own: your time, body, money, gifts and future are his to direct (6:19–20). That is a claim, and it is also a comfort. Because you are his, he takes responsibility for you: he feeds, guards, corrects and keeps what belongs to him (John 10:27–29). It means your identity is settled not by your job, your politics, your tribe or your failures, but by whose you are. And it means every other loyalty, to family, church, nation or leader, is real but secondary, held under him. When you are unsure what to do, ask the simple question: what would my Owner want?

In a sentence. and you are of Christ, and Christ is of God.

On a Tuesday. You belong to Christ. When someone tries to claim your loyalty, whether a leader, a cause or a party, remember whose you are. And when you feel alone or worthless this week, say it to yourself plainly: I am Christ’s. Nobody can take that away, because you did not give it to yourself.

For worship. So the chapter that opened by calling them infants ends by telling them what they own. It began with jealousy over preachers and ends with the world, life, death, the present and the future signed over to a squabbling congregation in a port city, not because they had grown up, for they plainly had not, but because they were Christ’s. And he is God’s. He did not seize the position; he was given everything by the Father and gave it away to us, and when it is all finished he will hand the kingdom back, so that God may be all in all. There is no grasping anywhere in the Godhead. Everything the Son has, he has from the Father, and everything you have, you have from the Son, and the whole vast movement of it runs outwards, from a God who has never once needed anything and has never stopped giving (John 17:10; 1 Corinthians 15:28).

3.text: <sup>1</sup>But I, brothers, could not address you as spiritual people, but as people of the flesh, as infants in Christ.<sup>2</sup>I fed you with milk, not solid food, for you were not ready for it. And even now you are not yet ready,<sup>3</sup>for you are still of the flesh. For while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?<sup>4</sup>For when one says, “I follow Paul,” and another, “I follow Apollos,” are you not being merely human?<sup>5</sup>What then is Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.<sup>6</sup>I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.<sup>7</sup>So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God who gives the growth.<sup>8</sup>He who plants and he who waters are one, and each will receive his wages according to his labor.<sup>9</sup>For we are God’s fellow workers. 4.title: Servants of Christ, Spectacles to the World
4.overview:
Paul finishes his answer to the factions by telling the Corinthians how to think about their leaders. Apostles are Christ’s servants and the managers of God’s revealed truth, and what counts for a manager is faithfulness. Paul is not troubled by the Corinthians’ assessment of him, or even by his own clear conscience, because the Lord is his judge, and on the last day he will expose hidden motives and give each person whatever praise is due. So the Corinthians must stop judging prematurely and stop puffing themselves up over one teacher against another, for everything they have is a gift.

Then Paul turns to biting irony. The Corinthians act as if they have already arrived, rich and reigning like kings, while the apostles look like condemned prisoners paraded at the end of a procession: hungry, ill-clothed, beaten, homeless, labouring with their hands, treated as the scum of the earth, yet blessing those who curse them. He writes not to shame them but to warn them as a father. They may have countless tutors, but only one father in the gospel, so they should imitate him. He is sending Timothy to remind them of his ways, and will come himself soon to see whether the arrogant have any real power, since God’s kingdom is a matter of power, not talk. Should he come with a rod, or with love and gentleness?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Servants and Stewards: The Judgment That Matters
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: People should regard Paul and his fellow workers as Christ’s servants, entrusted with managing God’s revealed secrets, and the one thing required of such managers is that they prove faithful. Paul cares very little whether the Corinthians or any human court evaluates him; he does not even judge himself. His conscience is clear, but that does not prove him innocent; the Lord is the one who judges him. So they should not pass verdicts before the time. When the Lord comes he will bring hidden things to light and reveal the purposes of every heart, and then each person will receive whatever commendation comes from God. Paul has used himself and Apollos as an example so that they learn not to go beyond what Scripture says and not to be proud of one leader against another. What makes anyone superior? What do they have that they did not receive? And if it was a gift, why boast as if it were not?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatological Judgment and Its Present Implications

Paul’s refusal to pre-judge himself or others (vv. 3–5) is not relativism but eschatological realism. The final judgment has not yet been rendered; therefore all present judgments — including self-assessment — are provisional. Reformed theology has always warned against both false confidence (I know I am right) and false despair (I know I am condemned): both pre-empt the judgment that belongs to God alone. The practical implication is freedom: neither to be destroyed by human criticism nor to be puffed up by human praise, because neither the critic nor the flatterer is the judge.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians were evaluating Paul and finding him wanting, not by the standard of faithfulness but by the standards of rhetorical eloquence and visible success. Paul refuses the evaluation: you are not my judge; the Lord is. Now: Ministry evaluation by attendance, public approval, or conference invitations is the contemporary equivalent. The minister who structures his ministry around what will get him praised by his peers has already chosen the wrong judge. The only evaluation that matters is the Lord’s — and it will assess what the heart actually was.

verseByVerse.quote: This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is how one should regard us, as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 4 finishes Paul’s answer to the divisions of chapters 1–4. First, ministers are servants and stewards; what matters is faithfulness, and only the Lord can judge it, at his coming. So the Corinthians must stop ranking their teachers (vv. 1–5). Second, everything they have was received as a gift, so they have no ground for pride (vv. 6–7).
