But discipline must never be harsh, hasty or used to protect leaders, and it never replaces calling the police when a crime has been committed.

In a sentence. For the kingdom of God is not a matter of talk but of power. What do you prefer? Shall Paul come to you with a rod of discipline, or shall he come in love and with a gentle spirit?

On a Tuesday. Is there a correction God has been making in your life gently, through a verse that keeps coming back, a friend’s word, a troubled conscience, that you have been putting off? Respond now, while it is still the gentle word. And if you have authority over others, as a parent, a manager or an elder, notice Paul’s order: warn clearly, show your love plainly, give time to respond, and only then use the rod, and even then with sorrow rather than satisfaction.

For worship. The chapter closes where it began, with a servant. It opened with stewards who own nothing and administer everything, and it ends with one of them holding real power and asking permission not to use it. He learned that from someone. The One who had every right to come with a rod to a world in open rebellion came instead as an infant, worked with his hands, was reviled and blessed, was made a spectacle last of all, and the only rod that has yet fallen in full fell on him: he was pierced for our transgressions, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5). The King of the kingdom of power comes to his people in gentleness, because the rod has already been spent on his own back.

5.title: The Leaven of Immorality: Church Discipline and the Holiness of God
5.overview:
Paul now deals with a scandal. A man in the church is living with his father’s wife, probably his stepmother, a relationship forbidden by the law of Moses and condemned even by Roman society. Worse, the church is proud of itself instead of grieving. Perhaps they thought their freedom in Christ meant the body did not matter. Paul, though absent, has already made his judgement: when they assemble with the Lord’s power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him outside the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord.

Paul uses a Passover picture. Just as Jewish households swept every scrap of yeast out of the house before the feast, the church must get rid of the old yeast of sin, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. Then he corrects a misunderstanding of an earlier letter. He never meant them to avoid all contact with immoral people in the world, which would mean leaving the world altogether. He meant that they must not share fellowship with someone who claims to be a believer but persists in serious sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge those inside.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has heard that there is sexual immorality in the church of a kind not even found among pagans: a man is living with his father’s wife. And instead of mourning and removing him, they are proud. Though absent in body, Paul is present in spirit and has already judged the man. When they gather in the name of the Lord Jesus, with Paul’s spirit and the Lord’s power present, they are to hand him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Their boasting is wrong. Do they not know that a little yeast works through the whole batch of dough? They must clear out the old yeast so that they may be a new, unleavened batch, as in fact they are, for Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed. So they should keep the festival, not with the old yeast of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.theology:
Church Discipline as a Gospel Act

The Reformed tradition has always identified church discipline as one of the marks of the true church (alongside Word and sacraments). Calvin’s Institutes IV.12 grounds discipline in the same logic Paul uses here: the holiness of the community is not a human achievement but a participation in the holiness of Christ who dwells in it. Excommunication is not the final word against the sinner but the penultimate word, designed to produce repentance. The church that refuses to discipline its members — in the name of grace, tolerance, or avoiding conflict — is, paradoxically, acting without grace: it is allowing the leavening of unrepentant sin to compromise the whole community and denying the sinner the painful mercy of confrontation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian pride in tolerating this relationship may reflect the influence of the “strong” in the community — those with social status and rhetorical sophistication who had reinterpreted gospel freedom as moral permissiveness. The man involved may have been a patron of the church, someone whose loss the community feared. Paul overrides all such calculations: the gospel has higher priorities than keeping wealthy members comfortable. Now: The contemporary church’s allergy to any form of discipline is well-documented and widely lamented. Churches afraid to confront unrepentant sin in their members have, ironically, become communities shaped more by the fear of conflict than by love for the sinner.

verseByVerse.quote: It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans, for a man has his father’s wife. And you are arrogant! Ought you not rather to mourn? Let him who has done this be removed from among you.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 5 turns from divisions to a case of open, scandalous sin, and to the church’s failure to deal with it. A member is living with his stepmother, and the church is proud of its tolerance instead of grieving (vv. 1–2). Paul, though absent, has already judged the case: when they gather in the Lord’s name and power, they must hand this man over to Satan, putting him out of the church, so that his sinful nature may be destroyed and he may be saved on the day of the Lord (vv. 3–5). Sin tolerated spreads like yeast through dough; since Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, the church must clean out the old yeast and live in sincerity and truth (vv. 6–8). Finally, Paul clears up a misunderstanding of an earlier letter: the call to separation applies not to unbelievers in the world, but to anyone who calls himself a brother and lives in open, unrepentant sin. God judges outsiders; the church must judge its own (vv. 9–13). This chapter is the New Testament’s clearest teaching on church discipline, and at its centre stands not a rule but a Lamb: the whole hard chapter rests on the blood of Christ, sacrificed for a people he means to make clean.

It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you. “Actually” is holōs, everywhere, widely: it is common knowledge. Paul has not been reading private letters or listening at doors; the thing is being talked about across the region. “Sexual immorality” is porneia, the broad word for any sexual sin outside marriage.

And of a kind that is not tolerated even among pagans. This is the sting. Paul’s point is not only that it breaks the law of Moses, though it does. It is that it breaks the standards of pagan Corinth. Roman law prohibited such a marriage outright, and Cicero treats a comparable union inside a family as a crime almost beyond belief. Corinth was a city with a reputation for vice across the whole Mediterranean, and this was over the line even there. The church had managed to be more permissive than a port town famous for permissiveness.

For a man has his father’s wife. The wording is careful, and it matters: not his mother but his stepmother, the father either dead or divorced. The law of Moses forbade it explicitly (Leviticus 18:8; Deuteronomy 22:30). “Has” is a present tense, which suggests an ongoing relationship, perhaps living together or even married, settled rather than a single lapse. And since Paul says nothing about disciplining the woman, she was probably not a believer; the church has authority only over its own members (v. 12).

And you are arrogant! Here is the real subject of the chapter. Not the man: he is dealt with in three verses. The congregation. They were not agonising over this, or divided about it, or quietly ashamed of it. They were proud. “Arrogant” is physioō again, puffed up, the word Paul has used against them all through chapter 4. How could a church be proud of this? The likeliest explanation runs straight out of the previous chapters. This was a church that prized its own spiritual sophistication and had a theology of freedom it was pleased with: the body did not matter spiritually (6:12–13), grace was so large and liberty so complete that it could accommodate even this, and a congregation that took it in its stride was proving how far beyond ordinary scruples it had travelled. There may have been a more sordid factor too: a man in such a marriage was likely wealthy, perhaps a patron the church could not afford to lose. Whatever the mechanism, the shape is permanent. There is a kind of tolerance that presents itself as maturity and is actually cowardice with a theology attached.

Ought you not rather to mourn? The word is pentheō, the verb for grieving a death, the word used of mourners at a funeral. This is the most instructive thing in the passage, because it names the right emotion, and it is one almost nobody reaches for. Consider the two responses available when serious sin surfaces in a church. One is what the Corinthians did: absorb it, explain it, be relaxed about it. The other is what churches more often do: outrage, gossip, the energetic circulation of the details, and a certain relish. Paul asks for neither. He asks for grief, the response of people who have lost something they loved and are standing at a graveside. Grief cannot be faked and cannot be enjoyed. Outrage is pleasurable; that is why it is so popular. Indifference is comfortable. Mourning is neither, and it is the only one of the three that has any love in it: you do not grieve over someone you were not attached to.

Let him who has done this be removed from among you. The man must be put out of the fellowship of the church. Mourning does not replace action; it is the only right soil for it. The grief Paul asks for is not a feeling that leaves everything as it was, but the sorrow of people who love the man and the Lord too much to pretend.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church should expel members for every sin. All believers sin, every day. Church discipline is for serious, open sin persisted in without repentance, after patient warning (Matthew 18:15–17). Nor does mourning mean a congregation should wallow in collective guilt. It means it should feel the weight of what has happened in its family, and act out of that weight rather than out of anger or embarrassment.

Why was the woman not disciplined too? Almost certainly because she was not a member of the church. Paul says plainly that the church’s responsibility is for those inside it, and that God judges those outside (vv. 12–13). That does not make her sin less serious, and it does not mean she is beyond the reach of the gospel. It means the church’s formal discipline applies only to those who profess Christ and have joined themselves to his people. Toward her, as toward every unbeliever, the church’s task is to proclaim the gospel and pray.

What should an ordinary member do when there is a scandal in the church? First, do not spread it. Talking about the details with people who are not part of the solution is gossip, however concerned it sounds (Proverbs 16:28). Second, pray, both for the person caught in the sin and for the leaders who have to handle it. Third, if you know something your leaders need to know, tell them directly and privately. Fourth, check your heart: aim for the grief Paul asks for, not the interest or superiority that comes so easily. And if the sin is a crime, especially any abuse, it must be reported to the police; the church’s discipline never replaces the law.

In a sentence. It is actually reported that there is sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that even pagans do not tolerate: a man is sleeping with his father’s wife. And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have gone into mourning and have put out of your fellowship the man who has been doing this?

On a Tuesday. When sin is exposed in your church, do not gossip or shrug. Grieve, and pray for repentance. Here is a test for the next time you hear that a Christian you know has done something serious. Watch the first movement of your heart in the four seconds before you have composed a response. If it is a flicker of interest, or of superiority, or of relief that it was not you, then whatever you go on to say about the sin, you have not yet reached the emotion this verse asks for. And a church full of people who cannot mourn is not fit to do what Paul is about to command (2 Corinthians 12:21; Galatians 6:1).

For worship. The God who asks his church to mourn over sin is the God who mourned over it first. The Lord Jesus wept over Jerusalem, and grieved at the hardness of men’s hearts, and he did not stop at grief. He took the sin that his people had made light of and bore its full weight on the cross, where it was never treated lightly at all. He loves his church too much to let her be proud of what is killing her, and his holiness and his tears are not two different things. They are one love, and it is the love that has made us his.
verseByVerse.note: “His father’s wife” probably means his stepmother. The law of Moses forbade it, and Roman law condemned it too.

verseByVerse.quote: For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though absent in body, I am present in spirit; and as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus and my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus,

For though absent in body, I am present in spirit. It is worth saying at once what this is not. Paul is not claiming a mystical projection of himself across the Aegean, nor some strange power of remote attendance. He is saying what any of us mean by being with someone in spirit, in thought and concern, but with an added weight: his apostolic authority genuinely travels in the letter being read aloud (Colossians 2:5). When they hear this document, they are hearing him.

And as if present, I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did such a thing. The verdict is not being submitted for discussion. “Pronounced judgment” is kekrika, from krinō: I have judged, decided. Paul has weighed the case and reached a conclusion, and he can do so from a distance because the facts are not in dispute. The thing is being openly and publicly done. No further investigation is needed when a man is living with his stepmother in plain sight.

When you are assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus. Now notice something that governs the whole doctrine of church discipline and is regularly missed: Paul does not act. He has pronounced the verdict, and the carrying out of it waits for something: when you are assembled. The apostle with unquestioned authority does not remove the man by letter. He tells the congregation to gather and do it. Discipline in the New Testament is a corporate act of the gathered church, not a private decision taken by a leader, and this cuts in two directions at once. It cuts against churches that will not act: the congregation cannot hand this to the minister and then complain about him, nor treat it as somebody else’s department. And it cuts against the leader who acts alone. A great deal of damage has been done in churches by men who decided a case privately and announced the outcome, and this verse gives them no cover whatever. The Lord himself built the same safeguard into the procedure: the escalating steps of Matthew 18 end with tell it to the church, not tell it to the pastor (Matthew 18:17).

And my spirit is present, with the power of our Lord Jesus. Then the two things that make such a gathering more than a disciplinary hearing. It is in the name of the Lord Jesus: convened on his authority, not the church’s own. And it proceeds with the power of our Lord Jesus, which is exactly the promise attached in Matthew: where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them (Matthew 18:20). That famous sentence is not, in its context, chiefly a comfort about small prayer meetings. It is a guarantee given to a church doing this very thing, and it is the most sobering possible reason for doing it carefully. When a church disciplines rightly, Christ acts through it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is present as a ghost. It means his authority and judgment are joined with the church’s action. Nor does it give any church a power of its own; the church acts only in Christ’s name, by Christ’s word, and when it acts against his word its verdict carries no weight in heaven.

Who actually carries out discipline, the elders or the whole church? Christians organise this differently, and honest believers disagree. Congregational churches, including many Baptists, read this verse and Matthew 18:17 as giving the final act to the gathered membership, led and guided by its elders (2 Corinthians 2:6 speaks of a punishment by the majority). Presbyterian churches see the elders, the church’s representatives, acting on behalf of the congregation. Others mix the two. But the common ground is wide and it is the point of this verse: discipline is never the act of one man alone, it is done before the Lord with his authority, it involves the church, and it is done openly and carefully, not in secret.

In a sentence. For Paul’s part, even though he is not physically present, he is with you in spirit. As one who is present with you in this way, he has already passed judgment in the name of our Lord Jesus on the one who has been doing this. So when you are assembled and he is with you in spirit, and the power of our Lord Jesus is present,

On a Tuesday. If you are a church member, you are not a spectator. You belong to a body that Christ has made responsible for its own life, and that includes the hard things. Pray for your church leaders as they exercise care and discipline, attend when the church gathers to decide, and refuse both the shrug and the private campaign. If you are a leader, never move without the body, never move without Christ’s word, and never move in any spirit except the grief of verse 2. An assembly gathered in his name, with his power present, is not a tribunal. It is a church standing in the presence of its Lord, doing the hardest thing he ever asked of it (Matthew 18:15–20; 2 Corinthians 2:6).

For worship. Christ is present in his gathered church with authority. The risen Lord does not govern his people from a distance, as a founder whose rules are kept by his heirs. He stands among them when they meet, holding the keys of the kingdom, and he lends his own power to their obedience. The church that bows to his word is never alone in the room. He who walks among the lampstands has promised to be there, and his presence is both the church’s greatest safety and her most holy fear.

verseByVerse.quote: you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
you are to deliver this man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord.

You are to deliver this man to Satan. It is one of the most alarming sentences in the New Testament, and every clause needs handling. To deliver to Satan does not mean handing a soul over to damnation, and Paul’s own final clause forbids that reading. The whole letter has been describing two spheres: the community where Christ dwells by his Spirit (3:16), and the world outside, which lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19; Ephesians 2:2). To be excluded from the assembly is to be put out of the first and into the second: removed from the protection, the fellowship, the Lord’s Table and the prayers of God’s people, and left in the open. Inside the church he was under the care of the body; outside, he is exposed. Paul uses the same phrase once more, of Hymenaeus and Alexander, who had made shipwreck of their faith (1 Timothy 1:20).

For the destruction of the flesh. This phrase is genuinely disputed, and honesty requires saying so. Some take it of physical suffering, even death, on the pattern of the judgments in Acts 5 or later in this letter (11:30). Others take “flesh” (sarx) in Paul’s usual moral sense, the sinful nature, so that what is to be destroyed is the appetite itself, by being allowed to run to its own bitter end. The second fits Paul’s vocabulary better and fits the purpose clause far better, and it describes something we have all watched. A man protected from the consequences of what he is doing will continue; a man who is left to feel what it actually costs may come to his senses. It is the road of the prodigal, who needed the pigs before he wanted the father (Luke 15:14–17). The misery of being cut off may break the power of his sin and bring him to repentance.

So that his spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord. Then the clause that governs everything. Read the sentence again with it at the front and it changes character entirely. This is not the church washing its hands of a man. It is the last available means of grace, applied because everything gentler has failed. Excommunication in the New Testament is not the opposite of seeking someone’s salvation; it is an instrument of it, the surgeon’s knife, used because the alternative is worse and used with the intention of a cure. The goal of discipline is restoration and salvation, not destruction. It is a severe mercy.

What happened next. No treatment of this verse is honest without the sequel. Writing to the same church a while later, Paul deals with a disciplined man, perhaps this one, though commentators are divided. The discipline had worked. And Paul’s instruction is emphatic: the punishment has been enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow; reaffirm your love for him. And he adds a reason that ought to be written over every case of church discipline in history: so that we would not be outwitted by Satan (2 Corinthians 2:5–11). Notice where Satan is in each passage. In 1 Corinthians 5 he is the instrument God uses to bring a man home. In 2 Corinthians 2 he is the danger of a church that will not let a repentant man back. The devil can work either side of this, and the second failure is the commoner one.

Where Christians differ: church discipline. Many churches today never practise discipline, thinking it unloving or judgmental. Others practise it harshly, for minor issues. Verdict: Church discipline is commanded by Christ and the apostles (Matthew 18:15–17; 2 Thessalonians 3:6, 14–15; Titus 3:10). It is one of the marks of a true church, alongside the preaching of the word and the right use of the sacraments (Belgic Confession 29). Its purposes are the restoration of the sinner, the purity of the church, and the honour of Christ (Westminster 30.3). It should be done carefully, in stages, with love and prayer, and only for serious, persistent, unrepentant sin.

The guard against cruelty. A guard is needed, because this text has been used to justify real cruelty. Shunning as punishment, families broken apart, people pursued for years, the machinery of control: all of it has claimed this verse. The test is the purpose clause. If a church disciplines without longing for the person’s return, without a route back, without telling him plainly what repentance would look like and how gladly he would be received, then whatever it is doing, it is not this. Paul’s aim is a man saved in the day of the Lord, and everything that does not serve that aim is somebody else’s idea.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church can damn someone or curse them. Only God judges the soul. It means the church formally recognises that the person is acting as an unbeliever, and treats him as one in need of the gospel, calling him to repent and come home.

Can a true Christian be put out of the church? Yes. Paul’s hope that the man’s spirit will be saved suggests he may be a genuine believer in serious, stubborn sin. True Christians can fall grievously for a time, as David did (Westminster 17.3). But God does not let his own go. One of the ways he brings them back is through the discipline of his church, which he uses to make them feel the misery of their sin and to turn them home. So the doctrine that God keeps his people to the end does not make discipline unnecessary; discipline is one of the means by which he keeps them. Whether a particular person is truly born again is finally known to God, and will be shown by whether he returns.

Can someone who has been put out ever come back? Yes, and the church should long for it and make it easy to see the way. The door in this passage opens both ways. In 2 Corinthians a disciplined man walked back through it and the church was told to forgive him, comfort him and reaffirm its love (2 Corinthians 2:7–8). Restoration should follow real repentance, which shows itself in turning from the sin, not merely in regret at the consequences. When it comes, the church should welcome the person as the father welcomed the prodigal, without probation by suspicion and without endless reminders of the past.

What if I was disciplined unfairly? Churches are made of sinners, and they can be wrong. A church can act hastily, without proper process, for things Scripture does not condemn, or to protect its leaders. If that has happened to you, remember chapter 4: it is the Lord who judges you (4:4). A wrong human verdict does not change your standing before God. Seek to understand what was said, examine yourself honestly before the Lord, and, if you can, ask for the matter to be reviewed or talk with wise believers from outside the situation. If reconciliation is impossible, it is right to find a faithful church elsewhere. And ask God to keep you from bitterness, which can do more harm than the injustice.

In a sentence. hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you are ever disciplined, see it as God’s severe mercy, not his rejection. If you see it done, pray for the person’s return, and be the first to welcome him when he comes. And if you are reading this as the person who was put out: the door is not locked. The way back is the way every Christian ever came to God, repentance and faith in Christ, and there are people who will be glad to see you walk through it (Luke 15:17–20; Hebrews 12:11).

For worship. The God of this verse is the God who disciplines the son he loves (Hebrews 12:6), and who will go into the far country after a straying child rather than let him perish there. He uses even the power of Satan as a tool in his hand to bring his people home, and the devil, who meant to destroy, finds that he has only served the purpose of the Shepherd. The day of the Lord, which Paul names here, is the day when every one of Christ’s sheep is counted in, and not one is missing. Our Father’s severity is always aimed at our salvation, and his arms are always open at the end of it.
verseByVerse.note: To “deliver to Satan” means to put the man out of the church into the world, where Satan rules, in the hope that he will repent.

verseByVerse.quote: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump, as you really are unleavened. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

Your boasting is not good. Paul returns to the pride of verse 2. Their boasting is unfitting, especially with this sin in their midst. A church that is congratulating itself while one of its members is destroying himself has its eyes in the wrong place. And the word Paul uses for “boasting” here can mean the thing boasted of: the very matter they are proud of is rotten.

Do you not know that a little leaven leavens the whole lump? A proverb, which Paul uses also in Galatians 5:9. Leaven (zymē) is not the dried yeast in a modern packet but a lump of old fermented dough kept back from the last baking and worked through the new. The image is domestic and exact, and it explains why Paul will not let this pass as one man’s private business. Leaven works invisibly and it works completely. You cannot put a small piece in one corner of the dough and have the rest unaffected; given time it is through everything, and there is no way of taking it out again. Paul is describing what tolerated sin does to a congregation.

How the leaven spreads. It is worth being precise about the mechanism, because the danger is not that everyone in the church will commit that particular sin. It is that the standard moves. Once something serious has been publicly accommodated, it becomes the new floor. Everything less than it is now unmentionable, because how do you raise a small matter in a church that has swallowed a large one? A single unaddressed case does not produce one hypocrite; it produces a congregation in which nothing can be said about anything. And the young believer watching learns that the church’s words about holiness are not meant.

Cleanse out the old leaven that you may be a new lump. Then Paul reaches for Passover, and the metaphor is chosen with care. Before the feast every Jewish household removed all leaven from the house (Exodus 12:15, 19; 13:7). In later practice this became a deliberate search, by lamplight, through every room for any crumb, which was then removed and burned. Not a general resolve to be purer: a search, room by room, for a specific thing, undertaken because a lamb was about to be killed. The church must remove the sinner and the sin he represents.

As you really are unleavened. Do not hurry past this clause, because it is the engine of all New Testament ethics and it is the reverse of how we naturally think. Paul does not say: purify yourselves in order to become clean. He says: you are unleavened, so get the leaven out. The status comes first and the effort follows from it. In Christ they are already a new, unleavened lump: holy, sanctified (1:2). The Corinthians are not working towards a holiness they might one day possess; they are being told to match a holiness already given them by the sacrifice. Become what you are. Every command in this letter stands on a statement of fact like that one, and a Christian who reverses the order will spend his life trying to earn a thing he was given at the start.

For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed. Everything in the chapter rests on this clause, and it is the only reason the search is worth conducting. Consider what stood behind the original feast. A night in Egypt; a lamb chosen and killed in every house; blood struck on the doorposts; a family inside eating in haste with their belongings packed; and death moving through the streets, and passing over every door where the blood was (Exodus 12). Nobody inside those houses was safer than anybody else because of their character. The blood was on the door or it was not. And every Passover for fourteen centuries afterwards was a rehearsal, a nation sitting down each year to eat the meal of a rescue that had already happened, with a lamb on the table that could never actually take away anything. Then John saw Jesus walking by the Jordan and said, behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). He died at Passover, at the time the lambs were being killed (John 19:14), and not a bone of him was broken, as the law required of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:46; John 19:36). The lamb was always him. Fourteen hundred years of suppers were pointing at one afternoon outside Jerusalem, when the blood went on the doorposts of the world.

What does it mean that Christ is our Passover lamb? It means that he died in our place, so that the judgment we deserved passed over us. In Egypt, the firstborn in a house marked with blood was spared, not because he was innocent, but because a death had already taken place in that house: the lamb had died instead. That is what happened at the cross. God’s just judgment against our sin fell on Christ, our substitute, and everyone sheltering under his blood by faith is spared (1 Peter 1:18–19; Romans 3:25). And the Passover was not only rescue from death; it was the beginning of a journey out of slavery. Christ’s blood frees us from the guilt of sin and also brings us out from its rule.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we keep the Jewish Passover, or must clear our kitchens of yeast. Christ has fulfilled it. The Lord’s Supper is the new covenant meal (11:23–26), and the old leaven we put away is sin, not bread.

In a sentence. Your boasting is not good. Don’t you know that a little yeast leavens the whole batch of dough? Get rid of the old yeast, so that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.

On a Tuesday. Is there one sin in your life you have quietly accommodated: a habit, a resentment, a way of handling money or truth, that you no longer even fight because it has become the floor? Leaven is never content with one corner. Go looking for it the Passover way, specifically, room by room, and bring it to Christ. And remember the order: you are not cleaning the house to earn the lamb. The lamb has been sacrificed, and that is why you clean.

For worship. Christ our Passover lamb was sacrificed for us. The Lamb chosen before the foundation of the world went willingly to the slaughter, and his blood is on the doorposts of every believer’s house. When the judgment of God passes through, it finds that death has already been there, and it passes over. We are spared, not because we were better than the Egyptians, but because the Lamb took our place. Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, for by his blood he ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 5:9, 12).
verseByVerse.note: Before Passover every Jewish household removed all leaven (yeast) from the house.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us therefore celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

Let us therefore celebrate the festival. It is an unexpected way to finish a paragraph about excommunication, and the choice of image tells you a great deal about how Paul understood the Christian life. The Passover was not a single evening. The lamb was killed, and then came seven days of unleavened bread, the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Exodus 12:15–20): a whole week of feasting that flowed out of the sacrifice. Paul takes that structure and applies it. Christ has been sacrificed, once, finished; and what follows is not a fast but a festival, and the festival is now. The Christian life is a continual feast: joyful, grateful, holy. A great many Christians would describe their faith in almost any terms other than feasting: duty, effort, struggle, a certain grimness endured in hope of better later. Paul says the sacrifice has been made, and the church is therefore at a feast, and the only question on the table is what is being served with it.

Not with the old leaven, the leaven of malice and evil. Then the striking thing, which catches every reader who is paying attention. Having spent seven verses on a case of gross sexual immorality, Paul names the leaven to be cleared out as malice and evil. Not immorality: malice. The word is kakia, ill will, the settled disposition to want someone’s harm; and evil is ponēria, active wickedness. Having every right to name the obvious sin, he names the one the congregation had not thought to look for, and it is the sin of the respectable. The man in verse 1 was one person. The malice was general, and it is what had made the church proud rather than grieving in the first place. This is the pattern all through the letter. The Corinthians were exercised about other people’s spectacular failures and entirely comfortable with their own settled unkindness. It is possible to be scrupulous about the sins one has no appetite for.

But with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Against that Paul sets two words. Eilikrineia, sincerity, means unmixed, unalloyed, with no second layer; it may come from the idea of something held up to the sunlight and found to have no flaw. And alētheia, truth, is the match between what a person is and what he appears to be. A life with no hidden yeast. Which makes the required cleansing far more searching than the removal of one man. A church can conduct discipline impeccably and still be full of the leaven this verse names: it can put out the immoral member and go on with its factions, its cold shoulders, its long-running grudges and its carefully maintained impressions.

What it does not mean. It does not mean holiness is a burden. It is a feast, a celebration of what Christ has done. Nor does sincerity mean saying every thought aloud; it means having no hidden agenda, no second face, no life behind the life.

What does malice look like in ordinary life? Rarely like open hatred. More often it is the small pleasure you feel when someone you dislike stumbles; the story you tell that makes another person look slightly worse; the grudge you keep fed by rehearsing it; the cold silence that punishes; the joke with an edge. It is wanting, even a little, for someone else not to do well. Paul lists it among the things to put away (Ephesians 4:31; Colossians 3:8), and the way to put it away is not only to stop but to replace it: to pray for that person’s good by name, to speak well of them when they are absent, and to forgive as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32).

How can holiness be a feast when it feels so hard? Because what you are putting away is the stale bread, and what you are given is better. The fight against sin is real, and it can be painful. But it is the struggle of someone clearing the table for a banquet, not of a prisoner breaking stones. Every sin you put away was a thief at the feast, taking your joy. The Lord who commands holiness is the Lord who spread the table, and he invites you to it with the words of the old prophet: come, buy and eat without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). Duty and delight are not opposites here. The command is to enjoy what Christ has done in the way that fits it.

In a sentence. Therefore let us keep the festival, not with the old bread leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

On a Tuesday. Live today as a celebration. Throw out the old yeast of grudges and hidden sins. Live openly, honestly, joyfully. And conduct the search the Passover way, room by room and for something specific. Not “am I broadly a decent Christian”, which nobody has ever answered usefully. Rather: is there a person whose difficulty would not entirely displease me? Is there a version of myself I keep up in public that those who live with me would not recognise? Those are leaven, in the two exact categories Paul names, and this is a feast, and the householder is expected to go looking with a lamp before he sits down (Matthew 23:25–28).

For worship. The sacrifice is finished and the feast has begun. The Lamb who was slain is also the Host at the table, and he has not invited his people to a fast of anxious striving but to a festival that will never end. One day it will be the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the bread there will have no trace of the old leaven in it at all. Even now, every honest, sincere, forgiving life is a few crumbs of that bread on earth, and every one of them was baked in his kindness.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul clarifies what he wrote in an earlier letter about not associating with sexually immoral people. He did not mean people of this world who are immoral, greedy, swindlers or idolaters; to avoid them entirely they would have to leave the world. He meant that they must not associate with anyone who calls himself a brother or sister but lives in sexual sin or greed, worships idols, slanders, gets drunk or swindles, and they should not even eat with such a person. It is not Paul’s business to judge outsiders; God will judge them. But the church must judge those inside it, and, as the law says, expel the wicked person from among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Church’s Jurisdiction and God’s Jurisdiction

Paul’s distinction between inside and outside the community (v. 12–13) defines the scope of church discipline with precision. The church is not called to police the world; it is called to maintain the integrity of its own fellowship. “God judges those outside” — this is not indifference to the world’s sin but a recognition that the church is not the world’s court of law. The church’s mission to the world is evangelism, not judgment; its internal discipline is precisely what enables it to be a credible witness in the world it is trying to reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul had already written a previous letter (now lost) on this subject, and the Corinthians had misapplied it. Misapplied teaching on holiness tends in two directions: either becoming a withdrawal sect (refusing all contact with sinful unbelievers) or collapsing into permissiveness (refusing all internal accountability). The Corinthians had managed both: they read the earlier letter as a call to leave the world, and they were lax about discipline inside the church. Now: The same confusion persists: churches that are either socially withdrawn from the world (failing at evangelism) or internally undisciplined (failing at community). Paul’s answer is a third way: engaged with the world in love, honest with the community in accountability.

verseByVerse.quote: I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people— not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters, since then you would need to go out of the world.

I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people. The letter in question is not in our Bibles. Paul had written to Corinth before this, and the document is lost. “Associate” is synanamignymi, to mix together with: close, ongoing fellowship. The command itself was clear enough. What we have is the Corinthians’ misreading of it, and the misreading is instructive.

Not at all meaning the sexually immoral of this world. Told not to associate with the sexually immoral, they had apparently applied it to Corinth at large, perhaps deliberately, so that the instruction became impossible and could be ignored altogether. Paul’s correction is dry to the point of comedy. He did not mean the people of the city. He meant something nearer home.

Or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. Paul widens the list. The greedy (pleonektai) are those who always want more, at others’ expense. Swindlers (harpages) are robbers and extortioners, people who grab. Idolaters are worshippers of false gods. He sets sins of money and of worship alongside sexual sin, and that should stop us from ever treating sexual sin as the only kind that counts. A church that would discipline adultery but never greed has not read this verse.

Since then you would need to go out of the world. He is pointing out that the policy is unworkable. In that city, a rule of no contact with immoral people would empty the market, the workshop, the street and most families. You would have to leave, which some later Christians duly tried, taking themselves off to the desert, and which every separatist movement since has attempted in some form. And notice what Paul does not do. He does not say: it would be admirable but impractical. He rules it out as a misunderstanding of the command. The Christian is not meant to withdraw from unbelievers, and the whole New Testament is against it. The Lord prayed not that his disciples should be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one in it (John 17:15). He himself was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, which was intended as an insult and was simply an accurate description of how he spent his time (Matthew 11:19). And Paul will shortly tell this church to accept dinner invitations from pagan neighbours (10:27).

Strict and open in the wrong places. Here is what makes this passage permanently useful: the shape of the Corinthian error. They were strict where they should have been open, and open where they should have been strict. Rigorous, in theory, with outsiders who had never professed anything; entirely relaxed about a member living in public sin. Precisely inverted. That inversion is not a first-century curiosity. It is the standing temptation of religious communities, and it runs both ways. There are churches that are ferocious about the sins of the surrounding culture, well informed, indignant, quick to denounce, and unable to have a hard conversation with one of their own. And there are churches so anxious not to seem judgmental that they have no internal accountability at all, while being quietly disdainful of the world they are supposed to be reaching.

Where Christians differ: the lost letter. Some argue that if an apostolic letter was lost, the New Testament canon must be incomplete. Verdict: Not everything an apostle wrote was meant by God to be Scripture for the whole church in all ages. God, in his providence, preserved exactly the books he intended to be the canon (Westminster 1.2, 1.8). The canon is closed and complete, sufficient for all faith and life (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The lost letter’s point is preserved here anyway.

Does a lost letter mean part of the Bible is missing? No. Paul, like any pastor, wrote a great deal that was true and useful and not meant to be Scripture: notes, arrangements, greetings, earlier instructions. Inspiration is not a claim that every sentence Paul ever wrote was meant for the canon. What God intended his church to have, he gave and preserved, and nothing we need for salvation or for godly living has been lost. You can open your Bible with full confidence that it is the complete word God meant you to have.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should approve of the world’s sins, or join in them. It means they should not try to escape the world, but live in it as witnesses, distinct in life and close in love.

Can I have close friends who are not Christians? Yes, and you should. Jesus did. Friendship is one of the main ways the gospel travels. What Scripture warns against is being bound together with unbelievers in ways that pull you away from Christ: being unequally yoked (2 Corinthians 6:14), which applies most clearly to marriage, and letting bad company corrupt good morals (15:33). So ask two questions about any friendship. Am I influencing them toward Christ, or are they drawing me away from him? And would I be free to speak of Christ, and to say no to sin, in their company? If the answers are good, enjoy the friendship and pray for your friend.

In a sentence. Paul wrote to you in his letter not to associate with sexually immoral people, not at all meaning the people of this world who are immoral, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world.

On a Tuesday. Do not hide from unbelievers. Love your non-Christian neighbours, colleagues and friends, and be salt and light among them. Here is a test, and it shows which error is yours. Count your actual friendships, not acquaintances or colleagues but people whose houses you have been in, and ask how many of them are not Christians. If the honest answer is none, you have drifted out of the world in the way this verse forbids, whatever your theology of engagement says. Then ask when you last spoke, kindly and directly, to a fellow believer about something that was doing them harm. Most of us find one of those two answers uncomfortable, and which one it is tells us which half of Paul’s correction we needed (John 17:15–18).

For worship. The Son of God did not keep his distance from sinners. He came into the world, ate at their tables, touched their lepers, and let a woman of the city weep on his feet, and he was never once stained by any of it. His holiness was not the fragile kind that has to hide; it was the kind that heals what it touches. He has sent his people into the same world in the same way: as the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you (John 20:21). We are not taken out of the world, because he means to save people in it, and he goes with us.
verseByVerse.note: The earlier letter Paul mentions has not survived.

verseByVerse.quote: But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother if he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler—not even to eat with such a one.

But now I am writing to you not to associate with anyone who bears the name of brother. Now the command itself, and the decisive words are “bears the name of brother”. That is the whole distinction. Not the immoral of the world, who have professed nothing, but the person inside, who calls himself a Christian, claims to belong to Christ, and whose life publicly contradicts it. The separation is from professing believers who live in open, unrepentant sin.

If he is guilty of sexual immorality or greed, or is an idolater, reviler, drunkard, or swindler. Look at the list, because it is more uncomfortable than we let it be. Paul adds two names to his earlier list: reviler (loidoros, one who abuses others with words, a verbal bully) and drunkard (methysos). These describe a pattern of life, not a single fall. And sitting in the middle of the catalogue, between an idolater and a drunkard, is the man with a vicious tongue. Paul has put the church member who savages people verbally in the same list as the man in verse 1, and greed beside them both. We would never have compiled it that way, and that is the point. A congregation will act on scandal and will tolerate a reviler for thirty years.

Not even to eat with such a one. In that world a shared table was not a casual arrangement. It was the public sign of acceptance, friendship and common life. And the reference very probably includes the church’s own meal, the gathering at which the Lord’s Supper was taken, as well as ordinary social meals. The church must not carry on as if nothing were wrong. The man is to find that the fellowship whose signs he has been receiving is closed to him, precisely so that he notices that something is wrong and feels the seriousness of his sin (2 Thessalonians 3:14–15).

About the unrepentant, not the struggling. Two guards are essential here, because this verse has done real damage in careless hands. The first: this is about the unrepentant, not about the struggling. Nothing here touches the Christian who is fighting a sin and losing, who is ashamed, who keeps confessing and keeps failing. That person is not a candidate for this passage; he is a candidate for Galatians 6:1, restoration by the spiritual in a spirit of gentleness. The category Paul is describing is settled, public and defended: a man who has decided, and who expects the church to accommodate it. If you are reading this with a guilty conscience about a sin you hate, this verse is not about you, and the fact that you hate it is the proof.

The church’s table, not the family’s bonds. The second guard: this concerns the church’s corporate fellowship, and it is not a licence to destroy natural bonds. Paul is regulating the assembly’s table, not abolishing the duties of a parent, a child or a spouse, and the New Testament never asks anyone to stop loving their family. Notice too what he does not say. He does not say have no contact, cut him off, or refuse to speak. When he writes about a similar case elsewhere he gives the tone explicitly: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). That sentence should govern the whole practice. The aim is not to make the person feel hated. It is to make the contradiction unmistakable: to withdraw the signal that everything is fine, while leaving no doubt that he is wanted back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean refusing all contact, or treating him as an enemy. Family members still have family duties. It means the church withdraws the normal signs of Christian fellowship until there is repentance. And it does not mean any individual Christian may decide on his own to shun someone; this follows the church’s proper process.

Must I stop having meals with a grown-up child who professes faith and lives in serious sin? No. Paul is speaking about the church’s fellowship, not about the bond between parent and child, which God himself made. You may and should go on loving your child, having them in your home, and caring for them. What changes is that you cannot pretend all is well with their walk with Christ. Speak honestly, and more than once, but not at every meal; pray without ceasing; and keep the door wide open. If the church has acted, support its discipline by not treating it as unimportant, while showing your child that your love has not moved an inch. That is the very balance Paul asks for: warn him as a brother.

Am I a “reviler” if I lose my temper? Not in the sense Paul means. Every Christian sins with his tongue (James 3:2), and a believer who loses his temper, is grieved, apologises and fights it is not the person in this list. The reviler is someone whose pattern of life is verbal abuse: who habitually belittles, demeans, intimidates or rages at others, and who sees nothing wrong with it. That pattern is serious enough to call for discipline, and it is especially serious in a home, where words can be a form of abuse. If you recognise yourself in that description, do not wait to be confronted. Confess it to God and to those you have hurt, seek help, and put it away.

In a sentence. But now Paul is writing to you that you must not associate with anyone who claims to be a brother or sister but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or slanderer, a drunkard or swindler. Do not even eat with such people.

On a Tuesday. Pray for anyone you know who calls himself a Christian but lives in open sin. Pray for genuine repentance, and ask yourself whether your friendship has quietly signalled to him that everything is fine. This is a difficult thing to do well, and it is the reason the chapter began by asking for grief rather than outrage. Only mourners can be trusted with this. Anybody who finds it satisfying should not be doing it (Galatians 6:1).

For worship. The table from which the unrepentant are kept back is the Lord’s own table, and it is holy because of the One who spread it. He paid for every seat with his body and blood, and he guards it, not to keep sinners away, for every guest at it is a forgiven sinner, but to keep it what it is: a feast of reconciliation, not a place to pretend. And he keeps his place at the head of it, waiting for every wandering brother to come back, with a robe and a ring and a fattened calf.

verseByVerse.quote: For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? God judges those outside. “Purge the evil person from among you.”

For what have I to do with judging outsiders? Paul draws the boundary in a single sentence, and it settles the jurisdiction. Outsiders are unbelievers. It is not the church’s job to discipline the world. The church is answerable for the church. The world is answerable to God directly, and he needs no assistance. This is not indifference to the world’s sin: the same apostle will describe the judgment of God on human wickedness at length in Romans 1. It is a recognition that the church has not been appointed the world’s magistrate. Our commission to those outside is announcement, not enforcement: we tell them what God has done in Christ. Their accounts are not ours to audit.

Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge? The church is responsible for its own members. “Judge” here means to exercise discipline, to assess conduct by God’s word and act on it, not to condemn anyone eternally. Belonging to a church is not a private arrangement between a believer and God; it is joining a family that has promised to watch over one another.

God judges those outside. Unbelievers are in God’s hands. He will judge them, rightly, at the last day. And there is a practical release in that which many Christians need. A great deal of religious energy is spent being indignant about people who never claimed to be anything else: monitoring the culture, keeping score, keeping up a running commentary on the sins of those outside. Paul’s question is quietly deflating: what have I to do with judging outsiders? Not your court. Our task toward them is to preach the gospel, and the hours are better spent on that.

Purge the evil person from among you. Then the closing citation, which Paul has been building towards. It comes from Deuteronomy, where the phrase recurs like a refrain (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7; 19:19; 22:21, 24; 24:7), used when Israel had to remove a serious offender. Israel was a nation as well as a covenant people, and there the purging was often capital: the offender was put to death, and the community was cleansed by his removal. Notice what Paul does with it. He keeps the seriousness and changes the penalty. The church is not a state, holds no sword, and executes nobody; what it can do is exclude. So the new covenant form of this command is at once as grave as the old and far more merciful, because a man put outside the camp can come back, and a man stoned outside the camp cannot. The whole of discipline in the New Testament is a death sentence commuted to a temporary exclusion, with the door left unlocked.

Outside the gate. And that is not an accident of temperament. It is a consequence of the sacrifice in verse 7. The reason the church does not need to purge anybody with a stone is that the death the covenant required has already been died, by someone else, once. The pattern of Deuteronomy is that the evil is taken outside the camp and dealt with there, and the people are made clean. And there was a day when someone was led out of the city, in the name of the community’s purity, and executed outside the walls between two criminals. He was not the evil person. He was the only one in the story who was not, and he went out anyway, in the place of the man in verse 1 and the arrogant congregation in verse 2 and every reader of this page. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not speak out about sin in society, or that the church has no prophetic voice. Christians may and should speak for justice, for the unborn, for the poor, for marriage, and they may vote and serve as citizens. It means church discipline applies only to church members, and that the church does not try to govern the world by its own discipline.

How does this fit with “Judge not”? They are about different things. In 4:5 Paul forbids passing verdicts on the hidden purposes of the heart, which only the Lord can see. Jesus forbids the hypocrite’s censorious judging, and tells him to take the log out of his own eye so that he can see clearly to help his brother (Matthew 7:1–5). Here Paul requires the church to deal with the open, unrepentant conduct of someone who claims to be a brother. Christians must not judge hearts; they must judge conduct by Scripture, inside the church, humbly and for the sinner’s good.

So how should I treat a non-Christian who lives in the sins on Paul’s list? With love, honesty and patience, as someone who needs the same Saviour you needed. Do not expect him to live by a standard he has never accepted, and do not make his morals the first subject you raise. His deepest problem is not his behaviour but that he does not yet know Christ, and the gospel is what changes behaviour. Be his friend, be honest when he asks what you believe, and pray for him. If he comes to faith, then he will come under the church’s care and its call to holiness, and he will find, as every Christian has, that the Lord who calls us to purity also gives the power for it (6:11).

In a sentence. What business is it of Paul’s to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside? God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked person from among you.”

On a Tuesday. Hold yourself and fellow believers to God’s standard. Be gentle and gracious with unbelievers, who do not yet know Christ. If you notice that most of your moral energy this week has gone on people outside the church, a politician, a celebrity, a neighbour’s lifestyle, turn some of it inward: to your own heart first, and then to the loving care of your own church family.

For worship. The purging that actually cleansed the people of God was not the removal of a sinner from the assembly. It was the Lamb, carried out through the gate at Passover, bearing in his body the judgment that belonged inside the camp. The Holy One was counted with the transgressors, so that transgressors might be counted among the holy. Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured (Hebrews 13:13), for the Lord who was cast out for us has made a home for us where no one who trusts him will ever be put out again.

6.title: Lawsuits, Liberty, and the Temple of the Spirit
6.overview:
Two more problems show the Corinthians living by the standards of their city rather than of Christ. First, church members were suing each other in the public courts. In Roman Corinth, civil litigation was a contest of status: the wealthy and well connected usually won, and lawsuits were a way to humiliate rivals. Paul is appalled that believers, who will one day judge the world and even angels, cannot settle disputes among themselves, and that they would rather drag one another before unbelieving judges than suffer wrong. He reminds them that the unrighteous, including thieves and swindlers, will not inherit God’s kingdom, and that some of them used to be exactly that, before they were washed, made holy and justified in Christ by the Spirit.

Second, some were using slogans like “all things are lawful for me” and “food for the stomach and the stomach for food” to justify sleeping with prostitutes, as if what the body does did not matter to the soul. Paul answers that the body belongs to the Lord and will be raised. A believer’s body is a member of Christ, and union with a prostitute makes the two one flesh. So they must run from sexual immorality. Their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit; they are not their own; they were bought at a price, and must honour God with their bodies.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul is shocked that when a believer has a dispute with another, he dares to take it before unbelieving judges instead of before God’s people. Do they not know that the saints will judge the world, and even angels? Then surely they are competent to settle everyday matters. Why appoint as judges those whom the church has no reason to respect? Is there really no one wise enough among them to decide between brothers, so that brother sues brother in front of unbelievers? The very fact that they have lawsuits against each other is already a defeat. Why not rather be wronged or cheated? Instead they themselves wrong and cheat, and they do it to their own brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Saints Will Judge the World: Present Implications

Paul’s argument from eschatology — “do you not know that the saints will judge the world?” (v. 2) — is a characteristic move: the future reality of the believer’s status shapes present behaviour. The saints who will participate in Christ’s eschatological judgment (Dan 7:22; Rev 20:4) have already, in their union with Christ, been granted a dignity that makes recourse to pagan courts for petty disputes absurd. The inconsistency Paul exposes is not merely practical but theological: why would those destined for cosmic judicial authority submit their neighbourhood disputes to judges who do not acknowledge Christ?
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Roman legal culture in Corinth was a social arena where disputes were used to assert status and damage opponents. Going to court was not merely a legal act but a social strategy. Paul refuses the framework: the cross creates a community in which the willingness to absorb loss is a greater display of power than the ability to win in court. Now: The Christian instinct to reach for legal remedies when wronged by a fellow believer is understandable but reveals how deeply the world’s categories of justice and self-protection have shaped us. Paul’s question — “Why not rather suffer wrong?” — is among the most countercultural sentences in the NT.

verseByVerse.quote: When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?
verseByVerse.commentary:
When one of you has a grievance against another, does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases?

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 6 deals with two more failures that show the Corinthians had not grasped what it means to belong to Christ. First, believers were suing one another in pagan courts. Paul is appalled: the saints will one day judge the world and even angels, so they ought to be able to settle disputes among themselves; better still, they should be willing to be wronged rather than wrong a brother (vv. 1–8). Second, he reminds them that the unrighteous, the sexually immoral, idolaters, thieves, the greedy and others, will not inherit God’s kingdom. Some of them had been such people, but they have been washed, sanctified and justified in Christ and by the Spirit (vv. 9–11). Third, he takes apart the Corinthian slogans that excused sexual sin: all things are lawful, food for the stomach. The body is for the Lord. It will be raised; it is joined to Christ; it is a temple of the Holy Spirit; it was bought with a price. So flee sexual immorality and glorify God in your body (vv. 12–20). Everything in the chapter hangs on what Christ has done and who he has made his people: future judges of the world, washed sinners, limbs of his own body, a purchased possession in which God himself has come to live.

The setting. Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt. Lawsuits were often used by the wealthy and powerful against those of lower status, and judges could be swayed by bribes or social rank. Roman civil litigation in a provincial city was not first of all a search for justice; it was an arena in which social standing was asserted and rivals were damaged. The wealthy man with connections and a hired advocate generally won, and everybody knew it. Taking a brother to court was a way of shaming him publicly, and of using your position against somebody with less of it.

When one of you has a grievance against another. “Grievance” is pragma, a matter, a case: a civil dispute, probably about property or money (v. 7). So when the Corinthians took their disputes to court, they were not merely choosing an inconvenient venue. They were importing into the church the exact mechanism by which the powerful of that city kept the weak in their place, which is what this whole letter has been about since the first chapter, where not many were powerful and not many were of noble birth (1:26).

Does he dare go to law before the unrighteous instead of the saints? “Dare” is tolmaō: to have the audacity, the nerve. Paul is not opening with an argument; he is opening with astonishment that anyone would think of it. “The unrighteous” is not name-calling. It is Paul’s standing category for those outside Christ, unbelieving judges outside God’s people, and he uses it to make a point about competence. These judges do not share the standard by which the case ought to be decided. They can apply Roman law. They cannot ask what love requires, or what the cross makes fitting between two brothers. The saints, fellow believers in the church, can.

Or do you not know that the saints will judge the world? Then the argument from the greater to the lesser. This is one of six times in this chapter that Paul asks, do you not know? (vv. 2, 3, 9, 15, 16, 19). It is a startling claim, and Paul assumes they have been taught it. Its roots are in Daniel’s vision, where judgment is given to the saints of the Most High (Daniel 7:22), and in the Lord’s own promise that his followers would sit on thrones (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 20:4). At the last day believers will share in Christ’s judgment of the world. Their part in it is not independent authority but a consequence of union with Christ: where he sits, those who are in him sit.

And if the world is to be judged by you, are you incompetent to try trivial cases? The word for trivial is the smallest available: everyday disputes, tiny compared with the last judgment. Paul’s logic is simple and unanswerable. People appointed to a share in the final judgment cannot plausibly claim they are unqualified to sort out a disputed debt. And that quietly exposes the real problem, which was not competence. A church that could produce men wise enough to settle the matter was choosing not to, because at least one party did not want a fair settlement. He wanted to win, and the court was where winning was available.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never use the courts, or that crimes should not be reported to the authorities. Paul himself appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and Romans 13 gives the state authority to punish wrongdoers. Paul is speaking of civil disputes between believers.

What about legal processes that are not one brother suing another? Paul condemns a believer taking another believer to court to win a private grievance without first letting the church settle it. An insurance claim, the legal formalities of a divorce that has biblical grounds, probate and similar matters are not what he is describing. And if a fellow member refuses every attempt at reconciliation and church judgment, Jesus says he is to be treated as one outside the church (Matthew 18:17); the believer is then no longer suing a brother who is acting as a brother. Even then, verse 7 still asks whether it might be better simply to suffer the wrong.

Does “the saints will judge the world” mean believers decide who is saved? No. Salvation and condemnation belong to God alone, and Christ is the Judge (John 5:22; Acts 17:31). Scripture does not give us the details of how the saints share in his judgment. It most likely means that, united with Christ, they will reign with him, agree with his verdicts and take part in them as his people, the way the twelve are promised thrones (Matthew 19:28). It is not a licence to pronounce on anyone’s eternal destiny now. Its purpose here is to show the Corinthians how great their calling is, and how small their quarrels look beside it.

In a sentence. If any of you has a dispute with another, do you dare to take it before the ungodly for judgment instead of before the Lord’s people? Or do you not know that the Lord’s people will judge the world? And if you are to judge the world, are you not competent to judge trivial cases?

On a Tuesday. If you have a dispute with a fellow Christian, go to them first, and then to wise believers, before going public. And here is a test for any Christian in a dispute with another. Ask whether you are looking for a resolution or for a verdict. They are not the same thing, and you can usually tell which you want by noticing whether you would accept an outcome in which nobody was declared right. The Corinthians had access to brothers who could have helped them. They preferred a venue that would produce a loser.

For worship. The Judge of all the earth has promised to share his throne with people who were once in the dock. The saints who will judge the world are sinners whom Christ took out of condemnation, clothed in his righteousness and seated with himself. He was judged by an unrighteous court so that they might sit in a righteous one, and the dignity he gives them is not earned but inherited. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood, and made us a kingdom, be glory and dominion for ever (Revelation 1:5–6).
verseByVerse.note: Roman civil courts were public, costly and often corrupt; lawsuits were a way for the powerful to win status.

parallels.desc: judgment was given for the saints of the Most High

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that we are to judge angels? How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life!

Do you not know that we are to judge angels? Paul drops it in as though it were common knowledge, which tells us it had been part of his teaching at Corinth. It is one of the most extraordinary throwaway lines in the New Testament, and he does not stop to explain it. Which angels? Almost certainly the fallen ones: the beings Peter describes as committed to chains of gloomy darkness to be kept until the judgment, and Jude in the same terms (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). There is a day appointed for their sentencing, and Paul says believers will have a part in it. Believers will share in Christ’s judgment even of them. It is an astonishing dignity.

The measure of it. Take the measure of that for a moment. These are creatures of an order above us: older, stronger, without bodies, with a knowledge of the created order no human being has ever approached. The Corinthians were being intimidated in a provincial courtroom by men with money and social connections. Paul reminds them that they are destined to sit in judgment on beings beside whom a Roman magistrate is nothing whatever. The powers that have terrorised the human race since Eden will one day stand before the Lamb, and his people will be seated with him.

How much more, then, matters pertaining to this life! The phrase is biōtika: the ordinary business of living, money, property, contracts, boundaries, the stuff of daily life. If you will judge angels, you can handle property disputes. And notice how Paul uses this vast claim. Not to make them feel important: this whole letter is an assault on their sense of importance. He uses it to make their behaviour look absurd. People with that future are squabbling over these things in front of pagans.

The disconnection Paul attacks. Most of us never think in these terms at all. We have a working sense of our own significance, and it is built almost entirely out of present things: the job, the income, the standing among people whose opinion we track. Scripture’s account of what a believer is destined for has almost no grip on an ordinary week. That is precisely the disconnection Paul is attacking. He is not asking them to feel grand. He is asking them to let the size of the future put the present in proportion, because a man who genuinely believed he would one day share in the judgment of angels would find it very hard to keep up a two-year grievance about a boundary wall.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will be judges independently of Christ. They share in his judgment, as his people united to him. Nor does it mean believers are greater than angels in themselves; it means that in Christ, the Son who became man, redeemed humanity is raised to a place the angels serve (Hebrews 1:14; 2:5–9).

Will we judge the holy angels too? There is no hint of that. The holy angels have never sinned, and they serve God’s people now (Hebrews 1:14). Paul is most probably thinking of the fallen angels who await judgment. Some think the word “judge” here also includes the idea of ruling, so that redeemed humanity, in Christ, will have a place of honour over the whole created order. Either way, Scripture does not give us details, and it is wise not to build theories on one sentence. The point is clear without them: your future is so great that your present quarrels should look small.

In a sentence. Do you not know that we will judge angels? How much more the things of this life!

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing that has most occupied your mind this week: the slight, the money worry, the argument you keep re-running. It is almost certainly a matter pertaining to this life. Not unimportant; Paul does not say these things do not matter, only that they are the small end of the scale. Then set beside it the sentence in this verse. There is a courtroom coming in which you will be seated, in Christ, over powers that have troubled the human race since Eden. The contrast is not meant to shame you for caring about your week. It is meant to loosen its grip (Romans 8:18).

For worship. God has destined his people for such dignity that they will judge angels. The Son of God did not take hold of angels, but of the offspring of Abraham (Hebrews 2:16): he became one of us, not one of them, and in him human nature has been lifted above the heavens. The one who was made for a little while lower than the angels is now crowned with glory and honour, and those he is bringing to glory will share his throne. Not one of them deserved it. All of them will have it.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you have such cases, why do you lay them before those who have no standing in the church? I say this to your shame.
