No. Desire for one’s husband or wife is part of the good creation; God made the man and the woman, brought them together, and they were naked and not ashamed (Genesis 2:25). A whole book of the Bible, the Song of Songs, celebrates married love without embarrassment. What is sinful is desire turned toward someone who is not your spouse, or desire allowed to rule rather than serve. Paul’s point is that God has given a holy place for this desire, and that pretending to be above it does not make a person more spiritual; it makes him more vulnerable.

In a sentence. Now for the matters you wrote about: “It is good for a man not to have sexual relations with a woman.” But since sexual immorality is occurring, each man should have sexual relations with his own wife, and each woman with her own husband.

On a Tuesday. If you are married, notice whether you have quietly absorbed the Corinthian slogan: whether some part of you thinks the physical side of your marriage is less holy than the praying side, something to be tolerated rather than given thanks for. Give thanks for it instead, out loud, to God. And if you are single, notice whether you have absorbed the opposite lie of Corinth’s other party: that desire must be obeyed. Neither is the gospel. The body is for the Lord, in the marriage bed and outside it.

For worship. God is not embarrassed by the bodies he made. He formed the man from the dust and the woman from his side, and he looked on what he had made and called it very good. He invented the delight of a husband and wife in one another, and he guards it with his law because he values it, not because he grudges it. And the same God took a body himself: the Son was born, ate, slept, wept and was laid in a tomb, and rose again in a body that the disciples could touch. Every human body is honoured by that. The Lord who wrote this chapter for anxious Corinthians is not a cold lawgiver measuring how little pleasure his people can survive on. He is the Creator who gives his children all things richly to enjoy, and the Redeemer who bought the whole of them, body included, to be his own.
verseByVerse.note: From here Paul answers questions the Corinthians had sent him in a letter. The ESV notes that “to have sexual relations” is literally “to touch.” The quoted saying was probably a slogan of some at Corinth.

parallels.desc: it is not good that the man should be alone

verseByVerse.quote: The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights, and likewise the wife to her husband. For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does.

The husband should give to his wife her conjugal rights. “Conjugal rights” is literally what is owed (opheilē), a debt word. Paul is describing an obligation each spouse has toward the other, not a claim each has on the other, and the difference is the whole verse. Sexual relations in marriage are a duty each spouse owes the other. And notice who is addressed first: the husband, and his duty to his wife. In a world where a man’s desires were assumed to be the point, Paul begins with what a husband owes.

And likewise the wife to her husband. Complete mutuality. Each owes the other, in the same terms.

For the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does. “Have authority” (exousiazō) is the same verb Paul used in 6:12, where he refused to be dominated by anything. In marriage each gives the other a claim on their body. In the Greco-Roman world this first half was unremarkable. A wife’s body was understood to be at her husband’s disposal, and no one would have argued the point.

Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. The second half had no parallel anywhere. A husband’s body was his own; his liberties outside the marriage were assumed and largely unpoliced, with slaves, prostitutes and mistresses all quietly allowed for. Paul says a husband’s body belongs to his wife, in precisely the terms and with precisely the force that hers belongs to him. Read the two halves again and notice that they are exactly symmetrical. That single word likewise did more to dignify women than any legislation of the period. It establishes equal mutual belonging in the marriage bed. And it means the passage cannot be read as a charter for a husband’s demands, because whatever it grants him it grants her in the same breath and the same sentence.

What it does not mean. It does not mean either spouse may force or coerce the other. The passage is about giving, not taking. Love does not insist on its own way (13:5), and husbands must love their wives as Christ loved the church (Ephesians 5:25). Abuse is never justified by this verse. These verses have been used to do serious harm. They have been quoted to wives, usually by husbands and occasionally by pastors who should have known better, to argue that a woman has no right to refuse, that her consent is not required, that saying no is a sin. Some who read this page will have had this text used against them in exactly that way. It will not carry the weight. The whole framing is mutual: two people who have each given themselves away, each responsible for the other’s good. And the very next verse governs how this works in practice, and the governing phrase there is by agreement. A man who uses verse 4 to override his wife’s no has taken a verse about mutual self-giving and turned it into a lever, and he has quietly ignored the half of it that binds him.

If this verse was used against me, what do I do? First, hear it plainly: forced or pressured sex in marriage is not what Paul is describing, and it is not your duty to submit to it. It is a sin against you, and where it involves force or threat it is also a crime. You are not to blame for refusing it. Tell someone you trust, a pastor or elder, a wise friend, a doctor or counsellor, and if you are in danger, seek safety first and contact the authorities. A church that hears this should protect you, not send you back to explain yourself. And if you have carried guilt for years because a verse was twisted against you, lay it down. The Lord who wrote these words is the one who binds up the broken-hearted (Psalm 147:3), and he never handed anyone a lever.

The real teaching is more searching. The positive teaching is worth having plainly, because it is more demanding than the arguments people have about it. Marriage in the New Testament involves a real handing-over of the self, and it works only when both are doing it. The obligation is to give, and neither spouse is anywhere given permission to take. It is the marriage bed version of what Paul says of the whole church: in humility count others more significant than yourselves, looking not only to your own interests but also to the interests of others (Philippians 2:3–4).

In a sentence. The husband should fulfil his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body but yields it to her husband. In the same way, the husband does not have authority over his own body but yields it to his wife.

On a Tuesday. The test here is directional, and it is answerable. In your marriage, are you chiefly aware of what you are owed or of what you owe? Paul frames the entire subject in terms of a debt you carry toward the other person, and a marriage in which both are thinking that way has almost no room left for the arguments this passage usually gets dragged into. So ask yourself, this week, not whether your spouse is giving enough, but whether you are giving yourself to your spouse generously, or holding back. Love gives.

For worship. Behind the likewise of this verse stands a Bridegroom who did not insist on his rights. Christ had every claim on his bride and came to give rather than to take: he loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). He handed over his own body, on a cross, for a people who had given him nothing. Every Christian marriage in which a husband and wife yield themselves to each other is a small echo of that self-giving, and every marriage that falls short of it is still held inside a greater marriage that will not fail, where the Lamb has given everything and his bride is clothed in what he gave.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not deprive one another, except perhaps by agreement for a limited time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer; but then come together again, so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

Do not deprive one another. “Deprive” (apostereō) means rob or defraud, the same verb Paul used a chapter earlier of the Corinthians cheating their brothers in the law courts (6:7–8). To withhold yourself from your spouse is treated here as a kind of theft. That is strong, and it is worth sitting with, because withholding is one of the commonest instruments in an unhappy marriage and it is almost never named. It is deniable, requires no words, and can be maintained for years while both people pretend nothing is happening. Paul calls it fraud.

Except perhaps by agreement for a limited time. Then the single exception, and it comes with three conditions, every one of which limits it. By agreement: both, freely. This is the phrase that settles the argument raised at verse 4, because Paul’s picture is never one spouse deciding for the other. For a limited time: with an end, agreed in advance, not an indefinite drift. And for a spiritual purpose, which the next clause names.

That you may devote yourselves to prayer. A season of special prayer, perhaps with fasting. A positive spiritual purpose, not leverage, punishment, or the slow retreat that most such withdrawals actually are.

But then come together again. Paul assumes the resumption. Abstinence in marriage is the exception, not the rule: a parenthesis in a normal life, not a higher state to be aspired to.

So that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control. Paul names the danger without embarrassment. A marriage in which this has been allowed to lapse is a marriage with a door left open, and there is somebody who tries doors. Satan uses unmet desire to tempt to adultery and other sins. And notice that Paul does not say because of your sin. He says because of your lack of self-control, which is simply a statement about how human beings are made, offered without condemnation. He is being protective, not accusing. Paul is realistic about human weakness, and his realism is a form of love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean sexual relations are less spiritual than prayer. Both are good, and both are received from God with thanksgiving. It means that devotion to prayer should not become an excuse to neglect a spouse. And this verse is not a lever either. It is addressed to both, it requires agreement, and the man who quotes it at his wife has misunderstood it as thoroughly as the woman who ignores it. Nothing here permits pressure or coercion.

Two readers, two words. This verse lands very differently depending on where you are standing. To the one who has been quietly withholding, sometimes for reasons that felt entirely justified, because of hurt, or exhaustion, or a long-running grievance that was never resolved, this verse is a summons to say so out loud. Not to comply resentfully, which Paul asks for nowhere in this passage, but to stop conducting the argument in silence and have it in words. And to the one on the other side, who has been going without and has begun to feel foolish for minding: it is not foolish, and Scripture does not treat it as a trivial want. A verse of the Bible exists to say that this matters and that its absence is a danger to both of you.

What if one of us cannot, through illness, pain, trauma or age? Then this verse is not a rule to be enforced against a suffering spouse. Paul is addressing the deliberate withholding of a gift that could be given, not the inability to give it. Where there is physical illness, pain, the after-effects of childbirth, depression or past abuse, love will be patient and gentle, will seek medical and pastoral help, and will find other ways of tenderness. A husband who presses an unwell or traumatised wife is not obeying this verse; he is breaking the one before it. And the spouse who goes without for such reasons should take that longing to God honestly, and to a trusted counsellor if needed, rather than let it harden into resentment or wander elsewhere.

In a sentence. Do not deprive each other except perhaps by mutual consent and for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again so that Satan will not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.

On a Tuesday. The remedy Paul prescribes is not compliance. It is a conversation the two of you have been avoiding, and quite possibly a prayer you have never prayed together. If something has gone quiet in your marriage, name it gently this week, without accusation, and ask what the other needs. And if you are married, pray together, even briefly, even awkwardly. Husbands, live with your wives in an understanding way, so that your prayers may not be hindered (1 Peter 3:7).

For worship. The God of this verse watches over marriages with a jealous care. He knows the door that Satan tries, and he has not left his people to stand guard alone; he has given them each other, and given them prayer, and given them his Spirit. And he is the Bridegroom who never withholds. Christ does not give himself to his church by measure, or keep his love in reserve as a weapon, or go quiet in a grievance. His heart is open to his people always, and his intercession for them never lapses (Hebrews 7:25). Two are better than one, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken (Ecclesiastes 4:9–12), and the third strand in every Christian marriage is the Lord himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another.

Now as a concession, not a command, I say this. Paul stops to mark the status of what he has just written, and the habit is worth noticing because he keeps it up all chapter. He will distinguish the Lord’s charge from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25), and here he flags that the preceding advice is permission rather than obligation. “Concession” (syngnōmē) means allowance or permission. What is “this”? Most likely the permission to abstain for a time for prayer (v. 5): that is allowed, not required. Paul does not command it. Some take it more broadly of the marriage counsel in general. Either way, the point is that Paul is scrupulous about not binding consciences where God has not bound them, which is a discipline in short supply among religious teachers of every century.

I wish that all were as I myself am. Paul was unmarried as he wrote. Whether he had never married or was a widower, he does not say. As a former Pharisee, and if he was a member of a council that voted (Acts 26:10), he may once have been married, since such men usually were. He found singleness a great freedom for ministry, and he is honest that he considers his own state advantageous, for reasons he will give at length from verse 32.

But each has his own gift from God. Then the sentence that stops him from turning his preference into a rule, and it is the most important thing in these two verses. The word is charisma, a grace-gift, the same word Paul will use of the gifts of the Spirit in chapter 12. That means marriage is a gift and singleness is a gift. Paul does not say only singleness is a gift. Not one gift and one deficiency; two gifts, differently distributed, both from God.

One of one kind and one of another. God gives different callings to different people. That single word settles more than most of what is said about this subject in churches. A married Christian is not the standard from which single Christians are a variation, and a single Christian is not someone waiting in a corridor for real life to begin. Both are described here as people who have been handed something.

Where Christians differ: is celibacy holier? The medieval church came to treat celibacy as a higher, more spiritual state, and required it of clergy. Verdict: Paul values singleness highly, but he calls both singleness and marriage gifts from God. Neither is holier. Forbidding marriage is described as a teaching of demons (1 Timothy 4:1–3), and church leaders may be married (1 Timothy 3:2; 9:5). The Reformers rightly restored the honour of marriage, including for ministers. Each believer should seek to serve God in the calling he has given.

What it does not mean. It does not mean singleness is a gift only for those who feel no desire. It means God gives each person their present situation as his gift, to be used for him. A great deal of clumsy teaching has been built on this verse. Single Christians are regularly told they must have the gift of singleness, and the phrase is then used to mean that they should therefore not mind, and that wanting marriage is a failure to accept their gift. Many people hear this and think: then I do not have it, because I mind very much. But notice that Paul does not describe a gift of contentment with one’s state. He describes the state itself as the gift. The single Christian who longs to be married has not thereby forfeited or misidentified anything. He is simply a person in the condition God has him in, wanting something good that he does not have. That is not a spiritual failure. It is the ordinary experience of most people alive, married and unmarried both, about something.

How do I know whether I have the gift of singleness? If you are single today, you have it today; that is what Paul means by gift. The question is not a hidden feeling you must detect in yourself, which is unanswerable and produces only anxiety. It is the one Paul will put in verse 17: what is the life the Lord has assigned me now, and what does faithfulness in it look like? You may pray for marriage, look for it wisely and gladly receive it if God gives it; that too would be his gift. Some people find over years that God has given them a settled freedom in singleness (Matthew 19:11–12), and they may embrace it with joy. Neither path needs to be decided on a feeling.

In a sentence. Paul says this as a concession, not as a command. He wishes that all of you were as he is. But each of you has your own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that.

On a Tuesday. Whether you are single or married today, see it as God’s gift to you for now, and use it for him. Name one way your present state frees you to serve that the other would not, and do something with it this week. And if you are in a church, notice how you speak to and about those whose state differs from yours. One kind and another kind: both handed out by the same Giver.

For worship. God is not a reluctant distributor of leftovers. Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17), and he hands out lives the way the Spirit hands out gifts in the church: as he wills, to each one individually (12:11), with no one forgotten and no one given the wrong thing. The single believer and the married believer stand side by side in front of the same open hand. And the Son who received both gifts from his Father’s hand, the single life of a carpenter and preacher and the bride he is gathering for himself, lived the one perfectly and is preparing the other with infinite joy.

verseByVerse.quote: To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the unmarried and the widows I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

To the unmarried and the widows. The unmarried (agamoi) may mean widowers here, paired with widows, or all unmarried people. Paul repeats his own preference, and again as counsel rather than command.

I say that it is good for them to remain single, as I am. “Good” (kalos) means fine, fitting, admirable: not commanded, but a good option.

But if they cannot exercise self-control, they should marry. “Exercise self-control” (enkrateuomai) is a word used of athletes in training (9:25). If someone is not able to live a chaste single life, marriage is the right path, and there is no virtue in a heroic celibacy you cannot sustain.

For it is better to marry than to burn with passion. The sentence everyone remembers, usually quoted with a certain amusement. The verb is pyroō, to be on fire. Some have taken it of the fire of judgment, but the sense here is almost certainly the ordinary one: consuming desire that will not leave a person alone. Not burn in hell. Paul is entirely unembarrassed. If desire is running your life, marry; that is part of what marriage is for. Strong desire is a legitimate reason to marry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is a second-best choice for the weak. It means God has provided marriage for the many who are called to it. The verse is often read as though Paul regarded marriage as a licensed outlet for people of weak character. He is answering a question, in a context, about people who are already struggling, and his answer is the pastoral one, not the complete one. The apostle who wrote this also wrote that marriage images the union of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:32), which is the highest thing anybody has ever said about it.

Marriage will not put the fire out. More urgently, the verse is not a promise that marriage will solve the problem. A great deal of unhappiness has been caused by young Christians who read this verse as an instruction to marry quickly in order to have their desires resolved, and who then discover that marriage does not extinguish desire, does not guarantee a satisfying sexual life, and adds a second person with her own history, tiredness and struggles. Paul says marrying is better than burning. He does not say marrying will stop the fire. Lust is a matter of the heart, and a married man can still look at a woman with lustful intent (Matthew 5:28). Marriage is a God-given place for desire, not a cure for sin.

And what if marriage is not open to me? There is an honest word owed to the reader for whom this verse offers no route at all. Paul’s advice presupposes that marriage is available. For many it is not: through circumstance, through a lack of anyone godly to marry, through same-sex attraction, or through a spouse who is present but with whom this part of life has ended through illness. Such a reader can find this verse almost mocking: the remedy is named and the door is shut. Scripture does not pretend that is easy, and neither should we. What it does say is that no one has been promised the fulfilment of every legitimate desire in this life; that the Lord who requires this of some was himself a single man, tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15); and that his grace is said to be sufficient precisely where the thorn is not removed (2 Corinthians 12:9). That is not a tidy answer, and it is not meant to be. But it is better than the two things such readers are usually offered, which are a demand to feel differently and a promise God has not made. And God has a word for those the world counts as without a future: to the eunuchs who hold fast his covenant he promises a name better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that shall not be cut off (Isaiah 56:4–5).

How strong does desire have to be before I should look to marry? Paul is not setting a threshold; he is giving permission. If you find that the desire for intimacy is a constant pressure, that it drives you toward pornography or fantasy or compromise in relationships, that is a clear sign that you should prayerfully and actively seek marriage, and there is nothing unspiritual about doing so. Talk to mature believers, pray, and take sensible steps to meet godly people. At the same time, fight the sin now: marriage is not a reward for those who first become pure, but neither is the struggle a reason to marry the first person who is willing. Marry in the Lord (v. 39), and marry someone you can love for a lifetime.

In a sentence. Now to the unmarried and the widows Paul says: it is good for them to stay unmarried, as he does. But if they cannot control themselves, they should marry, for it is better to marry than to burn with passion.

On a Tuesday. If you are single and long to be married, bring that desire to God honestly, and do not be ashamed of it. If you are struggling, do not fight alone: tell one trusted Christian friend. And if you are married, ask how you can make your church a place where single people are neither pitied nor pressured, but welcomed into homes, prayed for by name, and trusted with real work.

For worship. The Lord knows the frame of every single believer reading this, for he knows our frame and remembers that we are dust (Psalm 103:14). He does not sneer at desire or demand that it vanish. He walked through this world as a single man, with every human longing, and he was without sin, so that he can sympathise and so that his perfect obedience can be counted to those who fall. And he has promised a marriage to every one of his people, the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–9), where no believer will be single and none will be alone. Whatever fire is burning now, it is burning in someone already betrothed to Christ, and the Bridegroom is coming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: To married believers Paul passes on the Lord’s own command: a wife should not separate from her husband, and if she does she must remain unmarried or be reconciled; and a husband must not divorce his wife. To others, in cases Jesus did not address, Paul gives his own apostolic instruction. A believer married to an unbeliever who is willing to stay should not divorce. The unbelieving spouse is made holy through the believer, and so are their children. But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so; the believer is not bound in such cases, for God has called us to peace. And who knows whether the believer may yet save the unbelieving spouse?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Command and Apostolic Judgment

Paul’s careful distinction in vv. 10 and 12 (“not I, but the Lord” vs. “I, not the Lord”) is a fascinating window into apostolic hermeneutics. It does not mean that vv. 12–16 are less authoritative Scripture — Paul is writing under inspiration. It means that vv. 10–11 apply a dominical teaching directly, while vv. 12–16 extend the principle to a situation Jesus did not address. Both are authoritative; they are transparent about their different relationship to the dominical tradition.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Divorce was common and easy in the Roman world, and Corinth’s fluid social culture made marriage instability familiar. The question of what to do in a mixed marriage — especially if the unbeliever wanted out — was live and urgent for many in the community. Now: The “Pauline privilege” continues to be one of the most practically significant and debated passages in NT ethics, applied to situations ranging from desertion to abuse. The governing principle — God has called you to peace — is a pastoral starting point, not a blank cheque.

verseByVerse.quote: To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord): the wife should not separate from her husband (but if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband), and the husband should not divorce his wife.

To the married I give this charge (not I, but the Lord). Paul is doing something specific: he is citing the recorded teaching of Jesus (Mark 10:9–12; Matthew 5:32; 19:6–9). The Lord had addressed this directly: whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery against her (Mark 10:11). Where Paul has a word from Christ he says so and rests on it. “Married” here means where both spouses are believers; he will deal with mixed marriages in verse 12.

The wife should not separate from her husband. “Separate” (chōrizō) was a common word for divorce at that time; there was little legal distinction in Greek and Roman practice between walking out and divorcing. And notice that Paul addresses the wife first. Under Roman law at Corinth a woman could initiate divorce, which she could not do under Jewish law, so Paul speaks to her directly, as a person with agency and responsibility. Some Corinthian women may have wanted to leave their husbands to live a more spiritual, celibate life, under the influence of the ascetic slogan of verse 1.

But if she does, she should remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. This parenthesis is the most practically important clause in the passage. If a believing wife does leave without biblical grounds, she has two options: stay single or be reconciled. She is not free to marry someone else. And notice what that concedes. Paul states the rule and then, in the same breath, deals realistically with its being broken. He does not pretend that a command settles what people will actually do. There will be separations; here is what to do when there has been one. And the door he leaves open is reconciliation. The situation is not treated as closed.

And the husband should not divorce his wife. “Divorce” (aphiēmi) means send away. The same rule for husbands. In Greek and Roman law, divorce was easy for both sexes, and among Jews the school of Hillel allowed a man to divorce his wife for almost any reason. Christ forbids it. What the passage will not support is the assumption most people actually live by, that a marriage may be ended because it has failed: because the love has gone, or the two have grown apart, or one of them is unhappy. Scripture never treats marriage as a contract that lapses when it stops delivering. Christ’s own reason is that God joined them, and what God has joined, let not man separate (Mark 10:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is ignoring the exception Jesus gave for sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9). He is giving the general rule, without listing every exception. Taken alone this passage says no exceptions. But it is not alone. The Lord himself, in Matthew’s record, adds one: except for sexual immorality. And Paul is about to add another in verse 15, where a believer is deserted by an unbelieving spouse. So the historic Protestant position, that Scripture permits divorce on those two grounds and no others, adultery and wilful desertion (Westminster 24.5–6), is built from the whole of what is written rather than from any one text, and it is the reading followed here. Nor does it mean a spouse must stay in danger. Separation for safety from abuse is not the same as seeking divorce, and church leaders and the authorities should help.

What about abuse? The charge that a wife should not separate does not require anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. Abuse is never to be tolerated in a Christian home or excused by a Christian church. Leaving to be safe is not the separation Paul forbids, and a church must never send a victim back to an abuser or counsel her to submit to violence, threats or cruelty. Abuse is a crime as well as a sin; it should be reported to the authorities, and the abuser should face the church’s discipline. Whether persistent, unrepentant abuse ends the marriage itself is a harder question. The grounds for divorce remain the two Scripture gives, adultery and desertion. But many Reformed pastors and church courts have judged that a spouse who makes the home unsafe and will not repent has in fact deserted the marriage while remaining under the same roof, abandoning every promise he made. That is a judgement about whether desertion has occurred, not a third ground, and it is weighty enough that it should be made with the elders of the church, never alone and never in a hurry. What is never in doubt is the first step: get safe.

May the innocent party remarry after adultery? Paul’s instruction to remain unmarried or else be reconciled is given to the one who has separated without grounds. Where a marriage has been broken by a spouse’s adultery, Jesus’ words in Matthew 19:9 imply that the innocent partner who divorces and remarries does not commit adultery, and the historic Protestant confessions conclude that remarriage is then permitted, as if the offending party were dead (Westminster 24.5). Others hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives, appealing to verse 39 and to Mark 10:11–12. The first view is the more likely, because Jesus’ exception would mean little if the marriage bond remained intact. Even then divorce is permitted, not commanded; forgiveness and reconciliation after adultery are often possible and always beautiful.

I have already remarried after a divorce that did not fit these grounds. What now? Do not break up the marriage you are in. A second wrong does not undo the first, and the vows you have now made are real vows before God. Repent honestly of any sin in how it began, without excuses and without endless self-punishment; receive Christ’s forgiveness, which is as full for this as for anything else; and set yourself to keep the vows you have made, faithfully, for life. If there are children or a former spouse affected, ask what you can still do to act justly and kindly toward them. Your pastor can help you think it through.

If you are divorced. The pastoral word matters more than the argument, because of who actually reads a page like this. If you are divorced, and particularly if you look back and know that your own sin was part of why, understand what this passage is and is not doing. It is telling the church what marriage is. It is not a sentence passed on you, and it does not put you outside the reach of what this letter has already said: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (6:11). That verse was written to people whose past included the things in the list, and it is not amended for the divorced. Divorce is not the one sin the New Testament leaves outside the reach of forgiveness, and a divorced believer is not on a permanent second tier before God. Any teaching that leaves a repentant believer with that impression has strayed from the gospel this same letter preaches. The command in verse 10 is for a marriage you are in. The mercy in 6:11 is for a life you have already lived.

In a sentence. To the married Paul gives this command (not he, but the Lord): a wife must not separate from her husband. But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.

On a Tuesday. If your marriage is hard, do not look for a way out; look for help. Seek counsel early, before the hardness sets, from a pastor or a wise older couple, and pray, and work toward reconciliation. Take the specific thing you keep arguing about and ask what your own part in it is. But if your marriage is not hard but dangerous, do not wait: get yourself and your children safe, and tell someone today.

For worship. Behind this charge is the faithfulness of God himself. He is the husband who did not divorce his people when they played the harlot; he sent Hosea to buy back an unfaithful wife as a picture of what he would do (Hosea 3:1). The LORD hates divorce because he is the God of covenant (Malachi 2:16), and he kept his covenant with a bride who broke it every day. And at the cross the Bridegroom paid the price of his bride’s unfaithfulness in his own body, so that she could be presented to him without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27). Every Christian who keeps a hard marriage is telling a small, true story about him. And every Christian whose marriage has broken, by their own fault or another’s, is held by a Husband who has never yet let go of anyone he took.
verseByVerse.note: Paul cites Jesus’ own teaching on divorce.

verseByVerse.quote: To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To the rest I say (I, not the Lord) that if any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him.

To the rest I say (I, not the Lord). The phrase alarms some readers, so it is worth being clear about what it does and does not mean. Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer after the wedding; the situation could hardly have arisen in Galilee. So Paul gives his own apostolic ruling. This does not mean it has less authority, or that Paul is offering a private opinion the church may take or leave. It means Paul cannot quote a saying of Jesus, but he speaks with the authority Christ gave him, and he will end the chapter claiming that he too has the Spirit of God (v. 40; 14:37). So the distinction is about the source of the teaching, not its authority. And its presence is a mark of Paul’s honesty: a lesser man would simply have asserted that the Lord had said it.

If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. In a city like Corinth people were converted out of pagan households, and very often one spouse believed and the other did not. What then? The believer is now joined for life to someone who does not share the thing that has become the centre of their life. Some new believers may have thought they must leave an unbelieving spouse, perhaps fearing they were defiled by the union. Paul’s answer is emphatic and it runs in one direction: stay. The condition is the only one: she consents to live with him. The believer is not to initiate the ending. If the unbeliever is content to remain, the marriage remains.

If any woman has a husband who is an unbeliever, and he consents to live with her, she should not divorce him. The identical instruction to the woman, in the same words, because the situation and the duty are symmetrical. And her situation was the harder. In the ancient world a wife was expected to follow her husband’s religion; a woman who turned from his household gods to Christ was in a hard place, and might be seen as disloyal or even subversive. But she should stay if he is willing.

Ezra reversed. The force of this is easy to miss unless you know what had happened before. There was an Old Testament precedent for exactly this situation, and it went the other way. When the returned exiles were found to have married foreign wives, Ezra had them put away, wives and children both, as an act of covenant faithfulness (Ezra 10:1–3). Any Jewish believer at Corinth would have known that story, and might reasonably have concluded that the holy thing to do was to end a marriage to a pagan. Paul reverses it. Under the new covenant the direction of contamination has changed, and the next verse will say why. Holiness is no longer a fragile thing to be protected by separation. It is a stronger thing that spreads.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers may marry unbelievers. Paul forbids that (v. 39; 2 Corinthians 6:14). He is speaking of those already married when one came to faith. Nor does it mean that a believer must remain in a home where he or she is being abused; the safety counsel on verses 10–11 stands for mixed marriages too.

What if my unbelieving spouse opposes my faith, but does not leave? Then stay, and be wise. Opposition is not desertion, and mockery or coldness, painful as they are, do not end a marriage. Paul assumes many believers were living with spouses who disliked the new faith. Keep worshipping and keep loving; do not use your faith as a weapon in arguments, and do not hide it either. Where your spouse forbids something Scripture does not require on a particular day, be flexible; where he or she demands what God forbids, gently and firmly obey God (Acts 5:29). Ask your church to stand with you in prayer and practical help. And if opposition becomes threats, control or violence, that is abuse, and you should seek safety and counsel at once.

In a sentence. To the rest Paul says this (he, not the Lord): if any brother has a wife who is not a believer and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her. And if a woman has a husband who is not a believer and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him.

On a Tuesday. If you are in that marriage now, and there are many, including some who became Christians after they married, the instruction is not to look for an exit, and not to treat the marriage as a mistake to be corrected. It is to stay, and to be the sort of husband or wife the rest of the New Testament describes, and to leave the outcome where verse 16 will put it. That is a hard assignment and it is not a hopeless one. Peter writes to precisely this reader and does not tell her to argue: they may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives (1 Peter 3:1–2). And if you are not in that marriage, pray this week by name for someone who is.

For worship. The God who once told Israel to separate from the nations has now come among the nations to make them his own. He is not afraid of contact with the unclean; he sent his Son into the world precisely to touch it. And he stations his people in pagan households not by accident but as an embassy, his light set on a stand in a dark house. The marriage that a frightened believer thought was an obstacle to discipleship may, in his providence, be its field. He is the Lord of the house as well as the church, and he has put one of his own beside every unbelieving husband and wife who is willing to stay.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus had not addressed marriages where one partner became a believer; Paul applies his authority as an apostle.

verseByVerse.quote: For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife, and the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.

For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife. This is the reason the believer is to stay, and it is a startling one. It is also widely misunderstood, so the first thing to establish is what it cannot mean. It does not mean the unbelieving spouse is saved. Paul settles that himself two verses later, where he wonders whether the believing partner may yet save their spouse (v. 16), which would be an odd thing to wonder about someone already saved. Nobody is redeemed by marriage. Salvation is not transmitted by association, and every person stands before God on their own. So what does “made holy” mean? The word is the ordinary one for sanctified: set apart. It means the unbeliever is set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing spouse. The believer was evidently worried that the union itself was defiling, that living with a pagan, sharing a bed and a table with someone outside the covenant, made the whole thing unclean and the children along with it. Paul says the influence runs the other way. The believer is not defiled by the marriage; rather, the marriage is sanctified, set apart, acceptable to God, honourable and undefiled. And the unbeliever is exposed every day to the gospel and to the influence of a godly spouse (v. 16).

And the unbelieving wife is made holy because of her husband. The same in reverse.

Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy. If the marriage were unclean, the children would be too. But the children of a believing parent are holy: set apart, under the influence of the gospel and a believer’s care, and in that sense distinct from the children of two unbelievers. They are not outsiders.

The direction of transfer. That reversal is worth pausing on, because it runs all through the Gospels. Under the old order, touching a leper made you unclean. When Jesus touched one, the leper was made clean (Mark 1:40–42). The direction of transfer changed when he arrived, and this verse is that same change applied to a mixed marriage in a Greek city. In the new covenant, holiness is not a delicate condition that contamination destroys; it is the stronger force in the room. If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump (Romans 11:16).

Where Christians differ: holy children and baptism. Some argue from this verse that the children of believers are in the covenant and should therefore be baptised as infants. Verdict: The verse says the unbelieving spouse is also made holy, yet no one would baptise an unbelieving spouse. So holy here cannot mean qualified for baptism. It means set apart in a special relation to God’s people and blessing. Baptism in the New Testament is for those who repent and believe (see on Acts 2:38–39). The app holds this credobaptist reading, while recognising with charity that paedobaptist brothers and sisters read the covenant signs differently. The verse was not written to settle that question, and it should not become the thing this chapter is about.

What it does not mean. It does not mean children of believers are automatically saved. They need to be born again and believe, like everyone else. But they are greatly privileged: they hear the gospel from their earliest days, are prayed for by name, and see what a Christian life looks like up close.

What about my children if my spouse is not a Christian? This verse was written for exactly your fear. Your children are not disadvantaged before God because only one parent believes; they are set apart, because you are there. Teach them the Scriptures as Timothy’s mother and grandmother did, apparently with a father who was a Greek (Acts 16:1; 2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15). Pray with them, take them to church where you can, and let them see the faith lived gently rather than argued with their other parent. Be honest that you and their father or mother see things differently, without belittling your spouse. And pray for their salvation, and for your spouse’s, with real hope.

The comfort of an anxious believer. What the verse is actually for is the comfort of an anxious believer, and that is how it should be preached. If you are the only Christian in your house, you have almost certainly wondered whether your family is somehow outside: whether your children are at a disadvantage, whether your marriage is a compromise God tolerates rather than blesses, whether the whole arrangement is second-best. Paul’s answer is that your household is set apart because you are in it. Your presence there is not a problem to be managed; it is the reason the place is holy.

In a sentence. For the unbelieving husband has been sanctified through his wife, and the unbelieving wife has been sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but as it is, they are holy.

On a Tuesday. If you are the only believer in your home, your presence matters. God has placed you there for your family’s good. So be present: not preaching at the table, but praying in the morning, kind in the evening, cheerful, honest and forgiving in between. Let your house see what a sanctified life looks like before they hear what one sounds like.

For worship. When Christ came, holiness began to run downhill into unclean places. He touched lepers and they were cleansed; he ate with sinners and they were forgiven; he took the defilement of the world upon himself on the cross and gave his own purity in exchange. That same overflowing holiness now runs through ordinary houses in which one person loves him. The Holy One is not threatened by the unclean. He is the One who makes clean, and he has never yet entered a house without blessing it.
verseByVerse.note: “Made holy” does not mean saved, but set within the sphere of God’s blessing through the believing partner.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. God has called you to peace.

But if the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. Paul has spent three verses telling the believer to stay. Now he deals with the case where staying is not in their power, and the tone changes entirely. “Separates” (chōrizō) means divorces, departs. If the unbeliever insists on leaving, permanently, do not try to force them to stay. Let them go. The believer is not to pursue, obstruct or fight to hold a marriage the other person has ended. That is a hard permission, and it is a permission, not an instruction to give up easily; the whole preceding paragraph assumes the believer wants the marriage to continue.

In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved. “Enslaved” (douloō) means bound as a slave is bound: ou dedoulōtai, not under bondage. The believer is not bound to the marriage. This is a strong word: the believer is free. At minimum, the deserted believer is freed from the obligation to keep the marriage going, from any duty to chase, or to remain in limbo indefinitely waiting.

God has called you to peace. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read God has called us to peace. Either way, God does not call believers to endless conflict trying to hold on to a spouse who has left. This is the clause that governs the whole verse, and it is easily hurried past. It means that where reconciliation is genuinely impossible, where the other person has gone and will not come back, God is not requiring you to conduct a war, or to live permanently in an unresolved conflict, or to keep hold of something being pulled out of your hands. There is a kind of pious tenacity that looks like faithfulness and is actually a refusal to accept a loss God has permitted. Paul releases the deserted believer from it. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all (Romans 12:18); and when it does not depend on you, peace is still your calling.

Where Christians differ: desertion and remarriage. Some say a deserted believer may separate but never remarry while the former spouse lives. Verdict: Not enslaved means the marriage bond is broken, and the deserted believer is free to remarry, in the Lord. Paul uses similar language about being free to remarry after a spouse’s death (v. 39; Romans 7:2–3). Scripture recognises two grounds for divorce with freedom to remarry: sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9) and wilful desertion by an unbelieving spouse that cannot be remedied by the church or civil authority (Westminster 24.6). Divorce is always a tragedy, and churches should handle each case with care and wise counsel. The reading matters enormously to real people, and it should not be left vague. To say a deserted person is not enslaved while still holding them to a bond they cannot escape and did not break would be a strange kind of freedom; the Reformers read it this way, and that reading is followed here. Those who read it more narrowly are not to be dismissed, but the deserted should not be left in limbo by a church afraid to say anything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer may push an unbelieving spouse to leave, or use this as an excuse to end a hard marriage.

What counts as desertion, and what if the one who left calls himself a Christian? Desertion is a settled, wilful abandonment of the marriage: leaving and refusing to return, or refusing to live as husband or wife at all, despite patient efforts at reconciliation. A row, a few weeks apart, or a spouse who is difficult but present is not desertion. And if the one who leaves professes faith, the church should treat it as a matter of discipline (Matthew 18:15–17): call him to return, and if he persists, he is to be treated as an unbeliever, and the same freedom follows. A spouse who makes the home unsafe through persistent, unrepentant abuse has, in the judgement of many Reformed churches, deserted the marriage while still living in it. In every such case the victim should seek safety first, and the counsel of the elders, and the church should not leave the deserted to decide alone.

The loneliest seat in church. A word to that reader, because this is one of the loneliest situations in church life. The person who has been left often carries a double burden: the desertion itself, and a persistent sense that a better Christian would have held the marriage together. They watch other people’s marriages and wonder what they failed to do. Read the verse again. Paul does not ask what you might have done differently. He does not treat the departure as evidence about you. He addresses you as someone who has had something done to them, releases you from the obligation to fix what you did not break, and tells you that the God who called you called you to peace, which is precisely what you have been unable to feel, and precisely what he intends you to have.

In a sentence. But if the unbeliever leaves, let it be so. The brother or the sister is not bound in such circumstances; God has called us to live in peace.

On a Tuesday. If you have been left, let the church carry some of it with you: ask your elders for counsel, accept the meals and the help with the children, and let one or two friends ask how you really are. If someone in your church has been left, do not avoid them because you do not know what to say. Say that you are sorry, and then show up, again and again. Blessed are the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9), and sometimes making peace means helping someone carry a loss they did not choose.

For worship. If you have been abandoned, God has not abandoned you. He is the one who says, I will never leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), and he said it as the Lord who was himself forsaken. Christ was deserted by every friend he had in the garden, and on the cross he cried out to his Father in the words of the psalm, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? He went through the darkest desertion there has ever been so that no one who belongs to him would ever be left by God. The God of peace has called you to peace, and he is the one who will give it: the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guarding your heart and mind in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:7).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “God has called us to peace.”

verseByVerse.quote: For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

For how do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? The sentence can be read two ways, and both are grammatically possible. Commentators have divided over it for centuries, and it is worth setting out honestly because the pastoral force differs. Read hopefully, it is an argument for staying, attached to verses 12–14: who knows, you might win him to Christ, so stay if he is willing (1 Peter 3:1–2). Read soberly, it is a comfort for letting go, attached to verse 15: how can you know that you will save him? You cannot, so do not hold a departing spouse hostage to a hope you have no way of guaranteeing. The second fits verse 15 more closely; the first fits the whole passage’s encouragement to stay. Paul may well have intended both to be heard by the two different readers who would need them.

Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife? “Save” here means be God’s instrument in bringing them to salvation, as Paul says he became all things to all people that by all means he might save some (9:22). What is beyond dispute is the astonishing thing the verse takes for granted: that a Christian may be the human means by which their own husband or wife comes to Christ. Paul does not say it is likely. He says it is possible, and he says it in a way that assumes his readers had seen it happen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believing spouse can save their partner by their own power. Only God saves. But God often uses a faithful spouse. One plants, another waters, but God gives the growth (3:6–7).

A question, not a promise. That possibility is worth holding carefully, because it can be turned into a burden it was never meant to be. The verse says how do you know? which is a question, not a promise. It does not guarantee that a faithful wife will win her husband. Some do; some pray for forty years and bury a man who never came. To promise otherwise is to make the verse say what it explicitly refuses to say. But it also forbids the opposite conclusion, which is the one most people in that situation eventually drift into: that it is settled, that he will never change, that after this many years there is no point. You do not know that either. The verse cuts against certainty in both directions, and leaves the outcome where it belongs.

If my spouse dies without believing, did I fail? No. You were never given the power to save anyone, and Scripture does not lay that weight on you. The question in this verse is meant to free you from it. Grief over a spouse who died without professing Christ is real and deep, and you should not pretend otherwise. But you may leave that person with the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25), and who knows things about the last hours and the hidden heart that you do not. Your faithfulness was not wasted. It was seen by God, it was a witness, and it was the obedience he asked of you.

In a sentence. How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or, how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?

On a Tuesday. How does a believer live in that marriage? Not by campaigning. Peter’s instruction to precisely this reader is that a husband may be won without a word, by conduct (1 Peter 3:1–2), which is not a ban on ever speaking, but a warning that the sermon delivered over dinner for the fifteenth time is not the instrument God is most likely to use. What is being asked of you is a long, unspectacular faithfulness in the same house: to be someone whose Christianity has visibly made them kinder, more patient, less easily provoked and more generous than they were before, and to keep asking God for the one thing you cannot do yourself. Live with gentleness and quiet faithfulness. God may use it to win them.

For worship. You are not able to save your husband or your wife. Paul’s question makes that plain, and it is a mercy that he does, because it lifts off you a weight you were never given. Someone else saves people. Salvation belongs to the LORD (Jonah 2:9), who opens blind eyes and raises the dead, who opened Lydia’s heart by the riverside and turned a jailer’s house upside down in a night. He does not need our cleverness and he is not hindered by our weakness. Your part is to be in the house, and to ask, and to leave the rest in hands that have never failed to finish what they began.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — Live as You Were Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul states a general rule he teaches in every church: each person should live the life the Lord assigned and in which God called him. If a man was circumcised when called, he should not try to undo it; if uncircumcised, he should not seek circumcision. Neither counts for anything; what counts is keeping God’s commands. Each should remain in the situation in which he was called. A slave who was called should not let it trouble him, though if he can gain his freedom he should take it. For a slave called by the Lord is the Lord’s freed person, and a free person called is Christ’s slave. They were bought at a price, so they must not become slaves of human beings. Each should remain with God in the condition in which he was called.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Relativisation of Social Status by the Gospel

Paul’s refrain — remain as you are — is not social conservatism but theological prioritisation. The gospel relativises every earthly status by subjecting it to a higher identity: in Christ. This does not mean social structures are indifferent (Paul does not say slavery is good), but that the gospel’s transformative work operates from the inside out, transforming the meaning of every condition before changing the condition itself. This is the seed from which the ultimate abolition of slavery grew in Christian history: not immediate political revolution but the recognition that the slave is Christ’s freedman, which eventually made the institution of slavery theologically intolerable.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: First-century Christianity attracted people across the entire social spectrum, from Lydia the merchant to Onesimus the slave. The question of whether conversion required a change of social status was real and practically urgent. Paul’s answer guards against two errors: treating social change as spiritually necessary (legalism applied to status), and treating social change as spiritually forbidden (quietism about injustice). Now: The principle “remain as you are” guards against the modern Christian anxiety that effectiveness for God requires a different job, a different social location, a different cultural context. You were placed where you are by Providence; bloom there.

verseByVerse.quote: Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. This is my rule in all the churches. Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God.

Only let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him. Here is the governing principle of the whole chapter, and of verses 17–24 in particular. Everything else, the married, the single, the widowed, the mixed marriage, the slave, is an application of this one sentence. Notice the two verbs. “Assigned” (merizō) means apportioned, dealt out: God has given each person their place in life. “Called” points to the moment God called them to faith. Your circumstances are not an accident you must escape before your real Christian life can begin. They are a distribution, made by someone, on purpose. Becoming a Christian does not mean you must change your outward situation. Serve God where you are.

This is my rule in all the churches. Not a special rule for Corinth, or a concession to its peculiar troubles, but the way Paul teaches everywhere (4:17).

Was anyone at the time of his call already circumcised? Let him not seek to remove the marks of circumcision. Paul reaches for the test case of circumcision, and it is a shrewd choice, because it was the most emotionally loaded status marker in his world. Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to disguise their circumcision, to avoid mockery at the public baths and gymnasiums where men exercised naked (1 Maccabees 1:15). A Jewish believer among Gentile Christians might feel his circumcision embarrassing now. Paul says: a Jewish believer need not become a Gentile.

Was anyone at the time of his call uncircumcised? Let him not seek circumcision. A Gentile convert, on the other hand, might feel a second-class member of a faith with Jewish roots, and be tempted to acquire the mark. A Gentile believer need not become a Jew (Galatians 5:2–6). The identity you brought with you is not the problem.

For neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but keeping the commandments of God. A startling statement for a Jew, since circumcision was itself a commandment, and startling from the man who fought the circumcision party to a standstill in Galatia. He is not contradicting himself. Paul means the moral commandments, the law of love, which applies to all: in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but only faith working through love (Galatians 5:6), and a new creation (Galatians 6:15). Ethnic identity markers do not matter before God; obedience does. What he denies is that the mark carries any standing; what he affirms is that obedience does, not as the ground of acceptance, but as the substance of a life that has been accepted.

The obstacle we imagine. The practical force of this principle is considerable, because most of us are quietly convinced that our circumstances are the obstacle. If I were married. If I were single. If I had the other job, the other health, the other family, the other church: then I could serve God properly. Paul’s answer is that the life you are in is the life you were assigned, and faithfulness in it is not a holding pattern until the real thing starts. There is no arrangement of circumstances in which obedience becomes easy, and none in which it becomes impossible. Paul himself learned in whatever situation he was to be content, in plenty and in hunger (Philippians 4:11–12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians can never change jobs or circumstances (see v. 21). It means that our outward situation is not what makes us acceptable to God, so we need not rush to change it. This verse can be misheard as fatalism, and Paul corrects that himself in two verses. He is about to tell a slave to take his freedom if he can get it (v. 21), and he has already told the burning single person to marry (v. 9). The principle is contentment, not paralysis. You may change your circumstances; what you may not do is treat your present circumstances as a reason to postpone obedience.

Does this mean I should not leave a job that is wrong for me, or a sinful one? No. If your work requires you to sin, you must leave it, as tax collectors stopped cheating and soldiers stopped extorting when they repented (Luke 3:12–14). If it is lawful but you have a good opportunity to move, you are free to take it, prayerfully and without guilt. What Paul forbids is the restless conviction that God cannot use you until your situation changes, and the habit of making the next change the precondition of obedience. Ask two questions: is this situation sinful? If not, am I free and wise to change it? And meanwhile, serve Christ wholeheartedly where you are.

In a sentence. Nevertheless, each person should live as a believer in whatever situation the Lord has assigned to them, just as God has called them. This is the rule Paul lays down in all the churches. Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man uncircumcised when he was called? He should not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commands is what counts.

On a Tuesday. You do not need a new situation to serve God. Serve him in the job, family and place you are in today. The test is a simple substitution, and it is answerable now. Take the sentence you most often say to yourself about what is missing: when I have this, I will be able to do that. Then ask what obedience actually looks like this week, in the life you have, with the people who are already in it. That question has an answer, and the other one never has. Godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6:6).

For worship. The God of this verse is the Lord of every assignment. He fixed the boundaries of the peoples and the times of their dwelling (Acts 17:26); he set the Jew in his Jewishness and the Greek in his Greekness, the slave in his household and the free man in his, and then he called each of them by name into one family. In Christ there is no tier of the circumcised above the uncircumcised, no first-class and second-class believers. And the Son himself accepted an assignment none of us would have chosen: the carpenter’s shop in Nazareth, thirty hidden years, a ministry among the poor, and a cross. He did not wait for better circumstances to obey his Father. He obeyed in the ones he was given, perfectly, all the way to death, and every ordinary place where his people now serve him has been made holy by the place where he served.
verseByVerse.note: Some Jews under Greek influence had surgery to hide their circumcision.

verseByVerse.quote: Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. (But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity.)

Each one should remain in the condition in which he was called. The principle repeated, and now applied to the hardest case in that society.

Were you a bondservant when called? Do not be concerned about it. A bondservant (doulos) is a slave. It is a jarring sentence to a modern ear, and it should not be softened prematurely. Perhaps a third of people in Corinth were slaves, and the church contained many such people. Roman slavery was not based on race; people became slaves through war, debt or birth, and many were freed by the age of thirty. Some slaves were educated professionals: doctors, teachers, managers of estates. But slaves had no legal rights and could be badly treated, beaten, sold and used. Paul tells them not to let their status trouble them, and he can say that only because of what he is about to say in the next verse about who they actually are. You are fully a Christian, with full dignity before God.

But if you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of the opportunity. Then the parenthesis, and it changes the whole tone. The ESV notes that the sentence can also be read make use of your present condition instead, meaning stay a slave even if offered freedom. The Greek is genuinely elliptical; it says something like rather use, without stating what is to be used. The ESV’s main reading is more likely: freedom is better, so take it if you can. Manumission was common in that world, and Paul tells a Christian slave who gets the chance to take it without hesitation. And he goes on at once to say do not become slaves of men (v. 23), which would make little sense if he meant them to refuse liberty.

Neither quietism nor indifference. This is not quietism, and it is not indifference to injustice. Paul does not say slavery is good, or that a slave should refuse liberty out of piety. He says two things at once, and both are needed: your condition does not define you, and if you can be free, be free. Lose the first half and you get a Christianity in which nothing can be borne until it is fixed, in which a believer’s peace depends entirely on his circumstances improving. Lose the second and you get the far uglier thing that has actually happened in history: this text quoted by slaveholders to tell slaves that Christianity required them to stay put and be content. It required nothing of the kind, and the parenthesis in this verse is the refutation of it.

Where Christians differ: did the Bible approve of slavery? Some say the New Testament approved of slavery because it did not demand its abolition. Verdict: The New Testament did not call for violent revolution, but it planted principles that undermine slavery: all humans bear God’s image; slave and free are equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11); masters must treat slaves justly, knowing they have a Master in heaven (Ephesians 6:9); slave-trading is condemned (1 Timothy 1:10); and here slaves are encouraged to gain freedom. Christians like William Wilberforce rightly drew on these truths to fight for abolition. The race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, built on kidnapping, was condemned by the law of Moses itself (Exodus 21:16). The New Testament’s way with this institution was not endorsement but undermining. Paul sends a runaway back to his master with instructions to receive him no longer as a bondservant but as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). Those sentences, believed, dissolve the thing from within, and eventually did.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should accept injustice passively. It means our worth and calling do not depend on our circumstances. Christians may and should work for justice for the oppressed, as the prophets demanded (Isaiah 1:17), while refusing to make their own peace with God depend on how the work turns out.

What about the circumstances I cannot change? For the ordinary reader the transfer is straightforward, and it applies to any circumstance you did not choose and may not be able to change: the job you are stuck in, the illness, the family situation, the years that are not going the way you planned. Paul’s counsel is neither resignation nor restlessness. Do not let it define you, and if a door opens, walk through it without guilt. Contentment is not the refusal of a better situation. It is the freedom to live well in this one while the door stays shut. Pray for the change; take lawful steps toward it; and meanwhile refuse to let it tell you who you are.

In a sentence. Each person should remain in the situation they were in when God called them. Were you a slave when you were called? Don’t let it trouble you, although if you can gain your freedom, do so.

On a Tuesday. Take the circumstance you most resent and say two sentences about it to God. First: this does not define me; I am yours. Second: if you open a door, I will walk through it. Then do one faithful thing inside the situation today. And pray for those who are enslaved or exploited today, in trafficking, forced labour and debt bondage, and ask whether there is any practical way you can help them.

For worship. Thank God that in Christ your worth does not depend on your status. The Lord of glory took the form of a doulos himself (Philippians 2:7), was sold for the price of a slave, thirty pieces of silver (Exodus 21:32; Matthew 26:15), and died the death Rome reserved for slaves. He went to the bottom of every human ladder so that no believer, however low, could ever be beneath his notice or beyond his love. In his kingdom the last are first, and the slave in the back row at Corinth was seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6). That is why Paul could say, do not be concerned about it: the slave already had a throne.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the second sentence can also be read “make use of your present condition instead.” Slaves could sometimes buy or be granted their freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. You were bought with a price; do not become bondservants of men. So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God.

For he who was called in the Lord as a bondservant is a freedman of the Lord. Now Paul explains why a slave need not be consumed by his status, and the explanation is one of the great paradoxes of the New Testament. “Freedman” (apeleutheros) is a freed slave. A Roman freedman still owed duties to the patron who had freed him, and bore his name; here the patron is the Lord. The slave who becomes a Christian is spiritually free: freed from sin, guilt and death by the Lord. He owns nothing, his time is not his own, he may be sold next month, and he is, in the only sense that finally matters, a free man sitting in that room. He has the highest freedom there is. If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed (John 8:36).

Likewise he who was free when called is a bondservant of Christ. And the free person who becomes a Christian is now Christ’s slave, under his total ownership. The citizen with property and standing beside the slave has been bought and now belongs to somebody. Both halves are conversions of status, and they run in opposite directions. Within the church the two most important social categories in Corinth had been not merely relativised but crossed over. Each man had received what the other had. There was, in the end, nothing left to rank. Every believer is both free and a slave, whatever their social status.

You were bought with a price. As in 6:20. Christ purchased us with his blood. Paul used that phrase one chapter earlier of the body; here he uses it of the whole self, and draws a different conclusion.

Do not become bondservants of men. Because you are owned by Christ, you must not let yourself be owned by anybody else. Literally, do not sell yourself into slavery, a common way of escaping debt; and more deeply, do not let human opinions or powers control you spiritually. You belong to Christ. And notice that this is addressed to people who were, in the plainest legal sense, already owned by other men. Paul is not talking about their legal position; he is talking about the interior one. A slave may belong to a master in Corinth and be, in his soul, a free man who serves Christ. A free citizen may be legally answerable to nobody and be entirely enslaved: to opinion, to advancement, to the fear of what people will think.

The fear of man. This is where the verse reaches most readers, because almost nobody reading it is legally owned and almost everybody is servile about something.
