The commonest form is the one Scripture names as its own snare: the fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Proverbs 29:25). It is the settled habit of arranging your life around other people’s approval: saying the thing that will land well, softening a conviction because of who is listening, taking on more than you should because you cannot bear to disappoint, measuring yourself daily by an audience whose opinion you did not choose and cannot control. That is what Paul forbids, and he forbids it on the ground of ownership rather than of self-respect. The argument is not you are worth more than that. It is you are not for sale, because you have already been bought. If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10).

So, brothers, in whatever condition each was called, there let him remain with God. The third statement of the principle (vv. 17, 20, 24). “With God”: in his presence, before him, with him. The most important thing is not your situation, but that you are with God in it. A slave with God is better placed than an emperor without him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good. It means that the gospel relativises social status: in Christ, the slave is free and the free man is a slave. Nor does belonging to Christ mean that a Christian should be indifferent to an employer, a parent or a government; Christ himself tells us to honour those over us. It means that no human authority owns your conscience.

How do I serve Christ at work if my boss is the one I answer to? You do the work your employer gives you, honestly and well, but you do it for a different Master. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Colossians 3:23–24). In practice that means working when no one is checking, refusing to lie or cut corners even when it is expected, treating colleagues with respect, and accepting unfair treatment without bitterness while pursuing any just remedy available. If your employer requires you to sin, you must refuse, because he did not pay for you. Christ did.

In a sentence. For the one who was a slave when called to faith in the Lord is the Lord’s freed person; similarly, the one who was free when called is Christ’s slave. You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of human beings. Brothers and sisters, each person, as responsible to God, should remain in the situation they were in when God called them.

On a Tuesday. At work, you serve your employer, but your true master is Christ. Work for him (Colossians 3:23–24). And run this test on your week. Find the point at which you were not honest, or not obedient, or not generous, because of what somebody would think. Then ask who your master was at that moment. The name will be a person, or a group, or a version of your reputation you are maintaining, and the verse’s reply is that whoever it was, they did not pay for you.

For worship. Somebody else did pay, at a price mentioned at the end of chapter 6: not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:18–19). Having paid it, he set a slave free and made a free man his own, and in his church the two of them sit down together, and neither can any longer say what he used to be. You were slaves of sin, and you have become obedient from the heart (Romans 6:17–18) to a Master whose yoke is easy and whose burden is light. There is no freedom like belonging to him, and no slavery like belonging to anyone else.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–40 — The Unmarried, the Betrothed, and the Widows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the question of those who have never married, Paul has no command from the Lord, but gives his judgement as one the Lord has made trustworthy. Because of the present crisis, he thinks it good for people to stay as they are. Those who are married should not seek to separate; those who are free should not look for a wife. But marrying is no sin, though married people will face hardship, and Paul wants to spare them. The time is short. From now on, married people should live without being absorbed in marriage, mourners as if not mourning, the joyful as if not rejoicing, buyers as if they owned nothing, users of the world as if not engrossed in it, because the world in its present form is passing away. Paul wants them free from anxiety. The unmarried can focus on the Lord’s affairs and how to please him; the married must also think about the world and how to please their spouse, so their interests are divided. He says this for their benefit, not to restrict them, but so that they may serve the Lord with undivided devotion. A man engaged to a woman may marry her if he feels he should; it is no sin. But one who has firmly decided not to marry does well too. Marriage is good, but staying single is better in present circumstances. A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives, but if he dies she is free to marry anyone she wishes, provided he belongs to the Lord. Paul thinks she will be happier if she stays as she is, and he believes he too has God’s Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Eschatological Relativisation and Christian Freedom

Paul’s “as if not” framework is one of the most pastorally liberating texts in the NT for the believer under pressure. It is not an ascetic refusal of the world’s goods but an insistence that no good and no loss in this age has the last word. Marriage, mourning, rejoicing, buying — all are real; none are final. The person who holds them “as if not” is not less engaged with life but more free in it, because their ultimate security is not invested in any of them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s counsel to the betrothed (“do not seek a wife”, v. 27) and to the widow (“she is happier if she remains as she is”, v. 40) was given “in view of the present distress” — the compressed time between the first and second coming, with its attendant pressures. He is not issuing universal commands but pastorally calibrated counsel. Now: The eschatological urgency has not diminished — we are closer to the end than Paul’s Corinth was. The counsel to hold earthly goods and relationships lightly, in undivided devotion to the Lord, is not less relevant but more.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the betrothed, I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is.

Now concerning the betrothed. The marker again, and a new question from their letter. “Betrothed” is literally virgins (parthenoi): unmarried young women, probably those engaged to be married, and by extension the young unmarried generally.

I have no command from the Lord, but I give my judgment. Jesus had not spoken directly on this. Paul gives his considered advice (gnōmē, opinion, judgement). Paul is careful in exactly the way he was at verse 12, and the carefulness itself teaches something. There is a difference between what God has clearly commanded and the wise application of Christian principle to a situation Scripture does not directly address. A teacher who blurs the two, presenting his own judgment with the authority of a command, is doing something Paul refuses to do even when he is confident.

As one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. Paul is a trustworthy guide, made so by God’s mercy. His trustworthiness is not a quality he claims for himself; it is mercy received, from the Lord who found him on the Damascus road doing the opposite. His advice is inspired wisdom, even if not a command (v. 40).

I think that in view of the present distress it is good for a person to remain as he is. The “present distress” (anankē, necessity, pressure) may refer to famine, persecution or the general trouble of the last days. There were famines in Greece around this time, and hostility toward the young church was real; and the next paragraph will describe the whole age between Christ’s comings as short and passing. Whatever it was, it made marriage and family life especially hard. Paul’s advice is: stay as you are, for now. The honest answer is that we cannot be certain what the distress was, and it matters less than it seems, because Paul’s reasoning holds under any of them. He is not laying down a timeless rule that Christians should not marry. He is giving situational counsel, in view of a particular pressure, and the word he uses elsewhere describes hardship and persecution (2 Corinthians 6:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s advice here has no authority. It means it is wise counsel given for a specific situation, not an absolute command for all times. It models something we are generally poor at: pastoral advice that is explicitly tied to circumstances and does not pretend to be universal. Paul is not saying marriage is inferior. He is saying that in a season of acute difficulty, adding the responsibilities and vulnerabilities of a family is a real consideration, and a Christian is free to weigh it.

How do I decide something Scripture does not settle? There is a quiet permission in this paragraph for anyone facing such a decision. A great many of the choices that actually shape a life, whom to marry, whether to marry, which work, where to live, when to move, are not commanded either way. Christians often want them to be, and go looking for a verse or a sign that will remove the responsibility of choosing. Paul’s example is more freeing than that. He weighs the circumstances, applies the principles, reaches a judgment, states it as a judgment, and leaves the other person free. So: rule out what Scripture forbids; ask what love and wisdom commend; seek counsel from mature believers; consider the circumstances honestly; pray; and then decide, trusting that God guides those who seek him even when no voice speaks (Proverbs 3:5–6; Romans 14:5). That is what wisdom looks like when there is no command, and Christian maturity is largely made of it, since most of life is lived in exactly that territory.

In a sentence. Now about virgins: Paul has no command from the Lord, but he gives a judgement as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy. Because of the present crisis, he thinks that it is good for a man to remain as he is.

On a Tuesday. Take the decision currently on your mind that Scripture does not directly settle. Write down what Scripture does say that bears on it, what wise and godly people you trust have said, and what the circumstances honestly are. Then make a judgement, say it as a judgement, and stop waiting for a sign. Ask God for wisdom in your big decisions, especially in hard times. He gives it generously, without reproach (James 1:5).

For worship. The Lord whose mercy made Paul trustworthy is the same Lord who takes persecutors and makes them pastors. Paul had once been a blasphemer and a violent man, and he received mercy (1 Timothy 1:13); the very trustworthiness he offers the Corinthians is a monument to grace. And the God who does not legislate every choice is not leaving his people to guess. He is treating them as sons and not as infants, giving them his word, his Spirit and his church, and trusting them to walk in wisdom. He is the Father of lights, generous with wisdom to all who ask, and his providence is underneath every decision his children make in faith.
verseByVerse.note: The “present distress” may refer to famine, persecution or the pressures of the last days.

verseByVerse.quote: Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that.

Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek to be free. If you are married, or engaged, do not try to get out. The principle of verse 17 applied once more: do not make a project of changing your situation.

Are you free from a wife? Do not seek a wife. If you are unmarried, do not rush to find a spouse, given the present distress.

But if you do marry, you have not sinned, and if a betrothed woman marries, she has not sinned. Then, immediately, the qualification, and it is emphatic, because Paul knows exactly how his counsel is likely to be heard. Marriage is not sin. Paul is firm against the ascetics in Corinth. He says it twice, once for each party. This is a man who has spent much of the chapter commending singleness, and who is now anxious that nobody should conclude that marrying is a failure. He will not have his preference turned into a burden on anyone’s conscience. That instinct runs through the whole chapter, and it is rare. Paul holds a strong personal conviction, states it plainly, argues for it, and then repeatedly and deliberately protects the freedom of those who will decide differently. Very few teachers manage that. The usual pattern is to state a preference and then let the weight of one’s authority do the rest.

Yet those who marry will have worldly troubles, and I would spare you that. Literally, trouble in the flesh (thlipsis, pressure, affliction, the word used of persecution and hardship): the pressures and anxieties of married and family life, especially in hard times. Paul wants to spare them that. Pastoral care, not a rule. And this is Paul being honest in a way that Christian teaching about marriage often is not. Marriage is regularly commended to young believers as the destination, the completion, the arrival, and the sermon usually stops at the wedding. Paul says plainly that it brings trouble. Not that it is a mistake; he has just said twice that it is no sin. But it doubles the number of people whose suffering you feel as your own. It introduces the possibility of losses you would not otherwise have been exposed to. Every married person eventually discovers that they have given hostages. And I would spare you that is affection, not disparagement. It is a pastor who has watched people carry things, wishing they did not have to.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is bad. It means it carries burdens as well as joys. He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favour from the LORD (Proverbs 18:22); and he who finds a wife finds trouble in the flesh too. Both are true at once.

Does free from a wife include the divorced? Some read it that way, but the paragraph is about the betrothed and the unmarried (v. 25), so Paul is most likely thinking of those who have not yet married or have been widowed. Remarriage after divorce is settled not by this verse but by verses 10–15 and Matthew 19:9, on the grounds of adultery or desertion.

Honesty is a kindness. The honesty works in two directions. To the single reader, it removes the fantasy that marriage is where the difficulty ends, which is worth knowing, because that fantasy makes singleness far heavier than it needs to be, and makes marriages far more disappointing than they need to be. To the married reader who is in the middle of the trouble, the illness, the strain, the years of difficulty with someone you have promised not to walk away from, it says that you have not discovered a defect in your marriage. Paul told you this would be part of it, in writing, in advance. What you are carrying is not evidence that something has gone wrong. It is what he meant.

In a sentence. Are you pledged to a woman? Do not seek to be released. Are you free from such a commitment? Do not look for a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned; and if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. But those who marry will face many troubles in this life, and Paul wants to spare you this.

On a Tuesday. If you are thinking of marriage, count the cost as well as the joy. Both are real. Talk with a married couple a decade or two ahead of you and ask them honestly what was hard, and what carried them. If you are married and in a hard season, say to your spouse this week: this is what Paul said it would be, and I am still here.

For worship. The Lord who warns of trouble in the flesh is not a God who stands at a distance from it. He entered our flesh and took its troubles: he had a mother who wept at his cross, brothers who did not believe him, a household in Nazareth that thought him out of his mind. He knows the weight of loving people in a fallen world, because he has carried it. And he is the one who brings every marriage’s trouble to an end, not by abolishing love but by perfecting it, in a kingdom where there will be no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain (Revelation 21:4). Until then, he walks with his married people in the fire, as he walked with three men in the furnace, and they are not consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is what I mean, brothers: the appointed time has grown very short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none, and those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing, and those who buy as though they had no goods, and those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. For the present form of this world is passing away.

The appointed time has grown very short. “Appointed time” (kairos) is the decisive season rather than clock time: the season between Christ’s first and second comings. “Grown very short” (synestalmenos) means compressed, drawn together, and the verb is one used of furling sails: canvas taken in as a ship nears harbour. The remaining stretch has been shortened. The end is on its way. This shapes everything.

From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none. Then five clauses in the same startling form, and taken flatly they would be monstrous. They must not be taken flatly. Paul cannot mean neglect your wife: he has already insisted in this chapter that spouses owe each other themselves (v. 3), and elsewhere he tells husbands to love as Christ loved the church. He means not letting marriage become their ultimate concern. Marriage is for this age only; in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage (Matthew 22:30).

And those who mourn as though they were not mourning, and those who rejoice as though they were not rejoicing. Grief and joy are real, but not final. Paul cannot mean suppress your grief, when Scripture is full of lament and he himself writes of sorrow upon sorrow (Philippians 2:27). He cannot mean refuse to be glad, in a Bible that commands rejoicing more often than almost anything else. The Christian mourns, but not as others do who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13), and rejoices without clinging. And the inclusion of mourning is the tenderest thing in the paragraph. Grief is not exempted because grief is unimportant; it is included because grief, too, has a horizon. The thing you are mourning is real and the mourning is right, and it is not the last word about the person you have lost. There will be a morning when the arrangement in which that loss was possible has passed away.

And those who buy as though they had no goods. Buy, but hold possessions loosely. You are a steward, not an owner.

And those who deal with the world as though they had no dealings with it. “Have no dealings” (katachraomai) means use fully, use up. Use the world, its goods and systems, but do not be absorbed by it.

For the present form of this world is passing away. “Form” (schēma) is outward shape, arrangement, the way things are currently configured, like a scene in a play before the set is changed. The world as it now is will not last (1 John 2:17). Not that the world is worthless or that matter is evil; it is the arrangement that is temporary. What is passing is the shape, not the substance: creation itself will be set free, not discarded (Romans 8:21). What Paul is doing is relativising, not abolishing. Marry, grieve, celebrate, buy, work, and do not let any of it become the thing you are ultimately living for, because none of it is going to survive in its present form.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be cold, detached or careless. It means they should live with eternity in view, holding everything in this world with an open hand. The practical effect of believing this is not detachment but proportion. A man who holds his possessions loosely can still enjoy them; he simply does not panic when they go. A woman who holds her plans loosely can still make them; she is not destroyed when they change.

Did Paul think Christ would return in his lifetime? He did not know, and he never set a date. He taught that the day would come like a thief in the night (1 Thessalonians 5:2) and was always to be expected, and in other letters he speaks calmly of his own death (2 Corinthians 5:1–8; Philippians 1:23). The appointed time has grown very short because, since the resurrection, the church has been living in the last days, and every generation since has lived with the end in view. That is not a mistaken timetable. It is the posture every generation of Christians is called to: watchful, unhurried, with lamps lit.

In a sentence. What Paul means, brothers and sisters, is that the time is short. From now on those who have wives should live as if they do not; those who mourn, as if they did not; those who are happy, as if they were not; those who buy something, as if it were not theirs to keep; those who use the things of the world, as if not engrossed in them. For this world in its present form is passing away.

On a Tuesday. A test that fits in a sentence. Take the thing that currently has the most power to make or ruin your year: the outcome you are waiting for, the possession, the relationship, the plan. Ask what would remain of your life if it were removed tomorrow. If the honest answer is nothing much, then that thing has moved from being a gift to being a foundation, and Paul’s five clauses are aimed precisely at it. Hold it with an open hand today, and give thanks for it as a gift.

For worship. The sails have been taken in. Everything on this ship is worth having and none of it is worth building on, because the port is close. And the One who is waiting in the harbour is not a stranger. He is the Lord who said, surely I am coming soon (Revelation 22:20), the Bridegroom whose return will make every earthly marriage look like the sketch it was, every grief turn out to have been temporary, and every possession seem trivial beside him. Lord, let me know my end, and what is the measure of my days (Psalm 39:4): not to frighten us, but to turn our eyes to the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3:1). Only he, and his kingdom, will last, and in him we shall have everything.

verseByVerse.quote: I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I want you to be free from anxieties. The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife,

I want you to be free from anxieties. “Free from anxieties” (amerimnos) means without care. That is Paul’s stated motive for everything he has been saying about singleness, and it should govern how the rest is heard. His advice is pastoral. He is not trying to recruit ascetics; he is trying to spare people worry.

The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. Here “anxious” (merimnaō) is used positively: concerned for, devoted to. The single person can give full attention to the Lord’s work. The argument is refreshingly unspiritual: it is about time and attention, not about holiness.

But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife. Worldly things here are not sinful things, but the things of ordinary life: providing, caring, household concerns. Pleasing your wife is not a worldly ambition in any pejorative sense; it is a Christian duty, and the same apostle commands it. A married man rightly has to think about pleasing his wife. That is his duty, not his sin. “Worldly” here simply means belonging to this present arrangement, the ordinary, legitimate, time-consuming business of a shared life. So the point is not that marriage is spiritually inferior. It is that marriage takes attention, and attention is finite. The single Christian has one set of claims on his time; the married Christian has two, and the second one is a person with her own needs, opinions, tiredness and hopes. That is not a defect in marriage. It is marriage.

What it does not mean. It does not mean married people cannot serve the Lord, or that pleasing a spouse is unspiritual. It means their attention is rightly divided. Paul’s observation is simply accurate, as any honest married Christian will confirm. There are decisions a single believer can take alone and quickly, where to live, how much to give away, what risk to run, how much time to spend in service, that a married one cannot take at all without agreement.

To each reader. Each tends to misread the other’s situation. To the single reader, particularly one who did not choose it: this is Paul naming something real that you already possess, and it is not a consolation prize. You have a freedom of movement and attention that is genuinely useful to God, and a great deal of the church’s most demanding work has always been done by people who were free to do it. That does not remove the loneliness. But it means your situation is not merely an absence; there is something in your hands. To the married reader: the division of interests is not a failure of devotion that you should be repenting of. The attention you give your wife or husband is not stolen from God. It is the form your obedience takes, and Paul is not calling you back from it. What he asks is honesty that the cost exists. Many married Christians drift for years without admitting that their capacity for other things has genuinely narrowed, and then feel a low-grade guilt about it that they never examine.

Is it wrong to be anxious, then? Jesus told us not to be anxious about our life (Matthew 6:25), and Paul tells us to be anxious about nothing but to pray about everything (Philippians 4:6). Here, though, Paul uses the same word for legitimate concern: the care a man rightly has for his wife and the care a single believer has for the Lord’s work. The difference is between care carried to God and care that has replaced God. Concern for your family is right; anxiety that forgets your Father knows what you need is not. Bring the concern to him and let him carry the weight.

In a sentence. Paul would like you to be free from concern. An unmarried man is concerned about the Lord’s affairs, how he can please the Lord. But a married man is concerned about the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife,

On a Tuesday. If you are single, use your freedom for the Lord: offer a ministry, a home, an evening, a holiday, something a married friend could not easily give. If you are married, pleasing your spouse is part of pleasing the Lord; do it without guilt. And for either reader, ask Paul’s own question: where is my anxiety actually going this week? Not which state is better, which is not the question he is asking. Simply: what am I currently worried about, and does the list look like the life of somebody who belongs to Christ in the situation he has assigned? Seek first the kingdom of God (Matthew 6:33).

For worship. The Lord is worth undivided care. He is the one thing needful that Mary chose at his feet while Martha was distracted with much serving (Luke 10:41–42), and he will not take that from her. And he is the Lord who cares for us without division. His attention is never finite; he numbers the hairs of every head and the sparrows that fall, he hears the single believer at midnight and the married believer in the school run, and not one of his people is ever at the back of his mind. We may be free from anxiety because he is never free from caring for us. Cast all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you (1 Peter 5:7).

verseByVerse.quote: and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and his interests are divided. And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you, but to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord.

And his interests are divided. Pulled in two directions: the Lord and his wife. Both are legitimate.

And the unmarried or betrothed woman is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to be holy in body and spirit. Holy here means devoted to God, set apart for his service, in her whole person. And Paul applies the argument to women in exactly the same terms as to men, which is itself worth noticing. In a world that defined a woman almost entirely by her household, Paul assumes an unmarried Christian woman has her own devotion to the Lord, her own concerns, and her own spiritual vocation.

But the married woman is anxious about worldly things, how to please her husband. The same for wives. Both are legitimate.

I say this for your own benefit, not to lay any restraint upon you. Then the sentence that governs the entire chapter and rescues it from every misuse it has suffered. The word behind “restraint” is vivid: brochos, a noose or halter, the loop thrown over an animal to bring it under control. Paul is not trying to trap them or impose rules; he has no intention of putting a rope round anybody’s neck. That is the safeguard he has been building toward since verse 6, and it is what makes this chapter safe to read. Everything Paul has said about the advantages of singleness is offered as counsel for the reader’s benefit, not as a standard by which anyone is to be measured, and certainly not as a rule the church may impose.

But to promote good order and to secure your undivided devotion to the Lord. “Good order” (euschēmon) is what is fitting, seemly, well-formed. “Undivided devotion” (aperispastōs) means without distraction, the opposite of Martha, who was distracted with much serving (Luke 10:40); the root suggests sitting close beside someone, attending on them. His aim is that each one be wholly devoted to Christ. This is where the paragraph lands, and the phrase is the goal of the whole chapter. Not singleness. Not marriage. Devotion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are automatically more devoted, or that married people cannot be devoted. It means singleness offers a particular opportunity for undistracted service.

The noose thrown anyway, in both directions. What Paul forbade is precisely what happened, for centuries. The chapter was read as establishing celibacy as the higher path, marriage as the concession for the weak, and a two-tier Christianity with the unmarried at the top. Whole systems of spirituality were built on it. Paul wrote this sentence to prevent exactly that, and it was ignored. And the same danger runs in the opposite direction now, which is why the verse still matters. In many churches the noose is thrown over the single. There are congregations in which an unmarried adult is treated as a problem to be solved, is asked with wearying regularity whether there is anyone yet, is quietly excluded from the real business of church life which is assumed to be families, and is made to feel that his or her life has not properly started. That is a restraint Paul forbids just as firmly, and it is far commoner among us than enforced celibacy.

So which is better, marriage or singleness? Paul has refused that question repeatedly and in as many ways as he can find. The question is what undivided devotion looks like for the person you actually are, in the situation the Lord has assigned you. For one reader that will mean a freedom of time and movement to be spent rather than hoarded. For another it will mean loving one person faithfully for forty years in a way nobody outside the house will ever see. Neither is the higher path. Both are the same devotion, and the God who assigned them is not comparing.

In a sentence. and his interests are divided. An unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about the Lord’s affairs: her aim is to be devoted to the Lord in both body and spirit. But a married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband. Paul is saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but that you may live in a right way in undivided devotion to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Look at your church through the eyes of its single members this week. Are they invited into homes, trusted with leadership, asked about their work and their walk with God rather than only about whether they are seeing anyone? Fix one thing. And whatever your own situation, name one distraction that most often pulls you from attending on the Lord, and set it aside for one evening to sit at his feet.

For worship. One thing have I asked of the LORD, that will I seek after: that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to gaze upon the beauty of the LORD (Psalm 27:4). He is worth that undivided gaze, and he has made it possible for every one of his people, married or single, because he first fixed his own undivided devotion on us. Christ set his face to go to Jerusalem and was not distracted from the cross by any lesser good. He gave himself without reserve, so that his people might belong to him without reserve. And he lays no noose on anyone. His yoke is easy, and the only cords he uses are cords of kindness, the bands of love (Hosea 11:4).

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed, if his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry—it is no sin. But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control, and has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better.

If anyone thinks that he is not behaving properly toward his betrothed. These three verses are among the more obscure in the letter, and honesty requires saying so before anything else. The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally virgin, and that the passage could also be read of a father deciding whether to give his virgin daughter in marriage. The difficulty is that the Greek does not make explicit who the parties are. Two readings have held the field. The older one takes it of a father and his unmarried daughter, a man deciding whether to give her in marriage, which in that culture was his decision to make. The other, which the ESV follows, takes it of a man and the woman he is engaged to, a couple deciding whether to proceed with the marriage or remain betrothed without marrying. The second fits the immediate context better, since Paul announced at verse 25 that he was turning to the betrothed, and it fits the language of strong passions more naturally. But the question is not finally settled, and a reader who meets a different rendering in another Bible is not meeting an error.

If his passions are strong, and it has to be, let him do as he wishes: let them marry, it is no sin. If desire is strong, marry. No sin. Once more Paul removes the guilt from the decision before anyone can attach it. He has been doing this all chapter, and it is a striking pastoral instinct: every time he commends the harder path, he immediately protects those who will not take it.

But whoever is firmly established in his heart, being under no necessity but having his desire under control. If he is settled, not under pressure, in control of his desire, and has decided not to marry. The conditions are worth reading closely, because they are all internal and all mark a free decision rather than a suppressed one. Firmly established: settled, not wavering. Under no necessity: not driven to it by pressure from anyone. Having his desire under control: genuinely able, not merely determined to try. Which quietly rules out a great deal of what has passed for celibacy in the history of the church. Paul’s version is chosen freely, from a settled heart, by someone under no compulsion and not fighting a losing battle. Vows extracted from the young, or imposed by an institution, or undertaken as a spiritual achievement, meet none of his three conditions.

And has determined this in his heart, to keep her as his betrothed, he will do well. To remain engaged but not marry, in view of the present distress, is also good.

So then he who marries his betrothed does well, and he who refrains from marriage will do even better. Both good; singleness, in the present distress, is better for undivided devotion. Better here is not morally better, but more advantageous in that situation. And it is important that both verbs are positive. Paul is not contrasting a good decision with a bad one, or even a good one with a neutral one. He is contrasting good with better, and the better is the practical advantage he set out in verses 32–35, in the circumstances he named in verse 26.

What it does not mean. It does not mean marriage is morally inferior. Paul says marrying does well. Nor does it give a modern engaged couple a reason to drift in a long engagement with no end in view. In a world where engagement is not a legal bond, the principle is simply this: decide prayerfully, keep yourselves pure, and do not keep each other waiting without cause.

We are engaged, but one of us is now unsure. What should we do? Take it seriously and slowly, and speak honestly. An engagement is a serious promise, and it should not be broken lightly or by a sudden mood. But it is not yet a marriage, and it is far better to end an engagement than to enter a marriage one of you cannot enter in good faith. Pray together and separately; talk with a pastor or a wise married couple who know you both; ask whether the doubt is about this person, about marriage itself, or about fear. If you end it, end it kindly, take responsibility, and do not leave the other in uncertainty. If you go on, go on gladly, as Paul says: it is no sin.

In a sentence. If anyone is worried that he might not be acting honourably toward the virgin he is engaged to, and if his passions are too strong and he feels he ought to marry, he should do as he wants. He is not sinning. They should get married. But the man who has settled the matter in his own mind, who is under no compulsion but has control over his own will, and who has made up his mind not to marry the virgin, this man also does the right thing. So then, he who marries the virgin does right, but he who does not marry her does better.

On a Tuesday. If you are engaged and unsure, pray, seek counsel, and know that both marrying and waiting can honour God. There is something freeing in the whole shape of this passage for anyone facing a decision of this kind now. Scripture here does not tell you which to choose. It tells you that both roads are open, that neither is sin, that the practical considerations are real and worth weighing, and then it puts the decision in your hands and refuses to make you feel guilty about it either way. Whatever you do, do it in faith, for whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

For worship. The God of this passage is kind to the undecided. He does not trap young people with impossible choices, or punish them for choosing the good instead of the better. He sets two good roads before them and walks down whichever one they take in faith. That is the gentleness of a Father, and it is the gentleness of the Good Shepherd, who leads his sheep beside still waters and in paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. Whether we marry or refrain, he does well by us, always, and his goodness and mercy follow us all the days of our lives.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “betrothed” is literally “virgin,” and that the passage can also be read of a father deciding whether to give his daughter in marriage.

verseByVerse.quote: A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes, only in the Lord.

A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. Marriage is lifelong (Romans 7:2). Paul restates its permanence in a single clause, and the verb is the binding word, a different one from the word he used of the deserted believer in verse 15, who is not enslaved.

But if her husband dies, she is free to be married to whom she wishes. Death ends the marriage bond. A widow may remarry freely. The widow is not still bound; she is free, and Paul says so without qualification or any suggestion that remarriage would be a lesser choice. He says the same thing in Romans, using marriage as an illustration precisely because the principle is so clear (Romans 7:2–3). That deserves saying plainly, because widows have often been made to feel otherwise: that remarrying would be a betrayal of the person they buried, or a failure of devotion. Scripture attaches no such shame to it. Remarriage after a spouse’s death is honourable, and Paul elsewhere positively counsels younger widows to marry (1 Timothy 5:14).

Only in the Lord. Then the three Greek words that carry the weight. “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer. The freedom is real and it has one boundary: she may marry whom she wishes, provided he belongs to Christ. A Christian may not marry an unbeliever (2 Corinthians 6:14). This applies to all believers, not only widows. It is stated almost in passing, as something Paul assumes his readers already accept, and it is the New Testament’s consistent position, the same principle behind the warning against being unequally yoked with unbelievers.

Why only in the Lord? The reason is not snobbery about outsiders, which would sit very oddly in a letter that has just told believers to stay married to unbelievers, and will tell them to accept dinner invitations from pagans (10:27). The reason is what marriage is. If it is a union of two whole persons at every level, then a marriage in which the deepest thing about one of them is not shared by the other is divided at the root: not impossible, not without love, but permanently unable to be what marriage is for. Put it concretely, because this is one of the decisions on which young Christians most often reason badly. It means the person you marry will be the one you cannot pray with about your child’s illness. It means every Sunday is negotiated. It means the thing that matters most to you is a subject you learn to leave alone, and that leaving it alone becomes a habit, and habits of that kind do not stay confined to Sundays.

Two different situations. Notice the difference between this verse and verses 12–13, because they are often confused and the distinction is the whole point. If you are already married to an unbeliever, whether you married before conversion or after, Paul’s instruction is emphatically to stay, and God’s blessing is on that household (v. 14). What he addresses here is a decision still to be made. The first is a providence to be lived faithfully; the second is a choice, and the choice has a rule. And if you married an unbeliever in disobedience, you are still married; repent of the disobedience, not of the marriage, and live in it faithfully under verses 12–16.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a widow must remarry. Paul’s next verse suggests she may be happier single.

What about dating? Since dating is the road to marriage, a Christian should not begin a romantic relationship with someone Paul’s rule would forbid him or her to marry. The relationship is the first step, and a heart once given does not easily turn back. Someone already in such a relationship should be honest that it cannot go where it is heading, and end it kindly. And the rule is not satisfied by a partner who merely calls himself a Christian. Only in the Lord means someone whose life shows that he belongs to Christ: who loves the Lord, is part of a church, and wants to grow. Do not marry someone in the hope that he will become a believer afterwards.

In a sentence. A woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, but he must belong to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. If you are single and hoping to marry, commit to marrying only in the Lord, and pray for a godly spouse; and say so to a friend who will hold you to it when your heart is tempted otherwise. If you know a widow or widower, do not assume what they should do; ask how they are, and support whichever path they take in the Lord. So this is one of the few places in the chapter where Paul gives a command rather than a judgment, and it is the more striking for the freedom that surrounds it. Whom you marry, when you marry, whether you marry: all left open, all yours, all no sin either way. One boundary, stated in a single phrase, and it is the only one he draws.

For worship. The Lord who draws this boundary is the Bridegroom who wants his people’s marriages to be what his own is: two made one at the deepest level, sharing everything. He gives the widow her freedom, and he is himself a husband to the widow and a father to the fatherless (Psalm 68:5). And the only in the Lord which marks out a Christian marriage is the same phrase that marks out the whole Christian life. We live in the Lord, work in the Lord, marry in the Lord and die in the Lord, and blessed are the dead who die in the Lord (Revelation 14:13). Every part of our lives is held inside his.
verseByVerse.note: “Only in the Lord” means to a fellow believer.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

Yet in my judgment she is happier if she remains as she is. Paul gives his opinion one last time, and one last time he labels it as an opinion. Note the word he chooses: “happier” (makarios, here in the comparative), the word behind the Beatitudes, blessed. Not holier. Not more useful. Not more pleasing to God. In the present distress, Paul thinks a widow is better off single, free for the Lord: more blessed, given the circumstances he described at verse 26 and the undivided attention he described at verse 35. And he says so as a man who wants her happiness rather than as one imposing a standard.

And I think that I too have the Spirit of God. A touch of irony, and it is gently disarming. The Corinthians were the great claimants of the Spirit: the party of spiritual people, confident of their insight, quick to assess their apostle and find him wanting. Paul, having just spent forty verses declining to bind anybody’s conscience, ends by remarking mildly that he too has the Spirit, thank you. But it is not merely irony, and the sentence does real work. Paul has been careful all chapter to distinguish the Lord’s command from his own judgment (vv. 10, 12, 25, 40), and a reader might reasonably conclude that the judgment parts are simply Paul’s private view, take it or leave it. This last clause forbids that. His judgement is Spirit-guided. Here, in what he calls his opinion, he is still writing inspired Scripture. He is claiming, quietly, that the whole chapter is apostolic.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unsure whether he had the Spirit. “I think” is a modest way of making a firm point.

Is everything in this chapter binding on me, then? It is all God’s word, but not all of it is a command, and Paul has told you which is which. Where he speaks as the Lord’s command, as on divorce (vv. 10–11) and marrying only in the Lord (v. 39), you must obey. Where he gives his judgment, as on whether to marry or stay single in the present distress, you receive it as inspired, wise counsel that God wants you to weigh seriously, and you remain free to decide either way without sin, because he says so (vv. 28, 36, 38). Both kinds of word are Scripture; that is exactly why you may trust both the commands and the freedoms.

Looking back over the chapter. This is a fair place to look back from, because the chapter is one of the most humane in the Bible. It has told a church full of people at every stage of life, married, single, widowed, divorced, deserted, enslaved, engaged, married to unbelievers, that not one of them is in the wrong place. It has repeatedly refused to make one state superior to another. It has said you have not sinned to those who marry, not enslaved to those who were left, holy to those who feared their household was not, do not be concerned to those who owned nothing, and no restraint to everybody. And behind all of it stands the single sentence at its centre: let each person lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him, and to which God has called him (v. 17). Assigned. Called. Not left over, not settled for, not what remains after the plan failed.

In a sentence. In Paul’s judgement, she is happier if she stays as she is, and he thinks that he too has the Spirit of God.

On a Tuesday. If you have lost a spouse, know that God cares for widows and widowers (Psalm 68:5). Your single life can be blessed and fruitful, and the church needs what you have learned. Whatever your circumstances this evening, name them to God as his assignment, and ask him what faithfulness in them looks like tomorrow.

For worship. The circumstances you are in tonight, the marriage that is hard work, the house that is quiet, the person you are still waiting for, the person you have buried, were distributed by someone who knows exactly what he is doing and who has never yet given anybody the wrong life. The Lord of this chapter did not marry, had nowhere to lay his head, was deserted by everyone he loved, and died single and childless in his early thirties. He was despised and rejected, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). He is not asking anyone here to accept a smaller portion than he took himself. And he took that portion in order to give us his: the Spirit who is the guarantee of our inheritance, a place at the wedding supper of the Lamb, and a share in the joy of the Bridegroom who will present his whole church to himself in splendour. Blessed is everyone, married or single, who is in him.

8.title: Knowledge, Idols, and Love for the Weak
8.overview:
The next question from the Corinthians’ letter is about food offered to idols. Some background makes it vivid. In a Greek or Roman city, most meat came from animals sacrificed at temples: part was burned for the god, part went to the priests, and much of the rest was eaten at banquets in the temple dining rooms or sold in the meat market (the macellum, whose inscription has been found in Corinth). Temples were also the restaurants and party venues of the city; papyrus invitations survive asking guests to dine “at the table of the lord Sarapis”. Excavations at Corinth’s temple of Asclepius found dining rooms with couches. For a Christian, refusing every such meal could mean cutting yourself off from trade guilds, family celebrations and civic life.

Some Corinthian believers, proud of their knowledge, argued that idols are nothing and there is only one God, so they could eat anywhere. Paul agrees with their theology, and gives one of the most important statements of Christian belief: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ. But knowledge without love puffs people up. Not every believer has that confidence; some, long used to idols, still feel that eating such food is worship, and if they follow the example of the “strong” against their conscience, they are damaged. A believer for whom Christ died must not be ruined by another’s freedom. So Paul would rather never eat meat again than cause a brother to fall. (Chapter 10 will add that actually taking part in idol feasts is forbidden.)

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Knowledge Puffs Up, Love Builds Up
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On food sacrificed to idols, Paul quotes the Corinthians’ claim that “we all have knowledge”, and warns that knowledge inflates people, while love builds them up. Anyone who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he should; but whoever loves God is known by him. So, about eating such food: they say an idol is nothing in the world and there is no God but one. Paul agrees. Though there are many so-called gods and lords in heaven and on earth, for believers there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we live, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we live.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Christological Shema and the One Lordship

The confessional statement of vv. 5–6 is a watershed in NT christology. Paul takes the foundational monotheistic confession of Israel — “the LORD our God, the LORD is one” (Deut 6:4) — and distributes it between the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. God the Father receives the title “one God” with the phrase “from whom are all things and for whom we exist”; Jesus Christ receives the title “one Lord” with the phrase “through whom are all things and through whom we exist.” Both titles draw on the divine prerogative of creation. This is not bitheism or subordinationism; it is the Shema expanded to include the Son within the identity of the one God of Israel — which is exactly what Nicaea later defended.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The “strong” at Corinth were the theologically sophisticated — probably a mix of those with a Jewish background (who knew the idol was nothing) and educated Gentiles who had absorbed the Stoic critique of popular religion. Their knowledge was real. Their pride was realer. Now: The Reformed tradition is not immune to the Corinthian disease of knowledge-pride. The person who has worked through the doctrines of grace and arrived at the Reformation’s conclusions is in real danger of making theological correctness a platform for contempt of those still confused. Paul’s question applies: have you been known by God? (v. 3). That is the only knowledge that ultimately matters.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 8–10 answers another question from the Corinthians’ letter: may Christians eat food that has been offered to idols? Chapter 8 lays the foundation. Some Corinthians had knowledge: there is only one God, idols are nothing, so food offered to them is harmless. Paul agrees with their theology (vv. 4–6), and in doing so he writes one of the highest confessions of Christ in the New Testament: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made. But knowledge on its own puffs up; love builds up (vv. 1–3). Not every believer has this knowledge; some, with a past in idol worship, still feel that eating such food is taking part in idolatry, and their weak consciences are defiled if they eat (v. 7). So the strong must not use their freedom in a way that leads a weak brother to act against his conscience, and so to ruin. To sin against a brother like that is to sin against Christ, who died for him (vv. 9–12). Paul’s own resolve: if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat (v. 13). Chapter 9 then gives Paul’s example of giving up rights, and chapter 10 adds a warning about real idolatry. Behind the whole chapter stands the Lord who had every right and laid it down for his brothers.

The setting. Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple. Animals were sacrificed; part was burned, part went to the priests, and the rest was eaten at a temple feast or sold at the market. Social life in Corinth revolved around such meals: trade guild dinners, birthday parties and civic festivals were often held in temple dining rooms. Civic life, trade, family celebration and religious observance were not separate departments. To refuse such meals could cost a Christian business, friends and social standing; a man who refused all such meat was withdrawing from a great deal of ordinary life. So the question was live, and it divided the church.

Now concerning food offered to idols. Another question from their letter. The word is eidōlothyta, idol-sacrifices: a Jewish and Christian word, with a sneer built into it. Pagans called the same food simply sacred offering.

We know that “all of us possess knowledge”. Probably another Corinthian slogan, and Paul opens not by answering the question but by quoting the confident party. They were proud of their theological knowledge (gnōsis), and they were not wrong about the facts.

This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up. The key principle of chapters 8–10, and the sentence that governs the next three chapters. The two verbs are chosen with care, and they are opposites in a particular way. Physioō is the inflation word Paul has used repeatedly of this church (4:6, 18–19; 5:2): something swollen with air, like a balloon, larger than its substance justifies. Oikodomeō is the building word from chapter 3: laying one course on another, like a house, until something stands. Both make a thing bigger. Only one makes it stronger. Inflation is quick and impressive and there is nothing inside it; construction is slow and unglamorous and it holds weight. Knowledge used without love becomes pride. That is Paul’s judgment on knowledge held without love, and it is not a criticism of knowledge. He is about to affirm that the strong party’s theology is entirely correct.

If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know. The trap here is exquisite and inescapable. The very confidence that you have understood a matter is itself the evidence that you have not understood it as you should, because knowing as one ought includes knowing what knowledge is for. A man using his theology to feel superior has missed that entirely, however accurate his conclusions. Those who are proud of their knowledge show that they do not really understand. True knowledge of God humbles and produces love. If I understand all mysteries and all knowledge, but have not love, I am nothing (13:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge is bad, or that Christians should not study theology. It means knowledge must serve love. Paul himself is about to teach some of the deepest theology in the letter. The problem is never too much truth; it is truth held in a closed fist.

A warning for readers of theology. This lands with peculiar force on people who read commentaries. There is a version of the Christian life that consists almost entirely of acquiring correct positions, on grace, on election, on baptism, on whatever the current dispute is, and then holding them against people who have not yet arrived. It can be sustained for decades. It feels like maturity, because information is accumulating. And it is precisely what Paul is describing. The Reformed tradition is not exempt; if anything it is exposed, because its doctrines are genuinely clarifying, and the clarity is genuinely enjoyable, and a man who has worked through them can very easily begin to regard other Christians as the not-yet-arrived. Paul’s verdict on that man is not that his doctrine is wrong. It is that he does not yet know as he ought.

So should I stop arguing for what I believe is true? No. Paul argues hard throughout this letter, and truth matters enough to contend for (Jude 3). The question is not whether you speak but why and how. Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15), aiming at the other person’s good rather than at winning; listen before you correct; distinguish the doctrines on which the gospel stands from the ones on which faithful Christians differ; and be willing to lose an argument rather than a brother. If you notice that you enjoy someone else being wrong, stop and pray before you say anything more.

In a sentence. On the question of meat sacrificed to idols: the Corinthians claim that they all have knowledge, but knowledge on its own makes people proud, while love builds others up. Anyone who thinks he has mastered something has not yet understood it as he should.

On a Tuesday. When you know you are right about something, ask: am I using this knowledge to build others up, or to puff myself up? And a test that is uncomfortably easy to run. Take the doctrinal position you hold most firmly and most enjoy holding. Then ask what it has actually built: not what it has settled in your own mind, but who has been strengthened by your holding it. Name a person. If nobody comes to mind, the thing may still be true and you may still be right, and it has been inflating rather than building. Pursue what makes for peace and for mutual upbuilding (Romans 14:19).

For worship. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3), and he never once used them to make anyone feel small. The one who knew everything, who knew what was in man and needed no one to tell him, took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet. In him knowledge and love are not rivals; they are one perfect life. He knew the Father as no one else ever has, and he spent that knowledge building up fishermen, tax collectors and prostitutes into a house for God. Every true thing we learn about him is meant to make us more like that, and the knowledge of God which he gives is a knowledge that kneels.
verseByVerse.note: Much of the meat sold in the market had first been offered in a pagan temple; temples also had dining rooms used for banquets and celebrations. The quoted phrases are probably Corinthian slogans.

verseByVerse.quote: But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.

But if anyone loves God. The contrast to verse 2. What matters is not how much you know but whether you love God.

He is known by God. The sentence does not go where the grammar leads you to expect. Paul has been talking about knowledge; the natural completion is: if anyone loves God, he knows God. Instead the direction reverses, and the subject changes. You were expecting a statement about your knowing. You get a statement about God’s. It is one of the great turns in Paul, and he makes it elsewhere too. Writing to the Galatians he begins the same way and corrects himself mid-sentence: now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God (Galatians 4:9). He evidently could not leave the first formulation standing. The deepest reality is not our knowledge of God but God’s knowledge of us: his loving, choosing, personal knowledge (2 Timothy 2:19; Romans 8:29). Our love for God is the evidence that he first knew and loved us. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19).

The full Hebrew weight. “Known” here is not the possession of information about somebody; it is the language of relationship, of choosing, of intimate acquaintance. It is what God says to Jeremiah: before I formed you in the womb I knew you (Jeremiah 1:5); and what he says of Israel: you only have I known of all the families of the earth (Amos 3:2). Being known by God is being loved, chosen and dealt with personally. And it puts the weight in the right place. Knowledge that puffs up is knowledge of which I am the subject: my grasp, my understanding, my position, my achievement. The moment the sentence turns round, the whole basis of that inflation is removed. What is fundamental is not that I have understood God but that he has known me.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God only learns about us when we love him. He knew his people before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). It means that love for God is the sign that we are known by him.

I feel I understand so little. Does God know me? This verse was written for you. Some Christians live with a low, persistent anxiety about the quality of their grasp of God. They read, and forget what they read. Their theology feels thin next to other people’s. They could not defend the faith if pressed, and are not sure they have understood justification properly even after years. And underneath is the suspicion that their standing with God is proportional to how well they have got hold of him, and that their hold is not very good. Paul takes the whole question away. The security of your relationship with God has never rested on the firmness of your grip. It rests on his. You are known, and you were known before you knew anything, and nothing about the quality of your understanding alters it. The one mark Paul looks for is not knowledge at all: if anyone loves God. Do you love him, however feebly? Then he knows you.

And how do I know whether I love God? Not chiefly by the strength of your feelings on a given day. Love for God shows itself in wanting him, coming back to him when you have strayed, grieving over sin because it offends him, delighting in his word even when you understand little of it, loving his people, and wanting to obey: if you love me, you will keep my commandments (John 14:15). Peter, after failing badly, could only say, Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you (John 21:17). That is enough. And even weak love is a sign of something stronger beneath it: his love for you came first.

In a sentence. But whoever loves God is the one God knows as his own.

On a Tuesday. The plainest believer in the room can answer this verse, and the most learned often cannot. So this week, when you feel the urge to measure yourself against someone who knows more, or less, than you, stop and say to God: you know me. Then tell him simply that you love him, and ask him to make that love grow. It was, at bottom, why the confident party at Corinth were in the wrong even while being right: they had a great deal of information about a God who knew them, and had not noticed that being known was the whole of it.

For worship. You are known by God. Not just known about, but known and loved. O LORD, you have searched me and known me; you know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar (Psalm 139:1–2). He knew you when you were being knit together in your mother’s womb, and before that, before the foundation of the world, when he chose you in Christ. The Good Shepherd knows his own by name, and they know his voice, and he laid down his life for them (John 10:14–15). The firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: the Lord knows those who are his (2 Timothy 2:19). Your grip will slip a thousand times. His never has.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.” For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—

Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols. Paul returns to the topic and states the theology, and it is worth registering that he agrees with the strong party without reservation.

We know that “an idol has no real existence”. Probably another slogan: an idol is nothing in the world. Paul endorses it. The wooden thing in the temple is not a god. There is no real god behind the statue; there is nobody there; the meat that passed in front of it has not been altered in any way (Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8). Paul agrees, though in 10:20 he adds that demons are behind idol worship.

And that “there is no God but one”. The confession of Israel (Deuteronomy 6:4), the bedrock of Israel’s faith and now of the church’s. Monotheism is foundational.

For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth. Gods in heaven: sun, moon, Zeus, Apollo. On earth: deified emperors, local gods, heroes. Paul is granting that these beings are real as objects of worship.

As indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”. In one sense they exist: people worship them, and they hold real power over people’s lives. “Lords” (kyrioi) was a title for mystery-religion deities like Serapis, and for the emperor. The pantheon existed in the sense that people believed in it, temples were built for it, and lives were organised around it. Zeus had no existence; the worship of Zeus was one of the most powerful forces in that society. Both things are true at once.

Nothing, or demons? A careful reader will notice a tension here, and it should not be smoothed over. Two chapters later Paul will say something that sounds like the opposite: what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God, and he does not want the Corinthians to be participants with demons (10:20). So which is it? Both, and the two statements answer different questions. In what it is, the idol is nothing: no deity corresponds to it, and the food is not contaminated. But spiritually, idolatry is not therefore harmless, because a real enemy is happy to occupy the space a false god vacates. The image is empty; the worship is not. That is why Paul can say in chapter 8 that the meat is neutral and in chapter 10 that attending the temple feast is participation in something evil. It was never the meat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean idolatry is harmless because idols are nothing. Paul will warn that behind idols are demons (10:19–21). Nor does it mean that other religions are harmless paths to the same God; there is one God, and the gods of the nations are not him.

How idolatry works now. That distinction has a great deal of modern use, because it is exactly how idolatry works today. Few people reading this are tempted by a statue. But the things we organise our lives around, money, career, a child’s success, the good opinion of others, a political cause, are in themselves nothing whatever, and the devotion given to them is real, and it does real damage. An idol is not usually a rival god. It is a good thing that has been asked to do a job only God can do, and it always fails, and the failing is what wrecks people. The money does not steady you. The career does not justify you. The child cannot bear the weight of being your reason for living. There was nothing there to bear it, exactly as Paul says.

How can I tell if something has become an idol? Ask what you cannot imagine being content without; what you most fear losing; what you run to for comfort when you are low; where your money and spare thoughts go without effort; and what makes you angriest when it is threatened. A good thing has become an idol when losing it would feel like losing your life, or when you would disobey God to keep it. The remedy is not usually to throw the good thing away, but to put it back in its place under God, to thank him for it, and to find in him what you were asking it to give.

Isaiah’s carpenter. Scripture’s mockery of idols is not merely polemic but pastoral. Isaiah’s carpenter cuts down a tree, burns half of it to roast his dinner, and bows down to the other half asking it to save him (Isaiah 44:14–17). It is comic, and the point of the comedy is compassion: a man is asking a piece of firewood to do for him what only God can do, and he will not be answered. Those who make them become like them (Psalm 115:8).

In a sentence. So, about eating food sacrificed to idols: we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is only one God. There may be many so-called gods and lords in heaven or on earth, and people do treat many as gods and lords,

On a Tuesday. Our culture has its own gods and lords: money, pleasure, success, image, comfort, approval. Name one in your life, the one you would least like to be named, and dethrone it today: tell God what you have been asking it to give you, and ask him for it instead.

For worship. The idols have mouths but do not speak, eyes but do not see, ears but do not hear (Psalm 115:5–6). Our God is in the heavens; he does all that he pleases (Psalm 115:3). He speaks, and the worlds come into being; he sees the sparrow fall; he hears the faintest prayer of the weakest of his children. The gods of Corinth had temples on every hill and could not answer when spoken to. The living God has no statue and needs none, because he has shown his face in his Son. To turn from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9) is to wake from a dream about firewood into the presence of the One who is real, and who is love.

parallels.desc: the LORD our God, the LORD is one

verseByVerse.quote: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.

Yet for us there is one God, the Father. For Christians, against all the so-called gods, there is one God. This is one of the most remarkable sentences in the New Testament, and its force is invisible unless you know what Paul is quoting.

From whom are all things and for whom we exist. The Father is the source of all creation, and its goal. We exist for him: from him and through him and to him are all things (Romans 11:36).

And one Lord, Jesus Christ. Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus. Every Jew recited the Shema twice daily: Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). It was the confession that separated Israel from every nation around her, the thing Jews had died rather than compromise. In the Greek Bible it contains two crucial words: theos, God, and kyrios, Lord, the standard rendering of the divine name. Paul takes them and applies God to the Father and Lord to Jesus. He has not added a second deity alongside the first; that would be the abandonment of monotheism, and he has just insisted two verses earlier that there is no God but one. He has put Jesus inside the confession, distributing its own words between Father and Son. Jesus is included within the one God of Israel’s confession. Nothing prepares you for a first-century Jew doing that. Whatever else Paul thought about Jesus of Nazareth, he thought the divine name belonged to him, and he thought it so naturally that he can say it in passing, in the middle of a discussion about meat, without pausing to defend it.

Through whom are all things and through whom we exist. Then the prepositions, and they are not decoration. Of the Father: from whom and for whom, the source and the goal. Of Christ: through whom, the agent of creation and of our new existence. All things were made through him (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2). And through him we exist as new creatures, redeemed. Only God creates; creation is the exclusive prerogative of God in the Old Testament, and it is here assigned to Jesus without qualification. So Jesus is God.

Where Christians differ: the deity of Christ. Groups such as Jehovah’s Witnesses argue that this verse distinguishes Jesus from the one God, making him a lesser being. Verdict: Paul is not separating Jesus from the one God of Israel but including him within it. He divides the words of the Shema between the Father and the Son, and gives the Son the divine work of creation. This is the earliest Christian confession of the Trinity in seed form. The Father and the Son are distinct persons, but one God, with the Holy Spirit (Nicene Creed; Westminster 2.3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father is not Lord, or the Son not God. Both titles belong to both. Paul uses them to distinguish the persons while affirming one God. Nor does it leave out the Holy Spirit, whose deity Paul affirms elsewhere in this letter (2:10–11; 12:4–6).

Why does this belong in an argument about meat? Paul is not making a doctrinal excursion. The strong party’s freedom rests on this: if all things are from the Father and through the Son, then a piece of meat cannot belong to anybody else. It was made by Christ. Passing it in front of a carved image does not transfer the title. The earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof (Psalm 24:1; 10:26). And that is a more cheerful doctrine of creation than many Christians actually hold. There is a strain of piety that treats the physical world as spiritually suspect, food, pleasure, beauty, the body, as though holiness consisted in wariness. Paul’s answer is that every good thing came through Christ and belongs to him, and that the enemy has never made anything and cannot own what he did not make.

How do I explain the Trinity simply to a friend? Say what Scripture says, without pretending to explain everything. There is one God (Deuteronomy 6:4).
