The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God, and they are not three gods but one God in three persons, who speak to one another and love one another (Matthew 3:16–17; 28:19). This verse shows it in miniature: Israel’s one God, confessed now as Father and Lord Jesus. Avoid analogies like water, ice and steam, which suggest one person in three modes. It is a mystery, not a contradiction, and it is precisely what makes the gospel possible: the Father sent the Son, the Son gave himself, and the Spirit brings us to both.

In a sentence. but for us there is only one God, the Father, the source of everything and the goal of our life, and only one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom everything was made and through whom we have our life.

On a Tuesday. Take one ordinary good thing today, a meal, a walk, the face of someone you love, and say over it: this came from the Father, through the Son, and it is for him. Receive it with thanks. And when you pray, notice that you come to the Father through the Son, because there is one God and one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

For worship. Confess it today: one God, the Father; one Lord, Jesus Christ. There is one God and he is a Father. There is one Lord and he is the carpenter from Nazareth, through whom the universe was made and through whom the people at Corinth were now alive: the same hands. The hands that flung the stars into place were the hands that broke bread in Galilee and were nailed to a Roman cross. The gods of Corinth had made nothing, not one blade of grass. And the God who made all of it, and owns all of it, was known to that fractious little congregation by name, and had died for them. Worship the Father through the Son, for of him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever.
verseByVerse.note: Paul expands Israel’s confession “the LORD is one” to include Jesus Christ as the one Lord.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Weak Brother and the Limits of Freedom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But not everyone has this knowledge. Some, used to idols until recently, still think of the food as offered to an idol when they eat it, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not bring us closer to God; we are no worse off if we do not eat and no better off if we do. But they must be careful that their freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak. If someone with a weak conscience sees a knowledgeable believer eating in an idol’s temple, he may be encouraged to eat idol food himself, and so the weak believer, a brother for whom Christ died, is destroyed by the other’s knowledge. Sinning against fellow believers in this way, wounding their weak consciences, is sinning against Christ. So if food makes a brother fall, Paul will never eat meat again, so as not to make him fall.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Weak Brother and the Limits of Christian Freedom

The category of “weak brother” in Paul is not a permanent spiritual classification but a pastoral description of someone whose conscience is not yet formed to the level of theological maturity the gospel makes possible. The strong are not forbidden to exercise their freedom; they are required to consider the effect of their freedom on those still developing. This is not a silencing of the theologically mature but a school in cruciform love: the pattern of Christ, who “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor” (2 Cor 8:9), is the paradigm for the voluntary limitation of legitimate freedom in love for the weak.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific situation — food offered to idols in a pagan temple context — is culturally remote for most Western Christians. But the principle is not: the more mature members of any community regularly face the question of how to use their freedom in ways that do not damage those who are less free. Now: The contemporary applications range from alcohol (where an alcoholic is in the room) to entertainment choices (where a recovering addict might be triggered) to musical styles in worship (where real spiritual associations exist for some). The principle is constant: love for the weak sibling takes precedence over the exercise of genuine freedom.

verseByVerse.quote: However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.

However, not all possess this knowledge. In theory, all believers know there is one God. But not all have absorbed it deeply enough to feel free. The theology of verses 4–6 is correct, and Paul has just endorsed it. He now points out that correct theology is not evenly distributed, and that this fact is itself a pastoral reality the strong must reckon with.

But some, through former association with idols. “Former association” (synētheia) means habit, being used to something. Gentile believers who had worshipped idols all their lives could not shake the feeling that eating such food meant joining in worship. These are converts out of paganism, and not long out. For most of their lives that meat had been part of a religious act they took part in: the procession, the temple, the smell of it, the sense of being in the presence of a god. Their minds now accept that the idol is nothing. Their instincts have not caught up, and instincts formed over thirty years do not dissolve because a doctrine has been explained.

Eat food as really offered to an idol. When they eat, they feel it is an act of idolatry. They do not experience it as neutral nutrition. They experience it as going back, and something in them registers the act as betrayal.

And their conscience, being weak, is defiled. “Weak” (asthenēs) means not strong enough to be free. “Defiled” (molynō) means stained. If they eat against their conscience, they feel guilty, and in fact they sin, because they act against what they believe is God’s will: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

The doctrine of conscience. This needs stating plainly, because it is widely misunderstood. The conscience is not infallible. It is the faculty that judges our actions against the standard we actually hold, and that standard can be badly formed, over-scrupulous, or simply mistaken, as it is here, since the food is genuinely harmless. And yet, and this is the crucial point, a conscience that is wrong must still not be violated. The man who eats while believing it wrong is defiled, not because the food defiled him but because he has trained himself to act against his own conviction. What he has learned is that his conscience can be overruled when it is inconvenient, and that lesson does not stay confined to meat. A man who has taught himself to proceed against his conscience once will do it again, in a matter where the conscience was right. So the way to deal with a mistaken conscience is not to override it but to instruct it. It is educated by Scripture, slowly, until conviction and truth line up, and until then it is to be respected even in its error.

Food will not commend us to God. Probably another slogan of the strong, which Paul accepts. Food does not bring us closer to God.

We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do. Eating is spiritually neutral. So the strong lose nothing by giving it up, which is the hinge of the whole argument that follows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a weak conscience is good. It is weak. But it must be respected and gently instructed, not overridden. Nor does weak mean less spiritual or less loved; it means a conscience that has not yet caught up with the freedom Christ has given.

Am I the weak one or the strong one? Most of us are both, in different matters. You may be free about a glass of wine and troubled about Sunday shopping, or the other way round. On any given question, the strong believer is the one who rightly understands that Scripture leaves it free; the weak believer is the one whose conscience still forbids what God allows. Neither is a permanent rank. The strong must not despise; the weak must not judge (Romans 14:3). Both must grow: the weak in understanding, the strong in love.

Where it applies today. There are Christians who cannot do things that other Christians do freely, a drink, a film, a Sunday activity, a form of music, not because Scripture forbids it but because their history makes it impossible for them. The former alcoholic, the convert from a religion where certain foods were sacred, the believer who came out of the occult and cannot bear certain images: these are today’s weak brothers. The mature response is neither to mock the scruple nor to pretend it is a command of God. It is to recognise that a real person is carrying a real formation, and to be gentle with it.

In a sentence. Yet not everyone grasps this. Some, still used to idols, eat such food as though it were truly offered to an idol, and because their conscience is weak, it is stained. Food will not bring us nearer to God: we lose nothing by not eating, and gain nothing by eating.

On a Tuesday. Be patient with Christians whose past makes them sensitive about things you are free in. Their scruples may come from a painful history. And ask the honest personal question too: is there something you have talked yourself into doing while a small voice was still objecting? Paul’s concern here is not chiefly the act. It is what happens to a man who learns to proceed anyway. If your conscience is troubled, stop, search the Scriptures, and ask a mature believer. Do not train yourself to ignore it.

For worship. The Lord is gentle with consciences. A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench (Isaiah 42:3). He does not drag his weak children forward faster than they can walk; he carries the lambs in his arms and gently leads those that are with young (Isaiah 40:11). And he gave his people consciences as a gift, a voice that echoes his law, and then he cleansed those consciences with his own blood so that they could serve the living God without fear (Hebrews 9:14). The goal of our instruction is love that issues from a pure heart and a good conscience and a sincere faith (1 Timothy 1:5), and the One who gives all three is patient beyond telling.

verseByVerse.quote: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?

But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak. “Right” (exousia) means authority, liberty, a genuine entitlement. Paul concedes it is theirs. He has spent five verses establishing that they are correct, and he does not now take it back. What he questions is not whether they may, but what happens when they do. “Stumbling block” (proskomma) is something in the path that trips a man who did not see it. And the image is exact, because nobody sets out to trip anyone. The strong Corinthian is not trying to damage his weaker brother; he is simply exercising a liberty in front of him without thinking about the effect.

For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple. The scenario is specific. The strong were not only eating idol meat at home but attending meals in temple dining rooms. Archaeologists have found such dining rooms at the temple of Asclepius in Corinth. This is not the marketplace and it is not a private dinner, both of which Paul will permit in chapter 10 (10:25–27). It is the temple dining room, the most public and most religiously loaded venue available. The strong believer is sitting there, entirely convinced that the god is nothing, enjoying his freedom and quite possibly enjoying the demonstration of it. And the weak brother walks past and sees him.

Will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols? “Encouraged” is literally built up (oikodomeō), the same word as love builds up (v. 1), now used with bitter irony. The strong think they are building up the weak by showing freedom, but they are building them up to sin. The weak man is indeed built up: emboldened to do a thing his conscience still condemns, on the strength of another Christian’s example. He has been constructed into a wall that will fall on him.

How influence actually works. The damage is not done by argument. Nobody persuaded the weak brother of anything. He simply watched somebody he respected doing it, concluded it must be all right, and did it against his own conviction. That means every Christian is teaching all the time, whether or not they intend to. The younger believer in your church is not principally learning from what you say about holiness. He is learning from what he watches you do with your evenings, your money, your speech when you are annoyed, and your freedom.

What it does not mean. It does not mean eating in a temple is fine as long as no weak brother sees. In chapter 10 Paul will say that eating at temple feasts is in fact participating with demons (10:20–21). He is answering the strong on their own ground first, and will go further later.

How do I know whether my freedom will trip someone? It cannot be answered in the abstract, which is why Paul gives no list. The same action is fine in one setting and destructive in another, and the only way to tell is to know the people you are among. Love here requires attention. Ask who is present, what their history is, how young they are in the faith, and whether they are likely to copy you against their own conscience. When you do not know, you can ask them gently. And when you are unsure, it is rarely a loss to hold back. The strong Corinthian’s failure was not chiefly theological. He had not looked round the room.

In a sentence. But be careful that your freedom does not trip up those whose faith is weaker. If someone with a weak conscience sees you, who know better, eating in an idol’s temple, won’t he be emboldened to eat what has been sacrificed to idols?

On a Tuesday. The question this passage puts is not am I entitled to do this? The strong were entitled, and Paul says so twice. The question is who is watching, and what will they conclude? Think of one younger Christian who watches you, a child, a new believer, a colleague who knows you go to church, and ask what your example this week will build in them. Decide never to put a stumbling block or hindrance in the way of a brother (Romans 14:13).

For worship. The Lord Jesus is the one who never once put a stumbling block before the weak. He was free as no one has ever been free, Lord of the Sabbath and of every food, and he used his freedom only to heal, to feed and to lift up. He paid a tax he did not owe so as not to give offence (Matthew 17:27). Where we clumsily trip one another, he walks among his people setting the fallen on their feet, and he is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). Our example is mixed; his is perfect, and his is the one his people are finally built up by.

verseByVerse.quote: And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died. Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.

And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed. “Destroyed” (apollymi) is the ruin word, the one used of perishing. Paul is not describing embarrassment or a setback. He is describing a man being wrecked. The weak believer, acting against conscience, falls into sin and is spiritually ruined, perhaps drawn back into idolatry. The mechanism was set out in the previous verse: emboldened by watching a stronger believer, he acts against his conscience; having done it once he does it again; the habit of overriding conviction spreads to matters where the conviction was right; and a man who has learned that his conscience may be silenced when it is inconvenient is on a road that leads somewhere. That is how people are destroyed: not usually by a decision, but by a series of small permissions. The very knowledge the strong were proud of becomes the weapon that ruins him.

The brother for whom Christ died. The supreme reason, and the phrase that ends the argument. Set the two things side by side, which is exactly what Paul is doing. On one side, a man’s liberty to eat a particular piece of meat: genuine, defensible, correct. On the other, a person so valuable that the Son of God went to a cross for him. He is your brother, and Christ loved him enough to die for him. Will you not give up a meal for him? The strong Corinthian had never framed it that way. He was thinking about a principle, and he was right about the principle. He was not thinking about a person, and the person had a price attached that made the principle look very small.

Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak. “Wounding” (typtō) means striking, beating. To push a weak conscience is to beat it.

You sin against Christ. And there is the last step, which the Corinthians would not have anticipated at all. The offence does not stop at the brother. It travels. Christ is so united to his people that sin against them is sin against him (Matthew 25:40, 45; Acts 9:4). Paul has said this before in the letter: believers are members of Christ, limbs of his body (6:15), and you cannot damage a limb without the head registering it. It is the same thing the risen Christ said to Saul of Tarsus on the Damascus road, and Saul never got over it. He had never touched Jesus of Nazareth. He had been arresting Christians in Jerusalem and was on his way to do the same in Damascus, and the voice said: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? The man who wrote this verse had been on the wrong side of that sentence, and it is quite possibly why he puts it so strongly here.

Where Christians differ: can a brother for whom Christ died perish? Some take this verse as proof that Christ died for some who will finally be lost. Verdict: Paul describes the real tendency of the strong person’s action: it would lead the brother to ruin. The warning is real. But Scripture also teaches that Christ’s death infallibly saves those for whom he died (Romans 8:32–34; John 10:15, 28), and God uses warnings like this one as means to keep his people. The point is that the strong should treat every brother as someone precious enough for Christ to die for. This is consistent with definite atonement and the perseverance of the saints. Paul is not inviting speculation about whether the weak brother will finally be saved. He is telling the strong that their freedom could push someone toward ruin, and that this is a sin against Christ (Romans 14:15, 20). God keeps his sheep, and one of the ways he keeps them is through brothers who heed warnings like this one.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the weak have no responsibility. They too should grow in knowledge. But the strong must not take advantage of their weakness.

No private injuries. The sobering conclusion is that there is no such thing as a private injury within the church. The sharp remark, the cold shoulder maintained for two years, the person you have quietly written off: none of it stops with them. Christ counts what is done to his people as done to himself, which is a terrifying thought for the offender and an immeasurably comforting one for anyone who has been on the receiving end. And it applies well beyond food. Whenever a Christian is about to insist on being right at another believer’s expense, in an argument, in a church meeting, in a family, this sentence is the corrective. Not are you right? but: what did the person you are about to run over cost him?

I think I have caused someone to stumble. What should I do? Confess it to God, and receive his forgiveness; Christ died for your sin against your brother too. Then, where it is wise, go to the person, own what you did without excuse, and ask their forgiveness (Matthew 5:23–24). Stop the thing that was harming them, at least in their presence. If they have fallen into sin because of your example, help them back gently, and pray for them by name. Do not drown in guilt: the Lord who warns is the Lord who restores, and he can use even this to teach you love.

In a sentence. So this weak believer, the brother Christ died for, is ruined by your knowledge. When you sin against your brothers like this and bruise their fragile consciences, you are sinning against Christ himself.

On a Tuesday. Before you exercise a freedom, look at the person beside you and remember: Christ died for him. Do the same before you speak in the next argument. Put the name of the person you find most difficult in your church into this phrase, the brother for whom Christ died, or the sister, and say it aloud. It changes the temperature of everything.

For worship. Christ died for him: the weak, slow, scrupulous believer the strong had overlooked. The Lord of glory set his love on people of no account, and he holds them so close that a blow to their conscience lands on him. He is the head who feels every wound in his body, the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine for the one, the high priest who bears the names of his people on his heart. No one in his church is beneath him. And if he so values the weakest of them that he would die for them, then he so values you. His blood has set a price on every believer, and it is beyond all reckoning.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble. “Stumble” (skandalizō) means cause to fall into sin. Paul turns from argument to personal example. He does not conclude with a policy. He concludes with himself, and with a statement so absolute that it settles the matter by example rather than by rule.

I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble. “Never” is emphatic: never, to eternity, as emphatic in the Greek as in English, reaching to the end of the age. Not I will be careful. Not I will use discretion. Never. Not just idol meat, but any meat, if it would cause a brother to fall. Paul is willing to give up a right entirely for love’s sake. And notice that he has moved from the second person to the first. He has spent twelve verses telling the strong what they should consider; he ends by telling them what he himself will do. It is much harder to resent a man who has already gone further than he is asking you to go. And it cost him something real. Meat was not an everyday item for most people, but for the man who could afford it, giving it up permanently was a genuine loss, and Paul volunteers it without hesitation, for the sake of a weaker Christian whose name he may not even know. This leads into chapter 9, where he shows how he has given up other rights for the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul became a vegetarian on principle, or that anyone can forbid others anything by claiming offence. The point is the real danger of leading a brother into sin.

Does this give the most easily offended person a veto? No, and this guard is needed, because the verse can be turned into an instrument of exactly the opposite kind. Read carelessly, it puts the most easily offended person in any congregation in complete control. If anyone’s disapproval obliges everyone else to stop, the church is governed by whoever is prepared to be upset, and every genuine liberty can be shut down by someone announcing that they find it a stumbling block. That is not what Paul is describing, and the difference is in the passage. His weak brother is not someone who disapproves; he is someone in danger of being led into sin against his own conscience and destroyed by it (vv. 10–11). Being scandalised is not the same as being tripped. A man who says I disapprove of what you are doing is making a criticism; a man who is about to act against his own convictions because of your example is in danger, and only the second is in view here. Nor does Paul suggest the weak should stay weak. Romans 14, the fullest treatment of the same question, puts obligations on both sides: the strong must not despise the weak, and the weak must not pass judgment on the strong (Romans 14:3). Neither is given the whip hand. And where someone insists on a scruple as a rule for the whole church, as the circumcision party did, Paul resists them to the face (Galatians 2:11–14).

A harder thing than a rule. What is left, when both errors are excluded, is something harder than a rule and better: a willingness to lose a genuine right for the sake of a particular person, decided case by case, by people who are paying attention to each other.

In a sentence. So if what Paul eats would cause his brother to fall, he will give up meat for good, rather than make his brother fall.

On a Tuesday. Name one freedom you value that you could set aside this week, for one particular person, without any loss to your soul: the drink at a meal with a friend who is fighting addiction, the film when the young people are watching, the sharp joke in front of someone fragile. Set it aside quietly, without announcing your sacrifice. That is what love does.

For worship. The pattern is not Paul’s invention. He is doing in miniature what his Lord did entirely. One who had every right, to glory, to be served, to be spared, did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:6–7). The strong at Corinth were asked to give up beef for a brother. He gave up heaven for enemies, and never once insisted on his rights. He set aside the glory he had with the Father before the world existed, and went down to the manger and the cross, so that weak, stumbling people could be lifted up and seated with him. Every right we lay down for a brother is a small shadow of his great descent, and he is worthy of every one.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning food offered to idols: we know that “all of us possess knowledge.” This “knowledge” puffs up, but love builds up.<sup>2</sup>If anyone imagines that he knows something, he does not yet know as he ought to know.<sup>3</sup>But if anyone loves God, he is known by God.<sup>4</sup>Therefore, as to the eating of food offered to idols, we know that “an idol has no real existence,” and that “there is no God but one.”<sup>5</sup>For although there may be so-called gods in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many “gods” and many “lords”—<sup>6</sup>yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist.<sup>7</sup>However, not all possess this knowledge. But some, through former association with idols, eat food as really offered to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.<sup>8</sup>Food will not commend us to God. We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do.<sup>9</sup>But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.<sup>10</sup>For if anyone sees you who have knowledge eating in an idol’s temple, will he not be encouraged, if his conscience is weak, to eat food offered to idols?<sup>11</sup>And so by your knowledge this weak person is destroyed, the brother for whom Christ died.<sup>12</sup>Thus, sinning against your brothers and wounding their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, if food makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat, lest I make my brother stumble.

9.title: Rights Surrendered: The Apostle as Slave to All
9.overview:
Chapter 9 can look like a digression from idol food, but it is Paul’s example. He has just said he would give up meat rather than harm a brother. Now he shows that he lives that way. As an apostle he has every right to financial support: to food and drink, to bring a wife on his travels like Peter and the Lord’s brothers, and to be paid like a soldier, a farmer or a shepherd. The law of Moses says the same, the temple priests lived from the offerings, and Jesus himself commanded that preachers of the gospel should live by it. Yet Paul has used none of these rights in Corinth, because he would rather die than give anyone a reason to say he preached for money.

His freedom is spent in serving others. He has made himself everyone’s slave to win as many as possible: to Jews he lived as a Jew, to Gentiles as one outside the Mosaic law (though never outside God’s law, since he is under Christ’s law), to the weak as weak. He does it all for the gospel. Then Paul turns to the Isthmian Games, held every two years just outside Corinth. Athletes train with fierce self-control for a wreath that withers. Christians run for a crown that lasts, so Paul disciplines his body, lest after preaching to others he himself should be disqualified.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks whether he is not free, whether he is not an apostle who has seen Jesus the Lord, and whether the Corinthians themselves are not the result of his work in the Lord. Even if others doubt his apostleship, the Corinthian church is the seal that proves it. To his critics he offers this defence. He and Barnabas have the right to be fed, the right to take a believing wife with them like the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Peter, and the right not to work for a living. No soldier pays his own wages, no one plants a vineyard without eating its grapes, no shepherd goes without milk. The law of Moses says not to muzzle an ox while it threshes, and that was written for our sake, so that workers can expect a share of the harvest. If Paul has sown spiritual seed among them, it is not too much to reap material support. Others enjoy this right; Paul more so. Yet he has not used it, but puts up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ. Those who serve in the temple eat from its offerings, and in the same way the Lord has commanded that those who preach the gospel should get their living from it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Right of Ministers to Financial Support

Paul’s argument from Deuteronomy 25:4 (“You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain”) follows a characteristic pattern in his hermeneutics: the OT command for the benefit of animals carries an “how much more” application to human ministers of the gospel. The principle that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7, quoted by Paul in 1 Tim 5:18) is embedded in the creation order and confirmed by the Lord’s own command. The Reformed tradition has always insisted on adequate financial support for ordained ministry as a matter of justice, not charity — grounded precisely in passages like this.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The travelling sophist in Corinth charged fees for his teaching; the apostle who did not was, paradoxically, suspected of being less legitimate — not worth paying. Paul’s refusal to accept payment actually undermined his status in the eyes of some Corinthians, which is why he defends the right even while refusing to exercise it. Now: The principle cuts in two directions: congregations should support their ministers generously; ministers should never let financial considerations drive their preaching agenda. The apostle who can preach without anxiety about whether his congregation will like what they hear is the freest preacher in the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 9 can look like a change of subject, but it is Paul’s personal illustration of the principle of chapter 8: give up your rights for the sake of others. The strong in Corinth insisted on their right to eat. Paul shows that he, an apostle, has far greater rights: to be supported financially, to bring a wife on his travels, to stop working with his hands. He proves these rights from common sense, the law of Moses, temple practice and the command of the Lord himself (vv. 1–14). Yet he has given them all up, so as not to hinder the gospel. His reward is to preach free of charge (vv. 15–18). More than that, he has made himself a slave to all, becoming like a Jew to Jews, like a Gentile to Gentiles, weak to the weak, all things to all people, to win some (vv. 19–23). Finally, he uses the picture of athletes in training: the Christian life demands self-discipline, so that we win the imperishable prize and are not disqualified (vv. 24–27). And through it all shines the pattern of Christ, who though he was free made himself a servant of all, and gave up everything to win a people for God.

Not a digression. The chapter opens with four questions fired off without pause, and a reader coming from chapter 8 may wonder what has happened. Paul was discussing food offered to idols; suddenly he is defending his apostleship. Seeing why unlocks the whole chapter. Paul has just asked the strong at Corinth to surrender a genuine right for the sake of a weaker brother (8:13). He now spends twenty-seven verses demonstrating that he has done exactly that himself, on a far larger scale and at real cost, and the demonstration requires him first to establish that the right was genuinely his. You cannot admire a man for refusing something he was never entitled to.

Am I not free? Free as the strong claimed to be (8:9). The question has been at issue since 6:12. Paul has the same freedom, and more.

Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Some in Corinth questioned Paul’s apostleship. An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord (Acts 1:21–22). Paul saw him on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3–6; 1 Corinthians 15:8), and he treats that as an appearance of the risen Christ no less real than those given to the Twelve.

Are not you my workmanship in the Lord? Then the fourth question, and it is the one that lands. The Corinthian church itself is proof of his apostleship. It exists because of his ministry. The people questioning his credentials are his credentials. There would be no church at Corinth to hold an opinion about Paul if Paul had not come to Corinth. Every person in the room who was sitting there rather than in a temple was evidence, and the argument is unanswerable because the jury is the exhibit.

If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord. A seal (sphragis) authenticated a document, like a signature or a wax stamp: the mark that proved it was what it claimed to be. Their conversion is God’s seal confirming Paul’s apostleship. A changed community is the authentication of a ministry.

The wound underneath. There is something worth noticing beneath this. Paul is defending himself to people he led to Christ. That is a particular kind of pain, and anyone who has invested years in someone who later turned and questioned their motives will recognise it: the parent whose grown child reinterprets the whole childhood, the mentor whose protégé now explains what was really wrong with him. Paul does not conceal that it stings; the questions have heat in them. But notice where he goes with it. He does not withdraw, does not write them off, and does not reduce his commitment to them. He is about to spend the rest of the chapter explaining how much he has given up for people who are currently examining him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who plants a church is an apostle in Paul’s sense. Paul’s apostleship rested on seeing the risen Lord and being commissioned by him directly. That office ended with the apostolic generation.

Are there apostles today? Not in this sense. An apostle in the sense Paul means had seen the risen Lord and been sent by him in person (15:8; Acts 1:21–22). No one can meet that now, and Paul calls himself the last of them (15:8). The office belonged to the church’s foundation, which was laid once (Ephesians 2:20), and it continues in the only way it can: through the apostolic writings in Scripture. The word is sometimes used today loosely, of missionaries or church planters, and in that sense it is harmless. But anyone claiming apostolic authority to add to Scripture or to rule the churches should be refused. We have the apostles; they speak to us in the New Testament.

In a sentence. Is Paul not free? Is he not an apostle? Has he not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you yourselves not the result of his work in the Lord? Others may doubt him, but you cannot; your very existence as a church in the Lord is the stamp that proves him an apostle.

On a Tuesday. The best evidence of anyone’s ministry is changed lives. Thank God for those who brought the gospel to you, and tell one of them this week. And if you are carrying the hurt of ingratitude from someone you served, ask what you have done since. The natural movement is to protect yourself: to give less, care less, keep a little back. Paul’s answer to being doubted by his own converts was to go on spending himself on them (2 Corinthians 12:15), and to write them, a few chapters later, the greatest chapter on love ever composed.

For worship. Paul’s seal was a church that had not existed until Christ called it out of the temples of Corinth. Every Christian is that kind of evidence. The risen Lord who met a persecutor on the Damascus road is still making new creations out of idolaters, and every one of them is a signature in his hand, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3). He was rejected by those he came to save, and he did not withdraw; he went on loving his own to the end. The apostle who would not stop giving to an ungrateful church had learned it from him.
verseByVerse.note: An apostle had to have seen the risen Lord. A seal authenticated a document.

verseByVerse.quote: This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is my defense to those who would examine me. Do we not have the right to eat and drink?

This is my defense to those who would examine me. The words are legal. “Defense” (apologia) is the speech for the defence, a legal reply. “Examine” (anakrinō) means cross-examine, the same word Paul used at 4:3, where he said it was a very small thing to him to be judged by them or by any human court. Some critics were questioning Paul, perhaps because he refused payment, which they took as a sign he was not a real apostle.

Indifferent about himself, not about the trust. At first sight the two passages pull apart. In chapter 4 he refuses to be tried by the Corinthians; here he mounts a defence. The difference is what is at stake. When it was his own standing, whether they thought well of him, he was serenely indifferent; the Lord is the judge. But his apostleship is not his personal property. It is the authority by which the gospel came to them, and if it can be dismissed then so can everything he taught. So he defends the office while remaining unmoved about the man. That distinction is useful for anyone who has to decide whether to answer a criticism. There is a great deal of criticism a Christian should simply let go, and reaching for a defence is usually vanity dressed as principle. But there are times when something is being undermined that is not yours to surrender: the truth of what you taught, the good name of a work God gave you, the safety of people in your care. Paul’s rule seems to be: be indifferent about yourself, and not indifferent about the trust.

Do we not have the right to eat and drink? Now the case begins, and it opens at the most basic level. The first right: to receive food and drink at the church’s expense. “We” includes Barnabas and others. “Right” (exousia) is the key word of chapters 8–9, the same word used of the strong Corinthians’ liberty in 8:9, which is precisely the link Paul is building. And notice the modesty of the claim. Not a stipend, not a house, not a position. Food and drink. The apostle to the Gentiles is establishing, at length and against opposition, that he would have been entitled to his dinner. And he went hungry rather than take it (4:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was defending himself out of pride. He was defending the gospel’s integrity and showing the strong how to give up rights. Nor does any use of this chapter that ends in comfort rather than in the freedom to preach without fear keep the thread. The passage does underwrite the proper support of gospel workers, as Paul will say plainly at verse 14, but the man defending it chose to work with his own hands (Acts 20:33–34).

When should I defend myself against criticism? First, ask honestly whether the criticism is true, in whole or in part; if so, receive it as a gift and change. If it is false and only your pride is hurt, you can usually let it go and leave your reputation with God (1 Peter 2:23). But if a falsehood threatens the gospel, the people in your care, or a work God has entrusted to you, then speak: calmly, truthfully, without attacking back, and preferably to the person directly. And whatever you do, do not let the hurt shrink your love for the critic.

In a sentence. This is Paul’s answer to those who put him on trial: Do we not have the right to be given food and drink?

On a Tuesday. Think of the last criticism that stung you. Ask the two questions: was any of it true? and was anything at stake besides my pride? Then act accordingly. And thank God for those who serve you in the word, and ask how you can support them, beginning with something as plain as a meal.

For worship. The Lord Jesus stood before his examiners and, for himself, opened not his mouth; like a sheep before its shearers he was silent (Isaiah 53:7). Yet when the truth was at stake he spoke it plainly, even to the high priest. He was indifferent to his own reputation and passionate for his Father’s glory, and the Judge of all the earth allowed himself to be cross-examined by sinners. He who has every right to food and drink, to whom the cattle on a thousand hills belong, had nowhere to lay his head. And now he spreads a table for his people and serves them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?

Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife. Literally, a sister, a wife: a Christian wife. The right to marry, and to have her travel with him at the churches’ expense.

As do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas? Three things in that sentence repay attention, and the first is almost always missed: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him on ministry, supported by the churches. It is no surprise if you have read the Gospels: soon after calling Peter, Jesus heals his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30–31), and a man does not have a mother-in-law without a wife. Paul mentions it here as the normal arrangement. Second, the brothers of the Lord. Paul refers to them as a known group with a recognised ministry, as Luke does (Acts 1:14). They were Jesus’ half-brothers, James, Joses, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3), who came to faith after the resurrection (John 7:5; Acts 1:14). James became the leader of the Jerusalem church and wrote a letter in our Bible; Jude wrote another.

Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living? Third, only Barnabas and I. Paul and Barnabas both worked with their hands (Acts 18:3; 20:34). Are they the only ones without the right to be supported? It is the one mention of Barnabas in this letter, and it is affectionate. These two were the exception, the pair who supported themselves by their trades rather than drawing on the churches. And it is quietly moving that Paul names him. By now the two had parted company after a sharp disagreement over John Mark (Acts 15:36–39). Writing to a church that may never have met Barnabas, Paul reaches back and puts them in the same sentence as fellow labourers who made the same sacrifice. He does not pretend the split never happened, and he does not let it edit the record. He is capable of remembering honourably a man he could no longer travel with, and of asking, later, for the very Mark they quarrelled over, because he was useful (2 Timothy 4:11).

Where Christians differ: married ministers and the brothers of the Lord. The Roman Catholic Church requires celibacy of most of its priests, and teaches that Mary remained a virgin for life, so that the brothers of the Lord were cousins or children of Joseph by a previous marriage. Verdict: This verse shows that the apostles, including Peter, whom Rome regards as the first pope, had wives. Church leaders may marry (1 Timothy 3:2). Requiring celibacy of ministers has no basis in Scripture. As for the brothers of the Lord, the natural reading is that they were sons of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus (Matthew 1:25; 13:55–56). Mary is to be honoured as blessed among women, but nothing in Scripture requires her perpetual virginity. It is worth saying without heat: those who hold the tradition do so out of reverence for the Lord’s mother, which is not a bad motive. But it is not what the words naturally say, and not what any first-century reader would have assumed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single ministers are less qualified. Paul himself was single. It means marriage is no barrier to ministry.

I have fallen out with a fellow Christian. How should I speak of him now? Like Paul speaks of Barnabas: truthfully and honourably. You do not have to pretend the disagreement never happened, or that you were wrong if you were not. But you can refuse to let the quarrel rewrite the good you once did together, speak well of him where you honestly can, refuse to gossip, pray for him, and keep the door open. Paul and Barnabas differed sharply over a judgement, not over the gospel, and both went on serving Christ. Some separations of that kind are not sin; bitterness about them always is. If reconciliation is possible, pursue it.

In a sentence. Don’t we have the right to bring a believing wife with us, as the other apostles, the Lord’s brothers and Peter all do? Or are Barnabas and Paul the only ones who must earn their own keep?

On a Tuesday. Pray for your pastor’s marriage and family. Ministry places heavy strains on them, and a minister’s wife and children often carry burdens no one sees. Do one practical kindness for them this month. And think of one person you have parted from: say something honourable about them to God today, and to someone else if you can.

For worship. The Lord’s own brothers did not believe in him while he walked among them. They thought he was out of his mind. And then the risen Christ appeared to James (15:7), and the brother who had scoffed became a pillar of the church and called himself a servant of the Lord Jesus Christ. That is the grace of the Lord: patient with his own family, conquering unbelief in his own house, and turning sceptics into apostles’ companions. And it is the same grace that holds together quarrelling servants like Paul and Barnabas, and gives Mark a second chance. He wastes no one he has called.
verseByVerse.note: Peter (Cephas) was married, and his wife travelled with him. The Lord’s brothers included James and Jude.

verseByVerse.quote: Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?

Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Three questions, three trades, one point. Soldiers were paid and supplied by the state. Paul begins his case not with Scripture but with what any Corinthian already knows. Nobody funds his own military service.

Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? The farmer eats from his crop. Nobody plants a vineyard and then buys grapes.

Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk? The shepherd drinks from his flock. In every trade in the world, the worker eats from the work. And the three are not chosen at random. Each has an old association with ministry, and all three pictures are used elsewhere of it. The soldier: no soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him (2 Timothy 2:3–4). The vineyard and the farmer: Israel is God’s vineyard through the Old Testament (Isaiah 5:1–7), and Paul has already called the church God’s field (3:6–9; 2 Timothy 2:6). The shepherd: the standing image for those who lead God’s people, from Ezekiel 34 to Peter’s charge to shepherd the flock of God (1 Peter 5:2). So Paul has quietly described the ministry three times while appearing to talk about ordinary occupations. Gospel work is warfare, cultivation and care, and the labourer in each is fed by what he tends.

Starting from common life. The shape of the argument says something about how Paul thinks. He does not open with revelation and then illustrate it; he opens with what everybody can see and moves upward. Scripture comes in the next verse, and the Lord’s command at verse 14, but he begins where his readers already are, with soldiers and farmers and goats. It is the same instinct that made his Lord talk about seeds, lamps, coins, sheep and a man building a tower. The world is God’s, and it is arranged in such a way that ordinary things carry the shape of spiritual ones.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers should be in it for the money; they are to shepherd not for shameful gain, but eagerly (1 Peter 5:2). It means support is a fair right.

The long gap between labour and fruit. Each of the three trades involves a long wait between work and return. The soldier campaigns for a season before anything is settled; the vineyard takes years before the first harvest; the shepherd works through the night and the milk comes in the morning. None of them is paid at the moment of effort. That is a fair picture of most Christian work, of most Christian parenting, and of most praying. You put in what you have, and the fruit is not immediate and may not be visible for a very long time. But it belongs to the work. Let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up (Galatians 6:9).

I have served for years and see no fruit. Is it wasted? No. The fruit of Christian service is often slow, hidden and later than we would like, and some of it will only be seen on the last day. God does not measure your work by visible results but by faithfulness, and he has promised that your labour in the Lord is not in vain (15:58). Keep planting. Ask God honestly for fruit and for the grace to wait for it. Ask a trusted friend whether anything should change in how you serve. But do not mistake slowness for failure. Many of the people you have taught and prayed for will one day tell you what you never knew you did.

In a sentence. No soldier pays his own wages; no one plants a vineyard and goes without its grapes; no shepherd keeps a flock and never drinks its milk.

On a Tuesday. If you serve in any way, in a Sunday school class, a home, a prayer list, a ministry no one notices, thank God that he provides for his workers, and trust him to supply your needs and to give the fruit in his time. If you are supported by a church, give thanks; if you support others, do it gladly.

For worship. The God of this verse is the Lord of soldiers, vineyards and flocks, and he is himself all three to his people. He is the LORD of hosts who fights for them, the vinedresser who tends his vine with care, and the Good Shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. He never asks his servants to labour without fruit, because he himself is the reward of all their labour. And he has written the shape of his kingdom into ordinary things, so that every field and flock and soldier on the march preaches that the One who called us will also feed us.

verseByVerse.quote: Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.

Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same? Common sense has made the case; now Paul grounds it in Scripture. Not just common sense: Scripture says it too.

For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain”. From Deuteronomy 25:4, an unlikely verse to reach for. The picture is of a threshing floor. Oxen threshing grain walked over it, or pulled a sledge over it, to separate grain from husk, and the grain was right there under their feet all day. A tight-fisted farmer might tie the ox’s mouth shut. A muzzle would stop it eating as it worked. God’s law forbade it: let the ox eat. The animal doing the work eats from the work.

Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Paul’s startling aside. Read flatly it sounds like a dismissal of animal welfare, and it must not be taken that way, because Scripture will not have it. Paul does not mean God does not care about animals (Psalm 145:9; Jonah 4:11). This is the God who feeds the ravens and clothes the lilies, who knows when a sparrow falls, who ends the book of Jonah by remarking that Nineveh contained much cattle, and whose law commands rest for the working animal on the Sabbath (Luke 12:24, 27; Matthew 10:29; Exodus 23:12). Whoever is righteous has regard for the life of his beast (Proverbs 12:10). God is very much concerned for oxen. Paul is using a form of argument his readers would recognise, in which a rhetorical question sets aside the lesser matter to reach the greater. The sense is: is this only about oxen? He means that the law’s deeper purpose is not merely about oxen.

Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake. The principle behind the law: workers should share in the fruit of their labour. It expresses a principle God built into the world about labour and its fruit, and if he applies it to a beast at a threshing floor then he certainly applies it to a man in a pulpit. If that applies to oxen, how much more to people. This is an argument from the lesser to the greater. Paul uses the same verse for elders’ pay in 1 Timothy 5:18.

Because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop. Every worker works in hope of a share. That phrase is worth carrying about. Hope is what makes labour possible. A man breaking ground in February is looking at nothing but mud, and what keeps him going is a harvest he cannot see. Take away the expectation and the ploughing stops. That is what Paul says God has written into the arrangement of things, and it is a great comfort in a letter that has already said the growth belongs to God alone (3:6–7). You are not asked to work without prospect. The Christian teaching a class, visiting the housebound, raising children in the faith, or praying for a village is a ploughman working in hope, and the hope is not wishful. It rests on the character of a God who arranged the world so that even an ox eats while it works.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is allegorising the law and ignoring its plain meaning. He draws out the principle behind it, which the law intended (Romans 15:4). The ox is still to be fed.

How should I read the Old Testament laws, then? As Paul does here. He does not treat Deuteronomy as an archive of obsolete regulations. He treats it as written for our sake, addressed ultimately to the church (10:11; Romans 15:4). That does not mean every civil or ceremonial law is binding on Christians in its original form; the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel’s civil laws belonged to a nation. But every law reveals something of God’s character and wisdom, and usually a principle that still applies. So ask of any Old Testament command: what does this show about God? What principle of love to him or to neighbour lies under it? And how is it fulfilled in Christ? All Scripture is profitable (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

In a sentence. Is this only human reasoning? Doesn’t the law teach it too? Moses wrote, “Do not muzzle the ox while it threshes the grain.” Is God’s real concern here the oxen? Surely he is speaking for our benefit: whoever ploughs or threshes should be able to do it expecting a share of the harvest.

On a Tuesday. Pick one short Old Testament law this week, perhaps in Deuteronomy 22 or 24, and read it slowly with Paul’s questions: what does this show about God, and what was it written for our sake to teach? And whatever your work, plough in hope today. The God who feeds the ox will not forget you.

For worship. Thank God that his law is full of kindness, even to animals. The LORD is good to all, and his mercy is over all that he has made (Psalm 145:9). He wrote a clause into his covenant to protect an ox at a threshing floor, and if he cared for the ox, how much more for the ploughman. And thank him that it was written for your sake. The God of Sinai is not a remote legislator but a Father who has been thinking of his children all along, and every page of his law, down to the muzzled ox, was written with the church in mind and fulfilled in Christ, who worked in hope and will see the fruit of the anguish of his soul and be satisfied (Isaiah 53:11).
verseByVerse.note: Oxen threshing grain walked over it on the threshing floor; the law let them eat as they worked.

parallels.desc: you shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain

verseByVerse.quote: If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.

If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you? Spiritual seed, the gospel, yields a material harvest, financial support. The exchange is stated as plainly as it can be, and the disproportion is the argument. Paul gave them the gospel: the knowledge of God, the forgiveness of sins, eternal life. In return he might reasonably have expected dinner. A small return for a great gift (Romans 15:27; Galatians 6:6).

If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Other teachers in Corinth were receiving support. Paul, their founder, has a stronger claim. That is very often how it goes: the man who founds the work at his own expense watches his successors receive what he went without.

Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right. The surprise, and the hinge of the chapter. Everything since verse 3 has been building the case, and here it is surrendered. Not modified, not partially claimed, not used at all. Paul has the right, but refuses to use it. This is the point for the strong.

But we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ. Two words carry the weight. “Endure” (stegō) means bear, put up with; it is a word for covering something and so bearing up under it, the same word as love bears all things (13:7). It is the language of a roof holding under rain, and it means Paul is describing not a preference but a load he carries. “Obstacle” (enkopē) is literally a cutting-in, used of breaking up a road to stop an army’s advance: a roadblock. Paul’s fear is that something might be dug across the path of the gospel, and his own legitimate income was, in that city, exactly such a hazard. In Corinth, travelling teachers often charged fees and were seen as greedy. The travelling sophist charged for his lectures, and everyone knew the pattern: an impressive man arrives, gathers an audience, takes their money, moves on. If Paul had accepted support, he would have been placed in that category on the first day, and everything he said would have been heard as a sales pitch. Paul did not want anyone to think he preached for money. So he took a trade instead, made tents, and preached for nothing, and the message arrived without a price tag attached.

What it does not mean. It does not mean it is wrong for ministers to be paid. Paul defends the right and accepted gifts from other churches (2 Corinthians 11:8–9; Philippians 4:15–16). He refused it in Corinth for the gospel’s sake.

The principle under the practice. The specific application varies with the culture. Paul gave up a genuine right because in his particular setting it would have been misread. Not because it was wrong. Because of what people would conclude. And that puts a question to anyone who serves in any capacity. There are things you are perfectly entitled to, a payment, a recognition, a position, a defence of your reputation, and the question this verse asks is not whether you may have them. It is whether, in the eyes of the particular people you are trying to reach, having them would put something across the road.

Should Christians today avoid anything that looks like making money from the gospel? We should avoid anything that makes the gospel look like a product for sale. That means churches and ministries should be scrupulously honest with money, open in their accounts, modest rather than lavish, and never imply that God’s blessing can be bought (Acts 8:20). Preachers who live in luxury on the gifts of the poor, or promise wealth in return for donations, put exactly the roadblock Paul feared across the road. But fair support of faithful workers is not that; it is obedience. The test is whether money serves the gospel or the gospel serves money.

In a sentence. We sowed spiritual seed among you; is it too much to expect a material harvest? If others have that right, we have it more. Yet we never used it; we put up with anything rather than block the way of Christ’s gospel.

On a Tuesday. What right could you give up this week so that the gospel is not hindered? Perhaps the right to be thanked, to be paid back, to win the argument with a non-Christian colleague, or to keep your evening for yourself when a neighbour needs help. Name it, and lay it down quietly.

For worship. Paul went hungry rather than let anyone say the gospel was for sale, and in that he was only following his Lord. The gospel is free because it was infinitely costly to Christ. Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat, without money and without price (Isaiah 55:1). The Son of God endured the cross, bearing all things for his people, so that nothing would stand between them and the Father. He removed the greatest obstacle of all, our sin, and opened a road that no one can close. The least we can do is to keep our own small roadblocks off it.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.

Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple. Two final arguments, and Paul has saved the strongest for last. The first is from the temple. In Israel, the priests and Levites lived from the offerings and tithes (Numbers 18:8–32; Deuteronomy 18:1–5). They received no allotment of land; the LORD himself was their portion, and they lived from what was brought to the sanctuary. It was not charity. It was the system God designed, and it lasted for centuries. Pagan priests did the same.

And those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings? Priests ate portions of the sacrifices (Leviticus 7:6–10).

In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel. The final and highest argument: the Lord Jesus himself commanded it, when he said that the labourer deserves his wages (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). When the Lord sent out his messengers he told them to stay where they were welcomed, eating and drinking what was provided. And Paul quotes that same saying in a later letter alongside Deuteronomy, under the heading the Scripture says (1 Timothy 5:18), a striking sign of how quickly the words of Jesus were received with the authority of the Old Testament itself. Churches have a duty to support those who preach the gospel to them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gospel ministers are priests offering sacrifices. Paul uses the temple only as an analogy for support. Christ has offered the one sacrifice, once for all (Hebrews 10:12), and every believer now has access to God through him.

A command widely neglected. The practical conclusion should be stated plainly, because it is a matter of obedience. The Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should live by it. That is not a suggestion, and it is not the minister’s job to raise it, which is precisely the difficulty, since the one person who cannot comfortably make this argument is the one it concerns. Congregations are often careless here without ever intending unkindness. A minister’s pay is set once and quietly left behind by the cost of living. His housing is arranged so that he will retire with nothing. He is expected to look adequately prosperous and not to appear to want anything. Nobody decides any of this; it simply happens, in churches full of people who would be shocked to think they had disobeyed a command of Christ. And the principle runs beyond the paid minister to anyone the church leans on: the person who does the accounts, keeps the building, runs the young people’s work, and is thanked in general terms once a year.

Both edges. But the chapter cuts the other way too, and both edges must be kept. Paul establishes the right and then refuses it. So the minister who reads these verses and feels aggrieved has taken half the chapter. The freedom being described here is not the freedom to be well paid; it is the freedom Paul secured by declining payment, the freedom of a man who can say anything from a pulpit because nobody in the room is keeping him. That is the balance: let the church be generous as a matter of obedience, and let the preacher hold it loosely enough that it never once shapes a sermon.

How much should I give to my church? The New Testament does not set a percentage for Christians; it asks for giving that is regular, proportionate, cheerful and sacrificial (16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:3; 9:7). Many believers take the tithe, a tenth, as a sensible starting point and give more as they are able. Give first to the church where you are fed, since this verse makes that a duty, and then beyond it. Give in a planned way rather than only from what is left over. And if your circumstances are very tight, give what you can, gladly; the widow’s two coins were more than all the rest (Mark 12:43–44).

In a sentence. You know that those who work in the temple are fed from the temple, and those who serve at the altar receive part of what is offered there. In the same way the Lord himself directed that those who preach the gospel should be supported by it.

On a Tuesday. Give generously to support gospel ministry. It is the Lord’s command. If you are a church member or officer, ask quietly whether your minister is fairly paid and provided for in old age, and whether those who serve unpaid are thanked specifically and helped. If you are a minister, thank God for what you receive, and pray that it never shapes what you preach.

For worship. The Levites had no inheritance in the land, because the LORD was their portion. That is the deepest provision of all, and it is now the portion of every believer: the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup (Psalm 16:5). The One who commanded that his messengers be fed is the Bread of Life himself, who fed five thousand on a hillside and fed his disciples on the shore after the resurrection. He has never yet let one of his servants go without what they truly need, and he is the great High Priest who now serves at the true altar, not taking from us, but giving himself.

parallels.desc: the priests’ portion

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–23 — Becoming All Things to All People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul has not used any of these rights, and he is not writing to get them now; he would rather die than let anyone empty his boast. Preaching itself gives him no ground for boasting, because he is under compulsion; woe to him if he does not preach. If he did it willingly he would have a reward; but since he is entrusted with it as a duty, his reward is this: to offer the gospel free of charge and not use his rights. Though free from everyone, he has made himself everyone’s slave to win more people. To Jews he became like a Jew, to those under the law like one under it (though not under it himself), to those without the law like one without it (though not free from God’s law, being bound by Christ’s law), to the weak he became weak. He has become all things to all people so that by every possible means he might save some, and he does it all for the gospel, so as to share in its blessings.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missional Identification and the Integrity of the Gospel

Paul’s “all things to all people” has been both one of the most misused and most important principles in Christian mission. Misused, it becomes a pretext for theological drift — adjusting the content of the gospel to make it more acceptable. Properly understood, it describes the willingness to adjust the container — cultural form, communicative register, social entry point — while keeping the content constant. Keller’s ministry in Manhattan was an extended application of this principle: enter the cultural world of the highly educated secular professional, learn to speak their language, earn the right to challenge their assumptions — and preach the same crucified Christ that Paul preached in Corinth.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s concrete examples — becoming as a Jew, as under the law, as outside the law, as weak — map onto the social divisions within his own missionary world. He was not fixed in one cultural mode but radically adaptable in form while immovable in content. The Damascus road encounter made him a prisoner of the message; everything else was negotiable. Now: Contextualisation is the ongoing challenge of every missionary enterprise. The line between appropriate adaptation and compromising capitulation is real and requires constant discernment; but the failure to contextualise — treating one’s own cultural form of Christianity as the gospel itself — is at least as dangerous as over-adaptation.

verseByVerse.quote: But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!

But I have made no use of any of these rights. Paul is not hinting for money. He has deliberately refused.

Nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. He is not asking them to start paying him now. Paul has to add this clause, and the need for it is slightly comic. He has just spent twelve verses proving he is entitled to support, and he can hear how it will sound: a hint, a case being made, a man angling. So he closes the door: I am not asking.

For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting. The sentence is so emphatic that the Greek actually breaks off mid-sentence, which translations tidy up. Paul is agitated, and it is worth asking what has moved him so much. His boast (kauchēma) is not in himself, nor pride in his self-denial, but in being able to preach without charge. It is the one thing in his ministry he can call his own offering, and the next verse explains why he needs one.

For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. Preaching itself is no basis for pride, because he has no choice about it.

For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! “Necessity” (anankē) is compulsion, constraint, a necessity laid on a man from outside. This is one of the most revealing sentences Paul ever wrote about himself. He was going the other way, with letters in his pocket authorising arrests, and he was stopped in the road and turned round and given a commission he had not applied for. Christ commissioned Paul (Acts 9:15; 26:16–18). So he cannot boast in preaching, any more than a conscript can boast of enlisting. And woe to me is the language of the prophets. Like Jeremiah, who resolved to stop speaking and found the word was like a fire shut up in his bones, so that he was weary with holding it in and could not (Jeremiah 20:9), Paul cannot hold it in. Woe: he would be under God’s judgement if he refused.

One thing that was his to give. Within the compulsion Paul found one thing that was his to give: he could preach for nothing. That was not commanded. That was his, freely chosen, and he says he would rather die than have it taken from him. It is a window into a heart. Here is a man who has been given no choice about the central thing in his life, and who has responded not with resentment but by searching out something extra he could give, and then guarding it fiercely, because it was the only present he had.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached grudgingly. He preached with joy. But he knew he was under orders.

Does every Christian have this necessity to share the gospel? Not every Christian is called to be a preacher or an apostle, and Paul’s commission was unique. But every Christian has been entrusted with the gospel in some measure, and is to be ready to give a reason for the hope that is in him, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). The church as a whole is under the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20). For most believers this means speaking naturally of Christ to family, friends and colleagues, praying for opportunities, living so that the question is asked, and supporting those sent to preach. You need not feel guilty that you are not Paul; but you should not be silent either.

In a sentence. Paul has used none of these rights, and he is not writing in the hope of being paid now; he would rather die than lose this one thing he can take pride in. Preaching itself gives him nothing to boast about, because he is under orders: woe to him if he does not preach the gospel.

On a Tuesday. You too have been entrusted with the gospel. Share it, not for reward, but because you have been told to and because you love Christ. And think about the necessities of your own life: very little of what fills your days was freely chosen, the job that pays, the family that needs you, the health you have. Most people meet that with grumbling, or with a dutiful compliance that has no joy in it. Paul found, inside the thing he could not choose, one thing he could, and made that his offering. You cannot choose the work; you can choose to do it excellently when nobody checks. You cannot choose the illness; you can choose what people find when they visit. The necessity is not the enemy of joy. It is the field in which a freely given thing becomes possible.

For worship. The gospel came to Paul as an arrest, and that is the glory of it. Christ did not wait to be sought by the man breathing threats against his church. He came after him, knocked him to the ground, opened his eyes, and laid on him a necessity that became his joy. That is how sovereign grace works: it does not ask our permission to save us, and the chains it puts on us are the only freedom we have ever known. Christ himself said, I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God, for I was sent for this purpose (Luke 4:43). The Son lived under the same holy necessity, and he embraced it gladly, all the way to the cross, for the joy that was set before him.

parallels.desc: a burning fire shut up in my bones
