verseByVerse.quote: For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.

For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward. Paul works out the logic of his position. If preaching were his own free choice, like a volunteer, he could expect a reward, wages.

But if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship. A steward (oikonomos) was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s affairs; often a slave, not paid but obliged (4:1). A steward, given a charge he did not seek, has no claim to wages; he is simply obliged to be faithful with what was handed to him. Paul is a steward of the gospel. He preaches under compulsion, not for wages.

What then is my reward? So where is his reward? He asks it himself.

That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge. The answer is one of the most unexpected sentences in the letter. His reward is not something he receives. It is something he gives up. The wage he draws is the privilege of not drawing a wage. His reward is the joy of giving the gospel away, as it was given to him. A free gospel offered freely.

So as not to make full use of my right in the gospel. Paul’s reward is precisely in not using his rights. That is not how any of us naturally thinks about reward. Paul has been offered a genuine entitlement and has discovered that the pleasure of refusing it is greater than the thing itself would have been. He is not gritting his teeth through a sacrifice. He is describing something he enjoys.

More blessed to give. It is not a peculiarity of his temperament; it is the logic of the gospel working its way into a man’s appetites. The Lord said it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), a saying Paul quotes, and one which every Christian believes in principle and finds surprising in practice. Blessed, not merely commendable. There is a satisfaction on the giving side that is simply better than what is available on the receiving side, and people who have tasted it stop thinking of generosity as a cost. The ordinary Christian should not file this under apostolic heroics. Most people have felt it at least once: the anonymous gift, the favour that will never be known, the thing you paid for and let someone else be thanked for. There is a quiet gladness in it that receiving the same amount would not have produced. Paul organised a whole ministry around that discovery.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers who are paid have no reward. It means Paul found a special joy in giving up what he could rightly have claimed.

Is it wrong to serve God hoping for a reward? No. Jesus himself promises reward to those who give, pray and fast in secret (Matthew 6:4, 6, 18), and Hebrews says that whoever comes to God must believe that he rewards those who seek him (Hebrews 11:6). What is wrong is serving for the reward of human praise, or imagining that we earn salvation. The rewards Scripture holds out are gifts of grace, given by a Father who delights to honour what his own Spirit produced in us. And the greatest reward, as Paul found, is joy in God himself and in giving as he gives. To want that is not selfish; it is to want what God wants for you.

In a sentence. If he preached by his own choice, he could expect payment; but since he preaches under orders, he is simply a steward doing what he was given to do. So what is his reward? The joy of offering the gospel without charge, not using the rights it would give him.

On a Tuesday. A test, and it is a diagnostic of where your treasure actually is. Name something you have given away this year in such a way that nobody could return the favour or record the credit. Then ask what it felt like: not at the moment of deciding, which is usually reluctance, but afterwards. If nothing comes to mind, this verse describes a pleasure you have not yet drawn on, and it is one of the few in the Christian life that is available immediately. Do one such thing this week, and do not tell anyone (Matthew 6:3–4).

For worship. The gospel was given to you free. Give it away freely. And worship the God whose whole nature is giving. The Father gave his Son; the Son gave himself; the Spirit is given to all who believe. He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and he gives without counting, without reproach, without any hope of repayment from us. God loves a cheerful giver because he is one, and he is making us like himself. Every free gift Paul gave at Corinth was a small echo of the free gift of God, which is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.note: A steward was a household manager, entrusted with his master’s goods.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.

For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all. The sentence is built as a deliberate contradiction. Free (eleutheros): no one owns him, the word the whole chapter opened with. Yet he made himself a slave (douloō) to everyone, and the verb is not passive; nobody did this to him. A free man walked into servitude on purpose, because it was the only way to reach people. That is precisely the pattern of Christ, who took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7) and came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Christian freedom, in the New Testament, is never chiefly freedom from obligation. It is the capacity to take on obligations that nobody could have imposed on you.

That I might win more of them. “Win” (kerdainō) means gain, a business word: win for Christ. It appears five times in verses 19–22.

To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. Paul was a Jew, but in Christ he no longer depended on Jewish identity. Yet with Jews he kept Jewish customs: he circumcised Timothy (Acts 16:3), took a vow (Acts 18:18), joined in temple purification (Acts 21:23–26). Timothy had a Greek father, and his uncircumcision would have closed every synagogue door; Paul circumcised him freely, for access.

To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law). With people living by the law of Moses, he lived by it too, not as a way of salvation but out of love. But he was not under the law as a covenant or a means of righteousness (Romans 6:14; Galatians 2:19).

That I might win those under the law. The purpose was always to remove unnecessary barriers to the gospel.

Timothy and Titus. Set beside Timothy’s circumcision another episode. When certain men insisted that Titus, a Greek, must be circumcised as a condition of acceptance, Paul refused absolutely: to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Galatians 2:3–5). The same operation, opposite answers, and the difference is the whole doctrine of adapting to a culture in one comparison. When the question was how do I get near these people? Paul was endlessly flexible. When the question was what must a man do to be accepted by God? he would not concede a syllable, to anyone, ever. That is the line, and it is a clean one. Everything about the container may be adjusted: language, custom, diet, dress, the order of a service, the point at which you begin a conversation. Nothing about the content may be adjusted: the holiness of God, the reality of sin, the necessity of the cross, the call to repentance and faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul changed the gospel for different audiences. When the gospel itself was at stake, he refused to compromise (Galatians 2:3–5, 11–14). He adapted in matters indifferent, not in truth.

Flexibility in both directions. Notice that Paul’s flexibility ran both ways, which is the part we tend to forget. He became as a Jew to Jews and as one outside the law to Gentiles. He was not simply relaxing his own standards to reach the worldly; he was also taking on restrictions he did not personally need, in order to sit with the scrupulous. Both cost him something. Adapting that only ever moves in the direction of greater personal liberty is usually not gospel adaptation at all.

So how far should I adapt to reach my friends? As far as love requires and holiness allows. Learn their language, not only literally but in the words and questions that matter to them. Be at home in their homes and on their ground. Give up preferences that put them off without serving the gospel: your church jargon, your music, your habits, even lawful pleasures in their presence if they would stumble. But never join in sin to be accepted, never hide the hard parts of the gospel, and never let fitting in become the goal. If you find you have adapted so long that you have never mentioned Christ, you have stopped doing what Paul did.

In a sentence. Paul is no one’s slave, yet he has made himself everyone’s slave so as to win as many as possible. With Jews he lived as a Jew to win Jews; with those who keep the law he kept it too, though he himself is not under the law, so that he might win them.

On a Tuesday. What customs or preferences could you lay aside to help someone hear the gospel without unnecessary obstacles? Most of us have one way of speaking, formed by our own church culture, and we use it on everybody, and then conclude that people are hard-hearted when in fact they simply did not understand the words. Paul crossed the room to where people were standing. Ask when you last did, and cross one this week.

For worship. The free Son of God made himself the servant of all. He who was in the form of God did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being born in the likeness of men (Philippians 2:6–7). To the Jews he became a Jew, born under the law to redeem those under the law (Galatians 4:4–5). He learned a language, a trade, a village’s customs. He ate with Pharisees and with tax collectors. He came down to where we were, all the way down, and he did not change the truth by one word to make it easier. Every missionary who crosses a culture walks in footprints he left first.

verseByVerse.quote: To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law. To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.

To those outside the law I became as one outside the law. Those outside the law (anomoi, without law) are the Gentiles. With them, Paul did not keep Jewish food laws or customs; he ate with them (Galatians 2:12–14).

(Not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ). A vital qualification, and the safeguard sits inside the text rather than being imported by nervous commentators. Paul has just said he becomes as one without the law; he immediately makes clear that he is nothing of the kind. Paul was not lawless. He was under the law of Christ (ennomos Christou, in-lawed to Christ): the moral will of God as taught and fulfilled by Christ, summed up in love (Galatians 6:2; John 13:34). Freedom from Moses’ ceremonies is not freedom from God’s moral law. And the law of Christ is not a lighter code. It is the whole of what love requires, defined by his own life, and by the measure of the cross it is heavier, not lighter. A man may eat what he likes and still be under an obligation that reaches to laying down his life.

To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. The weak of chapter 8. Paul limited his freedom to serve them. And this one is different from the others. The Jew and the Gentile are cultural categories; the weak are the people with tender consciences, the easily damaged. Paul does not merely accommodate them; he joins them. He does not stand at a distance being patient with the scrupulous; he stands where they stand. We who are strong have an obligation to bear with the failings of the weak, and not to please ourselves; for Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:1–3).

I have become all things to all people. In every culture and with every kind of person, Paul adapted himself.

That by all means I might save some. “Save”: be God’s instrument in their salvation. “Some”: realistic. Not all will believe. Two things guard the famous phrase from the abuse it usually suffers. The first is the purpose clause, repeated again and again in four verses: that I might win, that I might win, that I might save. The flexibility exists for one reason. It is not a general amiability, not a desire to be liked, and not a strategy for avoiding conflict, and a man who adapts himself endlessly and never gets round to the gospel is not doing what Paul did; he is doing the opposite, using Paul’s words as cover. The second is the modesty of some. Paul has adapted himself in every direction he can think of, at real cost, and his stated expectation is some. That realistic word protects two kinds of people: the evangelist discouraged because the response is small, and the one tempted to think that if he only got the presentation right, everybody would come. Neither is how it works. You spend yourself, God gives the growth (3:6), and some are saved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul became a sinner to reach sinners, or adopted every cultural practice. He never joined in idolatry or immorality. It means he adapted in matters of liberty, never compromising the gospel or holiness.

If God has chosen his people, why does Paul work so hard to save some? Because God’s choosing is the reason evangelism succeeds, not a reason to stop. God ordains the means as well as the end, and the means is the preaching of the gospel (Romans 10:14–17). Paul knew the Lord had many people in Corinth (Acts 18:9–10), and that was why he stayed and preached there for eighteen months. Election does not make his effort pointless; it guarantees it will not be in vain. We do not know who the elect are, so we offer Christ freely to all, plead with them to be reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:20), and trust God to open hearts as he opened Lydia’s.

The opposite failure. There is a caution here for our own time that runs the opposite way to the usual one. Yes, this passage is misused to justify a Christianity that has quietly stopped saying anything difficult. But a common failure in conservative churches is the reverse: treating our own inherited cultural form, the music, the vocabulary, the dress, the assumptions about what a serious person is like, as though it were the gospel itself, and regarding anyone who does not fit it as not really interested. Paul dismantled his own preferences in every direction for the sake of people he wanted to reach. The question is not only whether we are willing to compromise the gospel. It is whether we are willing to be inconvenienced for it.

In a sentence. With Gentiles who do not have the law, Paul lived like them, though he is not free of God’s law but bound to Christ’s, so that he might win them. With the weak he became weak, to win the weak. He has become whatever each person needs him to be, so that by every possible means he might save some.

On a Tuesday. Pray by name for one person you would love to see saved, and ask what being all things to them would mean this week: an evening on their ground, a question about their life, a willingness to be bored or uncomfortable for them, a plain word about Christ when the moment comes. And thank God for missionaries who learn new languages and cultures to bring the gospel. Pray for one today.

For worship. The Lord who became weak to win the weak is the Saviour who was crucified in weakness and lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). He did not stand at a distance from our frailty. He was hungry, tired and tempted, wept at a grave and sweated in a garden, so that the weakest believer might know that his High Priest understands. And he does save some: a great multitude that no one can number, from every nation, tribe, people and language (Revelation 7:9). Not one of them will be lost, because the One who came to seek and to save the lost has never failed at what he came to do.

verseByVerse.quote: I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.

I do it all for the sake of the gospel. Everything Paul does, every right he gives up, every adaptation he makes, serves the gospel’s advance.

That I may share with them in its blessings. “Share” (synkoinōnos) is a fellow partaker. The little word with is doing a great deal of work, and it changes the picture of the apostle entirely. Paul wants to share in the blessings of the gospel together with those he wins. He is not above them, but a fellow sinner saved by grace. He is not standing outside the gospel handing it to other people. He is inside it with them, receiving the same thing he is offering, dependent on the same mercy, sustained by the same promises. The man who has just described himself as under compulsion, enslaved to all, going hungry and preaching for nothing, is not a functionary distributing a benefit he does not need. He is a beneficiary who has been given the job of telling others where he found it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul earned his salvation by his ministry. He wants to be a partaker of the gospel’s blessings, which come by grace.

The danger of handling holy things. This is a necessary corrective to something that happens to nearly everyone who works with the things of God for long enough. It happens to ministers most visibly: the Bible becomes raw material for Sunday, prayer becomes something conducted publicly on behalf of others, and a man can go months handling the gospel professionally without once being addressed by it. But it is not confined to the paid. It happens to the Sunday school teacher who only ever reads to prepare, to the parent whose faith has become entirely a matter of passing something on to the children, to the long-standing member who hears every sermon as an assessment of the preacher rather than a word to himself. The tell is a subtle change in how you hear things. You listen to a sermon and think, that would help so-and-so. You read a passage and immediately consider who needs it. In itself that is a good instinct; it is love. The danger is when it becomes the only way you receive anything, and the thought this is about me stops arriving altogether. Keep a close watch on yourself and on the teaching (1 Timothy 4:16).

How do I keep the gospel fresh for myself when I have known it for years? Go back to it as a sinner, not as an expert. Confess specific sins regularly, so that forgiveness stays real rather than theoretical. Read Scripture sometimes with no task in view, asking only what God is saying to you. Sing the great hymns about the cross and mean them. Spend time with new believers, whose wonder is contagious. Take the Lord’s Supper as a hungry man, not as a spectator. And pray Paul’s own prayer, that you may know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19). The gospel does not grow old; we grow dull, and the Spirit is able to wake us again.

In a sentence. He does all this for the gospel’s sake, so that he may share its blessings along with them.

On a Tuesday. Let the gospel shape your choices today: your words, your spending, your time. And run a test this Sunday. During the next sermon, notice how many times you think about somebody else and how many times about yourself. When you next open the Bible outside any preparation, if you do, notice whether you are reading for material or for food. Taste and see that the LORD is good (Psalm 34:8).

For worship. The apostle to the Gentiles, in the middle of listing everything he had given up for other people, stopped to say that he was in it for himself as well. There is no other honest way to do this work, and there is nothing to be ashamed of in it, because the blessings of the gospel are inexhaustible. There is enough in Christ for every preacher and every hearer, every apostle and every slave, and none of them will ever reach the bottom of it. Paul, who had seen the risen Lord, still needed the same mercy as the newest convert at Corinth, and found it every morning new. Great is his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–27 — The Discipline of the Athlete
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the athletic games. In a race all the runners run, but only one wins the prize, so they should run to win. Every competitor trains with strict self-discipline, and they do it for a wreath that will wither; believers do it for a crown that will last for ever. So Paul does not run aimlessly or box like someone throwing punches at the air. He disciplines his body and makes it his servant, so that after preaching to others he himself will not be disqualified.
verseByVerse.theology:
Assurance and Effort: The Perseverance of the Saints

The warning of v. 27 — “lest I myself should be disqualified” — has been debated in relation to the doctrine of perseverance. Reformed theology does not take this as a threat to genuine believers’ final security but as the description of the means by which that security is maintained: the God who sovereignly keeps his people does so through their own disciplined effort, not instead of it. The warning is the mechanism of perseverance: those who are genuinely elect will take the warning seriously, run hard, and thereby demonstrate and maintain their calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians lived in the shadow of the Isthmian Games and would have immediately understood the competitive imagery. Paul makes the comparison in order to shame them slightly: the athletes prepare with greater earnestness for a temporary prize than the Corinthians apply to an eternal one. Now: The contemporary church has, in many quarters, lost the language of spiritual discipline entirely — afraid that any emphasis on effort sounds like works-righteousness. Paul’s athletic imagery corrects this: grace produces effort; the free gift of the gospel generates the runner’s willingness to run hard.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it. Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.

Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? The image would have needed no explanation at Corinth. The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years, among the great festivals of the Greek world, and Corinth hosted them. Everyone reading this letter had seen the athletes train, had watched the races, and knew exactly what the prize looked like. In a race, only one wins.

So run that you may obtain it. Run the Christian race with the same intensity as a runner aiming to win. And a guard is needed at once, because the analogy has a limit Paul plainly does not intend. The point is not that only one Christian is saved; that would contradict everything in the letter. The point of comparison is the manner of running, not the number of winners. Run wholeheartedly, like a man who means to win, rather than like someone jogging round because attendance is expected.

Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. “Self-control” (enkrateuomai) comes from the same root as the self-control in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). Athletes trained for ten months, with strict diet and discipline; at Olympia they swore to it. Nobody turned up on the day. They say no to many good things for the sake of the prize.

They do it to receive a perishable wreath. What strikes Paul is the disproportion between the effort and the prize. At the Isthmian Games, the winner’s crown was made of wild celery, withered, or in some periods of pine. It soon decayed. Ten months of denial, and the reward was a handful of leaves that browned within a week and was thrown out. Men gave years to that.

But we an imperishable. Our crown is eternal life and glory: the crown of righteousness, the crown of life, the unfading crown of glory (2 Timothy 4:8; James 1:12; 1 Peter 5:4). If athletes sacrifice so much for a wilting wreath, how much more should we? And the comparison is not chiefly a rebuke of athletes; it is a rebuke of us. People will discipline themselves ferociously for something they know is temporary, and Christians will hardly discipline themselves at all for something that is not. Consider what people you know are prepared to give up for a marathon, a qualification, a business, a physique, a musical instrument: the early mornings, the diet, the years. Then consider what the same people find impossible for prayer or Scripture, and notice that the difference is not the time available.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation is earned by effort. The prize is given by grace. But the Christian life is not passive; grace trains us to strive (Philippians 2:12–13; Titus 2:11–12). Some Christians are so anxious not to fall into works-righteousness that any talk of discipline sounds to them like a threat to grace. This passage settles it. Nobody supposes an athlete’s training earns him the right to enter the stadium. The training is what a man does because he is in the race, not in order to be admitted to it.

What does spiritual training actually look like? Ordinary, regular, deliberate practices that put you where God has promised to meet you. Daily Scripture reading and prayer, at a set time if possible. Faithful attendance at the Lord’s Day worship, the preaching and the Lord’s Supper. Memorising verses. Occasional fasting. Generous giving. Honest friendship with a believer who can ask you hard questions. Saying no to things that dull you, often your phone or your screen. None of these earns anything; all of them are means of grace. Start small and keep going: train yourself for godliness, for it holds promise for the present life and for the life to come (1 Timothy 4:7–8).

In a sentence. You know that in a race many run, but only one takes the prize. Run like that, to win. Athletes in training deny themselves in everything, all for a crown that wilts; we do it for one that will never fade.

On a Tuesday. The question is simply whether you are training for anything. Not whether you feel spiritual, and not whether you are trying hard in some vague way, but whether there is any actual, deliberate, scheduled practice in your life aimed at godliness, of the kind an athlete would recognise as training. What would that look like for you this week: early prayer, Scripture memory, fasting from your phone? Choose one, write it down, and begin tomorrow. Train for the imperishable crown.

For worship. The crown that awaits the Christian does not wilt, because the One who gives it does not change. Christ ran the race first, looking to the joy that was set before him, and endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God (Hebrews 12:2). He wore a crown of thorns so that his people might wear a crown of life. And on the last day his saints will cast their crowns before the throne, because they will know whose victory it really was. Worthy are you, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honour and power (Revelation 4:11).
verseByVerse.note: The Isthmian Games, second only to the Olympics, were held near Corinth every two years. Winners received a wreath of pine or dried celery.

verseByVerse.quote: So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air. But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.

So I do not run aimlessly. “Aimlessly” (adēlōs) means uncertainly, without a clear mark: Paul runs toward a clear finish line. Two negatives here, and both describe activity without contact: the runner with no finish line in view, the boxer throwing punches at nothing. Effort is being expended; nothing is happening.

I do not box as one beating the air. A shadow-boxer swings at nothing. Paul lands real blows against real enemies. That is a fair description of a good deal of religious life. It is entirely possible to be busy in a church for thirty years, to attend everything, to be tired from it, and to be shadow-boxing. Paul’s alternative is not more energy. It is aim.

But I discipline my body and keep it under control. “Discipline” (hypōpiazō) literally means to give a black eye, to strike under the eye. Translations soften it. Strong language: Paul treats his own body’s sinful desires as an opponent in the ring. “Keep under control” (doulagōgeō) means lead as a slave. Having just called himself a servant to all (v. 19), he now makes a servant of his own body. His body serves him, not the other way round. That must not be misread as contempt for the body. This is the same apostle who has just called it a temple of the Holy Spirit and insisted that the Lord is for it (6:13, 19). He is not describing the self-punishment of a man who thinks flesh is evil. He is describing an athlete’s relation to his own appetites: the body is a magnificent servant and a ruinous master, and the training consists in keeping it in the right position.

Lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified. “Preaching” (kēryssō) is the herald’s word; the herald announced the rules and called the contestants at the Games. “Disqualified” (adokimos) means failing the test, not standing up to examination, rejected as counterfeit. Paul fears the herald might himself be disqualified from the race, and he applies the word to himself. It is the most sobering sentence in the chapter. And notice the exact danger he names, because it is specific and it is his own: after preaching to others. The peril of the herald is that he handles the truth so constantly that he stops being handled by it: that he can describe repentance without repenting, and warn against sins he is quietly committing, and do it competently for years.

Where Christians differ: could Paul lose his salvation? Some take this as proof that even an apostle could fall away and be lost. Others say disqualified means only losing a reward. Verdict: Paul knows that a person can preach to others and yet prove not to be genuine (Matthew 7:22–23). So he takes his own holiness seriously. The warning is real, and is one of the means God uses to keep his people persevering. True believers will not finally be lost (Romans 8:30; Philippians 1:6), but they persevere by heeding such warnings, not by ignoring them. Assurance and diligence go together (2 Peter 1:10). Scripture is emphatic that those whom God justifies he also glorifies, that no one can snatch Christ’s sheep from his hand (John 10:28), and this letter itself grounds the Corinthians’ security in the faithfulness of God, who will sustain them to the end (1:8–9). The warning is not idle machinery; it is one of the instruments, and it works precisely by being taken seriously. A man who reads this and thinks that could not happen to me has misunderstood it. A man who reads it and disciplines himself is the very man the warning was written to preserve. The fence at the cliff edge is not useless because nobody has gone over.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil. It means sinful bodily desires must be ruled, not obeyed.

This frightens me. How can I know I will not be disqualified? Look away from yourself to Christ, and then look honestly at your life. Your safety rests on his faithfulness, not on the strength of your discipline: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6). The very fear that makes you want to take holiness seriously is a sign of life; hypocrites rarely worry about this. So rest in his promises, and respond to the warning as Paul did, by fighting real sins with real means. Confess them, flee temptation, keep company with believers, and keep coming to Christ. The person who goes on trusting him and fighting sin, however imperfectly, is not the one this verse is about.

In a sentence. So Paul does not run without a goal, and he does not throw punches at the air. He trains his body hard and makes it serve him, so that after calling others to the race he himself will not be found unfit for the prize.

On a Tuesday. Name the one bodily appetite that most often masters you: food, sleep, lust, the phone, anger that runs through the body before the mind can stop it. Decide on one concrete blow you will land against it this week, and tell someone. And if you teach or lead others, ask God to help you take your own holiness seriously, and ask a trusted friend to ask you about it.

For worship. The chapter that began with a man defending his rights ends with him afraid of himself. He had seen the risen Christ, planted churches across the empire and written Scripture, and he still thought it necessary to keep his body under and his aim clear. That is not anxiety. It is what a man looks like who takes both the prize and the race seriously. And at the end of his life the same man could write, I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith, and there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (2 Timothy 4:7–8). He finished because Christ kept him. The Lord who calls his people to run is the Lord who runs beside them, lifts them when they fall, and will not let one of them be lost at the finishing line. To him who is able to keep you from stumbling be glory and majesty, now and for ever.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are not you my workmanship in the Lord?<sup>2</sup>If to others I am not an apostle, at least I am to you, for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.<sup>3</sup>This is my defense to those who would examine me.<sup>4</sup>Do we not have the right to eat and drink?<sup>5</sup>Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the brothers of the Lord and Cephas?<sup>6</sup>Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working for a living?<sup>7</sup>Who serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard without eating any of its fruit? Or who tends a flock without getting some of the milk?<sup>8</sup>Do I say these things on human authority? Does not the Law say the same?<sup>9</sup>For it is written in the Law of Moses, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” Is it for oxen that God is concerned?<sup>10</sup>Does he not certainly speak for our sake? It was written for our sake, because the plowman should plow in hope and the thresher thresh in hope of sharing in the crop.<sup>11</sup>If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it too much if we reap material things from you?<sup>12</sup>If others share this rightful claim on you, do not we even more? Nevertheless, we have not made use of this right, but we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel of Christ.<sup>13</sup>Do you not know that those who are employed in the temple service get their food from the temple, and those who serve at the altar share in the sacrificial offerings?<sup>14</sup>In the same way, the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the gospel should get their living by the gospel.<sup>15</sup>But I have made no use of any of these rights, nor am I writing these things to secure any such provision. For I would rather die than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting.<sup>16</sup>For if I preach the gospel, that gives me no ground for boasting. For necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!<sup>17</sup>For if I do this of my own will, I have a reward, but if not of my own will, I am still entrusted with a stewardship.<sup>18</sup>What then is my reward? That in my preaching I may present the gospel free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the gospel.<sup>19</sup>For though I am free from all, I have made myself a servant to all, that I might win more of them.<sup>20</sup>To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews. To those under the law I became as one under the law (though not being myself under the law) that I might win those under the law.<sup>21</sup>To those outside the law I became as one outside the law (not being outside the law of God but under the law of Christ) that I might win those outside the law.<sup>22</sup>To the weak I became weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, that by all means I might save some.<sup>23</sup>I do it all for the sake of the gospel, that I may share with them in its blessings.<sup>24</sup>Do you not know that in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it.<sup>25</sup>Every athlete exercises self-control in all things. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable.<sup>26</sup>So I do not run aimlessly; I do not box as one beating the air.<sup>27</sup>But I discipline my body and keep it under control, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified.

10.title: Israel’s Warning, the Lord’s Table, and the Glory of God
10.overview:
Paul completes his answer about idol food. The strong in Corinth felt secure: they were baptised, they shared the Lord’s Supper, they knew idols were nothing. Paul warns them with Israel’s story. The whole generation that left Egypt enjoyed God’s privileges: led by the cloud, brought through the sea, fed with manna, given water from the rock, which Paul says was Christ himself. Yet most of them died in the wilderness, because they fell into idolatry, sexual immorality, testing God and grumbling. Their story was written as a warning for us. Whoever thinks he stands should watch out, though God is faithful and will always provide a way through temptation.

So: flee idolatry. At the Lord’s Supper believers share in Christ’s blood and body and are made one body. Israel’s sacrifices likewise bound worshippers to the altar. Idols are nothing, but behind pagan sacrifice stand demons, and believers cannot share both the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Then Paul gives practical rules. Food bought in the market may be eaten without asking questions, for the earth belongs to the Lord. At an unbeliever’s dinner, eat what is served, unless someone points out that it was sacrificed, and then abstain for the sake of that person’s conscience. In everything, eating or drinking, do all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them of Israel in the exodus. All the people were under the cloud and all passed through the sea; all were, as it were, baptised into Moses in the cloud and the sea; all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink, from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ. Yet God was displeased with most of them, and their bodies were scattered in the wilderness. These things are examples to warn us not to crave evil as they did: not to be idolaters, as when the people sat down to feast and rose up to revel; not to commit sexual immorality, as when twenty-three thousand died in one day; not to put Christ to the test, as some did and were killed by snakes; and not to grumble, as some did and were destroyed by the destroying angel. These events happened to them as examples and were written down to warn us, on whom the climax of the ages has come. So anyone who thinks he is standing firm should take care not to fall. Every temptation they face is the common lot of humanity, and God is faithful: he will not let them be tested beyond what they can bear, but with the temptation will also provide the way out, so that they can endure it.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Pre-Existent Christ and the Typology of the Wilderness

Paul’s identification of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (v. 4) is a claim that the Son of God was the agent of God’s sustaining grace before the incarnation — the “Angel of the LORD” tradition of the OT now understood christologically. This is christological pre-existence applied to redemptive history: the same Christ who died on the cross was present and active in the wilderness, providing the spiritual sustenance that Israel squandered. Reformed typology has always read the OT this way: Christ is not absent from the old covenant; he is present as promise, type, and mediator.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who were attending temple meals — eating idol food in an actual pagan temple — needed to hear that spiritual confidence is not the same as spiritual safety. Israel had more obvious privileges than any of them and still fell. Now: The sacramental Christian who trusts in regular communion and baptism as automatic guarantees of spiritual health — without the disciplined effort, the watchful sobriety, the dependency on God that Paul describes — is making exactly the Israelite mistake. The sacraments are genuine means of grace, not magic shields.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea,

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 10 completes Paul’s answer about food offered to idols, and adds a sharp warning. The strong Corinthians felt safe: they had knowledge, baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Paul reminds them of Israel in the wilderness. All Israel had their own baptism and their own spiritual food and drink, with Christ himself present; yet most of them fell in the desert through idolatry, immorality, testing God and grumbling. Their story was written as a warning: let anyone who thinks he stands take care not to fall. Yet God is faithful and always provides a way of escape from temptation (vv. 1–13). So flee idolatry. The Lord’s Supper is a real participation in Christ’s body and blood, and pagan sacrifices are offered to demons; you cannot share the Lord’s table and the table of demons (vv. 14–22). Then Paul gives practical rules: eat whatever is sold in the market, and what an unbeliever serves you at home, without asking questions; but if someone points out that it was sacrificed, do not eat, for his conscience’s sake. Whatever you do, do it all to the glory of God, and seek the good of others so that they may be saved (vv. 23–33). And through the whole chapter walks one Person: the Rock who followed Israel in the desert, the Lord whose table is spread for his people, the Son who did not seek his own advantage but gave himself for many.

The athlete and the graveyard. Paul has just described himself in the language of an athlete who could still be disqualified (9:27). Now he turns and says, in effect: this is not a nightmare I invented. It happened. And it happened to the most privileged generation that ever lived.

For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers. A formula Paul uses when something important is coming (12:1; Romans 11:25), and here it is a gentle sentence with a hard edge. The Corinthians prided themselves on being aware: on knowledge (8:1), on insight, on having worked out that an idol is nothing. Paul does not attack their knowledge. He tells them there is a piece of history they have not factored in.

That our fathers. Paul is writing to a mostly Gentile church, and he calls the wilderness generation our fathers. That is not a slip. The church is the continuation of the people of God; whoever belongs to Christ is Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:29), and Israel’s history is the church’s family history. A Corinthian dock worker who had never seen Jerusalem was being told that Moses was his ancestor and the Red Sea was part of his story.

Were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea. Count the word all. It comes five times in four verses. All under the cloud. All passed through the sea. All baptised into Moses. All ate. All drank. Paul is not describing a spiritual elite; he is describing every last person in the camp, including the ones who would be dead within the year. Stand there for a moment. The pillar of cloud is overhead: not a metaphor, but a visible column of the presence of God, guiding them by day and standing between them and Pharaoh’s army by night (Exodus 13:21; 14:19–20). Ahead, the sea has stood up on both sides. They walk out on the seabed on dry ground, and the water that drowned the Egyptian army does not touch them (Exodus 14:21–22). Cloud above, water on either hand: they are, says Paul, surrounded, and he uses the word for baptism to say so.

And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea. Baptised into Moses is a striking phrase, and it needs unpacking, because it is not water baptism. Israel did not get wet; the Egyptians did. To be baptised into someone is to be bound to that person, so that his deliverance becomes your deliverance and his story becomes the story you live inside, just as Christians are baptised into Christ and joined to him (Romans 6:3). Israel came out of that sea belonging to Moses, their leader and mediator, in a way they had not belonged to him when they went in. They had a mediator, a rescue, a covenant sign, and a visible God. If church membership, the font and the table could save anyone, that generation was safe. Which is exactly the point Paul is setting up. Everything in these two verses is genuine. None of it is criticised. The cloud was real, the sea was real, the belonging was real, and the word nevertheless is coming in verse 5.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism automatically saves. That is the very point Paul is about to make: they were all baptised, yet most were destroyed.

Who this passage is for. It is easy to file it under other people. It is for the man who was sprinkled as a baby and has the certificate in a drawer. It is for the woman who was baptised in a river at seventeen in front of a weeping congregation. It is for the family that has not missed a Sunday in a decade, whose children know the songs, who take the bread and the cup every month without fail. Paul’s point is not that these things are worthless; he is about to call them spiritual food and spiritual drink. His point is that Israel had the equivalent of every one of them, in a more spectacular form than any church has ever seen, and it was possible to have the lot and perish anyway. The cloud did not make anyone love God. It only made him impossible to ignore.

Does this passage settle how baptism should be done? Not directly, and it is wise not to make it carry more than it does. Israel was neither immersed nor sprinkled; they walked through on dry ground. Paul uses the word baptism for union with a mediator, not for a method. This app holds to believer’s baptism by immersion on other grounds: the New Testament pattern of baptising those who repent and believe (Acts 2:41; 8:12), and the picture of burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:4; Colossians 2:12). Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise the children of believers, read the covenant differently, and we honour them as fellow servants of the same Lord. What both sides agree on here is the point Paul is making: no form of baptism, however it is done, can stand in for faith.

In a sentence. Paul wants you to remember, brothers and sisters, that our forefathers were all under the cloud and all went through the sea; all of them were baptised into Moses in the cloud and the sea.

On a Tuesday. Israel’s history is your family history. Read the Old Testament as the story of your own spiritual ancestors, not as a museum of other people’s mistakes. And take stock of your own privileges honestly: the Christian home, the good church, the Bible on the shelf, the baptism and the table. Thank God for every one of them. Then ask the question this passage is about to press: has all of this led me to trust and love Christ himself, or has it only made him familiar?

For worship. The God of this chapter did not save his people by sending instructions. He went with them. He hung over them in a cloud, held back the sea with his own wind, and walked them through on dry ground while their enemies drowned behind. Every privilege in these verses is a gift from his hand, given to a people who had done nothing to deserve it. And the deliverance at the sea was only a shadow. The greater Moses has passed through deeper waters than the Red Sea, the waters of death itself, and all who are joined to him by faith come up out of them on the other side.

parallels.desc: the pillar of cloud
through the sea on dry ground

verseByVerse.quote: and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ.

And all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. The privileges keep coming, and now they are edible. The food is the manna from heaven (Exodus 16); the drink is the water from the rock (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11). Paul sees them as Israel’s equivalent of the Lord’s Supper, which is why he describes them in the same breath as their baptism. Spiritual here does not mean immaterial. The manna could be gathered in a jar, and it went bad if you hoarded it. The water from the rock was wet. The word means supplied by the Spirit: food and drink that no farmer grew and no well yielded, arriving because God sent them, and pointing beyond themselves to Christ, the true bread from heaven (John 6:31–35). For forty years an entire nation woke up in a desert that grows nothing and found breakfast on the ground. Not once. Every morning, something like twelve thousand mornings, Sabbaths excepted, until the day they ate the produce of Canaan and it stopped (Joshua 5:12).

For they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them. Paul now says something that would be reckless if it were not true. Two questions come up here, and both deserve straight answers. First, is Paul repeating a Jewish legend? There was a later rabbinic tradition that the rock of Exodus 17 literally rolled along behind Israel, a boulder on tour, providing water. Paul does not endorse that. He is reaching for what the tradition was clumsily reaching for. Water came from a rock at Rephidim near the beginning of the journey (Exodus 17:6) and again at Meribah near the end of it, forty years later (Numbers 20:11). The rocks were different rocks in different places. What followed them was not a stone; it was the One who gave the water, and he was there at both ends of the wilderness and every dry mile in between.

And the Rock was Christ. Second, why call him the Rock at all? Because that is God’s own name in the song Moses sang over this very generation: the Rock, whose work is perfect; the Rock that bore you, whom you forgot (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 18; compare Psalm 78:35). And at Rephidim the LORD said he would stand before Moses on the rock (Exodus 17:6). Paul takes a divine title out of the Old Testament, a title reserved for the LORD, and lays it on Jesus of Nazareth without a word of apology. This is not the New Testament borrowing an image. It is the New Testament identifying a person. It affirms both Christ’s deity and his eternal pre-existence, and verse 9 will confirm it: Israel put Christ to the test.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the physical rock was literally Christ. It means the one who gave them water was Christ, and the rock was a sign of him.

How could Christ be with Israel centuries before he was born? Because the Son did not begin to exist in Bethlehem. He is the eternal Word who was with God and was God in the beginning (John 1:1), through whom all things were made. At Bethlehem he took a human nature to himself; he did not come into being. Before that, he was already at work among his people. Jesus himself said that Abraham rejoiced to see his day, and that before Abraham was, I am (John 8:56–58). So when Israel was led, fed and watered in the desert, the Son was not watching from a distance and waiting for his turn. He was the one doing it. The God of the Old Testament and the Saviour of the New are not two characters. They are the same Lord.

Before there was a manger, there was a rock in a desert. The Son of God stood in a waterless place beside a people who had already decided he was not worth trusting, and opened a spring for them. He would do it again on a hill outside Jerusalem, where the rock struck was himself, and what came out was not water only (John 19:34). He fed the men who would grumble at him by evening. He gave drink to the throats that would curse him by nightfall. There has never been a season of the world’s history in which he was not doing this.

In a sentence. All of them ate the same food from heaven and drank the same God-given drink, for they drank from the spiritual Rock that went with them on their journey, and that Rock was Christ.

On a Tuesday. Read the wilderness stories in Exodus and Numbers looking for him. When the manna falls and the water flows, you are watching Christ provide for people very like you. And when you are in a dry place yourself, remember who stood on the rock. He has not stopped giving water in deserts.

For worship. The Christ who gave Israel water in the wilderness gives living water still, and he gives it to the thirsty, not to the deserving (John 7:37). He was struck so that his people might drink. He has followed his people through every desert they have ever crossed, unseen and unthanked, and he has never once run dry. Blessed be the Rock of our salvation.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition told of a rock that followed Israel through the wilderness; Paul says the true source of their water was Christ.

parallels.desc: bread from heaven
water from the rock

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased, for they were overthrown in the wilderness.

Nevertheless, with most of them God was not pleased. Everything turns on one word. Nevertheless. All had the privileges; most perished. Paul says most, and the word is almost a mercy, because the arithmetic is worse than it sounds. Of the fighting men who came out of Egypt, two entered the land: Caleb and Joshua (Numbers 14:29–30). Two. Out of a muster of more than six hundred thousand men of fighting age (Numbers 1:46). Note also the restrained phrase God was not pleased. It is a mild-sounding verb for a fearful outcome, and the mildness is deliberate. God does not rage. He is simply not pleased, and a generation ends. The displeasure of God is quiet, and it is heavier than anything else in the world.

For they were overthrown in the wilderness. The verb is a picture word, taken from Numbers 14:16: katestrōthēsan, strewn, scattered, laid out flat, bodies spread across a desert floor. Put a figure on it. Something like forty funerals a day, every day, for thirty-eight years. There was never a week in that generation’s life without a burial party going out at dusk. The children who came into Canaan had grown up hearing that sound. And every one of those people had been under the cloud. Every one had walked through the sea on dry ground. Every one had eaten the bread of heaven that morning. Whatever the sacraments do, they did not do this.

Privilege is not armour. This is the sentence the confident Corinthians needed and did not want. They had concluded that spiritual privilege was a kind of insulation: that a man who had been baptised, who ate at the Lord’s table, who had the Spirit and could speak in tongues, was in a category where serious spiritual danger no longer applied. Paul answers with a graveyard. He does not deny that the privileges were real. He denies that they were armour.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that all who died in the wilderness went to hell. Moses died in the wilderness under God’s displeasure, and Moses is on the mountain of transfiguration (Deuteronomy 34:5; Luke 9:30). Miriam and Aaron died there too, and they were God’s servants. To be shut out of Canaan was a real and terrible judgment, but Canaan is not a picture of heaven in any simple way, and Paul is not conducting an inquest into individual souls. He is making one point, and it is enough on its own: privileges without faith and obedience do not protect from God’s judgment, and God’s manifest favour to a group is no guarantee about any particular person in it.

Were these people ever truly God’s? Some were, and many were not, and that is exactly the danger. Israel was a covenant people, but not everyone inside it had faith. The letter to the Hebrews explains what went wrong: the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened, and they were unable to enter because of unbelief (Hebrews 3:19; 4:2). The church today is the same kind of mixture. It is possible to sit among God’s people, sing their songs and share their table, and never have trusted Christ yourself. The answer is not to doubt every Christian around you, but to make sure of your own heart: to come to Christ himself, not merely to his people.

In a sentence. Yet God was displeased with most of them, and their bodies were left scattered in the desert.

On a Tuesday. Being baptised, taking communion and attending church are great privileges, but they do not save by themselves. Make sure you truly trust Christ. Ask yourself plainly: if every outward thing were taken away, the church, the habits, the reputation, would there be anything left between me and God? If the answer frightens you, that fear is a door, not a wall. Go through it to Christ today.

For worship. The God who is not pleased with privilege alone is the God who was well pleased with his Son (Matthew 3:17). Everything that generation lacked, he possessed: faith that never failed, obedience that never wavered, love for the Father that never cooled in the desert. And the favour that rests on him rests on everyone who is in him. Those who could never please God in themselves are accepted in the Beloved, and the displeasure that scattered bodies across the wilderness fell, in the end, on the one body on the cross.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these things took place as examples for us, that we might not desire evil as they did.

Now these things took place as examples for us. The word is typoi, types, patterns: the mark a die leaves when it stamps a coin. These events really happened, and the wilderness was not merely a bad patch of history that happens to be instructive. God shaped those events so that the pattern pressed into them would still be legible centuries later, to people who would never see a desert. The Old Testament is not raw material we are cleverly applying. It was struck this way on purpose.

That we might not desire evil as they did. Notice what the stamp says. Paul reaches past the four sins he is about to list and names the thing underneath them. It was not, first of all, that Israel worshipped a calf or slept with Moabites. It was that they craved. The Greek is epithymētas kakōn, cravers of bad things. One of the first great collapses in the wilderness was a food riot. They despised the manna and wanted fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions and garlic (Numbers 11:5), and they wanted them so badly that they said out loud they had been better off as slaves. God gave them quail until it came out of their nostrils, sent a plague, and the place was named the Graves of Craving (Numbers 11:4–34). The Corinthians’ craving for temple meals is the same thing in a toga. Sin begins with desire, and desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin (James 1:14–15). Every sin in the rest of this chapter began there. So did every sin in Corinth. So does every sin in the reader.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament stories are merely moral fables. They are history that teaches. Nor does saying the Old Testament was stamped for us license treating every detail as a code to be cracked: the scarlet cord, the number of the pillars, the colours of the curtain. That kind of reading turns Scripture into a puzzle and the interpreter into a genius, and it produces sermons that could not have been preached by Moses. Paul’s typology is disciplined and it is moral: here is a people with advantages, here is what they did with them, here is what happened, and you are made of the same material. The pattern is not hidden. It is the plain sense of the story, pressed on a later generation. And the reason it presses is not that history repeats itself but that human hearts do. The desert is gone. The craving is not.

Is it wrong to want things? No. God made us creatures of desire, and he gives us good things richly to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17). Wanting food, love, rest, children or useful work is not sin. The problem in the wilderness was not appetite but what the appetite did. It wanted bad things, or good things on its own terms; it despised what God had given in order to demand what he had not; and it valued the gift above the Giver, to the point of preferring Egypt. A useful question is whether a desire can be brought to God in prayer and left with him. A desire that sulks when God says wait, or that would rather have the thing without him than him without the thing, has become craving.

In a sentence. These things happened as warning pictures for us, so that we would not crave evil the way they did.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it is uncomfortable because it is easy to run. Think back over the last week and ask: what did I want that I would have been embarrassed to pray for out loud? Not what did I do, but what did I want. That is the question this verse is asking, and it is asking it before any sin has been committed, while the whole thing is still only an appetite in a decent-looking person. Then bring that desire to God by name, and ask him for contentment with what he has given.

For worship. The God of the wilderness rained bread from heaven every single morning on people who complained about the menu. He is not stingy. He is the giver of every good and perfect gift, and he knows better than we do what will satisfy. And in Christ he has given the one thing that ends the craving at its root: himself, the bread of life, so that whoever comes to him shall not hunger (John 6:35).

parallels.desc: the graves of craving

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be idolaters as some of them were; as it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”

Do not be idolaters as some of them were. The first of the four wilderness failures, and Paul picks the one everybody knows: the golden calf (Exodus 32), at the very foot of Sinai, weeks after the people had heard God speak the commandments.

As it is written, The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. He is quoting Exodus 32:6, and he quotes the line about the meal because the Corinthians are arguing about meals. They ate a sacrificial feast before the calf and then played. But look closely at what the golden calf actually was, because almost everyone gets it wrong. Israel did not decide to swap the LORD for a Canaanite deity. Aaron built the calf and then announced that tomorrow would be a feast to the LORD (Exodus 32:5). They kept the name. They kept the God. What they changed was the terms: they would have him visible, manageable, on their own schedule, in a form they had chosen. That is idolatry, and it is a religious sin, committed in a worship service, by people who would have described themselves as devout.

Rose up to play. The last verb is worth a moment. Play is the polite translation of a Hebrew word that covers dancing, revelry, and what happens after the dancing. Exodus notes drily that the people had broken loose (Exodus 32:25). This is exactly what happened at Corinthian temple feasts: eating, drinking and immorality, in that order. The pattern is fixed, and Paul will repeat it in the next verse: worship on your own terms first, and the bed follows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feasting or playing is wrong in itself. Israel’s own calendar was full of feasts commanded by God, with rejoicing before him. It means feasting in idol worship is wrong, and that celebration cut loose from God tends to end somewhere he did not lead.

Today’s idols. The modern reader should not relax here. Nobody in the reader’s street is casting bullocks out of earrings. But an idol, as Tim Keller put it, is a good thing that has become an ultimate thing: anything you look to for what only God can give. Here is a way to find yours, and it is quicker than introspection. Finish this sentence honestly: if I lost this, life would not be worth living. Whatever fills that blank is receiving worship. It may be a wholly good thing: a marriage, a child, a reputation, a ministry. Good things make the strongest idols, because nobody thinks to suspect them. If that test feels too dramatic, here is a duller one that catches more people. An idol is not usually discovered by asking what you believe; it is discovered by looking at where the money goes when it is not needed elsewhere, where the free hours go when nobody is watching, and what you think about in the ten minutes before sleep. A person’s theology is on his lips. His worship is in his diary and his bank statement.

Stop feeding the rival. Notice the mercy in the way Paul frames it. He does not tell the Corinthians to manufacture a stronger devotion to God. He tells them to stop feeding a rival. Nobody has ever loved God more by trying harder to feel it; hearts warm to God when the thing that was absorbing the heat is set down. That is why the command in verse 14 will be flee, a thing you can actually do on a Monday, and not feel differently, which you cannot (compare 1 John 5:21).

Can I worship the true God in a wrong way? Yes, and that is the calf’s lesson. Aaron’s people meant the LORD, and they were still idolaters, because they worshipped him in a form he had forbidden (Exodus 20:4–5). It is possible to believe the right God exists and still shrink him down: to a God who only comforts and never commands, or who agrees with my politics, or who exists to make my plans succeed. The safeguard is simple to state: let God define himself, from his own word, and worship him the way he has revealed. Whenever I find myself thinking, my God would never, it is worth checking whether that sentence comes from Scripture or from me.

In a sentence. Do not worship idols as some of them did; Scripture says, “The people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.”

On a Tuesday. Watch where your celebrations take you. Do they honour God or something else? And run the blank test once this week: if I lost this, life would not be worth living. Whatever you wrote, hand it back to God in prayer as his gift, held with an open hand.

For worship. The LORD will not be made into a calf, because he is greater than anything that could be cast or carved. He is not manageable, and that is our safety: a God small enough to control would be too small to save. And yet the uncontainable God made himself visible after all, not in gold but in flesh. The image we were forbidden to make, he gave us himself, in the Son who is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15). We do not need a calf. We have seen his glory, full of grace and truth.

parallels.desc: they sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play

verseByVerse.quote: We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did, and twenty-three thousand fell in a single day.

We must not indulge in sexual immorality as some of them did. The second of the four sins. The episode is Numbers 25, at Baal of Peor, and Paul chose it deliberately, because it is this chapter’s exact problem in Old Testament dress. Read how it starts: the Moabite women invited the people to the sacrifices of their gods, and the people ate and bowed down to their gods (Numbers 25:1–2). It began with an invitation to dinner. The meal came first; the immorality came second; the idolatry was in both. A Corinthian believer accepting a temple invitation would have said he was only eating. Israel said the same, and twenty-four thousand of them were buried.

And twenty-three thousand fell in a single day. Twenty-four thousand, says Numbers, and there is the difficulty, because Paul writes twenty-three. It is a small thing and it deserves a straight answer rather than a cough, because a thoughtful reader will notice it and wonder whether anyone was going to mention it. First, notice that the two texts are not making the same claim. Numbers gives a total for the whole judgment: those who died by the plague were twenty-four thousand (Numbers 25:9). Paul adds a phrase Numbers does not have: in a single day. The plague was not the only killing in that chapter; the chiefs of the people were executed by judicial sentence as well (Numbers 25:4–5), and the plague itself ran until Phinehas stopped it. A day’s toll inside a larger total is not a contradiction of the total; it is a smaller number inside it, which is what one would expect. Second, both figures are round. Nobody counted twenty-three thousand nine hundred and eighty-one corpses. Ancient reporting rounds, and rounding to the nearer or the lower thousand is not error, any more than saying a stadium held forty thousand is a lie because the turnstiles read 40,412. This is not a contradiction.

The rough edge left standing. And notice what Paul does not do. He does not harmonise. He knew the book of Numbers thoroughly; he could have copied the number and nobody would ever have known. A man manufacturing a religion smooths his sources. Paul, writing to a hostile and clever church that would have loved to catch him out, leaves the rough edge standing. Small differences like this one are not cracks in Scripture’s credibility; they are fingerprints on it, evidence of real writers handling real records rather than a committee tidying after the fact.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the precise number is the point. The point is the scale of God’s judgment on immorality joined to idolatry. Twenty-three thousand people were alive at breakfast and dead by dark, and it started with an invitation they saw no harm in accepting.

Is this verse a sentence on me if I have already fallen into sexual sin? No, it is a warning, and warnings are given so that people can turn back. Paul wrote this to a church in which some had been sexually immoral, and only four chapters earlier he told them: such were some of you, but you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God (6:11). The judgment at Peor fell on people who went on in their sin without repentance. For anyone who turns to Christ, the judgment has already fallen on him. Confess it plainly to God, break off whatever is feeding it, and if others have been wronged, seek to put it right. Then stand up as one who is forgiven, because you are.

In a sentence. Nor should we commit sexual sin as some of them did, and in a single day twenty-three thousand of them died.

On a Tuesday. Notice where your temptations begin, because they rarely begin with the sin itself. Peor began with a dinner invitation. Ask what the dinner invitation is in your life: the friendship that has started to feel secret, the late conversation, the app, the habit of looking. Decline the invitation, and you will rarely face the bed.

For worship. The holiness that struck at Peor is the same holiness that came down in mercy. At Peor, Phinehas stood between the living and the dead and the plague was stopped (Numbers 25:7–8, 11). A greater Priest has stood in that place for us, and the judgment did not merely stop at him; it was spent on him. Christ took the judgment our sins deserve, and he gives to the unclean his own purity. Blessed be the Lamb who makes the defiled clean and keeps them so.
verseByVerse.note: Numbers gives 24,000 as the total who died in the plague; Paul speaks of those who fell in a single day.

parallels.desc: Israel and the Moabite women

verseByVerse.quote: We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We must not put Christ to the test, as some of them did and were destroyed by serpents,

We must not put Christ to the test. The third sin. The verb is ekpeirazō, to test out, to try to the limit: to push God to see how far you can go before he acts. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read the Lord here, and a few read God; the ESV follows the reading with the strongest early support, and it is also the reading no scribe would have invented. A copyist might soften Christ to the Lord because the sentence startled him; nobody sharpens the Lord into Christ in an account of Israel in the desert. So the startling reading is almost certainly what Paul wrote, and it says the same thing verse 4 said: Christ was with Israel in the wilderness, and the one they were provoking in Numbers 21 was the Son of God.

As some of them did and were destroyed by serpents. The incident is worth having in front of you. Israel is on a detour around Edom, the road is long, and they say the thing that people say on long roads. They speak against God and Moses: why have you brought us up out of Egypt to die in the wilderness? There is no food and no water, and we loathe this worthless food (Numbers 21:4–5). The worthless food is the manna. They are complaining about the miracle. Fiery serpents come into the camp, people die, and the remedy God gives is a bronze serpent on a pole: look at it and live. Jesus took that image and applied it to himself: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that whoever believes in him may have eternal life (John 3:14–15).

What it is to test Christ. It is not doubt, and it is not asking hard questions; God is patient with both. Testing is what you do when you want to find out how far he can be pushed. It is defiant presumption, treating his patience as a margin you are entitled to spend, daring him to do something about your sin. Israel had watched him split a sea, and they were probing to see whether he would really follow through on his threats.

What it does not mean. It does not mean honest questions to God are wrong. Job and the psalmists asked him a great many, and he answered them. Testing God is not asking why; it is presuming on him.

The forgiveness factored in. Here is a test the reader can run on himself, and it is a searching one. Have you ever done something while quietly counting on being forgiven for it, the forgiveness factored in beforehand, part of the calculation, the cross treated as an allowance? That is not weakness. Weakness falls and is horrified. This is the sin of the confident, which is why it is in a chapter written for people who thought their knowledge kept them safe.

One more sign. Testing has a second form, quieter and commoner: the demand for one more sign. If God would just make this unmistakable, I would obey. Israel had a pillar of fire and asked for evidence. More proof has never yet produced obedience in anybody, because the problem was never the quantity of evidence. Jesus met this exact request in his own wilderness with the exact answer: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7). Where Israel failed the test in the desert, the true Son passed it.

Is it testing God to ask him for guidance or a sign? Not when it is asked humbly. Asking God for wisdom is commanded, and he gives generously (James 1:5). Gideon’s fleece is often cited, but notice that God had already spoken to Gideon plainly, and the fleece was a weak man’s request for reassurance, which God graciously granted rather than a method to copy (Judges 6:36–40). The sin is demanding a sign as the price of obeying what God has already made clear. If Scripture has spoken, the faithful response is to obey, not to ask for a second opinion. Where Scripture leaves the choice open, pray, seek counsel, use the mind God gave you, and trust him to guide.

In a sentence. We must not push Christ to see how far we can go, as some of them did and were killed by snakes.

On a Tuesday. Are you testing God, telling yourself that he will not mind just this once? Stop, and turn back. And if you have been waiting for a sign before obeying something God has already made plain, the sign you are waiting for is the verse you already have.

For worship. The comfort is buried in a frightening verse. The Christ these people provoked in Numbers 21 went into a wilderness of his own, hungry and alone for forty days, and would not provoke his Father even once. The obedience the reader has not managed has already been managed, and by the very person who was being tested in the desert. And the one they provoked is the one who was lifted up for them.
