Those who were bitten by their own rebellion are healed by looking at him. There is no other cure, and there has never been a sinner too poisoned for it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Lord.”

parallels.desc: fiery serpents among the people

verseByVerse.quote: nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
nor grumble, as some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer.

Nor grumble. The fourth sin, and of the four this is the one that looks out of place. Idolatry, immorality, testing God, and complaining. The word is gongyzō, to mutter, to complain under the breath, a word that sounds like what it describes. One of these is not like the others, or so it seems, until you notice that grumbling is the sin that killed more of that generation than any other. It was grumbling at the report of the spies that shut the door on the whole nation (Numbers 14:1–4, 29). Israel grumbled constantly in the wilderness, against God, Moses and Aaron. Perhaps the Corinthians were grumbling against Paul.

As some of them did and were destroyed by the Destroyer. After Korah’s rebellion, when the ground had opened (Numbers 16:31–33), the people grumbled about it the next day, and a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred (Numbers 16:41–49). The Destroyer (olothreutēs) is the destroying angel, the same figure who passed through Egypt on the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:23; Hebrews 11:28), now walking through Israel’s own camp.

Why God takes it so seriously. Because grumbling is never really about the food. It is a verdict. Every complaint carries an unspoken clause: this arrangement is wrong, and I would have arranged it better. The manna was on the ground that morning. The complaint was not that God had failed to provide; it was that his provision was beneath them. Grumbling is the sound a heart makes when it has reviewed God’s management and found it wanting. It is also the most respectable sin in the list. No church discipline case has ever been opened over it. A man can grumble his way through forty years of Sundays, about the music, the temperature, the preacher, the roster, the young people, the old people, and be thought a pillar. Israel grumbled their way to a desert grave and never once thought of themselves as rebels.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we cannot express sorrow or lament to God. There is a world of difference between grumbling and lament. A third of the Psalms are complaints, and some of them are savage: how long, O LORD, will you forget me for ever (Psalm 13:1)? God did not merely tolerate those words; he put them in the hymn book and gave them to his people to sing. So the difference is not the presence of pain in the sentence, and it is not the volume. The difference is direction and address. Lament is spoken to God, and it stays in the room with him; it argues, weeps, and will not leave. Grumbling is spoken about God, to everyone except him. Israel in Numbers 11 did not pray. They stood in their tent doorways and talked to each other.

The tell. It is simple and it is worth knowing: when something is wrong, who hears about it first? If the answer is God, that is a sufferer. If the answer is anyone else, that is a grumbler, and the way out is not to suppress the complaint but to redirect it, which is what the Psalms are for.

Is it grumbling to say my job is hard or my church has problems? Not in itself. Describing a hard thing truthfully is not a sin, and some problems need to be raised so that they can be fixed. The question is the spirit and the destination. Raising a concern with the person who can address it, for the sake of the good, is love. Repeating it to everyone else, with a shrug of contempt, for the pleasure of being aggrieved, is grumbling. One builds; the other corrodes. And a heart that has stopped noticing God’s gifts will find something to complain about in any job and any church on earth.

In a sentence. And do not complain against God, as some of them did and were wiped out by the destroying angel.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it takes about a minute. Replay yesterday’s conversations and count the sentences that were, at bottom, a review of God’s arrangements: the weather, the body, the salary, the family you were given, the church you are in. Then set that number against the number of sentences that were thanks. The ratio is a fair reading of where the heart is (compare Philippians 2:14–15). Then turn one complaint into a prayer today. Bring it to God honestly, with trust instead of grumbling.

For worship. The Destroyer passed over every house marked with blood on the night of the Passover, and he passes over still. Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed (5:7), and those sheltered under him are safe from the judgment their grumbling deserved. And the Son himself, given a cup more bitter than any wilderness hardship, did not mutter. He said, not my will but yours be done. His contentment in the Father’s will, perfect to the end, is counted to grumblers who trust him.

parallels.desc: the destroyer

verseByVerse.quote: Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now these things happened to them as an example, but they were written down for our instruction, on whom the end of the ages has come.

Now these things happened to them as an example. The word is typikōs, typically, as warning patterns, repeating the thought of verse 6 so that nobody misses it.

But they were written down for our instruction. Two claims sit in this sentence, and both are large. The first is about the Old Testament. The word nouthesia means warning, admonition, the kind of correction a father gives. It was written down for our instruction: not merely preserved, not merely available, but written with us in view (Romans 15:4; 2 Timothy 3:16). When Moses set down the account of the quail, the calf, the serpents and the plague, God intended the paragraph to be read by a Gentile believer in a port city some fourteen hundred years later, and by whoever is reading it now. That settles the question of whether the Old Testament is still the Christian’s book. Paul is arguing a live pastoral crisis in a Greek church out of the book of Numbers, and he expects it to land.

On whom the end of the ages has come. The second claim is about where we are standing. Literally, the ends of the ages have arrived at us. Christians live at the climax of history, where all the previous ages meet their fulfilment in Christ (Hebrews 9:26). The old age and the age to come are not separated by a tidy line in front of us; they overlap, and we are living in the overlap. The decisive act has happened: the Rock has been struck, the Passover Lamb has been killed, the tomb is empty. And the world is manifestly not yet put right: the wilderness is still a wilderness, the funerals still go out at dusk, and nobody is asked to pretend otherwise. This is what makes the warnings weightier rather than lighter. Israel had the shadow and fell. We have the substance. They had a rock in the desert; we have the crucified and risen Son and his Spirit living in us. Greater light is a greater privilege and a greater accountability, in that order and always together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament had no meaning for its first readers. It did, and they were judged by it. It means its full purpose is seen in Christ and his church.

Does the end of the ages mean Christ will return very soon? It means the last days have already begun, and they began with Christ’s first coming (Hebrews 1:2; Acts 2:17). The whole period between his ascension and his return is the last days. Nobody knows the day or the hour (Matthew 24:36), and Scripture forbids date-setting, but every generation of Christians lives at the end of the ages and must be ready. His return will be one public, visible event, when he comes to raise the dead and judge the world, not a secret coming in stages. So the right response is not to calculate but to watch: to live each ordinary week as people who may see him before it ends.

Numbers is not a museum. There is a practical consequence for how the Old Testament gets read, and it is worth stating because so many Christians have quietly given up on three-quarters of their Bible. A reader who works through the wilderness narratives asking what this tells me about people like me, dealing with a God like this, is reading it the way an apostle read it. He does not need a technique. He needs to believe verse 11: it was written down for him.

In a sentence. These things happened to them as warning pictures, and they were written down to warn us, who live when all the ages have reached their goal.

On a Tuesday. You live in the last days. Read the warnings of Scripture as written to you. Pick up the book of Numbers this month, the book most Christians skip, and read it as family history with your own name written in the margin.

For worship. There is a comfort in the timing. If the ends of the ages have arrived, then nobody is waiting for the interesting part of history to begin. Whatever the reader’s week looks like, and it may look like nothing at all, it is being lived after the decisive event and before the final one, in the short overlap where the outcome is settled and the fighting is still going on. The God who wrote Numbers with us in mind has been steering every age toward his Son, and the ages have not slipped from his hand. All of history was moving toward Christ, and all of it will be gathered up in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall.

Therefore let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall. This is the sentence the whole history has been building towards, and it is aimed with precision. Not at the struggling. Not at the man who knows he is weak and comes to church frightened of himself. It is aimed at the one who thinks that he stands; the verb means supposes, presumes, takes it as settled. In Corinth that was the confident believer with the correct doctrine of idols, sitting down to dinner in a temple and quite sure the theology covered him. Israel thought their privileges guaranteed safety. Self-confidence is the danger. Take heed (blepō) is simply watch out. Peter is the classic example: though they all fall away, I will not (Mark 14:29–31). Within hours he was warming his hands at the enemy’s fire.

Can a true Christian finally be lost? The question a Reformed reader will feel immediately should be answered rather than dodged. If Christ says no one will snatch them out of my hand (John 10:28), why the warning? The answer is that the warning is not an alternative to being kept. It is one of the ways God keeps his people. He does not preserve his own by making them immune to danger while they sleep through it; he preserves them by waking them up. Paul writes work out your own salvation with fear and trembling and then, in the same breath, for it is God who works in you (Philippians 2:12–13). Both halves are true and they are not in tension. The alarm that gets a family out of a burning house is not evidence that the fire brigade failed; it is how they were saved. This verse is an alarm, and God has been using it to keep people on their feet for two thousand years.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers should live in fear of losing salvation. It means overconfidence is dangerous, and humble watchfulness is the mark of the true believer. A true Christian may fall into grievous sin for a time, as David and Peter did, and suffer for it; but those whom God has truly called he keeps, and they are restored (Westminster 17.1, 3).

The frightened reader. This yields a strange and rather comforting test. If this verse frightens you, it is already doing its work, and you are not the person it is warning. The one in danger is the one who reads it and feels nothing, who assumes at once that it is about somebody else in the congregation. The man most likely to fall down the stairs is the one who says he could walk them in the dark.

The quiet kinds of confidence. Be careful of the particular kind of confidence Paul is naming, because it is not usually loud. It rarely says I could never fall. It says smaller things. It says that a certain sin is simply not in one’s temperament. It says that a friendship which would look questionable in someone else is fine here, because the people involved are mature. It says that a habit which flattened another Christian is manageable in a person with better theology. Every one of those sentences is the sentence of a man walking a wall in the dark, telling himself he knows where the edge is.

In a sentence. So if you think you are standing firm, watch out that you do not fall.

On a Tuesday. Take heed, not by working up anxiety about your standing, which helps nobody, but by doing the ordinary things a person does who knows he could fall: stay near the means of grace, keep short accounts, tell someone the truth about yourself, and stop rehearsing the sins you have decided you are no longer capable of (compare 9:27; Romans 11:20). Name the one sin you are most sure you would never commit, and ask God to guard you there too.

For worship. We do not stand by our own strength, and we never did. We stand because we are held. Christ is the one who is able to keep us from stumbling and to present us blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy (Jude 24). The hand that wrote this warning is the hand that will not let go. To him be glory, majesty, dominion and authority, before all time and now and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. And then, immediately, the promise. Paul has spent twelve verses making a Christian afraid of himself, and he will not leave him there for a single sentence longer. Temptation (peirasmos) covers testing, trial and temptation, and the context here is the pull toward sin. Common to man is anthrōpinos: human-sized, the sort of thing human beings get. This is the first mercy of the verse, and it goes straight to an ache most people carry in private: the conviction that mine is different. That whatever else is common, this particular pull, at this particular hour, with this particular history behind it, is a freakish thing that would horrify anyone I told. It is not. It has a name, other people have faced it and overcome, and some of them are sitting in your row. The loneliness is a lie, and it is the lie that keeps the sin fed, because a thing you believe is unique is a thing you will never say out loud.

God is faithful. Then the ground of the promise, and notice that it is not you. It is the same phrase that closed the opening thanksgiving of this letter (1:9), and it puts the weight of the sentence entirely on his character. Not our strength, but God’s faithfulness, is the foundation of hope.

And he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability. Check the verb, because it is not the verb people remember. This is not a description of your strength. It is a limit God imposes and polices, as he set limits on Satan with Job (Job 1:12; 2:6). He stands at the gate of every trial that comes at you and decides how much of it gets through. He knows our strength, and he will not allow more than his grace can enable us to bear.

But with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape. The word is ekbasis, a way out of a defile: the mountain pass that lets an army get clear of a valley it should never have marched into. With every temptation, God makes an exit. For the Corinthians, the way out of idolatry was to flee (v. 14). And in practice the door is usually further back than people look for it. Nobody is promised a supernatural exit at the last second; the escape is nearly always upstream. It is the second drink, not the twelfth. It is the reply typed at eleven at night, not the affair eighteen months later. It is the decision about what the laptop does after everyone else is asleep, not the moment of looking. Track any fall backwards and you will find the door standing open at a point that felt utterly harmless at the time.

That you may be able to endure it. Note the last clause, because it is not the one we would have written. Not that you may be able to avoid it. The goal is not always removal of the trial but endurance through it. Sometimes the escape God provides is a road out, and sometimes it is the strength to stand in the fire without bowing. Both are the way of escape. Both come from the same faithful God (Hebrews 2:18; 2 Peter 2:9).

Where Christians differ: can believers be overcome? Some take this verse to mean believers never actually fall into sin, or that if they do, they were never really tempted beyond ability. Verdict: God always provides a way to resist, so no believer can say, I had no choice. When believers sin, it is because they did not take the way out, not because God failed. This verse does not promise that believers never fall, but that they never have to. And it promises that God’s faithfulness will see them through (Westminster 17.3).

If there was always a way out, am I not guiltier? It is the objection an honest reader raises at once: if there was always a door, then every time I sinned I could have not sinned, and that only makes me guiltier. Yes. That is exactly what the verse says, and pretending otherwise would be no kindness. There was a door. But look at who is standing beside it. The same sentence that removes the excuse names God as faithful, and a God faithful enough to have built the door is faithful enough to forgive the man who walked past it (1 John 1:9). The verse takes away the alibi and hands over the Father in the same breath.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God never gives us more than we can handle in suffering. That popular saying is not in the Bible, and Paul himself flatly denies it about affliction: he was so utterly burdened beyond his strength that he despaired of life itself (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). God does give his children more grief than they can carry. That is often the point of it, because the next line is that we might rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead. So if you are reading this with a diagnosis in your hand or an empty chair at your table, this verse is not telling you that your load has been measured to fit your shoulders. The promise is about temptation to sin: God will always enable us to resist, by his grace.

Does God tempt me, then? No. God tests his people, to prove and strengthen their faith, as he tested Abraham (Genesis 22:1); but he never entices anyone to sin. Let no one say when he is tempted, I am being tempted by God (James 1:13). The same Greek word can mean a test or a temptation, and the same event can be both: God means it for our strengthening while the devil and our own desires mean it for our fall. Joseph’s brothers meant evil, and God meant it for good (Genesis 50:20). So in every pull toward sin, you can know that God has set its limit, is present in it, and has a purpose of good for you through it.

What if I genuinely cannot see a way out? Then the way out may be closer than you think and smaller than you expected. Very often it is simply to leave: the room, the conversation, the screen. Often it is to tell someone, today, because sin grows in secret and weakens in the light. Sometimes it is to pray out loud, short and honest: Lord, help me now. And when the escape is not removal but endurance, as with a long-standing desire that does not go away, the way out is to keep saying no, one day at a time, with others alongside you. You do not have to see the whole road. God has promised there is one, and he is faithful.

In a sentence. Every temptation you face is the kind others have faced. And God keeps his word: he will not let you be tempted past what you can bear, but when the temptation comes he will also make a way out, so that you can stand up under it.

On a Tuesday. When temptation comes today, look for the way out God has provided. Then take it, quickly. Better still, ask the question while you are calm: for the temptation I know is coming this week, where is the pass out of the valley, and what would I have to decide today to be standing in it? God has promised the way of escape. He has not promised to carry you through a door you refuse to look for.

For worship. God is faithful. Everything in this verse hangs on those three words, and they have never once failed. He was faithful to Israel in the desert when Israel was faithless. He was faithful to Peter on the night of the denials. And he has given us a High Priest who was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin, and who is able to help those who are being tempted (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15). The one who stands at the gate of every temptation is the one who walked through the worst of them for us and did not fall. We are not left alone in the valley. He made the way out, and he is the way.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — The Lord’s Table and the Demons’ Table
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So, dear friends, they must run from idolatry. Paul appeals to their good sense to judge what he says. The cup of blessing believers bless is a sharing in Christ’s blood, and the bread they break is a sharing in Christ’s body; because there is one loaf, they who are many are one body, for they all share the one loaf. Look at Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in the altar. Paul does not mean that idol food or idols are anything in themselves. He means that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons, not to God, and he does not want them to be partners with demons. They cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the cup of demons, or share the Lord’s table and the table of demons. Are they trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy? Do they think they are stronger than he is?
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Participation

Paul’s use of koinōnia in vv. 16–17 — the cup of blessing is a koinōnia in the blood of Christ; the bread is a koinōnia in the body of Christ — is the most precise language of eucharistic participation in the NT. It does not specify the mode of Christ’s presence, but it insists on its reality: something genuinely happens in the Supper that is a real sharing in what Christ accomplished. Reformed eucharistic theology (following Calvin rather than Zwingli) has insisted on this real spiritual presence: Christ is truly present in the Supper, giving himself to be received by faith.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Attending a civic dinner at a Corinthian temple was not optional for many members of the social elite; it was part of the patronage network on which their livelihood depended. Paul’s “flee idolatry” would have carried genuine social cost. Now: The situations where Christian participation in cultural or civic life involves implicit participation in what is spiritually incompatible are multiple and not always obvious. Paul’s principle — you cannot share in the Lord’s table and the demons’ table — is the test: what are you actually participating in when you participate in this?

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry. I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say.

Therefore, my beloved. Take the address first. My beloved, from a man who has just spent thirteen verses on graves in the desert. He is not a prosecutor. He is a father, and the sternness and the tenderness come from the same place; only someone who loves you tells you the graveyard story.

Flee from idolatry. Then the command, and it is the way of escape that verse 13 promised. It is worth noticing everything Paul does not say. Not study idolatry. Not manage it, negotiate with it, or test how close you can get. Not develop a mature theology of it, which is precisely what the strong Corinthians had done. Flee. The verb (pheugō) is a present imperative, keep on running, make it your standing policy, and it is the same verb he used in 6:18 about sexual immorality. Those are the only two things in this letter that Paul tells the church to run away from, and it is not an accident that they are the two that Corinth’s temple culture served up in the same room. For the Corinthians, it meant: stop attending temple feasts.

The brave thing and the stupid thing. Christians are told to stand and fight almost everywhere else: resist the devil, put on the armour, endure hardship. Here, no. Here the brave thing and the stupid thing are the same thing. Joseph did not reason with Potiphar’s wife or explain his convictions; he left his garment in her hand and got out of the house (Genesis 39:12). There is no medal for how long you stayed in the room.

I speak as to sensible people; judge for yourselves what I say. Sensible (phronimoi) means wise, thoughtful, and the Corinthians prided themselves on wisdom. Paul appeals to it. Having given a flat command, he now hands them the argument and invites them to check his working. That is a remarkable thing for an apostle to do, and it is a model for anyone who teaches: he does not want compliance without conviction. He is about to lay out the reasoning in the verses that follow, and he expects thinking people to follow it and agree.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only ancient-style idol worship is in view. Anything that takes God’s place is an idol: covetousness, Paul says elsewhere, is idolatry (Colossians 3:5; 1 John 5:21).

What fleeing looks like when the temple is gone. It looks like the boring, unspiritual, entirely practical measures that people are embarrassed to admit they need. Deleting the thing rather than resolving to use it better. Taking the other road home. Not being alone in that house. Telling one person the truth so that the secret has a witness. Handing over the card, the password, the key. None of that is glamorous, and all of it works in a way that resolutions do not, because it removes the opportunity instead of relying on the will, and the will is exactly the thing that has already proved unreliable.

Is that not avoidance rather than victory? The objection comes quickly: should a mature Christian not be able to stand in the room? But that question has the shape of the Corinthian error, which was to treat strength as something to be demonstrated. Scripture never asks anyone to prove he can stand beside an idol. The mature response to a fire is not to practise standing in it. Fleeing is the victory; it is simply a victory that gives nobody a story to tell.

Should I get rid of objects connected with my old life? Often, yes. When the Ephesians came to faith, those who had practised magic brought their books and burned them publicly, though they were worth a fortune (Acts 19:19). Objects have no power in themselves, and Paul has said so (8:4). But things that were used in false worship, occult practice or a besetting sin can be a standing invitation back, and getting rid of them is a clear, simple act of turning. There is no need to be superstitious about ordinary things with an odd history. The question is whether this object keeps a door open that Christ has closed.

In a sentence. So, dear friends, run from idolatry. You are thoughtful people; weigh what Paul says for yourselves.

On a Tuesday. Name one idol in your heart, and then name one concrete step of flight you could take before the day is out. Not a resolution; a step. Delete, cancel, hand over, leave, tell.

For worship. My beloved: that is how God addresses those he commands to flee. He does not drive his people from their idols with contempt; he calls them away with love, because he has something better for them than anything they are leaving. The One we flee to is the fountain of living waters, and the idols are broken cisterns that hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13). Blessed be the God who calls his runaways beloved, and runs to meet them on the road.

verseByVerse.quote: The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The cup of blessing that we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread.

The cup of blessing that we bless. A phrase lifted straight from the Jewish table. The cup of blessing was the name for a cup of wine drunk at the end of a meal with a prayer of thanksgiving, especially at Passover, very probably the cup over which the blessing was said after the meal. That is the cup the Lord took in his hands in the upper room, on the night the last Passover became the first Supper, and made it the cup of the new covenant (11:25). That we bless means: over which we give thanks to God.

Is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? Both questions in this verse are rhetorical, expecting the answer yes, and Paul needs that yes, because his whole argument about temple meals depends on a prior conviction: that eating and drinking at a table can be a real sharing in what the table represents. If the Lord’s Supper is only a memory exercise, then a temple dinner is only a dinner, and the strong Corinthians are right. The word he uses is koinōnia: participation, sharing, communion, having something in common with. The English word fellowship has been worn down until it means coffee after the service; the Greek word means a genuine joint holding, the way business partners hold a firm. Paul says the cup is a joint holding in the blood of Christ. To drink it is to share in the benefits of his shed blood: forgiveness and the new covenant.

The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? To eat the bread is to share in Christ himself, crucified for us. He did not hand his people a symbol of a distant event and leave them to remember it as best they could. He gives himself.

Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body. Then the sentence a divided church needs most. One loaf, shared by all, torn, and everyone eats from the same torn loaf. The Supper expresses and strengthens the unity of the church. Notice that the phrase body of Christ shifts its meaning between verse 16 and verse 17: from Christ’s crucified body to the church, his body. The one makes the other. Those who share in the body given for them become the body that belongs to him. That is a hard image to hold while maintaining that you are of Paul and he is of Apollos (1:12). The bread on the table is the standing argument against every faction in the room. You cannot eat from one loaf with someone all month and claim to have nothing to do with him.

For we all partake of the one bread. All believers share in one Christ, and so are one people. The unity of the church is not something we manufacture by agreeing with each other; it is something we receive by all being fed by the same Lord.

What actually happens at the table? It is worth answering carefully, because a reader has probably heard three answers and been told the differences are enormous.

Where Christians differ: what happens in the Lord’s Supper? Roman Catholics teach transubstantiation: the bread and wine become the actual body and blood of Christ. Lutherans teach that Christ’s body and blood are present in, with and under the bread and wine. Many evangelicals hold a memorial view: the Supper is only a reminder. Verdict: The bread and wine remain bread and wine (11:26–28 still calls it bread). But the Supper is more than a memorial: Paul calls it a real participation in Christ, and a reminder is not a participation. The Reformed view, taught by Calvin, is that Christ is truly present by his Spirit, and believers, by faith, really feed on Christ spiritually, receiving him and all the benefits of his death. Christ’s body is in heaven, but the Spirit lifts us up to commune with him (Westminster 29.7). Christ is truly present, not physically but spiritually, and truly given to faith.

Not nothing and not magic. Calvin was content to say he experienced the thing more surely than he could explain it. What that means at the table is this: when you eat, you are not performing a memory. You are receiving, by faith, the Christ who died, and he is giving himself to you as certainly as the bread is in your hand. The Christ who is present is a risen and ascended Christ who is not brought back down to be offered again, because the offering was made once for all (Hebrews 10:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a sacrifice repeated. Christ was offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10–14). The table is where the fruit of the sacrifice is given to us, not where the sacrifice is made again.

If Christ is not physically present, is the Supper only symbolic after all? No. Spiritual does not mean imaginary or less real. The Holy Spirit is the most real presence in the world; he is how Christ dwells in his people at all. In the Supper the Spirit truly unites believers to the living Christ, and faith truly receives him, as truly as the mouth receives the bread. The bread is a sign, but it is not an empty sign; God uses it as a means of grace, to nourish faith, deepen assurance and draw us closer to Christ and to each other. That is why the Supper is to be received often and with expectation, not treated as an occasional add-on to the sermon.

Who should come to the table? Those who have trusted Christ and been baptised as believers, who belong to his church, and who come in repentance and faith. It is not for the unbeliever, because the whole meal is a participation in Christ, and you cannot share in someone you have refused. But it is also not a prize for the spiritually accomplished. It is food for the hungry. The weak Christian who is fighting sin and trusting Christ should come; that is exactly who the bread is for. Paul will say more about coming in a worthy manner in 11:27–32.

In a sentence. When we give thanks over the cup, are we not sharing in Christ’s blood? When we break the bread, are we not sharing in Christ’s body? Since there is one loaf, we, though many, are one body, because we all share that one loaf.

On a Tuesday. At the next Lord’s Supper, come expecting to meet Christ. Feed on him by faith, and look around at the one body you belong to. If there is someone in that room you are refusing to be reconciled to, the bread is asking you a question. Begin to put it right before you eat.

For worship. Under it all is the thing itself. A cup of ordinary wine, in the hands of ordinary people, in a rented room in a Greek port, and what is being handed round is the death of the Son of God, given away as freely as bread at a family meal. He did not hoard it. He did not ration it. He took what it cost him to purchase and made it the most common thing on the table, so that the poorest believer in Corinth could hold it in his hand on the Lord’s Day and know it was his (Matthew 26:27–28; John 6:53–56). The Lord of glory spreads a table for sinners and feeds them with himself.
verseByVerse.note: “The cup of blessing” was the Jewish name for a cup of wine drunk with thanksgiving at a meal, including the Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the people of Israel: are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?

Consider the people of Israel. Literally, Israel according to the flesh: the nation of Israel in its worship. Paul is building a case with three tables on it, and this is the second. He has done the Lord’s table; now Israel’s; then the demons’. The principle he wants established is that eating from a sacrifice puts you in league with the altar it came from. And notice the tenderness of the word consider. Paul does not scold. He asks them to look at something they already know from the Scriptures and draw the obvious conclusion themselves. He is treating them, as he said in verse 15, like sensible people, even while telling them their sense has failed them.

Are not those who eat the sacrifices participants in the altar? The Old Testament practice behind this is the peace offering, and it is worth knowing, because most modern readers assume every sacrifice was burnt whole. It was not. In the peace offering, part went up on the fire to God, part went to the priest, and the rest was eaten by the worshipper and his household in a meal on the spot (Leviticus 7:15–16; Deuteronomy 12:17–18). It was a shared dinner with God as host. Nobody in Israel thought of it as a snack with religious decoration. To eat there was to be counted in, sharing in the worship, in fellowship with the God to whom it was offered.

What do I imply then? That food offered to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything? Paul steps in front of an objection before it is raised. He knows exactly what the clever ones in Corinth will say: you told us in chapter 8 that an idol has no real existence and there is no God but one, and now you are treating idol meat as though it were charged with something. His answer, coming in the next verse, is not a retreat. He still holds what he said in 8:4. He is not about to concede that the idol is real after all. He is about to say that the Corinthians drew the wrong conclusion from a true premise, and the gap between those two things is where a great deal of confident Christian foolishness lives.

A true statement is not a finished argument. It is worth pausing on that gap, because it is the intellectual habit this whole letter is correcting. An idol is nothing is true. Therefore I may eat in its temple does not follow, and no amount of insisting on the first sentence will make it follow. The Corinthians had learned to reason from a doctrine straight to a permission, without ever asking what else was true in the room. That is not knowledge; it is one piece of knowledge used as a lever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the meat itself is changed or defiled. The issue is the act of worship.

What about halal or other religiously slaughtered meat today? The principles of this chapter answer it. Meat sold in an ordinary shop or served at a friend’s table, even if a prayer was said at its slaughter, is simply food that belongs to the Lord (vv. 25–27); a Christian may eat it with thanks and does not need to investigate. What a Christian should not do is take part in a religious act: eat it as part of a festival offered to another god, or in a way that would be understood, by those watching, as joining in their worship. And if someone at the table makes a point of its religious meaning, and eating would confuse him or another believer, verse 28 applies: decline quietly, for his sake.

In a sentence. Think of Israel: those who eat the sacrifices share in what happens at the altar. So is Paul saying that idol offerings are anything, or that an idol is real?

On a Tuesday. What we take part in shapes our loyalty. Think about which tables you sit at, and what they mean: not only literal meals, but the gatherings, rituals and communities you give yourself to week by week. Ask what each of them is quietly counting you into.

For worship. In Israel’s peace offering, God was the host and his people sat down at his table. That has always been his intention: not merely to be obeyed from a distance, but to eat with his people. And in Christ the peace offering has been made once for all. He is our peace, and the God who once fed Israel at the altar now welcomes the nations to his table, and will one day sit down with them at the marriage supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).
verseByVerse.note: Worshippers ate part of many sacrifices, sharing a meal with God.

verseByVerse.quote: No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. I do not want you to be participants with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons.

No, I imply that what pagans sacrifice they offer to demons and not to God. Here is the correction, and it is precise. The strong Corinthians reasoned: the idol is nothing, therefore there is nothing at the altar, therefore the meal is empty of spiritual content. Every step of that but the last is right. Nothing at the altar is not the same as nobody at the altar. The statue is a block of stone with no more divinity in it than the quarry it came from, and something is nevertheless being transacted, because somebody is receiving what is offered, and it is not God. Behind idol worship stand real spiritual forces: demons (daimonia). Pagans think they worship gods; in reality they serve demons. Paul is not inventing this. He is quoting the same song of Moses he drew on in verse 4: they sacrificed to demons that were no gods, to gods they had never known (Deuteronomy 32:17). The Old Testament had already said both halves, no gods and demons, and held them together without embarrassment.

I do not want you to be participants with demons. Participants (koinōnoi) means partners, sharers: the same family of words as the participation in Christ in verse 16. Eating at a temple feast is fellowship with demons.

Is any of this still live? The question a modern reader will have should not be left hanging. The temples are museums now. But the impulse to reach past God for power or knowledge on terms he has not authorised has never gone out of fashion, and it is currently doing extremely well. The card reading booked as a laugh, the app that gives the daily horoscope, the ancestor shrine kept in the corner because the family expects it, the ceremony entered into on holiday because it seemed rude to decline. In every case the reasoning is the Corinthian reasoning: it is nonsense, so it is harmless. Paul’s answer is that the first clause does not deliver the second.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be afraid of demons, or think demons lurk in every object. That is a different error, and it makes for a frightened, superstitious Christian who has forgotten that Christ has already disarmed the powers and made a public spectacle of them (Colossians 2:15). It is a call to stop being naive. Deliberate participation in false worship is spiritual adultery.

Where is the line? Being present is not the same as taking part. A Christian may attend a friend’s wedding in a temple or a family funeral with rites he does not share, as a guest who loves the people there. He may not join in the worship itself: bowing to the image, offering incense, reciting the prayers, or eating what is presented to him as offered to the god (v. 28). Practices that are religious in their very content belong on the same side of the line, such as yoga built around chants and devotion to Hindu deities, even when it is sold as exercise; simple stretching is not the issue. When family pressure comes, the believer can explain gently that he honours them and will be there, but that he worships Christ alone.

You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. Temple feasts included drinking cups of wine poured out to the god. Then comes the sharpest pair of sentences in the chapter. Notice: not may not. Cannot. Paul is not laying down a rule that could in principle be broken discreetly. He is describing an impossibility, the way a man cannot be married to two women in one house and call it a marriage. The attempt does not produce a double portion. It produces the loss of the first.

You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Invitations to dinner at the table of the lord Serapis have been found from this period, written on papyrus, using exactly that phrase. Paul takes the pagans’ own language and sets beside it the table of the Lord, a phrase from the prophets for the Lord’s altar (Malachi 1:7, 12). Two tables, two hosts, two loyalties. Divided loyalty is impossible.

What about Halloween, or Christmas trees with pagan roots? The line in this chapter is participation in worship, not the distant history of a custom. Most customs in any culture have tangled origins, and a thing that was once religious can become simply ordinary, as the market meat did (v. 25). A Christmas tree in a Christian home worships no one. The question to ask of any practice is what it means now, to the people doing it and watching it: is it plain fun, or is it a celebration of death, the occult or a spiritual power other than Christ? Christians will draw these lines in slightly different places, and Romans 14 asks them not to despise one another for it. But nobody should take part in anything that is, in its present meaning, a rite offered to another power.

In a sentence. No, what Paul is saying is that pagan sacrifices are offered to demons, not to God, and he does not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the Lord’s cup and the demons’ cup too; you cannot eat at the Lord’s table and at the demons’ table.

On a Tuesday. Give your whole loyalty to the Lord’s table. Refuse every other altar. If there is a practice in your life that you have defended with the words it is only a bit of fun, ask honestly whom it is addressed to. If the answer is anyone or anything other than God, put it down.

For worship. There is a table that belongs to the Lord, and he has set it for us. The demons offer their meals in exchange for worship and give nothing back but bondage; the Lord gives his own body and blood and asks only that we come hungry. Christ has triumphed over every power that ever sat at a pagan altar, and he has made his people partners with himself. No other host has ever loved his guests enough to die for them.

parallels.desc: they sacrificed to demons that were not God

verseByVerse.quote: Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

Shall we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Two short questions, and Paul asks them and walks away without answering, which is how you ask a question that has already answered itself. The first is another line from the song of Moses, and from the same paragraph: they stirred him to jealousy with strange gods, and provoked him with their idols (Deuteronomy 32:16, 21). Israel did it, and was judged. It needs explaining, because jealousy is a word we now use only for a vice, and applying it to God sounds like an accusation. But there are two jealousies. One is envy: wanting what belongs to somebody else. That is never in God, and never can be, since everything is already his. The other is the jealousy of a husband for his own wife, and it is not a defect in him but the proof that the marriage is real (Exodus 20:5; 34:14). A man who watched his wife leave with another man and felt nothing at all would not be admirably calm; he would have stopped loving her some time ago. God’s jealousy is of that second kind. He has bound himself to a people at the cost of his Son’s life, and he will not be treated as one option among several. His jealousy is not petty, but holy love that will not share his bride with rivals.

Are we stronger than he? The second question is flatter and more frightening, and it is aimed at the strong in Corinth. You think you are strong. Are you stronger than God? Paul has just filled thirteen verses with corpses in the wilderness, so the reader knows what the question is doing. It asks a congregation of the confident whether they have thought about who it is they are provoking. There is a way of using Christian freedom that is not really freedom at all but a small experiment in whether God will actually do anything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s jealousy is like human jealousy, insecure and envious. It is the right zeal of the only true God for the love of those he redeemed.

Test it against the alternative. Suppose God were not jealous. Suppose he watched his people give their evenings, their money and their affections to whatever caught them, and felt nothing about it at all: benign, unbothered, endlessly accommodating. That God would be easier to live with, and he would be worth nothing, because his tolerance would be the measure of his indifference. Nobody has ever been comforted at a graveside by a deity who did not much mind.

Does God’s jealousy mean he resents the good things I love? No. He gave them to you. God is not jealous of your wife, your children, your garden or your work; he is jealous for your heart, that it should love him first, and love all these as his gifts. In fact, the things we love are safest when they are not our gods. A child who is loved as an idol is crushed by the weight of being someone’s whole meaning; a child who is loved under God can be loved freely. God’s jealousy guards our joys rather than competing with them.

In a sentence. Do we really want to stir up the Lord’s jealousy? Do we imagine we are stronger than he is?

On a Tuesday. God loves you too much to share you with rivals. Let that move you to loyalty, not fear. When you notice a rival rising in your heart, do not only resist it; tell God that you would rather have him, and ask him to make that true.

For worship. The two questions of this verse turn out to be one question asked twice. Is he strong? Yes: look at the wilderness. Does he care? Yes: look at the jealousy. A god who was strong and did not care would be a terror. A god who cared and was not strong would be a tragedy. The idols are neither, and neither is anyone else who has ever been worshipped. But our God is both. To be loved by someone who will not share you is a fearful thing and a safe thing at once. Cold gods let you drift. This one comes after his own. He is jealous because the cost of getting his people was his own Son, and he does not shrug about what he has bled for.

parallels.desc: they have made me jealous with what is no god

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–33 — Do All to the Glory of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul quotes the slogan “everything is permitted” and answers that not everything is beneficial or builds others up. No one should seek his own good, but the good of others. They may eat anything sold in the meat market without asking questions for conscience’ sake, because, as the psalm says, the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord. If an unbeliever invites them to dinner and they want to go, they may eat whatever is served without asking. But if someone tells them it was offered in sacrifice, they should not eat it, for the sake of the person who told them and for conscience, his conscience, not theirs. Why should Paul’s freedom be judged by someone else’s conscience, and why be blamed for food he thanks God for? Whether they eat or drink or do anything else, they should do it all for God’s glory. They should give no cause for stumbling to Jews, Greeks or the church of God, just as Paul tries to please everyone in everything, seeking not his own benefit but that of many, so that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
Soli Deo Gloria Applied to Ordinary Life

The Reformation’s fifth great watchword — soli Deo gloria, to God alone be glory — finds its Pauline root in v. 31. Every meal, every conversation, every commercial transaction, every athletic effort is capable of being an act of worship when performed in the right spirit and with the right orientation. The Reformed conviction that all of life is worship is the systematic development of this verse. The “sacred/secular divide” is not merely unhelpful; by Paul’s logic it is theologically incoherent: all of life, including the most mundane, is lived before the face of God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The practical guidelines of vv. 25–28 gave the Corinthians actionable wisdom for the specific daily situations they faced. The principle of “ask no questions” at the market protected them from unnecessary scrupulosity; the principle of sensitivity at the dinner table protected the weak and the unbeliever. Both together are shaped by the glory of God, not by personal preference. Now: “Do all to the glory of God” is not a cliché but a practice — a habit of asking, in any situation: how can this moment, this act, this conversation, be a participation in the glorification of God?

verseByVerse.quote: “All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“All things are lawful,” but not all things are helpful. “All things are lawful,” but not all things build up. Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor.

All things are lawful, but not all things are helpful. The slogan is back. It was quoted first at 6:12, and it is almost certainly the Corinthians’ own line, the sort of thing a church says when it has learned grace and is enjoying it. Paul now turns from the temple to the question of meat at home and in the market. He does not delete the slogan. He puts a comma after it. Twice.

All things are lawful, but not all things build up. The two tests he attaches are not is it permitted but something else entirely. Is it helpful: does it get anyone anywhere? And does it build up (oikodomeō), a construction word, the same root as edification: does anyone end up stronger because you did it? That is the test of love (8:1). Notice that both questions have someone else in them. The lawfulness question can be answered alone in a room. These cannot. And note the builder’s word. Paul could have said not all things are safe or not all things are wise. He uses this word all through the letter, and the picture is of a congregation as a structure going up, course by course, where the question about any action is not merely whether it damages anyone but whether it adds a stone. A great deal of Christian liberty is defended on the grounds that it hurts no one. That is a lower bar than the one in this verse.

Let no one seek his own good, but the good of his neighbor. Then the sentence that governs everything from chapter 8 to chapter 11, and it is a single short sentence. Love looks to others’ interests (Philippians 2:4; Romans 15:2). That is the whole ethic of the idol-meat discussion boiled down, and it is more radical than the way Christians usually apply it. The usual version is: enjoy your freedom, but be considerate. Paul’s version puts the neighbour’s good in the driving seat, not the passenger seat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should never care for our own needs. It means our own good must not override our neighbour’s. Paul has just spent a chapter telling the Corinthians to look after their own souls with great care: take heed lest you fall, flee idolatry, watch what you are participating in. Self-neglect is not the goal. What is forbidden is making your own good the deciding factor when someone else’s good is also on the table.

How do I know whether something builds up? Ask three questions about the people actually involved. Will this help them trust and obey Christ more, or make it harder? Will it draw them toward the church and its fellowship, or push them away? And would I be glad for them to copy me in this? You will not always know the answer, and you are not responsible for every possible reaction of every possible person. But when you know that a particular brother or sister would be hurt or misled, love lets that knowledge decide. And the question works positively too: building up is not only refraining from harm, but looking for the word, the visit or the gift that will strengthen someone.

In a sentence. “Everything is permitted,” you say, but not everything helps; not everything builds others up. No one should look out only for himself, but for the good of others.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test, and it works on any decision. Take the last time you defended something you were free to do. Play back the argument you made in your head. Whose flourishing was actually in view: his, or yours? Being right about your liberty and wrong about your neighbour is the exact position Paul has been dismantling for three chapters, and it is possible to hold it while quoting this very verse’s first half.

For worship. Christ did not please himself (Romans 15:3). He was the one Person who had every right to seek his own good, and he sought ours instead, all the way to the cross. The whole of the gospel is in this verse turned around: the Lord of all did not look to his own interests, but to the interests of those who had none to offer him. He is building his church, stone by stone, and every stone is a sinner he sought for its own good.

verseByVerse.quote: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eat whatever is sold in the meat market without raising any question on the ground of conscience. For “the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof.”

Eat whatever is sold in the meat market. After all that solemnity, a surprisingly relaxed instruction, and it is deliberate, because Paul is as concerned to protect the over-scrupulous as the over-confident. The word is makellon, the covered meat and fish market at the centre of the city; excavators at Corinth have turned up an inscription naming one. Much of the meat on those slabs had come from a temple, since sacrifices produced more carcasses than the priests and worshippers could eat and the surplus was sold on.

Without raising any question on the ground of conscience. A conscientious believer could spend his whole life anxious about his dinner, interrogating butchers, tracing provenance, going hungry on principle. Paul’s ruling is: do not ask. Not ask, and then decide. Do not ask. It is just food. Once it has left the temple, it carries no religious meaning. And there is a quiet pastoral kindness in that. Paul could have told them to investigate carefully and then decide with a clear conscience. He knows that for a certain sort of person the investigation never ends, and that a conscience kept permanently on duty does not become holier, only more exhausted. Sometimes the godly course is to close the question rather than to research it, and to eat the dinner in front of you with thanks.

For the earth is the Lord’s, and the fullness thereof. He gives the reason from a psalm (Psalm 24:1), and it is a psalm Jews used as a thanksgiving before meals. This is the answer to a fear that runs deeper than meat. The idol does not get to change the ownership of a cow. A false priest can mutter over a carcass all afternoon and he has not transferred the title; the beast belonged to God when it was born, belonged to God on the altar, and belongs to God on the slab. Nothing in the world has been successfully stolen from its Maker. All food belongs to God, not to idols, and it can be received with thanks, for everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

For the anxious reader. This is worth a great deal to the anxious reader, who is more common in the church than the arrogant one. It is the reader who wonders about the label on the package, the greeting the neighbour used, the second-hand furniture, the doorway that felt wrong. Paul’s rule for ordinary life is freedom without an investigation. Creation is God’s and it is good, and a Christian may eat it with thanks and stop performing background checks on his groceries. The world is not haunted. It is owned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean contradicting verses 14–22. There, the issue was taking part in temple worship; here, it is buying ordinary meat. One guard is needed, or this freedom will be stretched into something Paul has just forbidden. There is a difference between eating a piece of meat with a history and taking a seat at a rite: between buying a chop that once passed an altar and going to the altar. The first is a question about property, and God owns everything. The second is a question about allegiance, and no one may hold two. Paul is not inconsistent; he is drawing a line, and the line falls exactly where participation begins.

Does this mean Christians may eat any food at all, including what the Old Testament forbade? Yes. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and God taught Peter the same lesson in a vision (Acts 10:13–15). The food laws of Moses were part of the old covenant’s marking out of Israel, and they pointed to a holiness that Christ has now brought. So a Christian may eat pork, shellfish, or anything else with thanks. What remains is the law of love: if your eating would harm a brother, you may choose not to (Romans 14:20–21). And what remains is the call to self-control; freedom to eat anything is not a licence to be ruled by the stomach.

In a sentence. Eat anything sold in the market without asking questions for conscience’s sake, because the earth and everything in it belong to the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Thank God before you eat. Every meal is a gift from the Lord who owns the earth. And if you are the anxious kind, give yourself permission this week to stop investigating something God has already declared clean. Close the question and say grace.

For worship. The earth is the Lord’s. Every field of wheat, every herd on every hill, every fish in every sea, every loaf on every table belongs to him, and no idol has ever stolen a crumb of it. He feeds the whole world from his own hand, the just and the unjust, the thankful and the thankless. And the Christian at his kitchen table is a citizen of a world that has not been lost to darkness, because the Maker still owns it, and the Son who redeemed it is coming back to claim it in full.

parallels.desc: the earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof

verseByVerse.quote: If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—
verseByVerse.commentary:
If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go, eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. But if someone says to you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience—

If one of the unbelievers invites you to dinner and you are disposed to go. Note first what Paul assumes without arguing for it: that Christians will be having dinner in the homes of people who are not Christians, and that they may accept. This is a private home, not a temple. There is no warning attached, no list of precautions. The apostle who has just said flee from idolatry sees no contradiction in a believer sitting down at a pagan neighbour’s table. Fleeing idolatry is not the same as avoiding idolaters; he has already said so in this letter, and bluntly: to avoid them entirely you would need to go out of the world (5:10). Disposed to go (thelō, if you want to) leaves the decision genuinely open. Some invitations are not wise for a given believer at a given time, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But the default is yes.

Eat whatever is set before you without raising any question on the ground of conscience. The manners at the table are simple: eat what you are given and ask nothing. Do not interrogate your host; enjoy the meal, as Jesus told his disciples to eat what was set before them (Luke 10:8). A guest who cross-examines his host about the origin of the lamb is not being holy; he is being a poor guest, and the gospel is not served by it.

But if someone says to you, This has been offered in sacrifice. Then the one situation that changes everything. The word here is hierothyton, sacred offering, the polite pagan word, rather than the Jewish and Christian word for idol-food used elsewhere; it sounds like something said at the table, perhaps by the host, perhaps by another guest, perhaps half as a test of the Christian.

Then do not eat it, for the sake of the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience. Nothing about the meat has changed. The information has. Once somebody has put it into words, the meal has stopped being a meal and become a statement, and it will be read as one: that the Christian approves of idol worship, or does not take his faith seriously. Perhaps the speaker is a young believer watching to see what freedom looks like. Perhaps he is a pagan guest who has heard that these people worship one God and is curious whether it makes any practical difference. Either way, a person has just told you that this matters to him, and Paul’s instruction is to let it matter. The conscience in view is the other person’s (v. 29). Put the fork down. Say nothing pious. That is a useful principle well beyond first-century meat: the moment someone signals that a thing is loaded for him, your liberty stops being the only fact in the room.

How to decline. Two small things about how to do it. First, do it quietly. Paul gives no speech to accompany the refusal, and adding one would wreck it; a Christian who declines the dish and then explains at length why he is entitled to eat it but is graciously abstaining has kept the meat and taken the credit as well. Second, do not shame the host. The whole manoeuvre is for the sake of someone else’s conscience, and a refusal delivered as a verdict on the household undoes the very thing it was meant to protect.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid unbelievers’ homes. Paul encourages friendship. It means once the food is publicly identified as an offering, eating it becomes a statement.

What is the modern equivalent? The clearest one is alcohol. A Christian is free to drink wine in moderation; Scripture calls it a gift that gladdens the heart (Psalm 104:15), and drunkenness, not drinking, is the sin. But if you are at a meal with a friend who is fighting alcoholism, or with a young believer who has just come out of a drinking life and says so, the situation has changed. Your glass is no longer only a glass. Leave it empty that evening, without fuss or explanation, and enjoy his company. You have lost nothing, and he may have gained a great deal.

In a sentence. If an unbeliever invites you to a meal and you want to go, eat what is served without asking questions of conscience. But if someone tells you, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat it, for the sake of the person who told you and for conscience’s sake,

On a Tuesday. Say yes to the next invitation from an unbelieving neighbour, if you are free and it is wise. Go as a grateful guest. And if a moment comes at the table when your freedom would mislead someone, lay it down quietly and stay warm.

For worship. Underneath the etiquette is something larger. Paul is willing to be misunderstood, to look scrupulous to the free and lax to the strict, rather than harden one person’s conscience against Christ. He has already said he would never eat meat again if it came to that (8:13). Here he shows what it costs on an ordinary Thursday evening: not a heroic renunciation, just a hand withdrawn from a plate while nobody notices. And he learned it from his Lord, who ate with tax collectors and sinners, sat at the tables of people who despised him, and was called a glutton and a drunkard for his trouble, because he had come to seek and to save the lost. Blessed be the Friend of sinners, who came to our table so that we might sit at his.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not mean your conscience, but his. For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks?

I do not mean your conscience, but his. This is the hardest turn in the chapter, and it looks at first like Paul contradicting himself inside a single sentence. He has just said do not eat, and now he asks why anybody else’s conscience should govern him. The resolution is in this clause. Your own conscience is clear; you abstain for the other person’s sake.

For why should my liberty be determined by someone else’s conscience? This is the strong person’s objection, or Paul’s own reasoning, and either way he affirms it: in principle, my freedom is not ruled by others’ scruples. I am still free before God. What he surrenders in verse 28 is the use of his freedom on that occasion. What he refuses to surrender here is the freedom itself, and the verdict on it. His conscience is not remade by his neighbour’s. He does not walk away from that dinner thinking he was nearly defiled, or that the meat was in fact unclean after all. He walks away free, having chosen not to spend his freedom in front of someone it would injure.

If I partake with thankfulness, why am I denounced because of that for which I give thanks? Denounced (blasphēmeō) is spoken against, slandered. If I thank God for food, how can anyone condemn me? Paul’s point is that he gives up his freedom voluntarily, not because the other person’s conscience binds his, but to avoid having his good thing spoken of as evil (Romans 14:16). And there is a small warmth in with thankfulness. Paul’s instinct at a table is to give thanks, which is what a man does who believes verse 26: that the food, the evening and the world belong to God. He is not defending a right to indulge. He is defending a right to be grateful without apologising for it (Romans 14:22; 1 Timothy 4:4–5).

Two opposite disasters. The difference matters more than it may appear, because getting it wrong produces two opposite disasters. Collapse the distinction one way and you get the Christian who bulldozes: my liberty is real, therefore I will exercise it, and if that ruins you, learn some theology. Collapse it the other way and you get a church governed by whoever is most easily upset, where every scruple anyone raises becomes binding on everybody, and the strongest conscience in the room is the narrowest one. Paul will not have either. Love limits what I do with my freedom. It does not hand my conscience over to a committee.

What it does not mean. It does not mean others can control what Christians do. Liberty remains; love chooses how to use it.

Who is the weaker brother I should give way to? Not simply anyone who disapproves of me. In Paul’s argument the weak brother is someone who might be drawn, by my example, into doing what his own conscience still condemns, and so be damaged in his faith (8:10–11). That is very different from the person who has turned his own preferences into rules for everybody and is merely annoyed by my freedom. Jesus did not yield to the Pharisees over hand-washing or healing on the Sabbath (Mark 7:1–13; 3:1–6); when people try to bind consciences with man-made rules as if they were God’s law, love may require standing firm (Galatians 2:3–5). The question is always: would my action wound a fragile believer, or only offend a critic?

A rule the anxious can live by. This gives the anxious reader a rule he can live by, and it is a relief. When you give something up for the sake of another Christian, you are not conceding that he was right and you were wrong. You are not adding a rule to your own life. You are not obliged to feel guilty about the thing next Tuesday when he is not there. Paul abstains and remains free, and he tells the church he is doing both. Charity is not the same as agreement, and giving way is not the same as being convinced. The alternative, a conscience that quietly takes on every restriction anybody around it holds, ends in a Christian who cannot enjoy anything and cannot say why, and who is finally serving other people’s opinions rather than God. Paul’s way is harder and cleaner: know that you are free, and then choose, in this room, on this evening, for this person, not to use it.

In a sentence. Paul means the other person’s conscience, not your own. Why should my freedom be put on trial by someone else’s conscience? If I eat with thanks to God, why should I be condemned for something I thank him for?

On a Tuesday. Your freedom in Christ is real. Use it gladly, and lay it down gladly when love calls for it. If you have quietly adopted someone else’s scruple as your own law, out of fear of disapproval rather than conviction from Scripture, take it to God and ask whether he has actually bound you there.

For worship. The freedom Paul guards so carefully was bought at a price. For freedom Christ has set us free (Galatians 5:1), and the Son who sets free makes free indeed (John 8:36). He did not die to give us a new set of nervous rules, nor to let us trample one another. He died to make us sons and daughters who can eat at their Father’s table with thanks, and who are free enough to give that freedom away for love. Only the truly free can do that, and only Christ makes anyone truly free.

verseByVerse.quote: So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

So, whether you eat or drink. Three chapters of hard argument about butchers, dinner parties, weak brothers and demons come down to one sentence, and it is broad enough to cover a life. Notice where Paul starts: eat or drink, the most ordinary actions of life. He could have begun with prayer or preaching. He begins with chewing and swallowing, the most involuntary, animal, wholly unremarkable thing a body does, and says that this too can be done to the glory of God. If eating qualifies, nothing is excluded.

Or whatever you do. Everything: work, rest, play, speech, spending, sleep. The line between the sacred bits of life and the ordinary bits, which most Christians carry around without examining it, does not survive this verse. There is no part of a Tuesday that is off the map.

Do all to the glory of God. The governing purpose of the Christian life. To glorify God (doxa) is to show his worth, to honour him, to make him look as great as he is. The Westminster Shorter Catechism begins here: man’s chief end is to glorify God and enjoy him for ever (Q. 1). No part of life is outside this. The Reformers stressed that ordinary work and meals are as sacred as prayer when done for God; the milkmaid and the minister serve the same Lord.

What has to be true of a plate of food for it to glorify God? To the glory of God is exactly the sort of phrase that can be repeated for years without meaning anything, so let it be spelled out. That it is received rather than seized: taken as a gift from a hand, not a right that was owed. That it is eaten with thanks, spoken and meant, since everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Timothy 4:4). That it is enjoyed and not worshipped; there is a way of eating that is really an attempt to be comforted by something that cannot comfort. That it is not taken at someone else’s expense, which is the whole burden of this chapter. And that the one eating is content for God to be looking, which is a test that can be run on any activity in about four seconds.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must be constantly thinking about God in every second. A surgeon glorifies God by concentrating on the operation, not by thinking about theology during it. It means our whole life is offered to him, done in a way that honours him.

How do I glorify God in a dull job or a long day of chores? By doing it well, honestly and for him. Paul told slaves, who had the dullest and hardest work in the ancient world, to work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, because it is the Lord Christ they were serving (Colossians 3:23–24). The spreadsheet, the nappy, the shelf-stacking and the commute are not interruptions to the Christian life; they are where most of it happens. Do the work with integrity, treat the people around you with kindness, give thanks for the strength to do it, and rest when the day is done, trusting God with what is left undone. Nobody sees most of it. God does, and he is glorified by it.

In a sentence. So whatever you do, even eating and drinking, do everything for God’s glory.

On a Tuesday. Take the last hour of yesterday, whatever it contained: a meal, a screen, a task, a conversation, a queue. Ask what would have had to change for that hour to have been offered to God. Very often the honest answer is: nothing at all about the activity, and everything about the aim. That is not a loophole. That is the mercy of this verse. The Christian does not need a different life in order to have a life full of worship; he needs the one he has, turned in a different direction. At your next meal, pause and give thanks, and mean it.

For worship. This is finally why God gets glory from a man eating his dinner. Not because the dinner is impressive, but because the God who made the wheat and the fire and the mouth is being recognised at the moment his gifts are being used, by a creature who might have eaten in silence and thought himself self-supplied. Every honest thank-you at a kitchen table is a small correction of the world’s largest lie. And the God who is worthy of all this glory is the God who shared his table with us, who in Christ ate and drank among us, gave thanks for bread, and broke it. From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God, just as I try to please everyone in everything I do, not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved.
