Give no offense to Jews or to Greeks or to the church of God. Give no offence (aproskopoi) means not causing stumbling, putting no unnecessary obstacle in anyone’s way. Paul names three groups and covers the whole world with them: the Jew, the Gentile, and the church. He has already shown what each looks like in practice. He circumcised Timothy for the sake of the first (Acts 16:3), ate freely with the second (9:21), and would give up meat for ever for the sake of the third (8:13).

Just as I try to please everyone in everything I do. But this clause raises a genuine problem, and a reader who knows his Bible will spot it at once. To the Galatians Paul wrote that if he were still trying to please man, he would not be a servant of Christ (Galatians 1:10). Those cannot both be advice, so which is it? They are the same principle applied to opposite motives, and the tell is in what each sentence says the pleasing is for. In Galatians, the pleasing was a way of buying safety: certain men wanted to avoid persecution for the cross, so they trimmed the message and kept their position. The object of that exercise was themselves. Here the pleasing is not people-pleasing for approval but accommodating for their good (9:19–22).

Not seeking my own advantage, but that of many, that they may be saved. Here the object is stated outright. The goal is the salvation of others, and Paul’s whole life is shaped by it. He yields his preferences, his diet, his rights and his dignity to remove every obstacle between a person and Christ, and he will not yield one syllable of the gospel to remove an obstacle between himself and trouble.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding the offence of the cross (1:23). The gospel itself offends; we must not add needless offence of our own.

How far can I adapt to win people? As far as you like in everything that is truly indifferent, and not an inch in what God has commanded or forbidden. Paul changed his diet, his customs, his manner and his timetable for the sake of others; he would not change the gospel, join in sin, or hide the cross. So learn the culture of the people you love, eat their food, speak their language, enjoy their company, and drop the habits of your own background that are mere preferences. But never pretend to agree with what Scripture calls sin, and never soften the message so that Christ sounds less necessary. Adaptation is for the sake of the message, never at its expense.

In a sentence. Do not trip up Jews, Greeks or God’s church, just as Paul tries to accommodate everyone in all he does, looking not to his own benefit but to the benefit of many, so that they may be saved.

On a Tuesday. The test is not am I accommodating people? It is: who is this accommodation actually for? And it is easy to run. The next time you soften something, delay something, or leave something unsaid, ask which of these is more likely to be true at the end of it: that the other person is nearer to being saved, or that you are nearer to being comfortable. The first is apostolic. The second is what Galatians calls the end of being a servant of Christ. They can look identical from the outside and they are opposites inside. And pray for someone you want to see saved, asking God to show you what obstacle you could remove.

For worship. Behind both stands the pattern neither Corinth nor anyone since has improved on. The Son of God had every right and used none of them for himself; the one Person in history who was genuinely free spent his freedom entirely on the unfree, and had nowhere to lay his head (Romans 15:3; Philippians 2:6–8). He did not seek his own advantage. He sought many, that they might be saved, and he got them. Not one of those the Father gave him will be lost, and the multitude he sought will sing his praise for ever.

11.title: Head Coverings and the Lord’s Supper
11.overview:
Chapters 11–14 deal with problems in the church’s gatherings. The first concerns how men and women appear when they pray or prophesy. In the Roman world clothing and hair sent strong signals. A respectable married woman covered her head in public with a veil or the fold of her mantle; going uncovered could suggest immodesty or rebellion, and shaving a woman’s head was a mark of disgrace. Men, by contrast, did not cover their heads, except in some pagan rituals where Roman priests sacrificed with the toga drawn over the head. Some Corinthian women, perhaps reasoning that in Christ distinctions no longer mattered, were praying and prophesying uncovered. Paul grounds his answer in creation and in the order of headship, God, Christ, man, woman, while insisting that in the Lord men and women depend on each other.

The second problem was worse. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared evening meal in a wealthy member’s house. The host’s friends reclined in the small dining room and ate the best food early; latecomers, often slaves who had worked all day, crowded into the courtyard with little or nothing. Some went hungry while others got drunk. Paul says this is not the Lord’s Supper at all. He repeats the account of the Last Supper that he received from the Lord, reminds them that the meal proclaims Christ’s death until he returns, and warns that eating in an unworthy way, despising Christ’s body, brings judgement. They must examine themselves and wait for one another.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to follow his example as he follows Christ’s, and praises them for holding to the traditions he passed on. But he wants them to understand that Christ is the head of every man, the man is the head of the woman, and God is the head of Christ. A man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonours his head, and a woman who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonours hers; it is as shameful as having her head shaved, so if she will not cover it she might as well cut off her hair. A man should not cover his head, since he is God’s image and glory, while the woman is the glory of man, for woman came from man and was created for him. So a woman should have a sign of authority on her head, because of the angels. Yet in the Lord neither is independent of the other: woman came from man, but every man is born of woman, and everything comes from God. Paul asks them to judge for themselves whether it is fitting for a woman to pray uncovered, and points to nature: long hair is a disgrace to a man but a glory to a woman, given her as a covering. If anyone wants to argue, the churches of God have no other practice.
verseByVerse.theology:
Headship, Order, and the Trinity

Paul’s grounding of the male-female relationship in the Father-Son relationship (v. 3) is one of the most important and most debated texts in trinitarian theology. If “the head of Christ is God” describes an eternal subordination within the Godhead, it supports a permanent hierarchical ordering of human relationships. Most Reformed theologians have understood this as describing the economic Trinity (the Son’s voluntary submission in the incarnation and redemption) rather than ontological subordination within the immanent Trinity. Either way, Paul is using the divine relational order as the theological model for the ordering of human relationships in worship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The specific head covering practice was an expression of propriety and social order in a particular cultural context. A woman praying with her head uncovered may have signalled sexual availability or a rejection of the social ordering that the community needed to maintain for the sake of its witness. Now: The head covering practice is not directly applicable in most modern Western contexts. The underlying principle — that worship should reflect an ordered dignity appropriate to the God being worshipped, and that the differentiation of male and female is a gift to be honoured rather than erased — continues to speak into contemporary debates about gender in the church.

verseByVerse.quote: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 11 begins Paul’s teaching on public worship, which runs through chapter 14. Verse 1 closes chapter 10: imitate Paul as he imitates Christ. Then Paul addresses two problems in their gatherings. First, men and women praying and prophesying (vv. 2–16). Some Corinthian wives were throwing off the head covering, the visible sign in that culture of a married woman’s honour and her relation to her husband. Paul grounds his answer in an order God established: Christ is the head of every man, the husband is the head of his wife, God is the head of Christ. That order comes from creation, and is not cancelled by the gospel, though in the Lord men and women depend on each other completely. Second, the Lord’s Supper (vv. 17–34). The rich were eating and drinking their fill while the poor went hungry, turning the Supper into a display of social division. Paul reminds them of what the Lord himself handed down: the bread and cup proclaim his death until he comes. To eat in a way that despises his body is to eat judgment on oneself. So examine yourselves, and wait for one another. Over both halves of the chapter stands the same Lord: the Son who gladly does his Father’s will, and who on the night he was betrayed broke bread for those who would desert him.

The chapter division falls in the wrong place. This sentence is the last word of the argument that began at 8:1, and it is also the door into everything that follows.

Be imitators of me. The word is mimētai, from which we get mimic. Read on its own it sounds like the most arrogant sentence in the letter. No pastor could say it today without causing a scandal. But look at what Paul has just finished describing, because that is what he is offering to have copied: a man who gave up his right to be paid (9:12), his right to marry (9:5), his right to eat what he liked (8:13), and his right to be understood, so that people who were not his responsibility might be saved (9:19–23; 10:33). He is not saying admire me. He is saying watch what I gave up, and do that.

As I am of Christ. The second clause governs the first. It is the qualification and the source. Paul is not the original; he is a copy being held up, and he is careful to say so. The pattern is the Son of God, who did not please himself (Romans 15:3), who had every right there is and used none of them for himself, who emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:5–8). Paul is one step nearer in the chain, close enough to be seen. Imitate Paul only so far as he imitates Christ.

How the Christian life is learned. That matters more than it may seem, because it says something about how Christian obedience is actually learned. Nobody learns to be a Christian from a definition. People learn it the way they learn a trade or an accent: by being near someone who does it, long enough to catch it. Which is why Paul can write a letter and then say, in effect: now look at a life. And it is why the most important thing an older believer can offer a younger one is not advice but a visible life at close range. It also sets the terms for the two difficult passages that follow. Paul is about to talk about how men and women should appear in worship, and about a supper where the rich were humiliating the poor. Both are questions about whether a congregation will lay down its rights for the sake of others in the room. He has put the answer at the top of the page before asking the questions (Philippians 3:17; 1 Thessalonians 1:6).

Is it not dangerous to tell people to follow a man? An objection worth meeting, because it is a good one. The history of the church is littered with the wreckage of ministries built on a personality, and this very congregation had already split into fan clubs: I follow Paul, I follow Apollos (1:12). Paul knew that better than anyone; he had spent four chapters demolishing it. The safeguard is in the second half of the sentence, and it is a safeguard anyone can apply. Follow a Christian only as far as he is following Christ, and no further, which means you must know Christ well enough to see where the line falls. That is the difference between a disciple and a fan. A fan goes wherever his man goes. A disciple watches his man and keeps checking the pattern against the Master, and is ready to stop the moment the two diverge.

What it does not mean. It does not mean any leader can demand blind following. All human examples are measured by Christ.

Whom should I learn from? Not the most gifted person available, and not the most confident. Look for the one whose life shows the marks Paul has just described: rights not used, comfort spent on other people, a willingness to be thought less of. Gifts are impressive and they can be counterfeited. That pattern cannot. And if you cannot think of anyone near you, do not give up. Ask God to bring someone into your life; spend time with the older members of your church whom nobody notices; read the lives of faithful Christians from the past. Very often the person you need is already sitting a few rows away, and has simply never been asked.

In a sentence. Follow Paul’s example, as he follows the example of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Find a mature Christian whose life follows Christ, and learn from them. And live so that someone younger can learn from you. Ask yourself: if a new believer copied my week exactly, what would he learn about Christ?

For worship. Behind every faithful example stands the one perfect life. The Son of God is the original that every saint copies, and he never once needed a footnote telling us to imitate him only so far. He is the whole pattern, the image of the invisible God, the man in whom humanity was lived exactly as it was meant to be. And he does not merely set the example and leave us to it. By his Spirit he is forming himself in his people, so that the copies, faint as they are, grow slowly more like the original until the day we see him and are made like him.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.

Now I commend you because you remember me in everything. Praise first. It is worth noticing, because this letter has not been generous with praise and is about to become severe again in fifteen verses. Perhaps the Corinthians’ own letter claimed that they remembered his teaching, and Paul accepts the claim generously before correcting where they had gone wrong. And there is a real compliment buried in the sentence. This congregation, for all its arrogance, still cared what its founder thought. Nothing in the following chapters would be possible without that. A church that has stopped listening cannot be corrected; it can only be left. Paul writes the rest of this letter because he believes these people will still hear him. That is a fair question to put to any congregation and any Christian. Correction only works on people who are still in the room. The most dangerous position is not being wrong (the Corinthians were wrong about almost everything) but reaching the point where nobody is permitted to say so.

And maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you. Whatever else was wrong in Corinth, and the list is long, they had not thrown out the deposit. The word traditions makes some Christians uneasy, because it has been used to smuggle in doctrines the Bible does not teach. But the word itself is innocent and Paul owns it without embarrassment. Paradosis means something handed over: a parcel passed from one pair of hands to the next. Delivered (paradidōmi) is the technical term for passing on authoritative teaching, and he uses the same verbs in verse 23 about the Lord’s Supper and in 15:3 about the gospel itself: I received and I delivered. What is being handed on here is not a set of customs invented by the church but a deposit that came from Christ through the apostles, and is now preserved in the New Testament. That is the difference that matters. A tradition is trustworthy when you can trace the parcel back to a hand that had the right to fill it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church traditions not found in Scripture have equal authority with Scripture. Paul’s traditions are apostolic teaching, which we now have in written form (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Later church traditions must be tested by Scripture.

When tradition and the Bible pull apart. There is a rule here for that vexed question. Paul’s own test is simply whether the parcel came from the Lord: I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you (v. 23). Where a practice can be traced to that source it is binding, however inconvenient. Where it cannot, it may be genuinely valuable, since the church’s accumulated wisdom is not nothing, but it can never be made a test of obedience. Most congregational quarrels about how things are done would end within ten minutes if the parties agreed to sort their practices into those two boxes first.

A chain of hands. There is a debt in the verse worth pausing on. Everything the Corinthians had, they had been handed. So has every Christian since. Nobody in the history of the world has worked out the gospel from first principles; it reached each of us through somebody: a mother, a preacher, a friend who would not let the subject drop, a translator who died for the privilege. That is what a tradition is when it is healthy: not a dead weight but a chain of hands, and the only question that matters is whether you intend to be one of them.

In a sentence. Paul praises you for remembering him in everything and for holding to the teachings just as he passed them on to you.

On a Tuesday. Think of the people who handed the gospel on to you, and thank God for them by name. If any are still living, tell them. Then ask whose hands you are placing it into: a child, a friend, a younger Christian. Hold the apostolic teaching fast, and pass it on intact.

For worship. The faith was delivered once for all to the saints (Jude 3), and it has never been lost. Empires have fallen, churches have wandered, and Bibles have been burned, yet the same gospel that Paul handed to Corinth has reached us whole, because the Lord who gave it has kept it. He is the first hand in the chain, and he holds every hand after it. Thanks be to God, who has not left his church to invent its own message, but has spoken, and has guarded his word through every century to this day.
verseByVerse.note: “Traditions” means the teaching Paul had handed on to them.

verseByVerse.quote: But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.

But I want you to understand. A new teaching they had not grasped. Before any of the difficult application, Paul lays down the framework, and it needs handling slowly because a great deal is loaded onto the word head.

That the head of every man is Christ. The Greek is kephalē. In English, head has largely collapsed into one meaning: the boss. In Greek it carried more than that. It could mean the source of something, the way we still speak of the head of a river; it could mean the one who leads or represents; and in a body it is the part without which the rest cannot live. In this context head means one with authority and responsibility, as in Ephesians 1:22 and 5:23. Some argue it means only source. Both ideas may be present, since verses 8–9 speak of origin. But in Paul’s usage, headship includes leadership.

The head of a wife is her husband. Is Paul speaking of husbands and wives, or of men and women generally? The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean woman and wife, man and husband, and translators differ. The context, with its focus on the married woman’s head covering, suggests husband and wife. Headship in Scripture is a marriage relationship (Ephesians 5:23), not a rule that every woman is under every man. But the passage applies it in the church’s worship, where the order of creation shapes how all men and women take part. The husband has a God-given responsibility to lead his wife in love (Ephesians 5:23–25).

And the head of Christ is God. The sequence Paul gives shows why the word head cannot mean what the world means by boss. The Son, as incarnate Mediator, submits to the Father (15:28; John 5:19, 30; 14:28). Yet the Son is fully equal with the Father (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). This is the key to the whole passage, and it must be said plainly. Whatever this verse means, it cannot mean that a head is superior in worth to what it heads, because the third clause would then make Christ inferior to God, and the New Testament will not allow it. The Son is the exact imprint of God’s nature (Hebrews 1:3), in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily (Colossians 2:9). If the head of Christ is God can stand alongside I and the Father are one, then headship and equality are not rivals. Paul has picked the one relationship in the universe where perfect equality and willing order are both beyond dispute, and he has made it the model. Christ is not less than God because he submits to the Father; a wife is not less than her husband because she submits to him.

Where Christians differ: headship. Egalitarians argue that head means only source, and that Christ’s coming abolished all role distinctions between men and women. Verdict: Paul grounds this order in creation (vv. 8–9), not in culture or the fall, and compares it with the relation of the Father and the Son. Men and women are equal in worth, dignity and salvation (Galatians 3:28; 1 Peter 3:7). But God has given husbands the responsibility to lead their families, and qualified men the responsibility to lead and teach in the church (1 Timothy 2:12–13). This is the complementarian view: equal in being, distinct in role. Husbands must lead as Christ leads: by sacrificial love, not domination.

Where Christians differ: does the Son submit to the Father eternally? Christians differ over how far this reaches into the eternal life of God. Most Reformed theologians have been careful here: the Son’s submission is real, and it belongs to his mission, the sending, the incarnation, the obedience unto death, rather than being a subordination of nature within the Godhead, since the Father and the Son share one undivided divine essence. Others have argued for an eternal ordering of persons in authority and submission. It is a discussion worth conducting with great care and very little heat. Verdict: of those two views, the first is the more likely. Scripture plainly shows the Son submitting to the Father in his mission (15:28; John 5:19), but it never makes him anything less than fully God (Philippians 2:6). His submission belongs to the work of salvation he freely undertook, and it is no subordination of his being.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every woman must submit to every man. The headship here is in marriage (and, by extension, the church). It never justifies harshness or abuse.

Does headship mean the husband always gets the final say? In the rare case where a decision must be made, the two cannot agree, and nothing sinful is involved, yes: someone must bear the responsibility, and God has laid it on the husband. But a marriage that is constantly reaching for the final say has already gone wrong. Headship is first a responsibility, not a casting vote: to pray for his wife, to take the lead in loving, apologising and serving, to protect and provide, to care for her soul. A wise husband listens long, seeks his wife’s counsel as a gift from God, and very often defers to her judgment gladly. And no husband may ever ask his wife to sin; her first obedience is to Christ (Acts 5:29).

The shape love takes. What the ordinary reader should take from the verse is this, and it is enough to be going on with. Order is not the enemy of equality; it is the shape love takes when two equals are doing something together. The Son’s submission cost him everything and diminished him in nothing. It was not the loss of his dignity. It was the display of it (John 5:19; Philippians 2:6–8).

In a sentence. But Paul wants you to understand that Christ is the head of every man, the husband is the head of his wife, and God is the head of Christ.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, lead your wives as Christ leads you: with love that serves. Ask today what your wife needs from you, and do it before she has to ask. Wives, respect your husbands as the church honours Christ, and tell him what you see, because he needs your wisdom. And all of us: remember that the most powerful man in the room is the one with the most responsibility to serve.

For worship. Look at the head of Christ. The eternal Son, equal with the Father in power and glory, came gladly to do his Father’s will, and said, I always do the things that are pleasing to him (John 8:29). There was no resentment in it, no grasping, no loss. And Christ, the head of every man, exercises his headship by laying down his life. The order of heaven is an order of love, from the Father who sends to the Son who obeys to the Spirit who glorifies the Son. What a God, whose very greatness is displayed in giving, and whose authority looks like a towel and a basin and a cross.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek words can mean “woman” and “wife.”

verseByVerse.quote: Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.

Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head. Why would a covered head dishonour a man? In public worship, a man covering his head would dishonour both his physical head and his spiritual head, Christ. The likeliest background is the Roman custom in which a man leading pagan worship drew his toga over his head; a Christian man doing the same would look like a priest of the idols. Paul’s concern is what the sign said in that setting. Whether a man wears a hat in church today is a matter of courtesy, not of this text.

But every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head. In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and her honour as a wife; to remove it in public could suggest she was unattached or immoral. Her physical head and her husband were both shamed. Two things are established in this sentence, and the first is easily missed because it is assumed rather than argued. Women are praying and prophesying in the Corinthian assembly, out loud, and Paul does not object. He objects to how they are dressed while doing it. That is a striking thing to find in a letter often thought to silence women, and it needs to be held onto: the apostle’s correction here presupposes their audible participation and corrects only its manner.

Since it is the same as if her head were shaven. A shaved head was a sign of disgrace for a woman, perhaps associated with punishment for adultery or with certain pagan practices.

Garments speak. The second thing established here is that appearance in worship carries meaning. Paul assumes that what a person wears on his or her head in the assembly says something, and that saying the wrong thing brings dishonour. That assumption is the hinge of the whole passage, and it is the part most likely to be dismissed today as fussiness about hats. It is not fussiness. Every culture has clothing that speaks, which is why nobody wears a swimming costume to a funeral. Paul is not inventing the fact that garments talk. He is asking what these particular garments were saying in that room.

How can chapter 11 assume women speak, and chapter 14 tell them to be silent? This raises the hardest question in the chapter, and it should be answered here rather than left to ambush the reader three chapters on. Paul was not a fool, and the letter was read aloud in one sitting; whatever he meant, he did not think he was contradicting himself three chapters later. The resolution lies in noticing what kind of speech chapter 14 is actually discussing. That passage sits inside a paragraph about prophecy being weighed by the congregation (let the others weigh what is said, 14:29), and it ends by telling the women to ask their questions at home (14:35). It is regulating a particular activity in a particular part of the meeting: the public sifting and cross-examination of prophecies, an exercise of governing judgment over the congregation’s teaching. That is a different thing from praying and prophesying, which chapter 11 takes for granted that women do. So the two passages are addressing two activities, not one, and the seeming contradiction comes from reading silent as absolute when Paul has already shown, in this very verse, that he does not mean it absolutely. This will be taken up again where it is written, at 14:34.

Where Christians differ: women praying and prophesying. How does this fit with 14:34 (women should keep silent in the churches) and 1 Timothy 2:12? Verdict: Women may pray and contribute in the church’s life, and in New Testament times some prophesied (Acts 21:9). What is reserved for qualified men is the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church (14:29, 34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12). Since prophecy as new revelation has ceased with the closing of the canon, the question today concerns praying, sharing and teaching; women serve in many ways, but the office of elder and the authoritative preaching of the church belong to qualified men.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are spiritually inferior or have nothing to contribute. Paul expects them to pray and prophesy.

So what may a woman do in church today? A great deal, and churches that hold this verdict should say so as loudly as they say the limits. She may pray aloud in the gathering, read Scripture, share what God has taught her, lead in song, give testimony, and use every gift of mercy, administration, hospitality and wisdom God has given her. She may teach women and children, as Titus 2:3–5 commands the older women to do, and she may, like Priscilla with her husband, explain the way of God privately to a man who needs it (Acts 18:26). What she does not do is hold the office of elder or bring the church’s authoritative preaching. That is not a judgment on her gifts, many of which may exceed those of the men in the room. It is the shape God has given his household.

In a sentence. A man who prays or prophesies with something on his head shames his head; and a wife who prays or prophesies with her head bare shames her head, as much as if her head were shaved.

On a Tuesday. If you are a man, thank God for the women who pray in your church, and listen when they do. If you are a woman, do not hold back the gifts God has given you because some of the church’s offices are reserved; there is more for you to do in Christ’s church than any one life can finish. And all of us: ask what your appearance and manner in worship are saying, and whether they point to God or to yourself.

For worship. Men and women both pray to God in his church, and he hears them both with the same delight. In the gathered church, the daughters of the King lift their voices alongside his sons, as the prophet foretold: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17). The Spirit poured out at Pentecost was poured on both. Blessed be the God who has made of men and women one people of priests, every one with free access to his throne through the blood of his Son.
verseByVerse.note: In that culture a married woman’s head covering signalled her modesty and married status. Christians differ on how the principle applies today.

verseByVerse.quote: For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.

For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. Paul argues by reduction: if she is going to abandon the sign, she may as well go the whole way and take the shears to her hair, and everyone in Corinth knew what that meant, which is why the argument works. A shaved or cropped head on a woman in that world was a mark of disgrace; it was the look associated with women advertising a rejection of ordinary respectability. It is the ancient equivalent of saying that if you are going to leave the wedding ring at home, you may as well announce what its absence implies.

But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head. Since that would be shameful, keep the covering.

For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God. Then verse 7 gives the theological reason, and it is a sentence people stumble over. It comes from Genesis 1:26–27. Man was made in God’s image and reflects God’s glory.

But woman is the glory of man. Notice carefully what is not said. Paul does not say that the man is the image of God and the woman is not. Genesis, which he is quoting from, is explicit: God created man in his own image, male and female he created them (Genesis 1:27). Both bear it equally, and Paul knew that text better than his critics do. What he changes is the second noun. Man is the glory of God; woman is the glory of man. Glory here means that which honours and displays another: the honour that is reflected back. She was made from man and for him (vv. 8–9), and she brings him honour, as an excellent wife is the crown of her husband (Proverbs 12:4; Genesis 2:23).

A glory veiled before a greater one. His argument is about what should be on show in a worship service. When the church gathers, God is the one being honoured, so nothing should be visibly competing for that honour. The man, unveiled, reflects God. The woman, in that culture, reflected the honour of her husband, and Paul asks that this reflection be gently covered while God is being worshipped: not because it is shameful, but because it is glorious, and this is not the hour for it. Every other glory in the room dims when God is being praised. That is a strange logic to modern ears, but it is not a demeaning one. The covering is not a muzzle or a badge of inferiority. On Paul’s own account it is the veiling of a genuine glory in the presence of a greater one, which is exactly what the seraphim do with their wings in Isaiah’s temple, covering their faces before a holiness that outshines them (Isaiah 6:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean women do not bear God’s image or that their glory is only derived. Both sexes bear God’s image equally. Paul is speaking of their relation within creation’s order.

Is it wrong for a woman to have short hair today? Not in itself. Paul’s argument depended on what a cropped head meant in Corinth: disgrace, or a public rejection of being a wife. In most cultures today a short haircut on a woman says nothing of the kind. The principle that remains is that women and men should not try to erase the God-given difference between them, and should not use their appearance to make a statement against the order God has made. A woman with short hair who is glad to be a woman and honours her husband is not breaking this verse. A man or woman who styles themselves deliberately to blur the line between the sexes is going against its grain, whatever the length of their hair.

In a sentence. If a wife will not cover her head, she might as well cut off her hair; but if it is shameful for her to have her hair cut or shaved, she should cover her head. A man should not cover his head, because he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man.

On a Tuesday. Whether man or woman, you were made to display God’s glory. Live today in a way that honours him and those he has joined you to. Husbands, honour your wife as your glory, publicly and gladly. And when you gather for worship, let everything about you, clothes, manner and voice, say that God is the one being honoured.

For worship. Every glory in the room dims when God is praised, because he is the fountain of all glory. The man reflects him, the woman reflects the man, and both together reflect the God who made them in his image, male and female, a single portrait in two colours. But the brightest reflection of all is the Son, the radiance of the glory of God (Hebrews 1:3), in whose face the glory of God shines into our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6). We veil our own glories before his, and we are glad to, because his is so much greater.

verseByVerse.quote: For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.

For man was not made from woman, but woman from man. Paul now goes back to Genesis 2, and the reader should feel the weight of that move. He is not appealing to Corinthian manners, or to what the neighbours will think, or to what has always been done. He is appealing to how human beings were made, before there was a culture to have opinions about it. The first fact from the garden is that the woman was taken from the man: alone among human beings, neither formed from the dust as Adam was nor born as everyone since has been, but built by God out of the body of another, from Adam’s side (Genesis 2:21–23).

Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man. The second fact is that she was made for him, in answer to the first thing in the creation account that God calls not good: it is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a helper fit for him (Genesis 2:18).

From and for, read as Genesis reads them. Both facts have been used badly, so let both be read as Genesis reads them. From does not mean lesser. Eve came out of Adam’s side, and Adam’s response was not to assert rank but to break into the first poetry in the Bible: this at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh (Genesis 2:23). And for does not mean an instrument. The word Genesis uses for the woman’s role is helper (Hebrew ʿēzer), and it is worth knowing that the same Hebrew word is used most often in the Old Testament of God himself helping his people: our help and our shield (Psalm 33:20; 121:2). It is not a word for a subordinate assistant. It is a word for one who comes to the aid of somebody who cannot manage alone, which is precisely what the man could not do. It describes a role, not inferiority.

What Paul is establishing. His point in citing all this is narrow, and he is about to guard it himself. He is grounding headship in creation, which means the difference between men and women is not a social construction that a sophisticated congregation may dispense with. It reflects God’s design, it is written into how we were made, and it is therefore not the church’s to abolish. He is not saying it establishes rank in worth, and the very next sentence will make sure nobody thinks so.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women exist only to serve men, or that men owe women nothing. Verses 11–12 balance this immediately.

How this text has been misused. Something has to be said here, because pretending otherwise would be dishonest and would leave a wounded reader unhelped. Verses like these have been quoted by men to justify treating their wives as inferiors, to shut down every disagreement, and in the worst cases to demand submission to cruelty. That is not a misapplication at the edges; it is the exact reverse of what the passage teaches, and it ought to be named as the wickedness it is. The measure of headship in the New Testament is never the authority a man may claim. It is the death a man must die: husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). That is the standard, and it is a standard that ruins domineering before it starts. Christ’s headship over the church consisted of washing feet, absorbing insult, and being executed for people who had contributed nothing. Any man who quotes 1 Corinthians 11 to get his own way has picked up a verse about the Trinity and used it as a stick, and he will answer for it. Order in the Bible always runs downhill in service. It never runs downhill in privilege.

What if my husband is harsh or abusive? Then hear this clearly: nothing in this passage requires you to endure abuse, and no faithful church will ask you to. Headship is a calling to self-giving love, and a man who threatens, hits, controls or terrorises his wife has abandoned it. Your safety, and your children’s, comes first. It is right to leave a dangerous home, to call the police where a crime has been committed, and to tell your pastor or elders, who should protect you and confront him, not counsel you to go back and submit harder. Abuse is a grievous sin against God and against you. Whether a marriage broken this way may end in divorce is a further question, treated at 7:10–16 with the Westminster Confession’s teaching on adultery and desertion; but separation for safety is never disobedience to this text.

In a sentence. Man did not come from woman; woman came from man. And man was not created for the woman, but woman for the man.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, measure your headship by Ephesians 5:25 this week: what would it cost you to love your wife as Christ loved the church, today, in one specific thing? Do it. Wives, thank God that your role as helper is the very word he uses of himself. And if you know a home where this passage is being used as a weapon, do not stay silent; speak to someone who can help.

For worship. Thank God for his wise design in creating man and woman, different and fitted for each other. He did not make humanity in one lonely copy. He looked at the solitary man and said it was not good, and then, with his own hands, he built the woman and brought her to him, the first wedding, with God himself giving the bride away. And in that wedding he was painting a picture of a greater one: Christ, the last Adam, from whose wounded side his bride was born, and who loves her, nourishes her and cherishes her, and will present her to himself in splendour, without spot or wrinkle.

parallels.desc: a helper fit for him; she shall be called Woman

verseByVerse.quote: That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.

That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head. Two puzzles in one short verse, and neither should be hurried past. The first is the phrase rendered a symbol of authority. The Greek says simply that she ought to have authority on her head. The covering is a sign of her husband’s authority, but the older reading, a sign of someone else’s authority over her, is not the only one available. It is at least as natural to read it the other way round as well: the covering is her authority, the thing that gives her the standing to pray and prophesy in the assembly, under that order. On that reading the veil is not a leash but a licence. It marks her as a woman in her rightful place doing a rightful thing, and it silences the objection before it is raised. That reading fits the flow: Paul has been assuming since verse 5 that she prays and prophesies, and this is the garment that makes it unexceptionable.

Because of the angels. The second puzzle is one of the most contested phrases in all of Paul’s letters. It should not be passed over with a shrug, because a reader who meets it and gets no help will simply conclude that the Bible is obscure. Four readings have been offered. The most widely held today takes the angels as the appointed guardians of the created order, God’s agents in the world he has arranged. They are present when the church worships, they observe God’s order in the church (4:9; Ephesians 3:10; 1 Peter 1:12), and they have a stake in an ordering that reflects God’s design; to overturn it deliberately in a worship service would be a visible affront to the very servants charged with upholding it. A second reading, with a long history in the church, sees them as fellow worshippers: the church’s gathering joins a heavenly assembly where angels worship with perfect reverence, so decorum on earth honours the company we have walked into. Psalm 138:1 in the Greek reads: before the angels I will sing your praise; and Isaiah 6 and Revelation 4 and 5 show angels and the redeemed praising together. A third reading, the oldest, appeals to the strange episode of Genesis 6 and the Jewish traditions built on it, in which angels fell through desire for women; on this view the covering was protective. Paul knew those traditions (Jude 6; 2 Peter 2:4) and this reading was common in the early centuries, but it requires a speculative account of angels that the text does not supply. A fourth notes that the law was given through angels (Galatians 3:19), so their presence would call for the order the law required.

What it does not mean. It does not mean angels lust after women, as some ancient interpreters suggested from Genesis 6. The more likely meaning is that angels watch over worship.

Where the ordinary reader should land. The first two readings are the most defensible, and they share a conclusion. Whatever else the phrase means, it means that a Christian congregation at worship is not alone in the room. There are more present than can be counted on the chairs. That is the assumption behind the whole verse, and it is a bracing thing to carry into a Sunday morning: the singing is overheard, the reverence is observed, and the company is far larger and far older than the one you can see (Hebrews 12:22).

Should I pray to angels, or try to sense them? No. Angels are fellow servants, not objects of worship or prayer; when John fell at an angel’s feet, he was told at once to get up and worship God (Revelation 22:8–9). Scripture never invites us to seek contact with them, and an interest in angels that crowds out Christ is a road away from him (Colossians 2:18). What it does give us is a comfort and a dignity. The comfort is that they are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who are to inherit salvation (Hebrews 1:14). The dignity is that ordinary Sunday worship, in a small hall with a weak organ, is watched by heaven.

In a sentence. For this reason, and because the angels are watching, a wife should wear on her head a sign of authority.

On a Tuesday. When you worship, the angels are present. Worship with reverence and order. Next Sunday, before the first hymn, remind yourself who else is in the room, and sing like it.

For worship. We have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Hebrews 12:22–24). The angels have watched the whole story of redemption with longing, and they still look into it (1 Peter 1:12): the Creator made a creature, the Son made flesh, the holy one dying for the unholy. They do not need a Saviour, yet they never tire of watching him save. How much more should we, who are the ones he died for, join their song: worthy is the Lamb who was slain.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “because of the angels” is uncertain; angels were thought to be present at worship and to guard God’s order.

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.

Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman. And there is the guard, placed by Paul himself, in case anyone should take verses 8 and 9 and build a wall out of them. Nevertheless is the hinge. Everything just said about the garden stands, and it does not entitle anybody to independence or superiority. The word he uses cuts both ways with deliberate symmetry: not the woman apart from the man, not the man apart from the woman. In the Lord, in Christ’s new community, men and women need each other completely. Neither sex is a complete account of humanity, and neither can conduct its life as though the other were an optional extra.

For as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. Then Paul makes the point with a piece of homely wit. Yes, the first woman came out of a man. And every man since has come out of a woman, his mother. If anyone wants to argue about origins, the ledger balanced itself in the second generation and has stayed level ever since. Every man who has ever lived, including the ones in Corinth arguing about veils, was carried, delivered and fed by a woman. The apostle knows exactly what he is doing with that sentence. Mutual dependence.

And all things are from God. The last clause closes the account entirely. The whole arrangement traces back past both of them to the one who made the pair and gave them to each other, which means neither party has grounds for a boast, since neither invented himself. No room for pride on either side.

In the Lord. The phrase to hold on to is in the Lord. It is not a cancellation of what has gone before; it is the atmosphere in which what has gone before is now to be lived. Sin turned difference into domination, and the curse said as much on the way out of the garden (Genesis 3:16). In Christ the difference remains and the domination has no place. There is a kind of Christian teaching about men and women that quotes verses 8 and 9 loudly and lets verses 11 and 12 fall silent. Paul wrote all four, a few seconds apart, and the church is not free to keep only the half that suits it (Galatians 3:28; Ephesians 5:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean headship is cancelled in the Lord. Paul holds both: an order of headship and a deep mutual interdependence.

What dependence looks like when it is working. In a marriage it is a man who genuinely does not know what he thinks until he has heard his wife, and says so out loud in company. In a congregation it is a church whose men would notice within a fortnight if the women stopped, and are honest enough to admit that much of what holds the place together is being done by them. Dependence is not a compliment paid at an anniversary. It is a thing you can see in who gets consulted before a decision.

What does this mean for single people? Everything Paul says here applies to you as fully as to the married. You are not half a person waiting to be completed. You belong to a church in which men and women depend on one another as brothers and sisters, mothers and fathers in the faith, and you have gifts that the rest of the body cannot do without. A single woman is not under the headship of every man in the congregation; she is under Christ and the shepherding of her elders, as the men are. And the single man or woman can often show this mutual dependence most freely, in friendships, hospitality and service across the whole family of God.

In a sentence. Yet in the Lord woman is not independent of man, nor man of woman. Just as woman came from man, so every man is born of a woman, and everything comes from God.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the men and women in your life, and in your church, on whom you depend. Then tell one of them. If you are a man in leadership, ask the women in your church what they see that you are missing, and listen to the answer.

For worship. All things are from God. Not from Adam, and not from Eve. The difference between men and women is not a problem the church has to solve, nor a weapon either side may pick up. It is a piece of God’s workmanship, made deliberately, by someone who could have made us all identical and did not want to. He looked at what he had made, male and female, and called it very good before either of them had done anything at all. And when the Son came to redeem them both, he was born of a woman (Galatians 4:4): the eternal Word, through whom all things were made, carried, delivered and fed by a young mother in Bethlehem. The God from whom all things come came to us that way.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.

Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered? Once again Paul refers a matter to the congregation’s own judgment rather than settling it by decree, exactly as he did at 10:15. He appeals to their sense of what is fitting (prepō). He has given the theology; now he asks them to look at the thing itself and see whether it fits.

Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him. The appeal to nature has to be handled honestly, because a modern reader will object at once that nature does no such thing: hair grows on everyone, and plenty of cultures have thought long hair splendid on a man. The objection is fair, and the answer is that Paul is not making a biological claim. The word (physis) covers what is natural in the broad sense: the natural order of things as people generally sense it, the settled instinct of a people about what is fitting, the sort of thing that feels obvious long before anyone can argue for it. In Greek and Roman culture, long hair on men was associated with effeminacy. Paul is pointing at a shared sense of the fitting and saying that even that untutored instinct is pushing in the same direction as his argument. It is a supporting consideration, not the foundation; the foundation was laid in verses 3 and 8 to 12.

But if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? Long hair was considered a woman’s beauty and dignity, one of her recognised glories.

For her hair is given to her for a covering. A clause that has caused endless discussion. Some have concluded that Paul means the hair is the covering, and that no cloth was ever in view. That reads oddly against verse 6, where cutting the hair short is the alternative to covering the head rather than a way of doing it; the two cannot be the same thing if one is offered as the substitute for the other. The better sense is that nature itself gives women a covering, a God-given picture of the very thing the head covering signifies. Nature already drapes a woman’s head, and the fabric follows the pattern that the Creator drew first.

The kind of argument this is. Paul appeals to Christ, to creation, to the angels, and now to the ordinary human sense of what is seemly. He is not embarrassed to use the last of these. Christians sometimes speak as though only a proof text may be consulted, but the apostle here treats the shared instincts of decent people as a real witness: not the highest one, and never one that may overrule Scripture, but not nothing either (Romans 2:14–15).

Is long hair on a man therefore a sin? Scripture sets no hair length for men; the Nazirite let his hair grow long as a mark of devotion (Numbers 6:5). Paul’s concern is what a hairstyle signalled in Corinth: a man presenting himself as a woman. Where a style carries no such meaning, it is a matter of conscience and taste, and no Christian should judge another by the length of his hair.

Where Christians differ: must women wear head coverings today? Some churches require head coverings in worship today; most do not. Verdict: The principle is permanent: the distinction between men and women, and the husband’s headship, rooted in creation, should be honoured in worship. The specific form, a head covering, was the cultural expression of that principle in first-century Corinth, where an uncovered married woman sent a message of shame or rebellion. Where coverings carry no such meaning, the principle should be expressed in other ways: modest dress, and clear distinctions between men and women. Christians who wear coverings out of conviction should be respected.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there is a precise rule on hair length. It means men and women should not try to erase the God-given distinction between them.

What about dress more generally? The same principle reaches further than hair. The law of Moses forbade a man to wear a woman’s garment or a woman a man’s (Deuteronomy 22:5), and the concern was the same: not a particular cut of cloth, but the blurring of the line God drew between the sexes. What counts as masculine or feminine dress varies a great deal between cultures and centuries; trousers on a woman in many countries today are simply women’s clothes. So the question is not whether an item matches a rule from another time and place, but whether, here, it says I am glad to be the man or woman God made me, or says the opposite. And modesty applies to both sexes: dress for worship and for life in a way that does not draw attention away from God to yourself.

In a sentence. Decide for yourselves: is it fitting for a wife to pray to God bareheaded? Doesn’t the very nature of things teach you that long hair is a shame for a man but a glory for a woman? For long hair has been given to her as a covering.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for making you a man or a woman, and honour that distinction with joy. If you have felt pressure, from the world or from your own heart, to resent the body God gave you, bring that to him honestly; he made you on purpose, and he does not make mistakes. And be slow to judge other Christians over matters of dress and hair where Scripture has left room.

For worship. The Creator who painted the world did not make it grey. He made sea and land, day and night, male and female, and every difference was a gift. The ordinary instincts of decent people, the sense that some things are fitting and some are not, are faint echoes of his wisdom written into the world. And the same God who gave the woman her glory and the man his has crowned both with a greater one: in Christ they are fellow heirs of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7), and will shine together like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.

If anyone is inclined to be contentious. The last word on the subject, and it is not another argument. It is a door closing. Contentious (philoneikos) means fond of quarrelling, loving to win arguments. Paul expects some to argue.

We have no such practice, nor do the churches of God. Such practice is deliberately compact in the Greek, and both readings end in the same place. If it means the practice of contentiousness, Paul is saying: we do not do fighting about this, and neither does any other church. If it means the practice of women praying with uncovered heads, he is saying: no church anywhere does what you are proposing, so the innovation is yours alone. Either way the appeal is to the shared life of the churches, and either way it lands on the person who wants a fight. The churches everywhere follow this pattern. Corinth must not go its own way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that every church practice must be identical everywhere. It means churches should not break from apostolic patterns in order to be different.

Are Christian women meant to cover their heads in church today? This brings the passage to the question every reader has been waiting for, and it deserves an answer rather than an admiring description of how difficult it is. Begin with what does not change. The theology of verses 3 and 8 to 12 is rooted in the Trinity and in creation, and neither of those is a first-century custom. That men and women are equally God’s image, genuinely different, mutually dependent, and ordered in relationship to one another is not up for revision, and a congregation that quietly erases the difference between men and women has departed from Paul, whatever it is wearing. Now what does change. The visible sign is a different matter, and Paul’s own way of arguing suggests as much. He reasons from what is disgraceful, from what nature suggests, from what the churches do: the vocabulary of things that are legible in a particular place and time. A sign works only if people can read it. In first-century Corinth an uncovered head in worship said something specific and everyone in the room heard it. In most Western congregations today a hat says nothing whatever, and a woman who wore one to make Paul’s point would find that nobody received the message, which is the one thing a symbol must do.

So, practically. Where the covering is still meaningful, and there are cultures and congregations where it plainly is, wear it, and let nobody sneer at those who do; they are obeying Scripture in a way their neighbours can read. Where it is not, the principle must find a form that people can actually see: a church where men and women are equally welcome to pray and are not embarrassed to be different from one another; where the distinction is treated as a gift rather than an awkwardness to be managed; where dress and manner in worship are chosen with an eye to what honours God rather than what displays the wearer. And in either case, verse 16 governs: whatever conclusion a Christian reaches, he is not permitted to become contentious about it. The apostle who has just spent fifteen verses on the matter ends by refusing to let it become a battlefield.

What if my conviction differs from my church’s practice? Then follow your conscience quietly, and do not make it a cause. A woman who believes she should cover her head may do so in a church where few do, and the church should welcome her gladly. A woman who does not believe it is required should not be pressed to cover by the opinions of others. What neither may do is treat the other as less faithful, or turn the question into a campaign. That is exactly the contentiousness this verse shuts the door on. If the difference becomes a constant source of strife, talk to your elders with humility, and remember that the unity of the church is a weightier matter than this sign.

In a sentence. If anyone wants to argue about this, we have no other custom, and neither do the churches of God.

On a Tuesday. Avoid being the person who loves to argue. Seek the peace and unity of the church. Before you raise a disagreement, ask: do I want to win, or do I want my brother to flourish? If it is the first, wait until it is the second.

For worship. The God of the churches is not a God of confusion but of peace (14:33). He has not left his people to invent their worship from scratch in every city; he has given them one Lord, one faith, one baptism, and a shared life that runs from Jerusalem to Corinth to every congregation on earth today. And over all the quarrels of his people stands the Prince of Peace, who made peace by the blood of his cross, and whose church, for all its contentions, will be presented to him at last without a single division left.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Divisions at the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now Paul has no praise for them, because their meetings do more harm than good. He hears that when they gather there are divisions, and he partly believes it; there have to be differences, so that those who are genuine stand out. When they meet, it is not really the Lord’s Supper they eat, because each person goes ahead with his own meal, and one goes hungry while another gets drunk. Do they not have homes to eat and drink in? Or do they despise God’s church and humiliate those who have nothing? Paul will certainly not praise them for this.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord’s Supper as Enacted Gospel Equality

Paul’s critique of the Corinthian Supper is grounded in his theology of the cross. The Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death (v. 26) — the death in which the rich Son of God became poor for the sake of the poor, in which the Lord washed his disciples’ feet, in which social distinctions were overcome in the one body given for all. A Supper that reinforces social stratification is not merely socially unkind; it is a contradiction of what is being enacted. The body and blood of Christ at the table cannot be participated in rightly by those who simultaneously despise the members of his body gathered around the table.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The patronage culture of Roman Corinth structured even the shared meal around social hierarchy: the wealthy ate better food in the inner room; clients and dependents got lesser portions in the outer rooms. The Corinthians had imported this structure wholesale into the church’s gathering. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the place where the social equalisations of the gospel are most visibly enacted — or most visibly denied. The church where wealth, race, or education creates a gradient of welcome and participation has committed the Corinthian error at its most fundamental level.

verseByVerse.quote: But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part, for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.

But in the following instructions I do not commend you. Verse 2 opened with I commend you. This one opens by taking it back, and the echo is deliberate. Here Paul has no praise. Whatever they had held on to, they had lost the thing that mattered most.

Because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse. Sit with the accusation, because it is worse than it first sounds. Paul is not saying the meetings were dull, or badly run, or unhelpful. He is saying that these people would have been better off staying at home. Their gatherings were doing more harm than good. There is such a thing as a church service that leaves people further from God than it found them, and an apostle says so in writing. It is a shocking verdict on a church’s worship.

For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. The cause is named at once. Divisions (schismata) is the word of 1:10, but here the divisions are social: rich and poor.

And I believe it in part. That last phrase is a small masterpiece of pastoral care. Paul does not swallow the report whole and does not dismiss it. He has heard something, perhaps again from Chloe’s household (1:11); he knows that reports carry exaggeration; and he refuses both to pretend it is nothing and to convict them of everything alleged. Any pastor who has had to weigh what one member says about another will recognise the discipline in those five words.

For there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized. Then a genuinely hard sentence. Factions (haireseis) is the word from which heresies comes: parties, sects. This is not approval. Paul has been attacking the factions since chapter 1 and is not now blessing them. He speaks with irony and realism, and he is saying something about how God works even through what he hates. Trouble sorts people. When a congregation splits along the lines of money or personality or taste, it becomes visible who was there for Christ and who was there for the circle, and the sorting is not an accident but a providence. God permits the fracture and uses it as a sieve. It is the same principle as the wheat and the weeds growing together until harvest (Matthew 13:30), and the same comfort: a church going through an ugly season is not outside God’s hands.

Genuine. The word for genuine (dokimoi) is a metalworker’s word, used of metal that has been tested and approved. Nobody discovers what an alloy is made of while it sits on a shelf. It is found out in the fire, and a divided church is a furnace (1 John 2:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean factions are good. Paul condemns them. It means God can use even divisions to show who is true.

Should I leave a church that is divided? Usually not at the first sign of trouble, and never simply to escape discomfort. The passage gives three things to do instead. Do not conclude that God has abandoned the place; verse 19 says he is at work in the very thing that feels like collapse. Do not join a party, because the sifting is precisely between those who are for Christ and those who are for a camp. And ask the uncomfortable question that this verse presses: when the fire came, what did it show that I was made of? There are times when leaving is right: when the gospel itself is denied, when abuse is covered up, or when the leaders will not be corrected by Scripture. But most church troubles are a call to stay, pray, speak truthfully and seek peace. A season of trouble in a church is the only time most people ever find out what they were actually attached to.

In a sentence. In the following instructions Paul has no praise for you, for your meetings do more harm than good. First, he hears that when you gather as a church there are divisions among you, and to some extent he believes it. No doubt there have to be differences among you to show which of you have God’s approval.

On a Tuesday. Ask: does my church’s gathering leave people better or worse? What can I do to make it better? And the next time you hear a report about another member, do what Paul did: believe it in part, refuse to repeat it, and if it matters, go to the person.

For worship. The Lord of the church is the refiner who sits over the furnace and watches the silver (Malachi 3:3). He does not abandon his people in their quarrels; he uses even their divisions to purify them, and he will not stop until he sees his own face reflected in the metal. Blessed be the Christ who loves a divided church enough to refine it, and who has promised that the gates of hell will not prevail against it.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk. What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.

The setting. The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal, sometimes called the love feast (Jude 12). The wealthy hosted the church in their homes, and archaeology at Corinth helps us picture the room. A wealthy believer’s house had a dining room, the triclinium, which held perhaps nine or a dozen reclining on couches around a table. Everyone else went in the courtyard, the atrium, standing or on the floor. In Roman dining custom, the host’s high-status friends reclined in the dining room with the best food and better wine, while lower-status guests ate in the courtyard with lesser food. Nobody thought this shocking. It was simply how a dinner worked. Now add the working day. The wealthy could arrive when they liked. The poor, the slaves and labourers who made up much of the congregation, came when their work let them, which was late. So they walked in to find the meal eaten, the good wine gone, their brothers in the inner room flushed and full, and something left over for them if anything was.

When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat. That is one of the most devastating sentences ever written to a church, and it is worth feeling before it is explained. These people gathered on the first day of the week. They took bread and a cup. They said the words. And the apostle tells them that whatever they were doing, it was not the Lord’s Supper. They called it the Lord’s Supper, but in reality it was their own supper. The Lord’s meal had become a private party, and the thing had lost the right to its own name.

For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. Goes ahead (prolambanō) means takes beforehand, or devours. Each ate his own food without sharing.

One goes hungry, another gets drunk. Paul’s three flat observations describe the room exactly. The poor went hungry; the rich drank too much.

Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Then the anger breaks out, and Paul does not tidy it. The question opens with an exclamation, What!, which is of sheer disbelief. Four questions follow, one after another, and they are not gentle. If you want a private feast, have it at home.

Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? Notice where the sharpest word falls. Not on the drunkenness, bad as that is, but on those who have nothing. A man who arrives late and hungry and watches the meal end without him has been told something about his worth, and he has been told it at the table where Christ’s death for him is being celebrated. That is what Paul cannot bear. Their behaviour despised the church, God’s people, and shamed the poor. Social snobbery at the Lord’s table is contempt for God’s church. The Corinthians thought they were having a slightly untidy dinner. They were preaching, in actions, the opposite of the gospel they said with their mouths.

What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not. No praise.

The world’s seating plan. The sin is not really greed. It is the effortless importing of the world’s seating plan into the church. Nobody in that house had to decide to humiliate the poor; they only had to do what everyone in Corinth did, and let the ordinary arrangements stand. That is how it usually happens. Congregations rarely resolve to grade people by money or accent or schooling. They simply fail to notice that the surrounding culture has already done it for them, and do nothing to interfere (James 2:1–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should never share meals in church. It means the Lord’s Supper must not be turned into a display of social division.

Where does this happen today? Rarely at the communion table itself, and often everywhere around it. It happens at the coffee after the service, when the same circles form every week and the visitor stands alone with a cup. It happens when the church’s leaders are all drawn from one profession or one class, when the poorer members are served but never invited home, when the young families and the elderly never speak, when people from another country or another race are welcomed politely and never befriended. None of it is deliberate. All of it says, as Corinth did, that some here matter more than others. The remedy is not guilt but attention: look for who is on the edge, and go and stand there.

What if I am the one left out? Then know that the apostle is on your side, and so is the Lord whose table it is. Paul’s anger in these verses is anger on behalf of people like you. Your place at Christ’s table does not depend on whether anyone made room for you at the coffee urn; it was bought with his blood, and he does not grade his guests. It is still right to speak to an elder about how the church welcomes people, gently and honestly, and it is often worth taking the first step yourself towards one other person. But do not let other people’s neglect persuade you that you do not belong. You belong to Christ, and therefore to his body.

In a sentence. When you meet, it is not really the Lord’s Supper you are eating, because each of you rushes ahead with his own food, so one goes hungry while another gets drunk. Don’t you have homes for eating and drinking? Or do you look down on God’s church and shame those who have nothing? What can Paul say? Should he praise you? Certainly not for this.

On a Tuesday. Next Sunday, before you talk to your friends, find one person standing on their own and talk to them. Notice who your church naturally honours, and who it overlooks, and quietly honour the overlooked.

For worship. At the Lord’s table, rich and poor stand equal before Christ, because the Lord himself became poor. He who was rich, for our sakes became poor, so that we through his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He was born in a stable and laid in a feeding trough, ate with outcasts, and was buried in a borrowed tomb. He has never once humiliated those who have nothing; he has filled the hungry with good things and sent the rich away empty. His table is the one place in the world where the slave and the master eat the same bread, because both of them are beggars who have been fed by the King.
verseByVerse.note: The Lord’s Supper was eaten as part of a shared meal. The wealthy, free to arrive early, ate and drank before poorer members — often slaves — could come after work.

parallels.desc: your love feasts

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–34 — The Institution of the Lord’s Supper
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul passes on what he received from the Lord. On the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, which is for you; do this in remembrance of me.” After supper he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood; whenever you drink it, do this in remembrance of me.” Every time they eat this bread and drink this cup, they proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. So anyone who eats or drinks in an unworthy way will be guilty of sinning against the Lord’s body and blood.
