Each person should examine himself before eating and drinking, because whoever eats and drinks without recognising the body eats and drinks judgement on himself. That is why many of them are weak and sick, and some have died. If they judged themselves properly, they would not come under judgement. When the Lord judges, he disciplines them so that they will not be condemned with the world. So when they gather to eat, they must wait for one another. Anyone who is hungry should eat at home, so that their meetings do not lead to judgement. Paul will give further instructions when he comes.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Real Presence and the Reformed Understanding of the Supper

Calvin’s eucharistic theology, developed precisely in dialogue with this passage, insisted on a genuine but spiritual presence of Christ in the Supper — against both the Roman Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation (physical transformation of the elements) and Zwingli’s pure memorialism (the Supper as merely symbolic). Paul’s language of “participation” (10:16) and “proclaiming the Lord’s death” (11:26) supports a real, active, communicative presence of Christ at the table — where Christ genuinely gives himself to be received by faith, and where genuine nourishment of the soul takes place through the Spirit.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian abuse of the Supper — reducing it to a social meal stratified by class — was the practical outworking of their failure to grasp the gospel. When you understand that Christ died equally for the rich and the poor in your community, you cannot eat well while they starve at the same table. Now: The Lord’s Supper remains the church’s most powerful enacted proclamation of the gospel — which is why its abuse is so serious, and why its right practice (the community gathered equally around the cross) is so significant as a sign to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”

For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you. Paul stops arguing and starts reciting. The change of register is unmistakable; this is the language of something handed over intact. Received and delivered are the technical terms for handing on tradition (15:3), and from the Lord means the teaching originates with Jesus himself, passed on through the apostles. This is probably the oldest written account we have of that night, written about AD 54, before any of the Gospels, within about twenty-five years of the event, and already worn smooth by use in the churches.

That the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed. Of all the ways to date it. Not on the night of the Passover, though it was; not on the eve of the crucifixion, though it was. Paul fixes the Supper to the moment of treachery, and he does it because that is the point. Betrayed is paradidōmi, handed over: the same word as delivered. On the night he was handed over to death, he handed this meal to his church. While a man who had eaten with him for three years was arranging the price, Jesus was breaking bread for him and for the rest of them, none of whom would stand by him either. The Supper was not instituted in a season of loyalty. It was given on the worst night in the history of friendship, which is precisely why an unfaithful Christian may still come to it. And it is rooted in history: a real night, a real room, a real betrayal.

Took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it. He had given thanks. The Greek word is eucharisteō, which is where the old name Eucharist comes from. Jesus followed the Passover pattern of giving thanks over bread, and he gave thanks for it knowing what the bread meant and what the next eighteen hours held.

And said, This is my body, which is for you. Then the words that have divided the church for five hundred years. The question is what the small word is is doing, and a reader deserves a straight account rather than a fog.

Which is for you. Two small Greek words, hyper hymōn, carrying the whole gospel. Not merely a body broken, but a body broken for: on your behalf, in your place, instead of you. His body was given in death for us, in our place. This is substitution. And he said it to a room containing the man who would sell him, the man who would deny him, and ten men who would run.

Do this in remembrance of me. Remembrance (anamnēsis) is not just recalling, but calling to mind in a way that makes the past event present in its power, as Israel remembered the Exodus at Passover (Exodus 12:14; Deuteronomy 16:3). At every Passover a Jewish father told his children that this is what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt (Exodus 13:8), though he had never been there. So the Christian at the table does not merely recall a death long ago; he takes hold of it as his own.

Where Christians differ: This is my body. Roman Catholics take is literally: the bread becomes Christ’s body (transubstantiation), while continuing to look and taste like bread. Lutherans say Christ’s body is present in, with and under the bread. Zwinglians say it is purely a symbol, a vivid memorial of something now absent. Verdict: Jesus was physically present, holding the bread, when he said it; the disciples could not have understood him to mean the bread had become his body. Jesus often spoke in metaphors: I am the door, I am the vine (John 10:9; 15:1). The bread signifies his body. But it is not an empty sign: through it, by the Spirit and through faith, believers truly receive and feed on Christ (10:16; Westminster 29.7). Christ is spiritually and really present to faith.

Two observations that need no degree. They help enormously. First, when Jesus said these words, he was sitting at the table holding the loaf, with his body plainly in front of them, unbroken. Nobody at that table can have understood the sentence as a statement of chemistry, because the body it referred to was passing the plate. Second, this is how he regularly talked. He is the door, the vine, the light, the road. Nobody has ever thought he was made of timber. So the bread stays bread, and something entirely real is happening, because represents is far too thin a word for what the previous chapter called a participation in the body of Christ (10:16). The Reformed answer holds both, and it is not a compromise but the only position that keeps Paul’s own two statements in the same hand. What that means at the table is not a puzzle: the believer who takes the bread is receiving Christ, truly, by faith, through the Spirit, and the receiving is as real as the crumbs.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper is a re-sacrifice of Christ. He was offered once for all (Hebrews 9:25–28).

What should I actually do in my mind while I eat? Look back, look in, look around, and look forward. Look back to the cross: this body was given for me, in my place. Look in, with honest faith: I have nothing to bring, and I receive him gladly. Look around at your brothers and sisters, who eat the same bread and are one body with you. And look forward to the day he will eat it new with you in his kingdom. You do not need to feel something dramatic. You need only to take what is given, trusting the one who gives it. The Lord’s Supper is not a test of your concentration; it is his gift to your faith.

In a sentence. What Paul handed on to you came from the Lord himself: on the night he was betrayed, the Lord Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, given for you. Do this to remember me.”

On a Tuesday. You do not have to wait for Sunday to remember him. When you eat bread this week, let it remind you: his body was given for you. And if you have been unfaithful to him lately, remember on which night he gave this meal. He gave it to the unfaithful.

For worship. On the night he was betrayed, he gave thanks. Think of it. He knew the kiss that was coming, the trial, the whip, the nails, the darkness and the forsaking, and he lifted bread to his Father and gave thanks. There was no reluctance and no bitterness in the hands that broke it. He broke the bread because he was willing to be broken, and he gave it to the very men who would desert him, because it was for them. His body was given for you. Receive him with thanks, and adore the love that chose that night of all nights to say so.
verseByVerse.note: This is probably the earliest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”

In the same way also he took the cup, after supper. After supper: a small detail that tells us which cup this was. The Passover meal moved through a sequence of cups, and the one taken after the main course, the third cup, came to be called the cup of blessing, the same phrase Paul used at 10:16. Fourteen centuries of Israel had been drinking that cup annually in memory of a rescue from Egypt. On this night the host picked it up and quietly transferred it to himself.

Saying, This cup is the new covenant in my blood. No phrase in the Old Testament was more loaded with hope. Jeremiah had promised a day when God would make a new covenant, not like the one Israel broke, in which he would write his law on hearts rather than stone, everyone would know the LORD, and he would remember their sin no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Every Jew at that table knew the passage, and nobody knew when it would arrive. Jesus tells them, holding a wine cup, that it arrives tomorrow, and that the thing which will inaugurate it is his own death. Covenants in that world were cut with blood. Moses sprinkled the people with the blood of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). An agreement of any weight was sealed by a sacrifice, so that the parties should understand what they were undertaking. This one is sealed by the blood of one of the parties, poured out to secure the other party’s faithfulness as well as his own (Hebrews 9:15–22). That is not how any covenant in human history has ever worked.

What is a covenant? A covenant is a binding relationship with promises, sealed by an oath or a sacrifice. It is more than a contract, because it binds persons, not merely services; it is the kind of bond marriage is. God’s covenants are his gracious commitments to his people: I will be your God, and you shall be my people. The old covenant at Sinai depended on Israel’s keeping it, and Israel broke it. The new covenant does not fail like that, because Christ has kept its terms for us and his blood has paid for every breach. Its promises are forgiveness, a new heart, and knowing God personally. When you drink the cup, God is renewing his pledge to you: all this is yours in my Son.

Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me. The Supper is to be repeated regularly. As often as you drink it is also, incidentally, the nearest thing the New Testament gives to a rule about frequency, which is to say, no rule at all, only the assumption that it will be often. Some churches celebrate it weekly, others monthly or quarterly. Christians have settled this differently and charitably for centuries. What the phrase does exclude is a Supper kept so rarely that it becomes an occasion rather than a meal; the Lord assumed his people would need feeding regularly, and he was not wrong about them.

Where Christians differ: how often? Some churches hold the Supper weekly, believing that was the apostolic practice (Acts 20:7). Others hold it less often, to preserve its solemnity. Verdict: Scripture does not command a frequency. The early church seems to have celebrated it each Lord’s Day, and Calvin wished for weekly communion. Frequent celebration is a great blessing, as long as it is done with understanding and self-examination, not mechanically.

What should the cup contain? Jesus used the Passover fruit of the vine (Matthew 26:29), which in his day was wine, and wine is the fitting element. But the New Testament gives no rule about the vessel, and a church that uses grape juice for the sake of a recovering alcoholic or a troubled conscience has not broken the Supper. Nor does the Supper need to be a full meal: Paul tells the Corinthians to eat at home if they are hungry (11:34), separating the ordinary meal from the Lord’s table.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cup contains Christ’s literal blood. It signifies and seals the new covenant in his blood.

In a sentence. In the same way, after supper he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant sealed with my blood. Whenever you drink it, do it to remember me.”

On a Tuesday. You belong to the new covenant: your sins are forgiven and remembered no more. Live in that freedom today. When an old sin rises in your memory to accuse you, answer it with the cup: God has promised to remember it no more, and he sealed that promise in blood.

For worship. Israel remembered a lamb whose blood had been smeared on a doorframe so that death would pass over a household. The man saying these words would be dead by the following afternoon, in the city where the Passover lambs had just been killed. He knew it, held the cup steady, and called it the new covenant in my blood. There was no reluctance in the hand that lifted it (Luke 22:20). The God who made promises through Jeremiah kept them through his Son, at the cost of his Son’s life. He has written his law on our hearts, made himself known to the least of us, and buried our sins where he will never bring them up again. Glory to the Lamb, whose blood speaks a better word.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.quote: For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup. Paul adds his own comment to the tradition he has just recited, and it draws the Supper in two directions at once. Notice too that it is still called bread after the blessing.

You proclaim the Lord’s death. Backwards first. The verb (katangellō) is the word for announcing, publishing, preaching. The Supper is a visible sermon. It is not a private devotional moment with the eyes closed; it is a public announcement, and it is made with hands and mouths rather than words. Without words, it declares: Christ died for sinners. The Reformers called the sacraments visible words. A congregation eating together says something, out loud, to everyone watching: that a man died, that his death is the whole hope of these people, and that they are not ashamed of it. It is a sermon that even the illiterate can preach and no one can misquote. And notice which part of the story the Supper preaches. Not the teaching, not the miracles, not the example. The death. Christianity has never been able to make its central rite about anything else, however much it has wanted to at various times. Bread broken, wine poured: the symbols will not be repurposed.

Until he comes. Then forwards. Three words that turn the meal around. The Supper looks back to the cross and forward to the return. It has a built-in expiry date. It is provisional, a meal for the road between, and it will one day stop, not because it failed but because it will have been overtaken by the thing it pointed to. Christ himself said he would not drink of the fruit of the vine again until he drank it new in his Father’s kingdom (Matthew 26:29; Revelation 19:9). So every communion service is a table with an empty place at it, and every celebration is a prayer: Our Lord, come (16:22).

A meal of joy and of hunger. That is why the Supper suits the way a Christian actually feels. It gives real food and it leaves you wanting a fuller one; it says the rescue has happened and it says the party has not started yet. Anyone who has taken the bread and cup in a season of grief knows the strange fitness of it: this is the one act of worship that does not require you to pretend everything is well, because it is built around a death and a waiting. And there is the homesickness the reader may not have had a name for. Communion is designed to leave a person unsatisfied. Not because the food is poor but because it is a foretaste, and a foretaste is meant to make you hungry for the meal. That ache at the table is not a failure of devotion. It is the sacrament working.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Supper replaces preaching. Word and sacrament go together; the Supper confirms the word.

What if I feel nothing at communion? Then you are in good company, and you have lost nothing. The Supper does not work by the strength of your feelings but by the faithfulness of Christ, who gives himself to faith whether faith feels warm or cold. A starving man is nourished by bread even when he is too tired to taste it. Come, take, and believe the promise attached to it; that is all that is asked. Over time, many find that the quiet, repeated meal does its work below the surface, steadying faith in a way no single moment could. And sometimes the dryness is itself a call to come with more expectation: to prepare during the week, to read the passages beforehand, and to pray for eyes to see him.

In a sentence. Every time you eat this bread and drink this cup, you are announcing the Lord’s death until he comes back.

On a Tuesday. At the table, look back to the cross and forward to his coming. Between Sundays, live as people who are announcing his death: unashamed of it, resting on it, and longing for the day the empty place at the table is filled.

For worship. The Lord is coming. The one who died is not dead, and the one who left is not gone for good. Every loaf broken in every church across the world for two thousand years has been a sermon on his death and a pledge of his return, and the pledge will be kept. On that day the bread and cup will be put away, not because they failed, but because the Bridegroom himself will sit at the head of the table, and we shall see him face to face. Proclaim his death, and long for his return. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.

Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner. This verse has probably kept more Christians away from the Lord’s table than any other sentence in the Bible, and in almost every case it has done so by being read backwards. So it must be read carefully. The crucial word is an adverb. Paul does not write whoever is unworthy. He writes whoever eats in an unworthy manner. The word describes the manner, not the person. That distinction is the difference between a table and a locked door. And it has to be so, because if worthy people were the requirement, the table would be empty for ever. No one is worthy of the Supper by merit. Nobody has ever been worthy of the body and blood of the Son of God. That is the entire reason the body was broken. A Supper for the worthy would be a Supper for nobody, and Christ did not institute it in a room of worthy men; he handed it to a table of deserters. It is for sinners who trust Christ.

What is an unworthy manner? Paul is not speculating; he has spent six verses describing it. It is what was happening in Corinth: coming to the table while treating the people at it with contempt, despising the poor and treating the meal carelessly. Eating well in front of the hungry. Taking the sign of a death that levelled everybody, and using the occasion to display that you are not level with them at all.

Will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord. Guilty (enochos) means liable, answerable. To treat the Supper with contempt is to handle the holiest thing in the world carelessly, and to be answerable for it: to sin against the one it represents, as if siding with those who crucified him (Hebrews 6:6; 10:29).

Who should hesitate. So the person who genuinely should hesitate at the table is not the one who feels unworthy. It is the one who has an unhealed contempt for a brother and intends to keep it. It is the person carrying a grudge into the queue, or nursing a sin he has decided not to give up, and reaching for the bread as though none of that were in the room with him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only sinless people may come, or that struggling believers should stay away. The table is for repentant sinners. The danger is coming carelessly or in unrepentant sin.

If you have stayed in your seat. If you have read this verse and stayed in your seat because you knew yourself too sinful to come, hear this plainly: you have understood your own heart correctly and this verse wrongly. The table is not a reward for the clean. It is food for the starving, and a sense of your own unworthiness is very close to the qualification. Christ came to call not the righteous but sinners, and he invites the hungry to come and eat without money and without price (Matthew 9:12–13; Isaiah 55:1).

What if there is a sin I keep falling into? Then come, provided you are fighting it and not keeping it. There is a world of difference between the believer who hates his besetting sin, confesses it again and again, and keeps asking Christ for help, and the person who has made peace with a sin and intends to go on in it. The first is exactly who the Supper is for; it is given to strengthen weak faith in the fight. The second should not come until he has repented. If you are unsure which you are, the fact that you are asking with a troubled heart is usually a sign of the first. Speak to a pastor if it helps, confess the sin to God before you eat, and receive the bread as the pledge that Christ’s body was given for this sin too.

In a sentence. So anyone who eats the bread or drinks the Lord’s cup in a way that dishonours him will be answerable for sinning against the Lord’s body and blood.

On a Tuesday. Do not stay away from the table because you feel unworthy. Come as a sinner trusting Christ. Stay away only if you refuse to repent. And if there is a grudge you are carrying towards someone in your church, begin dealing with it this week, so that on Sunday you can come with empty hands.

For worship. The Lord’s table is guarded by his holiness and opened by his mercy. He is too holy to be treated with contempt, and too merciful to turn away a single sinner who comes hungry. He made himself the bread so that the unworthy could eat, and he made himself the sacrifice so that the guilty could be declared clean. No one has ever come to that table worthy. Everyone who has come trusting him has gone away fed.
verseByVerse.note: “Unworthy manner” refers to how they were eating — despising the poor — not to whether the individual was worthy.

verseByVerse.quote: Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.

Let a person examine himself. Examine (dokimazō) means test, prove, the same root as the genuine of verse 19: metal tested in the fire. Notice the shape of the sentence before anything else, because the shape is the pastoral point.

Then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. Examine yourself, and so eat. The point of self-examination is not to keep away, but to come rightly. The examination is not an alternative to coming. It is the way you come. Paul assumes the person who has examined himself will be at the table, not in the car park. This needs saying because a whole tradition of self-examination has grown up which ends in abstaining, and it has left sincere Christians sitting through communion with their hands in their laps for years, taking their exclusion as a mark of seriousness. It is not seriousness. It is a misreading, and it deprives the very people the meal was made for.

What am I actually looking for? Not a morbid inventory of every failure since the last Supper; that is introspection, and it ends where introspection always ends, with the self at the centre of the picture and Christ somewhere in the background. The examination Paul has in view is short and it faces outwards. A few questions will do it. Do I trust Christ, and not myself, for my standing before God? That is the first, and if the answer is yes, however shakily, the door is open. Am I repenting of known sin? Is there anyone in this room I am refusing to be reconciled to? That is the one Corinth failed, and if there is, deal with it, because the Lord himself said to leave the gift at the altar and go and settle it first (Matthew 5:23–24). Am I coming to honour Christ and his body, to receive rather than to perform? That last one catches the respectable.

Where Christians differ: who may come to the table? Some churches practise open communion, inviting anyone; others closed communion, inviting only members of that church or denomination. Verdict: The table is for baptised believers who trust Christ, are not under church discipline, and examine themselves. Churches should explain this clearly and invite all such believers, whatever their congregation. Unbelievers and those living in unrepentant sin should be lovingly warned not to partake (Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 173). This is called fencing the table.

A fence around a fire. The table belongs to the Lord, not to the church that sets it out, and the historic Reformed practice has been to welcome to it any baptised believer who trusts Christ, is walking with his people, and is not under discipline, and to say so openly, warmly, and with the warning of verse 27 attached. That is not a gate to keep the wrong people out. It is a fence around a fire, which is what you build when something is precious and hot.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you must achieve perfect assurance before coming. Weak faith is still faith. The Supper is given to strengthen it.

What about children who profess faith? In a church that holds believer’s baptism, as this app does, the order is baptism first, then the table. When a child gives a credible profession of faith, understands in a simple way what the gospel and the Supper mean, and shows the beginnings of a changed life, the elders and parents may well judge it right to baptise him, and then to welcome him to the Lord’s table. The age differs from child to child, and no church should rush or refuse it for the sake of a rule. Our paedobaptist brothers, who baptise infants, usually admit children to the Supper after a public profession of faith, and so arrive at a similar place by a different road. What both agree on is that the Supper is for those who can examine themselves and discern the body.

In a sentence. Each person should test himself before he eats the bread and drinks the cup.

On a Tuesday. Before the next Supper, take time to examine yourself in prayer, a day or two ahead rather than in the thirty seconds while the plate approaches. Ask the questions, confess what needs confessing, forgive whoever needs forgiving, send the message that needs sending. Then come gladly.

For worship. Right self-examination always ends at the same place: not with a verdict on yourself but with an empty hand held out. The bread has to be taken with an open palm; there is no other way to receive it, and there never has been. And the God who bids us examine ourselves has already examined us, and knows the worst, and has not withdrawn the invitation. He searched us and knew us, and still set the table. Every examination that ends in the hand of Christ ends in joy.

verseByVerse.quote: For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.

For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body. Everything turns on what the body means here, and the context has already answered most of it. Discerning the body may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, understanding what it means, or recognising the church as Christ’s body, which the Corinthians were despising by humiliating the poor (v. 22; 10:17). Both fit the context; perhaps Paul means both. The Corinthian failure was not a defective theory of the elements. Nobody in that church was being disciplined for a wrong view of how Christ is present in the bread. The failure was that they could not see the church. They ate in front of hungry members and did not perceive that those members were the body of Christ, the very thing Paul has been saying since 10:17, that the one loaf makes the many one body, and will say again at length in chapter 12. To fail to discern the body is to look around a congregation and not see Christ’s own people there.

The two senses held together. That said, the two senses are not really separable, and Paul is not choosing between them. The bread on the table and the people around it are called by the same name in this letter, and that is not a play on words. A man who does not grasp what the bread is will not grasp what the church is either; and a man who takes the bread seriously and the people contemptuously has not, in fact, taken the bread seriously. To eat without recognising that the meal is about Christ’s body given for us, and that it makes us one body, is to eat wrongly.

Eats and drinks judgment on himself. The word for judgment (krima) is not the word for damnation. It means a verdict, a sentence handed down: not necessarily eternal condemnation, but God’s judgment in the form of discipline, as the next verse shows. Verse 32 will explain that for the believer it is a Father’s correction, not a judge’s condemnation. That distinction is coming in three verses and is worth holding onto until it arrives.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the bread and wine are magically dangerous. It means God takes seriously how his people treat his table and his church.

Look up. That makes the practical test easier than the theology. Before the plate reaches you, look at the row in front and the row behind, and ask whether there is anyone there you are quietly writing off: the tedious one, the difficult one, the one who has been rude to you, the one whose politics you find intolerable, the one who has less money or less education than you and whom you have never once invited home. Those people are the body of Christ. Failing to see it is what this verse calls eating judgment.

The modern danger. There is a further application that our own age needs more than Corinth did. The modern danger at communion is not that we despise the poor member across the aisle; it is that we have forgotten he is there at all. Communion has quietly become a private transaction: head bowed, eyes shut, a personal moment between the individual and his Saviour, with the congregation an incidental crowd. That is not what Paul is describing. He assumes a meal where people look at each other. The bread on the plate has already been described as one loaf making one body (10:17). To receive it as though the person beside you were scenery is to miss the point in a gentler way than the Corinthians did, but to miss it nonetheless. Discerning the body is not only refusing to despise; it is bothering to notice.

Do I need to understand the theology of the Supper perfectly to discern the body? No. You need to know what it is about and whom it is for: that the bread and cup set forth Christ’s body and blood given for sinners, that he gives himself to faith through them, and that everyone who eats with you is one body with you in him. A child or a new believer can grasp that. What the verse warns against is not limited understanding but careless contempt: eating as though the meal were ordinary, and as though the people around you did not matter.

In a sentence. For anyone who eats and drinks without recognising the Lord’s body brings judgment on himself by doing so.

On a Tuesday. When you take the Supper, remember the body of Christ given for you, and the body of Christ around you: your brothers and sisters. This week, invite home someone from church you would not naturally choose. That is discerning the body with the door open.

For worship. The body that was broken on the cross is the body that holds the church together. Christ did not die for a collection of individuals who happen to sit in the same room. He died for his bride, his body, his one people from every nation, and he loves each member of it with the same love. When we look around the table and see one another, we are seeing what his death has made: a family that no human power could have built and no division can finally destroy. Glory to the Head, who has made us members of one another.
verseByVerse.note: “Discerning the body” may mean recognising the Lord’s body in the Supper, or recognising the church as his body.

verseByVerse.quote: That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.

That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. A startling statement. Paul makes a direct connection between how this church was behaving at the table and the sickness and deaths in its membership. God’s discipline had come on the Corinthians in the form of illness and even death. Died is literally fallen asleep, the Christian word for believers’ death (15:18, 20). He does not soften it and neither should any commentary. But it must be handled with great care, because the wrong lesson drawn from this verse has caused enormous and needless pain.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every illness is a punishment for sin. Scripture warns against that assumption. It does not license anyone to look at a sick Christian, or a sick child, and go hunting for the hidden fault. Jesus faced that assumption head on and demolished it. Asked whose sin had caused a man’s blindness, he answered that it was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:2–3). Told about Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen crushed by a falling tower, he asked whether his hearers thought the victims were worse sinners than everyone else, and answered his own question: no (Luke 13:1–5). The whole book of Job exists to destroy the theory that suffering is a reliable index of guilt. But it does mean that God sometimes disciplines his people through physical affliction.

A specific diagnosis, not a general theory. What Paul has here is a specific diagnosis, given by an apostle about a particular congregation whose particular sin had a particular consequence. He knew what he knew because God had shown him. Nobody today has that information about anybody else’s illness, and to imitate the diagnosis without the revelation is not faith; it is cruelty with a Bible verse attached. So if you are reading this from a hospital bed, or after a funeral, take the plain sense of the whole passage: this text is not an accusation aimed at you. If God has something to say to you, he is well able to say it, and he does not do it in code.

But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. What the verse does teach is that God takes his table seriously enough to intervene, and that his interventions with his own children are not punishments. Verse 31 offers the way of avoiding them, and it is the simplest thing in the world. Judged ourselves (diakrinō) means discerned, assessed, the same root as discerning in verse 29. If we examined ourselves honestly and repented, God would not need to discipline us. Honest self-appraisal now spares the need for correction later. The person who deals with his own sin is not dealt with.

But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined. Verse 32 gives the doctrine that makes the whole passage bearable, indeed comfortable. Disciplined (paideuō) means trained, as a father trains a child (Hebrews 12:5–11). God’s judgment on his people is fatherly correction, not final condemnation. Two different things are named in one sentence, and they must never be confused. Discipline belongs to sons; condemnation belongs to the world. God does not punish his children for sin in the sense of making them pay for it, because the punishment fell somewhere else, on a hill, once. What he does with his children is train them, and training hurts.

So that we may not be condemned along with the world. The purpose of discipline is to keep believers from final condemnation. Read the logic and it is astonishing: God let believers in Corinth become ill and let some of them die, in order that they should not be condemned with the world. Even the death of some Corinthian believers was discipline, taking them home rather than letting them go on dishonouring Christ; they were not condemned. Even the severest thing in the passage is a rescue. The hand that struck was holding on (Revelation 3:19).

Does God still discipline believers with sickness today? He may, but you can almost never know that a particular illness is discipline, and you should never conclude it about someone else. Most sickness in a Christian’s life is simply part of living in a fallen world, and God uses it to draw us nearer to him rather than to correct a specific sin. The right response to any illness is not a frantic search for hidden guilt but the ordinary, healthy practice of verse 31: ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, confess what he brings to mind, and then rest in his fatherly care. Pray for healing, use the doctors he has provided, and trust that whatever he allows, he means for your good (Romans 8:28).

In a sentence. That is why many of you are weak and sick, and a number of you have died. If we were honest in judging ourselves, we would not come under judgment. But when the Lord judges us, he is disciplining us, so that we will not be condemned with the world.

On a Tuesday. Make honest self-judgment a habit, not an emergency. At the end of the day, ask God to search you, name what he shows you, confess it, and receive his forgiveness. And if a time of hardship comes, read Hebrews 12:5–11 slowly: whatever else is happening, you are being treated as a son.

For worship. The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives. His hand is heavy only on those he is holding. And the condemnation that would have fallen on us with the world fell instead on his own Son, who was judged without mercy so that we could be judged only with a Father’s love. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Even our sicknesses and our deaths are in the hands of a Father who will not let us go.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another— if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another. After the institution narrative, the warning and the discipline, the remedy turns out to be a single short command. Wait for one another. The verb (ekdechomai) means wait for, and also receive, welcome. Do not start until all have arrived, and share with one another. The poor and slaves who came late must be welcomed. There is a lesson in the smallness of it. Paul has taken the Corinthians to the upper room, to Jeremiah’s new covenant, to the return of Christ, and to graves in their own congregation, and what he asks them to do about it is to sit still until the slaves get off work. That is what repentance usually looks like. Not a programme. A small, concrete, slightly inconvenient change in behaviour on the next occasion. And notice who is being asked to wait. Not the poor, who were already waiting. The comfortable, the ones with the leisure to arrive early, are told to hold their hunger for an hour so that the meal can begin together. The cost falls on the people with something to give up, which is the direction love always travels in this letter (8:13; 9:19; 10:24).

If anyone is hungry, let him eat at home. If you cannot wait, eat beforehand. Paul is drawing the distinction the Corinthians had lost. There is nothing wrong with a good dinner; there is something badly wrong with treating the Lord’s table as one. Satisfy your appetite in your own kitchen. The church meal is not for satisfying appetite at others’ expense. When the church gathers, you are not there to be fed in that sense, and what you do at that table is not about you at all.

So that when you come together it will not be for judgment. Gathering should bring blessing, not discipline.

About the other things I will give directions when I come. A quiet ending, and a reminder that a letter is not the whole of pastoral care. There were other issues about the Supper, and Paul would not settle them at a distance; some things need a face. He is coming, and they know it, and that expectation is itself part of the correction. Not everything was written down, but everything necessary was (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean churches must separate the Lord’s Supper from fellowship meals. But many churches did so later, partly to avoid such abuses.

What does waiting for one another look like in a church today? It looks like a hundred small courtesies that say: you matter here. Holding the service until the bus from the care home arrives. Keeping a seat for the latecomer with three small children. Making sure the food at the church lunch reaches the back table before seconds are offered at the front. Not starting the meeting before the person who works shifts can get there. Choosing, at the Supper itself, to receive the bread together rather than as isolated individuals. None of these is dramatic. All of them preach the same sermon that a Corinthian host preached when he put his bread down and waited.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, when you gather to eat, wait for one another. If anyone is hungry, he should eat at home, so that your meetings do not lead to judgment. Paul will sort out the other matters when he comes.

On a Tuesday. Wait for one another: notice who arrives late or sits alone at church. Make room for them. And think of one small, concrete change that would make your church’s gathering more welcoming to those who have least, and suggest it, or simply begin doing it.

For worship. It is worth ending the chapter where the chapter ends: with a wealthy Corinthian sitting on a couch with food in front of him, hearing footsteps in the courtyard, and putting the bread back down until the man with the calloused hands has come in and sat down beside him. Nothing grand happened in that room. But the death of the Son of God was preached in it, by two men starting to eat at the same moment. And the same sermon is preached wherever a congregation eats together on the level. The Lord of glory took bread on the night he was handed over, gave thanks for it, and broke it for people who were about to abandon him, and he has been setting that table ever since, in cathedrals and in kitchens, for anyone who will come hungry. He waited for us, long and patiently, while we were still far off. Blessed be the Host who waits for his guests.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ.<sup>2</sup>Now I commend you because you remember me in everything and maintain the traditions even as I delivered them to you.<sup>3</sup>But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God.<sup>4</sup>Every man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head,<sup>5</sup>but every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head, since it is the same as if her head were shaven.<sup>6</sup>For if a wife will not cover her head, then she should cut her hair short. But since it is disgraceful for a wife to cut off her hair or shave her head, let her cover her head.<sup>7</sup>For a man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God, but woman is the glory of man.<sup>8</sup>For man was not made from woman, but woman from man.<sup>9</sup>Neither was man created for woman, but woman for man.<sup>10</sup>That is why a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels.<sup>11</sup>Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman;<sup>12</sup>for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God.<sup>13</sup>Judge for yourselves: is it proper for a wife to pray to God with her head uncovered?<sup>14</sup>Does not nature itself teach you that if a man wears long hair it is a disgrace for him,<sup>15</sup>but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory? For her hair is given to her for a covering.<sup>16</sup>If anyone is inclined to be contentious, we have no such practice, nor do the churches of God.<sup>17</sup>But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse.<sup>18</sup>For, in the first place, when you come together as a church, I hear that there are divisions among you. And I believe it in part,<sup>19</sup>for there must be factions among you in order that those who are genuine among you may be recognized.<sup>20</sup>When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.<sup>21</sup>For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk.<sup>22</sup>What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing? What shall I say to you? Shall I commend you in this? No, I will not.<sup>23</sup>For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread,<sup>24</sup>and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “This is my body, which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me.”<sup>25</sup>In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me.”<sup>26</sup>For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.<sup>27</sup>Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord.<sup>28</sup>Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup.<sup>29</sup>For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself.<sup>30</sup>That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died.<sup>31</sup>But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged.<sup>32</sup>But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world.<sup>33</sup>So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another—<sup>34</sup>if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home—so that when you come together it will not be for judgment. About the other things I will give directions when I come.

12.title: One Body, Many Gifts, One Spirit
12.overview:
Paul turns to another question from their letter: spiritual gifts. The Corinthians were especially impressed by dramatic gifts, above all speaking in tongues, and treated them as marks of superior spirituality. Their pagan background explains some of this. Greek religion prized ecstatic experience: the prophetess at Delphi spoke in a trance, and the worship of Dionysus involved frenzy. Being carried away was taken as a sign of the divine. Paul begins with a test that has nothing to do with excitement: the Spirit always leads people to confess that Jesus is Lord.

Then he insists that the gifts are many but the giver is one, the same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God, and that every gift is given for the good of the whole church, not for individual display. He uses the familiar picture of the body, a common image in ancient politics for a community whose members must cooperate. In Corinth the picture had a local twist: at the temple of Asclepius, the god of healing, worshippers left clay models of the body parts they wanted healed, hands, feet, eyes, ears, and many have been dug up. Paul says the church is one body with many parts, all baptised by one Spirit. No member can say it does not belong, and none can say it does not need the others; the weaker parts are indispensable, and all share suffering and honour. God has placed gifts in the church as he chose, and not everyone has the same gift. They should seek the greater gifts, and Paul is about to show them a better way still, the way of love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Gifts of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul does not want them to be ignorant about spiritual gifts. They remember that as pagans they were swept along and led off to speechless idols. So he gives a test: no one speaking by God’s Spirit says “Jesus is cursed”, and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except by the Holy Spirit. There are different kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit; different kinds of service, but the same Lord; different kinds of working, but the same God works all of them in everyone. To each person the Spirit is shown in some way for the common good. To one the Spirit gives a message of wisdom, to another a message of knowledge, to another faith, to another gifts of healing, to another miraculous powers, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish spirits, to another different kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who distributes them to each person as he decides.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Trinitarian Source of All Gifts

The explicit trinitarianism of vv. 4–6 is remarkable as a casual structural feature of Paul’s argument: he assumes the Trinity without arguing for it. Reformed pneumatology has always grounded the discussion of spiritual gifts in this trinitarian framework: the gifts are not the Spirit’s autonomous productions but the common work of Father, Son, and Spirit. This prevents both the elevation of the Spirit over Christ (a common charismatic error) and the neglect of the Spirit’s ongoing work (a temptation in cessationist circles): all genuine gifts are simultaneously the work of the triune God.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Corinthian believers were apparently competing for the most impressive gifts, using spiritual gifts as social capital. Paul’s trinitarian grounding removes the competition from its foundation: you cannot boast in a gift that was sovereignly given to you by the Spirit who gives as he wills. Now: The same gift-competitive dynamic operates in charismatic and Reformed communities alike, in different directions: charismatics sometimes elevate dramatic gifts (tongues, healing) over quiet ones; cessationists sometimes elevate intellectual gifts (teaching, wisdom) over practical ones. Paul’s list refuses both hierarchies.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 12–14 answers the Corinthians’ question about spiritual gifts. They prized the spectacular gifts, especially speaking in tongues, as signs of spiritual superiority, and this was dividing and disordering the church. Chapter 12 lays the foundation. The test of the Spirit’s work is not ecstasy but the confession that Jesus is Lord (vv. 1–3). The gifts are many but come from one Spirit, one Lord, one God; each is given for the common good, and the Spirit distributes them as he wills (vv. 4–11). The church is one body with many members, all baptised by one Spirit into it. Every part is needed, the weaker and less honoured most of all, so that there is no division but mutual care (vv. 12–26). God has appointed different gifts and roles; not all are apostles, not all speak in tongues. Desire the greater gifts, those that most build up, and Paul will show the way that surpasses them all: love (vv. 27–31). And beneath the whole chapter lies the life of the triune God, Father, Son and Spirit, in whom there has never been rivalry, and the risen Christ, who did not need a body and chose to have one.

Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers. The phrase now concerning has appeared several times in this letter (7:1; 8:1), and each time it signals that Paul is turning to a question the Corinthians themselves put to him in writing. So these three chapters are an answer to a letter, not an unprompted lecture. The church had asked about spiritual gifts. What follows is the longest sustained treatment of the subject in the Bible, and it will take three chapters and pause in the middle for a hymn. Spiritual gifts is literally spiritual things or spiritual people (pneumatika), perhaps the Corinthians’ own word for the gifts they valued and the people who had them. Paul will soon use a different word, charismata, grace-gifts (v. 4), shifting the focus from spirituality to grace.

I do not want you to be uninformed. They thought they knew about spiritual things. Paul says they need teaching.

You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols. This verse is easily skipped and should not be, because it establishes the ground on which everything else stands. Paul reminds them what they used to be, and he chooses one detail out of everything he could have chosen: the gods they served could not speak. The word (aphōna) is mute, dumb, voiceless. The Old Testament says this about idols with something close to contempt: they have mouths, but do not speak (Psalm 115:5; Habakkuk 2:18). Elijah said it on Carmel with open scorn while four hundred and fifty men shouted at a silence that lasted all day (1 Kings 18:26–29). Stand in one of those temples for a moment. There is incense, and a crowd, and drums, and a statue with painted eyes that has never said a word to anybody. The priest interprets. The oracle is ambiguous. Whatever comes out of the ecstasy, nobody can check it, because the god in the room has no voice with which to confirm or deny anything at all.

However you were led. The phrase is not an aside. Led (agō) means carried off, driven, swept along by forces beyond their control. It admits that something did lead them. Pagan worship in Corinth was not dull; it involved genuine ecstatic states, frenzy, trance and utterance, especially in the cults of Dionysus. The Corinthians had seen impressive spiritual phenomena long before they had ever heard of the Holy Spirit, and that is exactly the problem Paul is about to address. A congregation full of former pagans had arrived in the church already trained to believe that the more overwhelming an experience is, the more divine it must be. They were grading the Spirit’s gifts by the standard of the temple they had left. But the Holy Spirit does not work by mindless compulsion; the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets (14:32).

Intensity is not evidence. That is a warning worth carrying into any discussion of the Spirit, then or now. Something can be powerful, sincere, moving, and entirely unconnected to God; the idols were mute, but the worship in front of them was not quiet. Being carried away by powerful spiritual experiences is not proof of the Holy Spirit. The question is never how strongly a thing was felt. The next verse gives the question that matters.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all strong experiences are demonic. It means experience alone is not the test. The test is what it says about Jesus.

How can people of other religions have powerful spiritual experiences? Because human beings are made for God and are deeply spiritual creatures, and because there are real spiritual powers in the world besides the Holy Spirit (10:20). Ecstasy, visions, healings and trances are reported in many religions, and Scripture never pretends otherwise; Pharaoh’s magicians copied some of Moses’ signs (Exodus 7:11, 22). So the presence of a spiritual experience settles nothing by itself. A Christian should neither be impressed by such things nor frightened of them, but should ask Paul’s question: what does this say about Jesus Christ? The Spirit of God always points to him.

Are emotions in worship wrong, then? Not at all. The Psalms shout, weep, dance and clap; the early church was filled with joy; and a Christian who is moved to tears by the love of Christ is responding rightly. Paul is not against feeling. He is against using feeling as the measure of God’s presence. The healthiest worship engages the mind and the heart together (14:15): it understands what it is singing, and it feels the weight and wonder of it. Strong emotion that rises from the truth about Christ is a gift. Strong emotion pursued for its own sake is the temple of Dionysus with Christian words.

In a sentence. Now about the gifts of the Spirit, brothers and sisters, Paul does not want you to be ignorant. You remember that when you were pagans you were swept off, in one way or another, to idols that cannot speak.

On a Tuesday. Do not judge spirituality by how intense it feels. Judge it by whether it honours Jesus. Think of the most powerful spiritual experience you have had, and ask what it left you believing about Christ, and how it changed the way you live. That is the measure of it.

For worship. Our God is not mute. The idols have mouths and do not speak; the living God has spoken, by the prophets, and in these last days by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). He spoke the world into being, he spoke the law from Sinai, he spoke the gospel through apostles, and he speaks still, every time his word is read and preached. We are not left guessing in a smoky temple. We have a God who talks to his people, and whose every word is true. Blessed be the speaking God, and the Word made flesh.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore I want you to understand. Here is the first test of genuine spiritual activity, and its brilliance is that it moves the question from the experience to the content. Not how did it feel, but what did it say about Jesus?

That no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says Jesus is accursed. Accursed is anathema. Whether anyone in Corinth actually shouted it is debated. Perhaps someone in an ecstatic state had said it and the church was shaken. Perhaps unbelievers in the synagogues were cursing Jesus and pressing Christians to do the same, as Paul himself once did (Acts 26:11). Perhaps Paul is naming the worst thing imaginable in order to establish the principle at its extreme. Whatever the source, the rule holds at both ends: the Spirit never speaks against Christ, and no one comes to confess Christ without him.

And no one can say Jesus is Lord except in the Holy Spirit. Take this half slowly, because it is the sweeter half. Jesus is Lord was one of the earliest Christian confessions (Romans 10:9; Philippians 2:11). Anyone can pronounce the syllables; parrots and hypocrites manage it. Paul means the confession that comes from a person who means it, who has genuinely handed the government of his life to a crucified Jew from Nazareth, submitting to him as God and master. That sentence, meant, cannot be manufactured. It is not the product of good arguments, a strong upbringing, or an emotional evening. It is the fingerprint of God on a human heart. Every believer who confesses Jesus as Lord has the Spirit. There are no second-class Christians without the Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who mouths the words has the Spirit (Matthew 7:21–23). It means sincere confession is the Spirit’s work. The mark of the Spirit is a Christ-centred life, not spectacular gifts.

What does Lord mean here? More than master or sir. The Greek word is kyrios, and it is the word the Greek translation of the Old Testament used for the name of God himself, the LORD. To call Jesus Lord in a church full of Jews and Gentiles who read that Bible was to give him the name that is above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). It was also costly. In the Roman world the cry was Caesar is Lord, and Christians who refused to say it, or who said Jesus instead, were sometimes killed for it. So the confession means three things at once: Jesus is God, Jesus has the right to rule me, and Jesus outranks every other power that claims my loyalty.

How do I know I am not simply talked into this? It is a question that troubles thoughtful Christians more than they usually say, and here is one honest place to look. If Christ is genuinely your Lord, not merely your preference or your heritage, then according to this verse somebody did that to you, and the somebody was the third person of the Trinity. The most ordinary Christian confession in the world is a supernatural event.

The practical use of the test. Corinth wanted a way to tell the Spirit’s work from spiritual theatre, and Paul gives them one that requires no special insight: listen to what is being said about Jesus. The Spirit’s whole business is to glorify Christ: he will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you (John 16:14). So a movement, a meeting, a teacher or a book that makes much of the Spirit and comparatively little of Christ has failed the only test the New Testament gives, however remarkable the phenomena. And a quiet congregation where Christ is honoured and trusted has passed it, however unremarkable the phenomena (1 John 4:2–3).

In a sentence. So Paul wants you to know that no one speaking by God’s Spirit says, “Jesus be cursed,” and no one can truly say, “Jesus is Lord,” except by the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Say it today, slowly and meaning it: Jesus is Lord. Then ask what in your week he is not yet allowed to rule, and hand it over. And when you next weigh a teacher or a book, ask first: how big is Christ in this?

For worship. The Spirit is the least self-advertising person in the universe. He is like a floodlight trained on a building at night: doing all the work, entirely unlooked at, and content that what people see is the building. If you can say Jesus is Lord from your heart, the Holy Spirit has been at work in you, opening blind eyes, softening a hard heart, and turning your face to the Son. Glory to the Spirit who glorifies Christ, and glory to the Christ whom every tongue will one day confess as Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
verseByVerse.note: “Jesus is Lord” was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.

Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit. Three sentences with the same shape, and the shape is the argument. Variety on one side, sameness on the other, three times over. Paul is doing something more than making a point about unity; he is showing where the unity comes from. Varieties (diaireseis) means distributions, different allotments. And gifts is charismata, from the word for grace: a gift is grace made specific, grace with a shape. The Spirit gives them.

And there are varieties of service, but the same Lord. Service is diakoniai, where we get the word deacon: a gift is not an ornament but a job. The gifts are for serving, under one Lord, Jesus.

And there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone. Activities is energēmata, from which we get energy: workings, effects. It is God actually doing something through a person, not a talent the person owns and operates. God the Father works through all.

The Trinity. Look at the three persons named. The same Spirit, the same Lord, the same God. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, laid out in one breath, in a paragraph about church squabbles, and Paul does not stop to explain or defend it. That is worth noticing in itself. The doctrine of the Trinity is sometimes presented as a late invention of arguing bishops. Here it is, twenty-odd years after the crucifixion, so settled in the apostolic mind that it can be used as a passing illustration in a letter about who is showing off in church. The gifts come from the triune God, and each person of the Trinity is involved in every gift. Unity in diversity in the church reflects unity in diversity in God.

Why the competition collapses. Put the three nouns together and the Corinthian competition collapses on the spot. If a gift is grace, nobody earned it. If it is service, it was never given for display. And if it is God working, then boasting about it is as odd as a chisel congratulating itself on the furniture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts, services and activities are three separate categories. They are three ways of describing the same thing: gifts of grace, used in service, by God’s power.

Should I pray to the Holy Spirit? You may, and the church has done so for centuries in hymns such as Come, Holy Ghost. The Spirit is fully God, and he may be worshipped and addressed. But the ordinary pattern of New Testament prayer is to pray to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit (Ephesians 2:18). And Paul’s three sentences quietly settle the worry behind the question, whether attention paid to one person is attention withheld from another. There is no dividing them up, because they are never working separately. The gift in your hands was given by the Spirit, is a service rendered to the Lord, and is God at work in you. One act, three persons, no seams. Whomever you address, you are speaking to the one God.

In a sentence. There are different kinds of gifts, but one Spirit gives them; different kinds of service, but one Lord is served; different kinds of working, but one God is at work in all of them in everyone.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test worth running on any church, including a healthy one. When the gifted people in a congregation gather, is the conversation about what God is doing, or about who is doing it? The two sound similar and they are not the same. Paul’s three sentences make the second sort of conversation not merely uncharitable but incoherent. Next time you talk about your church, try to speak of what God has done before you speak of who did it.

For worship. Look at what this means about the God being described. Within his own life there has never been a moment of competition. The Father is not diminished by the Son’s glory; the Spirit does not resent being the one nobody looks at; nothing in that fellowship has ever needed to be negotiated. And out of that life, unhurried, unthreatened, entirely at peace with itself, came a world, and a cross, and a church full of quarrelling people in a Greek port, handed grace with a shape and set to work. Thank the Father, the Son and the Spirit for every gift in your church, including those very different from yours, because every one of them came from the same overflowing life.
verseByVerse.note: Spirit, Lord and God appear together: the gifts come from the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

To each is given. Thirteen words in this verse, and two of them settle questions that trouble a great many Christians. To each. Not to some. Not to the impressive. Not to the ordained or the articulate or the ones who were converted dramatically. Every believer in Corinth, and this was a church containing slaves, dockworkers, and people Paul had already described as not wise, not powerful, not of noble birth (1:26), had received a manifestation of the Spirit. Every believer has received at least one gift. There are no giftless Christians. If you belong to Christ, something has been put into your hands. And is given: received, not earned.

Nobody simply attends. This is worth pressing, because a lot of people quietly believe otherwise about themselves. The usual reasoning runs: I am not a teacher, I do not sing, I have never led anything, I would not know what to say to a stranger about the gospel, therefore I am one of the ones who simply attends. This verse says that is not a category. It does not say every Christian has a prominent gift. It says every Christian has one.

The manifestation of the Spirit. Manifestation (phanerōsis) means display, showing. Each gift is a way the Spirit shows himself at work. When a member of your church comforts the grieving well, or keeps the accounts honestly, or explains a passage so that it opens, you are watching the invisible Spirit become visible.

For the common good. There is the purpose, and it is the phrase that ruins gift competition permanently. The word (sympherō) means for benefit, what helps. The Spirit does not hand out gifts as personal enrichment, spiritual souvenirs, or evidence of standing. A gift is given to one person for the benefit of other people. It is not the reward of the recipient; it is the property of the congregation, held in his hands for a while. A gift used for self-display has not merely been used badly; it has been used for the opposite of its purpose. This is the key to chapters 12–14.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer has a spectacular gift. Many gifts are quiet: helping, giving, showing mercy (Romans 12:6–8).

How do I find out what mine is? That is the practical question every honest reader wants answered, and it is usually left vague when it should not be. Not, in the first place, by introspection. The New Testament does tell a Christian to examine himself, but about his standing before God and his conduct at the Lord’s table (11:28; 2 Corinthians 13:5), never about which gift he has been given. Gifts are discovered in use, not in analysis. Four things will do more than any questionnaire. First, start serving something, anything the church actually needs, and notice what happens. Second, watch for the thing that leaves other people strengthened rather than merely impressed; that is the mark of a gift as against a talent. Third, ask two or three Christians who know you well and will tell you the truth, because gifts are far easier to see from outside than from inside. Fourth, notice what you keep being asked to do; congregations are usually better at spotting gifts than the people who have them. And notice what is not on that list: whether you enjoy it, and whether you are naturally good at it. Both are useful signs and neither is decisive. This is a manifestation of the Spirit, not a personality test, and the Spirit has been known to work through people who found the work difficult all their lives.

What if I am too old, ill or worn out to do anything? Then your gift has not been taken away; it may simply have changed shape. Some of the most fruitful members of any church are those who can no longer leave the house: who pray through the church list every morning, who write a card to the grieving, who telephone the lonely, who receive visitors with such faith and patience that the visitors go home strengthened. Suffering borne with trust in Christ is itself a ministry to everyone who sees it (2 Corinthians 1:3–6). The common good does not require energy. It requires a member who belongs to the body and is still, in whatever way is left, offering what God has given.

In a sentence. To every believer the Spirit shows himself through some gift, given for the good of all.

On a Tuesday. Your gift is not for you. Ask: who in my church needs what God has given me? Then do one thing about it this week. And if you have been telling yourself you are one of the ones who simply attends, retire that sentence. It is not true of anyone the Spirit has touched.

For worship. The Spirit is not stingy. He did not give gifts to the elite and leave the rest of the church to watch; he gave to each, the slave and the dockworker as much as the teacher and the host. Every Christian is a place where God has chosen to show himself. And every gift points back to the first and greatest gift, from which all the others flow: the Father’s gift of his Son, and the Son’s gift of his Spirit. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift.

verseByVerse.quote: For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,

For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom. The list begins, and Paul offers no definitions, which suggests the Corinthians knew what he meant. We have to work a little harder, and it is worth doing rather than hurrying past the names. The utterance of wisdom is, in the Greek, a word of wisdom (logos sophias): something said, not merely something possessed. Wisdom in this letter is not cleverness; Paul has spent two chapters saying that the wisdom of God is a crucified man (1:23–24; 2:6–7). So this gift is the ability to speak God’s wisdom, the capacity to say the thing that applies the gospel to the situation in front of you. Everyone has met it: the believer who is not especially learned but who, in a crisis, says the one sentence that helps.

And to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit. A word of knowledge (logos gnōseōs) is its companion: grasping the truth of God and being able to put it into words that hold. It is the ability to explain the truths of the faith, probably close to teaching. The Corinthians loved knowledge (8:1); Paul reminds them that even knowledge is a gift, not an achievement.

To another faith by the same Spirit. This is puzzling at first, since every Christian has faith. Paul must mean something beyond saving faith, which he never treats as a special endowment for some. The best sense is a special gift of faith: a particular God-given confidence for a particular thing, the believer who is certain God will provide for a work when everyone else is doing sums, and is proved right. It is the sort of faith Jesus described as moving mountains, and Paul will use exactly that image in the next chapter (13:2; Matthew 17:20).

To another gifts of healing by the one Spirit. Both nouns are plural in the Greek, which is itself instructive. Not the gift of healing, a standing power a man carries around, but gifts of healings: particular acts of mercy, given occasion by occasion, the ability to bring God’s healing in specific cases, as the apostles did (Acts 3:6–8; 5:15–16; 28:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean this is a complete list of gifts, or that each person has only one. Paul gives several lists, all different (Romans 12; Ephesians 4; 1 Peter 4).

Does God still heal? Yes. He is not less able than he was, and Christians should pray for the sick expectantly and without embarrassment, because they are told to: James tells the sick to call the elders to pray over them (James 5:14–15). That is different from a gift by which a person could heal at will, as the apostles did to confirm their message (Acts 5:15–16; 2 Corinthians 12:12). That sign gift belonged to the apostolic foundation and has ceased with it. So a believer should pray for the sick with confidence in God, and treat claims to a healing ministry with caution, testing them by Scripture and by what actually happens.

And does he always? Plainly not, and the New Testament is remarkably candid about it. Paul left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20). Epaphroditus nearly died, and Paul calls his recovery a mercy rather than an entitlement (Philippians 2:27). Timothy had a recurring stomach complaint and got advice about wine, not a healing (1 Timothy 5:23). And Paul himself asked three times for his own thorn to be removed and was told no, with a reason: my grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). That is enormously important for anyone who has prayed and not been healed, or who has been told that the failure was theirs. If the apostle who raised a young man from the dead at Troas (Acts 20:9–12) could not heal his own friend or himself, then unhealed sickness in a Christian is not evidence of a lack of faith. It is evidence that the gifts are given as he wills, and that the will in question is wiser than ours.

What is the difference between a spiritual gift and a natural talent? Sometimes very little on the surface, and a great deal underneath. God gives natural abilities to everyone, believers and unbelievers alike: a good mind, a fine voice, a head for figures. A spiritual gift is an ability the Spirit gives or takes up and uses, in a believer, for building up Christ’s body. Often the Spirit takes a natural talent and turns it to new ends, so that a teacher becomes a teacher of the word. Sometimes he gives what was never there before. The real difference is in the fruit: a talent impresses, a gift strengthens. When people go away from your service closer to Christ, rather than merely admiring you, the Spirit is at work.
