In a sentence. To one person the Spirit gives a message of wisdom, to another, by the same Spirit, a message of knowledge, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit,

On a Tuesday. Pray for the sick in your church this week, by name, expecting God to hear. And thank God for those in your church who speak wisely and explain the faith clearly; tell one of them how their words helped you.

For worship. Every gift on this list is a ray from one sun. The wisdom comes from Christ, who has become to us wisdom from God (1:30). The knowledge is the knowledge of the glory of God in his face. The faith rests on his faithfulness. And the healings are foretastes of the day when he will wipe every tear from every eye, and there shall be no more death, nor mourning, nor crying, nor pain. Whether he heals now or later, he heals, and every one of his people will rise whole. Blessed be the Great Physician, whose grace is sufficient.

verseByVerse.quote: to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.
verseByVerse.commentary:
to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues. All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.

To another the working of miracles. Five more gifts, and three of them will occupy the whole of chapter 14, so a short account here will do. The working of miracles is literally workings of powers (energēmata dynameōn): acts of power beyond healing, such as Paul striking Elymas blind (Acts 13:11) or raising Eutychus (Acts 20:9–12).

To another prophecy. Prophecy in the New Testament is not primarily prediction. It is speaking a message revealed by God for the church’s strengthening, encouragement and comfort (14:3), and it could lay bare the secrets of a heart so that an outsider fell down and worshipped (14:24–25). Crucially, Paul assumes it must be tested. Let the others weigh what is said (14:29) is not a thing anyone would say about Scripture. So whatever prophecy was in Corinth, it stood under the apostolic word and never beside it, and no congregational prophecy of this kind ever added a line to the Bible.

To another the ability to distinguish between spirits. The companion gift, and its presence in the list is telling: Paul assumes that not everything claiming to be from God is from God, and that some believers were given a nose for the difference. It is discerning which messages and powers are from God and which from false spirits (1 John 4:1), since prophecies needed testing (14:29). Verse 3 has already supplied the public test; this is the discernment that goes with it.

To another various kinds of tongues. Speaking in languages one has not learned, by the Spirit, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:4–11). These are the gifts Corinth prized most and understood least, and chapter 14 is Paul’s careful, unhurried treatment of them. It is enough to note here that he includes them without a hint of scorn; they are on the list, given by the Spirit, and he will say himself that he speaks in tongues more than any of them (14:18). Yet he lists them last, here and in verse 28, perhaps deliberately, since the Corinthians ranked them first.

To another the interpretation of tongues. The ability to explain what was spoken in a tongue, so the church could understand (14:13, 27–28).

All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills. Then the closing sentence, which governs the whole chapter. The Spirit decides. As he wills (bouletai): the Spirit is a person with a will, not a force or a power to be switched on. No one can demand a particular gift or boast in having one. There is real comfort in that clause and real rebuke. The rebuke is to anyone who thinks a gift reflects credit on its holder. The comfort is for anyone who has begged for a gift and not received it, and has been told by someone confident that the fault lies in his faith. The distribution is the Spirit’s free act. He is not a machine that dispenses on demand, and he has never given anybody grounds for despising a Christian who lacks something.

Where Christians differ: do the miraculous gifts continue? Continuationists hold that all these gifts are available today. Verdict: The gifts of miracles, healings, prophecy and tongues served as signs confirming the apostolic message while Scripture was being given (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). With the foundation of apostles and prophets laid and the canon closed, these revelatory and sign gifts have ceased as ordinary gifts in the church. God still heals in answer to prayer and does wonders as he pleases, and the gifts of wisdom, knowledge, faith, discernment, teaching, serving and mercy continue. This cessationist view is held charitably toward continuationist brothers and sisters, with whom we share the gospel.

Held with charity. Christians have differed over this for centuries, and both convictions are held by people who love the Bible and each other. The cessationist view rests on the church being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), and the question is taken up properly at 13:8–12. What this verse settles, whichever way a reader lands, is that no one may look down on another Christian over it. The Spirit apportions as he wills, and that clause has never yet been amended by a committee on either side.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God no longer works powerfully. It means his normal way now is through the word, prayer and the ordinary gifts.

What about Christians today who say they speak in tongues? Treat them as brothers and sisters, not as suspects. Many love Christ deeply, and the experience they describe is sincere. A cessationist will believe that what they experience is not the New Testament gift of real languages given as a sign, but a form of prayerful speech or devotion; a continuationist will see it differently. Both can agree on what Paul himself requires in chapter 14: that nothing in the church should be unintelligible without interpretation, that everything must be done decently and in order, and that no gift may ever be made the badge of the Spirit’s presence (v. 30). Where those rules are kept, the disagreement need not divide fellowship in the gospel.

What if someone says God told me? Listen carefully and humbly, and test it. God does guide his people, by his word, by wise counsel, by the circumstances he arranges, and by the Spirit’s inward work in their hearts and consciences. But an impression is not a revelation, and it never carries the authority of Scripture. If what someone believes God told them contradicts Scripture, it is not from God. If it agrees with Scripture, its authority comes from Scripture, not from the impression. And no one may bind your conscience with a word they say God gave them about your life. The canon is closed, and in it God has given us everything we need for life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3; 2 Timothy 3:16–17).

In a sentence. to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another discernment of spirits, to another speaking in different kinds of tongues, and to another the interpretation of tongues. All of these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who gives them to each person as he chooses.

On a Tuesday. Accept the gifts the Spirit has given you, without envy of others’ gifts. He chose wisely. And if you hold a firm view on the miraculous gifts, ask whether you hold it in a way that lets you embrace as brothers those who disagree. The Spirit who gave the gifts also gave the love that must govern them.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is Lord, the giver of life, and he gives as he wills. He does not need our permission, our programmes or our techniques. He laid the foundation of the church through apostles and prophets, with signs and wonders that confirmed their word, and he has built on it ever since with the steady power of the gospel preached, believed and lived. The same Spirit who rushed upon Pentecost now indwells the humblest believer, and his greatest work is still the one he never stops doing: taking dead hearts and making them alive to Christ. Every conversion is a miracle, and he is still working them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The body is one, though it has many parts, and so it is with Christ. All believers, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, were baptised by one Spirit into one body and were all given the one Spirit to drink. The body is not one part but many. If the foot said it does not belong because it is not a hand, it would still belong; if the ear said it does not belong because it is not an eye, it would still belong. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell? God has placed each part in the body just as he wanted. If all were one part, there would be no body. As it is, there are many parts but one body. The eye cannot tell the hand it does not need it, nor the head the feet. In fact the parts that seem weaker are essential, the parts we think less honourable we treat with more honour, and our less presentable parts are treated with more modesty, while the presentable ones need no special care. God has put the body together, giving greater honour to the parts that lacked it, so that there should be no division in the body, but its parts should care equally for each other. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part shares its joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Body of Christ: Ecclesiology and Soteriology United

Paul’s body metaphor is not merely sociological (a useful way to describe community life) but soteriological: the church is the body of Christ because the Spirit has baptised all believers into the one body of the crucified and risen Lord (v. 13). The union is real — not metaphorical — which is why the suffering of one member is genuinely felt by the whole (v. 26). The theology of the body of Christ is the foundation of Paul’s entire ethic of community: you cannot be indifferent to the suffering of a fellow member of Christ’s body any more than your left hand can be indifferent to the pain in your right foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had produced both contempt (the tongues-speakers dismissing those with lesser gifts) and despair (those with lesser gifts feeling excluded). Paul’s body metaphor addresses both directly: the despairers are told they belong; the contemptuous are told they need those they despise. Now: Every church community has its impressive and its unimpressive members by the world’s standards. Paul’s insight is that the one who seems indispensable and the one who seems marginal are both placed by the same God — and the functioning of the body requires both.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.

For just as the body is one and has many members. The image arrives, and Paul will spend the rest of the chapter on it. One body, many parts. The body was a familiar picture in ancient political writing for a united society, but Paul gives it a twist nobody had given it before.

So it is with Christ. Notice how the first sentence ends, because he does not finish it the way anyone expects. The natural conclusion is so it is with the church. What he writes is so it is with Christ. That is not a slip. The church is not merely like a body; it is his body (v. 27; Ephesians 1:22–23), so united to him that it bears his name, and Paul means the identification more literally than most of us are comfortable with. It is what the risen Lord said to a man on the Damascus road who had never laid a finger on him personally: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4). Saul had been arresting Christians in Jerusalem. Christ counted it as an assault on himself. The man who heard that sentence is the man writing this one.

For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body. In one Spirit, or by one Spirit. Two of Paul’s favourite words, all and one, are doing heavy work here, and they answer a question many Christians have been troubled by: is there a second experience after conversion, a baptism in the Spirit, which some believers have and others lack? Paul’s sentence is hard to get round. We were all baptised into one body, and he is writing to a church whose spiritual life was a shambles, with factions, a man in gross immorality, lawsuits and drunkenness at the Lord’s table. If any congregation could have been described as second-class in the Spirit, it was this one, and he says all of them have had it. Baptism in the Spirit, in this verse, is not an advanced stage. It is what happened to every Christian when he became one. It is the entrance, not the upgrade. This is the Spirit’s work of uniting us to Christ, of which water baptism is the sign.

Jews or Greeks, slaves or free. See what the Spirit does with the categories. Those were the deepest divisions in that world, ethnic and social, religious and economic, the two that still do most of the damage. The Spirit does not abolish the differences; a Jew was still a Jew and a slave still went back to his master. He does something better. He puts them in one body, so that the differences remain and stop being walls (Galatians 3:27–28; Ephesians 2:14–16).

And all were made to drink of one Spirit. The Spirit is like water poured out and drunk, the picture the prophets and Jesus himself used (Isaiah 44:3; John 7:37–39). All believers have drunk deeply of him; he is not sprinkled on the surface but taken in.

Where Christians differ: baptism in the Spirit. Pentecostals often teach that baptism in the Spirit is a second experience after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues. Verdict: Paul says all believers, including the immature Corinthians, were baptised in the one Spirit into the one body. Spirit baptism happens at conversion; it is the Spirit’s work of joining us to Christ and his body. It is not a second blessing for some. Believers may and should seek to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), which is different from the once-for-all baptism in the Spirit.

The hunger behind the question. That should be said clearly, and something else should be said just as clearly, because brothers and sisters who use the phrase differently are usually reaching for something real. Scripture plainly teaches repeated, fresh, powerful fillings of the Spirit after conversion. The same believers in Acts who were filled in chapter 2 are filled again in chapter 4 (Acts 4:31), and Christians are commanded to go on being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18), a present tense, a continuous thing, not a single event. So the hunger behind the question is right and should not be shamed. A Christian may and should ask for more of God. What he need not ask for is admission to a body he has already been baptised into.

What it does not mean. It does not mean water baptism unites us to Christ by itself. The Spirit does; water baptism signifies and seals it.

Then what is water baptism for? If the Spirit joins us to Christ at conversion, water baptism is the outward sign the Lord commanded for those who have been joined to him (Matthew 28:19). It pictures what the Spirit has done: washing, death to the old life, burial and rising with Christ (Romans 6:3–4). It is the believer’s public confession of faith and his entrance into the visible church. It is also a means God uses to strengthen faith and assure his people that they belong to him. That is why this app holds that baptism belongs to those who have professed faith in Christ, following the 1689 London Baptist Confession, while honouring paedobaptist brothers who baptise the children of believers. Baptism does not make anyone a Christian. It is how the Lord marks out those who are.

In a sentence. A body is one unit made of many parts, and though its parts are many they form one body; so it is with Christ. For we were all baptised by one Spirit into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, slaves or free, and we were all given the one Spirit to drink.

On a Tuesday. Pray today to be filled with the Spirit, not for a badge, but so that you may love Christ more and serve his body better. And look at the Christian you find most different from yourself, in background, race, class or politics: the Spirit has put you in one body with him. Treat him like it.

For worship. Christ is not a head without a body, and the church is not a body without a head. He has joined himself to his people so closely that what is done to them is done to him, and he has joined them to each other by the one Spirit they all drink. Jew and Greek, slave and free, the Corinthian docker and the reader of this page, all have drunk from the same river. Thank God that you were baptised by the Spirit into Christ’s body, together with believers of every race and class, and that no power in heaven or earth can cut you off from it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the body does not consist of one member but of many. If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body. And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.

For the body does not consist of one member but of many. Diversity is essential to a body. Paul now gives the body a voice, and the first thing it says is a complaint about itself.

If the foot should say, Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body. It is worth noticing whom Paul addresses first. Not the proud; they come at verse 21. The discouraged. The image was familiar: the Roman Menenius Agrippa was said to have calmed a rebellion of the common people with a famous fable of the body’s members refusing to feed the stomach. Paul uses it first for those who feel inferior: the foot envying the hand, the ear envying the eye. Listen to the logic of the foot. It has looked at the hand, admired what the hand can do, concluded that it cannot do any of it, and drawn the inference: therefore I am not really part of this. The reasoning feels like humility. It is not. It is a verdict passed on God’s arrangement by a body part that has decided it knows better.

That would not make it any less a part of the body. Paul answers with a shrug, and the reply is beautifully unimpressed. The foot’s membership is not a matter of the foot’s opinion. Feelings of not belonging do not detach anybody from Christ’s body, any more than a man’s low view of his own left foot detaches it from his leg. Belonging was settled by the Spirit’s baptism in verse 13, and it is not reopened every time a member feels unimpressive. Your feelings of inferiority do not change the fact that you belong. Those without spectacular gifts are no less part of Christ’s body.

What it does not mean. It does not mean feelings of inadequacy are sinful. It means they are untrue. Every believer belongs.

The foot talking. This is worth stating plainly for the sort of Christian who reads a passage on gifts with a sinking heart. If your reasoning has ever run: I cannot teach, I cannot sing, I have no story worth telling, so I am really just making up the numbers, that is the foot talking, and the apostle’s response is not to reassure you about your abilities. It is to tell you that the question of belonging was never yours to settle.

Comparison looks upward. Notice the comparison that started it. The foot did not compare itself to a foot. It compared itself to a hand, which is precisely the trick that makes the comparison useless and painful at once. Nobody is ever discouraged by comparing himself with someone doing the same job; discouragement comes from measuring yourself against a gift you were never given and then treating the shortfall as a personal failing. Comparison almost always looks upward and almost never sideways.

The quiet withdrawal. There is a practical consequence, and it is one of the quiet tragedies of church life. The foot in this parable does not merely feel bad. It withdraws. People who conclude they do not belong stop offering, stop coming forward, and eventually stop coming; and because they leave slowly and apologetically, nobody chases them. If that has been your own drift, the verse is addressed to you directly, and its answer is not a compliment but a fact: your leaving would not make you any less a part of the body, and it would leave the body without a foot. And there is something for everyone else in it too. The discouraged rarely announce themselves. They do not say I do not belong here; they say they are busy that week. A congregation that waits to be told will never find out. Which is why the ordinary work of asking a quiet member what he is finding hard, and meaning the question, is not small talk. It is body maintenance.

What if my church really does not seem to want me? Sometimes the problem is not the foot’s feelings but the body’s neglect, and it is right to say so. If you have offered to serve and been passed over, or been made to feel unwelcome, that is a failure the church must answer for, and verses 21–26 are written to it. But the answer to being overlooked is rarely to withdraw. Speak to an elder honestly and without bitterness; ask where help is actually needed; look for the people on the edges like yourself and befriend them. If after real effort a church persistently refuses to receive you, it may be right to seek another, but go to belong somewhere, not to belong nowhere. You are a member of Christ’s body, and you need a local expression of it, as it needs you.

In a sentence. The body is made of many parts, not one. If the foot says, “I am not a hand, so I don’t belong to the body,” it does not stop being part of the body. And if the ear says, “I am not an eye, so I don’t belong to the body,” it does not stop being part of the body.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you have nothing to offer your church, you are wrong. You belong, and you are needed. This week, offer to do one thing, however small. And if you know a member who has quietly started to drift, send a message today asking how they are.

For worship. Christ does not keep a list of his members ranked by usefulness. He bought every one of them with the same blood, and he knows the foot and the hand by name. The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one who has wandered, and he does not wait for it to apologise. Whatever you think of yourself, he has thought of you, and placed you in his body, and he will not let you go.
verseByVerse.note: The body was a familiar image in ancient politics for a united community.

verseByVerse.quote: If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?

If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? Paul argues by absurdity, and it is worth letting the absurdity land rather than treating it as a figure of speech. Picture it. A body that is one enormous eye. Not a better body, but a monster, and a helpless one, unable to hear a shout or smell smoke. Which is exactly what Corinth was trying to become. If tongues is the true mark of the Spirit, then the ideal congregation is one where everybody speaks in tongues and nothing else happens. Paul says: look at what you are asking for. A church where every member has the same gift is not a super-church. It is a church that has lost the ability to do everything that gift does not do.

If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell? Diversity is not a problem to be fixed; it is necessary. The argument works just as well against the opposite error, which is more common in sober congregations. A church where everyone is a teacher is a church that talks and never visits. A church of activists is one that never thinks. A church that has quietly decided which sort of Christian it approves of, and every church has one, is a body growing a second eye where an ear should be. The point is not that variety is pleasant. It is that variety is functional. God did not scatter different gifts around a congregation for the sake of interest. He did it because the work requires all of them, and no member has been given a gift that makes the others optional.

Senses the eye does not have. There is a second thing hiding in the two senses Paul names. Hearing and smell are not alternative ways of doing what the eye does; they are ways of knowing what the eye cannot know. An eye cannot detect a gas leak. This is why a church with a narrow range of gifts is not merely less varied but genuinely less aware: there are things about its own situation that it has no organ to perceive. The pastoral instinct that notices a family is in trouble, the practical instinct that notices the accounts are drifting, the discerning instinct that notices a teacher has begun to say something slightly wrong: these are different senses, and a body without them is not simply plainer. It is walking about with its eyes open and no idea what is happening. That is why the members a church finds least congenial are so often the ones it most needs. The person whose questions are awkward, whose concerns are always about the thing nobody else is worried about, whose temperament grates, may be the congregation’s sense of smell, and a body that silences him will not notice the smoke.

What it does not mean. It does not mean some gifts are unimportant. It means all are necessary.

Is it wrong for a church to be made up mostly of one kind of person? It is not wrong for a church to reflect the place where it is; a village church will look like its village. But it is wrong for a church to be content to be one kind of person, or to arrange itself so that others feel they do not fit. The gospel creates a people out of every tribe and language and nation (Revelation 7:9), and the local church is meant to be a foretaste of that. A church that finds it has become all one age, one class or one background should ask, without despair, whom it has been failing to reach or keep, and pray and work to widen its welcome.

In a sentence. If the whole body were an eye, how would it hear? If it were all ear, how would it smell?

On a Tuesday. Here is a test any congregation can run and few do. Look at who has left over the last five years, and who has quietly stopped coming. Then ask what kinds of people they were. If they were all one kind, the church has been growing a monoculture, and it will have lost the sense that those members carried before it noticed the loss. And personally: think of the member whose concerns most irritate you, and ask what he might be seeing that you cannot.

For worship. Thank God that your church is not made of people just like you. The God who made the eye and the ear, the hand and the foot, delights in variety; he never made two snowflakes, two faces or two saints alike. And his wisdom is many-sided, displayed through the church to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Ephesians 3:10). Every different member is another facet of that wisdom. A church full of different people, held together by one Lord, is a sight the angels look at with wonder.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. If all were a single member, where would the body be? As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.

But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose. Here is the answer to the discouraged foot, and it is not encouragement. It is doctrine. God arranged. The verb (tithēmi) is deliberate placement: the word for setting something where you have decided it should go. And then, in case anyone should think this happened at the level of general policy, Paul adds a phrase that makes it personal: each one of them. Not the body arranged in general, with individuals falling where they may. Each member, placed. Your place in the church is God’s decision, not an accident (v. 11).

What that means for an ordinary Christian. Sit with it. The gift you have was chosen for you. The gift you do not have was withheld on purpose. The congregation you are in, with its particular needs and its particular gaps, is the place you were set down. None of it is a leftover arrangement after the interesting decisions were made elsewhere. As he chose is the same note struck at verse 11, and it is the doctrine of God’s sovereign choosing applied to the most everyday thing imaginable: who does what on a Sunday. It cuts in two directions at once, which is how you can tell it is being used properly. To the person who is proud of his gift: you were handed it, and a man who is proud of a present has misunderstood the transaction. To the person who wishes he were somebody else: your wish is a complaint about the placement, and the one who did the placing knew exactly what he was doing.

A smaller life than you would have chosen. There is a particular ache this speaks to, and it is worth naming because most people carry it privately. It is the sense of having been assigned a smaller life than the one you would have chosen: a quieter role, a less visible service, a set of abilities that will never be remarked on. That is not a mistake in the distribution. The body has parts nobody has ever photographed, and it dies without them.

If all were a single member, where would the body be? A single member is not a body.

As it is, there are many parts, yet one body. Then the closing line, and it is the whole doctrine of the church in a handful of words. Unity and diversity together. Not many parts that ought to become one; many parts that already are. Unity is not the church’s achievement. It is the church’s starting condition, and everything Paul asks of the Corinthians is simply that they stop contradicting what is already true of them (Ephesians 4:3–4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean you cannot grow in your gifts or seek new ways to serve. It means you should accept your place with contentment. And one caution, since this doctrine can be turned into a cushion. God arranged is not a licence to refuse anything you have not been specially equipped for. Plenty of what a church needs done is not a gift at all; it is simply obedience, and it is required of everyone. Every Christian is commanded to give, to pray, to show hospitality, to speak the truth in love, to bear with difficult people, and to tell others about Christ, whether or not any of it comes easily. Nobody is excused from the ordinary duties on the grounds that generosity is not his gifting. Gifts describe how you will serve most fruitfully. They never describe the limits of what you will do. A hand that declines to help because carrying is properly the shoulder’s work has misread the whole chapter.

Should I move churches if my gifts are not being used? Rarely for that reason alone. God placed you, and the first question is whether you have offered what you have where you are. Gifts are often not used because nobody knows about them, and the remedy is to speak to your elders and start serving where help is needed, even in ways that are not your strongest. Some of the best gifts in a church grow out of years of doing whatever needed doing. There can be good reasons to move: a family move, a church that has departed from the gospel, or a real call to serve elsewhere. But a restless search for the congregation that will appreciate me is usually the foot talking again, and the place God has set you down deserves more patience than that.

In a sentence. But in fact God has placed every part in the body just as he wanted. If all were one part, there would be no body. As it is, there are many parts and one body.

On a Tuesday. God has put you exactly where he wants you in his church. Serve there gladly. Name one need in your church that is not a gift of yours but simply a duty, and do it this week.

For worship. The God who numbers the stars and calls them by name has placed each member of his church with the same care. He did not scatter his people at random; he arranged them, each one, as he chose, with a wisdom that sees the whole body and every joint and ligament. And he chose well, because he chose in love. The Lord who placed you is the Lord who died for you. Rest in his arrangement, because it is the arrangement of a Father who has never yet put a child in the wrong place.

verseByVerse.quote: The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”

The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you. Now the other failure, and Paul has held it back until now. The first speech was the discouraged member talking about himself. This one is the impressive member talking about somebody else: those who feel superior, the gifted eye looking down on the hand. Notice who is speaking. The eye and the head, the noble parts, the ones in the portrait, the ones that get named when people describe you. And notice whom they dismiss: the hand that does the work and the feet that do the walking. It is a precise little satire on the Corinthian situation, where the members with the visible gifts had concluded that the rest of the congregation was decorative.

Nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. The head, the most honoured part, cannot dismiss the feet. The spectacularly gifted cannot do without the ordinary members. The word to weigh is cannot. Paul does not say the eye should not say it, or that it is unkind to say it. He says the eye cannot, meaning the statement is not merely rude but false. An eye that announces it has no need of hands has said something untrue about itself. It will be needing those hands within the hour, and it will be needing them without ever noticing that it does.

What it does not mean. It does not mean head here refers to Christ, the head of the church. Paul is using the physical body as an analogy.

How contempt works in a church. It is not usually spoken. Very few people have ever said I have no need of you out loud to another believer, and anyone who did would be rebuked for it. It is expressed by omission: who gets consulted, who gets invited, who is treated as background. The sentence gets said by a seating plan, a rota, a conversation that stops when a certain person joins it. And there is a reason the impressive members are the ones warned here. The temptation to despise is not evenly distributed. It belongs almost entirely to the gifted, the busy and the capable, who can generally manage without help and so come to believe that they do.

What does repentance look like here? Not a warmer feeling about people you find tedious; feelings are not directly available to the will, and trying to manufacture them produces condescension, which is worse. Something more practical is required. Ask a member you have overlooked for advice about something that matters to you, and then take it. Put a name you have never put there onto the list of people whose opinion you seek. Sit somewhere else. Discover, by asking rather than assuming, what a person you had filed as marginal actually does with his week. Contempt is broken by finding out that the sentence was false, and the only way to find that out is to need the person and see what happens. The eye cannot argue itself into valuing the hand. It has to try picking something up.

In a sentence. The eye cannot tell the hand, “I don’t need you,” and the head cannot tell the feet, “I don’t need you.”

On a Tuesday. Here is a test with teeth. Think of the person in your congregation whose absence next Sunday would make the least difference to you. Now ask what would actually stop if that person stopped, and be honest, because you may well not know, which is itself the answer. The parts of a body you never think about are precisely the ones you find out about when they fail. Then go and find out.

For worship. The true Head of the church has never once said to any of his members, I have no need of you. He who needs nothing has chosen to need his people: to speak through their mouths, to serve with their hands, to walk on their feet into every street of the world. The Lord of glory washed the feet of his disciples, the lowest task in the house, and told them to do the same. Confess any pride that looks down on others in your church, and adore the humility of a Head who stoops to his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable, and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,

On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable. Paul now turns the world’s ranking upside down, and he does it with an observation anybody can verify on his own person. The parts that seem weaker are in fact indispensable; the word means you cannot do without them. Think of what is actually true of a body. The strong parts are the ones on show: the arms, the shoulders, the face. The parts you cannot survive without are soft, hidden and defenceless: the heart, the lungs, the brain, all of them tucked behind bone precisely because they could not take a blow. In the church, those who seem weakest may be the most vital: those who pray, the faithful elderly, the quietly serving.

And on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor. We clothe some parts more carefully; honour here may well mean clothing. This is Paul’s second observation and a delicate one: we spend more effort covering what is unpresentable than displaying what is presentable.

And our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty, which our more presentable parts do not require. The private parts are covered with special care; the face needs no covering. A man will leave his face bare in all weathers and would not dream of leaving the rest of himself so.

But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it. Then the theological punchline. Composed (synkerannymi) means blended, mixed together, as a painter mixes colours or a cook a dish. This is not human sentiment about the underdog. It is the design. God deliberately built compensation into the arrangement, so that the members with no natural standing receive an honour that is given rather than earned. So in the church, God honours the lowly, as he chose what is low and despised in the world (1:27–28). Which means a congregation that honours its unimpressive members is not being nice. It is being accurate.

Who are they? Be concrete, because vagueness here costs somebody something real. They are the housebound woman who has not been in the building for three years and prays through the church list every morning. The man with a learning disability whose questions in the Bible study slow everybody down. The elderly member whose memory has gone, who cannot follow the sermon, and who is still, on this verse, a load-bearing part of the body. The person who cleans up afterwards. The one who is simply hard work.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should despise the gifted. It means we should give special honour to those the world overlooks.

What does greater honour look like in practice? It looks like the overlooked being given the best, not the leftovers. Visiting the housebound as faithfully as the leaders are consulted. Asking the elderly to pray for specific things and then telling them how God answered. Making the building accessible before making it impressive. Thanking, by name and in public, the people who clean, count and set up. Seating the person with a disability where he can take part, not where he is out of the way. Listening to the slow question in the Bible study as though it might be the most important one asked, because it may be. Honour is not a feeling; it is attention, time and place given on purpose.

In a sentence. On the contrary, the parts that seem weaker are the ones we cannot do without, and the parts we regard as less honourable we treat with special honour; the parts we keep private we treat with special modesty, while the presentable parts need no such care. God has put the body together so as to give greater honour to the parts that lacked it,

On a Tuesday. Find the overlooked person in your church this Sunday and honour them. Ask their name if you do not know it, and remember it next week. If someone in your church is housebound, arrange to visit, and go to receive as much as to give.

For worship. The world grades people by what they contribute. Paul says the body of Christ is composed on the opposite principle, and he says it because of the cross. The pattern was set by a Lord who was despised and rejected, who had no form or majesty that we should look at him (Isaiah 53:2–3), and who turned out to be the one part of the whole arrangement that nothing could do without. A church that measures its members by prominence has forgotten what its own Head looked like. He was the stone the builders rejected, and he has become the cornerstone. This is the Lord’s doing, and it is marvellous in our eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.

That there may be no division in the body. Here is the purpose of the whole arrangement, and it is stated as God’s aim rather than as a target for the congregation: he composed the body that there may be no division in the body. Division (schisma) is the word of 1:10 and 11:18. The unity of a church is not a project that the members dreamt up. It is what God was after when he handed out the gifts in the first place.

But that the members may have the same care for one another. Care (merimnaō) is the word for anxious concern: each member concerned for the others, equally.

If one member suffers, all suffer together. Read it carefully: Paul does not say the members ought to suffer together. He says they do. It is a statement about how bodies work. And it is exactly true of the physical body, in a way that repays a moment’s thought. Stub one toe in the dark and the whole organism reacts: the breath catches, the eyes water, the hands reach, the voice makes a sound it did not plan. Nobody has to persuade the shoulder to care about the foot. The body does not hold a meeting about whether the injury is serious enough to warrant a response. It responds because the foot is not somebody else. When one believer suffers, the whole church should feel it (Romans 12:15; Hebrews 13:3).

A body with nerve damage. That turns the usual application inside out. The question this verse puts to a congregation is not are you being sympathetic enough? It is diagnostic. A church where a member can lose a job, a marriage or a child and the rest of the body carries on undisturbed is not an unkind body. It is a body with nerve damage, where the signal is being sent and nothing is arriving. That is a more serious condition than a failure of effort, and it is not cured by exhortation.

If one member is honored, all rejoice together. Note the second half, because it is the harder half in practice. Most Christians find it easier to weep with those who weep than to rejoice with those who rejoice. Sympathy costs nothing but time; gladness at another’s success costs you the comparison. When someone else in the congregation gets the thing you have prayed for and not received, the child, the recovery, the post, the invitation, the body’s health is measured by what happens in you at that moment, and it is measured more accurately there than at any funeral.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we feel every pain automatically. It means love makes us feel with others, and acts on it.

How does a body come to feel what its members feel? Not by resolving to. Nerves are built out of information, and the practical form of this verse is unglamorous: knowing people’s names, knowing what is happening in their lives, and asking again the following week. Suffering that nobody knows about cannot be shared, and a great deal of the suffering in most congregations is invisible because nobody has ever asked a second question. And the sharing runs in both directions, and neither direction is optional. A member who tells nobody anything has, with the best intentions, cut his own nerve. Privacy is not a Christian virtue in a body; it is how a limb goes numb. Letting people know that you are struggling is not weakness or self-indulgence, and this verse quietly requires it, because a body cannot suffer together with a member who has determined to suffer alone.

How can I rejoice when I am envious? Honestly, and by bringing the envy to God rather than pretending it is not there. Name it to him: Lord, I wanted that, and she has it, and it hurts. Then remember that the body’s blessing is your blessing; when another member is honoured, you are honoured in him, because you are not somebody else. Thank God for the specific good thing he has given that brother or sister, out loud if you can, and then do something kind for them. Gladness often follows the act rather than preceding it. And bring your own unanswered longing back to the Father who sees it; his love for you has not been reduced by his kindness to someone else.

In a sentence. so that there should be no split in the body, but each part should have equal concern for the others. If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honoured, every part shares in its joy.

On a Tuesday. Pray today for a suffering member of your church, by name, and then ask them a second question this week. And rejoice with one who has been blessed: send the message of congratulation you have been putting off.

For worship. The Head feels what the body feels. When Saul struck at the church, Christ in heaven cried out, why are you persecuting me? We have a High Priest who sympathises with our weaknesses, who wept at a friend’s grave, and who still carries his people’s sorrows as his own. And he rejoices over his people with gladness, and quiets them by his love, and exults over them with loud singing (Zephaniah 3:17). The body suffers and rejoices together because its Head does. Blessed be the Christ who has made us members of one another.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Varieties of Gifts: The Greater Gifts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them plainly that they are Christ’s body, and each one of them is a part of it. God has placed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and different kinds of tongues. Are all apostles, prophets or teachers? Do all work miracles, have gifts of healing, speak in tongues or interpret? Obviously not. So they should eagerly desire the greater gifts. And now Paul will show them the most excellent way of all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ordering of Gifts and the Priority of Love

The list of gifts in vv. 28–30, with its implied ordering (first, second, third), suggests that Paul does see a hierarchy of value in gifts — not because some are intrinsically superior but because some are more directly edifying for the whole community. Apostles and prophets lay the doctrinal foundation; teachers expound it; the other gifts serve the body in various ways. But the “still more excellent way” of chapter 13 is not a further gift above tongues and prophecy; it is the character quality that makes the exercise of any gift genuinely excellent.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian gift-competition had inverted the hierarchy: tongues (the most self-focused gift in Paul’s analysis) was being treated as the most prestigious. Paul’s list puts tongues last. The correction is not to dismiss tongues but to reorder values: gifts that build the community outrank gifts that edify only the speaker. Now: The principle applies in every community: the gifted teacher who uses his gift to impress rather than to build up the body has missed what gifts are for. The “excellent way” is available to every gift-user who submits his gift to love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.

Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it. Paul lands the metaphor. And the verb is the one to watch: you are. Not you should be, not you must strive to become, not you will be if you sort yourselves out. To this congregation, factional, arrogant, drunk at communion, tolerating scandal, the apostle says: you are the body of Christ. You, the Corinthian church, are Christ’s body. The identity comes first and the instructions come afterwards, which is the order the New Testament always uses and the reverse of the order that comes naturally to religious people. Then individually members of it. Both halves of that matter. You are not the body on your own; and you are not swallowed by it either. Christianity has never asked anyone to dissolve into a collective. A hand in a body is more itself, not less.

And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers. Appointed (tithēmi) is the same word as verse 18. This list is numbered, which the earlier one was not, and the numbering is doing something. The first three all have to do with the word of God: apostles, the foundational witnesses of Christ who received and delivered it (Ephesians 2:20); prophets, those who spoke revelation in the early church; and teachers, who explain it. These three word ministries come first because everything else in a church is built on what God has said, and they build the church most. Take the word out and the rest is activity.

Then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues. Two things in the list are easily overlooked and should not be. Helping (antilēmpseis, acts of assistance) is a word for practical aid to those in need, and Paul has just put it in the same list as miracles and healing. Administrating (kybernēseis) is a nautical word: it means steering, what a ship’s pilot does, leadership and guidance. So the person who keeps the accounts straight, arranges the rota and makes sure the widow gets visited is exercising a gift of the Holy Spirit, named alongside the spectacular ones by the apostle himself. A great many churches would be transformed by believing that sentence. And tongues come last. The Corinthians had the order upside down.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that those with lower-ranked gifts are less valuable as persons. The ranking concerns how much each gift builds up the church (14:5).

Are there apostles today? The office as Paul describes it had conditions attached that cannot now be met: an apostle had seen the risen Lord (9:1) and was commissioned directly by him, and the apostles together are called the foundation of the church, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20). A foundation is laid once; a building with a permanent foundation-laying department has a serious problem. So the office in that sense closed. The word also has a broader use in the New Testament, a sent one, a messenger of the churches (2 Corinthians 8:23), and that work has never stopped: church planters and missionaries doing today what Paul did at Corinth. Christians who use the title for such people usually mean the second thing, and the disagreement is often smaller than the vocabulary makes it sound.

And prophets? The prophets named here stand with the apostles as part of the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). They brought God’s revealed word to the churches before the New Testament was complete. That foundational, revelatory office has ceased with the closing of the canon. What continues is the ministry of the word: preachers and teachers who do not receive new revelation but faithfully explain and apply the revelation God has given once for all. When a sermon pierces your heart and you feel that God has spoken to you, he has, but through his written word, not beside it. That is why this app reads the third item on the list, teachers, as the living heir of the first two.

In a sentence. You are Christ’s body, and each of you is one of its parts. In the church God has placed first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, of helping, of guidance, and of different kinds of tongues.

On a Tuesday. Value the ministry of the word in your church. Pray for your teachers by name. And honour those who help and administer behind the scenes: find the treasurer, the rota-keeper or the person who unlocks the building, and thank them for exercising a gift of the Holy Spirit.

For worship. You are the body of Christ. The risen Lord has no other hands on earth than the ones he has joined to himself, and he has chosen to work through them. He gave apostles to lay the foundation, prophets to bring his word, teachers to open it, helpers to carry it into homes and steerers to keep the ship on course. Every one of these is his gift to his church, given after he ascended on high and led a host of captives, and gave gifts to men (Ephesians 4:8–12). He builds his church still, and it will stand.

verseByVerse.quote: Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Seven questions, and in Greek each is framed to expect the answer no. Paul is not wondering aloud. He is closing a door. Not everyone has the same gift.

Do all work miracles? Do all possess gifts of healing? No.

Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? The sixth question is the one Corinth cared about. Do all speak with tongues? No. Not every Christian speaks in tongues. That single syllable dismantles the whole system the church had built: the idea that one gift is the badge of the Spirit’s presence and that the believers without it are in the lower division. If the Spirit had intended tongues as the mark of genuine Christianity, he would have given it to everyone. He has not, and the fact that he has not is itself the argument.

Where Christians differ: tongues as the evidence of the Spirit. Some Pentecostal groups teach that speaking in tongues is the necessary evidence of being baptised in the Spirit. Verdict: Paul’s question expects the answer: no, not all speak in tongues. Yet all were baptised in the Spirit (v. 13). So tongues cannot be the required evidence of Spirit baptism. The evidence of the Spirit is confessing Jesus as Lord (v. 3) and the fruit of the Spirit, above all love (Galatians 5:22–23; 1 Corinthians 13).

The Corinthian error in other clothes. It is worth saying that this cuts both ways, and it should, because congregations have found more than one way to make the same mistake. Any church which decides that a particular gift is the test of spiritual seriousness has fallen into the Corinthian error, whatever the gift is. Some do it with tongues. Some do it with a certain kind of doctrinal precision, or evangelistic boldness, or emotional expressiveness in worship, or a particular pattern of daily devotions. In every case the same sentence answers it. Do all? No.

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts are unimportant. It means no single gift is for everyone, or proves spiritual status.

A release for the discouraged. There is a mercy in that no which the discouraged reader should take. The seven questions are usually read as a rebuke to the proud, and they are. But turn them round and they are a release for everyone who has spent years feeling second-rate in church. You were never meant to be able to do all of it. The Spirit did not distribute the whole list to anybody, and the apostle writing the sentence does not make himself the standard. There has only ever been one person who could do everything, and the whole point of the body is that he chose to do it through thousands of people who cannot.

In a sentence. Is everyone an apostle? Is everyone a prophet or a teacher? Does everyone work miracles or heal? Does everyone speak in tongues or interpret? Of course not.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the gift he gave you, and stop comparing it with others’. If you have been measuring your Christian life by a gift you do not have, put the measuring stick down. Measure it instead by verse 3 and by chapter 13: do you confess Jesus as Lord, and are you growing in love?

For worship. That is worth standing still in front of. Christ needed nothing. He could have preached every sermon, healed every sufferer, comforted every widow and administered every fund himself, and done all of it better than the whole church put together has ever done any of it. Instead he ascended, sent his Spirit, and handed the work out in fragments to fishermen and slaves and housewives and dockworkers, so that no one of them could manage without the others and none of them could manage without him. He did not need a body. He wanted one (Ephesians 4:15–16). Glory to the Head who has chosen to be honoured through such members.

verseByVerse.quote: But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

But earnestly desire the higher gifts. The first clause looks, at first glance, like a contradiction. Paul has spent thirty verses saying the Spirit apportions as he wills, and now he tells them to want the higher gifts. If the distribution is sovereign, what is the point of desiring anything? But the two sit together perfectly well, and in fact they always do in Scripture. God is sovereign over who is saved, and Christians are told to pray for the lost. He is sovereign over daily bread, and we are taught to ask for it. Sovereign distribution does not make desire pointless; it makes desire safe, because the asking is finally in the hands of someone who will not give a stone to a child asking for bread (Matthew 7:9). Earnestly desire (zēloō) means be zealous for. And note that the command is plural. Paul is not telling individuals to lobby for personal upgrades. He is telling a congregation what to want for itself. Some read the verb as a statement rather than a command: you are eagerly desiring the supposedly greater gifts, but Paul will show you a better way. Either way, the next clause redirects them.

What higher means. It obviously cannot mean more impressive after everything just said about eyes and feet. It means more useful to other people: those that build up the church most, such as prophecy and teaching. Paul will spell it out at 14:5: the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, because prophecy builds up the church. That is the whole scale. A gift ranks higher in proportion to how much good it does the person sitting next to you. By that measure the faithful visitor of the sick outranks a great deal that gets applauded.

And I will show you a still more excellent way. Then the last clause, and it is one of the great hinges in the Bible. More excellent (kath’ hyperbolēn) means beyond comparison, surpassing. Everything is set up for Paul to name the top gift. He does not. He steps off the ladder altogether, because the more excellent way is not a gift at all and cannot be distributed as he wills to some and not others. It is the way in which all gifts must be used: love. It is required of everybody, available to everybody, and without it the entire list is worth nothing, which is precisely what the next chapter opens by saying. So the sentence is doing two things at once. It is a promise, and it is a rebuke aimed at a church that had been arguing about rank. They wanted to know which gift was best. Paul is about to tell them that the question was wrong, and that a man may have every gift on the list, exercise them all with power, and be nothing whatever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is a gift for some. It is the way for all.

So should I pray for spiritual gifts? Yes, in the way Paul means. Pray, with your church, for the gifts that build others up: for wisdom to counsel, clarity to teach, compassion to visit, generosity to give, faith to persevere, and for God to raise up faithful preachers and leaders. Pray for these not as trophies but as tools, asking how you can be more useful to the people around you. And pray above all for love, because without it every gift is noise. The Father delights to give good gifts to those who ask him, and the best gift of all, the Holy Spirit, he has already given (Luke 11:13).

In a sentence. Be eager for the gifts that do the most good. And now Paul will show you a way that is better than all of them.

On a Tuesday. Seek gifts that build others up. But above all, seek love. Before you next serve in any way, pray a simple prayer: Lord, let me do this in love, for their good and your glory.

For worship. Notice, finally, the verb. I will show you. Not I will describe it, or define it, or commend it. Paul is about to put something in front of them and let them look at it, which is why chapter 13 is written the way it is: not as an argument but almost as a portrait, sentence after sentence of what love does and does not do. And the portrait, when it arrives, will turn out to be recognisable. There has been exactly one life that was patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not irritable, bearing all things and enduring all things to the end. The more excellent way has a face, and it is the face of Jesus Christ, who loved us and gave himself for us.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed.<sup>2</sup>You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led.<sup>3</sup>Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says “Jesus is accursed!” and no one can say “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit.<sup>4</sup>Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit;<sup>5</sup>and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord;<sup>6</sup>and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone.<sup>7</sup>To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.<sup>8</sup>For to one is given through the Spirit the utterance of wisdom, and to another the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit,<sup>9</sup>to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by the one Spirit,<sup>10</sup>to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another the ability to distinguish between spirits, to another various kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues.<sup>11</sup>All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills.<sup>12</sup>For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ.<sup>13</sup>For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body—Jews or Greeks, slaves or free—and all were made to drink of one Spirit.<sup>14</sup>For the body does not consist of one member but of many.<sup>15</sup>If the foot should say, “Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>16</sup>And if the ear should say, “Because I am not an eye, I do not belong to the body,” that would not make it any less a part of the body.<sup>17</sup>If the whole body were an eye, where would be the sense of hearing? If the whole body were an ear, where would be the sense of smell?<sup>18</sup>But as it is, God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose.<sup>19</sup>If all were a single member, where would the body be?<sup>20</sup>As it is, there are many parts, yet one body.<sup>21</sup>The eye cannot say to the hand, “I have no need of you,” nor again the head to the feet, “I have no need of you.”<sup>22</sup>On the contrary, the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable,<sup>23</sup>and on those parts of the body that we think less honorable we bestow the greater honor, and our unpresentable parts are treated with greater modesty,<sup>24</sup>which our more presentable parts do not require. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the part that lacked it,<sup>25</sup>that there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another.<sup>26</sup>If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together.<sup>27</sup>Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.<sup>28</sup>And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues.<sup>29</sup>Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles?<sup>30</sup>Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?<sup>31</sup>But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way.

13.title: The Most Excellent Way: Love
13.overview:
This famous chapter is often read at weddings, but it was written to rebuke a quarrelsome, proud church that valued spectacular gifts above everything. Paul sets it between his teaching on gifts in chapters 12 and 14, as the “more excellent way” in which every gift must be used. The Greek word for love here, agapē, was rare in ordinary Greek; the Christians filled it with new meaning from the love God showed in Christ. Read the chapter with Jesus’ name in place of “love” and it describes him; read it with your own name and it shows how far you fall short.

First Paul shows that love is essential. Tongues, prophecy, knowledge, mountain-moving faith, even giving away everything or sacrificing one’s body, are worth nothing without love. Then he describes love in action, mostly by what it does not do, and almost every phrase corrects something in Corinth: envy, boasting, arrogance, rudeness, self-seeking. Finally he shows that love lasts. Prophecy, tongues and knowledge are partial and temporary, suited to the present age, like a child’s speech or a dim reflection in a bronze mirror. When the complete arrives, at Christ’s return, they will give way to seeing God face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Paul could speak every human language and even the language of angels, but had no love, he would be no more than a noisy gong or a clashing cymbal. If he had the gift of prophecy and understood every mystery and all knowledge, and had faith enough to move mountains, but had no love, he would be nothing. If he gave away everything he owned and handed over his body to hardship, but had no love, he would gain nothing.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as the Form of All Virtues

Aquinas, following Augustine, called love (caritas) the form of all virtues — the quality without which no virtue is genuinely virtuous. Paul’s three strophes make the same point: spiritual gifts without love are not merely incomplete but negated. Reformed theology has grounded this in the law of love (Matt 22:37–40): the whole law is fulfilled in love, and therefore the whole Christian life, including the exercise of spiritual gifts, finds its telos and criterion in love. The gift that is not exercised in love has been severed from its own purpose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-speaker who exercised his gift in a public meeting, leaving the congregation uninstructed and himself privately edified, was exhibiting Paul’s noisy gong in practice. The spiritual trophy was real; the love was absent; the gift had become noise. Now: The preacher who loves the sound of his own voice more than the people he is preaching to, the theologian who loves winning arguments more than the person he is arguing with, the worship leader who loves the experience he generates more than the congregation he is leading — all are producing noise, not music.

verseByVerse.quote: If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 13 is the most famous chapter on love ever written, but it is not a wedding poem; it is a rebuke to a gifted, proud, divided church, set in the middle of Paul’s teaching on spiritual gifts (chapters 12 to 14). It has three movements. First, without love, even the greatest gifts and sacrifices are worthless: tongues become noise, prophecy and knowledge and faith amount to nothing, and giving everything away gains nothing (vv. 1–3). Second, love is described in action, fifteen verbs that read like a portrait of Christ and a mirror held up to the Corinthians: patient, kind, not envious, boastful, arrogant, rude, selfish, irritable or resentful; rejoicing in truth, bearing, believing, hoping and enduring all things (vv. 4–7). Third, love lasts forever. The gifts are for this age and will pass away when the perfect comes; now we see dimly, then face to face. Faith, hope and love remain, and the greatest is love (vv. 8–13). The word throughout is agapē: self-giving love that seeks the good of others, the love God showed in Christ. And the chapter that begins by pricing every gift the Corinthians were proud of ends by naming the eternal life of God himself.

The setting. This chapter is read at weddings, and there is nothing wrong with that. But it was written to a church that was tearing itself apart over which gifts were most impressive, and it lands like a blow. Chapter 12 has just taught that the Spirit gives different gifts to different members of one body, as he wills, for the common good, and it ended with a promise: I will show you a still more excellent way (12:31). Here it is. Chapter 14 will then apply it to the actual meetings of the church. So chapter 13 is not a detour into poetry between two practical chapters. It is the hinge on which the whole argument turns, and it begins by pricing everything the Corinthians were proud of.

If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels. Paul starts at the top, with the gift the Corinthians prized most. Not merely every human language, but the speech of angels: he grants his readers more than they were claiming, and then demolishes it. Notice that he writes I, not you. He puts himself in the dock first, which is how a pastor rebukes a church he loves.

Is there an angelic language? Paul is reaching for the most extreme case he can imagine, as he does in the next verse with all mysteries and faith that could remove mountains. He is not describing a language he or anyone else spoke, though some at Corinth may have believed their ecstatic speech was exactly that. When angels speak in Scripture, they speak words people understand (Luke 1:13; 2:10), so the verse gives no ground for an unintelligible heavenly tongue. The point is the argument from the greater: if even the speech of angels would be worthless without love, so is everything less.

But have not love. Love (agapē) is not mainly a feeling, but a self-giving commitment to another’s good, defined by God’s love in Christ: God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:9–10). The word was rare in ordinary Greek, and the New Testament filled it with new content. It is measured not by what it feels but by what it gives, and the measure of it is a cross.

I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. The gong and the cymbal are worth picturing, because the choice of instruments is not random. Instruments like these sounded in the pagan cults the Corinthians had come out of, especially the cults of Cybele and Dionysus: bronze, loud, resonant, and carrying no words. Corinth was famous for its bronze. Many in that congregation had heard such cymbals crash in a temple courtyard, and Paul is telling the man proud of his tongue that his gift, exercised without love, makes the same sound. Note the picture precisely. A gong is not silent. It is the loudest thing in the room, and that is the trouble with it: it fills a space, everyone turns round, and afterwards nobody can say what it said.

And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge. The stakes rise. Prophecy, the gift Paul ranks highest and which chapter 14 will rank above tongues (14:1, 5). Understanding all mysteries and all knowledge: not a great deal of theology but the whole of it, without gaps.

And if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains. Not saving faith here but wonder-working faith (12:9), the Lord’s own image for the largest faith imaginable (Matthew 17:20). Paul has listed the speaker, the prophet, the theologian and the miracle-worker, and he is about to put them all in the same column.

But have not love, I am nothing. The verdict is not the one anyone expects. Paul does not say that such a man has less than he thinks, or that his ministry is diminished. He says I am nothing: not my gift is nothing, but I am. The failure is not in the performance; it reaches back to the performer. A gifted person without love is spiritually zero. A man can be a first-class instrument and not be a Christian at all, and the gifts will not tell him which he is.

The gifts are no evidence about the man. That is a sobering thing to put to anyone who serves in a church, and it should be put personally rather than left in the air. It is entirely possible to preach well, pray in public with feeling, know your Bible thoroughly, give generously of your time, be thanked for all of it, and be nothing. The gifts are given as the Spirit wills (12:11), which means they say more about the Giver than about the man holding them. Judas was sent out with the Twelve with authority to heal (Matthew 10:1–4), and nobody at the Last Supper suspected him even as he left (John 13:27–30). Our Lord warned that many will say on that day that they prophesied and cast out demons in his name, and he will say he never knew them (Matthew 7:22–23).

What it does not mean. It does not mean gifts do not matter. Paul has just urged them to desire the higher gifts (12:31), and he will say it again (14:1). The gifts are good, they come from the Spirit, and the church needs them. It means gifts without love have no value before God and no value to the man who has them.

How can I tell whether my service is done in love? Ask who it is for. Love serves the person in front of it; pride serves its own reputation. A few honest tests help. Would I still do this if no one ever thanked me or knew it was me? Am I glad or deflated when someone else does it better? Do I notice the people I serve, their names and burdens, or only how it went? When the work is criticised, do I care first whether people were helped, or whether I was hurt? No one passes these perfectly. The point is not to stop serving until your motives are pure, which would mean never serving at all, but to bring the mixed motives to Christ and ask him to make love the reason.

In a sentence. If Paul could speak every human language and even the speech of angels, but had no love, he would be only a booming gong or a crashing cymbal. If he could prophesy, understand every mystery and know everything, and had faith enough to move mountains, but had no love, he would be nothing.

On a Tuesday. You may be gifted, knowledgeable and busy for God. Take the thing you do best in your church, the thing people thank you for, and ask who it was for the last time you did it. Then do one piece of service this week that no one will see and no one can thank you for, and watch what your heart does with the silence.

For worship. There was once a man with every gift in this list and more. He spoke as no man ever spoke, he knew what was in every heart, and his faith did not move mountains only because he had made them. And not one word he ever said was noise, because every word was love.
