He did not use his gifts to be admired; he used them to heal lepers, feed crowds and raise a widow’s son, and then he laid them all down and went to a cross. The more excellent way is not a technique. It is the way he walked, all the way to Golgotha, for people who had nothing to offer him but their need.
verseByVerse.note: Gongs and cymbals were loud instruments used in pagan worship.

verseByVerse.quote: If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.

If I give away all I have. Paul has finished with the gifts and moves to the deeds, and he goes straight to the two that no one has ever been able to top. The first is total divestment. Not generous giving; the verb (psōmizō) means to dole out in morsels, to feed, and suggests parcelling out everything you own, piece by piece, to feed the poor, until there is nothing left.

And if I deliver up my body to be burned. The second is martyrdom. A man walks into the fire rather than deny his Lord. Between them, these are the summit of what Christian devotion has ever been asked to produce, and they are the two acts that no congregation on earth would dare to question. Paul questions them.

A note on the text. A reader comparing translations will meet a difference here. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read deliver up my body that I may boast. Two Greek words differing by a letter or two lie behind the phrase, and the manuscript evidence is close. Burned fits the idea of martyrdom; boast fits the Corinthian pride, and is almost bleakly appropriate to the point: a sacrifice offered so that one has something to say about it. Either way the sentence works, and the meaning is the ultimate sacrifice of self.

But have not love, I gain nothing. It is possible to do the most extreme thing a human being can do and have the wrong reason for it. A man may give away his fortune because he cannot bear to be thought ordinary. A man may go to the stake because his own consistency has become the thing he worships, or because he cannot face what climbing down would cost him in front of people who are watching. Sacrifice proves that something mattered more than comfort. It does not prove what. Even generosity and martyrdom can be done for pride, reputation or self-justification, and our Lord warned against giving to be seen by others (Matthew 6:1–4).

Nothing, and then nothing gained. The phrase has been quietly changed. In verse 2 it was I am nothing; here it is I gain nothing. The first was about what a man is; this is about what he takes away with him. A whole life could be poured out, admired, written up, and yield its owner precisely nothing at the end, because the only currency that will still be legal tender on that day is love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving and sacrifice are bad, or that the martyrs were wrong. The church has been built on the blood of men and women who loved Christ more than life, and the poor have been fed by people who gave everything. It means motive matters. God looks at the heart, and he weighs not only what was given but why.

But if love is the one thing that counts, and I find little of it in me, what do I do? The answer is not to try harder to feel it, and the chapter never suggests that. Love is not generated from a standing start; it is received and then returned. We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). So the road to more love runs through more knowledge of his love: dwelling on the cross, on what he forgave you, on how fully he knows you and loves you anyway (v. 12). Ask him for it plainly, because it is the fruit of his Spirit (Galatians 5:22). And then do the loving thing while the feeling lags; affection very often follows obedience rather than going before it.

Should I stop giving until my motives are pure? No. Our motives this side of glory are always mixed, and if we waited for pure ones we would never give a penny or lift a finger. Keep giving and keep serving, and bring the mixture to God. Ask him to purify your heart as you go. The warning of this verse is not against giving; it is against trusting the giving, as though the size of the sacrifice could stand in for love or earn us something before God.

In a sentence. If Paul gave everything he had to the poor and even handed over his body to the flames, but did it without love, he would gain nothing.

On a Tuesday. Look at your giving, of money and of time. Is any of it arranged so that it will be noticed? Give something this week in a way that leaves no trace of your name, and pray for the person it reaches. Then thank God that he sees in secret, and that the unseen gift is not lost.

For worship. There was one sacrifice that was all love and nothing else. The Son of God gave away all he had: he who was rich became poor, so that we by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). He delivered up his body, not to win a name but to bear a curse, and he did it for people who were not watching with admiration but with mockery. If any self-giving ever deserved to gain something, it was his, and what he gained was us. Every lesser sacrifice that is done in love is only an echo of that one, and every sacrifice that lacks love is measured against it and found empty.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “deliver up my body [to death] that I may boast.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love is patient and kind. It is not envious, boastful or proud. It does not behave disgracefully, does not seek its own advantage, is not easily provoked, and keeps no record of wrongs. It takes no pleasure in wrongdoing but is glad when truth wins. It always protects, always trusts, always hopes and always perseveres.
verseByVerse.theology:
Love as a Christological Description

The point deserves full weight: replace “love” in vv. 4–7 with “Jesus Christ” and the sentences remain true. Christ is patient — he waited thirty years before beginning his public ministry; he bore with his disciples for three years; he endured the cross. Christ is kind — he touched lepers, welcomed children, ate with sinners. Christ does not insist on his own way — “not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). Christ does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth. Christ bears all things, believes all things (his faith was perfect toward the Father), hopes all things (the joy set before him, Heb 12:2), endures all things (the cross). Love is not primarily a commandment to be obeyed but a Person to be united with — and as Christ is formed in us (Gal 4:19), his character becomes our character.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s list is a mirror held up to Corinth. Every community that reads 1 Corinthians 13 should see itself in it — not as an aspiration but as a diagnostic. Where is the envy? The boasting? The resentment carried from meeting to meeting? The delight when a rival stumbles? The catalogue of love’s character is simultaneously a catalogue of the community’s failures. Now: The most powerful apologetic for Christianity in the twenty-first century is not a philosophical argument but a community that actually loves this way — that bears, believes, hopes, and endures. The watching world knows what love looks like; it is waiting to see if the church produces it.

verseByVerse.quote: Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant

Love is patient and kind. Now the portrait. And notice at once that in Greek every item is a verb, not an adjective. Paul does not say love is a patient thing; he says love acts patiently, behaves kindly, refuses to envy. This is not a description of a feeling. It is a description of conduct, which means it can be checked.

Patient. The word (makrothymeō) is a compound of long and anger: love has a long fuse. It is not the patience of waiting for a bus but the patience of putting up with people who wrong you, the same word the New Testament uses of God bearing with sinners for centuries (Romans 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9). The measure of it is not how you behave the first time someone irritates you but the fortieth.

And kind. The word (chrēsteuomai) means to be useful, gracious, actively doing good to others. The pair belongs together. Patience is what love does not do; kindness is what it does. Patience endures injury; kindness repays it with good. It is possible to endure someone indefinitely while giving them nothing at all, and there are marriages and churches held together on exactly those terms. Patience alone is endurance. Patience with kindness is love.

Love does not envy or boast. Put those two side by side and something surfaces. Envy (zēloō, to be jealous) is what this disease does when the other person has it; boasting is what it does when you have it. They look like opposites and they are the same illness in two positions, and the illness is the habit of measuring yourself against other people. The Corinthians envied one another’s gifts (3:3) and boasted in their gifts and leaders. The word behind boast (perpereuomai) is a rare one that means something like a windbag: the man who parades himself, who cannot let a story pass without improving his own part in it. Love rejoices in others’ blessings and has no need to advertise its own.

It is not arrogant. The verb is physioō, to be puffed up, inflated with air, and this is Paul’s signature word for Corinth. He has used it about their factions (4:6), about the men who thought he would not come (4:18–19), about their pride over the scandal in chapter 5 (5:2), and about their knowledge of idols (8:1). Now it appears in the list of what love is not, and Corinth would have recognised the word instantly. Love is humble because it is not the centre of its own attention.

A portrait of Christ. Every quality here was perfectly shown by Jesus. You can put his name in place of love and the sentences remain true: Jesus is patient and kind; Jesus does not envy or boast; he is not arrogant. He was patient with disciples who argued on the road about who was greatest, kind to a woman everyone else despised, and he never once paraded himself. Put your own name in, and you see how far you fall short, and how much you need him. The chapter is first a mirror and then a window: it shows you what you are not, and then shows you the one who is.

Am I meant to read my own name into this list? Yes, but as a mirror and not as a ladder. The list is not a set of rungs by which to climb into God’s favour; Christ has done that for you. It is a description of what his love looks like as it grows in his people. So read it with your name in, honestly, and let it drive you to him. Then read it with his name in, and rest. The Christian who does both is not crushed by the standard and is not careless about it either.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love tolerates everything, or that patience means never addressing a wrong. It means love responds to others with patience, kindness and humility, even when it has to say hard things.

In a sentence. Love is patient and kind. Love does not envy and does not show off; it is not proud.

On a Tuesday. Here is the test for this verse, and it takes ten seconds. Think of the person you find hardest in your congregation or your family. Now read the items again, with that person’s name after each verb. Am I long-tempered with him? Do I actively do him good? Am I glad when he does well? That is what the verse means, and it means nothing else. Love in this chapter is never a general benevolence toward humanity. It always has a name attached (1 John 3:18). Be patient and kind to that person today, deliberately, in one specific act.

For worship. The long fuse belongs first to God. He was patient with Israel through forty years in the wilderness, patient through the judges and the kings, patient with Jerusalem while it killed the prophets, and he is patient now, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). His kindness is not a mood but a deed: he sent his Son. And the Son, who had every right to boast, emptied himself and took the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7). Every line of this portrait was painted first in him, and he has never once been too proud to love us.

parallels.desc: love covers all offences

verseByVerse.quote: or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;
verseByVerse.commentary:
or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;

Or rude. Four more, and every one of them is a photograph of the Corinthian church. The word (aschēmoneō) means to behave disgracefully, in a way that is unseemly, that shames. The Corinthians were behaving shamefully at the Lord’s Supper, where some went hungry while others were drunk (11:21–22), and in their worship. It is striking to find manners in a list of Christian virtues, and it should give pause to a certain kind of believer who prides himself on being blunt. Rudeness is not a personality type in the New Testament; it is a failure of love. There is no gift, no calling and no strength of conviction that entitles a Christian to make another person feel small in front of others.

It does not insist on its own way. Literally, love does not seek its own things, and it is exactly the phrase Paul used at 10:24 and again at 10:33 (Philippians 2:4). This is the whole argument of chapters 8 to 10 compressed into a single phrase, and it is the hardest item on the list, because insisting on one’s own way rarely feels like selfishness from the inside. It feels like being right. The strong at Corinth were right about idols, were insisting on their rights, and were destroying people with it.

It is not irritable. The word (paroxynomai) gives us paroxysm; it means sharpened, provoked to a flash, easily angered, touchy. Everyone knows what this looks like: the person a whole household reads before speaking, the man whose mood determines the temperature of a room. It is usually treated as a temperament rather than a sin, and Paul files it here.

Or resentful. This is the one to slow down over, because the Greek is sharper than the English. Literally, love does not count up the wrong (logizetai to kakon). The phrase is an accountant’s: love does not reckon up the evil, does not enter the wrong in a ledger. And that is precisely what resentment is: not the memory of an injury, which is involuntary, but the keeping of it in a place where it can be produced later. Anyone can find out whether he is doing this. When a quarrel starts, does a list arrive? Are you able, without any preparation, to give the date and the wording of things said to you years ago? Nobody has that at his fingertips by accident. It is there because it was filed.

The ledger and the gospel. Behind the accounting image lies the gospel, which is why Paul reached for it. Logizomai is the very word used for righteousness being credited to believers in Romans 4, and of God not counting our trespasses against us (Romans 4:8; 2 Corinthians 5:19). The Christian is a person whose own ledger has been destroyed, not settled, not reduced, destroyed, and who is therefore in no position to keep one on anybody else. Forgiveness is the closing of an account you were entitled to keep open.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love ignores serious sin or abuse. Love confronts sin for the person’s good (Galatians 6:1), and it may need to remember facts for the sake of protection, justice or a report to the proper authorities. Keeping no record of wrongs is not the same as pretending nothing happened. But love does not nurse grudges, rehearse injuries, or hold them in reserve as weapons.

If I forgive, do I have to trust him again straight away? No. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Forgiveness is releasing the debt: you give up the right to punish, to repay, to keep the account open. It can be given at once, because Christ has forgiven you. Trust is rebuilt over time by changed behaviour, and wisdom may require boundaries while it is rebuilt, especially where someone has been harmed or is at risk. A wife can forgive a husband’s betrayal and still need time, honesty and counsel before trust returns. Forgiveness says: I will not hold this against you. It does not say: nothing has consequences.

What if the memory keeps coming back? Remembering is not the same as resenting. You cannot command your memory, but you can decide what to do when it arrives. When it comes, do not rehearse it, add to it, or imagine the speech you would make. Hand it back to God: Lord, I gave you this; I give it again. Pray for the person, even briefly. Many Christians have to forgive the same wrong many times before the feeling follows the decision, and that is not failure; it is what forgiving looks like in real life.

In a sentence. Love does not behave badly. It is not selfish, not quick to take offence, and keeps no list of wrongs.

On a Tuesday. Is there a record of wrongs you are keeping against someone? Name it to yourself honestly, the person and the item. Then bring it to God and close the account, as he has closed yours. And watch your temper in one place this week where you are usually the one others tiptoe around.

For worship. God had every entry. He did not need a ledger to remember what we had done; he knows it all. And he chose not to count it. The whole record of our debt was nailed to the cross (Colossians 2:14), and the one who could have produced every charge against us bore every charge himself. He was reviled and did not revile in return (1 Peter 2:23). He did not insist on his own way; he said, not my will, but yours. Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin, and blessed be the Lord who paid what he will not count.

verseByVerse.quote: it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.

It does not rejoice at wrongdoing. A single verse, and it exposes something most people have never admitted to themselves. Wrongdoing (adikia) is unrighteousness. Paul is not only talking about approving of sin. He is talking about the small, private pleasure that rises when something bad turns out to be true about somebody else. The verb is to be glad. And it is very hard to deny, because it is so quick: the flicker of satisfaction at hearing that a colleague’s promotion has fallen through, that a critic’s marriage is in difficulty, that a preacher you found insufferable has been found out. Nobody chooses that flicker. But the fact that it arrives uninvited is exactly what makes it such an accurate reading of the heart.

At Corinth it had a public form. The church had been arrogant about a case of gross immorality in its membership, a man living with his father’s wife, instead of mourning (5:2), and the factions were surely cheering when a rival group came off badly. But the private form is the commoner one, and it is the one this verse catches. Love takes no pleasure in sin, whether its own or others’.

The two-second test. Here is the sharpest test in the chapter. Bad news arrives about someone you have a grievance against. What happens in the first two seconds, before you have had time to arrange your face, before the appropriate sentence is composed? That flicker is a truer report on your love for that person than anything you would say about him out loud.

But rejoices with the truth. The positive is not the balance we would have written. The opposite of rejoicing at wrongdoing ought to be grieving at wrongdoing. Paul writes rejoices with the truth instead, and the truth is almost personified: love and the truth standing side by side, glad about the same things. Love is glad when truth prevails, the truth of the gospel and truthful living. Which settles a question that comes up constantly in Christian life: whether love and honesty are in tension, so that being loving means going quiet about what is true. This verse says they are allies. Love does not celebrate a wrong even when the wrong is convenient; it does not suppress a truth even when the truth is awkward. A love that requires lies is not love, and a truth-telling that takes pleasure in the damage is not truth-telling either (Ephesians 4:15; 2 John 1–3).

Gossip. There is a practical form of this sin that most Christians take part in without ever calling it what it is. Nobody says “I am glad this happened to him”. What people say is that they only mention it so that you can pray. The verse supplies a way of telling the two apart. Ask whether you would be disappointed to discover the report was false. If the correction would come as a relief, the interest was love. If it would come as a small deflation, the interest was the flicker.

So when may I speak about someone else’s sin? When speaking serves the person or protects others, and when you are speaking to someone who needs to know. Go to the person first where you can (Matthew 18:15). Speak to elders when the matter concerns the church’s care, and to the proper authorities when someone is in danger or a crime has been committed; love never hides abuse. Ask a wise friend for counsel without dressing the story up. What love does not do is pass the story along to people who can do nothing about it, add colour to it, or enjoy the telling. A useful question before you speak: is this person part of the problem or part of the solution?

How is the flicker killed? Not by scolding yourself for having it, which only drives it out of sight. It dies when the other person stops being a competitor, and he stops being a competitor when you genuinely believe that God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose (12:18). A man who is certain his own place was given him has nothing to gain by another man losing his.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is soft on doctrine. Love rejoices in truth, and so it cares that people believe and live the truth. Contending for the gospel is not a failure of love; it is one of love’s duties.

In a sentence. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but is glad whenever the truth wins.

On a Tuesday. When you hear of someone’s sin this week, refuse to enjoy it and refuse to repeat it; pray for him instead, by name. When you hear of someone’s faithfulness, rejoice, and tell him so. And when you next catch the flicker, confess it at once, simply, and thank God that he did not rejoice at your wrongdoing.

For worship. God has never once been glad at our fall. He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 33:11). When the son came home from the far country, the father did not savour the rags or rehearse the waste; he ran. And the Son of God is the Truth in person (John 14:6). In him love and truth are not rivals but one face. He told the woman at the well the whole truth about her life, and she ran into the town rejoicing, because the one who knew it all had not rejoiced over her sin but come to take it away.

verseByVerse.quote: Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

Love bears all things. Four verbs, each with all things attached, and the effect is of a wall that will not come down. Bears (stegō) is a roofing word: it means to cover, to keep the weather off, and so also to put up with. Paul used the same word of himself: we endure anything rather than put an obstacle in the way of the gospel (9:12). Love puts a roof over the person it loves, so that his failures are not exposed to everybody. That is not the same as pretending they are not there; it is refusing to broadcast them. Love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12) means that love does not repeat the story, and carries burdens instead.

Believes all things. Not gullibility, but a readiness to think the best, to give the benefit of the doubt where doubt genuinely exists. Love reads the other person generously and assumes the better explanation until it cannot. It does not assume the worst motives.

Hopes all things. When the evidence has run out, love goes on expecting God to do something with a person. It does not give up on people, because it trusts God’s power to change them. It is the parent still praying for a son twenty years after the last conversation.

Endures all things. The word (hypomenō) means to remain under a weight rather than get out from under it, to stand firm under pressure. Love keeps going when it is hard, persecuted or rejected. Love does not leave when loving becomes expensive. Christ endured the cross (Hebrews 12:2).

A guard on these four verbs. A guard has to be put on these four, because they have been used to do great harm and it would be dishonest to leave them undefended. Bears all things has been quoted at a woman to persuade her to keep silent about what is being done to her at home. Believes all things has been quoted to a congregation to persuade it that a credible allegation must be a misunderstanding. Endures all things has been used to send people back into danger. That is not what Paul means, and the proof is in his own letter. This is the man who, eight chapters earlier, told this church to put a man out of the fellowship for his sexual conduct and not even to eat with him (5:11–13). He names Alexander the coppersmith and warns Timothy about him (2 Timothy 4:14–15). He rebuked Peter to his face, publicly (Galatians 2:11). The apostle who wrote verse 7 did all of that, and he did not think he was contradicting himself.

What love does with wrongs. So the four verbs describe what love does with the wrongs it suffers, not what it does with the wrongs it discovers. Love will absorb an insult without publishing it. Love will not absorb an assault and call it patience. Believing all things means refusing to assume the worst about a person’s motives; it has never meant refusing to believe a victim, and using this verse to silence one turns it exactly on its head. Where someone is being hurt, love’s roof goes over the person being hurt, and the wrongdoer is brought into the light, which is itself the most loving thing that can happen to him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is naive, or must stay in danger, or must believe lies. All things means that in every situation love keeps bearing, trusting, hoping and enduring, within the bounds of truth and wisdom. Abuse is never to be tolerated or covered, and a person in danger should seek safety and help, from the church’s leaders and, where a crime has been done, from the police. Leaving danger is not a failure of love.

Does hoping all things mean I must believe a person will change? It means you never write anyone off as beyond God’s reach, and you keep praying for them. It does not mean you must pretend change has happened before it has, or put yourself back in harm’s way on the strength of a promise. Hope rests on God, not on the other person’s words. You can hope for a man’s repentance with all your heart and still wait to see its fruit before you trust him again (Matthew 3:8).

In a sentence. Love always shelters, always trusts, always hopes, and always keeps going.

On a Tuesday. Think of someone whose faults you know. Have you been covering them, or broadcasting them? Put the roof back on this week: say nothing about that person that you would not say in front of him. Think of someone you have given up on, and pray for him today, by name, as one who hopes. And if you are the one being hurt, love for yourself and for the one hurting you means telling someone who can help.

For worship. Read the four verbs once more, and see a face. It bore what was done to it without answering back. It went on believing the Father in the dark, when the Father’s face was hidden. It hoped when there was nothing visible to hope on, for the joy that was set before him. And it stayed under the weight until it was finished. Read that way, the verse is not a doormat. It is a description of the only love that has ever actually held, and it held for us. Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24), and he will bear with his people all the way home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love never fails. Prophecies will come to an end, tongues will stop, and knowledge will pass away, because our knowledge and our prophecy are only partial, and when completeness comes, the partial will be done away with. When Paul was a child he talked, thought and reasoned like a child, but when he became a man he put childish ways behind him. At present we see only a blurred reflection in a mirror, but then we shall see face to face. Now Paul knows in part; then he will know fully, just as he is fully known. And now these three remain: faith, hope and love. But the greatest of them is love.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Eschatology of the Gifts and the Permanence of Love

Paul’s teaching that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will pass away is often taken as the foundation of the cessationist argument — the gifts being provisional for an age of incomplete revelation and superseded when the perfect comes. Whether the perfect means the completion of the New Testament canon, the maturity of the church, or the return of Christ has been debated for centuries; but Paul defines his own terms in verse 12, where then is when we see face to face and know fully even as I have been fully known. Since no one began to see God face to face when the canon closed, this passage by itself does not settle the question, and the stronger arguments for cessation are made from Ephesians 2:20 and Hebrews 2:3–4 rather than from here. Those arguments are the stronger.

What the passage does settle is the structure: the gifts are for now, and love is for now and for ever. A church that pours its energy into the spectacular while neglecting love has it exactly backwards, clinging to the provisional and letting go of the permanent — and that is true of every party to the argument, whichever side it takes.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian community that prized tongues above all else was, on Paul’s analysis, investing heavily in something that would not survive the transition to the coming age, while neglecting the one quality that would. Now: The church that is rich in programmes, gifts, and spiritual activity but thin in genuine love has the Corinthian problem in contemporary dress. Every spiritual tradition — charismatic, Reformed, liturgical — can produce communities that are impressively gifted and loveless. Paul’s word is the same to all of them: love never ends; everything else is provisional.

verseByVerse.quote: Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.

Love never ends. The portrait stops and the argument resumes, and the hinge is the word never. The verb behind ends (piptō) means to fall, the way a leaf falls, or a flower, or a building. Everything else in the chapter has a collapse in its future. Love does not. It will never fail or become obsolete; it will continue into eternity, because God is love (1 John 4:8).

As for prophecies, they will pass away. Three things are named, and they are precisely the three the Corinthians had been ranking: prophecy, tongues, knowledge. Pass away (katargeō) means to be done away with, rendered inoperative, put out of use.

As for tongues, they will cease. Cease (pauō) simply means to stop.

As for knowledge, it will pass away. The same word as for prophecy. Our present partial knowledge will be replaced by full knowledge. Paul says all three have an expiry date, and this is a devastating thing to say to a church that had built its whole status system on them. The gifts they were fighting over were, on the apostle’s own account, temporary equipment.

Why the gifts pass away. It is worth being clear about the reason, because it is not that the gifts are inferior. They came from the Spirit, they were given for the common good, and Paul will tell this church to desire them earnestly and not to forbid them (14:1, 39). They pass away because they are the equipment of a journey, and journeys end. A map is a wonderful thing. Nobody consults one after arriving. That is the point that ought to survive every argument that has ever been conducted over this passage. Whatever a Christian concludes about when these gifts pass away, the apostle’s reason for raising the subject was not to settle a timetable. It was to tell a church obsessed with the temporary that it had its heart set on things with a shelf life, while neglecting the one thing that will still be standing when the sun burns out.

The last sermon. There is a picture worth carrying. The most gifted preacher who has ever lived will one day preach his last sermon, and there will never be any need for another. Every translation, every commentary, every sermon series, every one of these words will be as obsolete as a candle at noon. And the smallest act of love done by the least-noticed believer in the congregation will still be there, because it belongs to what is coming rather than to what is passing (1 Peter 1:24–25).

Does the different verb for tongues mean they stopped first? One detail of the wording is often pressed into service. Paul uses one verb of prophecy and knowledge, they will be rendered inoperative, and a different verb of tongues: they will cease, in a form that can suggest ceasing of themselves. Some have built on that the claim that tongues were to stop of their own accord at an earlier point than the other two. It is a slender foundation for a large conclusion; Greek writers use that form loosely, and Paul’s three clauses are plainly parallel in force. A doctrine should not be hung on a verb ending. The case for the cessation of these gifts, which this commentary holds, rests on other ground (see on vv. 9–10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean knowledge itself ends in heaven. We will know more, not less (v. 12). It means the present gift of partial knowledge will give way to something far greater, as starlight gives way to the sun.

Why is love the exception? Not because love is more useful. It is that the other three are things we do in a world where God is not yet seen, while love is what God is (1 John 4:8). Prophecy exists because we cannot see him; knowledge exists because we do not yet know him as we will; tongues exist because we are still on the road. Love existed before there was a road, in the giving between Father, Son and Spirit, and it will still be there when the road has been rolled up.

In a sentence. Love will never fail. But prophecies will come to an end, tongues will stop, and knowledge will be set aside.

On a Tuesday. Invest in what lasts. Look at how you spent your best energy this week, and ask how much of it went into things with a shelf life: reputation, possessions, being right. Then do one thing today that belongs to eternity: an act of patient, costly love toward someone who will not repay it. Gifts will end; love never will.

For worship. Before the mountains were brought forth, love was. The Father loved the Son before the foundation of the world (John 17:24), and in that love the Spirit was not a stranger. Creation was the overflow of it, and redemption was the cost of it, and the new creation will be the home of it forever. Everything that is passing serves what is permanent, and what is permanent is the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord, from which nothing in all creation will be able to separate us (Romans 8:39).

verseByVerse.quote: For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.

For we know in part and we prophesy in part. Even the best present gifts give only partial understanding. Paul includes himself: the apostle who received revelations knew in part.

But when the perfect comes. The perfect (to teleion) is the complete, the goal reached, the end for which a thing exists. It most naturally refers to the completion of all things at Christ’s return, when we see him face to face (v. 12).

The partial will pass away. When the complete arrives, the incomplete is no longer needed. The candle is not despised when the sun comes up. It is simply no longer lit.

The question everyone asks. Here is the verse Christians have argued over for centuries, and it deserves a straight account rather than a diplomatic fog. The question is simple to state: what is the perfect, and when does it come? On the answer hangs, for many, the question of whether gifts such as prophecy, tongues and healing continue in the church today. Three answers have been given. Some have said the perfect is the completed New Testament: once the last book was written, the church had God’s finished word and no longer needed revelatory gifts. Others have taken it as the maturity of the church, grown up out of its infancy. Others take it as the return of Christ and the state of things that follows.

Where Christians differ: what is the perfect? Some cessationists argue that the perfect is the completed New Testament canon, so that tongues and prophecy ceased when Scripture was finished. Continuationists argue that since the perfect is Christ’s return, the gifts must continue until then. Verdict: The perfect is best understood as the return of Christ and the age to come, when we will see face to face and know fully. This verse says that these gifts will certainly end by then; it does not say whether some of them might end sooner. The case for the cessation of the revelatory and sign gifts rests on other texts: the foundational and unrepeatable role of apostles and prophets (Ephesians 2:20), the confirmation of the apostolic message by signs (Hebrews 2:3–4), and the closing of the canon (Jude 3).

Why the perfect is Christ’s return. Paul himself defines his terms two verses later. Then we shall see face to face; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known (v. 12). Whatever else may be said, no Christian began to see God face to face when the book of Revelation was finished, and nobody alive knows God as fully as God knows him. The then of this passage is not a date in the first century. It is the day we see him. That has to be said even though it cuts against a conclusion some careful and beloved teachers have drawn, because honesty about a text matters more than tidiness. This passage does not, by itself, prove that the miraculous gifts ended with the apostles.

The case on other ground. But it would be equally dishonest to leave the impression that the case for their ceasing rests on this verse, because it does not, and the men who have made that case were not careless readers. Their argument runs on other ground. The apostles and prophets are called the foundation of the church, with Christ as the cornerstone (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. The signs and wonders of the first generation are described as God bearing witness to a message declared by those who heard the Lord (Hebrews 2:3–4), which suggests a purpose tied to that generation. The faith was once for all delivered to the saints (Jude 3). Scripture is sufficient, and a church expecting fresh revelation is exposed to every confident voice. And there is the honest observation that what is called prophecy or tongues in many places today bears little resemblance to what is described in Acts, where tongues were known languages (Acts 2:6–11). B. B. Warfield argued the case a century ago, and in our own day John MacArthur has argued it with conviction and love for the Word. These are serious arguments made by serious men, and they deserve a serious answer rather than a sneer.

The other side, fairly stated. The answer from the other side is also serious. Paul told this church plainly, do not forbid speaking in tongues (14:39), and told another church, do not quench the Spirit, do not despise prophecies, but test everything; hold fast what is good (1 Thessalonians 5:19–21). Those are commands, and continuationist brothers point out that no verse explicitly announces their repeal. And the observation that today’s claimed gifts often look nothing like the New Testament’s may, they argue, be an argument for testing them rather than for abolishing the category. Cessationists answer that commands addressed to churches with living apostles and prophets assume conditions that no longer hold, as the instructions about apostolic visits do. Godly men such as Wayne Grudem have held the continuationist view, and Martyn Lloyd-Jones was open to it; they have loved Christ and his word.

So where should an ordinary believer land? The cessationist case, made on that other ground, is the stronger, and it is the one followed here (see on Acts 5:12): the apostles and prophets were a foundation laid once, the signs attested their message, and the Scripture they gave is complete. Three further things can be said with confidence, and they are enough to live by. First, whichever conclusion a Christian reaches, this passage forbids him to look down on a brother who reached the other one; the chapter it sits in is about love, and a man who wins this argument uncharitably has lost the chapter. Second, no gift is the mark of the Spirit’s presence; that was settled at 12:3, and the mark is the confession that Jesus is Lord. Third, and this is Paul’s actual point, all of it is partial. Both sides of this debate are arguing about equipment for a journey that is nearly over, and the chapter was written to say so.

If the gifts have ceased, does God still heal and guide today? Yes. Cessationism does not mean God has stopped working. It means the particular gifts by which the apostles and prophets received new revelation and confirmed it with signs were for the foundation period. God still answers prayer, and he still heals the sick, sometimes in ways no doctor can explain; James tells us to call the elders and pray (James 5:14–15). He still guides his people, through his word, wise counsel, providence, and the Spirit’s illumination of Scripture. What he does not do is add new revelation to the Bible. A strong impression in prayer may be used by God, but it must be weighed by Scripture and never treated as his voice with the authority of Scripture.

What should I do if my church, or a friend, believes the gifts continue? Love them, and keep the main thing the main thing. Many continuationist believers are sound on the gospel, love the Bible, and put cessationists to shame in prayer and evangelism. Be clear about what you believe and why, but do not make it a test of fellowship among those who confess Christ crucified. Two things are worth watching for in any setting: whether claimed words from God are tested by Scripture and treated as below it, and whether Christ and the gospel stay at the centre. Where those hold, there is real unity to enjoy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Scripture is partial or imperfect. Scripture is complete and sufficient for this age (2 Timothy 3:16–17). But our knowledge, even with Scripture, is partial compared to seeing Christ. The map is perfect; our reading of it is still the reading of travellers.

In a sentence. Our knowledge is incomplete and our prophesying is incomplete; but when completeness comes, what is incomplete will be done away with.

On a Tuesday. The next time this subject comes up among Christians, decide beforehand that you will be the one who is patient and kind in the conversation. Say what you believe, plainly, and then turn the talk to the thing both sides long for: the day when we will see him.

For worship. Everything we have now is partial because he is not yet seen. But it is coming: the perfect, the complete, the end for which the world was made. The Bridegroom will come, and the church will need no more lamps. Every prophecy will have been fulfilled in the sight of its object, and every sermon will be finished because the One preached will be present. The partial is a pledge of the whole. Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “The perfect” most naturally refers to the completion of all things when Christ returns.

verseByVerse.quote: When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.

When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. An illustration, and it is regularly misused as a rebuke, as though Paul were telling the Corinthians to stop being childish, which he does elsewhere (3:1; 14:20) but not mainly here. Read it in its place: he is explaining what he means by partial. Notice that there is nothing wrong with the child’s speech. A three-year-old naming things is not lying. His thinking is real thinking, his reasoning is real reasoning, and within its own scale it works perfectly well. It is simply small. He is not mistaken about the world; he has less of it. That is right for a child.

When I became a man, I gave up childish ways. Gave up is katargeō again, the same word as pass away in verses 8 and 10. The present gifts are like childhood speech compared with the maturity of the age to come. There may also be a gentle rebuke in the background: the Corinthians, proud of tongues, were acting like children (3:1; 14:20).

True knowledge on a child’s scale. That is what Paul says about our present knowledge of God, and it is a wonderfully balanced thing to say. It rules out two errors at once. It rules out the confidence that imagines our theology has God taped, that the systems and the creeds have got him mapped and there is nothing left to be astonished by. And it equally rules out the fashionable humility that says nothing can really be known, that all our talk of God is guesswork. The child does know his mother. He simply does not yet know what she gave up for him, what she fears at three in the morning, or what she was like at twenty. So the Christian’s knowledge of God is true knowledge, and it is knowledge on a child’s scale. What comes next is not a correction of it but a growing up into it.

A quiet comfort. Nobody blames a child for being a child. The smallness is not a fault to be repented of; it is a stage to be outgrown, and the outgrowing is not something a child achieves by concentrating. It happens to him. Growing up is done to us, and so is this: when he appears we shall be like him (1 John 3:2).

Firm and light. There is a consequence for how a Christian holds his convictions. If our knowledge is genuine and partial, then two attitudes are ruled out and one is required. Ruled out is the man who will not commit to anything because certainty is arrogant; the child does know his mother, and hedging every sentence is not humility but evasion. Also ruled out is the man who treats his own grasp of a disputed question as though it were the view from the throne. What is required is conviction held firmly and carried lightly: believing what God has said with your whole weight, and holding your own conclusions about the harder questions with the awareness that you are, at present, three feet tall. Which is exactly the temper the previous verses were asking for. A church divided over prophecy and tongues is a nursery of children shouting about a subject on which every one of them is speaking like a child. That is not an argument for indifference. It is an argument for the kind of patience that this chapter has been describing all along.

How do I know which convictions to hold firmly and which lightly? Hold most firmly what Scripture states most clearly and what the church has confessed together through the ages: the Trinity, the deity and humanity of Christ, his atoning death and bodily resurrection, justification by faith alone, the authority of Scripture, his return. On these, a Christian stands without apology. Hold more lightly the conclusions that depend on harder texts and on which faithful Bible-believing Christians have long differed, such as the details of the gifts, church government, or the order of end-time events. Believe them, teach them, but do not treat the brother who differs as an enemy of the gospel.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the gifts are childish or bad. They are right for this stage, as childhood speech is right for a child.

In a sentence. As a child Paul talked, thought and reasoned like a child. When he grew up, he left childish ways behind.

On a Tuesday. Grow up in love. Leave behind childish attitudes: sulking, competing, showing off, needing to win. Pick one this week that you recognise in yourself and ask God to put it away. And next time you are tempted to speak about God as though you had him mapped, remember the three-year-old, and let wonder have a word.

For worship. We are children, and he is our Father. He does not despise the stammering of his little ones; he delights in it, as any father does in the first words of his son. And he has not left us to grow up alone. He has given us his Son as our elder Brother and his Spirit as the pledge of the maturity to come. One day the child will see his Father’s face and understand what the Father gave up for him, and then, at last, he will know how to thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.

For now we see in a mirror dimly. Corinth was famous for its bronze, and mirrors in that world were polished metal; every reader of this letter had looked into one. They did not work like ours. A bronze mirror gives you back a darkened, slightly warped version of a face: recognisably you, and never quite you. The phrase translated dimly (en ainigmati) is literally in a riddle, which is where the word enigma comes from. That is our present sight of God. Not blindness. We see him truly, through his word and works, but indirectly, like a reflection: a face in dark metal, and a riddle that is genuinely about him.

But then face to face. Refuse to let that phrase stay vague, because Scripture does not leave it vague and it is the hope of the whole Bible in three words. God spoke to Moses mouth to mouth, clearly and not in riddles (Numbers 12:8), and Paul’s word for dimly echoes that verse. Yet when Moses asked for the one thing more, please show me your glory, he was told, you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live; he was put in a cleft of rock, covered with a hand, and allowed to see the back of God going past (Exodus 33:18–23). That is the high-water mark of the old covenant. The greatest prophet in Israel’s history asked to see God’s face and was refused it. And the last page of the Bible says of ordinary redeemed people, without ceremony: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4). What Moses was not given, the least believer in the congregation is promised. We shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). This is what the church has called the beatific vision, the great hope of the Christian.

Whose face will we see? The face of God in Christ. The glory of God has already shone in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 4:6), and on that day we will see the Son, risen and glorified, with the marks of the nails still on him, and in him we will see the Father (John 14:9). We will not see the divine essence with bodily eyes, for God is spirit and infinite; but we will know him directly, without veil or riddle, in the face of the Lamb, as fully as creatures can.

Now I know in part; then I shall know fully. Know fully (epiginōskō) is to know thoroughly. Our knowledge will be complete, not infinite as God’s is, but without the distortions and gaps of the present.

Even as I have been fully known. Then the last clause, and it is the most tender sentence in the chapter. Sit inside that. God already knows us completely (8:3; Galatians 4:9). Every human being alive is caught in one of two positions, and there is no third. Either you are loved by people who do not fully know you, who love a version of you assembled from your better hours, or you are known by someone who has seen the worst and whose affection you can feel adjusting itself. The fear that runs underneath most human relationships is the same fear: if they knew everything, they would not stay. It is why people edit themselves in company, and why being loved often fails to settle anything. Paul writes, of God, I have been fully known. Past tense, already accomplished. There is no discovery still to come, no file not yet opened, nothing that will emerge in the last hour and change the verdict. The one who knows the whole of it, the thing you have never told anyone, the thing you would not put in a prayer, is the one who set his love on you before you had done anything at all.

The ground of the whole chapter. And that is the ground of everything this chapter has asked for. A person who is fully known and fully loved has nothing left to protect, and a person with nothing to protect can afford to be patient, kind, unenvious, and free of the ledger. Love like this is not squeezed out of the loveless by effort. It leaks out of people who have stopped being afraid of being found out.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become God or know everything. We will always be creatures, learning and adoring forever. But we will know God directly and truly.

Will we recognise one another? Scripture gives good reason to think so. If our knowledge then is fuller, not emptier, we will not know less than we do now. The disciples recognised Moses and Elijah on the mountain (Matthew 17:3–4); the risen Jesus was known by those who loved him; Paul expects to glory over the Thessalonians at Christ’s coming (1 Thessalonians 2:19). The relationships of grace are not erased but perfected. And every face we know will be turned the same way, toward his.

What happens to believers who die before that day? They are with the Lord at once, consciously and gladly. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). They do not sleep in unconsciousness, and there is no purgatory between. Yet the fullest face to face waits for the resurrection, when Christ returns and body and soul are reunited in glory (15:51–54).

In a sentence. For now we see only a dim reflection, as in a metal mirror; then we shall see face to face. Now Paul knows in part; then he will know fully, just as he is already fully known.

On a Tuesday. Think of the thing you most fear being known about you. Bring it to God in prayer, by name, and remember that he knew it before you told him and loves you no less. Then, in one relationship this week, stop protecting yourself a little: admit a fault, ask forgiveness, let yourself be seen. People who are fully known by God can afford it.

For worship. The Son of God knew exactly what he was buying. He looked at the whole record, not the edited version, the whole of it, and went to the cross for it anyway, so that on some morning still ahead he could stand in front of the people he died for with nothing hidden on either side, and be looked at. That is what he wanted. Not servants at a distance, but a face to face. You are fully known by God, and fully loved, and one day you will see him. Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8).
verseByVerse.note: Mirrors were made of polished metal and gave a dim, imperfect reflection; Corinth was famous for its bronze work. The ESV notes that “dimly” is literally “in a riddle.”

parallels.desc: with him I speak mouth to mouth, clearly, and not in riddles

verseByVerse.quote: So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three. Paul has just said that prophecy, tongues and knowledge will fall. Now he names three things that will not. Abide (menō) means to remain, to last. Unlike the gifts, these three are permanent features of the Christian life. The three appear together all over Paul’s letters: your work of faith and labor of love and steadfastness of hope (1 Thessalonians 1:3; 5:8; Colossians 1:4–5). And they map the Christian life onto time. Faith takes hold of what God has done. Hope leans forward to what he will do. Love does the present tense. Between them they cover everything a believer has.

But the greatest of these is love. The last clause needs explaining rather than admiring, because at first sight it is odd. Why is love greater? Faith saves; love does not. Faith is how a sinner is justified, and Paul of all people is not about to demote it. The answer is in the word abide. Consider what happens to each of the three when Christ returns. Faith is trusting a God you cannot see, and on that day you will see him, so faith will have become sight (2 Corinthians 5:7). Hope is waiting for what has not yet arrived, and on that day it will have arrived, so hope will have become possession (Romans 8:24). Neither is lost; each is swallowed by its own fulfilment. Love alone arrives unchanged. There is nothing love turns into, because there is nothing better than love to turn into. It is the only thing in the Christian life that will be doing in eternity exactly what it does now, which is why practising it is the one activity of this life that is not preparation for something else.

The deepest reason. Faith and hope are things creatures do; God has neither. He does not trust, because he knows, and he does not hope, because he holds. But God is love (1 John 4:8, 16): not merely loving, but love itself, in the unbroken giving between Father, Son and Spirit that was going on before there was anything else at all. Love is greatest because love is the one item on the list that is a description of God. Love is the bond of the age to come.

If love is greater, does it save us? No. We are justified by faith alone, not by our love. Faith is not the greatest virtue, but it is the empty hand that receives Christ, and Christ’s righteousness is what saves (Romans 3:28; 5:1). Love is the fruit, not the root. A faith that produces no love is dead (Galatians 5:6; James 2:17), but even the believer’s best love is imperfect, and if we had to stand on our love we would fall. We stand on Christ’s love for us, received by faith, and that love then begins to love through us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean faith and hope are unimportant. We are justified by faith alone (Romans 5:1), and hope is our anchor (Hebrews 6:19). But love is the goal of everything (1 Timothy 1:5).

Where the chapter has been going. The whole chapter has been leading somewhere other than self-improvement. It began by pricing the gifts and it ends by naming the eternal life of God, and it turns out that the patient, unenvious, unbookkeeping love it describes is not a standard the Corinthians were simply failing to reach. It is a Person, who was patient with them, who did not insist on his own way, who bore all things and endured all things, and who was at that moment holding that quarrelsome church together with his own hands.

In a sentence. So these three remain: faith, hope and love. And the greatest of them is love.

On a Tuesday. At the end of today, ask not just: did I believe? did I hope? But: did I love? Name one person you loved well today and thank God for the grace that did it; name one you did not, and confess it, and plan one concrete act of love for that person tomorrow. Then go to sleep resting in his love, not yours.

For worship. They wanted to know which gift was the greatest. He gave them himself and called it the more excellent way. Faith will one day give way to sight, and hope to having, but love will go on, because the One who loved us before the world began will go on loving us when the world has been made new. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). To him, the Love that never ends, be glory forever.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal.<sup>2</sup>And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.<sup>3</sup>If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing.<sup>4</sup>Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant<sup>5</sup>or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful;<sup>6</sup>it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth.<sup>7</sup>Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.<sup>8</sup>Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away.<sup>9</sup>For we know in part and we prophesy in part,<sup>10</sup>but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.<sup>11</sup>When I was a child, I spoke like a child, I thought like a child, I reasoned like a child. When I became a man, I gave up childish ways.<sup>12</sup>For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.<sup>13</sup>So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love.

14.title: Prophecy, Tongues, and the Order of Worship
14.overview:
Having shown that love is the way all gifts must be used, Paul applies it to the Corinthians’ worship, which had become noisy and confusing as many people spoke in tongues at once. His test is simple: what builds up the church? Tongues spoken without interpretation build up only the speaker, because no one else understands; prophecy, spoken in ordinary language, strengthens, encourages and comforts everyone. Like a flute that plays no recognisable tune, or a bugle with an uncertain call, unintelligible speech helps nobody, and a visitor cannot even say “Amen” to a prayer he does not understand. Paul himself speaks in tongues more than all of them, but in church he would rather say five words people can understand than ten thousand in a tongue.

He quotes Isaiah, where foreign speech was a sign of God’s judgement on unbelieving Israel, and warns that a visitor who walks into a room full of tongues will think they are mad, whereas prophecy may expose his heart and bring him to worship God. Then he gives practical rules. Each person may contribute, a psalm, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation, but everything must build others up. Only two or three should speak in tongues, in turn, with interpretation; two or three prophets should speak and the others weigh what they say. God is a God of peace, not disorder. Women should keep silent in this setting, apparently in the weighing of prophecies. Paul’s instructions are the Lord’s command, and everything should be done decently and in order.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul tells them to make love their aim, and to desire spiritual gifts eagerly, especially prophecy. Someone who speaks in a tongue speaks to God, not to people, because no one understands; he utters mysteries by the Spirit. But someone who prophesies speaks to people, building them up, encouraging and comforting them. The tongue-speaker edifies himself, but the prophet edifies the church. Paul would like every one of them to speak in tongues, but he would rather they prophesied. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.theology:
Intelligibility as a Prerequisite for Edification

Paul’s governing principle for corporate worship — intelligibility — has deep theological roots. The God who speaks is a God who communicates; the Word became flesh precisely to be heard and understood. Worship that renders the word of God inaccessible to the gathered community is, at a structural level, working against the grain of the incarnation. The Reformers’ insistence on vernacular worship (against the Latin Mass) was an application of precisely this principle: if the people cannot understand what is being said and done, they cannot be edified.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian preference for tongues in corporate worship was driven by the same status-seeking that produced the faction fights: tongues was the impressive gift, the spectacular performance. Paul’s preference for prophecy is a preference for the communal over the spectacular, the edifying over the impressive. Now: The principle of intelligibility has applications beyond tongues: jargon-laden sermons, inaccessible liturgy, and culturally opaque worship practices all fail the same criterion. Does the person who attends understand what is happening? Are they being built up?

verseByVerse.quote: Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 14 applies the love of chapter 13 to the Corinthians’ worship. Their gatherings were chaotic: many speaking in tongues at once, with no interpretation, so that no one understood and outsiders thought them mad. Paul’s principle is that everything in worship must build up the church, and only what is understood can build up. So prophecy, which speaks God’s word intelligibly, is greater than uninterpreted tongues (vv. 1–5). Unintelligible sounds are as useless as a bugle with no clear note; pray and sing with the mind as well as the spirit (vv. 6–19). Tongues without interpretation are a sign of judgement on unbelievers, while prophecy convicts them and brings them to worship (vv. 20–25). Then come practical rules: two or three speakers at most, one at a time, with interpretation and weighing; women are not to take part in judging what is said; and all things must be done decently and in order, because God is a God of peace (vv. 26–40). Behind it all stands a God who speaks, who made the world by his word and came to us as the Word, and who wants to be understood.

Pursue love. Two commands, and it matters that they are both here. After a chapter saying that the gifts without love are worth nothing, the obvious inference would be to stop caring about the gifts. Paul heads that off in his first sentence. Love is not an alternative to gifts; it is the way gifts are to be used. Both verbs are strong. Pursue (diōkō) is a hunting word: chase it down, run after it. Love from chapter 13 is the aim of everything.

And earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy. Earnestly desire is the verb behind our word zeal. So the Christian is to be zealous about both, and there is a definite order: love first, gifts within it. Love does not cancel gifts; it directs them. Then the whole chapter’s argument in one phrase: especially that you may prophesy. That is a startling preference to put to this church, and it will take the rest of the chapter to justify. But the reason is simple enough to state now, and it will not change: prophecy can be understood by the people in the room, and so it builds them up.

For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God. Without interpretation, a tongue is addressed to God, in prayer or praise, not to the congregation. That is why Paul will describe it as praying, singing and giving thanks (vv. 14–16) rather than as teaching.

For no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit. Understands is literally hears: no one grasps it. Mysteries here means things hidden from the hearers, not understood by them; not riddles, but the things of God spoken in a form that is closed to those listening. In the Spirit (or in his spirit, as the ESV notes) means by the Spirit’s enabling.

What tongues were. The reader deserves an honest account of what tongues actually were, because the chapter assumes a knowledge we no longer have. The Greek word is simply tongue (glōssa), the same word used for a language. At Pentecost the gift produced recognisable human languages: visitors from many regions each heard the mighty works of God in his own language (Acts 2:6–11). In Corinth the effect in the room was different, because there was no foreigner present who knew the language, so no one understood, and a separate gift of interpretation was required. Paul speaks of various kinds of tongues (12:10). Four things can be said with confidence, and they are enough. It was genuine speech, given by the Spirit. It was addressed to God, not to the congregation. It was unintelligible to hearers unless interpreted. And it was never the badge of a real Christian or the proof of an advanced one.

Where Christians differ: what were tongues? Some think the Corinthian tongues were ecstatic, non-human speech; others that they were real human languages as at Pentecost. Verdict: At Pentecost, tongues were known human languages, understood by foreigners (Acts 2:6–11). Paul’s own analogy here is foreign languages (vv. 10–11), and interpretation means translation. So the most natural reading is that tongues were real languages the speaker had not learned. Paul’s mention of tongues of angels (13:1) is a hypothetical extreme, not a description of the gift.

Not the mark of the Spirit. What cannot be said is that tongues are the sign of a Spirit-filled Christian. That was settled two chapters ago: not all speak with tongues (12:30), and the mark of the Spirit is the confession that Jesus is Lord (12:3). Corinth had made a distinction out of a distribution, and the whole chapter is a patient dismantling of it.

Is the private prayer language some Christians speak of today the same thing? This commentary holds that it is not. The tongues of the New Testament were real languages, given by the Spirit as a sign gift belonging to the apostolic foundation of the church (see on 13:8–10), and there is no warrant in Scripture for a separate private prayer language for later believers. Many sincere Christians who practise something they call tongues love Christ deeply, and they should be treated as brothers and sisters, not mocked. But no Christian needs such an experience to pray fully and freely. The Spirit helps every believer in his weakness and intercedes for him (Romans 8:26), and you may pour out your heart to your Father in your own words.

What it does not mean. It does not mean tongues were useless. Paul values them (v. 18). But in the gathered church, they must be interpreted.

In a sentence. Make love your aim, and eagerly seek the gifts of the Spirit, above all prophecy. Someone speaking in a tongue is speaking to God, not to people, since no one understands; by the Spirit he speaks things hidden from his hearers.

On a Tuesday. In all your speech this week, at church and elsewhere, aim to be understood and to build others up. Before you speak in a Bible study or a church meeting, ask one question: will anyone be stronger for this?

For worship. Our God is not a God who mumbles. He spoke, and light was. He spoke to the fathers by the prophets, and in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son (Hebrews 1:1–2). He has given us a Book in human words and sent his Spirit so that we might understand it. Every good gift he gives, he gives in love, and every gift is meant to carry his love from one heart to another. Blessed be the God who wants to be known, and who has made himself known in Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation.

On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people. Here is the contrast that governs the chapter. Tongues speaks to God; prophecy speaks to people, in their own language. Both are real, both were given by the Spirit, and only one of them does anything for the person in the next seat.

For their upbuilding. Notice how Paul defines prophecy. He does not define it by its source, or by how it feels, or by whether it predicts anything. He defines it by its effect, and he names three effects. That is a remarkable way to identify a gift, and it gives the church a usable test: look at what happened to the people who heard it. Upbuilding (oikodomē) is the builder’s word again, building up in faith and maturity, and it is the key word of the chapter (vv. 3, 4, 5, 12, 17, 26): the congregation is a structure going up, and this speech adds a course of stone.

And encouragement. Encouragement (paraklēsis) is close to the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the one called alongside. It means coming up beside someone and putting strength into him, whether by urging or by comfort: exhortation, urging on.

And consolation. Consolation (paramythia) is the plain word for what you say to the grieving: comfort for the sorrowing and discouraged.

The test of the effect. Stand those three next to the popular idea of prophecy and the difference is striking. Prophecy as most people imagine it is dramatic, predictive, and slightly alarming. Prophecy as Paul describes it leaves a congregation stronger, braver and comforted. A word that leaves people frightened, confused, or impressed with the speaker has not passed this test, whatever it claimed about its source.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prophecy was only encouragement and never correction. It could expose sin (vv. 24–25). And it does not mean prophecy is the same as preaching, though they share these purposes. Preaching expounds a text that is already given. Prophecy in this chapter was something said into a particular room on a particular day, which then had to be weighed by the others (v. 29), a thing no one would ever say about Scripture. So whatever else must be settled about this gift, it was subject to Scripture and never an addition to it.

If prophecy has ceased, what does this verse ask of me? A great deal. What is not in dispute is that these three effects are wanted, and that any Christian may aim at them. Even a believer entirely certain that the gift itself has ceased may take verse 3 as a description of what preaching should do and what his conversation after the service ought to do. Somebody in the room this Sunday needs to be built up, somebody needs courage, and somebody needs consoling, and the words that do it, drawn from Scripture, are the nearest thing to this verse that most of us will ever handle (1 Thessalonians 5:11; Hebrews 3:13).

In a sentence. But someone who prophesies speaks to people, to strengthen, urge on and comfort them.

On a Tuesday. Think of one person you will see this week who is struggling. Take one verse of Scripture that has strengthened you, and give it to them, plainly, with a sentence about why it helped. That is upbuilding, encouragement and consolation in an ordinary week.

For worship. The Holy Spirit is the Comforter, the one called alongside, and he has never once spoken to God’s people except to build them up in Christ. Through prophets and apostles he gave us the Scriptures, and through the Scriptures he still strengthens the weak, urges on the weary and consoles the grieving. Blessed be the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction (2 Corinthians 1:3–4), and whose word is never empty.

verseByVerse.quote: The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church. Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.

The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself. Read the first half slowly, because it is easily heard as a sneer and it is not one. Paul is not saying the tongue-speaker is being selfish. He is stating a fact about what the gift did: the speaker might be edified in some way, perhaps through the experience of praising God, even without understanding the words. But that is not the purpose of gifts, which are for the common good (12:7). The problem is not the gift. It is the setting. Corinth had taken something that built up the individual and made it the centrepiece of the gathering, and the gathering exists for a different purpose.

But the one who prophesies builds up the church. Prophecy serves everyone in the room.

Now I want you all to speak in tongues, but even more to prophesy. Nobody expecting a crackdown expects that sentence. Paul does not despise tongues. But he does not mean all will (12:30); it is a wish, like his wish that all were single as he was (7:7). He is not trying to remove anything. He is trying to reorder it, which is the harder and better kind of correction, and much rarer in churches than either enthusiasm or suppression.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets. Greater here means more useful to the church. And there is the qualifier that shows exactly where the ranking comes from. Interpreted tongues are no longer inferior to prophecy, because interpreted tongues do what prophecy does: the room understands and is built up. So the greatness Paul is measuring is not intrinsic to the gift at all. It is entirely a question of how many people benefit. The same gift moves up or down the scale depending on whether anyone else in the room can follow it.

So that the church may be built up. The test for everything. That principle reaches a great deal further than tongues, and it is worth applying to things nobody would call a spiritual gift. The sermon full of allusions the congregation cannot catch. The prayer meeting conducted in a register that a newcomer could not join. The music pitched where only the musicians can sing it. In every case the activity may be excellent, and the same question decides the matter: is anyone else being built by this, or only the one doing it?
