What it does not mean. It does not mean self-edification is wrong. A Christian who is strengthened in private prayer and Bible reading is doing exactly what he should. It means public worship is for building up others.

Is it wrong to go to church for what I get out of it? Not wrong, but incomplete. You should come hungry, wanting to be fed by the word and to meet God, and he delights to feed you. But this chapter adds a second reason for being there: the others. Every believer comes as a member of a body, with something to give as well as something to receive (12:7). The two are not rivals. The Christian who comes to serve is very often the one who goes home most fed, and the one who comes only to consume is often the first to complain that he got nothing.

In a sentence. Someone who speaks in a tongue strengthens himself, but someone who prophesies strengthens the church. Paul would be glad if all of you spoke in tongues, but gladder still if you prophesied. Prophecy does more good than tongues, unless the tongue is interpreted so that the church is built up.

On a Tuesday. When you serve in church, ask: does this build others up, or mainly me? Look at one thing you do regularly at church and ask whether it could be made easier for a newcomer to follow, and then make it so.

For worship. The Lord Jesus never did a single thing for show. When he prayed, he prayed for his disciples to hear (John 11:42; 17:13). When he spoke, the common people heard him gladly. His whole life was spent building up others, and his death was the foundation of the church he is still building. On this rock I will build my church, he said (Matthew 16:18), and every stone that is laid by a word of love is laid by his hand.

parallels.desc: would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks what good it would do them if he came speaking in tongues and brought no revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching. Even lifeless instruments, a flute or a harp, must play distinct notes to be recognised, and if a trumpet sounds an unclear call, who will prepare for battle? It is the same with them: unintelligible speech is talking into the air. There are many languages in the world, all meaningful, but if Paul does not understand a language he and the speaker are foreigners to each other. Since they are eager for spiritual gifts, they should seek to excel in those that build up the church. So anyone who speaks in a tongue should pray for the power to interpret. If Paul prays in a tongue, his spirit prays but his mind is unproductive. So he will pray and sing both with his spirit and with his mind. Otherwise, how can an outsider say “Amen” to his thanksgiving if he does not know what is being said? He may give thanks well, but the other person is not built up. Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than all of them, but in church he would rather speak five words that teach others than ten thousand in a tongue.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Corporate Criterion and the Nature of Worship

Paul’s insistence on intelligibility in corporate worship reflects a deep theological conviction about the nature of Christian assembly: it is not a private spiritual experience shared simultaneously by many individuals but a genuinely corporate event in which the whole body is built up together. Worship is not merely my encounter with God in the presence of other people; it is our encounter with God as a body. This corporate dimension requires intelligibility: I cannot say “Amen” to what I cannot understand, and a community of “Amens” is the sign that the body is genuinely worshipping together.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian tongues-enthusiasts were essentially importing an individual spiritual practice into the corporate meeting without consideration for the community’s ability to participate. Paul’s five-to-ten-thousand ratio is not a rule to be calculated but a principle to be embodied: always ask, in corporate worship, whether what is done can be received and responded to by the whole community. Now: The principle applies to any element of worship that prioritises the experience of some over the edification of all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?

Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues. Paul puts himself in the frame, which is his habitual courtesy in this letter. He does not say that when you speak in tongues you are useless. He says: suppose I turn up and do it.

How will I benefit you. What good would it do? The idea of benefit is the key, and it is not new: the same question, what is helpful, whose advantage is served, governed the argument about idol meat (10:23, 33), and it governs this one. Paul is not asking whether an activity is spiritual, permitted, or sincere. He is asking whether anyone is better off.

Unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching? Four things he could bring instead, and they are not four synonyms. Revelation is something disclosed by God; knowledge is grasp of the truth; prophecy is that truth spoken into this room now; teaching is the patient explanation that makes it hold. Revelation and prophecy are messages from God; knowledge and teaching are the explanation of truth. Between them they describe how the word of God actually reaches a congregation, and every one of them has this in common: the hearer understands.

A God who speaks. Behind the whole argument lies something about the character of God, and it settles more than this chapter. Our God speaks. He is not the mute idol of 12:2. He made the world by speaking, he gave a book, and when he came in person he came as the Word. Everything about him leans toward being understood. A form of worship that makes God’s truth inaccessible to the people present is not merely inconvenient; it is running against the grain of who he is.

The Reformation and the ploughboy. That conviction did real work in history. It is why the Reformers fought for services in the language of the people, and why William Tyndale vowed that a boy driving the plough would one day know more of the Scriptures than the learned cleric he was arguing with. A Latin liturgy in an English village fails this verse exactly as an uninterpreted tongue in Corinth failed it: the words may be true, reverent, and beautiful, and the man in the back row goes home with nothing.

Things that are nobody’s fault. The same test can be turned on things done with no bad intent at all. A preacher who quotes Greek without translating it, a prayer packed with phrases a person would only know from having grown up in church, a hymn whose language was ordinary in 1780 and is now a puzzle: each of them leaves somebody in the building outside the conversation. The remedy is small and unglamorous: explain the word, give the reference, say what you mean. And notice that Paul is asking about benefit, not about interest. A congregation can find a sermon interesting and go home with nothing to do, nothing to believe more firmly, and nobody comforted. Interest is not the test. Somebody stronger by the end is the test.

What it does not mean. It does not mean experience has no place in worship. Joy, sorrow, awe and love belong there. It means understanding must be central, and experience must rise out of truth understood.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, if Paul came to you speaking in tongues, what use would he be to you, unless he brought you some revelation, knowledge, prophecy or teaching?

On a Tuesday. Pray by name for those who preach and teach in your church, that they would be clear. And when you explain your faith to a friend this week, drop the church words and say it in the language you would use about anything else that mattered to you.

For worship. The eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and he spoke in Aramaic to fishermen. He told stories about seeds and coins and lost sheep, so that a child could follow him and a scholar could never exhaust him. He did not hide God behind a veil of words; he is the radiance of God’s glory, the exact imprint of his nature. Thank God for clear teaching, and above all for the clearest Word of all, who has made the Father known (John 1:18).

verseByVerse.quote: If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?
verseByVerse.commentary:
If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?

If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played? Two pictures, and Paul chose them well. The first is a flute or a harp producing sound without distinction, notes that do not resolve into a tune. Everyone has heard it. An orchestra tuning up is a wonderful noise and nobody hums it on the way home. There is nothing wrong with any individual sound; what is missing is the shape that makes sound into music. Paul says that is what uninterpreted tongues do to a service.

And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle? The second picture is sharper, because it has consequences. A bugle in a camp was not decoration; it was command. Different calls meant advance, retreat, gather, stand to. And an army only marches if the call is distinct. A bugler who blows something ambiguous does not produce a slightly confused response; he produces a camp of men looking at each other while the enemy comes over the ridge.

From taste to survival. The change of image is the point. The flute makes indistinctness a matter of aesthetics; the bugle makes it a matter of survival. Paul is telling a church that treats clarity as a matter of taste that it is in fact a matter of readiness. A congregation that cannot make out what is being said cannot obey it. Which lands on anyone who speaks to God’s people, and it lands as a duty rather than a style preference. Clarity is not a gift some preachers happen to have. It is the whole job. A sermon that is admired and not understood has failed in the way the bugle failed, and nobody in the congregation will be able to say what they are supposed to do on Monday. The Levites in Nehemiah’s day read from the Law clearly and gave the sense, so that the people understood the reading (Nehemiah 8:8).

The silver trumpets. The trumpet image was not a figure of speech to Israel. God gave Moses two silver trumpets with a fixed code of signals: both blown together summoned the whole congregation, one alone summoned the chiefs, an alarm meant the camps on the east should set out (Numbers 10:1–7). Lives were arranged around the certainty that the same sound meant the same thing every time, and the trumpet was blown in war so that Israel would be remembered before the LORD (Numbers 10:9). Which is why muddled teaching is a more serious failure than it feels. A congregation that cannot tell what its Bible requires does not become mildly less informed; it becomes an army that will not move. And the people most damaged are always the ones with the least background: the new believer, the visitor, the man who came in troubled and needed one clear sentence and was given a beautiful fog.

What it does not mean. It does not mean instruments are wrong in worship. Paul uses them as an illustration, and the instrument is not blamed for having no mind of its own; he calls these lifeless things. The people in the church are not lifeless. They can choose to be distinct, and this chapter tells them to.

What if I am not a gifted speaker? Clarity is not eloquence. It is saying one true thing in a way the listener can take home. You do not need a fine voice or a large vocabulary; you need to know what you mean and say it plainly. Before you speak about Christ, ask yourself: what is the one thing I want this person to understand? Then say that, in ordinary words, and stop. Some of the clearest witnesses in the church have been people who would never call themselves speakers at all.

In a sentence. Even lifeless instruments like the flute or harp: if they do not sound distinct notes, how can anyone tell the tune? And if the trumpet’s call is unclear, who will get ready for battle?

On a Tuesday. Speak clearly about Christ. An unclear witness leaves people confused. If someone asked you today what the gospel is, could you say it in three sentences? Try writing them down, and then say them to someone this week.

For worship. There is a trumpet that will give no uncertain sound. The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a cry of command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the sound of the trumpet of God (1 Thessalonians 4:16). On that day no one will mistake the call. Until then, he has given his church a clear gospel to sound: Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day. Blessed be the Captain who gives his soldiers a plain word, and who will himself sound the last trumpet.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet sounded signals to soldiers in battle.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning, but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.

So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible. Intelligible (eusēmos) means clear, distinct, easily recognised. Paul applies the pictures to Corinth.

How will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air. There is the phrase that sums up the whole chapter, and it is more desolate than it first sounds. Speaking into the air: wasted words, like a boxer beating the air (9:26). Not speaking nonsense, and not speaking wickedly. Speaking real words that reach nobody: sound going out into an empty room and simply dispersing.

There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning. Notice the concession he makes first, because it is generous and deliberate. Languages here (phōnai) is literally voices, sounds. Every human language means something. He is not saying that tongues were gibberish. Every one of those languages is a real language, full of poetry and law and love and grief, to somebody. The problem is never with the language. It is with the gap.

But if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me. The word for foreigner is barbaros, and its origin is a small joke at the Greeks’ expense. It is imitative: to a Greek ear, foreign speech sounded like bar-bar-bar, so a foreigner was a barbarian, a person who made noises. Anyone who has stood in a market or a hospital corridor in a country whose language he does not speak knows the feeling exactly: surrounded by meaning, cut out of all of it, reduced to guessing at faces. The comparison with human languages also supports the view that tongues were real languages.

Strangers in God’s house. Now put that feeling in a church. The gift that Corinth prized most highly was producing, in the person sitting three feet away, the loneliness of a stranger in a foreign country, and producing it in the one place on earth where nobody is supposed to be a foreigner. This is the church Paul has already told that Jews and Greeks, slaves and free were baptised into one body (12:13), and in Christ they are no longer strangers and aliens but fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God (Ephesians 2:19). Now they had invented a new way to be strangers to each other, and they were proud of it.

Any church can manufacture barbarians. The application is not confined to tongues, and it is worth putting bluntly to a congregation that would never dream of the Corinthian error. It happens through unexplained jargon, through in-jokes and shared history, through a way of praying that outsiders cannot join, through assuming everyone knows where the book is kept and what the notice means. None of it is malicious. All of it says the same thing to the person standing at the back: you are not from here.

What it does not mean. It does not mean tongues were meaningless. They had meaning, but the hearers could not understand it without interpretation.

How can our church help a newcomer not feel like a foreigner? Small things do most of the work. Say who is speaking and what is happening next. Give page numbers and Bible references, and explain a word like justification or communion the first time it is used. Make sure someone sits with a visitor, shows him where to find the reading, and talks to him afterwards about something other than the weather. Invite him for lunch. Each of these says what Paul wants said: you are welcome here, and this is meant for you too.

In a sentence. It is the same with you. Unless your tongue speaks words people can understand, how will they know what you are saying? You will just be talking into the air. There are many languages in the world, and each has meaning; but if Paul does not know the language, he and the speaker are foreigners to each other.

On a Tuesday. Next Sunday, look for the one person in church who seems most like a foreigner, whether new, alone, or different from the rest, and go and speak to him first.

For worship. At Babel God confused the languages, and the nations were scattered. At Pentecost he spoke the one gospel in many languages, and the nations began to be gathered. And at the end, John saw a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language, standing before the throne and crying with one voice: salvation belongs to our God (Revelation 7:9–10). The Lamb has made foreigners into family. Thank God for every translator who has carried his word into another tongue, and above all for the Saviour who has made us fellow citizens of one city.

verseByVerse.quote: So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.

So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit. One verse, and it is a model of how to correct people without crushing them. Literally, Paul says you are zealots for spirits. The Corinthians were enthusiastic about spiritual experiences. Look at what Paul affirms before he redirects. Since you are eager: he takes their eagerness as given, and he does not condemn it. He could easily have said: your appetite for spiritual experience is the whole problem, calm down. Many pastors would. Instead he treats their hunger as the raw material and simply turns it round: you want the Spirit’s manifestations, so excel at the thing his manifestations are for.

Strive to excel in building up the church. Redirect your zeal. Do not seek gifts for your own spirituality, but to build others up. Excel (perisseuō) means to abound, to overflow, to have more than enough. Paul takes the Corinthian instinct to outdo one another and does not abolish it either. He gives it a new field. If you must compete, compete at this: who can do the most good to the people in this room. Which is an almost comic reversal when you think about the church it was written to. Here is a congregation ranking itself by gifts, and the apostle proposes a different league table, and the people at the top of it will be the ones nobody has been counting. The member who has quietly rebuilt the confidence of a family going through a bad year is winning this competition. He does not know there is one.

The test. It can be applied to any activity in a church. Not was it spiritual? Not did I feel God in it? Simply: who is stronger because of it? If the honest answer is nobody, the thing may still be innocent, but it has not yet been what this verse is asking for.

A word for the flat. There is a warning in the verse for the opposite temperament too, and it should be said, because in most sober congregations there are more of these people than there are Corinthians. Some Christians are eager for nothing at all. They have never longed for more of God, never asked him for anything they could not arrange themselves, and mistake their flatness for maturity. Paul does not commend that. He does not say stop being eager; he says be eager about the right thing, which assumes the eagerness is there to be redirected. So the verse asks two questions rather than one. Am I eager? And is my eagerness pointed at the people around me?

What it does not mean. It does not mean zeal is bad. Paul channels it rightly.

How do I find out what I can do to build up my church? Start where you are and with what is in front of you. Ask your elders where there is need, and offer to fill it. Notice what others thank you for, and what you find yourself caring about when no one asks you to. Pray for the people around you by name, and you will soon see what they need. Most building up is done in ordinary ways: a meal taken round, a child taught, a hand held at a funeral, a verse given at the right moment. Faithfulness in small things is how gifts are discovered.

In a sentence. So since you are keen on the Spirit’s gifts, aim to overflow in the ones that build up the church.

On a Tuesday. Channel your enthusiasm for God into building up others in your church. Pick one family or person in your congregation this week and do one concrete thing to strengthen them.

For worship. The Spirit is never idle. He came at Pentecost like wind and fire, and he has been building Christ’s church ever since, stone by living stone (1 Peter 2:5). He took fishermen and tax collectors and made them pillars, and he takes the zeal of ordinary believers and turns it toward the good of others. Thank God that he does not quench our eagerness but redeems it, and that the zeal of the Lord of hosts will finish the house he has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.

Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret. The instruction is practical: if you have the one gift, ask God for the other, so that what you are doing can be shared and the tongue can benefit others.

For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful. My spirit is the inner person moved by the Spirit. Mind (nous) is the understanding. Unfruitful (akarpos) means producing no fruit, no understanding for himself or others. The phrase has been made to carry a great deal. It does not mean the speaker has left his mind behind, or that he is in a trance and not responsible. Paul’s own next sentence rules that out, because he says I will four times. This is a man deciding what to do, which is not a description of anyone overwhelmed. Unfruitful means the mind is not producing anything the congregation can pick up.

What am I to do? Paul’s conclusion follows, and it is neither of the two answers people usually reach for.

I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also. Both. Not a choice. Worship should engage the whole person, heart and understanding. Paul refuses the two great mistakes about worship in a single sentence. The first mistake is to want the spirit without the mind: worship as pure experience, where thinking is felt to interrupt the feeling, where the aim of a service is a state and doctrine is an obstacle to it. The second is to want the mind without the spirit: worship as instruction only, correct and cold, where a congregation could sing about the blood of Christ with the expressions of people reading a timetable, and where any warmth is suspected of being manipulation. Both are amputations, and both are common, and each is usually adopted as a reaction against the other. Paul will not have either.

Singing with the mind. Notice that he applies the rule to singing as well as praying, which is where most Christians meet it. Singing with the mind means singing words we understand and mean, letting the word of Christ dwell in us richly as we sing (Colossians 3:16; Ephesians 5:19). Anyone who has arrived at the end of a hymn with no memory of the middle verse knows how possible it is to sing with neither. Sing praises with understanding, says the psalm (Psalm 47:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean emotion is bad in worship. It means emotion must be joined to understanding. Nobody has ever been truly moved by something he did not take in, and the deepest feelings in worship come from truths most clearly grasped.

I often feel nothing when I sing. Is my worship worthless? No. Feelings rise and fall with tiredness, health and grief, and God does not measure worship by them. What he asks is that you mean what you sing, that you sing truth with your mind engaged and your will offered to him. Sometimes that is all a weary believer can give, and it is a true offering. Keep singing truth, and pay attention to the words. Very often warmth returns as the mind is filled with what God has done, and on the days it does not, the Spirit still carries your praise to the Father.

In a sentence. So someone who speaks in a tongue should pray for the ability to interpret it. If Paul prays in a tongue, his spirit prays but his understanding gets nothing from it. So what will he do? He will pray with his spirit and with his understanding; he will sing with his spirit and with his understanding too.

On a Tuesday. There is a simple discipline in it. Before the service, read the words of what you are about to sing. During the prayers, mean the Amen. Afterwards, ask what was said. That is praying with the mind, and it does not cost a Christian one degree of warmth.

For worship. Christ sang with his mind and his spirit. On the night he was betrayed, after the Supper, he sang a hymn with his disciples, very likely the psalms that end the Passover (Matthew 26:30), and he meant every word: the LORD is my strength and my song; I shall not die, but I shall live. He offered his whole self to the Father, mind and heart and body, and he offers our poor worship to the Father now, perfected by his own. Blessed be the God who made us whole people and redeems us whole.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying? For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.

Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit. Praising God in a tongue. Paul brings the argument down to one word, and it is a word every congregation says without thinking about it.

How can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving. Amen is Hebrew, and the church took it over from the synagogue without translating it, which is itself a small marvel: the same syllables have been said by God’s people for three thousand years. It means something firm, reliable, sure: so be it. It was the congregation’s response to prayers (Nehemiah 8:6; Psalm 106:48). When one person prays aloud and the congregation says Amen, they are not being polite. They are signing the prayer. It becomes theirs. Nehemiah records the whole assembly answering Amen, Amen, lifting up their hands, and bowing their heads with their faces to the ground. And Paul’s word for the outsider (idiōtēs) means an ordinary person, uninstructed, someone occupying the position of the uninitiated: the enquirer, the newcomer, the person who came because a friend asked him.

When he does not know what you are saying? You cannot say Amen to what you do not understand. So the outsider who cannot say Amen has not merely missed a nice moment. He has been excluded from the congregation’s prayer: present at it, unable to join it. The one guest in the building who most needed to be included has been quietly left out by the thing everyone else found most exciting.

For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up. The fairness of verse 17 keeps the whole rebuke honest. Paul concedes the point completely. The thanksgiving is real, it is directed to God, and God has heard it. Nothing about it is fake. The prayer itself may be fine before God, but it fails in its public purpose, and in a gathering of the church, that is decisive.

Sincerity is not the test. This is the sentence to carry out of the chapter, because it applies to a hundred things that are not tongues. It is possible to do something in a church service that is entirely genuine, entirely God-directed, entirely sincere, and still wrong, because of who else was in the room. Sincerity is not the criterion Paul uses anywhere in these three chapters. The criterion is always the person next to you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean saying Amen is a mere formality. It is the whole congregation’s agreement with the prayer.

Should I say Amen out loud in church? Yes, if your church’s practice allows it, and most do. The congregation’s Amen is a biblical act, and saying it aloud is a way of joining the prayer and encouraging the one who led it. Where a church’s custom is quieter, a silent Amen from the heart is still yours to give. What matters is that you have followed the prayer and mean it. If a prayer contains something you cannot agree with, you are not obliged to sign it; but for most prayers, an honest Amen is one of the simplest ways to share in worship.

In a sentence. Otherwise, when you praise God in the spirit, how can someone who does not understand say Amen to your thanksgiving, since he does not know what you are saying? Your thanks may be fine, but the other person gains nothing from it.

On a Tuesday. Here is a test with immediate application. Think of the last time you took part audibly in a gathering: a prayer, a reading, a comment in a study, a testimony. Could a nervous newcomer with no church background have said Amen to it, and known what he was agreeing to? If not, the fault was not his. And when someone leads prayer in church this Sunday, listen and say Amen from the heart.

For worship. Jesus Christ is himself the Amen, the faithful and true witness (Revelation 3:14). All the promises of God find their Yes in him, and that is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory (2 Corinthians 1:20). Every Amen a congregation has ever said rests on him. He is the one prayer the Father has always answered, and in him our weakest thanks become firm and sure.
verseByVerse.note: “Amen” (“so be it”) was the congregation’s response to prayer and thanksgiving.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.

I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you. This is the verse that stops the argument from being a caricature, and it should be allowed its full force before anything is built on it. Paul is not criticising tongues out of jealousy or lack. He had the gift abundantly: more than all of you, said to the congregation in the New Testament most famous for it. And his attitude to it is not tolerance but gratitude: I thank God. Whatever a reader concludes about the gift today, he is not entitled to a lower view of it than the man who wrote this chapter of restrictions. Every rule in this chapter comes from someone who prized the thing he was regulating.

Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others. In church: in the gathered congregation. Two words that divide the whole question. Paul is not weighing tongues against prophecy in the abstract; he is asking what belongs in a public gathering. The same activity can be excellent in one setting and out of place in another, and the distinction is not hypocrisy but wisdom. Instruct (katēcheō, from which we get catechise) means to teach. And note the aim: in order to instruct others. Paul is not praising brevity for its own sake, and this verse is no charter for the person who thinks sermons should be shorter. He is praising speech that lands somewhere. The measure is not length but transfer: whether something that was in one head is now in another.

Than ten thousand words in a tongue. Ten thousand (myrioi) is the largest Greek number word, and the ratio is a deliberate absurdity: five against ten thousand, two thousand to one. He is not proposing a calculation. He is saying that in the assembly, comprehensible speech and incomprehensible speech are not on the same scale at all: that five intelligible words which teach somebody outweigh an entire evening of the other.

Five words. Five words is worth sitting with. It is one short sentence. In English, Christ died for our sins (15:3) is exactly five. Paul is saying that a single plain sentence, understood by a struggling believer, is of more value in a church than a display that lasts all night. Any Christian can manage five words. That is the point of choosing such a small number. There is real freedom in this for anyone who has ever felt they had nothing to offer in a church. You do not need ten thousand words. You do not need a platform, a gift you can name, or a way with an audience. Five plain words that instruct one person are, on the apostle’s own scale, worth more than the most impressive thing that happened in Corinth that year.

Where did Paul speak in tongues, then? He has just spent seventeen verses saying the gift does not belong in the assembly without interpretation, so his use of it must have been chiefly elsewhere: perhaps in his own prayers, perhaps in his mission among people of other languages, where tongues could function as at Pentecost. The text does not tell us. What it does tell us is that the apostle who travelled constantly, was beaten, imprisoned and shipwrecked, and carried the anxiety of all the churches, gave thanks for every gift God had given him and used each for its purpose.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul encouraged private tongues as a superior form of prayer for later believers. He simply says public worship is for understanding. His gift belonged to the apostolic age, and the believer today who has no such gift has lost nothing in prayer; the Spirit helps us all to pray (Romans 8:26).

In a sentence. Paul thanks God that he speaks in tongues more than any of you. But in church he would rather speak five words that make sense and teach others than ten thousand words in a tongue.

On a Tuesday. Think of the five words of truth that changed your life, or the one sentence of Scripture that has held you up most. Share them with someone today, and tell him why.

For worship. Five words were enough on the lips of our Lord. It is finished, he said (John 19:30), and in Greek it was one word, and it was the most instructive word ever spoken. He did not need ten thousand words to save us. He spoke the word of the cross, and the word of the cross is the power of God (1:18). Thank God for five clear words that changed everything: Christ died for our sins.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul urges them to stop thinking like children; they should be infants in evil but adults in their thinking. Scripture says that God would speak to his people through people of strange tongues and foreign lips, and even then they would not listen. So tongues are a sign, not for believers, but for unbelievers, while prophecy is for believers, not unbelievers. If the whole church meets and everyone speaks in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers come in, they will say the believers are out of their minds. But if everyone prophesies and an unbeliever or outsider comes in, he will be convicted and judged by all, the secrets of his heart will be laid bare, and he will fall down and worship God, declaring that God is really among them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Worship and Witness

Paul’s concern for the unbeliever who might walk in to the church meeting is a significant ecclesiological statement: corporate worship is not only for the already-converted. The community that worships in such a way that the outsider can be addressed, convicted, and drawn to worship is doing something the tongues-heavy meeting cannot do. This does not make evangelism the primary purpose of corporate worship — the primary purpose is the glorification of God — but it recognises that intelligible worship of the living God is inherently missionary in its effect.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meetings were apparently chaotic — multiple tongues-speakers simultaneously, no interpretation, no order. Paul’s Isaiah citation turns their spiritual pride upside down: the tongues without interpretation is a sign associated with divine judgment, not divine favour. Now: The church that makes its corporate worship impenetrable to the outsider — whether through uninterpreted ecstatic experience, impenetrable theological jargon, or cultural inscrutability — is failing the unbeliever who walks through the door. The word of God should be the thing that disturbs, not the incomprehensibility of the proceedings.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.” Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.

Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. A beautifully turned rebuke. Corinth thought of itself as spiritually advanced, and Paul tells them they are behaving like toddlers, drawn to whatever is loudest and shiniest, which is exactly how a small child assesses value. Their fascination with tongues was childish (13:11).

Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature. He adds the one respect in which he does want them childish: in evil, be infants. Be innocent like babies about evil, the sort of person who has to have wickedness explained to him, but grown up in understanding (Romans 16:19; Matthew 10:16).

In the Law it is written. The Law here means the Scriptures, for the quotation is from Isaiah. And the setting must be known or the argument makes no sense. Isaiah is preaching to the drunken leadership of Israel, and they mock him: his plain speech sounds to them like baby talk, a string of nonsense syllables (Isaiah 28:9–10). Very well, says God: if my clear word through a prophet is only babble to you, you shall have a message you genuinely cannot understand. He means the Assyrian army, whose foreign speech would soon be heard in their streets (Isaiah 28:11–12). Moses had warned of the same: a nation whose language you do not understand (Deuteronomy 28:49). Unintelligible language was the judgement. It was the sound of God having stopped speaking to them in words they could follow.

By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people. And even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord. Foreign tongues were God’s judgement on unbelief: Israel refused to listen to God’s clear word through the prophets, so God would speak to them through the unintelligible language of invaders.

Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers. That unlocks verse 22, which otherwise seems to contradict what comes next. When Paul says tongues are a sign for unbelievers, he does not mean tongues are a good way to reach them. He means they function as the sign they functioned as in Isaiah: a mark of people who are outside, hearing sounds that carry nothing to them. It is a sign of judgement, not of welcome. When unbelievers hear tongues they cannot understand, it confirms them in their unbelief and alienation. At Pentecost, tongues also signalled that the gospel was going to the nations, and that judgement was coming on unbelieving Israel.

While prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers. Prophecy is a sign for believers in the opposite way: the mark of a God who is present with his people, showing his favour, and speaking to them in words they understand. And as verses 24–25 show, it also brings unbelievers to faith. Which is why the next verse can say that unbelievers walking into a room full of tongues will conclude the church is mad. That is not a contradiction of verse 22; it is the demonstration of it. The sign does exactly what Isaiah said such a sign does: it leaves the outsider outside.

A famine of hearing. There is a sobering thing here for any church, quite apart from tongues. The most frightening judgement God ever brings on a people is not fire. It is unintelligibility: a famine of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11), a pulpit full of noise, a religion that has stopped saying anything. That can happen to a congregation without anybody deciding it, and the people inside are usually the last to notice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean tongues were meant to convert unbelievers. Paul says uninterpreted tongues make outsiders think the church is mad (v. 23).

What does it look like to be mature in thinking? It means weighing things by Scripture rather than by how impressive they are. A child is drawn to noise and novelty; a mature believer asks what is true, what builds up, and what honours Christ. It means being able to hold a disputed question patiently, to distinguish what is central from what is secondary, and to resist being swept along by whatever is exciting this year. And it goes with innocence about evil: the mature Christian is not the one who knows the most about sin, but the one who knows the most about Christ.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, stop thinking like children. Be babies when it comes to evil, but adults in your thinking. The law says that through people of foreign speech and through the lips of strangers God will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to him. So tongues are a sign, not for believers but for unbelievers; prophecy, however, is for believers, not unbelievers.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you have been most drawn to in your Christian life this year: a speaker, a style, an experience. Then ask the grown-up question: has it made me know Christ better and love his people more? And guard your innocence: turn away this week from one thing you watch or read that makes you knowing about evil.

For worship. God has not stopped speaking to us. He could have left us to the babble of our own unbelief, as he left the mockers in Jerusalem. Instead he spoke at last in his Son, plainly and finally, and when we would not hear, he sent his Spirit to open deaf ears. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Hebrews 3:15). Thank God that he speaks to you clearly in his word, and that his patience still calls.
verseByVerse.note: “The Law” here means the Scriptures. In Isaiah, foreign speech — the Assyrian invaders — was a sign of judgment on those who refused to listen.

parallels.desc: by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people

verseByVerse.quote: If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,
verseByVerse.commentary:
If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,

If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues. The whole church: perhaps the gathering of all the house churches in one place. All speaking in tongues: the chaos Paul is correcting.

And outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds? Paul asks them to picture their own meeting through the door. Someone has come, perhaps a neighbour, perhaps a husband who finally agreed to come once. He steps in, and every person in the room is speaking words he cannot understand, all at the same time. What does he conclude? Out of your minds (mainomai) means mad, raving, like the frenzy of pagan cults he knew. Not that the doctrine is false; he has not heard any doctrine. He will simply decide that these people are unhinged, and he will go home, and he will not come back. And here is the sting: he was never given the chance to reject Christ. He rejected a room. Unbelievers often attended Christian gatherings, and worship should be understandable to them.

The offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles. That deserves to be said plainly, because the objection is always available that the world finds the gospel foolish anyway. It does; Paul said so at 1:23. But there is a difference between the offence of the cross and the offence of a shambles, and this chapter exists to say that a church may not confuse the two. If people are put off, let it be by Christ crucified, and not by the fact that nobody explained anything.

But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters. The second scenario, and everything is different. Notice that it is not one gifted speaker doing the work. If all speak God’s word intelligibly, one by one (v. 31), the whole congregation is speaking words that build up, encourage and console.

He is convicted by all. Convicted (elenchō) is a courtroom word: exposed, shown his sin, as the Spirit convicts the world (John 16:8).

He is called to account by all. Called to account (anakrinō) is another: examined, searched. God’s word through his people searches him. Nobody has cross-examined him. Nobody has singled him out; the whole point is that the congregation is talking about God to each other, and the truth spoken plainly begins doing its own work on a man who came in only to keep somebody company. He came to observe and finds himself on trial, which is what always happens when the word of God is intelligible in a room (Hebrews 4:12–13).

An ordinary mechanism. It is worth noticing how ordinary it is. Nothing in these two verses requires a special word of knowledge about the visitor. It requires a congregation in which people are plainly saying true things about God to one another, and a man who happens to be in the room while they do it. The conviction is the word’s own work, not the speaker’s insight. Which is a comfort to anyone who has ever felt that evangelism requires a technique he does not have. The most effective thing a congregation can do for the friend it has finally persuaded to come is not to arrange something special for him. It is to be, on that particular Sunday, a body of people who genuinely mean what they are saying, and to say it in words he can follow.

What it does not mean. It does not mean worship should be designed mainly for unbelievers. The gathering is for God’s people to worship him. But it should be clear, so that unbelievers present understand and are confronted.

Should our services be changed to suit visitors? Not their substance, but their clarity. The church must not water down the gospel, drop the hard parts of Scripture, or turn worship into entertainment to keep outsiders comfortable; that would remove the very word that converts them. But everything should be done so that a visitor can follow it: plain language, explained terms, readings he can find, and a warm welcome. Aim for a service that a believer finds deeply nourishing and a stranger finds understandable. Those two aims are not rivals; the clearest worship serves both.

In a sentence. So if the whole church meets and everyone speaks in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers come in, won’t they say you are mad? But if everyone is prophesying and an unbeliever or outsider comes in, he will be convicted of sin by all and brought under judgement by all,

On a Tuesday. Invite an unbelieving friend to church. Pray that God will speak to them through his word. And on the Sunday you bring someone, sing as if you mean it, listen as if it matters, and speak to your friend afterwards about what was said.

For worship. The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, and no creature is hidden from his sight (Hebrews 4:12–13). He does not need our cleverness to reach a sinner; he needs only his word spoken plainly. The same voice that called Lazarus out of the tomb calls dead men to life through the plain speech of ordinary believers. Blessed be the God whose word does its own work, and who still adds to his church day by day those who are being saved.

verseByVerse.quote: the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.

The secrets of his heart are disclosed. This is what Paul wants a church service to do, and it is far more ambitious than most of us expect on a Sunday morning. God’s word exposes hidden thoughts (Hebrews 4:12). The unbeliever feels: this is about me. God knows me. Not published: disclosed, made plain, brought into the light. And disclosed to whom? Chiefly to himself. Anyone who has sat under plain preaching and had the sensation of being described knows exactly what this means. Nothing supernatural has to be assumed about the speaker. The word of God has a way of walking into a man’s private rooms and turning on the lights, and the effect is that he stops listening to what is being said about people in general and starts hearing about himself.

And so, falling on his face, he will worship God. Not nodding. Not thoughtfully agreeing. This is the posture of awe and surrender, of a man who has met something and lost his footing: the posture of Ezekiel by the river, of John on Patmos, of every person in Scripture who found himself unexpectedly in the presence of God.

And declare that God is really among you. Then the sentence that Paul wants said about a congregation. It is not the sentence anyone expects him to want. It is not these people are warm, or that was a fine argument, or they made me feel welcome. Every one of those is good and none of them is this. He wants the visitor to walk out having concluded that God was in the building. The goal of worship is that outsiders recognise God’s presence: not through chaos or showmanship, but through his word convicting hearts.

The nations coming in. The words the visitor speaks are not new. Surely God is in you, and there is no other, is what Isaiah promised would one day be said by outsiders about Israel, foreigners bowing down and confessing that God was there and nowhere else (Isaiah 45:14). Zechariah saw ten men from every nation taking hold of the robe of a Jew and saying they had heard that God was with him (Zechariah 8:23). Paul takes those promises and lays them on a house church in a Greek port. The nations coming in has begun, and it is happening in an ordinary room, one man at a time.

Say something true, and let God be extraordinary. Here is what a church can take from it, practically. The thing most likely to convert the person who visits is not the excellence of the arrangements, the quality of the music, or the skill of the welcome, though all of them help and none should be neglected. It is a congregation talking plainly about a God who is actually there. Corinth thought the way to impress an outsider was to show him something extraordinary. Paul says the way is to say something true, and let God be extraordinary.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prophecy is the only way unbelievers are converted. The preaching of the gospel does the same today, and the Spirit uses the plain word of Scripture in every age to lay hearts bare and bring sinners to their knees.

Does God want me to feel exposed in church? He wants you to be known, so that you can be healed. Being searched by the word can be painful: a sermon names the sin you hoped was hidden, and you feel as if everyone can see. But the purpose is never to shame you; it is to bring you to the One who already knows and has come to forgive. The visitor in this verse is not crushed and sent away. He falls down and worships. Conviction is the doorway, and on the other side is mercy. When the word finds you out, do not run; confess, and come to Christ.

In a sentence. and the secrets of his heart will be laid bare. Then he will fall down and worship God, exclaiming that God is really here among you!

On a Tuesday. Pray this week that your church’s worship would be so filled with God’s word that visitors say: God is really here. And pray for yourself, that when the word lays your own heart bare on Sunday, you would not defend yourself but bow.

For worship. There has never been a service anywhere that God attended reluctantly. He is the God who searches hearts, and the God who receives the sinner on his face. The woman at the well said, come, see a man who told me all that I ever did (John 4:29), and she said it with joy. Christ is the one before whom every secret will be disclosed, and the one who has borne every secret sin of his people. To be found out by him is to be found by him. God is really among us, in Christ, by his Spirit, and that is the wonder of the church.

parallels.desc: God is with you only
we have heard that God is with you

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Orderly Worship and Final Rules
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When they meet, each person may bring a hymn, a teaching, a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation, but everything must be done to build up the church. If anyone speaks in a tongue, there should be two, or at most three, one at a time, and someone must interpret; without an interpreter the speaker should keep quiet in church and speak to himself and to God. Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should weigh what is said. If a revelation comes to someone else who is sitting there, the first speaker should stop. They can all prophesy in turn, so that everyone learns and is encouraged. The spirits of prophets are under the prophets’ control, because God is not a God of disorder but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints, women are to keep silent in the assemblies; they are not allowed to speak but should be in submission, as the law also says. If they want to learn something, they should ask their husbands at home, for it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. Did the word of God begin with the Corinthians, or are they the only people it has reached? Anyone who thinks he is a prophet or spiritual should acknowledge that what Paul writes is the Lord’s command. Anyone who ignores this will himself be ignored. So they should eagerly desire to prophesy and not forbid speaking in tongues, but everything should be done in a fitting and orderly way.
verseByVerse.theology:
God as the Ground of Ordered Worship

The theological ground for orderly worship — “God is not a God of confusion but of peace” — is a direct application of the doctrine of God to liturgical practice. The triune God is the most perfectly ordered being there is: the three persons in eternal, loving, ordered communion. Worship that is chaotic and disorderly is, at a deep level, a misrepresentation of the God being worshipped. Conversely, worship that is ordered, intelligible, and participatory is an enacted icon of the divine order. The Reformers understood this: the liturgical reforms of Geneva and Zurich were not mere preference but a theological conviction that worship should reflect the character of the God it addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian meeting was apparently chaotic: multiple simultaneous tongues, no weighing of prophecies, a general air of competitive spiritual display. Paul’s practical rules — two or three, in turn, with evaluation — are not bureaucratic restrictions but pastoral wisdom about how a community can actually benefit from the gifts God has given it. Now: “Decently and in order” is the guiding principle for every aspect of church life, from Sunday worship to congregational meetings to pastoral care. Order is not the suppression of the Spirit; it is the condition in which the Spirit’s gifts can be received and used by the whole community.

verseByVerse.quote: What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.

What then, brothers? Paul stops arguing and gives practical instructions, and he begins by describing. The description is one of the most interesting sentences in the New Testament about what a church meeting looked like.

When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. A picture of early Christian worship, with many participating. A hymn (psalmos, perhaps a psalm or a new song), a lesson (didachē, teaching), a revelation (a prophecy), a tongue, and its interpretation. Each one has: people arrived with something. It is a room of contributors, not an audience. Whatever else was wrong at Corinth, and the list has been long, nobody was there as a spectator. And Paul does not put a stop to it. That is the thing to notice, given everything he has just said about their disorder. He regulates what he finds, and the regulation is a single clause.

Let all things be done for building up. The rule for everything (oikodomē). Not let all things be done sincerely, or reverently, or with excellence. For building up. The phrase that has governed the whole chapter, and it is measured on other people.

Where Christians differ: how should worship be ordered? Some take this verse as the model for open, participatory worship, with anyone contributing. Others hold to the regulative principle: worship should include only what God commands, led by qualified men. Verdict: The apostolic church had more open participation, partly because of the revelatory gifts then active. With the canon closed and those gifts ceased, the core elements of worship are those God has appointed: reading and preaching the Scriptures, prayer, singing psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, the sacraments, and giving (Westminster 21.5). Worship should be ordered, led by those God has called, and above all edifying. Within that, the congregation participates fully in singing, prayer and Amen.

The criterion and the format. The binding instruction here is not the format but the criterion. Paul lays down no order of service, no timings, no minimum number of contributions. He insists on one thing: that everything done should build people up. And the New Testament plainly places teaching at the centre, since it lists teachers before most other gifts (12:28) and tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation and to teaching (1 Timothy 4:13).

A rebuke to passivity. The picture is nonetheless a rebuke to passivity, and most of us need the rebuke more than we need the format. Whatever the Sunday structure, the question what am I bringing? is a fair one to put to any Christian on the way in. It need not be a platform contribution. It may be a conversation prepared for a person you know is struggling, a burden carried into the prayers, an invitation to lunch, a heart prepared to sing and to listen. The instinct of verse 26 is that believers come to a gathering with something in their hands, and that instinct survives every difference of tradition.

What is the regulative principle? It is the conviction that God alone decides how he is to be worshipped. In ordinary life we may do whatever Scripture does not forbid; in public worship we offer what Scripture appoints. The reason is that worship is God’s, not ours to invent: Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorised fire and died (Leviticus 10:1–2), and Jesus condemned worship built on human traditions (Mark 7:7). This does not freeze every detail; the time of the service, the order of elements, the tunes and the building are matters of wisdom. But the elements themselves, reading, preaching, prayer, singing, the Lord’s Supper and baptism, giving, are what God has given, and they are enough.

What it does not mean. It does not mean worship should be a free-for-all. Order is required (v. 40).

In a sentence. What then, brothers and sisters? When you gather, one has a song, another a teaching, another a revelation, a tongue or an interpretation. Everything must be done to build up the church.

On a Tuesday. Come to church ready to contribute: with a heart to sing, pray and listen, aiming to build others up. On Saturday evening, read the passage to be preached if you know it, pray for one person you will see, and decide whom you will speak to after the service.

For worship. The church is the temple of the living God, and every member a living stone. The Lord Jesus walks among the lampstands (Revelation 2:1); he is present when his people gather in his name (Matthew 18:20). He has given gifts to men, apostles and prophets once for the foundation, and evangelists, pastors and teachers still, to equip the saints for the work of ministry, for building up the body of Christ (Ephesians 4:11–12). Every Sunday is his work, and he is building a house that will stand forever.

verseByVerse.quote: If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.

If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three. The rules, and they are strikingly specific for a man who has just affirmed the gift so warmly. A maximum number: two, or at the outside three, in one meeting, which implies that Corinth had been running many more. Not a whole service of tongues.

And each in turn. One at a time, not all together, which implies they had been speaking over one another.

And let someone interpret. Always with interpretation, without which the whole thing stops. If interpretation is what makes tongues useful, a congregation should want interpreters and pray for them (v. 13). Paul’s rules are not designed to reduce the gift to nothing. They are designed to make it useful.

But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church. No interpreter, no tongue. Speakers must control themselves. Notice what these rules assume. If a person can be told to wait his turn, then he is able to wait his turn, which Paul will say outright at verse 32. The Spirit does not seize people and make them speak against their will, and no one in that congregation could plead that he had no choice. That single assumption quietly settles a great deal, then and since. Any claim to a spiritual experience that cannot be paused when the elder raises his hand has already been answered by this verse.

And speak to himself and to God. Quietly, privately, in his own heart. Notice the tone of the last clause, because it is easy to hear as a dismissal and is not one. The tongue-speaker without an interpreter is not told his gift is bogus, or that he should be ashamed of it. He is told where it belongs. What it may not do is take up the congregation’s time producing nothing for anybody.

Is this the room? That is a model for how a church should handle a great many things that are good in themselves and unsuited to the assembly. A believer’s favourite doctrine, his particular burden, his favourite emphasis, the experience that changed his life: none of these need be denied to be given their proper place. The question is never only is this real? The question is also is this the room?

The love of restraint. There is a further thing hidden in the numbers, and it applies far beyond tongues. Two or three, and no more, even of a good thing, even of a thing the Spirit gave. Paul assumes that a congregation’s time is finite and that not everything genuine can be fitted into it. Somebody with something real to offer will have to go home without offering it, and that is not a tragedy; it is what happens in a room with other people in it. That restraint is a form of love, and it is one of the harder ones. It means holding back something you were looking forward to, because the meeting has already had enough of that kind of thing. The person who can do that has understood the chapter better than anyone who merely agrees with it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean speakers were overwhelmed and could not help it. The gift was under the speaker’s control.

What should a church do today if someone stands up and speaks in a tongue? The elders should act gently and by Paul’s own rules. A church that holds, as this commentary does, that the gift has ceased will not make room for it in its services, and will explain why kindly and privately. But even a church that allows it is bound by this chapter: no more than two or three, one at a time, always with interpretation, and silence otherwise. Whatever is said must be weighed by Scripture. And the person concerned should be treated as a brother or sister, not shamed in front of others.

In a sentence. If anyone speaks in a tongue, two or at most three should speak, one after another, and someone must interpret. If there is no interpreter, the speaker should keep quiet in the church and speak only to himself and God.

On a Tuesday. Spiritual zeal never excuses disorder. Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit. In your next church meeting or Bible study, practise restraint: let someone else speak first, and leave one good thing unsaid if the time is better given to another.

For worship. The Spirit of God is the Spirit of power and love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7). He does not drive his people like the frenzied crowds of the pagan temples; he leads them as a shepherd leads his sheep. And the Son, who had all authority, did not grasp at the floor. He waited thirty years in Nazareth before he spoke in public, and at his trial he was silent. Blessed be the Lord whose strength is perfectly governed, and who teaches his people the beauty of holding back for love.

verseByVerse.quote: Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said. If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,

Let two or three prophets speak. Prophecy gets the same numerical limit as tongues, and then something tongues did not get.

And let the others weigh what is said. Weigh (diakrinō) means to sift, to evaluate, to discern. Prophecy in the Corinthian assembly was to be examined by the congregation. New Testament congregational prophecy was not automatically accepted; it had to be tested against apostolic teaching (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21; 1 John 4:1). That one instruction settles more about the nature of this gift than any definition could, and it must be held onto firmly, because it is where a great deal of harm has been done in the church.

Nobody weighs Scripture. Nobody sifted Isaiah to see how much of him to keep. If a prophecy in this room was to be tested by the people listening, then this gift was not on the same footing as the written word of God, which is not weighed but obeyed. And a man who claims to speak for God in a way that places him beyond examination has misunderstood what he is claiming. Thus says the Lord, said in a manner that forbids questioning, is precisely what this verse rules out.

How is it weighed? Four questions do most of the work. Does it agree with Scripture? Anything that does not is finished at once, whatever accompanied it. Does it exalt Christ, or the speaker? Does it build up, encourage and console, which is what Paul said prophecy does (v. 3)? And what is the speaker like: is this a person whose life commends what he says? The Bible never asks anyone to accept a spiritual claim without examination, and the Berean Jews are commended precisely for checking an apostle against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11).

If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent. Courtesy and order: one speaker at a time. If something is given to a person sitting down, the one on his feet stops. That is a small rule with a large implication. It means no one has the floor by right. And the mark of a man who is truly hearing from God is that he does not mind sitting down.

For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged. Taking turns allows everyone with a word to give it, and everyone to benefit. There is the purpose again, and both halves matter. Learning without encouragement produces a congregation that is informed and flat. Encouragement without learning produces one that is cheerful and hollow. Paul asks for both from the same activity, which is a high standard and the right one.

Is there prophecy today? The gift of prophecy, like tongues, belonged to the apostolic foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and with the completion of Scripture it has ceased. That does not make this passage useless. When someone says the Lord told him something, the church still has to weigh it, and the tests are the ones Paul’s instruction implies: does it agree with Scripture, does it exalt Christ, and does it build up? An impression may be sincere and even wise, but it is never a word that binds anyone’s conscience. The voice that binds the conscience is the voice of God in Scripture.

What should I do when a Christian friend says God told him something about me? Listen graciously, and then weigh it. Thank him for caring enough to speak. Ask whether what he says agrees with Scripture and whether it is wise; talk it over with your elders or a mature believer if it matters. If it is a call to repent of something Scripture forbids, take it seriously, because it may be God’s word to you through Scripture whatever the friend calls it. If it is a claim about whom to marry, where to move, or what will happen, you are not bound by it. Your guide for life is the Bible, and you need not fear disobeying God by setting aside a word that Scripture does not give.

What it does not mean. It does not mean everyone in the church was a prophet (12:29). All who had the gift could take their turn.

In a sentence. Two or three prophets should speak, and the others should carefully weigh what is said. If a revelation comes to someone else who is sitting there, the first speaker should stop. You can all prophesy in turn, so that everyone may learn and be encouraged,

On a Tuesday. Weigh everything you hear in church, and everywhere else, by Scripture: the sermon, the podcast, the book, the Christian celebrity, and your own feelings. Open your Bible this week to check one thing you have been told, as the Bereans did.

For worship. The Lord has given his church a word that does not need to be sifted, because it is the very breath of God (2 Timothy 3:16). Every other voice is weighed by it, and it is weighed by none. He has not left us at the mercy of the loudest speaker in the room; he has given us a sure word, more fully confirmed, to which we will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts (2 Peter 1:19). Thank God for the Scriptures, and for the Spirit who opens them.

parallels.desc: test everything

verseByVerse.quote: and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,

And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. Two of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone who has to lead a church. This is the answer to the one defence the Corinthians could still have offered, and it is the defence that has been offered ever since: I could not help it. The Spirit came on me. Are you telling me to quench the Spirit? Paul’s answer is that the prophet is in charge of his own mouth. Prophets were not overpowered by the Spirit; they could control when and whether they spoke. This has to be true, or Paul’s rules would be unenforceable: you cannot tell a man to wait his turn if he genuinely cannot.

The Spirit’s signature. It exposes something important about how the Holy Spirit works, over against every counterfeit. The pagan oracle was possessed; the priestess at Delphi was taken over, and her loss of control was taken as the proof of the god’s presence. The Holy Spirit does not do that. He never overrides a person; he restores him to himself. Self-control is the last item in the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23), and a spiritual experience that removes it is not evidence of more of the Spirit but of something else altogether. The man from whom Jesus cast the legion was found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed and in his right mind (Luke 8:35). That is the Holy Spirit’s signature.

For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. Then the theological ground. Confusion (akatastasia) is disorder, chaos, the word used of riots and political upheaval. Paul does not settle the question of order by taste, or by temperament, or by what is customary. He settles it by the character of God. God’s character shapes worship. He is a God of order and peace, and worship is meant to be a true statement about the one being worshipped; a congregation in uproar is making a false one.

Peace is not the same as quiet. The guard must be set here too, because this sentence has been used to smother things it was never aimed at. Order is not the same as predictability. A church can be so orderly that nothing whatever happens in it: where no one would ever weep, or stay behind, or say anything that was not on the sheet. That congregation has not obeyed this verse; it has merely avoided the problem the verse addresses. Paul is regulating a fire, not a filing cabinet, and he will end the chapter by forbidding them to put the fire out (v. 39).

As in all the churches of the saints. This phrase may end the sentence about God’s peace, or begin the next about women, as the ESV takes it. Either way, Corinth must conform to the practice of all the churches. It is reminded that it is not the only congregation in the world, and that its practice is not its own invention to make. It is an unglamorous point and a healthy one. A church that does something no other church anywhere does should at least ask itself why.

What it does not mean. It does not mean worship should be dull or rigid. Order serves peace and joy.

But what about when people in the Bible were overwhelmed by God? They were often overwhelmed in awe: Isaiah cried woe is me, John fell at Christ’s feet as though dead (Revelation 1:17). But they were never turned into puppets. Isaiah answered here I am, send me; John was raised up and told to write, and he wrote clearly. Being deeply moved by God is right and good, and tears in worship are no disorder. What Paul rules out is the claim that the Spirit makes a person act against his own control and against the order of the church. The Spirit humbles us, but he never dehumanises us.

In a sentence. Prophets are in control of their own spirits, because God is not a God of disorder but of peace, as in all the churches of God’s people.

On a Tuesday. Bring peace and order to your home and work, as reflections of the God of peace. Look at one place in your life that is chaotic, your mornings, your money, your words when you are tired, and take one step this week to bring it under the peace of God.

For worship. God is not a God of confusion. From the first page of the Bible he has been bringing order out of chaos: the Spirit hovering over the deep, light separated from darkness, the waters given their bounds. He is the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep (Hebrews 13:20). In him there is no frenzy, no anxiety, no loss of control: only the perfect harmony of Father, Son and Spirit. And he is making his church a picture of that peace, so that the world may look and see what he is like.
