verseByVerse.quote: the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.
verseByVerse.commentary:
the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.

The women should keep silent in the churches. Few passages in the Bible are harder, and the reader who has been waiting since chapter 11 for this to be faced deserves it faced rather than hurried. The difficulty is not the culture. It is Paul. Three chapters ago, in this same letter, he regulated the way women should be dressed when they pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5), and he did not object to their doing it. A man does not lay down guidance for how women should pray aloud in church and then, three chapters later, forbid them to open their mouths. So this cannot be total silence. Whatever this passage means, it cannot mean the flat opposite of what he wrote a few pages earlier, and any reading that produces that result has gone wrong somewhere.

Look where these verses sit. The context is the weighing of prophecies (v. 29). That weighing was a public, judicial act: the assembly sitting in judgement on what had been said, testing a claim to speak for God. Women should not take part in that public judging and questioning, which carried teaching authority over the congregation.

For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. No single verse is quoted. Most likely Paul means the order of creation in Genesis 2, which he cites elsewhere for the same principle (11:8–9; 1 Timothy 2:13), and which stands in the Law in the sense of the five books of Moses. The principle is headship, not culture alone.

If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. And notice what verse 35 regulates: asking questions. The instruction is not addressed to praying or prophesying at all; it is addressed to the cross-examination and questioning that went with the weighing. Wives questioning or challenging prophets, perhaps their own husbands, in public would undermine order and headship. Paul directs their questions to the home, assuming women should learn. And the practical setting fits the ancient room, where most women had far less schooling than the men, and where an honest question called across a courtyard could stop the meeting.

For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church. Speak here in the sense of the public judging and questioning just described.

Four readings. Four readings are on the table. Some have taken it as a universal ban on women speaking in church; that founders on 11:5, and also on the fact that Christians who hold it do not actually apply it: the women in such congregations sing, confess the creed, and answer Amen. Some have suggested the two verses were not written by Paul at all, noting that a few manuscripts place them after verse 40. That displacement is real and worth knowing, but every manuscript we possess contains the verses somewhere, so they cannot simply be removed. Some read verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian slogan that Paul quotes in order to demolish it in verse 36. It is an ingenious reading, but the letter gives no signal that a quotation has begun, and verse 37 calls what he is writing the Lord’s command. The reading that fits the passage best takes it from its own context, in the paragraph about weighing prophecy.

Where Christians differ: women’s silence. Some take this as an absolute ban on women speaking at all in church. Others say it was a cultural rule for disruptive Corinthian women and no longer applies, or even that it was not written by Paul. Verdict: The verses are in all the manuscripts, though a few move them after verse 40. Since Paul allows women to pray and prophesy (11:5), this is not a ban on all speech, but on women taking the role of authoritatively judging prophecy and teaching in the gathered church, which belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:11–12). This is the complementarian position. Women may sing, pray, testify, and serve in countless ways. The principle is grounded in creation, not merely culture.

Read that way, the two passages agree. A woman may pray and prophesy in the assembly (11:5). She is not to exercise the congregation’s governing judgement over the church’s teaching, which belongs with the same ordering Paul roots in creation elsewhere (1 Timothy 2:12).

What does this mean for a church today? The restriction concerns the authoritative teaching and judging of doctrine in the gathered church, which Paul elsewhere reserves to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12). It does not forbid women to pray aloud, read Scripture, sing, give testimony, teach other women and children (Titus 2:3–5), or speak in a members’ meeting. And since prophecy has ceased, the part women once played in praying and prophesying (11:5) is now their full share in the church’s prayer and praise.

And women with no husband to ask? Paul’s point is to keep the meeting orderly, not to keep women from learning. A single woman, a widow or a wife whose husband does not believe should be taught by the elders and by other mature believers, as every member should. Many churches give opportunity for questions after the service or in classes, and that fits Paul’s concern exactly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are less intelligent or spiritual, or that their questions are unwelcome. Paul wants them to learn. The same apostle wrote that in Christ there is neither male nor female (Galatians 3:28), greeted Junia as well known to the apostles (Romans 16:7), and honoured Priscilla, Phoebe, Euodia and Syntyche for their labour alongside him (Romans 16:1–4; Philippians 4:2–3). Equal in worth and in Christ; different in calling within the church and the home.

A misuse to refuse. This passage has been used to shame women into silence far beyond anything Paul wrote, and that misuse has done real damage. A congregation where women are afraid to speak at all has not obeyed this text; it has ignored chapter 11. And headship in Scripture is never a licence for control. It is the self-giving love of Christ for his church (Ephesians 5:25). A husband who uses this verse to belittle or dominate his wife has turned it upside down, and abuse is never to be tolerated or covered in the name of submission.

Why would God give men and women different roles if they are equal? Because difference is not inequality, and the Trinity shows it. The Son is fully equal with the Father, yet he gladly does the Father’s will (11:3; John 6:38). Ordered roles among equals are not a scar on creation but part of its beauty. God made man and woman both in his image (Genesis 1:27), and he gave them to each other as partners with different callings, so that the home and the church might picture Christ and his bride. The man is called to lead by laying down his life, the woman to honour that leadership freely, and both to serve. Where this is lived in love, it is not a cage but a dance.

In a sentence. Women should not speak in the churches when prophecies are being judged. They are not given that role, but should accept the order the law teaches. If they want to ask about something, they should ask their husbands at home, for it is not fitting for a woman to take that part in the church.

On a Tuesday. Husbands, be ready to discuss Scripture with your wives at home. Make your home a place of learning together: ask your wife what she took from Sunday’s sermon, and listen. Sisters, ask your questions, and do not let anyone tell you that your understanding of God does not matter; it matters to him.

For worship. The Son of God took the place of the servant, though he was equal with God, and he was not less for it. He gave himself up for his bride, to sanctify her and present her to himself in splendour (Ephesians 5:25–27). In his church, men and women alike are heirs together of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7), and every ordered calling is a reflection of the love within the Godhead, where the Father sends, the Son gladly obeys, and the Spirit delights in both. Blessed be the God whose order is love.
verseByVerse.note: Paul has already assumed that women pray and prophesy in worship (11:5). Interpreters differ on what speaking is forbidden here; many take it as the public judging of prophecies just mentioned (v. 29).

verseByVerse.quote: Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?

Or was it from you that the word of God came? Two questions, dripping with irony, and they are the sting in the tail of the whole chapter. This verse is often skipped in the argument about the two before it, and it should not be, because it tells us what Paul thought the Corinthians’ real problem was. It was not tongues. It was independence. Behind every fault in this letter lies a congregation that had come to believe it was the centre of things: that its practices were its own to invent, its judgements its own to make, and its founder’s instructions a matter for consideration. The Corinthians acted as if they were the source of God’s word, free to make their own rules. They were not.

Or are you the only ones it has reached? Did the gospel start here? Are you the only place it has got to? Both answers are humiliating and both are obvious. The word of God came to Corinth from somewhere else, brought by a man who had received it himself, and it had already reached a great many other cities where the churches did not do what Corinth was doing. They were one church among many, receiving the same word, and must follow the same practice. The link with verse 33 is exact: as in all the churches of the saints, and now, are you the only ones? Paul is placing this congregation back among its peers. Whatever they had concluded about worship, they had concluded it alone, and that alone was a warning sign.

Novelty is worth examining. Which is a useful thing to hold up to any church, and it is not an argument for mere conformity. Truth is not decided by counting congregations, and there have been moments, the Reformation among them, when a few were right and the many were wrong. But a church that finds itself doing something no other body of Christians anywhere has thought necessary should at least ask whether the Spirit really has told it alone. The same Spirit is at work in the church in the next town, and in the churches of the last twenty centuries.

Private certainty. There is a humility in this for individuals too. The believer convinced that he has seen something in Scripture that the whole church has missed is occasionally right and is usually a man who has been reading alone for too long. Paul’s questions are worth asking of any private certainty: did this begin with me, and am I the only one it has reached?

What it does not mean. It does not mean local churches have no freedom in practical matters. It means they cannot overrule apostolic teaching.

How do I tell faithful conviction from mere novelty? Ask three questions. First, does Scripture plainly teach it, read in context, or am I building on one verse? Second, have faithful Christians in other times and places, people who loved the Bible as much as I do, seen it too? The creeds and confessions are a great help here. Third, would my elders and wise believers in my church recognise it, or am I hiding it from them? Not every old view is right, and not every new insight is wrong. But a conviction that cannot be found in Scripture plainly, has no friends in church history and must be kept from the church’s leaders deserves deep suspicion.

In a sentence. Did the word of God begin with you? Are you the only people it has reached?

On a Tuesday. Trace how the gospel reached you: the parent, the friend, the preacher, the book. Thank God for each link in the chain, and pray for one person to whom you might pass it on.

For worship. There is a warmer thing in the verse than the sarcasm suggests. The word of God came to Corinth. It arrived. Somebody carried it across the Aegean to a city with a bad reputation and no interest in it, and Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his entire household, and many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptised (Acts 18:8). Nobody in that congregation had generated a word of it. That is true of every Christian who has ever lived. There is no self-made believer. The word went out from Jerusalem by the will of the Father, through the death and resurrection of the Son, in the power of the Spirit, and it has run to the ends of the earth. We did not invent it. We received it, and that is grace.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.

If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual. Paul now supplies the test he knew would be needed, because he could predict exactly who would object to this chapter. It would be those who claim spiritual gifts, the people most confident of their own spirituality.

He should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord. So he sets a trap and states it openly. Do you consider yourself a prophet? Do you consider yourself spiritual? Then here is how that claim is checked: you will recognise that what I am writing is the Lord’s command. Any spirituality that arrives at a different conclusion from apostolic instruction has failed at the only point where it could ever have been tested. A true prophet will recognise apostolic authority, and any prophecy that contradicts the apostle is false.

A large claim about this letter. Notice how large a claim that is. Paul does not present these chapters as his best judgement, his temperament, or a policy for a difficult congregation. He calls them a command of the Lord. That is the apostolic authority the whole New Testament rests on: not that these men were wise, but that they were sent, and that what they wrote to the churches carries the weight of the one who sent them. Peter already counted Paul’s letters with the other Scriptures (2 Peter 3:15–16). This shows that the apostolic writings, now our New Testament, stand above all claimed revelation.

If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized. Short and cold. Not recognised by God, or by the church as a true prophet. The manuscripts vary slightly here between he is not recognised and let him not be recognised, and the difference is small, because either way the man is outside the circle he was claiming to lead. He wanted to be acknowledged as a prophet. He is not acknowledged at all, and the passive voice leaves open by whom, which is the most uncomfortable thing about the sentence.

A self-refuting claim. The principle has a long reach and it is worth having, because it settles the commonest form of spiritual manipulation. Whenever anyone claims an authority, an insight or an experience that places him above correction from Scripture, this verse answers him. The claim refutes itself. A genuine work of the Spirit will always submit to the word the Spirit gave; the test is not whether a man sounds spiritual, but what he does when the Bible contradicts him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was arrogant. He speaks as Christ’s appointed apostle, and he speaks for Christ, not for himself.

How do I run this test on myself? Everyone has a place where Scripture cuts across something he wants: a grudge, a habit, a plan, an opinion held for thirty years. The question is what happens in that moment. A man who reaches for a reason why the passage does not quite apply to his own case has just learned something about the real source of his convictions, whatever else he believes about the Bible. And there is mercy in Paul’s verb. He says the spiritual man should acknowledge this, should come to see it, the way one recognises a face. He does not say he will agree at once, or without a struggle. Recognition can take a while. Bring your struggle to God honestly and keep reading until you bow.

In a sentence. Anyone who thinks he is a prophet or spiritually gifted should recognise that what Paul is writing is the Lord’s command. Anyone who ignores this will himself be ignored.

On a Tuesday. Test every claimed word from God, every feeling, every teaching, by Scripture. Scripture is the Lord’s command. Name one place where the Bible is currently cutting across your will, and pray today for the grace to yield.

For worship. The Lord Jesus said that heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not pass away (Matthew 24:35). He gave his apostles his Spirit to guide them into all the truth, and through them he gave his church a word that will never be overruled. Blessed be the Lord who has not left his church to the competing claims of the confident, but has put his own voice into a book that every believer can open, and who rules his people by it with the gentleness of a shepherd.

verseByVerse.quote: So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order.

So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy. The chapter ends with two commands and a governing principle, and the balance of them is the whole point. Earnestly desire is the same verb Paul opened with. After a whole chapter of regulation, Paul does not want a subdued church. He wants them hungry for the gift that builds people up.

And do not forbid speaking in tongues. That is a command, and it is placed exactly where a lesser writer would have put a ban. Tongues, rightly used with interpretation, were a genuine gift then. Paul has spent the chapter restricting the practice in the assembly, two or three, in turn, interpretation required, otherwise silence, and he closes by forbidding the church to forbid it. He knows perfectly well what happens when a congregation is corrected about an excess: it swings, and the next generation treats the thing as an embarrassment.

But all things should be done decently and in order. The last word, and it is a phrase from the drawing room and the parade ground. Decently (euschēmonōs) is fittingly, beautifully, with dignity. In order (kata taxin) is in proper order, like soldiers in ranks. The final word on worship. It is a sentence often quoted by people who want a quiet church, and it will not quite serve that purpose, because verse 39 stands in front of it. Order is what Paul wants around the fire, not instead of it.

Where Christians differ: does do not forbid tongues apply today? Continuationists argue that churches today must not forbid tongues. Verdict: Paul’s command applied when the gift was active. If the revelatory and sign gifts have ceased with the apostolic age, as argued on 12:10, the question is whether present-day phenomena are the same gift. Cessationists believe they are not. Churches should neither mock nor exclude continuationist believers, and all should agree on the principles here: everything must be understood, edifying, tested by Scripture, orderly, and done in love.

How does a church that believes tongues have ceased obey this command? By recognising that Paul was protecting a gift then active, and by holding the conclusion that it has ceased with humility rather than scorn. Even for those who conclude, as is argued here, that the sign gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation, this sentence should temper the way the conviction is held. The instinct to shut down anything that cannot be controlled is not a Christian virtue, and it is not what this apostle did with a church that had abused almost every gift it had. He regulated, and then he protected. In practice, elders should test any claim to tongues by Paul’s own rules in this chapter: speakers in turn, never more than two or three, always with interpretation, and silence otherwise (vv. 27–28). And earnestly desire to prophesy is obeyed today by longing for the clear, Spirit-given proclamation of the word that builds the church up.

The fire and the grate. That is the balance the whole chapter has been holding: a church that is neither chaotic nor cold, where the Spirit’s work is wanted and not feared, where what happens can be understood by a stranger at the back, and where every single thing is measured by whether anybody was built up. Corinth had the fire and no grate. Many congregations since have had a beautiful grate and no fire.

What it does not mean. It does not mean order is opposed to the Spirit. The Spirit is the author of order.

How can a cessationist church keep from becoming cold? By remembering that cessationism concerns certain gifts, not the Spirit himself. The Spirit is as present and powerful in the church today as at Pentecost: he convicts, regenerates, comforts, sanctifies, and makes the word come alive. A cessationist church should be the warmest of all, because it believes the Spirit speaks fully and sufficiently in Scripture. Pray for his blessing on the preaching, expect conversions, sing with heart and mind, and love one another fervently. The great revivals under Whitefield and Edwards, and the preaching of Spurgeon, came through men who looked for no new revelation, and they were not cold.

In a sentence. So, brothers and sisters, be eager to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But everything should be done in a fitting and orderly way.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s gatherings this Sunday: for the preacher to be clear and full of the Spirit, for the singing to be heartfelt and true, for visitors to understand, and for everything to be done in love. Then come with your own heart prepared, as part of the answer to that prayer.

For worship. Underneath it all is the God of verse 33: not a God of confusion but of peace, whose own life is perfect order and perfect love at once, who has never had to choose between liveliness and dignity. He gave gifts to men when Christ ascended on high (Ephesians 4:8–13), so that a room full of ordinary people might be built up into something that will last after every tongue has fallen silent. And on the last day the whole redeemed creation will worship him in perfect order and unbounded joy, ten thousand times ten thousand, every voice distinct and every voice one: worthy is the Lamb who was slain.

The one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in tongues, unless someone interprets, so that the church may be built up.<sup>6</sup>Now, brothers, if I come to you speaking in tongues, how will I benefit you unless I bring you some revelation or knowledge or prophecy or teaching?<sup>7</sup>If even lifeless instruments, such as the flute or the harp, do not give distinct notes, how will anyone know what is played?<sup>8</sup>And if the bugle gives an indistinct sound, who will get ready for battle?<sup>9</sup>So with yourselves, if with your tongue you utter speech that is not intelligible, how will anyone know what is said? For you will be speaking into the air.<sup>10</sup>There are doubtless many different languages in the world, and none is without meaning,<sup>11</sup>but if I do not know the meaning of the language, I will be a foreigner to the speaker and the speaker a foreigner to me.<sup>12</sup>So with yourselves, since you are eager for manifestations of the Spirit, strive to excel in building up the church.<sup>13</sup>Therefore, one who speaks in a tongue should pray that he may interpret.<sup>14</sup>For if I pray in a tongue, my spirit prays but my mind is unfruitful.<sup>15</sup>What am I to do? I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also.<sup>16</sup>Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say “Amen” to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?<sup>17</sup>For you may be giving thanks well enough, but the other person is not being built up.<sup>18</sup>I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you.<sup>19</sup>Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue.<sup>20</sup>Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature.<sup>21</sup>In the Law it is written, “By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.”<sup>22</sup>Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers, while prophecy is a sign not for unbelievers but for believers.<sup>23</sup>If, therefore, the whole church comes together and all speak in tongues, and outsiders or unbelievers enter, will they not say that you are out of your minds?<sup>24</sup>But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all,<sup>25</sup>the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you.<sup>26</sup>What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up.<sup>27</sup>If any speak in a tongue, let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret.<sup>28</sup>But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church and speak to himself and to God.<sup>29</sup>Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said.<sup>30</sup>If a revelation is made to another sitting there, let the first be silent.<sup>31</sup>For you can all prophesy one by one, so that all may learn and all be encouraged,<sup>32</sup>and the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets.<sup>33</sup>For God is not a God of confusion but of peace. As in all the churches of the saints,<sup>34</sup>the women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says.<sup>35</sup>If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church.<sup>36</sup>Or was it from you that the word of God came? Or are you the only ones it has reached?<sup>37</sup>If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord.<sup>38</sup>If anyone does not recognize this, he is not recognized.<sup>39</sup>So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues.<sup>40</sup>But all things should be done decently and in order.

15.title: The Resurrection of the Dead
15.overview:
Some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead. That fitted Greek thinking well. Many Greeks regarded the body as a prison for the soul; a philosophical pun called the body (sōma) a tomb (sēma). Salvation meant the soul escaping, not the corpse rising, and the Athenians laughed when Paul spoke of resurrection (Acts 17:32). In one of Aeschylus’ tragedies the god Apollo says that once a man has died and the dust has soaked up his blood, there is no rising again. The Corinthians probably still believed in Christ’s resurrection and in some spiritual life after death, but not in the raising of their own bodies.

Paul answers in four stages. First, the facts: Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day and appeared to Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred at once, James, all the apostles and finally Paul. Second, the consequences: if there is no resurrection, Christ was not raised, preaching and faith are empty, sins unforgiven, the dead lost, and Christians the most pitiable of people. Third, the plan: Christ has been raised as the firstfruits of the harvest; as all die in Adam, all in Christ will be made alive; he reigns until every enemy, death last of all, is defeated. Fourth, the body: like a seed and the plant that grows from it, the body sown in weakness will be raised in power, a body fitted for the Spirit, bearing the image of the last Adam. At the last trumpet the dead will rise and the living be changed, death will be swallowed up in victory, and so believers’ labour in the Lord is never in vain.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Resurrection of Christ: The Apostolic Testimony
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reminds them of the gospel he preached, which they received and on which they stand, and by which they are saved if they hold firmly to it, unless they believed in vain. He handed on to them, as of first importance, what he himself had received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Peter and then to the Twelve. After that he appeared to more than five hundred believers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have died. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all to Paul, as to one abnormally born. Paul is the least of the apostles and does not deserve the name, because he persecuted God’s church. But by God’s grace he is what he is, and that grace was not wasted; he worked harder than all of them, though it was God’s grace with him. Whether it was Paul or they, this is what they preached and what the Corinthians believed.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Foundation of Salvation

Paul’s phrase “Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures” is among the earliest creedal formulations we possess, pre-dating the letter (Paul received it). The resurrection “in accordance with the Scriptures” grounds both events in OT prophecy — Psalm 16:10, Isaiah 53, Hosea 6:2 being the primary candidates. The conjunction of death and resurrection is crucial: the resurrection is not an isolated miracle but the divine vindication of the atoning death. Without the resurrection, the death has no declared meaning; without the death, the resurrection has no redemptive content. Together they constitute the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek philosophical tradition was deeply ambivalent about bodily resurrection. The famous scene in Acts 17:32 — when Paul mentions the resurrection, some mock and some are interested — captures the standard Hellenistic reaction. The Platonic tradition prized the release of the soul from the body; the idea of the body being raised was not an upgrade but a retrogression to the bodily existence the soul was trying to escape. Paul’s case for the resurrection runs directly against this deeply embedded cultural instinct. Now: The modern version of the Greek objection is not philosophical but scientific: dead bodies do not rise. Paul’s answer is the same: the evidence of the witnesses. The question is not whether bodies normally rise but whether this specific body, on this specific morning, was raised by the God who created bodies in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand, and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 15 is the Bible’s fullest teaching on the resurrection. Some in Corinth, shaped by Greek thought that saw the body as worthless or a prison, were denying that believers will be raised bodily. Paul answers in five movements. First, the gospel itself rests on the bodily resurrection of Christ, attested by Scripture and by hundreds of eyewitnesses, including Paul (vv. 1–11). Second, if the dead are not raised, then Christ was not raised, faith is useless, sins are unforgiven, the dead are lost, and Christians are the most pitiable people alive (vv. 12–19). Third, Christ has in fact been raised as the firstfruits of the harvest; as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. He reigns now until every enemy, death last of all, is destroyed, and then he hands the kingdom to the Father (vv. 20–28). Fourth, the practical consequences: why else would believers risk their lives, or live holy lives (vv. 29–34)? Fifth, what will the resurrection body be like? Like a seed and the plant, it will be the same person, transformed: imperishable, glorious, powerful, spiritual, bearing the image of Christ, the last Adam (vv. 35–49). At the last trumpet, the dead will be raised and the living changed in an instant, and death will be swallowed up in victory. So be steadfast, for your labour in the Lord is not in vain (vv. 50–58). It is the chapter Christians have read at gravesides for two thousand years, and it ends not with a sigh but with a shout of thanks.

The setting. Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the dead (v. 12). Greeks generally believed the soul might survive, but bodily resurrection seemed absurd; when Paul spoke of it at Athens, some mocked (Acts 17:32). Some Corinthians may also have thought that they had already been raised spiritually and needed nothing more (4:8; 2 Timothy 2:18). Fourteen chapters of correction are behind Paul now: factions, immorality, lawsuits, marriage, idol meat, head coverings, the Supper, the gifts. Here he turns to the thing all of it rests on, and his tone changes completely.

Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you. Remind (gnōrizō) is to make known again. Paul is not about to tell this church anything new. Everything in this chapter, the longest and greatest in the letter, is material they already had and had stopped standing on. That is worth knowing, because Christians commonly assume that what they need is more information. The Corinthians were drowning in information; they had been taught by Paul for eighteen months (Acts 18:11) and by Apollos after him. What they needed was for somebody to walk them back to the first thing and make them look at it again. Most of the Christian life is like that. Very little of what steadies a believer in a hard year is new to him. It is the old thing, remembered at the right moment, by someone who troubled to say it again.

Which you received, in which you stand. Four verbs in this sentence, and together they are a small map of the Christian life. The gospel was preached: it came from outside, as news; nobody worked it out. It was received: taken by faith, as a gift is taken, which is the only posture available to a man being given something. It is what they stand in: the present tense of it, the ground under their feet, and Paul chooses that verb for a congregation that had been standing on its gifts, its wisdom and its teachers.

And by which you are being saved. The fourth verb is a present continuous. Salvation is not only something that happened to them at a meeting years ago but something still going on, to be completed in the resurrection.

If you hold fast to the word I preached to you, unless you believed in vain. Hold fast (katechō) is to keep a firm grip. In vain (eikē) is without cause, without result. The clause stops some readers cold. It sounds, at first hearing, as though everything is conditional, and a Christian troubled about his own perseverance can be badly frightened by it. So read what Paul actually says. He does not say you will lose what you have if you slip. He raises the possibility that some of them believed in vain: believed to no purpose, without effect, a profession that never had anything living in it. If the resurrection were false, their believing would be pointless; and if they let go of this gospel, they would show their faith was empty. That is a different thing from a believer falling out of God’s hand, which this apostle elsewhere says is impossible (Romans 8:38–39).

Holding fast is evidence, not cause. In the New Testament, holding fast is never the cause of being kept; it is the evidence of it. The people God keeps are the people who keep going, and he keeps them by making them keep going. So this clause is not a threat held over a frightened Christian; it is a question put to a comfortable one. And it has a searching form: not do you remember believing? but are you still holding on? The mark of a real faith is not the vividness of its beginning but the fact that it is still there (Colossians 1:23; Hebrews 3:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our grip rather than God’s. True faith perseveres because God keeps it: he will sustain you to the end, guiltless in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:8–9). But those who abandon the gospel show their faith was never real.

I am afraid I might not hold on. What then? The fear itself is a good sign. People who have truly let go of Christ are rarely troubled about it. Your holding on is not a matter of gritting your teeth; it is a matter of looking at Christ, and he holds you far more firmly than you hold him. No one will snatch his sheep out of his hand (John 10:28–29). So when you feel your grip weakening, do not stare at your grip. Go back to the gospel in verses 3 and 4, read it, pray it, and take the Lord’s Supper with his people. Faith is strengthened by being fed, and its food is Christ.

In a sentence. Brothers and sisters, Paul wants to remind you of the gospel he preached to you: you received it, you are standing on it, and through it you are being saved, as long as you keep holding firmly to the message he preached; otherwise your believing was for nothing.

On a Tuesday. Hold fast to the gospel today. Remind yourself of it: Christ died for your sins and was raised. Say it to yourself before you get out of bed, and say it again when the day goes wrong.

For worship. The gospel came to us from outside. We did not find it; it found us. God sent it across seas and centuries, through apostles and martyrs and ordinary believers, until it reached our door, and then he opened our hearts to receive it. He planted our feet on it, and he is saving us by it still, and he will not let it fail. The One who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6). Blessed be the God who keeps those who hold fast, by holding them.
verseByVerse.note: Some at Corinth were denying the future resurrection of the body; most Greeks thought the body was left behind at death.

verseByVerse.quote: For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,

For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received. Two words in that sentence are worth more than they look. Received and delivered are the standard vocabulary for handing on a fixed tradition, word for word, without adjustment: the same pair Paul used of the Lord’s Supper at 11:23. Paul is not composing here. He is reciting something he was given. Of first importance: at the very heart of the gospel.

How early is this creed? That matters more for the historical question than almost anything else in the New Testament. Paul is writing about twenty-five years after the crucifixion, around AD 54. But he did not invent this formula; he received it, which means it was already in circulation and already fixed when he was taught it, and he was taught it probably soon after his conversion, around AD 35, within a very few years of the event. This is not a legend that grew over generations. It is a summary that was being recited by Christians while the people who buried Jesus were still middle-aged. Now the clauses, and each is load-bearing.

That Christ died for our sins. Not merely died. The little word for (hyper, on behalf of, in place of) carries substitution: in our place, on our account. His death dealt with our sins: he bore the penalty we deserved. A death without that word is a tragedy; with it, it is an exchange.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The phrase appears twice, once for the death and once for the rising, and it means this was not an emergency. Isaiah had described a servant pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, who would see his offspring and prolong his days after making his soul an offering for guilt (Isaiah 53:5–12). The cross was God’s plan, not an accident. The plan is older than the crime.

That he was buried. The oddest item on the list, and the one people skip. Why include it in a summary this compressed? Two reasons. It settles that he was actually dead: there was a body, and men carried it, and it was heavy. And it means the resurrection was bodily: the body placed in the tomb was the body raised, leaving the tomb empty. A burial means a tomb, and a tomb has an address, and Jerusalem is a small city. The claim was placed where it could be checked.

That he was raised on the third day. Note the passive. Was raised (egēgertai) is perfect tense: God raised him, and he remains raised. Not only he rose, though that is also true, but the Father acting on the Son. The resurrection is the Father’s answer to the cross, and his verdict on it. On the third day: a specific, historical date. The third day is counted the way the ancient world counted, where any part of a day was a day. Jesus died on Friday afternoon, lay in the tomb through Saturday, and rose early on Sunday: Friday, Saturday, Sunday. The three days and three nights of the Jonah sign (Matthew 12:40) is the same span in a common Jewish idiom, not a stopwatch.

In accordance with the Scriptures. The rising too was foretold. The psalmist had said God would not let his Holy One see corruption (Psalm 16:10), which Peter preached at Pentecost (Acts 2:27). The servant of Isaiah, after his death, would see his offspring and prolong his days (Isaiah 53:10–12). Hosea had spoken of God raising his people up on the third day (Hosea 6:2), and Jesus himself pointed to the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:40).

Where Christians differ: the meaning of Christ’s death. Some see Christ’s death mainly as an example of love, or as a victory over evil powers, and reject the idea that he bore the punishment for sins. Verdict: Christ died for our sins. Scripture presents his death as many things, including example and victory, but at its heart it is penal substitution: he stood in our place, bearing the penalty of God’s just wrath against our sins, so that we might be forgiven and declared righteous (Isaiah 53:5–6; Romans 3:25–26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; Galatians 3:13). This is of first importance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection was a spiritual idea or vision. The burial and empty tomb rule that out.

Why is the gospel news rather than advice? Because it tells what God has done, not what you must do to reach him. Advice says: try harder, and you may get there. News says: it has been done; believe it. Every other religion is finally a kind of advice. The Christian gospel is a report of three events, a death, a burial and a resurrection, and an announcement of what they mean: your sins can be forgiven, because Christ has borne them. The commands of the Christian life are real, but they follow the news. You do not obey in order to be accepted; you obey because in Christ you have been.

In a sentence. For what Paul received he passed on to you as most important: Christ died for our sins as the Scriptures foretold; he was buried; and he was raised on the third day, as the Scriptures foretold;

On a Tuesday. Learn these two verses by heart this week, so that you can say the gospel to anyone in a breath. Then say it to one person who needs to hear it.

For worship. Christ died for my sins. Before the world was made, the Father had planned it, and the prophets had seen it from afar: the lamb led to the slaughter, the Holy One who would not see corruption. He was pierced for our transgressions, and laid in a borrowed tomb, and on the third day the Father raised him from the dead. Every promise of the Old Testament says yes in him. Recite this gospel slowly as a prayer of thanks: Christ died for my sins, was buried, and was raised. There is no better news in the world, and there never will be.
verseByVerse.note: Verses 3–5 are an early summary of the faith that Paul had received — within a few years of the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.

And that he appeared to Cephas. The witness list begins, and it begins with a scandal. Cephas is Peter, and the last thing the reader knows about Peter is that he stood by a fire in a courtyard and swore three times that he had never met the man. His denial is recorded in all four Gospels. And he is first on the list. Luke preserves the same detail: when the two from Emmaus got back to Jerusalem, the others told them the Lord has risen indeed, and has appeared to Simon (Luke 24:34). Nobody records what was said in that meeting, which is a mercy; some conversations are not for publication. But the fact of it is here, in one of the earliest Christian creeds we possess: the first apostle the risen Christ went to was the man who had denied him. It was an act of grace and restoration.

Tell his disciples and Peter. The angel at the tomb had already signalled it. Go, tell his disciples and Peter (Mark 16:7), and those two extra words are the gospel in miniature. Peter had disqualified himself and would have said so. Somebody made sure his name was spoken separately, in case he assumed the message was for the others and not for him. On the shore of Galilee the restoration was completed, three questions for three denials, and a commission: feed my sheep (John 21:15–17).

Then to the twelve. A careful reader stops, because at that point there were not twelve. Judas was dead. Thomas was absent from the first appearance (John 20:19–29). So the number is wrong, and someone will say so. The answer is that the Twelve had become a title rather than a headcount. It was the name of the group, the way a committee keeps its name when a seat is empty and a regiment keeps its number after a bad year. John uses it the same way, calling Thomas one of the twelve (John 20:24). The apostolic group as a whole saw him.

A rough edge that rings true. A man polishing a story does not leave a countable discrepancy in the second line of his creed. He writes the eleven, which is what Luke writes when he is being precise (Luke 24:33), and nobody ever raises the question. The rough edge is the mark of a formula that was in use among people who were there and knew perfectly well what it meant.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these were inner visions or hallucinations. Appeared (ōphthē, was seen) describes real sightings. Jesus ate with them and they touched him (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27).

Could the disciples have been mistaken or deceived? Consider what the alternatives require. Hallucinations are private experiences; they do not happen to groups in the same form, and they do not eat fish or invite touch. A stolen body would not explain why the men who knew where it was went to their deaths saying he was alive. Legend takes generations to grow, and this creed was fixed within a few years. And the disciples were not expecting a resurrection; they were hiding behind locked doors. Something turned frightened men into bold witnesses within weeks, in the very city where he was buried. The simplest explanation is the one they gave: he appeared to them.

In a sentence. and that he was seen by Peter, and then by the Twelve.

On a Tuesday. Jesus appeared first to the apostle who had failed him most. If you have failed him, he still comes to you. Name your failure to him today, and hear him say your name.

For worship. Two men, then, at the head of the evidence: a denier, and a group with a hole in it where a traitor used to be. He did not go to the Sanhedrin, or to Pilate, or to the crowd. He went back to his friends, and the first name on the list is the one who had let him down worst. The risen Christ does not begin with the loyal. He begins with the man who has to be told twice that he is still wanted, and he goes and finds him first. Such is the Shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine, and such is the love that rose from the dead.
verseByVerse.note: Cephas is Peter. “The twelve” was the title of the group even when only eleven were present.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.

Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time. A mass appearance, probably in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–17). It is recorded nowhere else in the New Testament, which is itself striking: Paul knows more than the Gospels chose to write down. Hallucinations are private; five hundred people do not share the same hallucination.

Most of whom are still alive. That is not a devotional remark. It is an invitation, and its tone is almost brisk. Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote, about twenty years later. The letter is going to a port city with constant traffic to Palestine. Paul is in effect saying: several hundred people saw this at the same time, they are not hard to find, and you may go and ask them. A man inventing a story does not name a crowd of living witnesses and mention that they can be interviewed. He locates his miracle somewhere quieter.

Though some have fallen asleep. Some had died. Fallen asleep is the Christian word for believers’ death: temporary, to be followed by waking at the resurrection.

Then he appeared to James. This one is quietly devastating. This is James the brother of the Lord, who ended up leading the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13–21; Galatians 1:19; 2:9) and was killed for it. And the Gospels record, without embarrassment, what he thought before that: not even his brothers believed in him (John 7:5). His family had at one point gone out to seize Jesus, saying he was out of his mind (Mark 3:21). Consider what it takes to change a brother’s mind. Nobody in the world is harder to convince that a man is the Son of God than the man who grew up in the same house, ate at the same table, and watched him be an ordinary older brother for thirty years. Scepticism about a sibling is not a theory; it is a lifetime of evidence. James went from that to leading the mother church of Christianity and dying rather than take it back, and this verse is the whole explanation: then he appeared to James.

Then to all the apostles. Perhaps at the ascension (Acts 1:3–9), including a wider group beyond the Twelve.

Why are the women not on the list? One thing the list does not contain is worth explaining, since a modern reader will notice it. All four Gospels say the women found the tomb empty, and Matthew and John record that they were the first to see him (Matthew 28:9; John 20:14–18). Paul is assembling something like a legal brief, and in that world a woman’s testimony carried little weight in a court, which is precisely why the fact that the Gospels kept the women in is such powerful evidence of honesty. Nobody constructing a case puts his least admissible witnesses at the front. They did it because that is what happened. And the Lord himself chose a weeping woman, Mary Magdalene, to be the first to see him and to carry the news to the apostles.

Where Christians differ: soul sleep. Some take fallen asleep to mean that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Verdict: Sleep describes the appearance of the body in death and the certainty of waking. But Scripture teaches that the souls of believers go immediately into the presence of Christ, conscious and at rest, awaiting the resurrection of the body (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Philippians 1:23; Revelation 6:9–11; Westminster 32.1).

Where are my Christian loved ones now? With Christ, consciously and gladly. When a believer dies, his soul goes at once to be with the Lord, which Paul calls far better (Philippians 1:23). There is no waiting room of unconsciousness and no purgatory of cleansing; Christ’s blood has cleansed them fully. They are at rest, free from sin and pain, in the presence of Jesus. Their bodies, meanwhile, rest in the grave, still united to Christ, waiting for the resurrection. So you grieve the parting, but you do not grieve as those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). They are more alive now than they ever were with you.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these were the only appearances. Paul gives an official list of witnesses.

In a sentence. After that he was seen by over five hundred brothers and sisters at once, most of whom are still living, though some have died. Then he was seen by James, then by all the apostles,

On a Tuesday. Your faith rests on public, testable history. When you are asked why you believe, do not begin with your feelings; begin with the witnesses. And pray for one sceptic you know, perhaps in your own family, as James once was in his.

For worship. Thank God for the eyewitnesses who saw the risen Lord, and for the Lord who showed himself to them. He did not hide in a corner. He stood on a hillside before five hundred, he sat at table with his brother, he let doubting Thomas touch his wounds. And he has written their testimony down for us, so that we who have not seen may believe and have life in his name (John 20:31). Blessed is the Lord who changes the hardest hearts, even a brother’s, by showing himself alive.
verseByVerse.note: Many of the five hundred could still be questioned when Paul wrote. James is the Lord’s brother, who had not believed during Jesus’ ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.

Last of all. Paul was the last person to whom the risen Christ appeared in this way. The resurrection appearances ended with him.

As to one untimely born, he appeared also to me. The word translated untimely born (ektrōma) is blunt in Greek: it describes an abnormal birth, a miscarriage or stillbirth, or a premature birth, a birth that came violently and out of season. It may have been a name his opponents used for him, the runt, the one who arrived wrong, and if so, he has picked it up and put it in his own creed. Paul does that repeatedly. He takes the insult and keeps it, because it fits. The Twelve had three years of walking beside Jesus, being taught, being corrected, being prepared. Paul had none of it. He was on a road with warrants in his bag, travelling to arrest people, and the risen Christ intercepted him mid-journey (Acts 9:3–6). His sudden, violent conversion on the Damascus road came outside the normal time of the appearances. He was not raised into apostleship; he was seized into it.

For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle. True humility, and there is no performance in it. Paul never forgot what he had been. Later he will call himself less than the least of all the saints (Ephesians 3:8) and, later still, the foremost of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15), and the striking thing is the direction of travel. The longer he walked with Christ, the smaller his estimate of himself became. That is the normal arithmetic of grace, and it runs the opposite way from the arithmetic of religion.

Because I persecuted the church of God. The persecution he names is not left in the abstract. He had hunted, imprisoned and helped kill believers (Acts 8:3; 22:4; 26:10–11; Galatians 1:13). Luke tells us what it looked like: witnesses laying their garments at his feet while a man was stoned to death (Acts 7:58); Saul ravaging the church, entering house after house, dragging off men and women and committing them to prison (Acts 8:3); still breathing threats and murder as he set out for Damascus (Acts 9:1). There were widows in Jerusalem who knew his name.

Humble, but not self-cancelling. Notice what he never does, though. He does not say he is not an apostle. He never trades his commission for the comfort of self-abasement, because the commission was not his to resign; it was given. A Christian can hold two things at once here: an honest low estimate of himself, and a settled certainty about what God has said about him. Losing either produces a distortion, arrogance on one side, false humility on the other, and both of them are finally about the same subject.

A hard fact for the sceptic. There is evidence in this verse as well as autobiography. Paul’s own conversion is one of the harder facts for a sceptic to place. Here is a trained, motivated, well-connected opponent, actively destroying the movement, with everything to gain by continuing, and he changes sides, loses his standing, and spends thirty years being beaten and imprisoned for the thing he was suppressing. Something happened on that road. He says he knows what it was.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s apostleship was inferior or doubtful. He saw the risen Christ and was commissioned by him. It means he knew he did not deserve it.

Can someone who has done terrible things really be forgiven? Yes, and Paul is the proof. He was complicit in murder and had violently persecuted Christ’s people, and Christ not only forgave him but made him an apostle. He says Christ did it precisely so that he might be an example to those who were to believe (1 Timothy 1:16). There is no sin so dark that Christ’s blood cannot wash it, for those who turn to him. Forgiveness does not erase every earthly consequence, and it does not make the past unimportant; Paul never forgot it. But it removes the guilt before God entirely. If you are carrying a past you cannot bear to look at, bring it to the One who met Saul on the road.

In a sentence. and last of all he was seen by Paul too, as by someone born at the wrong time. For Paul is the least of the apostles and does not even deserve to be called an apostle, because he persecuted the church of God.

On a Tuesday. Remember what you were before Christ found you. It will keep you humble and grateful. And if there is someone you have written off as too far gone, pray for him today. Saul was too far gone.

For worship. Whatever else grace is, it is not a general kindliness. It is specific enough to walk out onto a road and stop a man who is on his way to arrest more of the family. The risen Lord could have struck him dead. Instead he called him by name: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? And the persecutor became the preacher, and the man who held the coats at Stephen’s stoning wrote nearly half the books of the New Testament. The grace of our Lord overflowed for him (1 Timothy 1:14), and it overflows still, for the worst of sinners. To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honour and glory forever and ever.
verseByVerse.note: “Untimely born” describes an abnormal birth — Paul’s sudden, late calling.

verseByVerse.quote: But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.

But by the grace of God I am what I am. One of the great sentences of the Bible, and one of the most compressed in Paul, and it holds together two things that people are forever pulling apart. Everything Paul is, apostle, Christian, forgiven sinner, is God’s free gift. Nothing about him is self-made: not the apostleship, not the conversion, not the endurance, and not the letters. Everything traces back to an unearned kindness that intercepted him when he was going the other way.

And his grace toward me was not in vain. In vain (kenē) is empty. Grace produced results in Paul. Grace is never inert; where it truly lands, it does something.

On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them. Paul laboured more than the other apostles. Which sounds, on the face of it, like the boast he has just disowned, until the last clause takes it back without cancelling it. Grace does not make people lazy; it makes them work (Philippians 2:12–13).

Though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me. Even his hard work was grace at work in him. Do not resolve that tension by choosing a side; Paul refuses to. Grace is not an alternative to effort. Grace is what produces the effort. The man worked himself to exhaustion, and the working was itself the gift. It is the same grammar as work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13), and it is the answer to two opposite mistakes that Christians make with equal enthusiasm.

Two mistakes about grace. The first is the one that hears grace and concludes that effort is unspiritual: that a Christian should wait to be moved, that trying hard is a form of unbelief, that the disciplined believer is really relying on himself. Paul was the most exhausted man in the New Testament and he did not think so. The second is the one that hears work and quietly begins keeping score: that measures itself against other Christians, is pleased with its own diligence, and would be offended to be told that all of it was a gift. Paul had a genuine claim to that comparison and he made it in the same breath as its cancellation.

Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed. Verse 11 puts the whole apostolic company back on one footing. All the apostles preach the same gospel of the resurrection, and the Corinthians believed it. After all that autobiography, it does not matter which of them said it. The Corinthians had been dividing over exactly this, Paul, Apollos, Cephas (1:12), and here is the man himself waving the question away. The messenger is not the point. What was preached is the point, and it was the same from all of them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace makes human effort unnecessary. It means our effort is the fruit of grace, not the cause of it.

How do I work hard without trusting my work? Work as a son, not as a hired hand. A hired hand works to earn his wages; a son works because he already belongs to the family and loves his father. Begin each task by remembering that you are already accepted in Christ, so that nothing rides on your success for your standing with God. Then pour yourself into the work, asking for his strength. When it goes well, thank him; it was his grace. When it fails, confess any sin and rest; your acceptance never depended on it. That is how a Christian can be both tireless and at peace.

In a sentence. But by God’s grace Paul is what he is, and that grace was not wasted on him. He worked harder than all the others, yet not he, but the grace of God with him. So whether it was he or they, this is what we preach, and this is what you believed.

On a Tuesday. Say it today: by the grace of God I am what I am. Then work hard, by his grace. Take the task you have been putting off and do it this week, asking God for strength at the start and thanking him at the end.

For worship. Grace found a persecutor and made him a preacher. Grace found us dead and made us alive. Every good thing in any Christian, every prayer, every kindness, every hour of faithful work, is the grace of God that is with him. And the source of it all is the Son of God, who was full of grace and truth, and from whose fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16). Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to your name give glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Christ Has Not Been Raised
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the message is that Christ has been raised, how can some of them say there is no resurrection of the dead? If there is none, Christ has not been raised either; and if Christ has not been raised, the apostles’ preaching is useless and so is their faith. The apostles would be found to be false witnesses about God, since they testified that he raised Christ, which he did not do if the dead are not raised. If Christ has not been raised, their faith is futile and they are still in their sins, and those who have died believing in Christ are lost. If their hope in Christ is only for this life, they are more to be pitied than anyone.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Resurrection as the Confirmation of the Atonement

Paul’s logic in v. 17 — “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins” — grounds the significance of the resurrection in its relationship to the atonement. The death of Christ atones; the resurrection of Christ confirms and declares the atonement accepted. This is why Romans 4:25 says Christ “was raised for our justification”: the resurrection is the Father’s “yes” to the Son’s atoning sacrifice. Without the resurrection, Good Friday is a tragedy; with the resurrection, Good Friday is the pivot of history.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthian denial of bodily resurrection was probably influenced by Platonic body-soul dualism: if the soul is what matters, and it survives death, why would God re-attach it to a body? Paul’s argument is that this misunderstands both what salvation means (the redemption of the whole person, body and soul) and what happened to Christ (his body was raised, not merely his spirit). Now: The contemporary version of the Corinthian position often appears in Christian thinking that treats the soul’s going to heaven as the whole story and the resurrection as an afterthought. Paul’s insistence is that the resurrection body is the destination, and the intermediate state (soul in God’s presence before the resurrection) is the waiting room.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.

Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead? At last the actual problem, and the inconsistency in it. Some in Corinth were denying the resurrection of the dead: not, apparently, the resurrection of Jesus, which they seem to have accepted, but the idea that the rest of us will be raised bodily.

Why it felt reasonable to them. It was not stupidity. Educated Greeks had a settled view of the body, and it was low. The soul was the real self; the body was its container and, for many, its prison. There was a well-worn play on words for it, sōma sēma: the body is a tomb. On that view, death is not the enemy but the release: the soul finally gets out. Immortality of the soul, yes, gladly. But God putting you back into a body? That is not salvation; that is being re-arrested. So the Corinthian denial was not an attack on Christianity as they understood it. It was an attempt to keep the parts of it they liked and file the rest under the crude expectations of Jewish converts.

But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised. Paul’s reply is to show that the thing they wanted to keep cannot survive the thing they wanted to drop. The reasoning is exact. Resurrection of the dead is the category. Christ’s resurrection is an instance of it. If the category is impossible in principle, no instance of it happened, including that one. You cannot say such things do not occur, except once. Christ’s resurrection and ours stand or fall together.

And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain. In vain (kenos) means empty: hollow, with nothing inside. Not mistaken in a detail; containing nothing at all. An empty sermon and an empty faith, because faith is only ever as good as the thing it is resting on, and if the thing is not there the sincerity of the resting changes nothing. Christianity is not a set of moral teachings that work whether or not they are true. It rests on a historical event. If Christ is not raised, there is nothing left.

The easier letter Paul did not write. It is worth noticing what Paul does not do here, since it is what most of us would do. He does not tell the doubters that their faith can survive without the doctrine. He does not offer them a version of Christianity that keeps the ethics, the community and the comfort and quietly drops the miracle. There was an easier letter available to him and he did not write it. That is a courtesy to the reader, though it does not always feel like one. A faith that can be adjusted to fit whatever a generation finds credible has no power to contradict that generation, and therefore nothing to offer it. Christianity does not claim that believing is good for you. It stakes everything on an event, and it says so out loud, and it offers to be checked.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection is a matter of opinion. Paul treats it as fact, testable by witnesses.

Is it wrong to have doubts about the resurrection? Doubt is not the same as unbelief. Thomas doubted, and Jesus came to him and showed him his hands (John 20:27). If you have questions, bring them into the light: read the accounts in the Gospels, read a careful book on the evidence, talk to your pastor, and pray, Lord, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24). Paul’s own method is to invite inquiry, not to forbid it. The resurrection has been examined by sceptics for two thousand years and has not been explained away. What would be wrong is to settle into doubt as a comfortable place, or to treat the resurrection as optional. It is the centre.

In a sentence. If we preach that Christ was raised from the dead, how can some of you say that the dead are not raised? If there is no resurrection of the dead, then Christ has not been raised either. And if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is empty and so is your faith.

On a Tuesday. Your faith is not a feeling or a philosophy. It rests on a fact: Christ is risen. Stand on that today. When a doubt comes, do not ask first how you feel; ask what happened in Jerusalem on the third day.

For worship. Our hope is not a theory about the soul. It is a man who was dead and is alive forevermore, and holds the keys of Death and Hades (Revelation 1:18). The God who raised him is the God who gives life to the dead and calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17). He did not ask us to believe a comfortable idea. He did a thing in history, in a garden outside a city wall, and he has never undone it. Christ is risen, and our preaching is not empty, and our faith is not in vain.

verseByVerse.quote: We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.

We are even found to be misrepresenting God. Paul follows the logic down and it gets worse at every step. Literally, we are found to be false witnesses of God. If there was no resurrection, then the apostles have not merely been mistaken. They have been going round the Mediterranean telling people that God did something he did not do: putting words in his mouth, attaching his name to a fiction. They are liars, and liars about God.

Because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised. The apostles’ testimony is either true or a lie. No middle ground. Notice that Paul takes that possibility seriously enough to name it. He does not say the gospel is worth believing regardless. He says: if this did not happen, we are liars about the God we claim to serve. People do not usually die for what they know to be a lie, and the apostles suffered and died for this testimony.

For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised. Repeated for emphasis.

And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile. Futile (mataia) is useless, without result.

And you are still in your sins. Then he arrives at the worst consequence, and it is not the one most people would have guessed. Why should that follow? He died, after all. If the death is what pays for sin, why does the rising matter to the accounting? Because a death, by itself, tells you nothing about whether it worked. Two men were crucified beside him and their deaths paid for nobody. What the cross needed was a verdict: some public act by which the Father declared that the sacrifice had been received and the debt cleared. That is what the resurrection is. Paul says it plainly elsewhere: Jesus was delivered up for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25). Without it, there is no proof that sin has been dealt with. You would still be guilty.

The receipt. Think of it as a receipt. A man may pay an enormous debt and the payment does the work; but until the paper comes back stamped, the debtor has no way of knowing whether it went through. The empty tomb is the stamp. On Friday the price was paid. On Sunday the Father put it in writing, in a form that could be walked into and looked at.

A chapter about assurance. Which turns this into a chapter about assurance and not only about the afterlife. The Christian troubled about whether his sins are really forgiven is being pointed, by this verse, away from his own feelings and toward a garden outside Jerusalem. The question is not whether you feel forgiven. It is whether the tomb is empty. If it is, the matter is settled, and it was settled without consulting you. And notice how carefully Paul distinguishes two states that people confuse. He does not say that without the resurrection a Christian would feel unforgiven. He says you are still in your sins: a statement about the actual position, not the impression of it. Which cuts both ways, and the second way is the comfort. If the objective fact governs when the news is bad, it governs when the news is good. The believer who feels nothing on a grey Tuesday is not less forgiven than he was on the day he first wept over his sin. The tomb did not become less empty overnight.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the cross alone has no significance. It means the cross and resurrection belong together; the resurrection shows the cross worked.

What if I still feel guilty after I have confessed? Feelings of guilt can linger long after God has forgiven, through habit, through a tender conscience, through the accuser’s whispers, or through consequences that remain. Do not measure your forgiveness by your feelings. Measure it by Christ: he was raised, so the payment was accepted. If there is something still to put right with another person, put it right. Then tell your conscience what God has said: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). Faithful, because he promised; just, because Christ has paid. The feelings will often follow the truth in time.

In a sentence. More than that, we would be shown to be false witnesses about God, for we have testified that God raised Christ, which he did not do if the dead are not raised. If the dead are not raised, Christ was not raised either; and if Christ has not been raised, your faith is worthless and you are still guilty of your sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there a sin you keep confessing as though it had never been forgiven? Confess it once more, plainly, and then thank God aloud that Christ is raised and the debt is paid. Refuse to carry it out of the room.

For worship. Because Christ is raised, you are not in your sins. The Father has spoken his verdict over the cross, and it cannot be reversed: it is God who justifies; who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died, more than that, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who indeed is interceding for us (Romans 8:33–34). The stone was rolled away so that we could see the grave clothes lying there. Rejoice in your forgiveness today; it was sealed on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.

Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished. The argument stops being abstract. There were graves in Corinth with Christians in them: members of that congregation who had died in the few years since the church began, and whose families were still in the room when this letter was read out. Fallen asleep is the New Testament’s habitual word for the death of a believer, and it is not a euphemism designed to avoid the subject.
