It says something: that this condition is temporary and that there will be a waking. But Paul now removes that, for the sake of the argument, and states the alternative without softening it. If there is no resurrection, believers who have died are simply gone. No reunion, no future. Not asleep: finished. Every Christian funeral would be a lie. That is what the clever position in Corinth actually cost, and Paul makes them look at it. A doctrine can be discussed as an idea in a room full of healthy people. Take it to a graveside and you find out what it is.

A word on asleep. It is often misread. It describes how death looks from this side: the body lies down and will be woken. It does not mean the person is unconscious until the resurrection. Paul could say that to die is to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23), to be away from the body and at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Jesus promised the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43). The believer who dies is with Christ, consciously, now. What waits for the last day is the body.

If in Christ we have hope in this life only. If Christianity offers only benefits for this life: meaning, morals, community.

We are of all people most to be pitied. Not we are still better off. Not at least the ethics are good and the community is warm. Paul says that if this life is all there is, the Christian has made the worst bargain of anyone alive, and deserves not respect but pity. He had grounds for saying so. He had given up his standing, his safety, his prospects and his comfort; he would shortly list the beatings, the shipwrecks, the hunger and the sleepless nights (2 Corinthians 11:23–28). If there is no resurrection, that is not nobility. It is a man who threw his one life away on a rumour. Christians give up pleasures, face persecution, and stake everything on a future life. Paul does not accept that Christianity is worth it merely as a helpful way of life. It is true, or it is pitiable.

A comfortable Christianity indicted. The verse quietly indicts a kind of Christianity that is very common and very comfortable: the sort that values the faith for what it does now. It steadies a family, gives a shape to the week, provides friends and a moral framework and a sense of meaning. All of that is real, and Paul’s point is that a religion which delivers those things and nothing else is a pitiable arrangement, whatever its members say about it. This faith is not primarily a way to live. It is a claim that a dead man is alive, and everything else follows from that or falls with it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christianity has no benefits in this life. It does. But they are not the main point.

Does this mean the Christian life is miserable now? No. Paul is not saying believers are wretched in this life; he wrote elsewhere of joy, peace and contentment in all circumstances (Philippians 4:11–13). He is saying that the sacrifices of the Christian life only make sense if Christ is raised. The joy is real, but much of it is the joy of hope: the gladness of people who know where they are going. Take the destination away and the road becomes foolish. Keep it, and even suffering can be borne with joy, because it is working for us an eternal weight of glory (2 Corinthians 4:17).

In a sentence. Then those who have died believing in Christ are lost. If our hope in Christ is only for this life, we deserve more pity than anyone in the world.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one whose hope reaches beyond this life. What would you do differently if you truly believed in the resurrection? Do one thing this week that only makes sense if Christ is risen: give away something you would rather keep, forgive a debt, speak of Christ where it will cost you.

For worship. Our hope does not stop at the grave. Christ has gone through death and come out on the far side, and he has left the door open behind him. Because he lives, we also will live (John 14:19). The believers who have fallen asleep are not lost; they are with him, and they will rise. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Peter 1:3).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the first portion of the harvest of those who have died. Since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. As in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in turn: Christ first, then, at his coming, those who belong to him. Then the end will come, when he hands the kingdom over to God the Father after destroying every rule, authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, and the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Scripture says God has put everything under his feet; this plainly does not include God himself, who put everything under Christ. When all things have been subjected to him, the Son himself will also be subject to the one who put everything under him, so that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Adam/Christ Typology and the Scope of Redemption

The Adam/Christ typology here (cf. Rom 5:12–21) is the cornerstone of Paul’s understanding of both sin and salvation. Adam’s representative headship means that his sin brought death to all who are “in Adam” — which is every human being by natural birth. Christ’s representative headship means that his obedience, death, and resurrection bring life to all who are “in Christ” — which is every believer by the new birth. The scope is parallel but not identical: “in Christ shall all be made alive” refers to all who are in Christ, not to every human being universally. The typology demands that the domain of redemption be at least as real and significant as the domain of death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians who had lost members to death needed to know that those deaths were not permanent losses but sleeps awaiting a harvest. The firstfruits language gave them a specific, liturgically resonant image: the resurrection of Christ is God’s pledge that the full harvest of resurrection is coming. Now: The Christian stands at the graveside of a believer with the same confidence: the firstfruits have already appeared; the rest of the harvest is as certain as the God who made the pledge. The resurrection is not a hope against hope but a certainty grounded in a historical event.

verseByVerse.quote: But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.

But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead. Two words in Greek (nyni de, but now), and they turn the whole chapter. Paul has spent eight verses in a nightmare of his own construction: empty preaching, futile faith, unforgiven sin, dead friends gone for ever, a life thrown away. And then, without argument, he simply steps out of it. Not if, but in fact. The corridor of horrors was hypothetical. He was never in any doubt about the way out. Christ is risen.

The firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The image is agricultural and liturgical at once, and every Jewish reader knew it. On the day after the Sabbath following Passover, a single sheaf of the new barley was cut and brought to the priest and waved before the LORD (Leviticus 23:10–14). One sheaf, in a field still standing. It was not the harvest; it was the promise of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge that the rest would follow. The rest was coming, and the sheaf in the priest’s hands was the proof. Consider the timing of that ceremony, and then consider on which morning Jesus came out of the tomb. The feast of firstfruits fell on the very day Christ rose.

The first of a series. What the image does is change the category of the resurrection completely. It is not a miracle that happened to one exceptional person, a stand-alone wonder, best admired from a distance. It is the first of a series. Nobody waves a sheaf over an empty field. The resurrection of Jesus is God’s public statement that the harvest of the dead has begun, and it therefore says something about every Christian grave that has ever been dug. His resurrection is the first part of the great harvest; ours will follow.

For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead. Death came through Adam’s sin (Genesis 3; Romans 5:12). Resurrection comes through Christ, a man. Christ had to be truly human to undo what a human did.

For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive. Paul’s way of thinking about the human race is one of representation. Two men stand at the head of two humanities, and what each did counts for everyone belonging to him. Adam sinned, and death entered and spread to all who are in him, which is everybody, by birth. Christ obeyed, died and rose, and life comes to all who are in him, which is everybody who belongs to him, united to him by faith, by new birth. They will be made alive in resurrection glory.

Where Christians differ: will everyone be saved? Universalists read all in both halves the same way: as all die in Adam, all humans will be saved in Christ. Verdict: The two alls are defined by in Adam and in Christ. All who are in Adam die; all who are in Christ, those who belong to him (v. 23), will be made alive to glory. Paul is not saying every human will be in Christ. Scripture is clear that some will rise to judgement and eternal punishment (John 5:28–29; Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Paul here speaks only of the resurrection to life.

Whichever man you are joined to. The verse is saying that whichever man you are joined to, his outcome is yours. Nobody is standing on his own. Which is bad news read one way and the best news in the world read the other. You did not choose to be in Adam and you cannot argue your way out of it; the evidence is that you are going to die. But the same principle that ruins you is the principle that saves you, because being in Christ works exactly the same way: not by achievement, but by belonging (Romans 5:17–19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers will not be raised at all. All will rise, some to life, some to judgement (Acts 24:15). This chapter focuses on believers.

How do I know I am in Christ and not only in Adam? You come to be in Christ by faith: by turning from your sin and trusting him as your Saviour and Lord. The Spirit unites you to him, and his death, his righteousness and his resurrection life become yours. If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you are in him; faith is the hand, and Christ is the treasure it holds. Look for the fruit as well: a new love for him, a new hatred of sin, a desire for his people and his word. These do not make you his; they show that you are. And if you are not sure, come to him now. He has never turned away anyone who came.

In a sentence. But Christ really has been raised from the dead, the first part of the harvest of those who have died. Since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes through a man too. As everyone joined to Adam dies, so everyone joined to Christ will be made alive.

On a Tuesday. Next time you pass a churchyard, remember the sheaf. The harvest has begun. And if you have a Christian grave to visit, go and stand by it this week and say: firstfruits.

For worship. Christ is the firstfruits. Your resurrection is as certain as his. The first man brought death into the world, and the second man walked into death and broke it open from inside. He is the head of a new humanity, and every one who belongs to him will follow him out of the grave. The harvest is his, the field is his, and not one ear of grain will be lost. Praise him, the firstborn from the dead, that in everything he might be preeminent (Colossians 1:18).
verseByVerse.note: The firstfruits were the first sheaf of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the whole harvest to come — at the time of the Passover festival.

verseByVerse.quote: But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ. Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.

But each in his own order. Order (tagma) is a military word: a rank, a division, a company of soldiers moving in sequence. Paul is not being vague about the future; he is saying it has a shape and the shape has stages.

Christ the firstfruits. The first has happened. Christ’s resurrection is already accomplished, a fixed point in history behind us rather than in front of us.

Then at his coming those who belong to Christ. The second is still to come. At his coming (parousia, arrival, the word for a king’s visit to a city), all believers will be raised. And notice the definition of the group. Not those who achieved something, or understood something, or belonged to the right party in Corinth. Those who belong to Christ: the sole qualification is ownership, and it runs the right way round. They are his. This happens at one event, his return.

Then comes the end. The end (to telos) is the goal, the consummation of history.

When he delivers the kingdom to God the Father. A picture that ought to be better known than it is. Christ, having completed his work as Mediator, hands the kingdom to the Father. The whole long campaign, the incarnation, the cross, the empty tomb, the long centuries of the church, the resurrection of the dead, is a mission with a completion, and it ends with the Son handing the finished work to his Father. It is the language of a steward handing back an estate, or of a commander reporting to the one who sent him. And what is handed over is not a ruin salvaged from a fire. It is a kingdom: the whole thing, complete, every enemy dealt with and every subject alive.

After destroying every rule and every authority and power. Every power opposed to God: spiritual forces of evil, human rebellion, and death itself. Paul uses words like these elsewhere for more than parliaments and armies; they cover the spiritual forces behind the visible ones, the powers he says the Christian actually wrestles with (Ephesians 6:12). Every one of them goes. Not reformed, not negotiated with, not accommodated. Abolished.

A steadiness for anyone reading the news. The powers that presently look permanent, the regimes, the ideologies, the interests that seem able to outlast any opposition, and the darker things that stand behind them, are on a list, and the list has a completion date. Nothing on it is going to survive the arrival of the King, and none of it will require a second campaign (Colossians 2:15; Revelation 11:15).

Where Christians differ: the millennium. Premillennialists see a gap between his coming (v. 23) and the end (v. 24), filled by a thousand-year earthly reign of Christ. Verdict: The most natural reading is that the end follows Christ’s coming directly. Christ is reigning now (v. 25), from heaven, and will reign until his return, when the dead are raised and death is destroyed. This is the amillennial view: the millennium of Revelation 20 describes Christ’s present reign during the church age. There is one return of Christ, visible and public, not a secret rapture followed by a later coming.

The case on both sides. Premillennial Christians, many of them careful students of Scripture, read the word then as leaving room for an interval: Christ returns, raises his people, and reigns on earth for a thousand years before the end. They point to Revelation 20:4–6, where the saints came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years, and note that Paul’s word can mark a gap, since a long time has already passed between Christ’s resurrection and his coming. Amillennial Christians answer that Paul places the resurrection of believers at his coming and then the end, and the next verses say Christ must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet, the last being death (vv. 25–26); and death is defeated at the resurrection itself (vv. 54–55). If death is destroyed at Christ’s coming, there is no room after it for a further age in which death still reigns. That is why the amillennial reading is the more likely: Christ reigns now, and his coming brings the resurrection, the judgement and the end together.

Not a rescue from a write-off. There is a quiet correction here for the way Christians often picture the end. It is not principally a rescue in which a remnant is snatched out of a world written off as a total loss. It is a campaign that finishes, a work that is completed, and a Son with something to present to his Father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s rule ends. He hands the kingdom over in the sense that his mediatorial work is complete, but he reigns forever with the Father: of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1:33; Revelation 11:15).

If Christ is reigning now, why is the world still so evil? Because his reign is a campaign still under way. He has already won the decisive battle at the cross and the empty tomb, and he now rules from the Father’s right hand, gathering his people from every nation by the gospel and restraining evil. But the enemies are not yet all under his feet, and his people still suffer, as he did. The New Testament holds both together: he reigns, and we wait. The evil you see is real, but it is not winning; it is on borrowed time, and its end is already set. Meanwhile his kingdom grows like a mustard seed, quietly, in every place where sinners bow the knee to him.

In a sentence. But each in proper order: Christ, the firstfruits; then, when he comes, those who belong to him. Then the end will come, when he hands over the kingdom to God the Father, having destroyed every ruler, authority and power.

On a Tuesday. Every evil power you see is on borrowed time. Christ will destroy them all. Take courage. When the news frightens you this week, name the thing that frightens you and add four words: until he comes.

For worship. The kingdom is his, and the victory is his, and the end is his. He came once in weakness; he will come again in glory, and every knee will bow. The Son who was sent will come back to his Father bearing the whole redeemed creation in his hands, and he will say, as he said in the upper room, I have accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). The kingdom of the world will become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.

verseByVerse.quote: For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.

For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. From Psalm 110:1, the most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament: the LORD says to my Lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool. Christ is reigning now, at the Father’s right hand (Ephesians 1:20–22; Hebrews 10:12–13). Must (dei): it is God’s plan. His reign is now, not only in the future. The reigning Christ is at this moment putting his enemies under his feet, one after another, and he is working his way toward the grave.

The last enemy to be destroyed is death. Eight words that a great many people need and have never been given. Destroyed (katargeitai) means abolished, rendered powerless. Look at what death is called. Not a doorway. Not a natural transition, not a part of the circle of life, not a friend who comes at the end of a long day. An enemy, and the last one standing, the one still on its feet after everything else has fallen. Christ has already defeated it by his resurrection; at his return it will be abolished entirely (Revelation 20:14; 21:4).

Permission to hate death. That single word is worth more to a grieving Christian than a great deal of what is said at funerals. There is a way of speaking about death in religious circles that tries to make peace with it: that says it is only a change of address, that we should not be sad, that a believer ought to be serene. The Bible does not do this. The Bible calls death an enemy, and it gives the mourner permission to hate it. The Lord himself did. On his way to the tomb of a friend he was about to raise, knowing exactly what would happen, Jesus wept (John 11:35), and the word John uses of him a moment earlier suggests something closer to indignation than sorrow (John 11:33). He was not weeping about the outcome; he knew the outcome. He was standing in front of the thing itself, the enemy in a graveyard, doing to a family he loved what it does to everybody.

What death does. Be concrete about what it does, because vagueness here helps nobody. It takes a person who was in the room and makes the room empty. It ends the conversation in the middle. It takes a hand that has been held for fifty years and makes it cold in an hour. It leaves a chair, a coat, a handwriting, a voice on an old recording that is now unbearable to play. It is not tidy and it is not gentle and it does not care what anyone was in the middle of. So the Christian is not asked to pretend. He is asked to believe that the enemy is on a schedule. The last enemy to be destroyed: not tamed, not made bearable, destroyed, and last, because everything else goes first and this is the one that has to be dealt with at the end.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should not grieve death. Death is an enemy, and Jesus wept at Lazarus’s tomb (John 11:35). But we grieve with hope.

Is it a lack of faith to be afraid of dying? No. Death is an enemy, and it is natural to shrink from it; our Lord himself was in agony in Gethsemane. What faith does is not remove every fear but give it a horizon. For the believer, death has lost its sting (v. 55): it cannot separate you from Christ, and it will not keep you. Many Christians fear the process of dying more than death itself, and that fear can be brought honestly to God in prayer. He has promised to be with you in the valley (Psalm 23:4). Very often those who have feared most find, when the hour comes, that grace is given for it.

In a sentence. For Christ must go on reigning until he has put every enemy under his feet. The last enemy to be abolished is death.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend. Tell God that you hate what death has done, and then tell him that you believe it is on a schedule. If someone near you is grieving, do not hurry them toward serenity; sit with them, and remind them, when the time is right, that death is the last enemy, and it will be destroyed.

For worship. There will come a day on which there is no death anywhere in the universe, and no one will ever again have to be told that someone has died. Christ has gone into death’s own house and taken the keys. He reigns now, at the right hand of the Majesty on high, and every enemy is falling, and death will fall last. He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more (Revelation 21:4). Praise him, the King who must reign, until the last enemy lies under his feet.

parallels.desc: until I make your enemies your footstool

verseByVerse.quote: For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.

For God has put all things in subjection under his feet. The quotation is from Psalm 8:6, and the psalm is not, in the first place, about the Messiah. It is about human beings: what is man that you are mindful of him? And yet God has crowned him with glory and put all things under his feet (Psalm 8:4–6). It is creation’s job description for the human race, given in the garden and abandoned there. Adam was made to rule the world under God and instead handed it over. Paul applies the psalm to Christ, and the logic is the one running through this whole chapter. Christ is the last Adam, the true human being, doing at last what humanity was made for (Hebrews 2:6–9). Psalm 8 has not been wrenched out of context; it has finally found a man it fits.

But when it says all things are put in subjection, it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him. Then Paul stops to make a point so obvious it is almost comic, and yet it needs making: when Scripture says everything is put under him, that plainly does not include the One doing the putting. All things except God the Father, who did the subjecting. The Father is not among the things subdued.

When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him. Here is a sentence that has troubled readers for centuries, because it appears to make the Son permanently lesser. It does not, and the reason is the same one that answered the same question at 11:3. What is described here is not the Son’s nature but the completion of his mission. The Son, as Mediator, will hand his completed work to the Father and remain subject to him. He was sent; he came; he obeyed; he died; he rose; he reigns; he subdues; and when the work is finished he presents it all to the Father and takes his place in the order he has occupied willingly from the beginning. The Son who is the exact imprint of the Father’s nature (Hebrews 1:3) does not become less divine by handing over a completed kingdom. He is doing what he has always done, and it is the same Son who said, in a garden, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42).

That God may be all in all. That is the end of the story, the goal of history: God’s rule complete and unchallenged, filling everything (Ephesians 1:23; Colossians 3:11). And it is worth refusing to leave it as a phrase. It means a universe with nothing left in it that is not filled with God: no corner where he is absent, no life he does not saturate, nothing between him and his people, and nobody anywhere having to go looking for him. Every place where a believer has felt God to be distant will have been abolished, along with distance itself.

Where Christians differ: is the Son inferior to the Father? Arians, ancient and modern, use this verse to argue that the Son is a lesser being. Verdict: The subjection here is of the Son as incarnate Mediator, in his role of redemption, not of the Son in his divine nature. In his divine nature, the Son is equal with the Father, of the same substance (John 1:1; 10:30; Philippians 2:6). In his role as Mediator, he submits to the Father’s will (John 6:38). This is the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity, as summarised in the Nicene Creed and Westminster 2.3 and 8.2.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s kingdom will end, or that he will stop being king.

Will we still see and worship Jesus when God is all in all? Yes, forever. The Son does not disappear into the Father at the end. He remains the God-man, with his risen body, and the Lamb is on the throne in the new Jerusalem (Revelation 22:1, 3). God is all in all precisely in and through Christ: the glory of God is its light, and its lamp is the Lamb (Revelation 21:23). The handing over of the kingdom is not Christ stepping aside; it is the Son presenting his finished work to the Father, so that the whole of creation rings with the praise of Father, Son and Spirit. We will worship the Lamb who was slain for all eternity.

In a sentence. For Scripture says that God has put everything under his feet. When it says everything has been put under him, clearly this does not include God himself, who put everything under Christ. When he has done this, the Son himself will be made subject to the one who put everything under him, so that God may be all in all.

On a Tuesday. History is heading toward one goal: God all in all. Let that goal shape your goals today. Look at what you are planning this week and ask whether it fits a world that is heading toward God being everything; and where you feel God to be far away, remember that distance itself is on the list of things to be abolished.

For worship. The Son came to do the Father’s will, and he loved to do it. He humbled himself to the cross, and the Father highly exalted him. And at the end the Son, who has all things under his feet, will lay them all at his Father’s feet, not because he must but because he delights to, and the Father will be glorified in the Son, and the Spirit will fill all things, and God will be all in all. From him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen (Romans 11:36).

parallels.desc: you have put all things under his feet

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 29–34 — The Logic of Resurrection Living
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Otherwise, Paul asks, what are people doing when they are baptised on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why do it? And why do the apostles face danger every hour? Paul faces death every day; he swears it by his pride in them in Christ Jesus. If, humanly speaking, he fought wild beasts at Ephesus, what did he gain, if the dead are not raised? Then, as people say, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. They must not be misled: bad company corrupts good character. They should come back to their senses and stop sinning, because some of them have no knowledge of God; Paul says this to their shame.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection and the Rational Grounds of Christian Ethics

Paul’s argument here anticipates the famous wager logic: if there is no resurrection, Christian ethics (self-denial, risk, suffering for others) is irrational. The person who lives as if the resurrection were true is either right (and has invested wisely) or wrong (and has lived a meaningful but ultimately futile life). The Epicurean is consistent: if there is no resurrection, maximise pleasure now. Paul’s whole life is a living argument for the resurrection: his willingness to face death daily makes no sense on any other hypothesis.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul’s reference to “fighting with beasts at Ephesus” may be literal (arena animals) or metaphorical (violent opponents); either way it describes the real mortal danger of apostolic ministry. The question is: for what purpose? If the dead are not raised, the purpose has no transcendent ground. Now: Every Christian who chooses a harder path for the sake of the gospel — the missionary in a dangerous field, the pastor who refuses to compromise his convictions, the layperson who sacrifices career advancement for integrity — is making an implicit resurrection bet. Their lives only make sense if the resurrection is true.

verseByVerse.quote: Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Why are we in danger every hour?

Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? Verse 29 is the most obscure sentence in the letter, one of the most puzzling verses in the Bible, and over forty interpretations have been suggested. It is worth being honest about that rather than pretending to a certainty nobody has.

Three readings worth knowing. The plainest sense of the Greek is that some people at Corinth were being baptised as proxies for relatives or friends who had died unbaptised, in the hope that it would do the dead some good. Early writers such as John Chrysostom knew of such practices among heretical groups and condemned them. A second reading takes the small word for as meaning because of: new converts were being baptised because of the dead, moved to faith by the death of a believer whose hope had held to the end, or in order to be reunited with believing loved ones who had died. A third takes it as baptism with one’s own coming death and resurrection in view. Whatever it was, Paul does not approve the practice; he simply uses it to show the inconsistency of those who deny the resurrection.

If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf? Whatever it was, it only made sense if there was a resurrection. What can be said with certainty is how Paul is using it, and that is the part that matters. He is not teaching it. Notice that he does not say you or we but they: he holds the practice at arm’s length, neither endorsing nor attacking it here, and simply points out that whatever it is, it makes no sense at all unless the dead have a future. His argument is that the Corinthians’ own behaviour contradicts their stated theology. That is worth noting as a method, because it is a fair one. People are often better than their opinions, and one honest way to answer a bad idea is to show the person that he does not actually live as though it were true. Nobody grieves as if the dead were nothing. Nobody attends a funeral and behaves like a man who thinks a machine has stopped.

Why are we in danger every hour? Paul turns to his own life. Why would the apostles risk death constantly if there were no resurrection? The second argument runs to the end of verse 32. It is the same question turned on himself: what am I doing, if there is nothing after this?

Where Christians differ: baptism for the dead. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints practises proxy baptism for the dead, based on this verse. Verdict: Paul mentions the practice without endorsing it, and notice he says people, not we. Nowhere else does Scripture teach it. The New Testament is clear that each person must believe for themselves, and that after death comes judgement, with no second chance (Hebrews 9:27; Luke 16:26). Baptism is for those who personally repent and believe.

Holding a passage loosely. Two things are worth carrying away from a verse this obscure. The first is that it is possible to hold a passage loosely without holding the Bible loosely. Not every sentence in Scripture yields its meaning easily, and saying so is honesty rather than doubt. The doctrine of the resurrection does not rest on verse 29; verse 29 is a supporting argument, and Paul’s own case runs perfectly well without our knowing what the practice was. The second is a caution about the opposite error, which is real and does damage. A whole teaching has been built by one movement on this single obscure verse, against the plain sense of the rest of Scripture, which nowhere else suggests that anything can be done for the dead by the living. A doctrine erected on one difficult sentence, with nothing else in the Bible to support it, is a building on a very narrow footing.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an uncertain verse should be used to build a doctrine. Clear passages must interpret unclear ones.

Can I do anything for a loved one who died without Christ? Nothing can change a person’s state after death; Scripture gives no second chance and no way for the living to alter it (Hebrews 9:27). That is a hard truth, and it is right to grieve it honestly. But remember two things. You do not know what passed between that person and God in their last hours, and the thief on the cross shows how late grace can come. And the Judge of all the earth will do what is just (Genesis 18:25). Leave them with him. What you can do is pray for the living, and speak of Christ to those who are still within reach of the gospel.

In a sentence. Otherwise, what will those who are baptised for the dead do? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptised for them? And why do we put ourselves in danger every hour?

On a Tuesday. Notice this week one place where you live better than the opinions of the people around you, and one place where they live better than theirs. Then speak to one unbelieving friend about the hope of the resurrection while he can still hear it.

For worship. Thank God that salvation comes through personal faith in Christ, and that your loved ones who died in Christ will rise. No ritual of ours can open the gate of heaven; the gate was opened once, by the Son of God, when he passed through death and came out alive. Now is the favourable time, now is the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6:2), and the God who saves is still calling the living to himself. Blessed be the One who holds the keys of death, and who has never lost one whom the Father gave him.
verseByVerse.note: The meaning of “baptized on behalf of the dead” is disputed; most likely some Corinthians were being baptized as proxies for the dead. Paul mentions the practice without approving it, only to show that it assumes a resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”

I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day! A solemn oath. I die every day is not first a devotional phrase about self-denial. Paul is describing his working conditions. He faced the threat of death daily, and daily gave up his life for Christ (2 Corinthians 4:10–11; 11:23–27). He lived where a violent end was a daily possibility, and he is saying that a man in that position needs a reason. He swears to it, oddly, by my pride in you: he stakes the truthfulness of the claim on the one thing this difficult congregation would recognise as valuable, that he is proud of them. Even in the middle of an argument he tells them that.

What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition, since a Roman citizen was unlikely to be thrown to animals, and Paul does not mention it in his list of sufferings (2 Corinthians 11:23–27). Perhaps it refers to the riot of Acts 19 (Acts 19:23–41), or to opponents who acted like wild animals. Either way the sense is the same: he had been in a place where he did not expect to come out alive. What do I gain? That is the honest question, and it deserves an honest answer. Nothing. If the dead are not raised, Paul has purchased absolutely nothing with his life, and he says so without flinching.

If the dead are not raised, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die. The quotation is from Isaiah 22:13, and it is not a joke. Isaiah described a city under siege that ought to have been weeping and repenting, and instead threw a party: killing the oxen, drinking the wine, saying let us eat and drink. It is the exact philosophy that the ancient world had already worked out and that ours has rediscovered: if this is all there is, get what you can before the lights go out. This was the creed of the Epicureans and of many ordinary people. And Paul does not sneer at it. That is the striking thing. He treats it as the rational position for a man with no resurrection. If death is the end, then a life of self-denial for other people’s benefit is not admirable, it is merely a waste, and the person eating and drinking has understood the situation better than the martyr has.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians live morally only for reward. It means the resurrection changes everything about how we live.

Is it selfish to serve God for the sake of heaven? Not if heaven is God himself. The reward the Bible holds out is not a payment unrelated to the work, like money for a chore; it is the natural end of loving God: being with him, seeing his face, enjoying him forever. A man who marries for love is not mercenary because he looks forward to his wedding day. Jesus himself endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (Hebrews 12:2). To want Christ, and to be willing to lose everything else to gain him, is not selfishness. It is the very thing we were made for.

In a sentence. Paul faces death every day, brothers and sisters; he swears it by the pride he takes in you in Christ Jesus our Lord. If he fought wild beasts at Ephesus for merely human reasons, what has he gained? If the dead are not raised, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.

On a Tuesday. Here is a sharp question, and no one can answer it for someone else. If you knew for certain there was nothing after death, what in your life would you change? Whatever comes to mind is the part of your life currently being funded by the resurrection. And if nothing comes to mind, that is worth sitting with too. Because of the resurrection, you can give your life away. It is not wasted.

For worship. The Lord Jesus did not eat and drink because tomorrow he would die. He took bread and a cup, and gave them away, because tomorrow he would die for us. He laid down his life, and he took it up again, and because he lives, every life laid down for him is gathered up and kept. Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it (Matthew 16:25). Blessed be the Lord who has made self-denial wise and martyrdom victorious.
verseByVerse.note: Fighting with beasts at Ephesus is probably a picture of fierce human opposition; a Roman citizen could not normally be sent to the arena.

parallels.desc: let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.” Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.

Do not be deceived. Some in Corinth were being misled by those who denied the resurrection.

Bad company ruins good morals. The proverb is a line from the Greek poet Menander’s comedy Thais, and it was probably a common saying by Paul’s day, the sort of line everybody knew without knowing where it came from. Paul is not shy about using it. He does the same at Athens with the poets (Acts 17:28) and in Titus with a Cretan (Titus 1:12). Truth is truth wherever it turns up, and an apostle is free to borrow a good sentence from a playwright. But notice what the quotation is doing in an argument about the resurrection. It is a sentence about company, and that tells us something Paul assumes and we often do not: that people do not usually reason their way into a false belief. They drift into it, in company, over time. Those who deny the resurrection influence others toward sinful living.

How faith is usually lost. That is worth taking seriously, because most Christians who abandon what they believed did not do it in a library. It happened gradually, through friendship, through the desire to be thought reasonable by people they admired, through a slow adjustment of what could comfortably be said aloud. Nobody sits down and decides to stop believing in the resurrection. He starts spending time where it is quietly assumed to be embarrassing, and after two years he finds he has moved. Paul is not commanding a retreat from the world; he has already ruled that out in this letter (5:10). He is pointing at the particular company that is doing this particular damage, the confident deniers inside the church, and telling the congregation to stop finding them impressive.

Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right. Wake up (eknēphō) is what you say to a man sleeping it off: sober up, come round. Wrong beliefs about the future had made them spiritually drunk. It is an extraordinary thing to say to a congregation that thought itself the most spiritually advanced in Greece. He does not tell them they are mistaken. He tells them they are not properly conscious.

And do not go on sinning. Wrong doctrine leads to wrong living. Doctrine and ethics belong together.

For some have no knowledge of God. No knowledge (agnōsia) is ignorance, and it is ironic for a church that prided itself on knowledge. That is the diagnosis under the error. Behind the denial of the resurrection is not a difficulty with biology but an inadequate view of God: a God not big enough to raise the dead, which is to say not the God who made the world out of nothing. To deny the resurrection is to know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God (Matthew 22:29).

I say this to your shame. They should be ashamed. It is the second time in the letter Paul has used that phrase (6:5). A church full of knowledge, and some of its members do not know God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should avoid all contact with unbelievers. It means they should not be influenced by false teaching and bad examples.

How do I keep unbelieving friends without being pulled away? Be the influence rather than the influenced. Jesus ate with sinners, but he set the direction of the conversation. Keep your roots deep: be in the word daily, be in church weekly, and have Christian friends close enough to notice if you drift. Be honest about your faith early in a friendship, so that it is not something you have to hide. Watch for the warning signs: finding your convictions embarrassing, laughing at what grieves God, wanting their approval more than Christ’s. And if a particular friendship is steadily dragging you into sin, love may require distance. The goal is to win them, not to become them.

In a sentence. Do not be misled: bad company corrupts good character. Come back to your senses as you should, and stop sinning; for some of you are ignorant of God, and Paul says this to shame you.

On a Tuesday. Ask God to show you any influences in your life that are pulling you away from him: friends, feeds, books, shows. Name one, and decide this week what to do about it. And name one Christian friend who sharpens you, and spend time with him.

For worship. To know God is to know the One who raises the dead. He spoke, and the world came out of nothing; he breathed, and Adam stood up out of the dust; he called, and Lazarus walked out of the tomb. And he gave his Son to be the friend of sinners, the company that does not ruin but redeems. Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, but delights in the law of the LORD (Psalm 1:1–2), and more blessed still the God who calls us his friends.
verseByVerse.note: “Bad company ruins good morals” is a line from the Greek poet Menander.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Someone will ask how the dead are raised and what kind of body they will have. Paul calls that a foolish question: a seed does not come to life unless it dies, and what is sown is not the plant that will grow but a bare grain, of wheat or something else. God gives it the body he has chosen, and each kind of seed its own body. Not all flesh is alike: people, animals, birds and fish differ. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies with different splendour, and even sun, moon and stars differ in glory. So it will be with the resurrection. The body is sown perishable and raised imperishable, sown in dishonour and raised in glory, sown in weakness and raised in power, sown a natural body and raised a spiritual body. Scripture says the first man, Adam, became a living being; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. The natural came first, then the spiritual. The first man was made of earth’s dust; the second man is from heaven. Those of the earth are like the earthly man, and those of heaven are like the heavenly man. Just as believers have borne the image of the earthly man, they will bear the image of the heavenly one.
verseByVerse.theology:
Continuity and Transformation in the Resurrection Body

The Reformed tradition has insisted, against all forms of Gnosticism and spiritual idealism, on the bodily nature of the resurrection. The creeds confess “the resurrection of the body” — not the survival of the soul. Paul’s seed analogy establishes both poles: continuity (the seed and the plant are the same organism in different stages) and transformation (the glory of the plant exceeds anything visible in the seed). The specific body that is buried — your body, with its particular history, its particular wounds, its particular scars — is the body that will be raised. This is why the bodily resurrection of Christ is the paradigm: the same body that was crucified was raised — still bearing the wounds (John 20:27), yet transformed into resurrection glory.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Greek objection to bodily resurrection was that the body is the problem, not the solution; the soul’s liberation from the body is the goal, not its resurrection. Paul refuses this framing entirely: the body is God’s creation, declared good, destined for resurrection. The problem is not embodiment but mortality, not physicality but corruption. The resurrection is the redemption of the body, not its abolition. Now: Every theology that treats the goal of salvation as the soul going to heaven (leaving the body behind) has the Corinthian problem. The goal is the new creation, the resurrection body, the renewed earth — the full embodied flourishing of redeemed humanity in the presence of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?” You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

But someone will ask, how are the dead raised? Now the real objection, and Paul lets the sceptic put it in his own words, which is fair of him. It is not a stupid question. Bodies decay, are eaten by worms, scattered, burned. Bodies are lost at sea and eaten by animals and scattered so completely that not a molecule stays in place. The atoms that make up a man are borrowed and returned. Where exactly is the body that is going to be raised?

With what kind of body do they come? And what would such a body be like? The same decaying body? That sounded absurd to Greeks.

You foolish person! Foolish (aphrōn) means without sense. It is sharper in English than in Greek, and Paul is not calling him stupid for asking. The word describes someone reasoning without taking into account what he already knows: a man who has the answer in his own back garden and has not looked at it. The objection shows a failure to think, and to know God’s power.

What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. Here is the answer: the analogy of a seed. Every farmer in the ancient world, and every gardener since, has watched this happen and never found it strange. You take a hard dry seed and you bury it in the ground. That is a funeral. It goes into the dark, it is covered over, and if you dug it up a fortnight later you would find it soft and rotting and finished. And out of that comes a green shoot, and then a stalk taller than the seed ever was, carrying thirty seeds of its own. The objection assumes that burial is the end of the story. The seed says otherwise, and it says it in every field the objector has ever walked past. Death is not the obstacle to the new life; in the only process any of us can actually observe, death is the doorway to it. The thing that looks like destruction is the mechanism. Burial is sowing.

A grain of wheat. Jesus said exactly this about himself, days before it happened: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). He was talking about his own burial, and about a harvest that would include the man asking this question.

Evidence from a seed. There is something worth noticing in Paul’s choice of evidence. He could have answered a question about the resurrection body from revelation; he had been caught up into the third heaven and had heard things he was not permitted to repeat (2 Corinthians 12:2–4). He answers it from a seed. God has arranged the world so that the hardest thing a person has to believe is acted out every spring in front of him, in mud, by vegetables. That is not an accident. The resurrection is not an alien intrusion into a universe that runs on other principles; it is a pattern written into the universe since the beginning, applied at last to the thing that matters most.

What it does not mean. It does not mean resurrection is a natural process. God does it (v. 38). The seed is an illustration.

Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated? It does not matter to God’s power; he will raise the cremated as surely as the buried, the lost at sea as surely as those in the churchyard. Many Christians, following the pattern of Scripture and of Christ’s own burial, prefer burial, because it pictures the sowing of a seed and honours the body as something God will raise. Others choose cremation for good reasons, and they do no wrong. What matters is that the body is treated with respect, and that the funeral speaks plainly of the hope of the resurrection.

In a sentence. But someone will ask how the dead are raised, and what sort of body they will have. How foolish! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.

On a Tuesday. When you bury a believer, you are sowing a seed. Grieve, but with hope of the harvest. Next time you plant something, or see a field in spring, stop for a moment and thank God for the sermon he preaches in the soil.

For worship. The God of the harvest is the God of the resurrection. Every spring he preaches it in the fields, and on one spring morning in Jerusalem he did it in a garden. The grain of wheat fell into the earth and died, and it has borne much fruit: a harvest from every nation. Thank God for the Seed that was buried, and for the harvest he will bring home, sheaf by sheaf, in the morning of the world.

verseByVerse.quote: And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.

And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain. Paul presses the picture, and the two halves of it answer the two halves of the objection. First: what you sow is not the body that is to be. A seed looks nothing like the plant. Nobody who had never seen it happen would predict a wheat stalk from a wheat grain. Hold a seed in your hand: it is small, brown, dry, hard, and entirely unremarkable. There is nothing in its appearance that suggests a green stem, a head of grain, a field moving in the wind. If you had only ever seen the seed, you would consider the plant a wild story. So the question with what kind of body do they come? has an answer, and part of the answer is: not one you could work out from looking at what goes into the ground. The resurrection body is not an improved corpse. It stands in the same relation to the buried body as harvest stands to seed-time: continuity and transformation, the same life in a different form.

But God gives it a body as he has chosen. God is the one who gives the new body. Resurrection is his power at work. And that is where the question of molecules and dust and scattered atoms is quietly settled. The wheat plant is not built only out of the material of the seed; the seed is spent, and the plant is made of soil and rain and air. Continuity is not a matter of the same particles being reassembled. It is a matter of the same God attending to the same person. Which means that a Christian may lay to rest a body ruined by illness, or burned, or lost at sea, or long since gone to dust in a churchyard whose stones are unreadable, and none of it is an obstacle of any kind. The God who is going to do this made the original body out of the ground in the first place and has never been short of material. He is not searching for anything. He knows exactly where every one of his people is.

And to each kind of seed its own body. Each seed becomes its own kind of plant: wheat becomes wheat. So each person will be raised as themselves, recognisably the same person, but transformed. This is a promise of particularity. Not one generic glorified shape issued to everybody. Its own. That answers a fear people do not usually put into words: that whatever is raised will not really be me, that eternity means being absorbed into something general, a soul among souls, a light among lights. Every seed in a field goes into the ground as itself and comes up as itself. Barley does not come up wheat.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection body has no connection to the present body. The seed becomes the plant; it is the same life. The body sown is the body raised.

Will I still be me? Yes. The resurrection is not the creation of a new person who happens to carry your name. It is you, body and soul, raised and made whole. Your soul has been with Christ since death, and on that day it will be reunited with your body, the same body, transformed. Your history, your relationships, the work of grace in you will not be erased. The risen Jesus was recognisably Jesus; he knew Mary by name and she knew him by his voice. So it will be with you, except that everything sin and death have spoiled will be gone.

In a sentence. When you sow, you do not plant the body that will grow, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. Then God gives it the body he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.

On a Tuesday. If you are anxious about what will happen to your body, or to someone you love, give the anxiety to God by name. He designed this body, he knows where every one of his people lies, and he is not improvising.

For worship. The choosing is God’s, which is the last comfort in the verse. The body you will have was designed by the same Person who designed this one, and he has had a very long time to think about it. He is not improvising at the graveside. He who knit you together in your mother’s womb (Psalm 139:13) will clothe you in glory, and you will praise him with a body fit at last for praise. God will give you a resurrection body as he chooses. Trust his wisdom and power.

verseByVerse.quote: For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.

For not all flesh is the same. A second analogy. God has made many kinds of bodies. Paul now widens the lens, and the argument is doing something specific: it is dismantling the assumption that the word body can only mean one thing.

But there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish. Echoes Genesis 1. Look around, he says. A man’s flesh and a fish’s flesh are both flesh and they are not remotely alike; the bird that can live in the air and the fish that would drown in it are both embodied creatures. God the Creator is able to make bodies of every kind suited to every sphere.

There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. Heavenly bodies: sun, moon, stars. Earthly: plants and animals and men.

But the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another. Each has its own splendour (doxa, glory, brightness). Their glories are of different orders altogether.

There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. Even among the heavenly bodies, there is variety: no two lights are the same. The point is that God has never worked with one template. A God with this much range in what he has already made is not likely to be stuck for a design when he comes to raise the dead. The objector at verse 35 was assuming that a resurrection body would have to be the same sort of thing as the body he currently has, and that assumption is the whole of his difficulty. If God can make all these, he can make a resurrection body with a glory beyond anything we know.

Difference is God’s habit. There is a note being sounded here that the Corinthians particularly needed, and Paul has been sounding it all letter. Star differs from star in glory. Difference is not a defect in God’s workmanship; it is his habit. He made a universe in which nothing is standardised: a church of eyes and ears and feet (12:17), and a sky in which no two lights are matched. A congregation that had been ranking one another by a single measure is being shown a night sky.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers will become stars, or that there will be ranks of glory among the saved based on merit, though some interpreters have taken it that way. Paul’s point is about God’s creative power. He is answering the question with what kind of body do they come? (v. 35), and the illustration is about kinds, not ranks. Scripture does speak elsewhere of rewards that differ (3:12–15), but every raised believer will bear the image of the man of heaven (v. 49).

Will there be rewards in heaven? Yes, but not the kind that make anyone envious. Scripture speaks of reward for faithful service (3:14; Matthew 25:21), but every reward is itself grace, for even our good works were prepared by God (Ephesians 2:10). No one will be second-class in glory, and no one will begrudge another; the elders in Revelation cast their crowns before the throne (Revelation 4:10). Every believer will be filled to the brim with joy, though the vessels may differ in size. The greatest reward of all is the same for everyone: Christ himself.

In a sentence. Not all flesh is alike: people have one kind, animals another, birds another, fish another. There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies; the splendour of the heavenly is one kind, the splendour of the earthly another. The sun has one splendour, the moon another and the stars another, and star differs from star in splendour.

On a Tuesday. Look at the night sky. The God who made the stars will make your resurrection body. And look at your church with the same eyes: stop measuring your brothers and sisters by a single standard, and thank God for one person this week who is gloriously unlike you.

For worship. There is something to be simply enjoyed in this passage, which too many commentaries hurry past. This is a tentmaker writing to a quarrelling church about a difficult doctrine, and he stops in the middle of it to look up. He notices fish and birds. He notices that the stars are not alike. The man who wrote the hardest arguments in the New Testament had his eyes open in the world, and thought God’s ordinary handiwork was worth putting into a sentence about the last day. The heavens declare the glory of God (Psalm 19:1). He determines the number of the stars and gives to all of them their names (Psalm 147:4), and he knows yours too.

verseByVerse.quote: So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.

So is it with the resurrection of the dead. The comparisons stop and the promises begin. Four contrasts follow (vv. 42–44) between the present body and the resurrection body; here are the first three, and each one names something a reader has felt.

What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. Perishable (phthora) is decay, corruption; imperishable (aphtharsia) is incorruption. The present body is on a schedule of decay and everyone knows it. It began wearing out at about twenty-five. The knee goes, the eyes go, the name of somebody you have known for forty years will not come. Whatever is done to slow it, and there is nothing wrong with slowing it, the direction is fixed. The resurrection body will have no such direction. It will not be a body kept young by effort. It will be a body with nothing in it that can wear out, that will never decay or die.

It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. This is the honest one, and it should not be softened, because anyone who has sat with the dying knows exactly what Paul means. There is very little dignity available at the end. There is the indignity of being washed by strangers, of a body that will not obey, of a mind that says the wrong word, of a person who was formidable and is now frightened of the stairs. A corpse is a humiliating thing. Death does not merely end a life; it humiliates it first. And into that Paul writes raised in glory, the same word used of the splendour of God himself. The raised body will shine with glory, like Christ’s (Philippians 3:21; Matthew 13:43). The body that was carried out of a ward with a sheet over it comes back radiant.

It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. Weakness is the daily one. The present body tires and fails; the dead body is utterly helpless. It is not only the sickbed; it is the ordinary ceiling every person lives under: wanting to help and being too tired, wanting to stay and having to sleep, wanting to do the good thing and finding that the body will not carry the will that far. Every human being alive is limited by an instrument that cannot keep up with him. Raised in power means the instrument will be equal to the person at last. The resurrection body will be full of strength.

Sown. Notice the verb governing all three. Not disposed of, not lost, not stored. Sown, which is a thing done by a farmer, on purpose, with a harvest in mind. Christians have buried their dead for two thousand years in that word’s shadow. A grave, on Paul’s account, is not a full stop but a planting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a different person is raised. It is sown and it is raised: the same body, transformed.

How should I care for my body now if it will be raised? With gratitude and respect, but without idolatry. Your body is not a prison to escape but a temple of the Holy Spirit (6:19) and a seed of glory. So feed it, rest it, exercise it, and do not abuse it with drunkenness or sexual sin. Care for the bodies of others too, the sick, the elderly, the disabled, because God will raise them. But do not worship youth or beauty, and do not despair as the body declines. Its weakness is not the end of the story. The wrinkles and the aches are the dishonour of the sowing, and the harvest is coming.

In a sentence. So it will be with the resurrection of the dead. The body is sown in decay and raised never to decay; sown in humiliation and raised in splendour; sown in weakness and raised in power.

On a Tuesday. Visit someone whose body is failing: in a hospital, a care home, or their own front room. Treat them with the honour due to one who will be raised in glory. And when your own body aches this week, tell it what Paul says: sown in weakness; raised in power.

For worship. Your weak, ageing body will one day be raised imperishable, glorious and powerful. Christ was sown in dishonour, stripped and mocked and hung on a cross, his body carried down by friends and laid in a borrowed grave. And he was raised in glory, in power, imperishable, never to die again. Death no longer has dominion over him (Romans 6:9), and because it has none over him, it will have none over us. He will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body (Philippians 3:21). Thank God for that hope.

verseByVerse.quote: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.

It is sown a natural body. The fourth contrast, and the one most often misunderstood, so it must be handled carefully. Natural (psychikos, soulish) describes a body animated by ordinary human life, suited to this age (2:14): breath, blood, appetite, sleep.

It is raised a spiritual body. A spiritual body is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit. It does not mean a ghost, a mist, a shining outline, or a soul that has escaped its container. Spiritual (pneumatikos) describes what governs and empowers it, not what it is made of. Paul uses the same word of spiritual people (2:15), who are not made of spirit. Which means the resurrection body is not less physical than the present one. If anything it is more so: more solid, more alive, more capable, because everything that currently drags at the body has been removed from it.

If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. Just as there is a body suited to this age, there will be one suited to the age to come.

One such body was examined. We are not guessing, because one such body exists and was examined. The risen Christ was not a vision. He told them to touch him, and said that a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Luke 24:39). He ate a piece of broiled fish in front of them (Luke 24:42–43), which is a strange thing for a phantom to do, and which reads exactly like a man proving a point. And when Thomas needed evidence, he offered the wounds (John 20:27).

He kept the scars. That last detail answers a question people carry and rarely ask. The one resurrection body we have any information about is marked, permanently, by what was done to it. Glorification did not erase the history; it healed it and kept the record. Whatever that means for the rest of us, it means the risen life is not an amnesia. The Lamb in heaven stands as though it had been slain (Revelation 5:6).

Where Christians differ: a physical resurrection? Some say the resurrection body is immaterial, a spirit body, and that Jesus’ resurrection was spiritual rather than physical. Verdict: Christ’s resurrection body was physical: he ate, was touched, had flesh and bones and the marks of his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27). The tomb was empty. Ours will be like his (Philippians 3:21). The spiritual body is physical, but transformed and wholly governed by the Holy Spirit (Westminster 32.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will be ghosts or disembodied spirits. That is the opposite of resurrection.

Will we know one another? The disciples knew him, sometimes at once, sometimes after a moment, and always in the end, and Paul assumes throughout his letters that Christians will be reunited and will recognise each other (1 Thessalonians 4:17–18; 2 Corinthians 4:14). Love does not end (13:8), and the people we have loved in Christ will be ours to love forever, more truly than now.

What about bodies wrecked by disease, dementia or disability? Verse 38 has already answered it: God gives it a body as he has chosen, and what is raised is raised imperishable, in glory, in power (vv. 42–43). Nothing that the fall put into a body is going to be raised with it. The child who never walked will run; the mind lost to dementia will know and praise and remember; the body broken by illness will be strong. And what age? Scripture does not say, and it is better to admit that than to invent. What it does say is enough: the body will be like his (Philippians 3:21). That is the whole promise, and it is a great deal more than a description.

In a sentence. It is sown a body fit for this life; it is raised a body ruled by the Spirit. If there is a body for this life, there is also a body for the Spirit’s life.

On a Tuesday. Thank God that he will redeem your body, not discard it. Honour your body now as one God will raise. And speak this hope to someone who is living with a body that does not work as it should: not as a pat answer, but as the solid promise of God.

For worship. The risen Lord ate fish on a beach at dawn, with the marks of the nails in his hands. He did not leave his body in the grave like a shell; he came out in it, glorified, and he took it with him into heaven, where a man now sits on the throne of the universe. He is the first of a new creation, and the Spirit who raised him will raise us. Our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20). Thank God that our bodies are not discarded but redeemed.
verseByVerse.note: A “spiritual body” is a real body wholly empowered by the Spirit, not a body made of spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.

Thus it is written, the first man Adam became a living being. Paul goes back to Genesis, and the difference between the two halves of his sentence is one word. Of Adam, Scripture says he became a living being (Genesis 2:7), a living soul (psychē zōsa), the word behind natural body. He received life; God breathed it into him and he stood up. Everything about the first man is on the receiving end: he was made from dust he did not gather, given breath he did not take, and put in a garden he did not plant.

The last Adam became a life-giving spirit. Of Christ, Paul says he became a life-giving spirit. Not merely alive: a source. Christ is the last Adam, the head of the new humanity (Romans 5:12–21). By his resurrection, he became the giver of life through the Spirit. Adam received life; Christ gives it (John 5:21; 6:63). The first Adam was a vessel; the last Adam is a spring. That is why the resurrection of Jesus is not simply the best example of resurrection but its cause. He does not stand at the head of the queue. He is the reason there is a queue.

What life-giving spirit means. Spirit here does not mean Christ is no longer bodily; it means he gives the Spirit’s life to his people. Paul is not saying that Christ turned into the Holy Spirit; the two remain distinct persons throughout his letters (2 Corinthians 13:14). He means that the risen Christ, in a body wholly alive with the Spirit, now gives life: he pours out the Spirit (Acts 2:33) and will raise his people by that same Spirit (Romans 8:11). Note also the title: the last Adam. Not the second, as though there might be a third. The human race has had two representatives and will have no more. Everything after Christ is a matter of which of the two you belong to.

But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. Verse 46 looks like a small logical aside and is doing real work. The order of history is first the natural, Adam and this age, then the spiritual, Christ and the age to come. Paul is establishing the order of God’s working, and it runs against the instinct of every religious person who has ever wanted to skip a stage. The ordinary comes first. The dust comes before the glory, the natural body before the spiritual one, the long unremarkable life before the transformation. God does not begin with the finished thing. That is a rebuke to the Corinthian error, which was to believe they had already arrived, already reigning, already filled, already beyond the ordinary business of bodies and patience (4:8). Some Corinthians thought they already had the spiritual in full. Paul says it comes later, at the resurrection.

Seed first, harvest afterwards. And it is a comfort to anyone who suspects his own Christian life is too plain to be real. The plainness is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the appointed order. Nobody gets the second without going through the first, and the Lord himself did not (Hebrews 5:8; Philippians 2:8–9). It is a rule with a wide application. The long apprenticeship before the work. The years of faithfulness nobody notices before the door opens. The decades of an ordinary marriage, an ordinary job, an ordinary congregation. Christians are forever looking for a shortcut past the natural into the spiritual, and there is not one; there is only the appointed sequence, and God is not in a hurry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Adam was created evil. He was good, but natural, not yet glorified. Christ brings humanity to its intended goal.

My Christian life feels ordinary. Am I missing something? Probably not. Most of the Christian life is meant to be ordinary: daily prayer and Scripture, weekly worship, faithful work, patient love at home, small acts of service. That is not second-rate Christianity; it is the natural before the spiritual, the seed before the harvest. If you are trusting Christ and walking with him, you are not missing a secret level. Seek more of him, certainly, and do not settle for coldness. But beware of anyone who promises a shortcut to glory now. The glory is coming, and it is far greater than any experience this life can give.

In a sentence. So Scripture says that the first man Adam became a living person; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. The spiritual did not come first, but the natural, and after that the spiritual.

On a Tuesday. You are now in Adam’s body but united to the last Adam. The best is still to come. Do today’s ordinary duties faithfully, as seed-time, and thank God for them.
