For worship. Thirty years in a carpenter’s shop came before three years of ministry. If the last Adam took the natural first and did not complain about the ratio, nobody else is being short-changed. He who is the fountain of life was content to receive his daily bread from the hand of his Father, to grow in wisdom and stature, to wait. And now he gives life to whom he will. Blessed be the last Adam, the life-giving Lord, from whom every Christian draws his breath.

parallels.desc: the man became a living creature

verseByVerse.quote: The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.

The first man was from the earth, a man of dust. Two men, two origins, and two families that look like their heads. Genesis says so and does not apologise for it: God formed the man of dust from the ground (Genesis 2:7), and told him after the fall that to dust he would return (Genesis 3:19). Every person carries the evidence. We are made of the same elements as the soil in the garden, we require constant maintenance from that soil in the form of food and water, and in the end we go back into it. There is a reason the funeral service says what it says over a grave: dust to dust.

The second man is from heaven. Not made of different material: he had a real body, born of a woman, that got tired and hungry and bled. He is from heaven in origin: he came from somewhere, which no other human being has ever done. Christ came from heaven, and his risen body belongs to the heavenly realm.

As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust. All Adam’s descendants share his earthly, mortal nature.

And as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. All who belong to Christ will share his heavenly, glorious nature.

Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven. One of the great sentences of the Bible. Image (eikōn): we were born in Adam’s likeness (Genesis 5:3). We have borne the first image all our lives, and we know its features intimately: mortality, weakness, the pull toward what we know is wrong, the face in the mirror getting older. Nobody had to be taught to bear that image. It came with the birth. The second is as certain as the first. Note the tense: we shall also bear, flat future, no condition attached. This is the same thing Paul says in Romans, that those God foreknew he predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:29), and what John says in one line: we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

A note on the text. Some manuscripts read let us bear, making it an exhortation; the ESV note mentions this. The future we shall fits the context of the resurrection better, and it is the reading the argument requires.

The gap closes. Measure that against what is actually broken. The man you have wanted to be and the man you are have never once been the same man; every Christian carries an internal record of the gap. On that day the gap closes. Not by lowering the standard, and not by a lifetime of gradual improvement finally arriving, but because the likeness of Christ, which has been worked into his people slowly and against resistance, will be completed in an instant and will hold. There will be nothing left in you that he would have to overlook.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we will become divine. We will be glorified humans, like Christ in his humanity.

If I will bear his image then, why try to be like him now? Because the Spirit is already at work forming that image in you, and you are called to cooperate with him. We all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). The resurrection completes what sanctification begins. And the hope itself is a motive: everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3). You do not become like Christ in order to be saved; you become like him because you are saved, and the finished likeness is promised.

In a sentence. The first man was from the earth, made of dust; the second man is from heaven. Those of the earth are like the earthly man, and those of heaven are like the heavenly man. And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so we will bear the likeness of the heavenly man.

On a Tuesday. One day you will look like Jesus. Let that hope purify you now (1 John 3:3). Pick one feature of Adam’s image you see in yourself this week, a temper, a habit, a fear, and bring it to Christ, asking him to make you more like himself.

For worship. The Son of God came down from heaven and took the dust on himself. He who was in the form of God was born in the likeness of men, and bore our image all the way to the grave. He did it so that we, the men of dust, might bear his. Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared (1 John 3:2). But we know whose face we will wear, and whose face we will see. Glory to the Man from heaven, who has made the children of Adam the brothers of the King.

parallels.desc: you are dust

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul declares that flesh and blood, our present mortal nature, cannot inherit God’s kingdom, nor can the perishable inherit the imperishable. He tells them a mystery: not all believers will die, but all will be changed, in a flash, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. The trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and the living will be changed. The perishable must be clothed with the imperishable, and the mortal with immortality. When that happens, the saying of Scripture will come true: death has been swallowed up in victory. Where is death’s victory, where is its sting? Death’s sting is sin, and sin’s power comes from the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. So, dear brothers and sisters, they must stand firm and immovable, always giving themselves fully to the Lord’s work, because they know their labour in the Lord is not wasted.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Foundation of Present Labour

The practical conclusion of the resurrection argument — “your labour is not in vain” (v. 58) — is the most comprehensive positive statement about Christian ethics in the letter. The resurrection does not merely give hope for the future; it validates the present. Every act of love, faithfulness, service, and endurance that has been poured out for Christ is stored up in a creation that will be renewed, not discarded. Herman Bavinck’s great theme was that grace restores nature: the resurrection does not annul creation but redeems and glorifies it.

Anthony Hoekema makes the same point in his study of biblical eschatology: the resurrection is the guarantee that present labour is not in vain, because the God who raised Christ will also raise and renew the creation in which that labour was performed. The resurrection does not make the present world irrelevant; it makes it eternally significant.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed to hear that the deaths of their beloved dead were not permanent losses, that their own present labour was not ultimately futile, and that the God who raised Christ had the power and the intention to complete what he had begun in them. The resurrection doctrine is not abstract comfort; it is the concrete ground of the community’s ability to bear all things, believe all things, hope all things, endure all things (ch. 13). Now: Every generation of the church faces the question that faces every human being: does my life mean anything beyond this brief span? Paul’s answer is the most radical possible: yes, because the God who raised Jesus from the dead is the God who inhabits your story, and he wastes nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,
verseByVerse.commentary:
I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,

I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God. Flesh and blood is a Hebrew phrase for human nature in its present weak, mortal state (Matthew 16:17; Galatians 1:16): not a slur on physical existence, which Paul has spent fifteen verses defending. It does not mean physical bodies cannot enter the kingdom; it means bodies as they now are, mortal and corruptible, cannot. They must be changed. It is not a moral judgement; it is a statement about fitness. You do not go deep-sea diving in a jacket.

Nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable. What decays cannot possess what is eternal. Transformation is necessary.

Behold! I tell you a mystery. A mystery in Paul is never a puzzle; it is a truth previously hidden, something that could not have been worked out and has now been disclosed by God. He is about to say something the church did not know.

We shall not all sleep. There is the new information. The entire chapter so far has assumed the pattern of death and resurrection: sown, then raised. But not every believer will die. There will be a generation of Christians alive when Christ returns, who will never be buried at all. They will not miss out on the transformation; they will simply reach it by a different road.

But we shall all be changed. All believers, dead and living, will be transformed. Changed (allassō) is transformed, exchanged, as one garment is exchanged for another.

Did Paul expect to be alive when Christ returned? He writes we because he speaks as one of the living church, which is always to be ready, and he did not know the day (1 Thessalonians 5:1–2). Elsewhere he speaks just as calmly of his own death (2 Corinthians 5:1–8; Philippians 1:21–23). We means believers generally; Paul did not know whether he would be alive then. He was not mistaken about a date; he never set one.

One with Thessalonica. This is where Paul’s teaching here joins hands with what he had already written to Thessalonica: the Lord descending with a cry of command and the sound of the trumpet, the dead in Christ rising first, and then those who are alive being caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). Christians of every persuasion share nearly all of it: that Jesus Christ will return personally, visibly and bodily; that the dead in Christ will be raised; that those alive will be transformed; that this will happen in an instant and at his initiative; and that no believer of any generation will be left out of it. That is what this passage teaches, and it is what Christians say together at a graveside.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the resurrection body is not flesh. Jesus’ risen body had flesh and bones (Luke 24:39). It means our bodies must be changed from mortality to immortality.

Will believers who are alive at his coming miss anything by not dying? No. They will not miss the resurrection; they will receive the same transformation in a different way. And those who have died will not be disadvantaged either: the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16). Both groups meet the Lord together, and both are changed into his likeness. Whether the Lord comes in your lifetime or you go to him first, you lose nothing. Either way, you will be with him and like him.

In a sentence. Paul declares to you, brothers and sisters, that flesh and blood as they are now cannot inherit God’s kingdom, nor can what decays inherit what never decays. Listen, he tells you a mystery: we will not all die, but we will all be changed,

On a Tuesday. Whether you die before Christ returns or are alive when he comes, you will be changed. Either way, the future is glory. Live today as if he might come before evening, not in fear, but in readiness: with sins confessed, quarrels made up, and your face turned toward the sky.

For worship. A mystery hidden for ages has been disclosed: the King is coming, and his people will be changed. Not one will be left behind in the grave, and not one will be left as he is. The God who planned it before the world began will do it in his own time, and the Son who promised it will keep his word. Behold, I am coming soon (Revelation 22:12). Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.

In a moment. Paul reaches for two measures of time and both of them mean the same thing: there will be no process. In a moment translates en atomō: in an uncuttable instant. It is the word from which we get atom, and it meant the smallest thing that cannot be divided further. Paul is saying the change will happen in a slice of time too thin to have parts.

In the twinkling of an eye. The homelier version of the same idea. As fast as a blink, or faster: the flicker, the involuntary movement of the eye that is over before it has been noticed. It is the fastest thing a person can observe in himself. The change will not be gradual.

The slowest and the fastest work of God. Both images say the same thing and it is worth pausing on, because it is not what anyone would have guessed. Everything else in the Christian life is slow. Sanctification takes decades and moves backwards on many days. Grief takes years. Prayers are answered over the course of a lifetime, or not visibly at all. The whole of a believer’s experience trains him to expect God to work at the pace of growing things. And then this. No preparation, no ramp, no gradual improvement. A woman who has spent eleven years unable to leave her chair, and in the next instant she is not merely well but imperishable. A man in a churchyard since 1840 whose stone is illegible, and in the same instant he is standing. The slowest work God does and the fastest work God does are both directed at the same person.

At the last trumpet. A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people (Exodus 19:16; Joel 2:1; Zechariah 9:14). In Israel it summoned the assembly, announced the king, and called the camp to move (Numbers 10). This one does all three at once. The last trumpet signals the end of history and the return of Christ (Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16). And there is something worth noticing in the word last: there will never be another summons after it, because there will never again be anyone who needs calling.

For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed. First the dead are raised, then the living are changed (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17). All together meet the Lord. And note who is doing what in the sentence. The dead do not rise by their own power; they will be raised, the same passive that was used of Christ at verse 4. Nobody in that vast company contributes anything to his own resurrection. They are not straining at the lid. They are called, and they come, because the voice that calls them is the voice that called light out of nothing and Lazarus out of a tomb (John 5:28–29).

Where Christians differ: the rapture. Many dispensationalists teach a secret rapture: Christ will come invisibly to take believers away before a seven-year tribulation, and then return again visibly later. Verdict: Paul says this happens at the last trumpet, which suggests the end, not a stage before further events. The New Testament describes one return of Christ, visible, public and glorious (Matthew 24:27, 30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; Revelation 1:7), at which the dead are raised, the living changed, and all are judged. There is no secret rapture. Believers will be caught up to meet the Lord in the air, to welcome him as he comes, and then be with him forever.

The case fairly stated. Christians who hold a pre-tribulation rapture point to promises that believers are not destined for wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9) and will be kept from the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world (Revelation 3:10), and many of them love the Scriptures and read them with great care. Others, including amillennial, postmillennial and historic premillennial Christians, see one coming. They note that Paul ties this moment to the last trumpet, the public trumpet of Christ’s coming (Matthew 24:31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16), and to the resurrection that ends death (vv. 54–55). The word for meeting the Lord in the air was used of citizens going out to meet an arriving king and escorting him into the city, not of being taken away from it. That is why the more likely reading is one coming of Christ, visible to all, at which the dead are raised and the living changed together. It is a poor use of a promise this size to make it the occasion of a quarrel among people who are all waiting for the same trumpet.

Will there be one resurrection or two? One general resurrection, at Christ’s return. Jesus said an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement (John 5:28–29). Paul spoke of a resurrection of both the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). This chapter dwells on believers, because its purpose is comfort and hope; but the same trumpet that raises the saints to glory summons all to judgement (Matthew 25:31–46). That is why the gospel is urgent now.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we know when it will happen. The day is unknown (Matthew 24:36).

In a sentence. in a flash, in the blink of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised never to decay, and we will be changed.

On a Tuesday. Live today as one who listens for a trumpet. Pray for one person who is not ready for it, and tell him of the One who is coming.

For worship. The certainty of this does not depend in the least on the strength of the faith of the person waiting for it. Everyone in the churchyard will be raised by the same voice, at the same instant, with the same ease. The Lord himself will descend; the archangel will cry out; the trumpet of God will sound. And the believing dead of every age, apostles and martyrs, mothers and children, the forgotten saints of a thousand village churches, will stand up in a moment, imperishable, and look on the face of their King. Listen for the last trumpet. Pray, Come, Lord Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: A trumpet announced great acts of God and summoned his people.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality. When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”

For this perishable body must put on the imperishable. Notice the verb: put on (endyō). It is the word for getting dressed: putting on a coat, a garment, clothing. Paul does not say the perishable body is discarded and a better one issued. He says it is clothed, and the thing underneath is still there (2 Corinthians 5:2–4). That matters, because it is the difference between resurrection and replacement. The Christian is not going to be swapped for a superior model of person. The same man who has struggled and prayed and failed and hung on is going to be dressed in immortality, and it will be him inside it. And this perishable body, Paul writes. He might have said the perishable. He says this: the body we have now. One imagines him gesturing at himself as he dictated, a man with a scarred back and failing eyes, saying: this one.

And this mortal body must put on immortality. Immortality (athanasia) is deathlessness. Only God has immortality in himself (1 Timothy 6:16); he will give it to his people.

Must. One word in these verses is worth pressing, because Paul repeats it: must. That is the language of necessity: not what is likely, or hoped for, or reasonable to expect, but what has to happen. Necessary to whom? Not to us; nobody here arranged anything. It is necessary because God has purposed a new creation and has determined that his people will live in it, and a perishable body cannot. The obligation sits on his side of the transaction. He has bound himself by his promise, and the raising of the dead is now something he will surely do, because he is the God who keeps his word.

When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality. Paul repeats it for emphasis, as a man repeats good news he cannot quite believe he is allowed to tell.

Then shall come to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. The quotation is from Isaiah 25:8, and it is worth knowing what surrounds it there, because Isaiah is describing a feast. On his mountain the LORD will make for all peoples a feast of rich food; he will swallow up the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations, and then: he will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces (Isaiah 25:6–8). The verb is worth having. Swallowed up (katapinō) is gulped down, devoured. Death is not defeated in a negotiated settlement. It is swallowed: taken in and gone, the way the sea takes something and closes over it. The thing that has swallowed every human being who ever lived is itself swallowed at last, and there is a rough justice in the image that Isaiah plainly intended.

The faces. The detail that most people need is the one about the faces. God is not described as issuing a decree about grief. He is described as coming close enough to wipe tears off individual faces with his own hand, which is what he is doing at the end of the Bible too (Revelation 21:4). Whatever else that day contains, it contains a God who has come near enough to touch the people who have been crying.

What it does not mean. It does not mean death is defeated by human progress. Medicine can delay it and comfort can soften it, but only God can swallow it up.

How do I hold on to this when I am grieving? Slowly, and with help. Grief does not obey arguments, and God does not ask you to stop grieving; he promises to wipe away tears, which means there will be tears to wipe. Read these verses aloud, even when they feel far off. Let others pray for you when you cannot pray. Visit the grave, if it helps, and say there what Paul says here. Mourn honestly, and keep company with the hope of the feast. The day is coming when the Lord will lift your face with his own hand, and the person you have lost in Christ will be at the table.

In a sentence. For this body that decays must be clothed with what never decays, and this mortal body with immortality. When that happens, the saying in Scripture will come true: Death has been swallowed up in victory.

On a Tuesday. At the next funeral you attend, remember: death will be swallowed up. It does not have the last word. And if you know someone who is grieving this month, send them Isaiah 25:8 with one line telling them you are praying.

For worship. On a hill outside Jerusalem, death opened its mouth and swallowed the Son of God. And it could not keep him down. On the third day he came out of the grave, and death was the thing that had been swallowed. One day his whole people will come out after him, clothed in immortality, and sit down at the feast on the mountain, and the veil will be gone from every face. He will swallow up death forever. Blessed be the God who wipes away tears with his own hand.

parallels.desc: he will swallow up death forever

verseByVerse.quote: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting? Paul turns and speaks to death directly, and the tone is not respectful. He is quoting Hosea (Hosea 13:14), and the two questions are a taunt song over defeated death: the sort of thing shouted after an enemy who has been beaten and is being watched off the field. Where is your victory? Death has had a total record. It has never lost a single engagement in the history of the world; every person it has come for, it has taken. And Paul stands in front of it and asks what it has won.

The sting. Then the word to concentrate on: sting. It is the word for the barb of a scorpion or a bee: not the size of the creature but the part that can actually kill you. The old illustration is still the best one. A bee that has stung has left its sting behind. It can still come at you; it can still fly at your face and make a grown man leave a picnic. What it cannot do is hurt you, because the thing that made it dangerous is gone. And a child who knows that will stand perfectly still while it buzzes round his head. That is precisely the Christian’s position. Death may still frighten, but it cannot destroy believers.

The sting of death is sin. Paul explains the mechanism rather than leaving it as a picture. What makes death deadly is sin. Death is the wages of sin (Romans 6:23). What makes death terrible is not that it ends the body; animals die and it is sad and it is not frightening in this way. What makes death terrible is that it is the doorway to judgement for a guilty person: it is sin that gives death its barb. Christ removed the sting by bearing our sin.

And the power of sin is the law. The law gives sin its power, by exposing it, condemning it, and even provoking it (Romans 7:7–13). Without the law, sin is not counted (Romans 5:13). The law is not the villain here; it is holy, righteous and good (Romans 7:12). But the law is what turns wrongdoing into a documented offence. It names it, measures it, and pronounces the sentence, and so it is the law that gives sin its legal force.

Follow the chain backwards. Death is fearful because of sin. Sin has its power from the law. And Christ has dealt with both: he kept the law we broke and bore the curse it pronounced (Galatians 3:13). So sin has no power to condemn believers, and death has no sting. Pull those two out and death is a bee with no sting. It is still an enemy. It can still frighten. It cannot destroy a Christian, and it never will.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is sin. The law is holy (Romans 7:12). But it condemns sinners.

What about those who die without Christ? For them death keeps its sting, because their sin remains on their own account. Death is then not a doorway to rest but to judgement, and Scripture warns plainly of conscious, eternal punishment (Matthew 25:46; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). That is why the gospel is not a pleasant extra but the most urgent message in the world. The sting is drawn only for those who are in Christ, who has borne their sin. If you are not yet trusting him, come to him now, while death is still at a distance. He receives all who come.

In a sentence. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law.

On a Tuesday. Taunt death today with Paul’s words. Its sting has been drawn by Christ. Say them aloud at the end of a hard day, and say them again when you hear bad news from a doctor.

For worship. Death drove its sting into the Son of God, and the sting stayed in him. He took into his own body the curse of the law and the wages of sin, and he exhausted them. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). Death still buzzes at us, but its barb is in the cross. O death, where is your sting? It is buried with the grave clothes in an empty tomb, and the Lord of life has gone out into the morning.

parallels.desc: O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting?

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

But thanks be to God. The argument stops. The proofs are finished, the objections are answered, and Paul does the only thing left to do. The only fitting response is thanksgiving (Romans 7:25).

Who gives us the victory. Read the verbs. Nobody in the sentence wins anything. The victory is given: handed over, made a present of, and it is given to people who were not on the field. The victory is a gift, not an achievement. This is not the language of a struggle in which the believer participated and finally prevailed. Every Christian who will ever be raised was, at the decisive moment, dead in trespasses and sins, and had contributed nothing to the outcome except the problem. And notice the tense: gives. Present. Not only will give, though the resurrection is future. God is giving us the victory now, over sin, death and the law. The victory is being handed over now, to people still in perishable bodies, still burying their friends, still afraid of the diagnosis. The thing has been settled and the settlement is in force.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ. The channel is named, as it always is in Paul: through his death, which removed sin’s sting, and his resurrection, which defeated death. His victory is ours. Not through our grasp of the doctrine, our steadiness under pressure, or the quality of our dying. Christians have died well and Christians have died badly, frightened, confused, heavily medicated, saying nothing memorable at all, and it makes no difference whatever to the outcome, because the victory was won by somebody else and is handed over as a gift. The word victory is a battlefield term: the outcome, the thing carried off the field. Paul uses it again in Romans and puts an even stranger word in front of it: in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us (Romans 8:37). More than conquerors. Not merely surviving the engagement, but coming out of it with more than was taken in.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never struggle with sin or face death. It means the outcome is certain.

What does victory look like on a hard day? It rarely looks like triumph. It looks like a believer who falls and gets up again, who confesses sin instead of hiding it, who keeps praying when prayer feels empty, who weeps at a graveside and still sings the hymn. Victory in Christ is not the absence of struggle but the certainty of the outcome. You may feel defeated and still be more than a conqueror, because the battle that decides everything has already been won. On the hardest days, do not look for the feeling of victory; look at the One who gives it, and thank him.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God! He gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the victory he has given you through Christ. Say it out loud. Write the verse where you will see it in the morning, and say it before you check the news.

For worship. He was dead. Properly dead, taken down by men who did this for a living and knew when a job was finished, wrapped with spices and shut behind a stone by people with no expectation whatever of seeing him again. Everything that has ever terrified the human race had done its complete work on him, and had done it with the full cooperation of the authorities, the crowd, and his own friends. And on the first day of the week he rose, and left the cloth that had been on his head folded up in a place by itself, and went out into a garden where a woman was crying, and said her name (John 20:7, 15–16). Thanks be to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

Therefore, my beloved brothers. Fifty-seven verses of the highest doctrine in the letter, and the conclusion is about Monday. The practical conclusion of the whole chapter. After rebuking them throughout the letter, Paul calls them beloved. That therefore is doing all the work, and it should stop anybody who has ever thought the resurrection is a subject for funerals only. Paul does not say: therefore look forward to heaven. He says: therefore get on with it.

Be steadfast. Steadfast (hedraios) is firmly seated, settled. Do not be shaken in your faith in the resurrection.

Immovable. Immovable (ametakinētos) is not to be moved. Two words meaning much the same thing, laid one on the other for weight: seated, settled, not to be shifted. Not moved by false teaching or hardship. This is the answer to a church that had been blown about by every teacher, every fashion and every clever argument all through this letter.

Always abounding in the work of the Lord. Abounding (perisseuō) is an overflow word. Not managing, not maintaining, not doing one’s bit: more than is required, spilling over the edge. Give yourself fully to the Lord’s work: serving, witnessing, loving. And note that a man is being told to spend himself in a body he has just been told is perishable, on the ground that the body is going to be raised. The doctrine does not produce detachment from this life. It produces holy recklessness in it.

Knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain. The clause the whole chapter has been travelling toward. Labour (kopos) is toil to exhaustion. Not in vain (ou kenos, not empty) is the same word as verse 14. The word in vain has been haunting this chapter. If Christ is not raised, the preaching is in vain, the faith is in vain (v. 14); Paul’s grace was not in vain (v. 10). Now it lands where the reader lives. Because Christ is risen, nothing done for him is wasted. Every act of faithful service will count in eternity.

Not in vain, concretely. That needs to be made concrete, because it is exactly the sort of promise that evaporates when it is left general. Consider the mother who has prayed for a son for thirty years and has watched him get worse. The man who taught a Sunday class of eight children for a decade and has no idea what became of any of them. The woman who nursed a husband through seven years of dementia, doing everything, thanked by nobody, remembered by a man who did not know her name. The believer who has held a difficult marriage together in private for a lifetime and will never be commended for it. The missionary who gave forty years to a place and left it with three converts and a small building. Every one of them has looked at what they have to show for it and thought: that was nothing. And every one of them has been wrong, on the authority of this verse. Not your labour will probably bear fruit eventually. Not God sees your effort even if it failed. Your labour is not in vain: the work itself is not lost, because it was done in the Lord, and what is done in the Lord belongs to a world that is not going to be thrown away but raised.

What it does not mean. It does not mean you will always see the results of your labour now. It means God sees and will reward it.

What counts as the work of the Lord? Far more than church activities. It includes preaching, evangelism and serving in the church, certainly. But it also includes any work done in the Lord: for his sake, in faith, by his strength. Changing a nappy, filling in a spreadsheet honestly, caring for an elderly parent, visiting a lonely neighbour, praying in secret, raising children in the faith. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward (Colossians 3:23–24). The question is not whether the task is religious, but whether it is done in him.

In a sentence. So then, dear brothers and sisters, stand firm. Let nothing shift you. Always give yourselves fully to the Lord’s work, because you know that what you do for the Lord is never wasted.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection means your ordinary faithfulness today matters forever. Get on with the Lord’s work. Take the task that most feels like nothing, the one no one notices, and do it today as an offering to the risen Christ.

For worship. That is what the empty tomb finally means for an ordinary Tuesday. The God who did not let his Son’s body stay in the ground is not going to let his people’s work stay there either. He wastes nothing, he forgets nothing, and he is going to raise all of it. The cup of cold water given in his name will not lose its reward (Matthew 10:42). The tears sown in prayer will be reaped in joy. And the Lord who laboured to the cross and rose from the grave will say to his tired servants, well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your master (Matthew 25:21). Blessed be the risen Lord, in whom no labour is ever in vain.

15.text: <sup>1</sup>Now I would remind you, brothers, of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, in which you stand,<sup>2</sup>and by which you are being saved, if you hold fast to the word I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.<sup>3</sup>For I delivered to you as of first importance what I also received: that Christ died for our sins in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>4</sup>that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures,<sup>5</sup>and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve.<sup>6</sup>Then he appeared to more than five hundred brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive, though some have fallen asleep.<sup>7</sup>Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles.<sup>8</sup>Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me.<sup>9</sup>For I am the least of the apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God.<sup>10</sup>But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me was not in vain. On the contrary, I worked harder than any of them, though it was not I, but the grace of God that is with me.<sup>11</sup>Whether then it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.<sup>12</sup>Now if Christ is proclaimed as raised from the dead, how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?<sup>13</sup>But if there is no resurrection of the dead, then not even Christ has been raised.<sup>14</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain.<sup>15</sup>We are even found to be misrepresenting God, because we testified about God that he raised Christ, whom he did not raise if it is true that the dead are not raised.<sup>16</sup>For if the dead are not raised, not even Christ has been raised.<sup>17</sup>And if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins.<sup>18</sup>Then those also who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished.<sup>19</sup>If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied.<sup>20</sup>But in fact Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.<sup>21</sup>For as by a man came death, by a man has come also the resurrection of the dead.<sup>22</sup>For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.<sup>23</sup>But each in his own order: Christ the firstfruits, then at his coming those who belong to Christ.<sup>24</sup>Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power.<sup>25</sup>For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet.<sup>26</sup>The last enemy to be destroyed is death.<sup>27</sup>For “God has put all things in subjection under his feet.” But when it says, “all things are put in subjection,” it is plain that he is excepted who put all things in subjection under him.<sup>28</sup>When all things are subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who put all things in subjection under him, that God may be all in all.<sup>29</sup>Otherwise, what do people mean by being baptized on behalf of the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized on their behalf?<sup>30</sup>Why are we in danger every hour?<sup>31</sup>I protest, brothers, by my pride in you, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord, I die every day!<sup>32</sup>What do I gain if, humanly speaking, I fought with beasts at Ephesus? If the dead are not raised, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”<sup>33</sup>Do not be deceived: “Bad company ruins good morals.”<sup>34</sup>Wake up from your drunken stupor, as is right, and do not go on sinning. For some have no knowledge of God. I say this to your shame.<sup>35</sup>But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body do they come?”<sup>36</sup>You foolish person! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies.<sup>37</sup>And what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel, perhaps of wheat or of some other grain.<sup>38</sup>But God gives it a body as he has chosen, and to each kind of seed its own body.<sup>39</sup>For not all flesh is the same, but there is one kind for humans, another for animals, another for birds, and another for fish.<sup>40</sup>There are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, but the glory of the heavenly is of one kind, and the glory of the earthly is of another.<sup>41</sup>There is one glory of the sun, and another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory.<sup>42</sup>So is it with the resurrection of the dead. What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable.<sup>43</sup>It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power.<sup>44</sup>It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body.<sup>45</sup>Thus it is written, “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit.<sup>46</sup>But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual.<sup>47</sup>The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven.<sup>48</sup>As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven.<sup>49</sup>Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven.<sup>50</sup>I tell you this, brothers: flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable.<sup>51</sup>Behold! I tell you a mystery. We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed,<sup>52</sup>in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable, and we shall be changed.<sup>53</sup>For this perishable body must put on the imperishable, and this mortal body must put on immortality.<sup>54</sup>When the perishable puts on the imperishable, and the mortal puts on immortality, then shall come to pass the saying that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”<sup>55</sup>“O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”<sup>56</sup>The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.<sup>57</sup>But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>58</sup>Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain.

16.title: The Collection, the Plans, and the Farewell
16.overview:
After the soaring end of chapter 15, the letter comes down to practical matters, which is itself a lesson: the hope of the resurrection makes ordinary faithfulness “not in vain”. First the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem (described more fully in 2 Corinthians 8–9). Each believer should set aside money regularly on the first day of the week, in proportion to income, so that there is no last-minute scramble when Paul comes; the church will choose its own trusted messengers to carry it.

Then Paul’s travel plans. He is writing from Ephesus, where a great opportunity has opened amid much opposition, and he plans to stay until Pentecost before travelling through Macedonia to Corinth, perhaps for the winter, when sea travel stopped. Timothy may arrive first and must be made welcome, and Apollos will come later. Paul gives five brisk commands, watch, stand firm, be courageous, be strong, do everything in love, and commends the household of Stephanas and the three men who brought the Corinthians’ letter. He sends greetings from the churches of Asia, from Aquila and Prisca and the church in their house, writes the final words in his own hand, pronounces a curse on anyone who does not love the Lord, prays the earliest Christian prayer, “Maranatha”, “Our Lord, come!”, and ends with grace and his own love.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Collection for the Saints
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: About the collection for the Lord’s people, the Corinthians should do what Paul told the churches of Galatia. On the first day of every week each of them should set aside a sum in keeping with their income and save it up, so that no collections need to be made when Paul arrives. When he comes, he will send the people they approve, with letters of introduction, to take their gift to Jerusalem. If it seems right for Paul to go too, they will travel with him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Collection as a Gospel Act

Paul’s collection theology, most fully developed in 2 Corinthians 8–9, grounds financial generosity in the grace of Christ: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Cor 8:9). The collection is not a tax but a participation in the logic of the cross — the voluntary sharing of material blessing across economic and ethnic lines that enacts the gospel’s claim that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek. The Gentile churches supporting the Jewish church in Jerusalem is the financial expression of Romans 15:27: “if the Gentiles have come to share in their spiritual blessings, they ought also to be of service to them in material blessings.”
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem church was impoverished, possibly as a result of the famine of Acts 11:28 or the social cost of Jewish Christians being excluded from economic networks following their conversion. The collection was an act of solidarity across the most significant social divide of the ancient world. Now: The principle of systematic, proportionate, habitual giving as a spiritual discipline remains the most practically effective and most theologically grounded approach to Christian financial stewardship. The “first day of every week” rhythm connects giving to worship — it is part of how the community orients itself toward God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.

Meaning first. 1 Corinthians 16 brings the letter to a practical close, and it is no less spiritual for being practical. After the soaring hope of the resurrection, Paul turns to money, travel plans and greetings, because the hope of chapter 15 is lived out in ordinary faithfulness. First, he gives instructions for the collection for poor believers in Jerusalem: regular, proportionate, planned giving each Lord’s Day, carried by trustworthy people (vv. 1–4). Second, he shares his plans to visit, and commends Timothy and explains Apollos’s delay (vv. 5–12). Third, he gives a burst of short commands: be watchful, stand firm, be courageous and strong, and do everything in love; and honour those who serve, like the household of Stephanas (vv. 13–18). Finally, greetings, a holy kiss, Paul’s own signature, a solemn warning, the ancient prayer Maranatha, and a closing word of grace and love (vv. 19–24). A letter that began with grace ends with grace, and its last word is love.

The setting. The collection was one of the great projects of Paul’s life. The believers in Jerusalem were poor: there had been famine (Acts 11:28–30), and Jewish believers who confessed Christ were often cut out of the family and trade networks that had supported them. So Paul spent years gathering money from Gentile congregations around the Aegean for a Jewish congregation most of them would never meet, and he cared about it enough to risk his freedom delivering it (Romans 15:25–31). He is not raising funds for his own ministry here. The money is going to strangers, and the strangers are of the people who had caused him the most trouble. The gift expressed the unity of Gentile and Jewish believers in one body.

Now concerning the collection for the saints. Another topic from their letter (now concerning, 7:1). After the resurrection, money. The transition looks jarring, and it is not; it is the same transition the whole letter has been making. Paul has just spent fifty-eight verses proving that the dead will be raised, and concluded that therefore no labour in the Lord is wasted. The very next thing he mentions is a hardship fund for a church some eight hundred miles away. The resurrection does not lift Christians above the practical. It sends them back into it with open hands.

As I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do. Corinth was not alone. The churches of Galatia, Macedonia and Achaia were all taking part (2 Corinthians 8–9). Four things follow in one sentence, and together they are the New Testament’s most practical paragraph on giving.

On the first day of every week. It is regular. Sunday, the day of Christ’s resurrection. The church gathered for worship on that day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10), and giving was part of it. This is one of the earliest pieces of evidence that the first day had become the Christian day of worship. Giving is attached to the resurrection day from the beginning.

Is Sunday the Christian Sabbath? Faithful Christians answer differently, and both views deserve a fair hearing. Many Reformed Christians, following the Westminster Confession (Westminster 21.7–8) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment still stands as a moral law, with the day changed to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection: the Lord’s Day is the Christian Sabbath, to be kept holy in worship and rest. Other Christians, including many Baptists and Reformed believers, see the Sabbath as a shadow fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and hold that while the apostolic habit of meeting on the first day is wise and good, no day binds the conscience as the Sabbath did (Romans 14:5–6). Both agree that the Lord’s Day is the day of the church’s worship, and that it is a gift to be treasured rather than a burden to be minimised.

Each of you is to put something aside and store it up. It is personal: each of you. Not the wealthy patrons, not a committee, not whoever feels moved. Everybody, rich or poor, gives. Regularly and deliberately, not on impulse.

As he may prosper. It is proportionate: more if you earn more. The sum is not fixed; it is scaled to income. That single phrase protects the poor from a demand they cannot meet and prevents the rich from discharging the duty with something they will not notice. Generous giving flows from God’s generosity to us (2 Corinthians 8:9; 9:7).

So that there will be no collecting when I come. And it is planned in advance, so that Paul’s arrival is not the occasion of a scramble. Planned giving means no high-pressure appeals later. There is a small pastoral wisdom here worth having: he does not want his visit remembered as the week they were asked for money.

Where Christians differ: tithing. Some teach that Christians are bound to give exactly a tenth, as under the law; others that no standard applies. Verdict: The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It calls for regular, proportionate, generous, cheerful giving, in response to grace (2 Corinthians 9:6–7). The tithe is a helpful starting point and a biblical benchmark, and many Christians rightly give more. Giving is part of worship on the Lord’s Day.

Why Paul names no figure. Paul had every opportunity to name a figure here and in two whole chapters on giving (2 Corinthians 8–9), and he never does. What he gives instead is this principle: as he may prosper. That is deliberately not a number, and it is harder rather than easier, because a fixed percentage can be paid and forgotten while a proportion has to be thought about every year the circumstances change. And notice what Paul actually appeals to when he wants to move people to generosity. Not a rule. A Person: you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The Christian does not give a percentage of his income to a cause. He gives, out of what he has been given, to people who have less, because that is precisely what was done for him, and the One who did it did not calculate a proportion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving earns God’s favour. It means grace makes us generous.

What if I am in debt or can barely pay my bills? Then give something, however small, and give it gladly; as he may prosper protects you from a demand you cannot meet. The widow’s two coins were worth more in Christ’s eyes than the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44). God does not want you to neglect your family or your honest debts to give (1 Timothy 5:8). Pay what you owe, live simply, ask for wise help with your budget if you need it, and give regularly what you can. As your circumstances improve, let your giving rise with them. The habit matters more than the amount.

In a sentence. Now about the collection for God’s people: do what Paul told the Galatian churches to do. On the first day of each week, each of you should set aside an amount in keeping with your income and save it, so that no collections need be made when he comes.

On a Tuesday. Plan your giving. Decide in advance what you will give each week, in proportion to what God has given you. Sit down this week with your income in front of you, pray, and set a figure; and include in it something for believers in need beyond your own church.

For worship. He who was rich became poor. The Son of God owned the cattle on a thousand hills, and he was born in a borrowed stable, laid in a borrowed tomb, and gave away his life for beggars. Every gift we give is an echo of his. Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift (2 Corinthians 9:15). The God who gave his own Son will not fail to supply every need of those who give in his name, and he loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.note: The collection was for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The first day of the week is Sunday, the day Christians met.

verseByVerse.quote: And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.

And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter. An administrative note, and one of the most quietly important sentences in the letter for anyone who has ever wondered how a Christian ministry ought to handle money. Accredit (dokimazō) means to approve after testing. Paul does not carry it. He, an apostle, with a direct commission from the risen Christ and every right to be trusted, arranges that the funds should travel in the hands of men the Corinthians themselves have chosen and formally accredited. He will not be alone with the money. And notice that the men who carry it are chosen by the Corinthians, not by Paul. It is their gift, and they appoint its escort. He is not managing them; he is serving an arrangement they own.

To carry your gift to Jerusalem. Gift (charis) is the word for grace. Giving is an act of grace (2 Corinthians 8:1, 6–7): it begins in God’s grace to us, and it carries grace to others.

If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me. The last clause has a quiet dignity. Even the question of whether the apostle travels with the delivery is left open, subject to what turns out to be wise. There is no assumption that his presence is required. In the end, Paul did go, with representatives from several churches (Acts 20:4; 24:17).

Financial integrity. Paul takes care that no one can accuse him of mishandling money. He explains why elsewhere, and the sentence deserves to be framed in every church office: we take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). Note the two audiences. A ministry must be honest before God: that is obvious. Paul adds that it must also be visibly, checkably honest before people who are not obliged to think well of it. Being innocent is not sufficient; the arrangements must be such that no reasonable person could suspect otherwise. Churches should handle funds with transparency and accountability, with more than one person responsible.

Apostolic practice. This is not modern governance imported into the Bible. It is apostolic practice, and the church has paid a heavy price whenever it has thought itself above such things. Every scandal in which a Christian leader has been found handling money alone, unaccountably, with the records in his own keeping, was preventable by a verse written in the fifties. And the practical form of it is unglamorous and cheap: two signatures rather than one, an audited account, published figures, a treasurer who is not the preacher, and no one, however trusted, however senior, however long-serving, ever alone with the cash. Not because Christians are suspected. Because the gospel is worth protecting from suspicion.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was untrustworthy. It means he was wise.

How can I know whether a ministry I give to is trustworthy? Ask the questions Paul’s practice answers. Is more than one person responsible for the money? Are the accounts audited and the figures available to givers? Do the leaders live in a way that matches what they ask of others? Is the ministry accountable to a church or a board that can say no? Does it tell you plainly what your gift will do? A trustworthy ministry will welcome such questions, as Paul did. A ministry that is offended by them, or that pressures you to give quickly and emotionally, has given you your answer.

In a sentence. When he arrives, he will give letters of introduction to the people you approve and send them with your gift to Jerusalem. If it seems right for him to go too, they will travel with him.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s treasurers and those who handle its finances. Thank God for their faithfulness. If you serve in such a role, check this week that no one, including you, is ever alone with the money.

For worship. The Lord Jesus was entrusted with the greatest treasure of all, the souls of his people, and he has not lost one of them (John 17:12). He kept every coin of his Father’s trust and gave a faithful account of all of it. In him there is no hidden thing, no secret ledger, no shadow of turning. Blessed be the faithful Steward of God’s house, who makes his people honest in little things because he has been faithful in all things.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul plans to come to them after passing through Macedonia. He may stay with them for a while, perhaps the winter, so that they can help him on his journey wherever he goes next; he does not want just a brief visit in passing, but hopes to spend some time with them, if the Lord permits. But he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a wide door for effective work has opened for him, and there are many opponents. If Timothy comes, they should make sure he has nothing to fear among them, for he is doing the Lord’s work as Paul is. No one should look down on him; they should send him on his way in peace so that he can return to Paul, who is expecting him with the brothers. As for Apollos, Paul strongly urged him to visit them with the brothers, but he was quite unwilling to go now; he will come when he has the opportunity.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Missionary Network and the Unity of the Gospel

Paul’s travel plans are not merely logistical; they reflect the theology of the one body of Christ extended across geography. The early church was not a collection of independent local congregations operating in isolation; it was a network of communities bound together by the gospel, by apostolic ministry, by financial sharing, and by personal relationship. Paul’s letters are themselves the literary expression of this network — the apostle’s presence extended across distance through writing.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The ease with which Paul mentions Timothy and Apollos as co-workers, and the genuine care he shows for Timothy’s reception, models the pastoral culture of the early church: mutual submission, personal warmth, collaborative ministry. Now: The temptation to treat Christian ministry as competitive rather than collaborative is ancient and persistent. Paul’s warmth toward Apollos — the man whose followers had been used as a weapon against him — is a lesson in the largeness of a gospel-formed heart.

verseByVerse.quote: I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia, and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.

I will visit you after passing through Macedonia. Travel arrangements, and they are more revealing than they look. Paul’s plan: from Ephesus, through Macedonia (northern Greece: Philippi, Thessalonica), then south to Corinth (Acts 19:21; 20:1–3).

And perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter. Sea travel stopped in winter; to winter somewhere was to be stuck there until spring. He did eventually spend three months in Greece (Acts 20:3), where he wrote Romans. And notice the warmth. This is the congregation that had divided into parties over his name, questioned his apostleship, taken each other to court, and got drunk at the Lord’s table, and Paul is planning to spend the winter with them. He is proposing to be shut in for months with the most difficult church he has.

So that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go. Help on my journey (propempō) means to provide for a missionary’s travel: food, money, companions. Paul was willing to receive this kind of help from them, even though he refused payment for his preaching (9:15–18).

For I do not want to see you now just in passing. He wants a long stay, not a quick visit. Their problems needed time. He could have managed a brief, efficient, well-controlled visit and moved on. He wants time with them instead. That is what a man says about people he loves, not about a problem he is managing.

I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits. Then the phrase that most needs saying. Paul makes plans. Detailed ones: a route, a season, a length of stay, and an expectation that the church will help him onward afterwards. There is nothing unspiritual about a diary, and this passage should settle it for anyone who has been taught that planning shows a lack of faith. But every plan he makes sits under a clause. James puts it more sharply: you do not know what tomorrow will bring; you ought to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (James 4:14–15). It is not a superstitious formula to be attached to sentences. It is a settled awareness that the diary is a proposal and not a contract.

When plans change. And in fact it did not go as written. Paul’s movements changed, the Corinthians were upset about it, and he had to defend himself in the next letter against the charge of being unreliable (2 Corinthians 1:15–2:1). Which is worth knowing, because it tells the reader what if the Lord permits costs. It is easy to say when the plan works. It has to be meant in advance, so that when the year goes differently there is something already in place to stand on.

What it does not mean. It does not mean planning is unspiritual. Paul planned carefully, and held his plans loosely.

How do I hold plans loosely without being unreliable? Make your plans carefully, keep your word wherever you can, and tell people honestly when circumstances change. Saying if the Lord permits is not an escape clause for breaking promises lightly; Paul was grieved when he was thought unreliable. It is a humble admission that God governs the future and you do not. So plan, commit, and work hard at what you have promised. When God’s providence closes a door, through illness, a change at work or a family need, accept it without bitterness, explain it kindly to those affected, and trust that his plan is better than yours.

In a sentence. After he goes through Macedonia he will come to you, since that is his route. He may stay a while with you, perhaps the whole winter, so that you can send him on to wherever he goes next. He does not want to make only a brief visit; he hopes to spend some time with you, if the Lord allows.

On a Tuesday. Make your plans today, and add sincerely: if the Lord permits. Look at your diary for this week, pray over it, and hand it to God. And plan time, not just a passing visit, with someone who needs it.

For worship. The Lord of heaven and earth holds every road, every season and every winter in his hand. The plans of the heart belong to man, but the answer of the tongue is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:1), and his counsel stands forever. And the Lord Jesus did not visit us in passing. He came and stayed, and dwelt among us full of grace and truth, and he has promised to be with us always, to the end of the age. Blessed be the God whose plans never fail, and who makes all things work together for good for those who love him.

verseByVerse.quote: But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.

But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover, in late spring. Paul wrote this letter in Ephesus, probably in the early months of the year.

For a wide door for effective work has opened to me. Two facts about the same situation, joined by and, and it is one of the most useful sentences in the New Testament for anyone trying to read his circumstances. A door is an opportunity for the gospel (2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3; Acts 14:27). Wide and effective (energēs, active, powerful): work that works, that gets somewhere. Ephesus was proving fruitful, and Luke records what that looked like: two years of daily teaching, the word spreading through the whole province of Asia, sorcerers burning their books in public (Acts 19:9–10, 19–20). Paul is not staying because the situation is interesting or because he has invested a lot in it. He is staying because something is actually happening, and he can tell the difference between motion and progress. That is a discernment many a ministry has lacked, and it costs years.

And there are many adversaries. The same city, the same season. Opportunity and opposition together. Within a short time the silversmiths would start a riot that filled the theatre for two hours and nearly cost him his life (Acts 19:23–41). Now notice how Paul relates the two clauses. Not a door has opened, but there is opposition, as though the second were a qualification of the first. He writes and. The adversaries are part of the report, and they are not a reason to leave; they are named in the same breath as the reason to stay.

Reading circumstances the right way round. Christians routinely read the two facts the wrong way round. A door opens, resistance follows, and the resistance is taken as evidence that the door was not from God after all: that if this were really his will it would be going more smoothly. Paul assumes the opposite. Where the gospel is actually advancing, something pushes back. Opposition is not a sign that God has closed the door; often it means the door is open. The absence of opposition is not the mark of God’s blessing; it may only be the mark of not having disturbed anything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek out conflict. It means they should not be surprised by it when the gospel advances.

How do I tell an open door with opposition from a closed door? The rule cuts both ways, and both halves are needed. Not every difficulty is proof that you are on the right road; some obstacles are God closing a door, and Paul himself was once forbidden by the Spirit to go where he intended (Acts 16:6–7). But opposition by itself never disqualified an opportunity. The test is not the size of the difficulty; it is what the difficulty is made of. Opposition from people who do not want the gospel to advance is evidence that it is advancing. A closed road, an exhausted body, a family that needs you at home, a door that simply will not open however hard it is pushed: those are different, and a wise Christian reads them differently, with prayer and the counsel of others.

In a sentence. But he will stay on at Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for fruitful work has opened to him, and there are many who oppose him.

On a Tuesday. Pray for open doors for the gospel in your city, and for courage in the face of opposition. Think of one good work you have been tempted to abandon because it became hard, and ask honestly whether the difficulty is a closed door or simply an adversary.

For worship. Christ is the one who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Revelation 3:7). He set before his church an open door, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. The riots of Ephesus came and went, the temple of Artemis fell into ruins, and the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily (Acts 19:20). Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, who opens wide doors and is stronger than every adversary.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.quote: When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.

When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you. Read that as a letter of introduction and it is almost protective enough to be touching. Paul is sending a young man into the hardest congregation he has, and he knows exactly what they are like, because he has spent fifteen chapters describing it. So he writes ahead. At ease (aphobōs) is without fear. The Corinthians could be intimidating. Timothy was young, and Paul would later have to tell him to let no one despise him for his youth (1 Timothy 4:12). By all appearances he was not a naturally commanding figure. He seems to have been prone to timidity; Paul writes elsewhere about his tears (2 Timothy 1:4) and tells him that God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control (2 Timothy 1:7). Corinth was a church that graded people by eloquence, presence and impressiveness, and before long some there would be saying that Paul’s own bodily presence was weak and his speech of no account (2 Corinthians 10:10). Timothy was walking into that.

For he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. The safeguard Paul offers is not a claim about Timothy’s gifts. He does not say Timothy is a fine preacher, or more capable than he looks. He says: he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am. The same work. That is the whole credential. Timothy carries Paul’s authority as his representative (4:17). Which is a standing rebuke to how congregations actually assess people, then and now. A church will weigh a visiting speaker’s confidence, accent, humour and bearing within about ninety seconds, and every one of those measures was in play at Corinth. Paul cuts across all of it with a question about what a man is doing.

So let no one despise him. Do not look down on him because of his youth or temperament.

Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me. Send him back with provisions and goodwill.

For I am expecting him with the brothers. Other companions were travelling with him.

A word for every Timothy. There is something here for anyone who has ever felt like Timothy walking in: too young, too quiet, too unimpressive for the room, aware that he is being measured against somebody more capable. He was, and he was right about it, and the apostle wrote ahead to the whole congregation about it. Timidity is not a disqualification. It is a thing the family is supposed to make allowances for.

What it does not mean. It does not mean young leaders are above correction. It means they should not be dismissed because of age.

What does putting someone at ease actually look like? It is work, and somebody has to decide to do it. Not merely refraining from crushing someone, but actively setting him at ease: being the person who goes over first, who asks the question that lets a nervous newcomer talk about something he knows, who does not leave him standing at the edge of a room with a cup in his hand. Learn his name and use it. Introduce him to one other person. Thank a young preacher for something specific in his sermon rather than offering a critique at the door. Pray for him, and tell him you are. Every church has a Timothy in it on any given Sunday. The command is not to admire him. It is to go and put him at ease.

In a sentence. When Timothy comes, make sure he has nothing to fear among you, for he is doing the Lord’s work just as Paul is. No one should treat him with contempt. Send him on his way in peace so that he can return to Paul, who is waiting for him with the brothers.

On a Tuesday. Encourage a young or timid Christian leader this week. Put them at ease. Write a note to a young person who serves in your church, telling them one way God has used them.

For worship. The Lord Jesus does not break a bruised reed or quench a smouldering wick (Matthew 12:20). He chose fishermen and a timid young man from Lystra, and he made them pillars of his church. He knows the frame of those who serve him, and he remembers that they are dust (Psalm 103:14). Blessed be the gentle Shepherd who carries the lambs in his arms, and who gives his fearful servants a spirit of power and love.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy was young and perhaps timid.

verseByVerse.quote: Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.

Now concerning our brother Apollos. A short verse, and remarkable in three directions at once. Perhaps the Corinthians had asked for Apollos to come. Remember who Apollos is in this letter. He is the other name in the faction fight, I follow Paul, or I follow Apollos (1:12), the eloquent Alexandrian (Acts 18:24) whose admirers had been used as a stick to beat Paul with. Four chapters were spent dismantling that party spirit. And here is Paul, at the end of the same letter, calling him our brother Apollos.

I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers. That is the first remarkable thing. Paul wanted Apollos to go, showing he had no jealousy. Paul and Apollos were not rivals, whatever the factions in Corinth thought (3:5–9). If there were any rivalry, it is entirely on the Corinthians’ side. Paul is actively trying to send his supposed rival to the church that prefers him.

But it was not at all his will to come now. The second remarkable thing is that Apollos said no. An apostle strongly urged him, and he declined, and Paul reports it without a word of complaint, without hinting that Apollos was being difficult, and without appealing to his own authority to overrule him. Apollos may well have had a good reason, and the obvious one is staring out of the text: a church divided into a Paul party and an Apollos party is not helped by the arrival of Apollos (1:12). Staying away may have been the most loving thing he could do, and it would have cost him a warm welcome. The Greek may also mean that it was not God’s will for him to come now.

He will come when he has opportunity. The third remarkable thing is the last clause. No coolness in it, no door shut. Two servants of the same Lord disagreeing about timing, and the friendship entirely intact. A great deal of damage in churches would be avoided if Christians could learn to let a no be a no without treating it as a verdict on the relationship.

Christian freedom among leaders. Even an apostle did not command Apollos. Christian workers are fellow servants, not a chain of command (3:5).
