Apostolic authority was real, and Paul had just used it heavily in this letter. But it did not extend to running another man’s diary. Where Scripture commands, there is no discretion; where it does not, a Christian is free to weigh a matter and reach a different conclusion from someone he respects, and neither man has sinned.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Apollos was disobedient. He used his own judgement.

How do I find God’s will when Scripture does not settle a decision? The way Apollos did. He did not receive a revelation telling him to stay where he was. He weighed a request from a man he respected, considered the situation, formed a judgement, and acted on it, and the New Testament records the outcome without a hint that he should have waited for something more supernatural. So where the Bible speaks, obey it. Where it does not, pray, use the mind God gave you, take advice (Proverbs 15:22), weigh the good of other people, and decide. Then get on with it, trusting God’s providence to overrule your mistakes. You do not need a sign to do a wise and lawful thing.

In a sentence. As for our brother Apollos, Paul strongly urged him to come to you with the others, but he was quite unwilling to go now. He will come when the time is right.

On a Tuesday. Is there a Christian whose no you have taken personally? Release it this week; let it be a no and not a verdict. And if you are paralysed over a decision Scripture leaves free, gather counsel, pray, and decide by Friday.

For worship. Thank God for leaders who put the unity of the church above their own popularity. Such men are only following their Master, who did not seek his own glory, who would not let the crowds make him king, and who withdrew when his presence would have fed the wrong kind of zeal. One plants, another waters, but God gives the growth (3:6–7). Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, whose servants are brothers and not rivals, and to whom alone belongs the glory.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul gives five short commands: stay alert, stand firm in the faith, be courageous, be strong, and do everything in love. He reminds them that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia and have devoted themselves to serving God’s people, and urges them to submit to such people and to everyone who joins in the work and labours at it. He is glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from the Corinthians; they have refreshed his spirit and theirs. Such people deserve recognition.
verseByVerse.theology:
Courage and Love: The Paradox of Gospel Character

The sequence of imperatives in vv. 13–14 — watchful, firm, courageous, strong, then loving — captures the full paradox of the Christian character that Paul has been cultivating throughout the letter. The cross demands both: the courage to stand for truth (as Paul has done in every hard section of this letter) and the love that is patient, kind, and bears all things (as chapter 13 demands). Neither without the other is Christian; together they describe the character of Christ himself, who drove the money-changers from the temple and wept on the way to Lazarus’s tomb.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Corinthians needed all five imperatives in exactly the order Paul gave them. They needed watchfulness against the false teachings threatening them; firmness against the cultural pressure to conform; courage to exercise church discipline; strength to endure the costs of faithful community. And they needed all of this wrapped in love, or it would produce the cold and harsh community that pride produces rather than the warm and strong community that grace produces. Now: Every generation of the church needs the same five imperatives in the same order. The church that is watchful and firm but unloving is a fortress, not a family. The church that is loving but not watchful and firm is a sentimentality, not a community.

verseByVerse.quote: Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. Let all that you do be done in love.

Be watchful. Five commands, fired off like an order of the day, and they are the whole letter compressed into two lines. Watchful (grēgoreō) is a sentry’s word: stay awake, keep looking. Watch for Christ’s return (Matthew 24:42), and against danger and false teaching. It is the same verb Jesus used in Gethsemane to men who could not manage an hour (Mark 14:34–38). A church is most in danger when it is comfortable, and Corinth had been asleep in exactly that way: a man in gross immorality in the membership and the church arrogant about it rather than mourning (5:1–2).

Stand firm in the faith. Not in your faith: in the faith, the thing believed, the deposit handed over, the gospel especially as defended in chapter 15. Do not be shaken (15:58). There is ground to hold, it is not the church’s to renegotiate, and the pressure to move it is constant and usually reasonable-sounding.

Act like men. One word in Greek (andrizomai), and it needs explaining, because a modern reader will stumble. It is built on the word for a man, and it means: be courageous, be mature, behave like an adult. In older English, quit you like men carried the same sense. It is a military word, used in the Greek Old Testament for be strong and courageous (Joshua 1:6–7; 2 Samuel 10:12), and God said it there to a man who was frightened. Here it is addressed to the whole church, men and women: be brave and mature, not childish (14:20). It is addressed to a church Paul has already called infants (3:1), and it means grow up and show some nerve.

Be strong. Be strong (krataioō) is passive in form: be strengthened. The strength is not manufactured. Paul says elsewhere exactly where it comes from: be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might (Ephesians 6:10).

Let all that you do be done in love. And then the fifth, which changes everything. Take the first four alone and you get a certain kind of Christian, and everyone has met him: watchful, immovable, courageous, strong, and impossible to be near. Vigilance without love becomes suspicion. Firmness without love becomes rigidity. Courage without love becomes belligerence, and there is a species of contender for the faith who is right about everything and has never comforted anyone. Take the fifth alone and you get the opposite failure: a church so anxious to be loving that it will not stand anywhere, cannot say a hard thing, and has quietly agreed that nothing is worth a disagreement. Paul will not have either. All four, and all four soaked in the fifth. Love, from chapter 13, governs everything.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only men should be brave. It means all believers are called to mature courage.

What does it mean for a man, in particular, to act like a man? The command is to the whole church, but it lands with special weight on men, because Scripture calls husbands and fathers to lead their homes and qualified men to lead the church (11:3; 1 Timothy 3:1–7). Biblical manhood is not swagger or control. It is courage in the service of others: standing firm in the truth, protecting the weak, taking responsibility instead of blaming, leading in prayer and in repentance, and laying down your life as Christ did for his bride (Ephesians 5:25). A man who uses strength to dominate or harm has not acted like a man in Paul’s sense; he has acted like a child with a weapon.

In a sentence. Keep alert; stand firm in the faith; be brave and grown up; be strong. And do everything in love.

On a Tuesday. Ask: am I standing firm? Am I brave? And am I doing it all with love? Think of one place where you have gone quiet out of fear, and speak; and one place where you have been firm without kindness, and soften.

For worship. That is the character of the Lord who drove the traders out of the temple and wept on the way to a friend’s grave. He was watchful in Gethsemane while his friends slept. He stood firm before the high priest and before Pilate. He set his face like flint toward Jerusalem. He was strong with the strength of his Father. And all of it was love: love for the Father, and love for us. Blessed be the Lion who is the Lamb, and who makes his frightened people brave.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints— be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints—be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.

Now I urge you, brothers. A personal appeal. Names at last. After fifteen chapters of problems, Paul points at some people who were getting it right.

You know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital. First converts is literally firstfruits (aparchē), the same word used of Christ in 15:20: the first family in southern Greece to believe. Paul had baptised this household (1:16), one of the very few he remembered baptising personally. And they had been at it ever since.

Does the household of Stephanas show that infants were baptised? It is sometimes cited for infant baptism, because Paul baptised the household (1:16). But the description here, a household that had devoted themselves to the service of the saints, describes believers, and nothing in either passage mentions children. The other household baptisms in Acts are likewise households that heard, believed and rejoiced (Acts 16:34; 18:8). This commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds that baptism is for those who personally repent and believe. Our paedobaptist brothers, who read the households in the light of the covenant promise to believers and their children, are honoured and beloved fellow servants, and we gladly labour alongside them.

And that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints. The verb Paul uses of them is the striking thing. Devoted (tassō) means they appointed themselves, posted themselves to the duty, set themselves to it. Nobody rostered them. No one asked. They looked at what the church needed and put themselves into the gap, and had apparently been doing it for years without a title.

Be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer. Then the instruction, and it is not the one anyone expects. Consider what that means in a congregation that had spent the whole letter arguing about status. Paul does not tell them to admire Stephanas, or thank him, or put him on a rota. He tells them to place themselves under the people who have proved themselves by serving: recognise and follow the leadership of those who serve faithfully. Leadership in the church is earned by service, not demanded by status. And note the reach of the last clause. The word for labourer means someone who works to the point of exhaustion. Paul is not building a hierarchy with two names in it. He is describing a whole category, and the qualification for it is simply that a person has worn himself out for the church.

A test for whom to follow. This supplies a test for anyone deciding whom to follow in a church. Not who is the most gifted speaker, or the most confident, or the one everybody quotes. Look for the household that has been quietly serving the saints for fifteen years and has never once been thanked from the front. Then note that the New Testament tells you to submit to people like that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who serves automatically holds office. Elders are to be appointed according to the qualifications of Scripture (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Titus 1:5–9). It means faithful servants deserve respect and should be followed.

Should I wait to be asked before serving? No. Stephanas did not wait. Churches are full of people whose gifts are real and whose service never begins, because nobody approached them and it felt presumptuous to volunteer. This verse quietly removes the excuse: the household Paul holds up as the model appointed themselves, and the apostle commends them for exactly that. Speak to your elders, see a need, and fill it. And a warning for those who are already serving. What Paul commends is not the work; it is the direction of it. They devoted themselves to the service of the saints: to people, not to a programme, a building, or a set of arrangements. It is entirely possible to be exhausted by church activity and never once to have served a person.

In a sentence. Paul urges you, brothers and sisters: you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and they have given themselves to serving God’s people. Submit to people like them, and to everyone who works and labours alongside them.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for faithful servants in your church. Honour and follow them. Name one household in your church that has quietly served for years, and tell them this week what their faithfulness has meant to you.

For worship. The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). He took a towel and washed his disciples’ feet, and then he went to the cross. Every household of Stephanas in every church is a small picture of him. And the One who served us best is the One we now gladly serve, the Servant who is Lord of all. Blessed be the Lord who made himself the servant of his saints.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence, for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.

I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus. These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul in Ephesus (7:1) and would carry his reply. They made the journey from Corinth to Ephesus, a crossing of some two hundred and fifty miles by sea, undertaken at their own trouble and expense.

Because they have made up for your absence. Their presence brought the church to him. And look what Paul says about it. He had been missing them. Not the letter, not the news: them. The apostle who has spent fifteen chapters correcting this church tells them that having three of their number in the room went some way toward filling a gap their absence had left.

For they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Refreshed (anapauō) is to give someone rest, the way a weight is taken off. Paul was in Ephesus with a wide door and many adversaries, carrying, by his own account, the daily pressure of anxiety for all the churches (2 Corinthians 11:28). Into that came three men from a difficult congregation, and he says they rested him. Some people bring life and encouragement wherever they go (Philemon 7, 20). It is worth asking what they actually did, since he does not say. There is no record of Fortunatus preaching or Achaicus writing anything. They travelled, they brought a letter, they stayed a while, they went home. Which is to say: the thing that lifted the weight off the greatest missionary in history was some ordinary Christians turning up.

Give recognition to such people. Honour them. Do not take them for granted. A last small command, and an easy one to obey. Notice them. Say so out loud. Every congregation has its Stephanas, and the reason they are rarely thanked is not unkindness but that quiet service is almost invisible by design: the work only becomes noticeable in the week it stops.

The traffic runs both ways. Keep hold of the direction this runs, because it is not what anybody expects. The letter has been a torrent of correction flowing from Ephesus to Corinth for fifteen chapters. Here, for a moment, it flows the other way: a struggling, arrogant, half-grown church sent three men across the sea, and they rested the apostle who was correcting them. Nobody is only a recipient in the body of Christ. The people being taught refresh the teacher; the ones being carried carry him back. Paul says as much to the Romans about a visit he was hoping for: that we may be mutually encouraged by each other’s faith, both yours and mine (Romans 1:12). He did not want anyone thinking the traffic went one way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only these three were faithful. They represent the kind of people to honour.

How can I refresh a pastor or missionary who is carrying too much? You do not need a gift for it. Go and see them. Take something. Stay a while, but not too long. Say the encouraging thing you have thought and never said, and be specific: a sermon that helped, a visit that mattered. Pray for them and tell them you are praying. Offer a practical help that removes a burden rather than adds a meeting. Protect their day off. It sounds too small to matter, and Paul put three men’s names in Scripture for doing it.

In a sentence. Paul was glad when Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus arrived, because they made up for your absence. They refreshed his spirit and yours too. Such people deserve recognition.

On a Tuesday. Be a refreshing presence. Visit someone this week and leave them encouraged. Choose someone in your church who carries a heavy load, and do one thing to lighten it.

For worship. Come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28). The Lord Jesus uses the same word, and he is the great Refresher of his people. He gives rest to the weary apostle and the weary mother alike, and he sends his people to one another as bearers of his rest. Blessed be the Lord who refreshes the souls of his saints, and who uses ordinary believers to do it.
verseByVerse.note: These three men probably brought the Corinthians’ letter to Paul.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The churches of the province of Asia send greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church that meets in their house, send warm greetings in the Lord, and so do all the believers there. They should greet one another with a holy kiss. Paul writes this greeting in his own hand. If anyone does not love the Lord, let him be under God’s curse. Our Lord, come! The grace of the Lord Jesus be with them, and Paul’s love be with them all in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Maranatha: The Eschatological Pulse of the Church

“Maranatha” is either maran atha (“Our Lord has come,” a declaration of the incarnation) or marana tha (“Our Lord, come!” a prayer for the Parousia). The context — following the anathema, preceding the benediction, echoing Revelation 22:20’s “Come, Lord Jesus” — strongly favours the prayer. The church that lives with the cross at its centre (ch. 1–2), that loves without condition (ch. 13), that proclaims the resurrection (ch. 15), lives with this prayer on its lips: come. The present is not all there is; the best is yet to come; the One who died and rose is coming again. Maranatha is the heartbeat of the community that has understood what Paul has been saying all letter long.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The early church’s Aramaic prayer preserved in a Greek letter to a Gentile church is a small but moving piece of evidence for the unity of the early church across language and culture. Jewish and Gentile believers shared the same prayer in the same words. Now: The prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” is a prayer Christians in every tradition and century have prayed. It is the prayer that the Revelation ends with; it is the prayer that this letter ends with. To pray it is to join the whole church across time — to live, with Paul, as one on whom the end of the ages has come, watching and waiting for the One whose coming makes all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord. All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

The churches of Asia send you greetings. Greetings, and they are not padding. This paragraph is a map of the early church. Asia was the Roman province around Ephesus, where churches had sprung up through Paul’s ministry: Colossae, Laodicea, Hierapolis. Churches, plural: a whole province of congregations that had not existed a few years earlier.

Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house. The church in their house, because for generations that is where churches met. Churches met in homes; there were no dedicated church buildings for some two centuries. A front room, some benches, a table, and a family who had space and were willing to have people tramping through it every week. Aquila and Prisca deserve to be known. They were a couple, tentmakers like Paul, expelled from Rome when Claudius drove the Jews out, who took him in when he arrived in Corinth after Athens (Acts 18:1–3; 2:3). They moved to Ephesus with him (Acts 18:18–19). They took the eloquent Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26): two tentmakers correcting a brilliant preacher, privately, and he took it. And Paul says elsewhere that they risked their necks for his life (Romans 16:4). Notice, too, that they are almost always named together, and that Prisca is often named first, which was not the ordinary order.

Send you hearty greetings in the Lord. They knew the Corinthians well, having worked there with Paul for eighteen months.

All the brothers send you greetings. The worldwide fellowship of believers.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. The family greeting of believers (Romans 16:16; 1 Peter 5:14). After all the divisions, this command is pointed: be reconciled and show it. The greeting was the ordinary affectionate greeting of that world, as it still is in much of the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and Paul’s addition to it is the important word: holy. In that room a slave and a slave-owner greeted each other this way. A Jew and a Greek did. The rich patron and the dockworker who arrived late for the supper did. The greeting was the one moment in the week when the world’s seating plan was visibly suspended, which is exactly what this letter has been fighting for since chapter 1, and it turns out the fight comes down to who you are willing to greet warmly on a Sunday morning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a literal kiss is required today. It means warm family affection.

So what should I actually do in a culture that does not kiss? Greet people. Warmly, in whatever way your place counts as warm: a firm handshake, a hug where it is welcome, a smile and a name remembered. And greet the ones you would not naturally have crossed the room for: the visitor, the elderly widow, the awkward teenager, the person you quarrelled with last month. Be pure and considerate in it; holy means no one should feel uncomfortable or used. That is the whole instruction, and a congregation can be transformed by ten people obeying it for a month.

In a sentence. The churches in Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Priscilla greet you warmly in the Lord, and so does the church that meets at their house. All the brothers and sisters here send greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.

On a Tuesday. Greet someone warmly at church this week, especially someone you have been at odds with. And if you have a home, ask God how it might be opened to his people, for a meal, a Bible study, or a lonely student on a Sunday afternoon.

For worship. Thank God for the worldwide family of believers. The Father has adopted children from every tongue and nation, and he has made them one household. In Christ the walls between Jew and Greek, slave and free, rich and poor have been broken down, and his people greet one another as family because they are family. Behold, how good and pleasant it is when brothers dwell in unity (Psalm 133:1). Blessed be the Father of the great household, who sets the lonely in families.
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.

I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. The pen changes hands. Letters in that world were normally dictated to a trained secretary, and Paul used one; the man who took down Romans even signs his own name in it (Romans 16:22). So this letter has most likely been in a professional’s handwriting: even, practised, easy to read. Now the apostle takes the pen himself, and the script on the papyrus visibly changes. He does this at the end of several letters as a signature, to prove the letter was genuine (Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17), and once he draws attention to it: see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand (Galatians 6:11).

The seal of a real correspondent. There is a practical reason for it. Forged letters were a real problem in the early churches, and Paul had to warn one congregation not to be shaken by a letter seeming to be from us (2 Thessalonians 2:2). His handwriting was the seal: the sign of genuineness, as he says elsewhere, in every letter of his (2 Thessalonians 3:17). A congregation that knew his hand could check. And there is a small evidential note in it too. This is not the sort of detail a forger includes. A man fabricating an apostolic letter has no reason to mention a change of handwriting he cannot produce, and every reason not to draw attention to the question of authenticity at all. The habit only makes sense for a real correspondent writing to people who had seen his hand before.

What the last lines are. There is more in it than security. Everything in this letter has been his: the rebukes, the arguments, the hymn to love, the great chapter on the resurrection. Now the last few lines are his in the other sense too: formed by his own fingers, on that sheet, in that room in Ephesus, by a man with a scarred back, who wanted these particular sentences to arrive in his own writing. And it is worth remembering what those sentences are going to be. He has picked up the pen in order to write a warning, a prayer, and two declarations of love to a church that had given him more grief than any other. He did not save his own handwriting for the easy people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only this verse is Paul’s. The whole letter is his, dictated to a scribe, and the whole of it is the word of God.

Does it matter that Paul used a secretary? Not for the authority of the letter. A secretary wrote down what Paul dictated, and Paul read and signed it; the words are Paul’s, and through Paul, the Lord’s (14:37). God inspired the Scriptures through the ordinary means of the ancient world, papyrus, ink, scribes and couriers, and he kept every word he intended. The verse is a reminder of what these documents physically were. Not a leather-bound book with gilt edges. A roll of papyrus, dictated over days, carried by hand across a sea, read aloud to a room of people who had been waiting for it, and at the bottom of the last sheet, larger and less tidy than the rest, the writing of a man they knew.

In a sentence. Paul writes this greeting in his own handwriting.

On a Tuesday. Write a note by hand to someone this week. A personal touch matters. Choose someone who has hurt you or whom you have found hard, and write them one line of genuine blessing.

For worship. God has not sent us a message from a distance in an impersonal hand. He wrote the law with his own finger on tablets of stone, and then he wrote it on our hearts by his Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3). And the Word himself became flesh, so that we might see his glory with our own eyes. Blessed be the God who signs his love in his own hand, and whose signature is the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters and added a closing greeting in his own handwriting as a mark of authenticity.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!

If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Two sentences, and the first is the hardest thing in the letter. Love here is phileō, warm affection. Accursed is anathema: devoted to destruction, handed over to the judgement of God. It is not a temper; it is a formal declaration, and Paul writes it in his own hand. A solemn warning. Lack of love for Christ is not a small matter. All who have no love for Christ, whatever their spiritual gifts or knowledge, are outside the kingdom.

What the verse does not say. Begin with what it does not say, because a tender conscience will misread it within seconds. It does not say if anyone does not love the Lord perfectly. It does not say if anyone’s love has grown cold, or if anyone struggles to feel anything in church, or if anyone has doubts. Every believer who has ever lived would be under that sentence, including the man writing it. It says has no love. None. Paul is describing the person for whom Jesus Christ is a matter of complete indifference: who may be in the congregation, may be perfectly orthodox, may know the arguments and enjoy the debates, and has no affection for him at all. That, and not weakness, is what falls under this word.

But it should not be softened. Paul is saying that the final question is not whether a person knows the right things about Jesus. This whole letter has been written to a congregation stuffed with knowledge and gifts, and here at the end the apostle names the one thing that cannot be substituted for. Christianity is not agreement. It is love for a Person, and there is no version of it in which that is optional.

Our Lord, come! Then, immediately, the other sentence, and Paul leaves it in Aramaic. The ESV notes that Our Lord, come! translates Maranatha: Marana tha, our Lord, come! (Revelation 22:20). Its survival is a small marvel. Here is a Greek letter to a Greek-speaking church in Greece, and this one phrase is left in Aramaic, untranslated, because everyone already knew it. It was a prayer of the earliest, Aramaic-speaking church in Jerusalem, and it had travelled across the Mediterranean without ever needing to be put into another language. It is among the oldest recorded prayers of the church, and it is two words long. And it shows something astonishing: Jewish believers, who would never pray to a mere man, were praying to Jesus as Lord, a powerful witness to his deity from the very beginning.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wishes damnation on people. He states God’s verdict, and then prays for Christ’s return, when that verdict will be carried out.

I am afraid I do not love Christ enough. Am I under this curse? No, and the fear is itself the answer. Nobody who has no love for Christ is troubled by a verse about not loving Christ. The people this sentence describes read it and feel nothing whatever, which is precisely the diagnosis. Your love will always be smaller than it should be, and smaller than his love for you. Do not try to manufacture feeling; look at him. Read of his life and death, think on what he has forgiven you, and ask the Spirit to pour God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5). We love because he first loved us (1 John 4:19). Love for Christ grows as we gaze at Christ.

In a sentence. If anyone does not love the Lord, let that person be under God’s curse. Come, Lord!

On a Tuesday. Do you love the Lord Jesus? Tell him so, in your own words, today. And pray for one person you know to whom he is a matter of complete indifference.

For worship. The prayer of the first believers is still the last prayer in the Bible, in Greek this time: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:20). The church has been saying it for two thousand years, and one day it will be interrupted. The One we pray to is the One who first loved us, who bore the curse for all who love him, so that no anathema remains for his people (Galatians 3:13). Pray with the earliest Christians: Maranatha, our Lord, come!
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Our Lord, come!” translates Maranatha, an Aramaic prayer of the earliest church.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.

The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Look at where this letter ends, and then look at where it began. It opened with grace to you and peace (1:3–4) and it closes with the grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Everything in between, the factions, the immorality, the lawsuits, the idol meat, the head coverings, the disgraceful supper, the tongues, the denial of the resurrection, rebuke and teaching alike, is enclosed by grace at both ends and flows from it. Whatever this church was, it was a church, and Paul never once wrote to them as though they were not.

My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Then the last line, and it is unlike anything else he wrote. A tender final word, unique among Paul’s letters, and it is addressed to the congregation that had given him the most pain. Count what he had taken from them. They had split into parties over teachers. They had questioned whether he was an apostle at all. They had tolerated a scandal that shocked pagans. They had sued each other in front of the city. They had got drunk at the Lord’s table while poor members went hungry. And they had written him a list of questions, several of which were really challenges. He answered every one of them, at enormous length, holding nothing back and softening almost nothing. And then he took the pen out of the secretary’s hand and wrote, in his own difficult script: my love be with you all. All. Not the ones who had stayed loyal. Not the party that still called itself his. The whole quarrelsome congregation, including the men who thought him a fool. Love, from chapter 13, is the last word.

In Christ Jesus. The last words say where such a thing comes from, because it does not grow in human ground. Paul had no natural stock of affection for people like this, and neither has anybody else. What he had was a share in the love of the One who had looked at a world exactly this arrogant, this divided and this ungrateful, and had not withheld himself from it.

Amen. So be it. Some manuscripts omit it, but it fits.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s rebukes were not serious. Love rebukes, and love embraces.

How do I love someone I have had to correct? Let the correction serve the love, not replace it. Before you speak, pray for the person and remind yourself of the grace you have received. Correct what is wrong plainly, as Paul did, without exaggeration or contempt. Then say, and show, that you are still for them: stay in touch, speak well of them to others, and be quick to rejoice in any change. If they reject what you said, keep loving them anyway, as Christ has kept loving you. A rebuke wrapped in grace and sealed with love is one of the kindest gifts one Christian can give another.

In a sentence. The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you. Paul’s love goes to all of you in Christ Jesus. Amen.

On a Tuesday. End hard conversations with grace and love, as Paul ended this letter. Think of someone with whom things are difficult, and send them a word of genuine love this week, without conditions.

For worship. Sixteen chapters of correction, and the last word is love. It was always going to be. That love reached Corinth from the throne of heaven, through the cross of Christ, and turned some of the least promising people in the Roman Empire into saints, and then came back out of them in a letter. It has reached us too. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit are with all who belong to him, from the first word of the gospel to the last trumpet. To him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus throughout all generations, forever and ever. Amen (Ephesians 3:21).

16.text: <sup>1</sup>Now concerning the collection for the saints: as I directed the churches of Galatia, so you also are to do.<sup>2</sup>On the first day of every week, each of you is to put something aside and store it up, as he may prosper, so that there will be no collecting when I come.<sup>3</sup>And when I arrive, I will send those whom you accredit by letter to carry your gift to Jerusalem.<sup>4</sup>If it seems advisable that I should go also, they will accompany me.<sup>5</sup>I will visit you after passing through Macedonia, for I intend to pass through Macedonia,<sup>6</sup>and perhaps I will stay with you or even spend the winter, so that you may help me on my journey, wherever I go.<sup>7</sup>For I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits.<sup>8</sup>But I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost,<sup>9</sup>for a wide door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many adversaries.<sup>10</sup>When Timothy comes, see that you put him at ease among you, for he is doing the work of the Lord, as I am.<sup>11</sup>So let no one despise him. Help him on his way in peace, that he may return to me, for I am expecting him with the brothers.<sup>12</sup>Now concerning our brother Apollos, I strongly urged him to visit you with the other brothers, but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity.<sup>13</sup>Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong.<sup>14</sup>Let all that you do be done in love.<sup>15</sup>Now I urge you, brothers—you know that the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and that they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints—<sup>16</sup>be subject to such as these, and to every fellow worker and laborer.<sup>17</sup>I rejoice at the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus, because they have made up for your absence,<sup>18</sup>for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. Give recognition to such people.<sup>19</sup>The churches of Asia send you greetings. Aquila and Prisca, together with the church in their house, send you hearty greetings in the Lord.<sup>20</sup>All the brothers send you greetings. Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>21</sup>I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.<sup>22</sup>If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!<sup>23</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you.<sup>24</sup>My love be with you all in Christ Jesus. Amen.
